1607436244732164|c6d4.headline: 4...Nd4 leaves e5 hanging; develop with 4...Nf6.
1607436244732164|c6d4.why: Moving the knight a second time removes e5's only defender, so 5.Nxe5 wins a pawn and then strikes at f7 with 6.Nxf7. 4...Nf6 develops the knight toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e4, leading to the quiet Giuoco Pianissimo after 5.d3; it is the choice in 89.6% of master games.
1607436244732164|c6d4.principle: A second knight move before the kingside knight is out must win something concrete; here it only abandons the e5 pawn.

1642112043242450|f6d5.headline: After 5.exd5, play 5...Na5 and take the bishop off f7
1642112043242450|f6d5.why: 5...Nxd5 opens the door to the Fried Liver: 6.Nxf7 Kxf7 7.Qf3+ drags the black king into the centre, and White brings more pieces with 8.Nc3 while it is stuck there. 5...Na5, the Polerio variation, moves the attacked knight out of the pawn's reach and hits the bishop on c4, ending its pressure on f7. After 6.Bb5+ c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 Black is a pawn down but has the more active pieces, and is considered equal.
1642112043242450|f6d5.principle: With White's knight on g5 and bishop on c4 both aimed at f7, drive the bishop off that diagonal before you open lines near your king.

1642112043242450|f6e4.headline: Save the c6 knight with 5...Na5, hitting the bishop
1642112043242450|f6e4.why: White threatens 6.dxc6, and 5...Ne4 doesn't address it: it moves the f6 knight onto a square where the g5 knight takes it with 6.Nxe4, and the c6 knight is still attacked. 5...Na5, the Polerio variation, is the theory's best move: it gets the knight out of the pawn's way and attacks the c4 bishop. After 6.Bb5+ c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 White is a pawn up, but Black has more active pieces and is considered equal.
1642112043242450|f6e4.principle: First check which of your pieces are attacked; when a pawn hits a knight, move that knight, ideally to a square where it attacks something.

1652894211754070|g1f3.headline: Hit f7 with 5.e6 before Black plays ...e6
1652894211754070|g1f3.why: 5.Nf3 is natural, but it gives Black time for 5...e6, which rules out e5-e6. After 6.O-O Ne7 7.Nc3 Bxd3 8.Qxd3 Nd7 9.Ne2 c5 the light bishops are off and Black hits d4: a comfortable Caro for Black. 5.e6 strikes while Black's e-pawn is still at home: taking with the f-pawn lets your bishop take on g6 with check and wreck Black's pawns. After 5...Qc8 6.exf7+ Bxf7 7.Nf3 Nf6 8.Ne5 e6 9.Nxf7 Kxf7 Black has lost the right to castle.
1652894211754070|g1f3.principle: Strike while the opponent's move order leaves a hole: Black's bishop came out before ...e6, so e5-e6 hits f7 right now.
sources: Jeremy Silman, Kt Maneuvers Against the Advance Caro-Kann (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/kt-maneuvers-against-the-advance-caro-kann?page=2

ideas.title: Strike with e6 before ...e6
ideas.text: Black's e-pawn hasn't moved, so e5-e6 hits f7 now: 5.e6, or 5.Bxg6 hxg6 6.e6. Either way Black's king ends up on f7.

ideas.title: The light-squared bishop question
ideas.text: Swapping the light bishops suits Black in the Caro Advance. Once ...e6 is in, Black takes on d3 anyway, as in 7...Bxd3.

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: With ...e6 played, Black hits d4 with ...c5 and ...Qb6, as in 9...c5 or 6...Qb6.

habit.why: 5.Nf3 is natural, but it gives Black time for 5...e6, which rules out e5-e6. After 6.O-O Ne7 7.Nc3 Bxd3 8.Qxd3 Nd7 9.Ne2 c5 the light bishops are off and Black hits d4: a comfortable Caro for Black.

strays.text: 5.Nf3 lets Black play 5...e6, and the chance is gone.

taught.why: 5.e6 strikes while Black's e-pawn is still at home: taking with the f-pawn lets your bishop take on g6 with check and wreck Black's pawns. After 5...Qc8 6.exf7+ Bxf7 7.Nf3 Nf6 8.Ne5 e6 9.Nxf7 Kxf7 Black has lost the right to castle.

enforces.text: The pawn hits f7 before Black can close the door with ...e6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bxg6 hxg6 is strong: Black gets the open h-file, but in the main line Black's king still ends up on f7 after 9.exf7+ Kxf7. It's nearly as good as the best move.
alternatives.after: 5.e6 is the same idea a move sooner; 5.Bxg6 hxg6 6.e6 then hits f7 the same way, so both work. 43% of club players choose 5.Bxg6.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain
alternatives.before: 5.f4 lets Black close the centre and play 6...Qb6 against d4 and b2, and later 8...Bxd3 9.Qxd3 Qa6 offers a queen swap on the light squares. The f4 pawn also shuts in your c1 bishop.
alternatives.after: 5.e6 uses the moment before ...e6; after 5.f4 e6 that chance is gone for good.

1652894211754070|h2h4.headline: Hit f7 with 5.e6; 5.h4 just lets Black swap bishops
1652894211754070|h2h4.why: 5.h4 threatens to chase the bishop, but Black doesn't wait: 5...Bxd3 makes the swap at once. After 6.cxd3 e6 7.h5 f6 8.Nf3 Nh6 9.Nc3 Nf7 Black is hitting e5, and your h-pawn push has done nothing. 5.e6 strikes while Black's e-pawn is still at home: taking with the f-pawn lets your bishop take on g6 with check and wreck Black's pawns. After 5...Qc8 6.exf7+ Bxf7 7.Nf3 Nf6 8.Ne5 e6 9.Nxf7 Kxf7 Black has lost the right to castle.
1652894211754070|h2h4.principle: Strike while the opponent's move order leaves a hole: Black's bishop came out before ...e6, so e5-e6 hits f7 right now.

1657768441002862|g7g6.headline: 3...Nf6 first: an early ...g6 lets the queen recapture on d4
1657768441002862|g7g6.why: 3...g6 lets White take back on d4 with the queen: after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Qxd4 the queen eyes your h8 rook down the long diagonal. Following 5...Nf6 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.e5 dxe5 8.Qxd8+ the queens come off, and your king has to take back and loses the right to castle. 3...Nf6 attacks e4 first, so after 4.d4 cxd4 White takes back with 5.Nxd4 and you reach the main Open Sicilian. You keep the choice of system, such as the Najdorf with 5...a6.
1657768441002862|g7g6.principle: Knights before bishops: develop the g8 knight first, and decide later whether your bishop goes to g7.

ideas.title: Hit e4 with ...Nf6 early
ideas.text: 3...Nf6 attacks e4 at once; after 4.d4 cxd4 White takes back with 5.Nxd4 instead of the queen.

ideas.title: Queen on d4 eyes h8
ideas.text: Once your g-pawn has moved, 5.Qxd4 hits h8 down the long diagonal, and you must block before developing freely.

ideas.title: Keep the Open Sicilian choices
ideas.text: After 3...Nf6 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 you choose your system, such as the Najdorf with 5...a6.

ideas.title: The pin on b5
ideas.text: In the 3...g6 line 6.Bb5+ pins the c6 knight, and 7.e5 opens the centre while your king is uncastled.

habit.why: 3...g6 lets White take back on d4 with the queen: after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Qxd4 the queen eyes your h8 rook down the long diagonal. Following 5...Nf6 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.e5 dxe5 8.Qxd8+ the queens come off, and your king has to take back and loses the right to castle.

strays.text: Nothing hits e4, so White can take back on d4 with the queen.

taught.why: 3...Nf6 attacks e4 first, so after 4.d4 cxd4 White takes back with 5.Nxd4 and you reach the main Open Sicilian. You keep the choice of system, such as the Najdorf with 5...a6.

enforces.text: The knight hits e4 before the d-pawns are traded.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...Nc6 develops, and after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 it becomes a Classical Sicilian, where 6.Bg5, 7.Qd2 and 8.O-O-O are White's main line. Masters play it 13% of the time, though the engine rates it a bit lower.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 usually transposes after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4, but it keeps c6 free for other setups, so the Najdorf with 5...a6 stays available.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...a6 aims for a Najdorf, but White isn't committed to 4.d4 yet and can choose a closed setup with g3, where ...a6 is less useful. Masters play it 18% of the time; the engine rates it slightly lower.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 makes White deal with e4 first, and after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 you get the Najdorf anyway.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...e6 heads for a Scheveningen, but after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 6.Be3 White sets up 7.Qd2 and 8.f3 with a quick attacking plan. Masters rarely play it (2%).
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 hits e4 at once and keeps both ...e6 and ...e5 setups open.

1694081511794223|g5e6.headline: Win the e6 pawn with 7.Qg4, not with the knight
1694081511794223|g5e6.why: 7.Nxe6 takes the pawn with the knight and leaves f2 guarded only by your king: 7...Bxf2+ 8.Kf1 Qd7 9.Nxc7+ Qxc7 10.Kxf2. You end up a pawn ahead, but your king can't castle and Black's pieces are active. 7.Qg4 hits e6 a second time, and now the 7...Bxf2+ trick just loses the bishop. After 7...Qf6 8.Qxe6+ Nge7 9.Qxf6 gxf6 you're a clean pawn up in an endgame with Black's pawns broken.
1694081511794223|g5e6.principle: Check what's loose on both sides: e6 is loose for Black and f2 for you, so win e6 with 7.Qg4, where the 7...Bxf2+ trick fails.

ideas.title: Pick off the loose e6 pawn
ideas.text: After 6...fxe6 nothing defends the e6 pawn. 7.Qg4 hits it a second time and wins it cleanly.

ideas.title: Watch the f2 trick
ideas.text: Only your king guards f2. With your knight on e6, 7...Bxf2+ pulls the king out; taking the bishop lets a queen check win the knight.

ideas.title: Keep your king able to castle
ideas.text: After 7.Qg4 your king can still castle; after 7.Nxe6 Bxf2+ 8.Kf1 it never can.

habit.why: 7.Nxe6 takes the pawn with the knight and leaves f2 guarded only by your king: 7...Bxf2+ 8.Kf1 Qd7 9.Nxc7+ Qxc7 10.Kxf2. You end up a pawn ahead, but your king can't castle and Black's pieces are active.

strays.text: The knight capture lets 7...Bxf2+ pull your king out and costs you castling.

taught.why: 7.Qg4 hits e6 a second time, and now the 7...Bxf2+ trick just loses the bishop. After 7...Qf6 8.Qxe6+ Nge7 9.Qxf6 gxf6 you're a clean pawn up in an endgame with Black's pawns broken.

enforces.idea: Pick off the loose e6 pawn
enforces.text: The queen wins e6 and your king keeps the right to castle.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qf3 eyes the open f-file but doesn't attack e6 at all. After 7...Qe7 8.Qh3 Kd7 Black's king steps up to guard e6.
alternatives.after: 7.Qg4 attacks e6 twice and wins it, while 7.Qf3 lets Black cover it with 7...Qe7 and 8...Kd7.
alternatives.idea: Pick off the loose e6 pawn

17066305934542|f3e5.headline: Save the bishop by taking on f7 with check
17066305934542|f3e5.why: 7.Nxe5 grabs a pawn but leaves your bishop hanging: 7...Nxc4 8.Nxc4 d5 hits the knight and opens the centre. After 9.Nxb6 axb6 10.d3 dxe4 11.dxe4 Qxd1+ the queens are off, your king has lost castling and your edge is gone. 7.Bxf7+ saves the bishop with check and wins a pawn; if the king takes, 8.Nxe5+ exposes it even more. After 7...Kf8 8.Nxe5 Qf6 9.d4 d6 10.Ng6+ Kxf7 11.Nxh8+ you pick up the h8 rook as well.
17066305934542|f3e5.principle: When a piece is attacked, see if it can move with check and win something: 7.Bxf7+ saves the bishop and takes a pawn.
sources: Georgios Souleidis and Karsten Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (New in Chess preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: 7.Bxf7+ moves the attacked bishop with check. If the king takes, 8.Nxe5+ checks again; after 7...Kf8 your knight takes e5 next.

ideas.title: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
ideas.text: Black threatens 7...Nxc4. Grabbing e5 ignores the threat; a check makes Black answer you first.

ideas.title: ...Na5 chases the bishop
ideas.text: After 6.b5 the knight jumps to a5 to hit your c4 bishop. Pushing b5 too early invites exactly this.

ideas.title: A king that can't castle
ideas.text: After 7...Kf8 Black's king can never castle, and in the engine line 10.Ng6+ forks king and h8 rook.

habit.why: 7.Nxe5 grabs a pawn but leaves your bishop hanging: 7...Nxc4 8.Nxc4 d5 hits the knight and opens the centre. After 9.Nxb6 axb6 10.d3 dxe4 11.dxe4 Qxd1+ the queens are off, your king has lost castling and your edge is gone.

strays.idea: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
strays.text: You take a pawn while Black takes your bishop.

taught.why: 7.Bxf7+ saves the bishop with check and wins a pawn; if the king takes, 8.Nxe5+ exposes it even more. After 7...Kf8 8.Nxe5 Qf6 9.d4 d6 10.Ng6+ Kxf7 11.Nxh8+ you pick up the h8 rook as well.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
enforces.text: The bishop leaves with check and takes f7, so you win material.

1706874451895020|c8g4.headline: Keep the pawn with 4...g6; 4...Bg4 runs into 5.Bd5
1706874451895020|c8g4.why: 4...Bg4 leaves the e4 knight and b7 loose, and 5.Bd5 hits both at once. After 5...Nf6 6.Bxb7 Nbd7 7.Bxa8 Qxa8 White has won a rook for the bishop and got the gambit pawn back. 4...g6 keeps the extra pawn and gets ready to castle after 5...Bg7. After 6.Re1 Nf6 7.Bf1 White has chased your knight back but has nothing concrete for the pawn.
1706874451895020|c8g4.principle: Before a developing move, check what is left loose: here the e4 knight and b7 can be hit together.

ideas.title: ...Bg4 pin versus f7 tactics
ideas.text: With White's bishop on c4 and your king uncastled, ...Bg4 is risky. Here 5.Bd5 hits the e4 knight and b7 at once.

ideas.title: Keep the pawn, then castle
ideas.text: You are a pawn up. Play ...g6, ...Bg7 and castle, and bring the knight back to f6 when it is hit.

ideas.title: Your e4 knight is a target
ideas.text: White will chase the e4 knight with 5.Bd5 or 6.Re1. Retreat it to f6 in time and keep the pawn.

habit.why: 4...Bg4 leaves the e4 knight and b7 loose, and 5.Bd5 hits both at once. After 5...Nf6 6.Bxb7 Nbd7 7.Bxa8 Qxa8 White has won a rook for the bishop and got the gambit pawn back.

strays.text: The pin ignores the c4 bishop, which forks e4 and b7 from d5.

taught.why: 4...g6 keeps the extra pawn and gets ready to castle after 5...Bg7. After 6.Re1 Nf6 7.Bf1 White has chased your knight back but has nothing concrete for the pawn.

enforces.text: Fianchetto and castle; the knight drops back to f6 when hit.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...d5 hits the c4 bishop and supports the e4 knight; after 5.Bd3 Bf5 you develop comfortably and stay a pawn up. The engine rates it about as good as the top move.
alternatives.after: 4...g6 and 4...d5 are about equal: 4...g6 aims for a fianchetto and castling, 4...d5 for a solid centre with 5...Bf5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nf6 brings the knight to safety before White can hit it, and you stay a pawn up; you finish developing and castle next.
alternatives.after: 4...g6 leaves the knight on e4 a move longer and retreats with 6...Nf6 when needed; both keep the pawn.

1711540021875497|b8c6.headline: Stop e4 with 3...Nf6; the knight on c6 lets White expand
1711540021875497|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 doesn't control e4, so White plays 4.e4 and gains space with 5.e5, kicking your knight; after 5...Ne4 6.Ne2 f6 Black has to push pawns to free the position. 3...Nf6 develops and guards e4, so White's knight on c3 is left blocking its own c-pawn with no central break. After 4.Qd3 Bb4 Black pins that knight and jumps in with 5...Ne4.
1711540021875497|b8c6.principle: In closed 1.d4 openings, keep control of e4 so White can't add a second centre pawn; the knight on f6 does that while developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Nc3

1743288401012634|e1h1.headline: Cash in on f7 with 5.Nxf7; 5.O-O lets Black castle
1743288401012634|e1h1.why: 5.O-O ignores the attack on f7 you set up with 4.Ng5, and 5...O-O covers it for good. After 6.d3 d5 7.exd5 Bg4 8.Nf3 Nxd5 the knight is back on f3 and Black has developed freely. 5.Nxf7 forks the d8 queen and h8 rook: after 5...Bxf2+ 6.Kf1 Qe7 7.Nxh8 you win the rook. Black fights back with 7...d5 8.exd5 Nd4, and Quintiliano gives 9.d6 as the right answer, but warns that after 9...Qxd6 Black has real complications and you must play very precisely.
1743288401012634|e1h1.principle: When your attack has created a real target, cash it in at once instead of making a quiet move that lets the opponent cover it.
sources: IM Renato Quintiliano, Is the Traxler Variation still viable? (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/newsroom/post/is-the-traxler-variation-still-viable-2?page=0

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: f7 is attacked twice and guarded only by the king. 5.Nxf7 forks queen and rook; 5.Bxf7+ drags the king up.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: Here f7 is a real target, which is why 4.Ng5 was played. A quiet move lets Black castle and cover it.

ideas.title: Kf1: out of reach of checks
ideas.text: After 5.Nxf7 Bxf2+, step to f1: taking the bishop with the king allows a knight check on e4.

ideas.title: Black's counter on f2
ideas.text: 4...Bc5 ignores f7 and aims at f2, hoping for wild play if you grab on f7 carelessly.

habit.why: 5.O-O ignores the attack on f7 you set up with 4.Ng5, and 5...O-O covers it for good. After 6.d3 d5 7.exd5 Bg4 8.Nf3 Nxd5 the knight is back on f3 and Black has developed freely.

strays.text: f7 was a real target; castling lets Black cover it.

taught.why: 5.Nxf7 forks the d8 queen and h8 rook: after 5...Bxf2+ 6.Kf1 Qe7 7.Nxh8 you win the rook. Black fights back with 7...d5 8.exd5 Nd4, and Quintiliano gives 9.d6 as the right answer, but warns that after 9...Qxd6 Black has real complications and you must play very precisely.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
enforces.text: The knight takes on f7 with a fork, and the rook falls.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bxf7+ is the masters' main choice (68%) and a safe way to win a pawn: after 5...Ke7 6.Bc4 Black's king can never castle. Black gets the f-file and quick development for it, and the engine rates one other move a little higher.
alternatives.after: Masters prefer 5.Bxf7+ (68%) because it is safe; 5.Nxf7 (21%) wins more material, but only if you know 6.Kf1 after 5...Bxf2+.
alternatives.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.d4 opens the centre; after 5...d5 6.Bxd5 Nxd4 7.Bxf7+ Ke7 8.Bc4 you are a pawn up, but Black's active pieces give practical chances.
alternatives.after: 5.Nxf7 cashes in the attack on f7 at once and wins more material, as long as you meet 5...Bxf2+ with 6.Kf1.
alternatives.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up

1783814385093536|d7d5.headline: Don't open the centre yet: 5...a6 takes b5 first
1783814385093536|d7d5.why: 5...d5 opens the centre while you have no pieces out: 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.exd5 exd5 8.Ne5 hits your pinned knight and the isolated d5 pawn. After 8...Bd7 9.Qxd5 Nxe5 10.Qxe5+ White has the pawn back and your king is in check in the middle. 5...a6 keeps White's bishop and knight off b5, so the check and pin from the habit line are gone. After 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.Be2 d6 8.O-O Be7 you develop behind a solid pawn front and keep the extra pawn; masters choose it most often (42%).
1783814385093536|d7d5.principle: White is ahead in development, so keep the centre closed for now: 5...a6 takes b5 away, while 5...d5 opens lines before your pieces are out.
sources: IM Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf
Albert Hoogendoorn, The Smith-Morra Gambit, Part I | http://www.chessvictory.com/SmithMorra.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith%E2%80%93Morra_Gambit

ideas.title: Take b5 away with ...a6
ideas.text: 5...a6 keeps White's knight and bishop off b5, the entry square Morra players use for checks, pins and jumps to d6 and c7.

ideas.title: The d6 hole
ideas.text: With your e-pawn on e6 and the d-pawn at home, d6 has no pawn guard. A white knight reaching b5 eyes d6 and c7.

ideas.title: Don't open the centre undeveloped
ideas.text: Opening lines helps the side ahead in development. 5...d5 opens the centre while none of your pieces are out.

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: White's main pawn break: e4-e5 grabs space and cramps you, as in 6.e5 after 5...d6, or 10.e5 in the main line.

habit.why: 5...d5 opens the centre while you have no pieces out: 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.exd5 exd5 8.Ne5 hits your pinned knight and the isolated d5 pawn. After 8...Bd7 9.Qxd5 Nxe5 10.Qxe5+ White has the pawn back and your king is in check in the middle.

strays.text: The centre opens while your pieces are at home, and the d5 pawn falls.

taught.why: 5...a6 keeps White's bishop and knight off b5, so the check and pin from the habit line are gone. After 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.Be2 d6 8.O-O Be7 you develop behind a solid pawn front and keep the extra pawn; masters choose it most often (42%).

enforces.text: The pawn covers b5 before White's pieces can use it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Nc6 develops and reaches the main Morra position; it's played in 38.5% of master games and is fully sound. One other move is slightly more popular.
alternatives.after: Both are main lines. 5...a6 (42%) takes b5 first; 5...Nc6 (38.5%) develops first and transposes to the main Morra tabiya.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Bb4 pins the c3-knight, but IM Langrock calls it dubious: 6.Qd4 hits the bishop and g7 at once, and after 6...Bf8 the bishop is back home.
alternatives.after: Langrock rates 5...Bb4 dubious, but the engine finds it level, because after 6.Qd4 Bf8 7.Qe5 d6 8.Qg3 White's queen has moved a lot too. 5...a6 is the calmer, more common choice.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...d6 is the Scheveningen setup and holds, but White strikes at once with 6.e5, gaining space after 6...Nc6 7.Bf4 d5.
alternatives.after: Masters prefer 5...a6 (42% to 9%), which keeps b5 covered and your d-pawn flexible; after 5...d6 you must be ready for e4-e5 every move.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Bc5 develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, but White can still cramp you with 6.Bf4 and later 9.e5, even with your d-pawn at home.
alternatives.after: 5...a6 is the most common master move (42%, against 9% for 5...Bc5). Both are sound; 5...Bc5 invites White's e4-e5 push.

1783814385093536|f8b4.headline: Morra: play 5...a6; 5...Bb4 runs into 6.Qd4
1783814385093536|f8b4.why: 5...Bb4 leaves the bishop loose, and 6.Qd4 hits it and g7 at once. You must retreat with 6...Bf8 or give up the bishop for the knight, and after 7.Qe5 Nc6 8.Qg3 the queen keeps eyeing g7 while you untangle. 5...a6 keeps White's knight off b5, so d6 can't be hit with a knight jump. After 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.Be2 d6 8.O-O Be7 you have a solid setup and the extra pawn, with White's e4-e5 break the thing to watch.
1783814385093536|f8b4.principle: Accept a gambit only if you can consolidate: make the safe move 5...a6 rather than a bishop sortie that White can hit.
sources: Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (excerpt) | https://www.scacco.it/data/attachments/7011/morra.pdf
Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit, 2nd ed. (New in Chess excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf

ideas.title: The Qd4 double attack
ideas.text: After 5...Bb4, 6.Qd4 hits the loose bishop and g7 at once: the bishop must retreat or take on c3.

ideas.title: Knight jumps to b5, d5, d6
ideas.text: With ...e6 played, d6 has no pawn guard and a knight jumping to b5 aims at it. 5...a6 takes b5 away first.

ideas.title: Morra setup: fast development, open files
ideas.text: For the pawn White gets quick development and the open c-file: 6.Bf4 aims at d6, then castling and 9.Rc1.

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: White's main pawn lever: e4-e5 gains space and kicks a knight from f6, as in 9...Nf6 10.e5.

habit.why: 5...Bb4 leaves the bishop loose, and 6.Qd4 hits it and g7 at once. You must retreat with 6...Bf8 or give up the bishop for the knight, and after 7.Qe5 Nc6 8.Qg3 the queen keeps eyeing g7 while you untangle.

strays.text: The bishop lands on a loose square where 6.Qd4 hits it and g7.

taught.why: 5...a6 keeps White's knight off b5, so d6 can't be hit with a knight jump. After 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.Be2 d6 8.O-O Be7 you have a solid setup and the extra pawn, with White's e4-e5 break the thing to watch.

enforces.idea: Knight jumps to b5, d5, d6
enforces.text: ...a6 takes b5 from the knight before d6 can be hit.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Nc6 is sound and popular with masters: it develops and covers d4, which rules out the queen jump there. After 6.Be2 d6 7.O-O Be7 8.Qb3 you have a standard Morra setup.
alternatives.after: 5...a6 first keeps b5 covered against knight jumps, and 5...Nc6 is just as good. Masters split almost evenly (42% to 39%).

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...d6 is sound and leads to the usual ...e6/...d6 Morra setups, though 6.e5 Nc6 7.Bf4 shows White can gain space at once. There is a slightly more flexible move.
alternatives.after: 5...a6 covers b5 first and leaves the d-pawn's decision for later. Both are sound; masters prefer 5...a6 (42% to 9%).

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Bc5 develops and is playable, but White often answers it with the space-gaining e4-e5, as in 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.a3 and later 9.e5.
alternatives.after: 5...a6 keeps your bishop home until you know where it is safe, and stops the knight jump to b5. Masters prefer it (42% to 9%), though both are sound.

1790000171764366|f3g5.headline: 5.Ng5 hangs to the queen; strike the centre with 5.d4
1790000171764366|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 puts the knight on a square Black's queen covers: the d8-g5 diagonal is open, so 5...Qxg5 wins a piece. With your light-squared bishop traded, the knight had no target on f7 or e6 anyway, and after 8.d4 Qxe4 Black takes a pawn too. 5.d4 hits e5 and opens the centre while Black's kingside pieces are still at home, and masters play it 71% of the time. After 5...exd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Bg5 e5 8.Nf5 your knight is centralised and then jumps to f5.
1790000171764366|f3g5.principle: Before a knight jump, check every enemy piece that reaches the landing square: the queen on d8 covers g5 along the open diagonal.
sources: Sean Marsh, Chess Opening Basics: The Philidor Defense (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-philidor-defense/

ideas.title: Mind the d8-g5 diagonal
ideas.text: ...d6 opened the diagonal from d8 to g5, and nothing stands on e7 or f6. A knight on g5 hangs to the queen.

ideas.title: Claim the centre with d4
ideas.text: Your edge is space and time: 5.d4 hits e5 while Black's kingside pieces are still at home. Masters choose it 71% of the time.

ideas.title: Hit the doubled e6 pawn
ideas.text: Black's doubled e-pawns are a target, so play fast: after 5...exd4 6.Nxd4 your knight eyes e6 and f5.

habit.why: 5.Ng5 puts the knight on a square Black's queen covers: the d8-g5 diagonal is open, so 5...Qxg5 wins a piece. With your light-squared bishop traded, the knight had no target on f7 or e6 anyway, and after 8.d4 Qxe4 Black takes a pawn too.

strays.text: The knight lands where Black's queen takes it for free.

taught.why: 5.d4 hits e5 and opens the centre while Black's kingside pieces are still at home, and masters play it 71% of the time. After 5...exd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Bg5 e5 8.Nf5 your knight is centralised and then jumps to f5.

enforces.text: The pawn strikes e5 and opens lines for your pieces.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.d3 is solid and guards e4; Wikibooks calls d3 the conservative choice in these lines. A more active move exists.
alternatives.after: 5.d4 is what masters play, 71% to 3%: it opens lines at once, while after 5.d3 Nf6 6.c3 Be7 7.O-O O-O Black finishes developing in peace.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.O-O is sound: you castle first, then 6.c3 and 8.Qb3 hit b7 and e6. Masters choose it in 16% of games; one move is more popular.
alternatives.after: 5.d4 strikes the centre first and castling can wait; masters prefer it, 71% to 16%.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 lets Black answer 5...c5 and clamp the centre, and after 6.a3 Nf6 7.b4 you are fighting on the wing instead.
alternatives.after: 5.d4 gets the pawn there before 5...c5 can stop it, so you open the centre on your terms.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.c3 is the Steinitz-type set-up: it opens b3 for your queen, and after 5...Nf6 6.Qb3 Qc8 Black must guard b7. Masters play it in 10% of games; one move is far more common.
alternatives.after: 5.d4 opens the centre at once instead of preparing it; 5.c3 is just as sound and often gets there later with 9.d4.

1890995340270663|d1d5.headline: The queen fork needs check: retreat with 9.Bb3 instead
1890995340270663|d1d5.why: 9.Qd5 is not check, so Black calmly guards the c5 bishop with 9...d6. After 10.Bxg8 Rxg8 11.Ng5 Qe8 you have traded your best attacking bishop and the c3 pawn is still Black's. 9.Bb3 saves the bishop from the king and keeps it on the diagonal toward g8. After 9...d6 10.Nxc3 you win back the c3 pawn with development, and Black's king can never castle.
1890995340270663|d1d5.principle: When the opponent's king has lost castling, keep your attacking pieces and develop: 9.Bb3 saves the bishop and 10.Nxc3 wins back a pawn.
sources: John Nunn, GM tutorial: Learn to play the Evans Gambit (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/john-nunn-learn-to-play-the-evans-gambit
Evans Gambit (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_Gambit

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: The queen fork on d5 works only with check. With the king on f8, 9.Qd5 is not check, and 9...d6 guards c5.

ideas.title: Save the bishop, keep the aim
ideas.text: Black's king attacks your f7 bishop. 9.Bb3 saves it and keeps it on the diagonal toward g8.

ideas.title: King in the centre: keep queens
ideas.text: Black's king has lost castling and stands on f8. Keep the queens on and bring pieces out, starting with 10.Nxc3.

habit.why: 9.Qd5 is not check, so Black calmly guards the c5 bishop with 9...d6. After 10.Bxg8 Rxg8 11.Ng5 Qe8 you have traded your best attacking bishop and the c3 pawn is still Black's.

strays.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
strays.text: Without check, the queen on d5 gives Black time for 9...d6.

taught.why: 9.Bb3 saves the bishop from the king and keeps it on the diagonal toward g8. After 9...d6 10.Nxc3 you win back the c3 pawn with development, and Black's king can never castle.

enforces.idea: Save the bishop, keep the aim
enforces.text: The bishop stays aimed at g8, and 10.Nxc3 follows.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 9.Bxg8 Rxg8 is a good choice: the bishop takes a knight before the king can take it, and 10.Ng5 with 11.e5 aims at the boxed-in king.
alternatives.after: The engine rates 9.Bxg8 at least as highly as 9.Bb3. The difference is the plan: 9.Bb3 keeps your bishop aimed at the king, 9.Bxg8 trades it and attacks with knight and pawns.
alternatives.idea: Save the bishop, keep the aim

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 9.Nxc3 is natural and sound: it wins back the c3 pawn and develops. Your f7 bishop is safe for now, since taking it walks into a queen check on d5 that hits c5.
alternatives.after: 9.Nxc3 is accepted too: it just changes the order. 9.Bb3 moves the attacked bishop first and 10.Nxc3 follows; either way Black's king can't castle.
alternatives.idea: King in the centre: keep queens

1891225405277048|f1c4.headline: After 2...b6, take the centre with 3.d4
1891225405277048|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 aims the bishop at the e6 pawn, and 3...d5 hits it at once. After 4.exd5 exd5 5.Be2 the bishop has moved twice, you no longer have a pawn on e4, and Black develops freely with 5...Bd6. 2...b6 does nothing to stop 3.d4, which builds a two-pawn centre; masters play it 93% of the time. After 3...Bb7 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 Be7 6.Qe2 your bishop and queen guard e4, and when Black hits it with 6...d5, 7.e5 gains space.
1891225405277048|f1c4.principle: When your opponent spends a move on the wing, occupy the centre with pawns before putting a bishop where a pawn can hit it.
sources: Matthew Astle, The Offbeat Owen's: 1.e4 b6 (Chessable blog) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/owens-defense/
Owen's Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen%27s_Defence
French Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Defence

ideas.title: Take the full centre with d4
ideas.text: 2...b6 doesn't contest the centre. 3.d4 puts a second pawn there before Black's ...d5 arrives.

ideas.title: Bishop on c4 hits a wall
ideas.text: 1...e6 prepares ...d5, which hits a bishop on c4. After 3...d5 4.exd5 exd5 it retreats with 5.Be2.

ideas.title: Guard e4 against ...b6 lines
ideas.text: Black's bishop will aim at e4 from b7. Your light bishop belongs on d3, backed by the queen, as in 4.Bd3 and 6.Qe2.

ideas.title: Gain space with e5
ideas.text: When Black finally hits e4 with 6...d5, 7.e5 gains space instead of swapping on d5.

habit.why: 3.Bc4 aims the bishop at the e6 pawn, and 3...d5 hits it at once. After 4.exd5 exd5 5.Be2 the bishop has moved twice, you no longer have a pawn on e4, and Black develops freely with 5...Bd6.

strays.idea: Bishop on c4 hits a wall
strays.text: The bishop runs into 3...d5 and has to move again.

taught.why: 2...b6 does nothing to stop 3.d4, which builds a two-pawn centre; masters play it 93% of the time. After 3...Bb7 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 Be7 6.Qe2 your bishop and queen guard e4, and when Black hits it with 6...d5, 7.e5 gains space.

enforces.idea: Take the full centre with d4
enforces.text: Two pawns in the centre before Black can challenge them.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 develops and guards e4, so it's sound, but there is a stronger move. After 3...Bb7 Black can pin the knight with 4...Bb4 and press e4.
alternatives.after: 3.d4 is the masters' choice (93%): it takes the centre first, and you guard e4 with 4.Bd3 and 6.Qe2, pieces Black can't pin.

1895778820316678|d1b3.headline: Stop Black castling with 8.Ba3, not 8.Qb3
1895778820316678|d1b3.why: 8.Qb3 aims at f7, but 8...O-O covers it, and the queen trip does nothing for your loose e4 pawn. After 9.cxd4 Nxe4 Black is two pawns up and your centre is half gone. 8.Ba3 uses the diagonal the b-pawn opened to stop Black castling, so Black spends 8...d6 to block it. Then 9.e5 Ne4 10.exd6 cxd6 11.Qe2 hits the e4 knight and you develop with tempo; Marin calls 8.Ba3 typical of the Evans, and masters choose it 60% of the time.
1895778820316678|d1b3.principle: In a gambit every move must gain time: 8.Ba3 stops Black castling, while 8.Qb3 lets Black castle and take e4.
sources: GM Mihail Marin, Beating the Open Games, ch. 7 (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-beating-the-open-games.pdf
GM John Nunn, Learn to play the Evans Gambit (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/john-nunn-learn-to-play-the-evans-gambit

ideas.title: Evans tempo moves: e5, Ba3, Qb3
ideas.text: 8.Ba3 uses the diagonal your b-pawn opened to stop Black castling; 8.e5 kicks the f6 knight. Each must leave nothing loose.

ideas.title: Evans: the centre is the payment
ideas.text: cxd4 rebuilds pawns on e4 and d4, but e4 must not be left hanging: 8.cxd4 Nxe4 grabs it.

ideas.title: Black wants to castle
ideas.text: 7...Nf6 develops and prepares ...O-O. Once Black's king is on g8, your pressure on f7 is gone.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: Queen on b3 and bishop on c4 aim at f7, but that only works while Black's king is still on e8.

habit.why: 8.Qb3 aims at f7, but 8...O-O covers it, and the queen trip does nothing for your loose e4 pawn. After 9.cxd4 Nxe4 Black is two pawns up and your centre is half gone.

strays.text: Black castles at once, and f7 is safe.

taught.why: 8.Ba3 uses the diagonal the b-pawn opened to stop Black castling, so Black spends 8...d6 to block it. Then 9.e5 Ne4 10.exd6 cxd6 11.Qe2 hits the e4 knight and you develop with tempo; Marin calls 8.Ba3 typical of the Evans, and masters choose it 60% of the time.

enforces.idea: Evans tempo moves: e5, Ba3, Qb3
enforces.text: The bishop takes f8 from Black's king and forces a reply.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 8.e5 kicks the f6 knight at once and is a good, popular move (31% of masters). After 8...d5 9.exf6 dxc4 10.fxg7 Rg8 the game gets very sharp.
alternatives.after: Masters prefer 8.Ba3 (60%), and Marin shows that the 8.Ba3 d6 9.e5 Ne4 order can gain a tempo over similar 8.e5 lines.
alternatives.idea: Evans tempo moves: e5, Ba3, Qb3

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 8.cxd4 rebuilds your centre, but leaves e4 loose: after 8...Nxe4 9.d5 Ne7 10.Qd4 Nf6 11.Bg5 you have to work to win back the pawn.
alternatives.after: 8.Ba3 first stops Black castling and keeps e4 from dropping at once; masters play it 60% of the time, 8.cxd4 only 9%.
alternatives.idea: Evans: the centre is the payment

1905410911939124|e1h1.headline: Push 6.f4 so Black's f-pawn can never reach f4
1905410911939124|e1h1.why: 6.O-O lets Black play 6...f4, which shuts in your c1 bishop and starts a pawn storm toward the king you just castled. After 7.h4 Be7 8.Qh5+ Kf8 9.Nc3 Nd4 10.Be3 Bg4 Black's pieces come out with threats against your queen. 6.f4 meets the f-pawn with your own, so 6...f4 never comes, your c1 bishop stays free and the f-file opens toward Black's uncastled king. In 6...fxe4 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.Qd2 Nb4 9.Bb3 exd3 Black grabs pawns, but you develop fast while Black's king is still in the centre.
1905410911939124|e1h1.principle: Ask what Black wants first: 6.f4 stops the ...f4 bind before it starts, while 6.O-O lets it happen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

ideas.title: Support the g5 knight
ideas.text: Your g5 knight hits f7 and e6, but no pawn supports it. 6.f4 gives it a pawn guard and stops Black's pawn advancing.

ideas.title: Black's ...f4 bind
ideas.text: If Black's pawn reaches f4 it shuts in your c1 bishop and starts a kingside pawn storm, as after 6.O-O f4.

ideas.title: Hit back in the centre
ideas.text: Black has spent moves on pawns. Open lines and develop fast, as in 6.f4 fxe4 7.Nc3, while Black's king is still on e8.

ideas.title: Don't take on f5
ideas.text: 6.exf5 gives up your central e4 pawn, and 6...Bxf5 develops Black's bishop with nothing lost.

habit.why: 6.O-O lets Black play 6...f4, which shuts in your c1 bishop and starts a pawn storm toward the king you just castled. After 7.h4 Be7 8.Qh5+ Kf8 9.Nc3 Nd4 10.Be3 Bg4 Black's pieces come out with threats against your queen.

strays.text: Castling ignores the threat, and 6...f4 locks in your bishop and storms your king.

taught.why: 6.f4 meets the f-pawn with your own, so 6...f4 never comes, your c1 bishop stays free and the f-file opens toward Black's uncastled king. In 6...fxe4 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.Qd2 Nb4 9.Bb3 exd3 Black grabs pawns, but you develop fast while Black's king is still in the centre.

enforces.text: The f4 pawn guards your g5 knight and opens the f-file.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.exf5 gives up your central e4 pawn, and 6...Bxf5 develops Black's bishop for free. After 7.Nc3 Qd7 Black castles long with easy play.
alternatives.after: 6.f4 meets the f-pawn with a pawn of your own and opens the f-file, instead of helping Black develop.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.Qh5+ looks scary, but 6...g6 hits the queen and it has to retreat with 7.Qe2. Black then advances the f-pawn anyway and keeps the bind, as in 8.Nf3 Bg7.
alternatives.after: 6.f4 stops Black's f-pawn for good without moving your queen; 6.Qh5+ just loses time to 6...g6.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Ne6 jumps into e6, but 6...Bxe6 7.Bxe6 trades it off. You get the bishop pair, but Black gains time with 7...Qf6, hitting your bishop, and then pushes the f-pawn.
alternatives.after: 6.f4 keeps your knight and stops Black's pawn for good; after 6.Ne6 the knight is swapped off and Black still gets in 8...f4.

1922438896562435|f1c4.headline: After 2...Nc6, take the whole centre with 3.d4
1922438896562435|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 runs into 3...d5, which hits the bishop: after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5 a6 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 7.Qe2+ Qe7 it has moved three times only to trade itself off, and Black has the bishop pair. You have no pawn left in the centre and Black is comfortable. 3.d4 takes the centre with pawns, and masters choose it 91% of the time. After 3...d5 4.e5 the knight blocks Black's c-pawn, so Black breaks with 4...f6, and after 5.Nc3 fxe5 6.Nxe5 Nxe5 7.dxe5 you keep a pawn on e5 and more space.
1922438896562435|f1c4.principle: When the opponent's knight blocks the pawn that would challenge your centre, put a second pawn in the middle at once.
sources: Schiller, Standard Chess Openings; Alekhine, New York 1927 (Google Books snippets) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%22Nc6+2.Nf3+e6+3.d4+d5+4.e5%22
Jeremy Silman, Nimzovich Defense, the Swing! (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/nimzovich-defense
Nimzowitsch Defense: Franco-Nimzowitsch Variation (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/nimzowitsch-defense/franco-nimzowitsch-variation/
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3

ideas.title: Take the centre with pawns
ideas.text: Black has handed you the centre, so put a second pawn on d4 before the bishops come out.

ideas.title: ...d5 hits a bishop on c4
ideas.text: With ...e6 in, ...d5 gains time against a bishop on c4, as in 3...d5 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5.

ideas.title: Nc6 blocks the ...c5 break
ideas.text: Black's knight stands in front of the c-pawn, so after 4.e5 Black can't hit your centre with ...c5 and turns to 4...f6.

habit.why: 3.Bc4 runs into 3...d5, which hits the bishop: after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5 a6 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 7.Qe2+ Qe7 it has moved three times only to trade itself off, and Black has the bishop pair. You have no pawn left in the centre and Black is comfortable.

strays.text: The bishop comes out before d4, and 3...d5 chases it.

taught.why: 3.d4 takes the centre with pawns, and masters choose it 91% of the time. After 3...d5 4.e5 the knight blocks Black's c-pawn, so Black breaks with 4...f6, and after 5.Nc3 fxe5 6.Nxe5 Nxe5 7.dxe5 you keep a pawn on e5 and more space.

enforces.text: With ...c5 blocked, Black can only hit your centre with ...f6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 develops and guards e4, so 3...d5 doesn't gain time on anything. It's sound, but there's a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 3.d4 takes the centre at once, and masters play it 91% of the time. 3.Nc3 often reaches a similar centre a move later, but after 4.d4 Nf6 5.e5 Ne4 Black's knight gets an active post.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.Bb5 gives up the bishop for the knight: after 3...a6 4.Bxc6 dxc6 Black has the bishop pair, and with the knight gone the c-pawn is free, so 5...c5 hits your centre.
alternatives.after: 3.d4 keeps the c6-knight where it blocks Black's c-pawn. After 3.Bb5 a6 4.Bxc6 that block is gone, and 5...c5 comes easily.

1931050112551786|e6e5.headline: Recapture 4...exd5: keep a pawn in the centre
1931050112551786|e6e5.why: 4...e5 leaves the d5 pawn hanging and lets White open the f-file: after 5.fxe5 Qxd5 6.Nc3 Qe6 you are simply a pawn down. Your queen keeps getting chased too, as in 7.b3 Nc6 8.Bc4 Qe7. 4...exd5 wins the pawn back at once and opens your c8 bishop's diagonal. After 5.Bb5+ Nc6 6.Nc3 Nf6 you have a free centre and equal chances; all 22 master games went 4...exd5.
1931050112551786|e6e5.principle: Hold the centre with a pawn: after 4.exd5, 4...exd5 takes back with a pawn and frees your c8 bishop, while 4...e5 just leaves a pawn hanging.
sources: Shaun Sedice, Playing the Grand Prix Attack (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/grand-prix-attack/
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. f4

ideas.title: Strike with ...d5
ideas.text: Against an early f4, ...e6 and ...d5 is the standard reply. After the trade on d5 you have a free centre.

ideas.title: Keep a pawn in the centre
ideas.text: After 4.exd5, take back with the e-pawn: a pawn on d5 holds the centre and opens the diagonal for your c8 bishop.

ideas.title: Bb5 against d5
ideas.text: White's plan against a d5 pawn is a bishop check from b5 and piece pressure. Develop fast with ...Nc6 and ...Nf6.

habit.why: 4...e5 leaves the d5 pawn hanging and lets White open the f-file: after 5.fxe5 Qxd5 6.Nc3 Qe6 you are simply a pawn down. Your queen keeps getting chased too, as in 7.b3 Nc6 8.Bc4 Qe7.

strays.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
strays.text: It gives up the d5 pawn instead of retaking it.

taught.why: 4...exd5 wins the pawn back at once and opens your c8 bishop's diagonal. After 5.Bb5+ Nc6 6.Nc3 Nf6 you have a free centre and equal chances; all 22 master games went 4...exd5.

enforces.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
enforces.text: The e-pawn takes back, and a pawn holds d5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
alternatives.before: 4...Qxd5 wins the pawn back and avoids an isolated d-pawn, but your queen gets chased: 5.Nc3 Qd8 sends it home. Sound, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4...exd5 takes back with a pawn, so no knight gains time on your queen, and your c8 bishop's diagonal opens. Every master game chose it.

1957522496653461|f8c5.headline: Develop 3...Nf6 first; 3...Bc5 runs into the fork trick
1957522496653461|f8c5.why: 3...Bc5 allows the fork trick 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 5.d4, which hits your bishop and knight at once. After 5...Qh4 6.dxc5 Qxe4+ 7.Be3 Ng4 8.Nc3 you have the pawn back, but White keeps the bishop pair and is ahead in development. 3...Nf6 develops a piece and hits e4, and the bishop still comes to c5 later, as in 4.g3 Bc5 5.Bg2 O-O 6.O-O. With your king castled you then take the centre with 6...Re8 7.c3 d5.
1957522496653461|f8c5.principle: Bring the king's knight out before the bishop: after 3.d3, a bishop on c5 is a target for the 4.Nxe5 and 5.d4 fork.
sources: Open Games with ...Bc5 (IM Sam Collins, ChessBase) | https://shop.chessbase.com/en/products/collins_open_games_with_bc5
Three Knights Game (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Knights_Game

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...e5/2._Nf3/2...Nc6

ideas.title: The fork trick
ideas.text: Against an early ...Bc5, White plays 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 5.d4: the pawn hits bishop and knight, and White wins the piece back with a better centre.

ideas.title: Knight before bishop
ideas.text: 3...Nf6 develops and hits e4. Once the knight is out, the bishop can still go to c5 safely, as in 4.g3 Bc5 5.Bg2 O-O.

ideas.title: Answer d4 by taking on d4
ideas.text: White's d-pawn reaches d4 in one move. A bishop on c5 is its target; meet the push with ...exd4, as in 5.d4 exd4.

ideas.title: Strike back with ...d5
ideas.text: 3.d3 is slow, so once you have developed and castled you can claim the centre yourself, as in 6...Re8 7.c3 d5.

habit.why: 3...Bc5 allows the fork trick 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 5.d4, which hits your bishop and knight at once. After 5...Qh4 6.dxc5 Qxe4+ 7.Be3 Ng4 8.Nc3 you have the pawn back, but White keeps the bishop pair and is ahead in development.

strays.text: The bishop on c5 before the knight on f6 invites 4.Nxe5 and 5.d4.

taught.why: 3...Nf6 develops a piece and hits e4, and the bishop still comes to c5 later, as in 4.g3 Bc5 5.Bg2 O-O 6.O-O. With your king castled you then take the centre with 6...Re8 7.c3 d5.

enforces.text: The knight comes out first, so ...Bc5 later no longer drops into a fork.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Answer d4 by taking on d4
alternatives.before: 3...d6 guards e5, so the 4.Nxe5 fork trick never comes up, but it is passive: after 4.Nc3 and 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 White gets the centre in one go. A more active move is stronger.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 develops a piece and presses e4 instead of only guarding e5. Masters choose it 72% of the time, 3...d6 only 4.5%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...h6 is a waiting move that develops nothing; it is fine only because 3.d3 is slow too, and after 4.a3 g6 5.c4 Bg7 White gains queenside space. A developing move is stronger.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 is just as safe but brings out a piece and hits e4, while 3...h6 spends a move masters don't spend.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...g6 is good: the bishop on g7 backs up e5 and ...d5 comes later, as in 4.g3 Bg7 5.Bg2 Nge7 6.O-O O-O 7.c3 d5. Masters play it 10.5% of the time, but another move is far more popular.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 and 3...g6 are close; the knight move develops at once and hits e4. Masters prefer it, 72% to 10.5%.

1976310622037328|c7c5.headline: Against Bg5, play ...c6; ...c5 hands White time
1976310622037328|c7c5.why: 5...c5 gives up a pawn for a while: 6.dxc5 Qa5 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Qd3, and White develops with tempo while your queen chases it. You only win it back with 9...dxc5, with White castled and well ahead in development. 5...c6 keeps d6 solid, so the d-file stays shut while f6 is pinned, and prepares b7-b5. After 6.h3 O-O 7.Bd3 Nbd7 8.a4 e5 you hit the centre once your king is safe.
1976310622037328|c7c5.principle: Don't open lines while you are behind in development: after 5...c5 6.dxc5 White develops with tempo while you win back the pawn.
sources: Pirc Defence - Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirc_Defence
Pirc Defense: Byrne Variation (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/pirc-defense/byrne-variation/

ideas.title: Keep it flexible with ...c6
ideas.text: Against 5.Bg5, ...c6 keeps d6 solid and prepares b7-b5 or the queen to a5. Castling and ...e5 can wait.

ideas.title: White gains time on c5
ideas.text: After 6.dxc5 your queen spends moves winning the pawn back, while 7.Bb5+ and 8.Qd3 develop White with tempo.

ideas.title: The Bg5 pin on f6
ideas.text: The g5 bishop pins your f6 knight against e7. Opening the d-file now helps White, so keep d6 solid.

ideas.title: White's Bh6 and h-pawn attack
ideas.text: After 5...O-O, White plays 6.Qd2 and 8.Bh6 to trade off your g7 bishop. Castling early gives that plan a target.

habit.why: 5...c5 gives up a pawn for a while: 6.dxc5 Qa5 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Qd3, and White develops with tempo while your queen chases it. You only win it back with 9...dxc5, with White castled and well ahead in development.

strays.text: White takes on c5 and develops with check and tempo.

taught.why: 5...c6 keeps d6 solid, so the d-file stays shut while f6 is pinned, and prepares b7-b5. After 6.h3 O-O 7.Bd3 Nbd7 8.a4 e5 you hit the centre once your king is safe.

enforces.text: d6 stays solid; the central break waits until you are castled.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...O-O is the club favourite, but it gives White a target: 6.Qd2 d5 7.exd5 Nxd5 8.Bh6 trades off your g7 bishop and 10.h4 follows.
alternatives.after: 5...c6 keeps castling in reserve, so White's bishop trade on h6 gains less. Masters still castle here in 24% of games; the engine prefers waiting.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...h6 asks the bishop to decide, and masters play it in 32% of games. The engine is less keen: 6.Be3 Ng4 7.Bc1 Nf6 8.h3 and 9.e5 gain White space.
alternatives.after: 5...c6 does something useful without spending moves on the bishop. Masters play the two about equally (34% and 32%); the engine prefers 5...c6.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Bg4 gets chased: 6.h3 Be6 7.Be3 O-O 8.Qd2, and 9.d5 hits the bishop again while White's attacking set-up is ready.
alternatives.after: 5...c6 keeps the c8 bishop home until it has a safe square, and leaves White no target to chase.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Nbd7 aims for ...e5, but with f6 pinned it doesn't work: after 6.h3 e5 7.Nxe5 you are simply a pawn down.
alternatives.after: 5...c6 prepares ...e5 the right way: in its line 8...e5 comes after castling and ...Nbd7, when the pin no longer costs a pawn.

1976310622037328|e7e5.headline: Against Bg5, play ...c6; an early ...e5 loses a piece
1976310622037328|e7e5.why: 5...e5 opens the centre with your king still on e8: 6.dxe5 dxe5 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 puts it on d8, where the g5 bishop pins your f6 knight. 8.Nd5 hits f6 again, and after 8...Be6 9.Bxf6+ Bxf6 10.Nxf6 you are a piece down. 5...c6 is the most common master move here (34%): it keeps d6 solid and prepares b7-b5. After 6.h3 O-O 7.Bd3 Nbd7 8.a4 you play 8...e5 only once you have castled and developed.
1976310622037328|e7e5.principle: Deal with the pin first: while the g5 bishop pins your f6 knight, opening the centre with 5...e5 lets White pile on f6.

ideas.title: Develop first, ...e5 later
ideas.text: Against 5.Bg5, castle and play ...Nbd7 before ...e5. Rushed, ...e5 walks into a queen trade with check.

ideas.title: The Bg5 pin on f6
ideas.text: Once your king lands on d8, the g5 bishop pins the f6 knight to it, and 8.Nd5 attacks f6 a second time.

ideas.title: White's Bh6 and h-pawn attack
ideas.text: After 5...O-O, White plays 6.Qd2 and 8.Bh6 to trade off your g7 bishop. Castling early gives that plan a target.

habit.why: 5...e5 opens the centre with your king still on e8: 6.dxe5 dxe5 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 puts it on d8, where the g5 bishop pins your f6 knight. 8.Nd5 hits f6 again, and after 8...Be6 9.Bxf6+ Bxf6 10.Nxf6 you are a piece down.

strays.text: Opening the d-file turns the pin on f6 into a lost piece.

taught.why: 5...c6 is the most common master move here (34%): it keeps d6 solid and prepares b7-b5. After 6.h3 O-O 7.Bd3 Nbd7 8.a4 you play 8...e5 only once you have castled and developed.

enforces.text: A quiet useful move; the central break waits until you are ready.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...O-O is the club favourite, but it gives White a target: 6.Qd2 d5 7.exd5 Nxd5 8.Bh6 trades off your g7 bishop.
alternatives.after: 5...c6 keeps castling in reserve, so White's bishop trade on h6 gains less. Masters still castle here in 24% of games; the engine prefers waiting.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...h6 asks the bishop to decide, and masters play it in 32% of games. The engine is less keen: 6.Be3 Ng4 7.Bc1 Nf6 8.h3 and 9.e5 gain White space.
alternatives.after: 5...c6 does something useful without spending moves on the bishop. Masters play the two about equally (34% and 32%); the engine prefers 5...c6.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Bg4 gets chased: 6.h3 Be6 7.Bb5+ and later 9.e5 Nfd7, and White gains space while your pieces are pushed back.
alternatives.after: 5...c6 keeps the c8 bishop home until it has a safe square. In the 5...Bg4 line you end up playing ...c6 anyway, with White's pawn already on e5.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Nbd7 aims for ...e5, but with f6 pinned it doesn't work: after 6.h3 e5 7.Nxe5 you are simply a pawn down.
alternatives.after: 5...c6 prepares ...e5 the right way: in its line 8...e5 comes after castling and ...Nbd7, when the pin no longer costs a pawn.

2036399053007590|b8c6.headline: In the French, follow 1...e6 with 2...d5 straight away
2036399053007590|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 lets White build the full centre with 3.d4, and after 3...d5 4.e5 the knight blocks your c-pawn, so the usual ...c5 against d4 is off. Your only lever is 4...f6, and after 5.c3 fxe5 6.Nxe5 Nxe5 7.dxe5 White's pawn sits on e5 and your kingside is loosened. 2...d5 hits e4 at once, before White has d4 in; masters play it 92% of the time. After 3.exd5 exd5 4.d4 Nf6 your c8 bishop is free, and 5.Bd3 c5 still hits d4.
2036399053007590|b8c6.principle: The e6 pawn is there to support ...d5: push it now and challenge e4 before White adds a second centre pawn.
sources: French Defense: Knight Variation (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/french-defense/knight-variation/
Knight Variation, French (C00): The 2.Nf3 Sidestep (Chessiverse) | https://chessiverse.com/resources/openings/knight-variation-french
Lukas Köpl, Review: Mastering the French Advance Main Line by Jan Werle (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/newsroom/post/review-jan-werle-french-advance?page=0

ideas.title: Black: break with ...d5 and ...c5
ideas.text: 1...e6 prepares ...d5. Play 2...d5 now to hit e4, and keep ...c5 ready against d4 later.

ideas.title: Take the full centre with d4
ideas.text: Given a quiet move, White plays 3.d4 with two pawns in the centre, and 4.e5 gains space.

ideas.title: Knight after the c-pawn
ideas.text: A knight on c6 blocks your c-pawn. After 3.d4 d5 4.e5 you'd have no ...c5 against White's d4-e5 chain.

ideas.title: ...f6 is a poor substitute
ideas.text: Without ...c5 your only lever is 4...f6, which loosens your king; after 5.c3 fxe5 6.Nxe5 White's knight lands in the centre.

habit.why: 2...Nc6 lets White build the full centre with 3.d4, and after 3...d5 4.e5 the knight blocks your c-pawn, so the usual ...c5 against d4 is off. Your only lever is 4...f6, and after 5.c3 fxe5 6.Nxe5 Nxe5 7.dxe5 White's pawn sits on e5 and your kingside is loosened.

strays.text: The knight blocks the c-pawn you need against White's centre.

taught.why: 2...d5 hits e4 at once, before White has d4 in; masters play it 92% of the time. After 3.exd5 exd5 4.d4 Nf6 your c8 bishop is free, and 5.Bd3 c5 still hits d4.

enforces.text: You challenge e4 right away and keep the c-pawn free.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2...c5 turns the game into a Sicilian: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 it's an Open Sicilian, so it only suits you if you know those lines. The engine calls it an inaccuracy.
alternatives.after: 2...d5 keeps the game French and is the masters' choice in 92% of games. They play 2...c5 6.5% of the time, so it is playable even though the engine marks it down.
alternatives.idea: Take the full centre with d4

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2...b6 lets White build the full centre with 3.d4, and after 4.Nc3 Bb4 5.Bd3 Nf6 6.e5 White gains space and kicks your knight.
alternatives.after: 2...d5 hits e4 a move earlier, before White has d4 in, and keeps the c8 bishop's diagonal open.
alternatives.idea: Take the full centre with d4

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2...c6 spends a move on a pawn that wants to reach c5 anyway: after 3.d4 and 4.Nbd2 Nf6 5.Bd3 c5 it has taken two moves, and 6.e5 gains space.
alternatives.after: 2...d5 challenges e4 at once; in the 2...c6 line you play the same breaks a move later.

2067858163173673|d4c6.headline: Save the knight with a threat: 6.Nb5 hits c7
2067858163173673|d4c6.why: 6.Nxc6 saves the knight from 6...Qxd4 but helps Black: 6...dxc6 opens the d-file and frees the c8 bishop. After 7.O-O Be6 8.Bb3 Bc5 Black develops easily and the queen on f6 is well placed. 6.Nb5 saves the knight and threatens to take on c7 with check, forking king and rook. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Kd8 Black must guard c7 with the king and can never castle.
2067858163173673|d4c6.principle: When a piece is attacked, look for a square where it saves itself and makes a threat: 6.Nb5 hits c7.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4

ideas.title: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
ideas.text: Black threatens 6...Qxd4. 6.Nb5 saves the knight and threatens to take on c7 with check, forking king and a8 rook.

ideas.title: Punish the early queen
ideas.text: 5...Qf6 brings the queen out before the minor pieces. Keep your knight active so the queen looks misplaced, rather than trading it off.

ideas.title: King stuck in the centre
ideas.text: In the engine line 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Kd8 Black guards c7 with the king and gives up castling.

ideas.title: Recapturing towards the centre
ideas.text: After 6.Nxc6 dxc6 Black opens the d-file and frees the c8 bishop, as in 7.O-O Be6.

habit.why: 6.Nxc6 saves the knight from 6...Qxd4 but helps Black: 6...dxc6 opens the d-file and frees the c8 bishop. After 7.O-O Be6 8.Bb3 Bc5 Black develops easily and the queen on f6 is well placed.

strays.idea: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
strays.text: You trade your active knight, and the threat on c7 never comes.

taught.why: 6.Nb5 saves the knight and threatens to take on c7 with check, forking king and rook. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Kd8 Black must guard c7 with the king and can never castle.

enforces.idea: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
enforces.text: The knight escapes and hits c7, so Black must defend.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Be3 guards the knight and is solid: after 6...Bc5 7.c3 Nge7 8.O-O O-O you reach a classical Scotch set-up. But Black's early queen move goes unpunished.
alternatives.after: 6.Nb5 is sharper: it makes a threat at once and costs Black castling, where 6.Be3 lets Black develop normally.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.c3 props up the knight and steers into a classical Scotch set-up: 6...Bc5 7.Be3 Nge7 8.O-O O-O. It is playable, but Black develops without trouble.
alternatives.after: Against an early ...Qf6 in the plain Scotch, Wikibooks calls the knight jump sharper than propping it up with the c-pawn, and here 6.Nb5 also costs Black castling, which 6.c3 does not.

2067858163173673|d4f3.headline: Save the knight with a threat: 6.Nb5 hits c7
2067858163173673|d4f3.why: 6.Nf3 saves the knight, but it is its third move while your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Nbd2 Nge7 8.O-O O-O Black is fully developed and level. 6.Nb5 saves the knight and threatens to take on c7 with check, forking king and rook. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Kd8 Black must guard c7 with the king and can never castle.
2067858163173673|d4f3.principle: When a piece is attacked, look for a square where it saves itself and makes a threat: 6.Nb5 hits c7.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4

2094672111620588|d4e5.headline: Answer 3...f6 with 4.Bc4, not the trade on e5
2094672111620588|d4e5.why: 4.dxe5 dxe5 settles the centre on Black's terms: the f6 pawn now holds e5 and Black's position is solid. After 5.Bd3 Be6 6.Qe2 Bd6 Black develops calmly and your edge is small. 4.Bc4 develops onto the a2-g8 diagonal that 3...f6 weakened, aiming at g8 where Black's king wants to go. After 4...Nc6 5.h3 Nge7 6.O-O exd4 7.Nxd4 you are castled and well ahead in development, the time Wikibooks says 3...f6 hands you.
2094672111620588|d4e5.principle: Black's ...f6 cost a developing move and weakened the king, so keep developing toward that weakness instead of trading the tension away.
sources: Bill Wall, 700 Opening Traps (archive.org) | https://archive.org/stream/700OpeningTraps/700%20Opening%20Traps_djvu.txt
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4

ideas.title: Keep the d4/e5 tension
ideas.text: After 4.dxe5 dxe5 the f6 pawn holds e5 for good. Keep the tension and use the time 3...f6 cost Black.

ideas.title: Use the open a2-g8 diagonal
ideas.text: 3...f6 opened the a2-g8 diagonal toward Black's king. 4.Bc4 aims at f7 and g8, where the king wants to castle.

ideas.title: Extend your development lead
ideas.text: Black has made three pawn moves and no piece moves. Castle and develop first, as with 5.h3 and 6.O-O, then open lines.

ideas.title: Black's cramped Philidor set-up
ideas.text: 3...f6 takes the g8-knight's best square, and the f8-bishop has only e7, so Black develops slowly.

habit.why: 4.dxe5 dxe5 settles the centre on Black's terms: the f6 pawn now holds e5 and Black's position is solid. After 5.Bd3 Be6 6.Qe2 Bd6 Black develops calmly and your edge is small.

strays.text: The trade lets the f6 pawn hold e5 for good.

taught.why: 4.Bc4 develops onto the a2-g8 diagonal that 3...f6 weakened, aiming at g8 where Black's king wants to go. After 4...Nc6 5.h3 Nge7 6.O-O exd4 7.Nxd4 you are castled and well ahead in development, the time Wikibooks says 3...f6 hands you.

enforces.text: The bishop lands on the diagonal 3...f6 weakened.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.d5 closes the centre, so Black's f6-e5 chain stands firm and the open lines that punish ...f6 disappear: 4...g6 5.Nc3 Nd7.
alternatives.after: 4.Bc4 keeps the centre fluid, so the time Black lost with 3...f6 still counts and the a2-g8 diagonal stays open.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 develops and keeps the tension; after 4...Be6 5.Be3 you stay clearly better. A slightly stronger move exists.
alternatives.after: 4.Bc4 puts a piece on the weakened diagonal at once; after 4.Nc3 Be6 Black covers it first. The engine rates the two moves close.

2107090482514507|c1e3.headline: Castle to break the pin on your c3-knight
2107090482514507|c1e3.why: 7.Be3 leaves the c3-knight pinned with your king still on e1. After 7...O-O 8.Qe2 Bxc3+ 9.bxc3 Black takes it with check, doubles your c-pawns, and most of your edge is gone. 7.O-O takes your king off the b4-e1 diagonal, so the c3-knight is no longer pinned to it. If Black still trades after 7...O-O 8.Qe2 b6 9.Bg5 Bxc3 10.bxc3, it comes without check and your g5-bishop already pins the f6-knight.
2107090482514507|c1e3.principle: Break a pin before the pinned piece is attacked again: castling takes your king off the b4-e1 diagonal and frees the c3-knight.
sources: IM Alberto Chueca, Scandinavian Defense | https://www.albertochueca.com/blog/scandinavian-defense/
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8

ideas.title: Break the pin by castling
ideas.text: The b4-bishop pins your c3-knight to the king. 7.O-O takes the king off that diagonal, so a later ...Bxc3 comes without check.

ideas.title: Pin against pin
ideas.text: Once you've castled, 9.Bg5 pins the f6-knight to Black's queen, so Black's pieces are tied up too.

ideas.title: Bishop shut in by ...e6
ideas.text: 4...e6 came before Black's c8-bishop got out, so it needs ...b6 and ...Bb7 to find a diagonal, as in the 7.O-O line.

ideas.title: Bishop pair vs doubled pawns
ideas.text: Black can take on c3 to double your c-pawns; you get the bishop pair in return, which is fine once your king is safe.

habit.why: 7.Be3 leaves the c3-knight pinned with your king still on e1. After 7...O-O 8.Qe2 Bxc3+ 9.bxc3 Black takes it with check, doubles your c-pawns, and most of your edge is gone.

strays.text: The king stays on e1, so 8...Bxc3+ comes with check.

taught.why: 7.O-O takes your king off the b4-e1 diagonal, so the c3-knight is no longer pinned to it. If Black still trades after 7...O-O 8.Qe2 b6 9.Bg5 Bxc3 10.bxc3, it comes without check and your g5-bishop already pins the f6-knight.

enforces.text: With your king castled, the c3-knight is a normal piece again.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Bd2 breaks the pin with a developing move, and after 7...a6 8.a3 Bd6 9.Qe2 b5 10.Ba2 Bb7 11.O-O-O you castle long. It's sound, but another move keeps more of your edge.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O breaks the pin and makes your king safe in one move. After 7.Bd2 you castle long on the side where Black has already pushed ...a6 and ...b5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Bg5 answers the pin with a pin of its own, and after 7...h6 8.Bh4 c5 Black hits your centre. It's sound, but another move keeps more of your edge.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O makes your king safe first and keeps the bishop pin from g5 for later, as in 9.Bg5, when Black can no longer take on c3 with check.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 7.a3 asks the bishop at once, but 7...Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 doubles your c-pawns with check, and Black develops calmly with 8...b6 and 9...Bb7.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O keeps your pawns whole for now; if Black trades on c3 later, you've already castled and developed.

2118572924932318|g7g6.headline: 4...g6 ignores 5.Ng5; develop the bishop with 4...Bc5.
2118572924932318|g7g6.why: White threatens 5.Ng5, attacking f7 together with the bishop on c4, and 4...g6 does nothing about it: after 5.Ng5 d5 6.exd5 Black loses a pawn. 4...Bc5 develops the bishop toward the centre and readies castling, transposing into the Giuoco Pianissimo.
2118572924932318|g7g6.principle: When a knight and the bishop on c4 can combine against f7, develop the pieces that let you castle instead of spending time on a pawn move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. d3

2122895618389281|c8f5.headline: Hit the d5 pawn at once with 3...c6
2122895618389281|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 develops but doesn't touch the d5 pawn, so White keeps it. After 4.d4 e6 5.dxe6 fxe6 you are still a pawn down and your e-pawn is weak. 3...c6 attacks d5 a second time, and after 4.d4 cxd5 the pawn is back. With 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bg4 you reach a Caro-Kann Panov-Botvinnik with your pieces pressing on d4.
2122895618389281|c8f5.principle: When the opponent props up an extra pawn, hit it with a pawn at once; the bishop can come out later.

ideas.title: Undermine the d5 pawn
ideas.text: 3.c4 props up White's extra pawn. Strike it at once with a pawn: after 3...c6 4.d4 cxd5 the pawn is back.

ideas.title: Pawn first, bishop later
ideas.text: Usually your bishop comes out before ...c6 and ...e6. Here it waits: 3...Bf5 leaves d5 alone and White keeps the pawn.

ideas.title: Target d4
ideas.text: Once White has pawns on c4 and d4, aim your pieces at d4, as in 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bg4.

ideas.title: White clings to d5
ideas.text: White's 3.c4 hopes to stay a pawn up. Against slow moves it works: 3...Bf5 4.d4 e6 5.dxe6 fxe6 leaves you a pawn short.

habit.why: 3...Bf5 develops but doesn't touch the d5 pawn, so White keeps it. After 4.d4 e6 5.dxe6 fxe6 you are still a pawn down and your e-pawn is weak.

strays.text: The bishop move leaves d5 alone, so White's extra pawn survives.

taught.why: 3...c6 attacks d5 a second time, and after 4.d4 cxd5 the pawn is back. With 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bg4 you reach a Caro-Kann Panov-Botvinnik with your pieces pressing on d4.

enforces.text: The c-pawn hits d5 at once and wins the pawn back.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...e6 is the Icelandic Gambit: after 4.dxe6 Bxe6 you give a pawn for a big lead in development. The engine marks it down, since after 5.Nf3 Qe7 6.Qe2 Nc6 7.d4 Bf5 8.Qxe7+ the queens come off and you are still a pawn short.
alternatives.after: 3...c6 wins the pawn back for sure, while 3...e6 keeps it a gambit. Masters play the two almost equally (53% and 47%) and books rate the Icelandic well, but the engine prefers 3...c6.

2162412998029713|f1c4.headline: 3...e6 prepares ...d5: put the bishop on d3, not c4
2162412998029713|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 runs into 4...d5, hitting bishop and e4 at once: after 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bd3 the bishop has moved twice to reach d3. Black has a free game after 6...Ne7 7.O-O O-O 8.Re1 Bf5, and most of your edge is gone. 4.Bd3, the masters' top choice (28.9%), guards e4 so ...d5 hits nothing loose. After 4...Nc6 5.e5 Nge7 6.Nc3 h6 7.h4 you hold space in the centre and start play on the kingside.
2162412998029713|f1c4.principle: Ask what your opponent's last move prepares: 3...e6 readies ...d5, so develop the bishop where that push won't hit it.
sources: GM Max Illingworth, The Mad Dog Attack vs. the Modern (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/blog/Illingworth/the-mad-dog-attack-vs-the-modern
Stjepan Tomic, The Bishop Attack: Modern Defense (Lichess) | https://lichess.org/video/On_UP9d9mi8
IM Andrew Martin, The Hippopotamus system of defence (ChessBase) | https://shop.chessbase.com/en/products/martin_hippopotamus
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...g6/2._d4/2...Bg7

ideas.title: Bishop to d3, not c4
ideas.text: With Black's pawn on e6, ...d5 hits a bishop on c4. On d3 it guards e4 and stays put.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 break
ideas.text: The e6 pawn prepares ...d5, attacking e4 and anything on c4, as in 4.Bc4 d5.

ideas.title: The h-pawn against the Hippo
ideas.text: h4 gains kingside space before Black castles, as with 7.h4 in the main line.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Black lets you keep pawns on e4 and d4, then hits them with ...c5 or ...d5, as in 4.Be3 d5 5.e5 c5.

habit.why: 4.Bc4 runs into 4...d5, hitting bishop and e4 at once: after 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bd3 the bishop has moved twice to reach d3. Black has a free game after 6...Ne7 7.O-O O-O 8.Re1 Bf5, and most of your edge is gone.

strays.text: On c4 the bishop is a target for 4...d5 and must move again.

taught.why: 4.Bd3, the masters' top choice (28.9%), guards e4 so ...d5 hits nothing loose. After 4...Nc6 5.e5 Nge7 6.Nc3 h6 7.h4 you hold space in the centre and start play on the kingside.

enforces.text: The bishop guards e4 from d3, where ...d5 can't chase it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 is flexible: the knight guards e4, so ...d5 is no threat, and after 4...d6 5.h4 h6 6.Bf4 you keep a good game.
alternatives.after: 4.Bd3 and 4.Nc3 are equally good; masters play 4.Bd3 a bit more (28.9% to 21.1%), and both guard e4 against ...d5.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
alternatives.before: 4.e5 grabs space but commits early: 4...d6 5.Qe2 b6 6.Nc3 Ne7 7.Qe4 d5 8.Qf4 c5 undermines the pawn while your queen moves three times.
alternatives.after: 4.Bd3 develops first; the push can still come later, as in 4...Nc6 5.e5, with your pieces following.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
alternatives.before: 4.Be3 is solid development, but 4...d5 5.e5 c5 gives Black a French-style counter against d4. Sound, though a slightly stronger move exists.
alternatives.after: 4.Bd3 guards e4 first, so ...d5 hits nothing loose and you aren't forced to push e5 at once.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
alternatives.before: 4.c3 backs up d4 and can lead to Geller's System; after 4...d6 5.a4 Nc6 6.a5 a6 the game stays balanced in the centre. Sound, though one move is slightly stronger.
alternatives.after: 4.Bd3 develops a piece instead of a pawn, and the 4.c3 line still plays 7.Bd3 later. Masters split 28.9% to 18.4%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Be2 keeps the bishop safe from ...d5, but after 4...d5 5.Nc3 dxe4 6.Nxe4 Black gets a French-like game. Sound, though one move is slightly stronger.
alternatives.after: From d3 the bishop also guards e4, which 4.Be2 doesn't, so Black can't simply take on e4.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
alternatives.before: 4.c4 grabs space like an Averbakh, but 4...d5 5.e5 Ne7 6.Nc3 c5 hits your centre from both sides.
alternatives.after: 4.Bd3 develops and guards e4, and keeps c3 for a pawn or knight to support d4, the pawn 6...c5 attacks in the 4.c4 line.

2173517444444160|b2b3.headline: Take the centre with 4.d4, not a slow 4.b3
2173517444444160|b2b3.why: 4.b3 is a slow wing move: after 4...Bg7 5.d4 O-O you play d4 anyway, a move later. Black then hits your centre with 6...c5 and gets an easy game after 7.O-O cxd4 8.Nxd4 Qa5. 4.d4 takes the full centre at once, the choice in 87.5% of master games. With 5.Be3 and 6.Qd2 you then aim for 8.Bh6 to trade off Black's g7 bishop.
2173517444444160|b2b3.principle: When the opponent fianchettoes and leaves the centre to you, occupy it with a second pawn before anything slower.
