ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Black lets you have e4 and d4 and hits them later with ...c5 and the g7 bishop. Take the full centre now, not with a timid wing move.

ideas.title: Be3-Qd2-Bh6 attack
ideas.text: With 5.Be3 and 6.Qd2 you prepare 8.Bh6 to trade off the g7 bishop, the key guard of Black's king.

ideas.title: Hit back in the centre
ideas.text: When you attack on the wing, Black strikes in the centre, as with 6...d5 7.exd5 Nxd5.

habit.why: 4.b3 is a slow wing move: after 4...Bg7 5.d4 O-O you play d4 anyway, a move later. Black then hits your centre with 6...c5 and gets an easy game after 7.O-O cxd4 8.Nxd4 Qa5.

strays.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
strays.text: A flank pawn move instead of taking the centre Black offers.

taught.why: 4.d4 takes the full centre at once, the choice in 87.5% of master games. With 5.Be3 and 6.Qd2 you then aim for 8.Bh6 to trade off Black's g7 bishop.

enforces.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
enforces.text: Two pawns in the centre before Black can hit them.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Bc4 develops toward f7 and is playable. Black can answer with 6...Bg4, pinning your f3 knight and pressing on the centre; there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 takes the centre first; masters choose it 87.5% to 10.9%. With the bishop on c4, Black gets the ...Bg4 pin on your knight.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.d3 guards e4 with a pawn and heads for a King's Indian Attack after 4...e5 5.g3 Bg7 6.Bg2. It is playable but passive, and 4...e5 gives Black a share of the centre.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 claims e4 and d4 at once; 4.d3 lets Black take the centre with 4...e5.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

2179133986956493|f1c4.headline: Guard e4 with 5.Bd3; 5.Bc4 drops the pawn
2179133986956493|f1c4.why: 5.Bc4 does not guard e4, and with a pawn on c3 instead of a knight you have no way to win it back: 5...Nxe4 6.O-O O-O 7.Re1 Nf6 8.Bf1. You have spent moves chasing the knight and are simply a pawn down. 5.Bd3 guards e4 and keeps your c3-d4 centre solid; masters play it in 84.3% of games. After 5...O-O 6.O-O Nbd7 7.Re1 e5 8.h3 you keep a small, safe space edge.
2179133986956493|f1c4.principle: After every opponent move, check which of your pawns are attacked and how many times they are defended.
sources: A Pirc Quirk (IM Jeremy Silman, chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/a-pirc-quirk
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7 (Wikibooks) | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...g6/2._d4/2...Bg7
Modern Defense (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Defense
Modern Defense: Geller's System (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/modern-defense/gellers-system/

ideas.title: Guard e4 before anything else
ideas.text: With a pawn on c3 rather than a knight, nothing guards e4. 5.Bd3, 5.Nbd2 or 5.Qc2 guard it; 5.Bc4 and 5.Bg5 do not.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Your c3-d4 chain holds the centre. Black will hit it with ...e5 or ...c5 and the g7 bishop, so keep it solid.

ideas.title: An early e5 just gets traded
ideas.text: With no f4 behind it, 5.e5 is simply traded: 5...dxe5 6.Nxe5 Nbd7, and Black develops freely.

habit.why: 5.Bc4 does not guard e4, and with a pawn on c3 instead of a knight you have no way to win it back: 5...Nxe4 6.O-O O-O 7.Re1 Nf6 8.Bf1. You have spent moves chasing the knight and are simply a pawn down.

strays.text: The bishop develops, but e4 is left for the f6 knight.

taught.why: 5.Bd3 guards e4 and keeps your c3-d4 centre solid; masters play it in 84.3% of games. After 5...O-O 6.O-O Nbd7 7.Re1 e5 8.h3 you keep a small, safe space edge.

enforces.text: The bishop guards e4 and develops in one move.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Nbd2 guards e4 with a knight and keeps the c3-d4 chain intact; masters play it in 10.3% of games. A more natural move exists.
alternatives.after: 5.Bd3 does the same job while developing the bishop; after 5.Nbd2 O-O 6.Bd3 you usually reach the same set-up.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: With no f4 behind it, 5.e5 is just traded: 5...dxe5 6.Nxe5 Nbd7, and Black has swapped off your centre pawn and develops easily.
alternatives.after: 5.Bd3 keeps the e4 pawn and the space it gives; 5.e5 gives it up for nothing.
alternatives.idea: An early e5 just gets traded

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.Bg5 leaves e4 unguarded: 5...Nxe4 wins a pawn and hits the bishop, which goes back with 6.Bh4, and e7 is well covered anyway.
alternatives.after: 5.Bd3 guards e4 before you develop the other bishop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Qc2 guards e4 with the queen and lets the bishop go to e2 with 6.Be2. It is sound, but a more natural developing move exists.
alternatives.after: 5.Bd3 guards e4 and develops a piece in one move, keeping your queen free; masters prefer it 84.3% to 5.1%.

2185074222383401|d2d3.headline: 4...Qe7 doesn't hold f7: take it with 5.Bxf7+
2185074222383401|d2d3.why: 5.d3 is too slow: Black kicks the knight with 5...h6, and after 6.Nf3 Nxe4 the e4 pawn is gone. 4...Qe7 does not really defend f7, which the bishop on c4 and the knight on g5 both attack. 5.Bxf7+ takes the pawn with check; after 5...Kd8 the knight on g5 protects the bishop, and Black's king has lost the right to castle.
2185074222383401|d2d3.principle: f7 is guarded mainly by the king, which cannot take a protected piece, so with bishop and knight both on it, the capture wins a pawn and castling rights.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5

2185074222383401|g5f7.headline: Take on f7 with the bishop, with check: 5.Bxf7+
2185074222383401|g5f7.why: 5.Nxf7 grabs the pawn and hits the rook, but lets Black open the game with 5...d5; after 6.Bxd5 Nxd5 7.exd5 Qxf7 the trades leave Black with active pieces and a safe king after 9...O-O. 4...Qe7 looks like it guards f7, but 5.Bxf7+ wins the pawn with check: the bishop is protected by the knight on g5, so neither the king nor the queen can take it. After 5...Kd8 Black's king is stuck in the centre and can no longer castle, and 6.Bb3 keeps the bishop safe.
2185074222383401|g5f7.principle: f7 is guarded only by the king and queen while the bishop on c4 and the knight on g5 both hit it; capture with the piece that gives check and stays protected.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5

2185447105552102|e1h1.headline: Push 6.e5 first: castling lets 6...dxe4 fork bishop and knight
2185447105552102|e1h1.why: 6.O-O leaves the tension alone, and 6...dxe4 forks your bishop on d3 and knight on f3. After 7.Bxe4 Nxe4 the queen can't take back because the b7-bishop guards e4, so you lose a piece for a pawn. 6.e5 pushes past the attack: the knight goes back to d7 and the fork is gone. After 6...Nfd7 7.c3 c5 8.Be3 you have a French-type centre with extra space on the kingside; masters play 6.e5 in 88% of games.
2185447105552102|e1h1.principle: Look at forcing moves first: 6...dxe4 forks your d3-bishop and f3-knight, so 6.e5 ends the threat before you castle.
sources: Christian Bauer, Play 1...b6 (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%22Qe2+e6+5.Nf3+d5+6.e5%22
Owen's Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen%27s_Defence
Matthew Astle, The Offbeat Owen's (Chessable blog) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/owens-defense/

ideas.title: Resolve ...d5 before castling
ideas.text: Black's ...d5 hits e4 a third time, and 6...dxe4 would fork your d3-bishop and f3-knight. Settle the tension now.

ideas.title: e5 kicks the f6-knight
ideas.text: With the queen and knight behind it, e5 gains space, drives the knight to d7 and locks the b7-bishop behind Black's d5-pawn.

ideas.title: Count attackers on e4
ideas.text: The d5-pawn and f6-knight hit e4, with the b7-bishop behind them; your bishop and queen guard it, one guard short.

ideas.title: Black strikes back with ...c5
ideas.text: After e5, Black hits d4 with ...c5 and ...Nc6; c3 keeps the centre, as in 7.c3 c5 8.Be3 Nc6.

habit.why: 6.O-O leaves the tension alone, and 6...dxe4 forks your bishop on d3 and knight on f3. After 7.Bxe4 Nxe4 the queen can't take back because the b7-bishop guards e4, so you lose a piece for a pawn.

strays.text: Castling ignores ...dxe4, which forks your bishop and knight.

taught.why: 6.e5 pushes past the attack: the knight goes back to d7 and the fork is gone. After 6...Nfd7 7.c3 c5 8.Be3 you have a French-type centre with extra space on the kingside; masters play 6.e5 in 88% of games.

enforces.text: The pawn kicks the knight to d7 and ends the threat on e4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.exd5 settles the tension and removes the fork, which is good, but there's a stronger move. After 6...Qxd5 7.a3 Nc6 8.Nc3 Qh5 Black's pieces are active and both sides castle long.
alternatives.after: 6.e5 keeps the b7-bishop locked behind the d5-pawn and gains kingside space; 6.exd5 opens its diagonal. Masters choose 6.e5 in 88% of games, 6.exd5 in 5%.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Nbd2 adds a third guard to e4, but 6...dxe4 7.Nxe4 Nxe4 8.Bxe4 Bxe4 9.Qxe4 Qd5 trades off your centre pawn and Black's b7-bishop, and the game is level.
alternatives.after: 6.e5 keeps the pieces on and the b7-bishop shut in, with space for you; the trades after 6.Nbd2 free Black's game.

221633201643279|d2d4.headline: Take the free pawn: 2.Bxb5 wins material and develops
221633201643279|d2d4.why: 2.d4 builds a centre but leaves the b5 pawn alone, so Black's gambit costs nothing. After 2...Bb7 3.Nd2 a6 Black has the long diagonal and queenside space without being a pawn down. 2.Bxb5 takes a pawn that nothing defends and develops your bishop at the same time. In the line 2...Bb7 3.d3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 you guard e4, keep developing and stay a pawn up.
221633201643279|d2d4.principle: Take an unsound gambit pawn when the capture also develops a piece and you can hold your centre afterwards.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b5 (Wikibooks) | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...b5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b5/2. Bxb5 (Wikibooks) | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...b5/2._Bxb5

ideas.title: Take the free pawn
ideas.text: The b5 pawn is attacked by your bishop and defended by nothing. 2.Bxb5 wins it while developing a piece.

ideas.title: Watch the long diagonal
ideas.text: Black's idea is 2...Bb7, hitting e4 and later g2, which your bishop no longer guards once it leaves f1.

ideas.title: Guard e4, stay a pawn up
ideas.text: After 2.Bxb5 Bb7, 3.d3 guards e4, and you stay a clean pawn up with easy development.

habit.why: 2.d4 builds a centre but leaves the b5 pawn alone, so Black's gambit costs nothing. After 2...Bb7 3.Nd2 a6 Black has the long diagonal and queenside space without being a pawn down.

strays.text: The b5 pawn survives, so Black gets the play without paying for it.

taught.why: 2.Bxb5 takes a pawn that nothing defends and develops your bishop at the same time. In the line 2...Bb7 3.d3 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 you guard e4, keep developing and stay a pawn up.

enforces.text: The bishop develops and wins the b5 pawn in one move.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2.Nf3 develops but lets Black hit e4 at once with 2...Bb7. In the line Black wins the e4 pawn back with 3...Bxe4, so the gambit has cost nothing.
alternatives.after: 2.Bxb5 takes the pawn before e4 comes under fire, so 3.d3 can still guard e4 and you stay a pawn up.

2219393363100507|f8d6.headline: Hit the centralised queen with 3...Nc6
2219393363100507|f8d6.why: 3...Bd6 leaves the pawn on g7 unprotected against the queen on d4, so 4.Qxg7 wins it, and the bishop also blocks Black's d-pawn. 3...Nc6 is the usual answer to the Centre Game: it develops with an attack on the queen, so White has to move it again and Black gains time.
2219393363100507|f8d6.principle: When the opponent's queen sits in the centre, develop a piece that attacks it and make it move again.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Qxd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Qxd4/3...Nc6

2227650220427205|d7d5.headline: Don't push ...d5 into three attackers; 5...h6 is the quiet move
2227650220427205|d7d5.why: 5...d5 drops a pawn: d5 is hit by the pawn on e4, the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4, and after 6.Nxd5 Nxd5 7.Bxd5 White has won it. 5...h6 is a useful waiting move that takes g5 away from White's knight and bishop, so Black can castle with 6.O-O O-O without worrying about a pin or a hit on f7.
2227650220427205|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a central pawn, count the attackers on its square: here three white pieces cover d5 and Black has fewer defenders.

2264630549471820|a2a3.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; 5.a3 wastes time and loosens e4
2264630549471820|a2a3.why: 5.a3 spends a tempo inviting 5...Bxc3, and after 6.dxc3 Nxe4 the e4 pawn is gone; White wins the knight back with 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7 8.Qd5+ Ke8 9.Qxe4, but has traded off the attacking bishop and Black has the easier game. 5.O-O gets the king safe and keeps the tempo: after 5...Bxc3 6.bxc3 Nxe4 7.Bd5 Nf6 8.Bxc6 dxc6 9.Nxe5 White has the pawn back with active pieces. It is the most common master move here.
2264630549471820|a2a3.principle: A pawn move like 5.a3 that neither develops nor fights for the centre needs a concrete reason; castling finishes White's kingside development instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

2264630549471820|c3b5.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; the c3 knight is e4's only guard
2264630549471820|c3b5.why: 5.Nb5 moves a developed knight again and abandons the e4 pawn, so 5...Nxe4 wins it for nothing. 5.O-O is the most common master move: it tucks the king away first. After 5...Bxc3 6.bxc3 Nxe4 7.Bd5 Nf6 8.Bxc6 dxc6 9.Nxe5 White wins the pawn back.
2264630549471820|c3b5.principle: Before moving a piece, count what it defends: if it is the only guard of a centre pawn, leave it and improve another piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

2326611116094961|c1e3.headline: Check on f7 first: 6.Bxf7+ before you guard the knight
2326611116094961|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 guards the knight but lets Black off the hook: 6...Qf6 7.c3 Nge7 8.O-O O-O is a normal, level Scotch-type game with Black fully developed. The tempo Black lost with 3...h6 and the weak f7 square are no longer worth anything. 6.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check, and taking with the king would drop the c5 bishop to a queen check on h5. After 6...Kf8 7.Nxc6 Qh4 8.Qf3 dxc6 9.Bg6+ Qf6 10.Qxf6+ Nxf6 you are a clean pawn up and Black can never castle.
2326611116094961|c1e3.principle: Before you answer a threat, look for your own forcing move: 6.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check, and the threat on d4 can wait a move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: 6.Bxf7+ takes a pawn with check. If the king takes, a queen check from h5 also hits the loose c5 bishop.

ideas.title: Check before you answer the threat
ideas.text: Black threatens 6...Bxd4. A check that wins a pawn comes first; the knight can be dealt with next move, as in 7.Nxc6.

ideas.title: A king that can't castle
ideas.text: After 6...Kf8 Black's king can never castle, and you keep the extra pawn even after the queens come off with 10.Qxf6+ Nxf6.

ideas.title: Black's pieces aim at f2
ideas.text: The c5 bishop already aims at f2. Given a free move, 6...Qf6 adds the queen and threatens mate there.

habit.why: 6.Be3 guards the knight but lets Black off the hook: 6...Qf6 7.c3 Nge7 8.O-O O-O is a normal, level Scotch-type game with Black fully developed. The tempo Black lost with 3...h6 and the weak f7 square are no longer worth anything.

strays.idea: Check before you answer the threat
strays.text: Guarding d4 at once skips the check that wins a pawn.

taught.why: 6.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check, and taking with the king would drop the c5 bishop to a queen check on h5. After 6...Kf8 7.Nxc6 Qh4 8.Qf3 dxc6 9.Bg6+ Qf6 10.Qxf6+ Nxf6 you are a clean pawn up and Black can never castle.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
enforces.text: The check wins a pawn, and taking the bishop would lose the c5 bishop.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.Nxc6 removes the attacker but lets 6...Qf6 in, threatening mate on f2 with the c5 bishop; after 7.O-O dxc6 Black develops freely.
alternatives.after: 6.Bxf7+ comes first with check and wins a pawn; 7.Nxc6 can follow next move, when Black's king has already lost castling.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.c3 adds a guard to d4 but does nothing for f2 or e4: 6...Nf6 7.Nxc6 bxc6 8.e5 Ne4 9.O-O Nxf2 breaks into f2 with the c5 bishop's help.
alternatives.after: 6.Bxf7+ strikes first with check instead of defending, so Black never gets time for 6...Nf6 and the raid on f2.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.Nf5 saves the knight but moves it a third time: after 6...d6 7.Nxg7+ Kf8 8.Nh5 Qh4 it is stranded on the rim while Black's queen hits f2 and e4.
alternatives.after: 6.Bxf7+ forces matters with check instead of spending a third knight move; you win a pawn and Black's king loses castling.
alternatives.idea: Check before you answer the threat

2326611116094961|d4c6.headline: Check on f7 first: 6.Bxf7+ before you trade knights
2326611116094961|d4c6.why: 6.Nxc6 answers the threat on d4 but lets 6...Qf6 in, threatening mate on f2 together with the c5 bishop. You must spend 7.O-O on defence, and after 7...dxc6 Black develops freely and the shot on f7 is gone. 6.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check, and taking with the king would drop the c5 bishop to a queen check on h5. After 6...Kf8 7.Nxc6 Qh4 8.Qf3 dxc6 9.Bg6+ Qf6 10.Qxf6+ Nxf6 you are a clean pawn up and Black can never castle.
2326611116094961|d4c6.principle: Before you answer a threat, look for your own forcing move: 6.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check, and the threat on d4 can wait a move.

alternatives.idea: Check before you answer the threat

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.c3 adds a guard to d4 but does nothing for f2 or e4: 6...Nf6 7.Nxc6 bxc6 8.e5 Ne4 9.O-O Nxf2 breaks into f2 with the c5 bishop's help.
alternatives.after: 6.Bxf7+ strikes first with check instead of defending, so Black never gets time for 6...Nf6 and the raid on f2.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.Nf5 saves the knight but moves it a third time: after 6...d6 7.Nxg7+ Kf8 8.Nh5 Qh4 it is stranded on the rim while Black's queen hits f2 and e4.
alternatives.after: 6.Bxf7+ forces matters with check instead of spending a third knight move; you win a pawn and Black's king loses castling.
alternatives.idea: Check before you answer the threat

2385998627357413|b2b4.headline: Gain queenside space with 7.a4; 7.b4 just hangs a pawn
2385998627357413|b2b4.why: 7.b4 puts a pawn where the c6 knight and c5 bishop both hit it and only the c3 pawn guards it, so 7...Nxb4 wins it. Taking back with the c-pawn opens the long diagonal for the bishop to hit your a1 rook, and after 8.a4 d5 9.exd5 Nxd5 Black is simply a pawn up. 7.a4 gains queenside space at no cost, prepares a later b4 or a5 and gives your bishop a retreat on a2. After 7...a5 8.h3 Kh8 9.Qh5 the game is level, and h3 comes only now that Black has castled.
2385998627357413|b2b4.principle: Count attackers and defenders before you push: b4 is hit twice and guarded once, while 7.a4 gains space safely.
sources: Georgios Souleidis and Karsten Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (New in Chess), pp. 11-13 | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf

ideas.title: Count the b4 pawn's guards
ideas.text: On b4 the pawn is hit by the c6 knight and the c5 bishop and guarded only by c3, so 7...Nxb4 wins it.

ideas.title: Slow Italian: build first
ideas.text: Gain space with a4 first: it costs nothing, gives your bishop a retreat on a2 and prepares b4 or a5 later.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: Black has castled and the h6 knight guards f7, so your g5 knight has no target. Build up around it instead of adding the queen.

ideas.title: Guard f7, chase the bishop
ideas.text: Black's knight wants a5 to hit your c4 bishop, as after 7.Qf3 Na5, so keep a retreat ready.

habit.why: 7.b4 puts a pawn where the c6 knight and c5 bishop both hit it and only the c3 pawn guards it, so 7...Nxb4 wins it. Taking back with the c-pawn opens the long diagonal for the bishop to hit your a1 rook, and after 8.a4 d5 9.exd5 Nxd5 Black is simply a pawn up.

strays.text: Two black pieces hit b4 and only the c3 pawn defends it.

taught.why: 7.a4 gains queenside space at no cost, prepares a later b4 or a5 and gives your bishop a retreat on a2. After 7...a5 8.h3 Kh8 9.Qh5 the game is level, and h3 comes only now that Black has castled.

enforces.text: Queenside space without giving up a pawn.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.O-O gets your king safe and keeps the g5 knight's options; after 7...Kh8 8.h3 a5 9.Qh5 knight and queen press on f7 and h7. It's fully sound.
alternatives.after: The engine rates the two moves equally. 7.a4 grabs queenside space first and 7.O-O castles first; in the 7.O-O line you play 10.a4 a few moves later anyway.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Nf3 brings the knight back, admitting the trip to g5 cost two moves. Black uses the time for 7...Kh8 and a later ...f5 break, as in 9.O-O f5.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 spends the move on useful queenside space; the g5 knight isn't attacked, so there's no need to spend a move bringing it back.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qf3 brings the queen out early, and 7...Na5 hits your bishop. After 8.Bd5 c6 it's kicked again and Black gains time.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 keeps the queen home and frees a2 as a retreat for your bishop if the knight comes to a5.

2446703153094283|b8c6.headline: Against 1.Nf3, keep your options open with 1...Nf6
2446703153094283|b8c6.why: 1...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, and after 2.d4 d5 3.c4 White gets a Queen's Gambit in which Black cannot use the c-pawn to support d5 or to strike back with ...c5. 1...Nf6 is the most flexible reply and the most popular among masters at 46%: it develops, stops White from playing e4, and keeps every pawn free, so Black can choose a setup such as 1...Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.g3 g6.
2446703153094283|b8c6.principle: The knight on f6 controls e4 and d5 without committing a pawn, while a knight on c6 in front of the c-pawn takes away Black's usual way to fight for d5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3
Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...Nf6

2446703153094283|e7e5.headline: After 1.Nf3, e5 just hangs; play 1...Nf6
2446703153094283|e7e5.why: 1...e5 puts a pawn where the knight on f3 attacks it and nothing defends it, so 2.Nxe5 wins it; theory calls it the dubious Ross Gambit. 1...Nf6 is the most flexible reply: it keeps the position symmetrical and leaves Black free to choose a setup later. Masters choose it in 46.4% of games.
2446703153094283|e7e5.principle: Before putting a pawn on a square, count: e5 is attacked by the knight and defended by nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...e5
Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...Nf6

2463215796795915|f1e2.headline: Take the undefended c5 pawn before Black trades it off: 6.dxc5
2463215796795915|f1e2.why: 6.Be2 is played by 40% of masters, but the engine rates it below 6.dxc5: it gives Black time for 6...cxd4 7.cxd4, the release the theory recommends. After 8.O-O Nge7 9.Nbd2 Bh5 10.h3 Qb6 Black piles up on d4 and your chance on c5 is gone. 6.dxc5 takes the loose pawn, and grabbing e5 at once loses to the b5 check trick, so Black first plays 6...a6. After 7.Nbd2 Nxe5 8.Be2 the pawns are level again, but 10.b4 supports your pawn on c5 and gains queenside space.
2463215796795915|f1e2.principle: Ask what Black wants: here 6...cxd4 to free the game, so take on c5 first and the release never comes.
sources: njswift, Advance Caro-Kann: The Botvinnik-Carls Defense, chapter 'The solid 4. c3' (Lichess study) | https://lichess.org/study/SZvZhdh3/4UOz513G
Siegfried Baumegger, Caro-Kann Defense - Advance Variation (Modern Chess) | https://www.modern-chess.com/opening/caro-kann-defense-advance-variation/
Jeremy Silman, Kt Maneuvers Against the Advance Caro-Kann (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/kt-maneuvers-against-the-advance-caro-kann

ideas.title: Grab c5 when it hangs
ideas.text: c5 is attacked by d4 and guarded by nothing, and 5...Bg4 doesn't stop 6.dxc5. Later 10.b4 holds your pawn on c5.

ideas.title: The b5 check trick
ideas.text: After 6.dxc5, grabbing e5 at once fails: you recapture on e5, and if Black takes your queen, a bishop check on b5 regains it.

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: Black's c5 pawn and c6 knight hit d4, and the g4 bishop eyes the f3 knight that guards it. Black wants ...cxd4 next.

ideas.title: Don't invite ...Bxf3
ideas.text: Your f3 knight guards d4. 6.h3 Bxf3 7.Qxf3 removes it and pulls your queen off the d-file, so 7...cxd4 wins a pawn.

habit.why: 6.Be2 is played by 40% of masters, but the engine rates it below 6.dxc5: it gives Black time for 6...cxd4 7.cxd4, the release the theory recommends. After 8.O-O Nge7 9.Nbd2 Bh5 10.h3 Qb6 Black piles up on d4 and your chance on c5 is gone.

strays.text: You develop instead, and 6...cxd4 removes the loose pawn for good.

taught.why: 6.dxc5 takes the loose pawn, and grabbing e5 at once loses to the b5 check trick, so Black first plays 6...a6. After 7.Nbd2 Nxe5 8.Be2 the pawns are level again, but 10.b4 supports your pawn on c5 and gains queenside space.

enforces.text: You take c5 before ...cxd4; the b5 check stops Black regaining e5 at once.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Bb5 pins the knight that attacks d4, but after 6...cxd4 7.Qa4 Qc7 8.Nbd2 Bd7 9.Bxc6 bxc6 10.cxd4 Black hits d4 again with 10...c5.
alternatives.after: 6.dxc5 removes the c5 pawn before ...cxd4; 6.Bb5 gives up your bishop for the knight and Black still gets at d4.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Be3 guards d4 once more, but 6...cxd4 7.cxd4 e6 is the release Black wants, and after 8.Bd3 Bb4+ 9.Nc3 f6 10.h3 Bxf3 Black hits both e5 and d4.
alternatives.after: 6.dxc5 changes the structure first; after 6.Be3 Black gets the freeing ...cxd4 that the theory recommends.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.h3 lets 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 cxd4 win a pawn: the knight that guarded d4 is gone and your queen has left the d-file.
alternatives.after: 6.dxc5 deals with the c5 pawn first; after 6.h3 Black's ...cxd4 comes with a pawn won.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Nbd2 develops, but after 6...cxd4 7.cxd4 Qa5 the knight is pinned, and after 8.Qb3 Qb4 9.Qxb4 Nxb4 10.Kd1 your king has lost the right to castle.
alternatives.after: 6.dxc5 takes the pawn before ...cxd4; 6.Nbd2 lets Black release the tension and then harass your king.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

2463215796795915|h2h3.headline: Don't spend a move on h3: take on c5 with 6.dxc5
2463215796795915|h2h3.why: 6.h3 asks the bishop a question Black is happy to answer: 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 cxd4 removes the knight that guarded d4 and wins the pawn. 8.Bb5 dxc3 9.e6 fxe6 10.O-O only throws in more pawns for some activity. 6.dxc5 takes the loose pawn, and grabbing e5 at once loses to the b5 check trick, so Black first plays 6...a6. After 7.Nbd2 Nxe5 8.Be2 the pawns are level again, but 10.b4 supports your pawn on c5 and gains queenside space.
2463215796795915|h2h3.principle: Black's play is aimed at d4, the base of your chain; don't invite the swap of its defender, and remove the c5 lever instead.

2465468553870240|c8f5.headline: Knight first: an early ...Bf5 leaves b7 to Qb3
2465468553870240|c8f5.why: 5...Bf5 leaves b7 without a defender, and 6.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 together. The natural 6...Qb6 drops the d5 pawn to 7.Nxd5 Nxd5 8.Qxd5, because swapping queens first runs into a knight check on f6. 5...Nc6 develops toward the centre and keeps the c8-bishop at home guarding b7, so a queen trip to b3 has nothing to win. After 6.Bf4 a6 7.Rc1 Nh5 8.Bd2 Nf6 9.Qb3 e6 10.e3 both b7 and d5 are covered.
2465468553870240|c8f5.principle: Develop the knight first: the c8-bishop's best square depends on whether b7 can be left without a defender.
sources: Slav Defense Traps (Chess Lab Academy) | https://www.chesslab.academy/openings/slav-defense/traps/
Why do people keep playing an early Bf5 in slav defense? (Lichess forum) | https://lichess.org/forum/general-chess-discussion/why-do-people-keep-playing-an-early-bf5-in-slav-defense
Opening Repertoire (Lakdawala & McDonald), Google Books snippet | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%22Developing+the+c8-bishop+early+can+be+dangerous%22

ideas.title: Early ...Bf5 drops b7
ideas.text: Once the c8-bishop leaves, b7 has no defender. 6.Qb3 then hits b7 and d5 together, and 6...Qb6 fails to 7.Nxd5.

ideas.title: Knight first, then the bishop
ideas.text: 5...Nc6 develops while the c8-bishop keeps guarding b7. The bishop can come out later, as in 5...Nc6 6.Bf4 Bf5.

ideas.title: The waiting move ...a6
ideas.text: In this symmetrical structure ...a6 after ...Nc6 is a useful waiting move that keeps White's bishop off b5, as in 6.Bf4 a6.

ideas.title: Ne5 hits a bishop on g4
ideas.text: A bishop on g4 gets hit by 6.Ne5, and after 6...Nc6 7.Nxg4 Nxg4 8.e4 White has the bishop pair and the centre.

habit.why: 5...Bf5 leaves b7 without a defender, and 6.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 together. The natural 6...Qb6 drops the d5 pawn to 7.Nxd5 Nxd5 8.Qxd5, because swapping queens first runs into a knight check on f6.

strays.text: The bishop leaves b7 loose while d5 is still under fire.

taught.why: 5...Nc6 develops toward the centre and keeps the c8-bishop at home guarding b7, so a queen trip to b3 has nothing to win. After 6.Bf4 a6 7.Rc1 Nh5 8.Bd2 Nf6 9.Qb3 e6 10.e3 both b7 and d5 are covered.

enforces.text: The bishop waits on c8 guarding b7 until ...Bf5 is safe.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...e6 holds d5 but shuts in your c8-bishop, and White pins your knight with 6.Bg5. After 6...h6 7.Bh4 g5 you have to loosen your kingside to break the pin.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 develops and keeps the c8-bishop's diagonal open for later. Masters play it 93% of the time, 5...e6 only 2.7%.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.idea: Ne5 hits a bishop on g4
alternatives.before: 5...Bg4 also leaves b7 loose, and 6.Ne5 hits the bishop at once. After 7.Nxg4 Nxg4 8.e4 Nf6 9.e5 White has the bishop pair and gains space with tempo.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 develops without giving White a target. The bishop comes out later, once b7 and d5 are safe.

2466581236058373|c8d7.headline: Block 5.Bb5+ with 5...Nc6: the bishop block runs into 6.Qe2+
2466581236058373|c8d7.why: 5...Bd7 blocks with the bishop, so 6.Qe2+ checks you again down the open e-file. After 6...Qe7 7.Bxd7+ Nxd7 8.Nxd5 the queen no longer guards d5 and White wins the pawn. 5...Nc6 blocks with a developing piece, so your c8 bishop isn't traded and the queen keeps guarding d5. After 6.O-O Nf6 7.d4 Bd6 8.Bg5 O-O you have castled, and after 10.dxc5 your active pieces have to make up for the isolated d5 pawn.
2466581236058373|c8d7.principle: Develop with every move: block the check with a piece that wants to come out anyway.
sources: Sicilian-phobia Part Two - Closed Sicilian (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/sicilian-phobia-part-two---closed-sicilian
Playing the Grand Prix Attack Against the Sicilian (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/grand-prix-attack/

ideas.title: Checks on e2 and b5
ideas.text: With the e-file open and your king on e8, 5.Bb5+ and 6.Qe2+ pin your pieces, and the d5 pawn drops.

ideas.title: Block with a developing piece
ideas.text: Answer the check with 5...Nc6: it develops, keeps your c8 bishop for later, and leaves the queen guarding d5.

ideas.title: Castle quickly
ideas.text: With the e-file open, get your king off e8 fast: 6...Nf6, 7...Bd6 and 8...O-O, as in the main line.

ideas.title: The isolated d5 pawn
ideas.text: Once the c-pawns are traded, d5 stands alone. White aims pieces at it; you answer with active pieces.

habit.why: 5...Bd7 blocks with the bishop, so 6.Qe2+ checks you again down the open e-file. After 6...Qe7 7.Bxd7+ Nxd7 8.Nxd5 the queen no longer guards d5 and White wins the pawn.

strays.text: The bishop block gets traded off, and the e-file check follows.

taught.why: 5...Nc6 blocks with a developing piece, so your c8 bishop isn't traded and the queen keeps guarding d5. After 6.O-O Nf6 7.d4 Bd6 8.Bg5 O-O you have castled, and after 10.dxc5 your active pieces have to make up for the isolated d5 pawn.

enforces.text: The knight develops while blocking, and the queen keeps guarding d5.

2471617853961957|e8e7.headline: Take the bishop on f7 with your king; nothing defends it
2471617853961957|e8e7.why: 7...Ke7 leaves the bishop alive, and 8.Bxg8 Qxg8 trades it for your knight, so White keeps the f7 pawn for free. Then 9.Nd5+ chases your king again, and after 9...Kf8 you are a pawn down and can no longer castle. 7...Kxf7 wins the bishop, because nothing defends it. White's trick 8.Nxe5+ dxe5 9.Qxg4 wins back your bishop and a second pawn, but after 9...Nf6 10.Qd1 Re8 you are still a piece for two pawns up.
2471617853961957|e8e7.principle: When a piece lands on f7 with check, count its defenders before stepping aside: with none, take it and meet the follow-up.
sources: Ihechikara Abba, The Chess Italian Game Handbook: Traps for White (freeCodeCamp) | https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/the-chess-italian-game-handbook-traps-for-white/

ideas.title: Take the f7 bishop
ideas.text: Nothing defends the bishop on f7. After 7...Kxf7 8.Nxe5+ dxe5 9.Qxg4 White gets only two pawns for the piece.

ideas.title: Bxf7+ is a desperado here
ideas.text: Your g4 bishop and d4 knight both hit the pinned f3 knight, so 7.Bxf7+ grabs a pawn rather than starting a real attack.

ideas.title: Nd5 hits a king on e7
ideas.text: A king on e7 walks into checks from d5, as in Legal's Mate: here 9.Nd5+ comes with tempo.

habit.why: 7...Ke7 leaves the bishop alive, and 8.Bxg8 Qxg8 trades it for your knight, so White keeps the f7 pawn for free. Then 9.Nd5+ chases your king again, and after 9...Kf8 you are a pawn down and can no longer castle.

strays.text: Stepping aside lets the bishop trade itself for your knight.

taught.why: 7...Kxf7 wins the bishop, because nothing defends it. White's trick 8.Nxe5+ dxe5 9.Qxg4 wins back your bishop and a second pawn, but after 9...Nf6 10.Qd1 Re8 you are still a piece for two pawns up.

enforces.text: The bishop has no defender, so the king takes it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7...Kf8 avoids the d5 check, but the bishop lives and the f3 knight escapes with tempo: 8.Nxd4 Bxd1 9.Ne6+ forks your king and queen, and White comes out ahead.
alternatives.after: 7...Kxf7 takes the bishop at once. With the king on f8, 9.Ne6+ forks king and queen, and White ends up ahead despite the label.

2480011064030415|f3g5.headline: Build with 5.c3; 5.Ng5 just loses time
2480011064030415|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 5...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 6.a4 Ne7 7.Nf3 c6 8.Bb3 Ng6 the knight is back on f3 and Black has used the time to castle and regroup. 5.c3 starts the slow Italian plan and keeps d4 for later. After 5...a6 6.a4 d6 7.O-O Ba7 8.Re1 O-O 9.Nbd2 you have the standard c3, d3 and a4 set-up, the most common choice of masters (42%).
2480011064030415|f3g5.principle: When Black can castle and cover f7, don't move the f3 knight twice: build up with c3, a4 and castling.
sources: NM Jeremy Kane, Bad Trades Amateurs Make In Chess | https://www.chess.com/article/view/bad-trades-amateurs-make-in-chess
Souleidis and Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf
Sergey Grigoriants, The Italian for insiders (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/the-italian-for-insiders

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: f7 is guarded by the king only until Black castles. After 5...O-O, taking on f7 gives two pieces for a rook and pawn.

ideas.title: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4
ideas.text: Play c3 and a4, castle and bring the b1 knight out via d2. Push d4 only once you are ready.

ideas.title: Black: a retreat for the bishop
ideas.text: Black answers a4 with ...a6 and ...Ba7, so the c5 bishop can't be trapped or kicked with gain of time.

ideas.title: Don't move a piece twice
ideas.text: Your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. Moving the f3 knight again gives Black free time.

habit.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 5...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 6.a4 Ne7 7.Nf3 c6 8.Bb3 Ng6 the knight is back on f3 and Black has used the time to castle and regroup.

strays.text: Black castles, f7 is covered, and the knight has to go back.

taught.why: 5.c3 starts the slow Italian plan and keeps d4 for later. After 5...a6 6.a4 d6 7.O-O Ba7 8.Re1 O-O 9.Nbd2 you have the standard c3, d3 and a4 set-up, the most common choice of masters (42%).

enforces.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4
enforces.text: c3 first, then a4, castling and the knight via d2.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.O-O is a good move: your king is safe, and the build-up goes on with 7.Re1 and 8.Nbd2. Masters play it in 34% of games; one other move is a bit more popular.
alternatives.after: Both moves are good and usually transpose: 5.c3 (42%) commits to the pawn set-up first, while 5.O-O (34%) castles and plays 6.c3 next.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bg5 develops with a pin on the f6 knight. After 5...h6 6.Be3 Bb6 you offer a bishop trade on the a7-g1 diagonal; it's sound, but masters prefer a more flexible plan.
alternatives.after: 5.c3 keeps the c1 bishop's options open and builds the pawn set-up, with a4 and d4 to come. Masters choose it 42% of the time, 5.Bg5 only 5%.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 develops and eyes d5: after 5...a6 6.Nd5 h6 the knight sits on a central square. It's sound, but masters prefer another move.
alternatives.after: 5.c3 keeps the c-pawn free so d4 can come later; with the knight on c3, its line has to move it again with 6.Nd5 before the pawn can advance.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

2566699904980904|f8g7.headline: Play 3...d6 first so 4.e5 can't kick your knight
2566699904980904|f8g7.why: 3...Bg7 leaves e5 uncovered, and 4.e5 kicks your knight with tempo: after 4...Ng8 5.Bf4 d5 6.Qd2 White has a big space edge and your knight is back home. The other retreat is no better, as 4.e5 Nh5 puts it on the rim. 3...d6 covers e5, so the knight stays on f6 and the game becomes a Pirc Defence, the masters' choice 76% of the time. After 4.Be3 a6 5.Be2 Bg7 the bishop still reaches g7, and the b-pawn can push against White's centre.
2566699904980904|f8g7.principle: A knight on f6 is a target for White's e-pawn: cover e5 with a pawn before you fianchetto.

ideas.title: e4-e5 kicks the f6 knight
ideas.text: If nothing covers e5, 4.e5 hits your f6 knight with tempo, and it has to go to g8 or h5.

ideas.title: ...d6 before ...Bg7
ideas.text: Play ...d6 first, so a later e5 push can simply be taken; only then put the bishop on g7.

ideas.title: Meet Be3 with ...a6 and ...b5
ideas.text: Against set-ups with 4.Be3, GM Nigel Davies plays ...a6 early, then pushes the b-pawn to hit e4 and a long-castled king.

habit.why: 3...Bg7 leaves e5 uncovered, and 4.e5 kicks your knight with tempo: after 4...Ng8 5.Bf4 d5 6.Qd2 White has a big space edge and your knight is back home. The other retreat is no better, as 4.e5 Nh5 puts it on the rim.

strays.text: The bishop comes out before ...d6, so nothing stops 4.e5.

taught.why: 3...d6 covers e5, so the knight stays on f6 and the game becomes a Pirc Defence, the masters' choice 76% of the time. After 4.Be3 a6 5.Be2 Bg7 the bishop still reaches g7, and the b-pawn can push against White's centre.

enforces.text: The pawn covers e5 first; the bishop comes to g7 a move later.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 3...d5 hits e4, but after 4.e5 Ne4 5.Nce2 the knight on e4 is short of squares, and you need 5...f6 to free it, loosening your dark squares.
alternatives.after: 3...d6 covers e5 so the push never comes. Masters play 3...d5 in 22% of games, but the engine rates it clearly worse here.

2583228623150903|d7d5.headline: Against 3.Bc4, develop with 3...Nc6 before pushing ...d5
2583228623150903|d7d5.why: 3...d5 opens the centre while d5 is hit by the c3 knight and the c4 bishop and guarded only by your queen. After 4.exd5 exd5 5.Qe2+ Be7 6.Nxd5 the check on the e-file wins the pawn. 3...Nc6 develops and prepares 4...Nf6 and a supported ...d5 later, the plan Ikeda and Astle give against 3.Bc4. After 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bb5 White moves the bishop again to avoid ...d5, and 6.Bxc6 Qxc6 leaves you the two bishops.
2583228623150903|d7d5.principle: Count attackers and defenders: d5 is hit twice and guarded once, so prepare ...d5 before pushing it.
sources: How I play against the Closed Sicilian (IM Junta Ikeda) | https://juntaikeda.substack.com/p/how-i-play-against-the-closed-sicilian
The Bowlder Attack: Bold move or beginner's folly? (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/bowlder-attack/

ideas.title: ...e6 blunts the c4 bishop
ideas.text: Your e6 pawn shuts the c4 bishop out of f7 and makes it a target for a later ...d5 or ...b5.

ideas.title: d5 is attacked twice
ideas.text: Right now the c3 knight and the c4 bishop both hit d5; after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Qe2+ there is no time to defend it.

ideas.title: Develop before ...d5
ideas.text: Bring out 3...Nc6 and 4...Nf6 first; then ...d5 comes with support and gains time on the bishop.

ideas.title: Chase the bishop with ...b5
ideas.text: The other main plan: 3...a6 and 4...b5 gain queenside space and chase the bishop, as in 4.Bb3 b5.

habit.why: 3...d5 opens the centre while d5 is hit by the c3 knight and the c4 bishop and guarded only by your queen. After 4.exd5 exd5 5.Qe2+ Be7 6.Nxd5 the check on the e-file wins the pawn.

strays.text: The pawn goes forward before any piece supports it.

taught.why: 3...Nc6 develops and prepares 4...Nf6 and a supported ...d5 later, the plan Ikeda and Astle give against 3.Bc4. After 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bb5 White moves the bishop again to avoid ...d5, and 6.Bxc6 Qxc6 leaves you the two bishops.

enforces.text: The knight adds a piece to the centre before the pawn moves.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...a6 is a main move (43% of master games): it prepares ...b5 to chase the bishop, as in 4.Bb3 b5 5.d3 Bb7. It is fully sound, and the move this card teaches is just as good.
alternatives.after: Both are main moves (48% and 43% of master games). 3...Nc6 develops at once and readies ...Nf6 and ...d5, while 3...a6 first gains queenside space.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Nf6 develops and hits e4, with ...d5 to follow; after 4.Nf3 a6 5.Be2 Qc7 6.e5 Ng4 the knight hops out and keeps hitting the centre. It is sound, but masters choose it only 7% of the time.
alternatives.after: 3...Nc6 develops the other knight first, so an early e5 push has nothing to chase, and masters prefer it (48% to 7%).

2615425569294719|c8f5.headline: Knights out first: 4...Bf5 drops b7 to Qb3
2615425569294719|c8f5.why: 4...Bf5 leaves b7 with no defender, and 5.Qb3 hits it and d5 together. After 5...Nc6 6.Nf3 Nf6 7.Qxb7 White has won a pawn. 4...Nf6 develops and guards d5 while the bishop still covers b7. After 5.Bf4 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bf5 the bishop comes out once both knights are developed, the main line masters play 76% of the time.
2615425569294719|c8f5.principle: Knights before bishops: in the Exchange Slav the c8-bishop guards b7, so develop a knight before ...Bf5.
sources: Slav Defense Traps (Chess Lab Academy) | https://www.chesslab.academy/openings/slav-defense/traps/

ideas.title: Bishop c8 guards b7
ideas.text: Your c8-bishop is b7's only guard. Once it leaves, 5.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 together.

ideas.title: Knight first, bishop later
ideas.text: Play ...Nf6 or ...Nc6 first; ...Bf5 comes a move or two later, as in 4...Nf6 5.Bf4 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bf5.

ideas.title: Keep e4 covered
ideas.text: A knight on f6 also hits e4, so White can't push 5.e4 as in the 4...Nc6 line.

habit.why: 4...Bf5 leaves b7 with no defender, and 5.Qb3 hits it and d5 together. After 5...Nc6 6.Nf3 Nf6 7.Qxb7 White has won a pawn.

strays.text: The bishop leaves b7 bare, and 7.Qxb7 wins a pawn.

taught.why: 4...Nf6 develops and guards d5 while the bishop still covers b7. After 5.Bf4 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bf5 the bishop comes out once both knights are developed, the main line masters play 76% of the time.

enforces.text: Both knights come out first, and only then 6...Bf5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nc6 is sound and keeps b7 guarded, but it lets White push 5.e4, and after 6.e5 Ne4 7.Be3 Bf5 8.g4 the game turns sharp. There is a more solid move.
alternatives.after: 4...Nf6 hits e4, so 5.e4 isn't possible. Masters play 4...Nf6 76% of the time and 4...Nc6 21%.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4...e6 keeps b7 guarded but shuts in your c8-bishop for good, and after 5.Bf4 Bd6 6.Bg3 Nc6 you have a passive, symmetrical game.
alternatives.after: 4...Nf6 develops and keeps the bishop free to come to f5 later, as in 6...Bf5.

2615583540108407|b8c6.headline: Answer 2.f3 with 2...d5 so that e4 costs White a pawn.
2615583540108407|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 lets White carry out the plan: 3.e4 builds a big centre and after 4.e5 Ng8 Black's knight is pushed back home. 2.f3 weakens White's kingside and takes the knight's natural square just to prepare e4, and 2...d5 makes that push fail: if 3.e4 dxe4 4.fxe4 Nxe4, Black is a pawn up.
2615583540108407|b8c6.principle: When White prepares e4 with a weakening pawn move, add a second guard of e4 with your d-pawn so the advance costs material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. f3

2615583540108407|g7g6.headline: Stop e4 with 2...d5 instead of letting White build a big centre
2615583540108407|g7g6.why: 2...g6 lets White build the centre f3 was aiming for: after 3.e4 d5 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4 White gains space and your knight is pushed back. In the line 5...c5 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.c3 you are cramped. 2...d5 guards e4, so White can only push it as a gambit, since 3.e4 dxe4 4.fxe4 Nxe4 just loses a pawn. In the line 3.Nc3 c5 4.e4 e6 5.Nge2 cxd4 6.Nxd4 e5 you hit the centre at once and gain time on the d4-knight.
2615583540108407|g7g6.principle: Contest the square your opponent's pawn move prepares: 2.f3 aims at e4, so 2...d5 guards it, while 2...g6 lets 3.e4 build a big centre.
sources: Paleface Attack: What should I do? (chess.com forum) | https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess-openings/paleface-attack-what-should-i-do

ideas.title: Stop e4 with ...d5
ideas.text: White's f3 prepares e4. With a pawn on d5 guarding e4, White can only push it as a pawn sacrifice.

ideas.title: Accept gambits, hit the centre
ideas.text: If White pushes anyway, take: 3.e4 dxe4 4.fxe4 Nxe4 wins a pawn, so White must gambit with 4.Nc3, the Blackmar-Diemer.

ideas.title: e4-e5 kicks the f6 knight
ideas.text: Once White has e4, e5 can chase your f6-knight back, unless a pawn on d6 can take on e5.

ideas.title: Strike back with ...c5
ideas.text: With d5 in, ...c5 hits d4 at once; club advice against this set-up is quick central play.

habit.why: 2...g6 lets White build the centre f3 was aiming for: after 3.e4 d5 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4 White gains space and your knight is pushed back. In the line 5...c5 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.c3 you are cramped.

strays.text: The fianchetto leaves e4 free for White's pawn.

taught.why: 2...d5 guards e4, so White can only push it as a gambit, since 3.e4 dxe4 4.fxe4 Nxe4 just loses a pawn. In the line 3.Nc3 c5 4.e4 e6 5.Nge2 cxd4 6.Nxd4 e5 you hit the centre at once and gain time on the d4-knight.

enforces.text: The pawn on d5 contests e4 before White can occupy it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Sound: if 3.e4 you reach a French-type position, though 4.e5 Ng8 can send your knight home. There's a more direct move.
alternatives.after: 2...d5 stops e4 at once instead of allowing a French where 4.e5 kicks your knight back. Masters choose 2...d5 in 83% of games.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Sound: it allows 3.e4 but covers e5, so your knight can't be kicked, and 3...e5 leads to a closed centre. There's a more active move.
alternatives.after: 2...d5 stops White's e4 centre altogether, while 2...d6 allows it and plays against it with 3...e5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Sound: it hits d4 at once, and if White pushes past, 3...e6 4.e4 exd5 5.exd5 d6 gives you a Benoni where f3 has cost White development. The engine prefers another move.
alternatives.after: 2...d5 stops e4 outright and keeps ...c5 for later, as in 3.Nc3 c5. Masters play 2...c5 in 6% of games, against 83% for 2...d5.

2671625836318681|b8c6.headline: Release the tension with 5...dxe4 before 6.exd5 wins d5
2671625836318681|b8c6.why: 5...Nc6 doesn't stop 6.exd5: after 6...exd5 7.Bb5 the c6 knight is pinned and your d5 pawn has only the queen to guard it. After 7...Bd7 8.Nxd5 the pawn is gone, since your queen can't take back while White's queen stands behind the d4 knight. 5...dxe4 swaps off the pawn White was about to win, and after 6.Nxe4 you have no weak pawns. In the line 6...a6 7.Bd3 Be7 8.O-O Nf6 you develop calmly and castle next.
2671625836318681|b8c6.principle: Check the opponent's threats first: 6.exd5 and 7.Bb5 win d5, so 5...dxe4 removes the target before you develop.
sources: How I play against the Closed Sicilian (IM Junta Ikeda) | https://juntaikeda.substack.com/p/how-i-play-against-the-closed-sicilian

ideas.title: White threatens exd5
ideas.text: Your d5 pawn is hit by e4 and the c3 knight; after 6.exd5 exd5 the pawn is isolated and 7.Bb5 follows.

ideas.title: Checks on e2 and b5
ideas.text: 7.Bb5 pins a knight on c6, or checks your king, while the e-file and the a4-e8 diagonal are open.

ideas.title: Take on e4, keep no weakness
ideas.text: 5...dxe4 swaps off the attacked pawn; after 6.Nxe4 you have no weak pawn and can develop calmly.

ideas.title: Develop and castle
ideas.text: Then come 7...Be7 and 8...Nf6, and castling, before White's pieces find a target.

habit.why: 5...Nc6 doesn't stop 6.exd5: after 6...exd5 7.Bb5 the c6 knight is pinned and your d5 pawn has only the queen to guard it. After 7...Bd7 8.Nxd5 the pawn is gone, since your queen can't take back while White's queen stands behind the d4 knight.

strays.text: The knight develops but leaves d5 to 6.exd5 and 7.Bb5.

taught.why: 5...dxe4 swaps off the pawn White was about to win, and after 6.Nxe4 you have no weak pawns. In the line 6...a6 7.Bd3 Be7 8.O-O Nf6 you develop calmly and castle next.

enforces.idea: Take on e4, keep no weakness
enforces.text: Trading the attacked pawn ends all play against d5.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Bb4 pins the c3 knight but doesn't save d5: after 6.exd5 Qxd5 7.Be2 Nc6 8.Nxc6 Qxd1+ 9.Bxd1 bxc6 your queenside pawns are split.
alternatives.after: 5...dxe4 trades the attacked pawn at once, so White never gets 6.exd5 and your pawns stay healthy.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5...Bc5 hits the d4 knight but leaves d5 and the bishop loose: after 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Nf5 Bxb5 9.Nxb5 Qa5+ 10.Nc3 White's knights are active and d5 soon falls.
alternatives.after: 5...dxe4 takes the attacked pawn off the board, so there is no 6.exd5 and no check on b5 to fear.

2692473875865858|c8f5.headline: Knight to f6 first: an early ...Bf5 leaves b7 to Qb3
2692473875865858|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 takes the only guard off b7 while the c3-knight already presses d5, so a queen on b3 hits both. After 4.Qb3 Qb6 5.Qxb6 axb6 6.cxd5 you are a pawn down, and the theory's 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 wins one too. 3...Nf6 guards d5 and covers e4, and with the bishop still on c8 a queen on b3 later finds b7 defended. After 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3 Nbd7 6.Bd3 dxc4 7.Bxc4 b5 you get a solid Semi-Slav with queenside play; masters choose 3...Nf6 in 88.6% of games.
2692473875865858|c8f5.principle: Before a piece leaves, check what it was guarding: the c8-bishop holds b7, and with the c3-knight pressing d5, 3...Bf5 lets a queen on b3 hit both.

ideas.title: Early ...Bf5 drops b7
ideas.text: Once the bishop leaves c8, b7 has no guard. 4.Qb3 then hits b7 and d5 together, with the c3-knight adding pressure on d5.

ideas.title: Knight to f6 before ...Bf5
ideas.text: 3...Nf6 guards d5 and covers e4. The bishop comes out only once a queen on b3 no longer wins anything, usually after ...e6 or ...dxc4.

ideas.title: ...Qb6 runs into Nxd5
ideas.text: Meeting the queen on b3 with ...Qb6 often fails: after 3...Bf5 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 Qb6, 6.Nxd5 wins the d5 pawn.

ideas.title: Watch White's e4
ideas.text: The c3-knight backs up an e4 push. Without a knight on f6 covering e4, White grabs the centre, as after 3...e6 4.e4.

habit.why: 3...Bf5 takes the only guard off b7 while the c3-knight already presses d5, so a queen on b3 hits both. After 4.Qb3 Qb6 5.Qxb6 axb6 6.cxd5 you are a pawn down, and the theory's 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 wins one too.

strays.text: The bishop leaves b7 unguarded while d5 is already under pressure.

taught.why: 3...Nf6 guards d5 and covers e4, and with the bishop still on c8 a queen on b3 later finds b7 defended. After 4.e3 e6 5.Nf3 Nbd7 6.Bd3 dxc4 7.Bxc4 b5 you get a solid Semi-Slav with queenside play; masters choose 3...Nf6 in 88.6% of games.

enforces.text: d5 gets its guard first; the bishop waits until a queen on b3 wins nothing.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...e6 guards d5 but shuts in your c8-bishop and leaves e4 open: 4.e4 Bb4 5.Bd2 Bxc3 6.Bxc3 and 7.e5 give White space and the bishop pair.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 covers e4 and leaves the bishop free to come out later. Masters prefer it, 88.6% to 4.5%.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...dxc4 is a known line: your c6 pawn can back up a pawn on b5, which can later push on to hit the c3-knight. But after 4.Nf3 e6 5.a4 Bb4 6.e3 b5 7.Bd2, 8.axb5 undermines your pawns and White wins the pawn back.
alternatives.after: Masters still play 3...dxc4 in 5.4% of games, but the engine prefers 3...Nf6, which keeps every Slav option, ...dxc4 included, for later.

269926073920586|c1e3.headline: Question the pinning bishop at once with 6.h3
269926073920586|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 lets Black keep the pin on f3 and develop with 6...e6 and 7...c6. After 8.h3 Bh5 9.Bd3 Nbd7 10.Qe2 Bb4 the bishop is still on the board, 10...Bb4 adds to the pin on your c3-knight, and most of your edge is gone. 6.h3, the choice in 90% of master games, makes the bishop decide now. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 c6 8.Bd2 Nbd7 9.O-O-O you have both bishops, an active queen and no pin on c3.
269926073920586|c1e3.principle: A pin ties your knight down; break it while that costs Black something, by hitting the pinning bishop with the h-pawn before Black can support it.
sources: A Chess Terrorist's Guide to the Center Counter (Chess Life) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%22Bg4+6.h3%22+Scandinavian+Qa5+%22Bxf3+7.Qxf3%22

ideas.title: Ask the Bg4 question with h3
ideas.text: h3 makes the g4-bishop decide now: after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you have the bishop pair and your queen is already active.

ideas.title: Bd2, long castling, pawn storm
ideas.text: Then 8.Bd2 unpins the c3-knight and 9.O-O-O follows; if the bishop retreats instead, g4 chases it to g6.

ideas.title: Black's pressure on d4
ideas.text: The g4-bishop eyes your f3-knight, a defender of d4; with ...Nc6 and ...O-O-O Black can pile up on the pawn.

ideas.title: The pin on c3
ideas.text: Black's queen on a5 pins your c3-knight to the king. A bishop on d2 breaks the pin; 6.Be3 does not.

habit.why: 6.Be3 lets Black keep the pin on f3 and develop with 6...e6 and 7...c6. After 8.h3 Bh5 9.Bd3 Nbd7 10.Qe2 Bb4 the bishop is still on the board, 10...Bb4 adds to the pin on your c3-knight, and most of your edge is gone.

strays.idea: Ask the Bg4 question with h3
strays.text: h3 comes two moves late, and the bishop simply drops back to h5.

taught.why: 6.h3, the choice in 90% of master games, makes the bishop decide now. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 c6 8.Bd2 Nbd7 9.O-O-O you have both bishops, an active queen and no pin on c3.

enforces.idea: Ask the Bg4 question with h3
enforces.text: Black must trade on f3 or retreat right now.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Be2 is passive: after 6...Nbd7 7.a3 c6 Black develops calmly, then trades with 8...Bxf3 9.Bxf3 e6, and your edge shrinks.
alternatives.after: 6.h3 makes Black decide right away instead of two moves later. Masters play it in 90% of games, 6.Be2 in 5%.
alternatives.idea: Ask the Bg4 question with h3

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Bd2 breaks the pin on c3, but 6...Qf5 7.Bd3 Bxf3 8.gxf3 wrecks your kingside pawns, and after 8...Qd7 9.Ne4 Qxd4 Black has won the d4 pawn.
alternatives.after: 6.h3 settles the bishop first, so after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you take back with the queen and your pawns stay whole.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: After 6.Bc4 Nc6 the knight joins the bishop against d4. Black trades on f3, castles long with 8...O-O-O, and after 9.d5 Ne5 the knight hits your queen and bishop. Your edge is gone.
alternatives.after: 6.h3 settles the bishop before Black's knight and rook join the attack on d4; masters play it in 90% of games, 6.Bc4 in only 2%.

269926073920586|f1e2.headline: Ask the g4 bishop at once with 6.h3
269926073920586|f1e2.why: 6.Be2 lets Black finish ...Nbd7 and ...c6 before deciding about the bishop. After 6...Nbd7 7.a3 c6 8.h3 Bxf3 9.Bxf3 you play h3 anyway, but two moves later. Black has developed in the meantime, and your edge has shrunk. 6.h3, the choice in 90% of master games, makes the bishop decide now. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 c6 8.Bd2 Nbd7 9.O-O-O you have both bishops, an active queen and no pin on c3.
269926073920586|f1e2.principle: A bishop that a pawn can attack is a target: hit it with the h-pawn right away, while the trade on f3 still costs Black something.
sources: A Chess Terrorist's Guide to the Center Counter (Chess Life) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%22Bg4+6.h3%22+Scandinavian+Qa5+%22Bxf3+7.Qxf3%22

ideas.title: Bd2, long castling, pawn storm
ideas.text: Then 8.Bd2 unpins the c3-knight and 9.O-O-O follows; if the bishop retreats instead, g4 chases it to g6.

ideas.title: Black's pressure on d4
ideas.text: The g4-bishop eyes your f3-knight, a defender of d4; with ...Nc6 and ...O-O-O Black can pile up on the pawn.

ideas.title: The pin on c3
ideas.text: Black's queen on a5 pins your c3-knight to the king. A bishop on d2 breaks the pin; 6.Be2 does not.

alternatives.after: 6.h3 settles the bishop first, so after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you take back with the queen and your pawns stay whole.

2731765578959899|c4b3.headline: Retreat 6.Bf1: guard g2 and stay out of the knight's reach
2731765578959899|c4b3.why: 6.Bb3 walks into 6...Nd4: the knight hits the bishop, guards b5, and a later c3 would just let it take on b3. After 7.d3 Bc5 8.Nc3 O-O 9.Nge4 Nxe4 10.Nxe4 Black is fully developed and your knight has been pushed back. 6.Bf1 guards g2, so if 6...Qxd5, 7.Nc3 gains time on the queen. After 6...Nxd5 7.Bxb5 Bb7 8.d4 exd4 9.O-O you have taken b5 with no queen fork, as masters do in 84% of games.
2731765578959899|c4b3.principle: Before you retreat, ask what Black wants: ...Qxd5 and ...Nd4. 6.Bf1 answers both, since g2 is guarded and ...Nd4 hits nothing.

ideas.title: Retreat to f1, guard g2
ideas.text: 6.Bf1 guards g2, so ...Qxd5 no longer hits two things, and the bishop can still take on b5 later.

ideas.title: The queen fork on d5
ideas.text: ...b5 lures your bishop away so that ...Qxd5 can attack the b5-bishop and g2 at once.

ideas.title: Watch for ...Nd4
ideas.text: On b3 or e2 your bishop is hit by ...Nd4, which also guards b5; Tait calls those retreats inferior.

habit.why: 6.Bb3 walks into 6...Nd4: the knight hits the bishop, guards b5, and a later c3 would just let it take on b3. After 7.d3 Bc5 8.Nc3 O-O 9.Nge4 Nxe4 10.Nxe4 Black is fully developed and your knight has been pushed back.

enforces.text: With g2 covered, Black has no queen fork on d5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Bxb5 takes the pawn, but 6...Qxd5 attacks the b5-bishop and g2 at once; Wikibooks marks it dubious.
alternatives.after: 6.Bf1 guards g2 first, so after 6...Nxd5 7.Bxb5 the pawn falls with no queen fork.

alternatives.after: 6.Bf1 keeps both your extra pawn and your bishop.

2731765578959899|c4b5.why: 6.Bxb5 takes the bait: 6...Qxd5 attacks your b5-bishop and g2 at once. After 7.Be2 Bb7 8.d3 Nd4 9.Nf3 O-O-O Black's queen and bishop rake the long diagonal and Black is fully developed for the pawn. 6.Bf1 guards g2, so if 6...Qxd5, 7.Nc3 gains time on the queen. 2731765578959899|c4b5.principle: Check what is loose before you grab: after 6.Bxb5 both the bishop and g2 are open to ...Qxd5.

27382415154004|d3d4.headline: Count the guards on d4 before you push
27382415154004|d3d4.why: 6.d4 pushes onto a square Black hits three times, with the pawn on e5, the knight on c6 and the bishop on c5, while White covers it only twice, so 6...exd4 simply wins a pawn. 6.Na4 goes after the bishop on c5 first: after 6...Bb6 7.O-O Nge7 8.Nxb6 axb6 one of d4's attackers is gone, and 9.d4 comes once it can be supported.
27382415154004|d3d4.principle: In the quiet Italian, push d4 only when you guard it as often as Black attacks it; otherwise trade off one of the attackers first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

275585188789254|f3d4.headline: 5.e5 kicks the f6 knight before you collect d4
275585188789254|f3d4.why: 5.Nxd4 takes the pawn back but leaves e4 with no defender, and 5...Nxe4 grabs it. Black keeps the extra pawn, and after 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Qe2 Qe7 8.O-O Nd6 9.Nc3 Qxe2 the queens come off. 5.e5 attacks the f6 knight, and after 5...d5 6.Bb5 Ne4 7.Nxd4 you have won your pawn back with space in the centre. Masters choose 5.e5 70% of the time.
275585188789254|f3d4.principle: When the opponent's extra pawn comes with weaknesses, play on the weaknesses first; the pawn can usually be won back afterwards.

ideas.title: Kick the f6 knight first
ideas.text: 5.e5 attacks the f6 knight. After 5...d5, 6.Bb5 pins the c6 knight and 7.Nxd4 wins your pawn back.

ideas.title: Don't leave e4 loose
ideas.text: Recapturing with 5.Nxd4 leaves e4 without a defender, and 5...Nxe4 takes it; Black stays a pawn up.

ideas.title: Black's extra pawn has weaknesses
ideas.text: Black is a pawn up, but the e5 square, the f6 knight and f7 are weak. Play on those first.

ideas.title: Ng5 hits f7 only when it hurts
ideas.text: Here 5.Ng5 is premature: 5...d5 6.exd5 Qe7+ 7.Kf1 costs you castling.

habit.why: 5.Nxd4 takes the pawn back but leaves e4 with no defender, and 5...Nxe4 grabs it. Black keeps the extra pawn, and after 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Qe2 Qe7 8.O-O Nd6 9.Nc3 Qxe2 the queens come off.

strays.text: The recapture leaves e4 hanging to 5...Nxe4.

taught.why: 5.e5 attacks the f6 knight, and after 5...d5 6.Bb5 Ne4 7.Nxd4 you have won your pawn back with space in the centre. Masters choose 5.e5 70% of the time.

enforces.text: 5.e5 hits the knight, then 7.Nxd4 regains the pawn.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Castling is the classical line: after 5...Nxe4 6.Re1 d5 7.Bxd5 Qxd5 8.Nc3 your pins on the d- and e-files give enough play for the pawn. There is a more popular choice.
alternatives.after: 5.e5 is played 70% of the time and wins the pawn back simply with 7.Nxd4. 5.O-O (27%) leads to sharper, balanced play.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.Ng5 goes straight for f7, but 5...d5 6.exd5 Qe7+ forces 7.Kf1, so you lose the right to castle, and 7...Ne5 hits your c4 bishop.
alternatives.after: 5.e5 gains time on the f6 knight while keeping your king safe. Wikibooks calls 5.Ng5 a misguided direct attack on f7.
alternatives.idea: Ng5 hits f7 only when it hurts

2781218480891122|g1f3.headline: Kick the e5 knight with 4.f4 and take the centre
2781218480891122|g1f3.why: 4.Nf3 lets Black trade the badly placed knight with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3, so Black's cramp eases. You keep some space after 5...d6 6.g4 h6, but the chance to drive the knight back with gain of time is gone. 4.f4 attacks the knight, and after 4...Ng6 5.Nf3 d6 6.Nc3 you have a big centre and a lead in development. Then 7.f5 kicks the knight again, and 7...Ne5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 leaves Black cramped behind your d5 and f5 pawns.
2781218480891122|g1f3.principle: A centralised knight without pawn support is a target: 4.f4 drives it back and gains space with tempo.
sources: Tim Harding, Steinitz in London | https://books.google.com/books?id=Dc7xDwAAQBAJ
Hans Renette, H.E. Bird: A Chess Biography | https://books.google.com/books?id=U2n7DAAAQBAJ
Geza Maroczy, Paul Morphy | https://books.google.com/books?id=rWHKEQAAQBAJ

ideas.title: Chase the knight with pawns
ideas.text: The e5 knight has no pawn support. 4.f4 drives it back with tempo and grabs space at the same time.

ideas.title: Don't swap Black's bad knight
ideas.text: Black's knight is short of squares. 4.Nf3 lets it trade itself off with 4...Nxf3+, and Black's cramp eases.

ideas.title: The big centre
ideas.text: Pawns on d5, e4 and f4 give you a big centre. In 19th-century games Steinitz and Bird followed up with c4, Steinitz with e5 too.

habit.why: 4.Nf3 lets Black trade the badly placed knight with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3, so Black's cramp eases. You keep some space after 5...d6 6.g4 h6, but the chance to drive the knight back with gain of time is gone.

strays.text: Black's misplaced knight gets traded off for your good one.

taught.why: 4.f4 attacks the knight, and after 4...Ng6 5.Nf3 d6 6.Nc3 you have a big centre and a lead in development. Then 7.f5 kicks the knight again, and 7...Ne5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 leaves Black cramped behind your d5 and f5 pawns.

enforces.text: The f-pawn hits the knight and gains space at the same time.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4.Bf4 lets Black defend with 4...d6, and after 5.Bxe5 dxe5 you've swapped your dark bishop for the knight without gaining any time.
alternatives.after: 4.f4 hits the knight with a pawn: it has to retreat, you gain space, and you keep both bishops.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 develops but gives Black time: after 4...d6 the knight can drop back to d7, and Black sets up with ...g6 and ...Bg7.
alternatives.after: 4.f4 kicks the knight at once and gains space with tempo; with 4.Nc3 first, Black uses the move for 4...d6 and the knight finds d7.

2782228191759896|g1f3.headline: e4 is attacked and unguarded: push 5.e5
2782228191759896|g1f3.why: With no knight on c3 and no bishop on d3, nothing guards e4, so 5...dxe4 wins a pawn. You can't take it back: after 6.Ne5 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Ne7 8.Bb5+ Bd7 Black stays a pawn up. 5.e5 steps out of the attack and gains space, reaching an Advance French with the c-file open; masters play it 66% of the time. After 5...Nc6 6.Nf3 Nge7 7.Nc3 Nf5 8.h4 Qb6 Black presses d4 while you play on the kingside.
2782228191759896|g1f3.principle: When a pawn is attacked, count its defenders: e4 has none, so push it, guard it or swap it, but don't ignore it.
sources: Sam Collins: The French Advance Structure (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/sam-collins-the-french-advance-structure-050613

ideas.title: Answer ...d5 by keeping e4
ideas.text: Black's d5 pawn hits e4 and no piece guards it. Push with 5.e5, guard with 5.Nc3, or swap with 5.exd5.

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: After 5.e5 Black hits d4 with ...Nc6, ...Nge7-f5 and ...Qb6; 6.Nf3 guards it.

ideas.title: Space for a kingside push
ideas.text: The e5 pawn gives you space; a later h4, as in 8.h4, starts play on the kingside.

habit.why: With no knight on c3 and no bishop on d3, nothing guards e4, so 5...dxe4 wins a pawn. You can't take it back: after 6.Ne5 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Ne7 8.Bb5+ Bd7 Black stays a pawn up.

strays.text: 5.Nf3 ignores the attack on e4, and 5...dxe4 wins it.

taught.why: 5.e5 steps out of the attack and gains space, reaching an Advance French with the c-file open; masters play it 66% of the time. After 5...Nc6 6.Nf3 Nge7 7.Nc3 Nf5 8.h4 Qb6 Black presses d4 while you play on the kingside.

enforces.text: The pawn steps forward out of attack and takes space.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.exd5 exd5 is safe: the pawns become symmetrical, each side with an isolated d-pawn, and after 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.Nf3 Nf6 the game is level. There's a more ambitious move.
alternatives.after: 5.e5 keeps a pawn in the centre and gives you space and kingside play; 5.exd5 leaves a level, symmetrical game. Masters still pick it 29% of the time, against 66% for 5.e5.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 guards e4 with a piece, but after 5...dxe4 6.Nxe4 Nf6 the centre opens and Black develops easily with 7...Bd7 and 8...Bc6.
alternatives.after: 5.e5 keeps the centre closed and gains space, instead of an open game where Black's light bishop comes to c6 freely. Masters play 5.Nc3 only 3% of the time.

2790758909279175|d1e2.headline: Jump 8.Nb5 at the d6 hole before Black plays ...a6
2790758909279175|d1e2.why: 8.Qe2 is the standard Morra move, but it threatens nothing, and 8...a6 takes b5 from your knight at once. After 9.a4 Qc7 10.h3 Nge7 11.Rd1 O-O Black has castled and keeps the extra pawn. 8.Nb5 threatens a knight check on d6, and since ...e6 and ...Bg7 no pawn or bishop guards that square. After 8...a6 9.Nd6+ Kf8 Black can't castle any more; Wikibooks also gives 8...Nf6 9.Qd6, threatening a knight fork on c7.
2790758909279175|d1e2.principle: When your opponent leaves a hole, hit it at once: ...g6 and ...e6 left d6 unguarded, so 8.Nb5 aims there before 8...a6 closes the door.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6
Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (sample pages) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf

ideas.title: Knight jump to d6
ideas.text: Black played ...e6 and ...Bg7 without ...d6, so no pawn or bishop guards d6. From b5 your knight checks there and Black loses castling.

ideas.title: ...a6 shuts the door
ideas.text: Black's answer is ...a6, taking b5 from your knight. One quiet move from you, and 8...a6 makes d6 safe.

ideas.title: Morra setup on autopilot
ideas.text: Queen to e2 and rook to d1 is the standard Morra setup, but against ...g6 with ...e6 a concrete hit beats finishing it.

ideas.title: Gambit pawn buys time
ideas.text: You are a pawn down for quick development and open lines. Spend that time on threats, or Black catches up and keeps the pawn.

habit.why: 8.Qe2 is the standard Morra move, but it threatens nothing, and 8...a6 takes b5 from your knight at once. After 9.a4 Qc7 10.h3 Nge7 11.Rd1 O-O Black has castled and keeps the extra pawn.

strays.text: It gives Black the one move, 8...a6, that makes d6 safe.

taught.why: 8.Nb5 threatens a knight check on d6, and since ...e6 and ...Bg7 no pawn or bishop guards that square. After 8...a6 9.Nd6+ Kf8 Black can't castle any more; Wikibooks also gives 8...Nf6 9.Qd6, threatening a knight fork on c7.

enforces.text: The knight heads for d6 before ...a6 can stop it.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 8.Bg5 attacks the queen, but 8...Nge7 blocks with a developing move. After 9.Qd2 a6 Black has taken b5 from your knight and keeps the extra pawn.
alternatives.after: 8.Nb5 makes a threat no developing move can meet: 8...a6 comes too late, because 9.Nd6+ follows anyway.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 8.Bf4 eyes d6, but it gives Black a free move: 8...a6 takes b5 from your knight, and after 9.Bb3 Nge7 10.e5 b5 Black is ready to castle.
alternatives.after: 8.Nb5 goes for d6 straight away; the bishop can come later, once Black's king is already stuck on f8.

2797760506254471|d2d3.headline: Take the free e5 pawn with 3.Nxe5, not 3.d3
2797760506254471|d2d3.why: 3.d3 leaves the loose e5 pawn alone and spends a tempo: 3...Nc6 defends it, and after 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe5 Nf6 your d-pawn has moved twice while Black's f-pawn took over e4. After 6.Bc4 d5 Black has a strong centre and the game is level. 3.Nxe5 wins the undefended pawn, and 3...fxe4 now fails to 4.Qh5+, so Black answers 3...Qf6 and has to keep moving the queen. After 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3 Qg6 7.f3 you develop with gain of time and attack Black's e4 pawn.
2797760506254471|d2d3.principle: Against an unsound gambit, take the pawn when the capture comes with a threat: after 3.Nxe5 Black has no time for 3...fxe4.
sources: GM Avetik Grigoryan, Latvian Gambit: The Refutation (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/blog/Avetik_ChessMood/latvian-gambit-the-refutation
Latvian Gambit (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latvian_Gambit

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5

ideas.title: Take the free e5 pawn
ideas.text: 2...f5 leaves the e5 pawn attacked and undefended. 3.Nxe5 wins it at once; quiet moves give Black a free hand in the centre.

ideas.title: Meet gambits with concrete threats
ideas.text: With the knight on e5, 4.Qh5+ down the open e8-h5 diagonal is a threat, so 3...fxe4 fails and Black must spend moves on the queen.

ideas.title: Black's ...fxe4 counterattack
ideas.text: Black's point is ...fxe4, hitting your knight. Give Black time and the f-pawn takes over e4 for free.

ideas.title: Undermine the e4 pawn
ideas.text: Once Black's pawn reaches e4 it is a target: in the main line 6.Nc3 and 7.f3 attack it while Black's queen wanders.

habit.why: 3.d3 leaves the loose e5 pawn alone and spends a tempo: 3...Nc6 defends it, and after 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe5 Nf6 your d-pawn has moved twice while Black's f-pawn took over e4. After 6.Bc4 d5 Black has a strong centre and the game is level.

strays.text: 3.d3 lets Black defend e5 with 3...Nc6 instead of losing it.

taught.why: 3.Nxe5 wins the undefended pawn, and 3...fxe4 now fails to 4.Qh5+, so Black answers 3...Qf6 and has to keep moving the queen. After 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3 Qg6 7.f3 you develop with gain of time and attack Black's e4 pawn.

enforces.text: The 4.Qh5+ threat forces Black to spend moves on the queen.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.exf5 wins a pawn too, but 3...e4 kicks your knight first, and after 4.Ne5 Nf6 5.Be2 Be7 Black covers h5 and develops quickly.
alternatives.after: Taking on e5 keeps your knight central with the 4.Qh5+ threat, so Black gets no time for ...e4. GM Grigoryan gives 3.exf5 some advantage but chose 3.Nxe5; masters agree, 76.4% to 7.9%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 is sound: it guards e4 and develops, and in the engine line 5.Ng4 and 7.Nxf6+ Qxf6 trade off Black's f6 knight. A stronger move exists, though.
alternatives.after: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn at once. GM Grigoryan answers 3.Nc3 with 3...Nf6 and finds a smaller edge for White, though the engine rates 3.Nc3 nearly as good; masters choose 3.Nxe5 76.4% to 3%.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 3.d4 is a reversed Falkbeer, says GM Grigoryan: 3...fxe4 hits your knight at once, and after it takes on e5, 4...Nf6 gives Black easy development.
alternatives.after: 3.Nxe5 takes first, so 3...fxe4 runs into 4.Qh5+ instead of hitting your knight. After 3.d4 the pawn reaches e4 with tempo.

2797760506254471|f1c4.headline: Grab e5 at once with 3.Nxe5; 3.Bc4 lets 3...fxe4 hit back
2797760506254471|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 ignores the e5 pawn, and 3...fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 hits your knight and the g2 pawn at once. After 5.d4 Qxg2 6.Qh5+ g6 7.Bf7+ Kd8 you are a pawn down and must keep attacking, and GM Grigoryan says 4...d5 is even better for Black. 3.Nxe5 wins the undefended pawn, and 3...fxe4 now fails to 4.Qh5+, so Black answers 3...Qf6 and has to keep moving the queen. After 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3 Qg6 7.f3 you develop with gain of time and attack Black's e4 pawn.
2797760506254471|f1c4.principle: Look at captures first: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn with the 4.Qh5+ threat, while a developing move gives Black time for 3...fxe4.

2816849754100076|g8f6.headline: Hit the bishop that aims at f7
2816849754100076|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 attacks the queen but leaves f7 guarded only by the king: 4.Qxf7# is mate. 3...d5 breaks the attack at its source by hitting the bishop on c4 with a pawn and opening the way for the c8-bishop; after 4.Bb3 Be6 that bishop covers f7 and Black has the better centre.
2816849754100076|g8f6.principle: Answer a threat with a move that also gains time: attacking the piece that aims at f7 removes the danger and frees your own development.

2823299714850307|b8c6.headline: Hit the base of White's pawn chain with 3...c5
2823299714850307|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 blocks your c-pawn, the one pawn that can hit White's d4, and gives White an easy game. After 4.Nf3 f6 5.Bb5 a6 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 the knight is gone and you have doubled c-pawns. 3...c5 hits the base of the chain at once, the choice of 95.8% of masters. After 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bd7 6.Be2 cxd4 7.cxd4 Nge7 your knight can go to f5 and add more pressure on d4.
2823299714850307|b8c6.principle: When White's pawns lock the centre on d4 and e5, strike the base of the chain with your c-pawn and keep that pawn free to move.
