ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: White's d4 pawn holds up the chain. Strike it with 3...c5, then add 4...Nc6 and ...Qb6 against it.

ideas.title: Knight after the c-pawn
ideas.text: A knight on c6 blocks your c-pawn. Push 3...c5 first and the knight still reaches c6 on move four.

ideas.title: Watch for Bb5 after ...f6
ideas.text: With your knight on c6, ...f6 invites 5.Bb5: after 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 you are left with doubled c-pawns.

ideas.title: White props up d4 with c3
ideas.text: White meets 3...c5 with 4.c3, so 6...cxd4 7.cxd4 puts a pawn back on d4. Keep adding pieces against it.

habit.why: 3...Nc6 blocks your c-pawn, the one pawn that can hit White's d4, and gives White an easy game. After 4.Nf3 f6 5.Bb5 a6 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 the knight is gone and you have doubled c-pawns.

strays.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain
strays.text: With the knight on c6, your c-pawn can't reach c5 to hit d4.

taught.why: 3...c5 hits the base of the chain at once, the choice of 95.8% of masters. After 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bd7 6.Be2 cxd4 7.cxd4 Nge7 your knight can go to f5 and add more pressure on d4.

enforces.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain
enforces.text: Pawn, knight and later ...Nf5 all bear down on d4.

283181713049681|g7g5.headline: Don't hang g5: mirror White with 2...g6
283181713049681|g7g5.why: 2...g5 puts a pawn where the f3-knight takes it for free: 3.Nxg5. After 3...d5 4.Nf3 you are a pawn down and your kingside is loosened. 2...g6 mirrors White's set-up and is the masters' top choice (42%). After 3.c4 Bg7 4.Bg2 c6 5.O-O O-O 6.d4 d5 your king is safe and your ...c6/...d5 centre is solid.
283181713049681|g7g5.principle: Don't push a pawn onto a square the enemy knight attacks unless it is defended.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...Nf6/2. g3 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._Nf3/1...Nf6/2._g3
The Réti Opening: How to Play It as White and Black (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/the-reti-opening-how-to-play-as-white-and-black/

ideas.title: Nf3 takes loose pawns
ideas.text: The f3-knight hits e5 and g5. A pawn pushed there with no defender is simply taken, as in 2...g5 3.Nxg5.

ideas.title: Mirror the fianchetto
ideas.text: Answer White's fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7; your bishop matches White's on the long diagonal.

ideas.title: Fianchetto plus c4 hits d5
ideas.text: White often adds c4 and d4, as in 3.c4 Bg7 4.Bg2 c6; your ...c6 backs up ...d5 and blunts the g2-bishop.

habit.why: 2...g5 puts a pawn where the f3-knight takes it for free: 3.Nxg5. After 3...d5 4.Nf3 you are a pawn down and your kingside is loosened.

strays.text: Nothing guards g5, so 3.Nxg5 wins a pawn.

taught.why: 2...g6 mirrors White's set-up and is the masters' top choice (42%). After 3.c4 Bg7 4.Bg2 c6 5.O-O O-O 6.d4 d5 your king is safe and your ...c6/...d5 centre is solid.

enforces.text: Your bishop goes to g7 to match White's on g2, and you castle.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...d5 is a sound way to take the centre, the masters' second choice (30%), as in 3.Bg2 c5 4.O-O e6. There is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: 2...g6 keeps it symmetrical and safe; 2...d5 takes the centre at once. Both are good.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 2...Nc6 lets White play 3.d4 comfortably, and after 5.c4 dxc4 6.O-O Bg7 7.Na3 White wins the c4-pawn back with a strong centre.
alternatives.after: 2...g6 doesn't block your c-pawn, so ...c6 and ...d5 can follow, as in 4...c6 and 6...d5.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 2...e6 shuts in your c8-bishop, and after 3.Bg2 d5 4.d4 c5 5.c4 dxc4 6.O-O Nc6 7.dxc5 you get a Catalan-type game where White has won the pawn back.
alternatives.after: 2...g6 leaves the c8-bishop free and gives you a solid fianchetto; masters choose it 42% of the time.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...b6 is a sound Queen's Indian-style fianchetto, and after 3.Bg2 Bb7 your bishop fights White's on the long diagonal. But 6.d4 O-O 7.d5 gains White space, and there is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: 2...g6 mirrors White on the kingside; masters play it 42% of the time, against 11% for 2...b6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...b5 is a sound Polish-style fianchetto that grabs queenside space: after 3.d3 Bb7 4.Bg2 your bishop is on the long diagonal. There is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: 2...g6 is the masters' main move, 42% to 7%; 2...b5 is a sharper side line.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...c5 leads to a symmetrical English after 3.c4 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5, a sound choice. There is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: 2...g6 keeps your centre solid; with 2...c5 your knight on d5 is hit after 5.Bg2 Nc6 6.Nc3.

2861143771416580|e7e6.headline: Take the free c4-pawn and hold it with ...b5
2861143771416580|e7e6.why: 4...e6 defends d5 but leaves the loose c4-pawn alone, and 5.e3 covers it for good. After 5...h6 6.Bxf6 Qxf6 you have the bishop pair but a passive game, and 8.f4 grabs space. 4...dxc4 takes a pawn no White piece defends. After 5.e3 b5 6.a4 Qb6 7.Be2 a6 your pawns on a6, b5 and c4 hold together, and masters choose this 43% of the time.
2861143771416580|e7e6.principle: Take a pawn when nothing defends it and you can keep it.
sources: Slav Defense: The Main Line Move by Move (Chess Lab Academy) | https://www.chesslab.academy/openings/slav-defense/moves/
Slav Defense Traps (Chess Lab Academy) | https://www.chesslab.academy/openings/slav-defense/traps/

ideas.title: Bg5 leaves c4 loose
ideas.text: White played 4.Bg5 before e3, so nothing defends c4: 4...dxc4 wins a pawn.

ideas.title: Hold c4 with ...b5
ideas.text: After 5.e3 b5 the extra pawn is backed up; 6.a4 Qb6 and 7...a6 keep b5 protected.

ideas.title: Bishop c8 guards b7
ideas.text: Your c8-bishop guards b7. Moving it with 4...Bf5 lets 5.Qb3 hit b7.

habit.why: 4...e6 defends d5 but leaves the loose c4-pawn alone, and 5.e3 covers it for good. After 5...h6 6.Bxf6 Qxf6 you have the bishop pair but a passive game, and 8.f4 grabs space.

strays.text: You skip the free c4-pawn, and 5.e3 defends it.

taught.why: 4...dxc4 takes a pawn no White piece defends. After 5.e3 b5 6.a4 Qb6 7.Be2 a6 your pawns on a6, b5 and c4 hold together, and masters choose this 43% of the time.

enforces.text: 5...b5 and 7...a6 keep the extra c4-pawn protected.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Bf5 develops actively, but 5.Qb3 hits b7, and after 5...Nbd7 6.cxd5 cxd5 7.Nf3 Qb6 8.Bxf6 Nxf6 9.Qxb6 the queens come off in a quiet game. There is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4...dxc4 grabs the loose c4-pawn first; after 4...Bf5 White plays 6.cxd5 and the chance is gone.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4...h6 questions the bishop, but 5.Bxf6 gxf6 doubles your f-pawns and loosens your kingside.
alternatives.after: 4...dxc4 wins a pawn instead of letting White damage your pawns with 5.Bxf6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nbd7 is sound, and masters play it 12% of the time, but 5.cxd5 Nxd5 6.e4 Nxc3 7.bxc3 gives White a broad centre. There is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4...dxc4 takes the pawn before White can play 5.cxd5; masters choose it 43% of the time.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Ne4 hits the g5-bishop at once, and after 5.Nxe4 dxe4 6.Qd2 f6 7.Bh4 e5 you strike back in the centre. It is as good as the move the drill wants.
alternatives.after: Both work: 4...dxc4 grabs a pawn and holds it with ...b5, while 4...Ne4 swaps knights and hits back with 7...e5. Masters prefer 4...dxc4, 43% to 17%.

2885293173565302|d2d3.headline: Play 4.c3 to prepare d4 against Black's c5 and e5 pawns
2885293173565302|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is passive: the d-pawn takes one step, so challenging Black's centre with d4 later costs another move. After 4...Be7 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.a4 Nf6 7.Bg5 Bg4 8.h3 Be6 Black has developed freely, the e6-bishop challenges yours and the game is level. 4.c3 prepares d4 and opens b3 for your queen. After 4...Nf6 5.Qb3 Qc7 6.d4 Nc6 7.d5 Ne7 8.Qc2 you have hit f7 and b7, gained space with the d-pawn and pushed Black's knight back.
2885293173565302|d2d3.principle: Fight for the centre: Black's c5 and e5 pawns control d4, so 4.c3 prepares d4 to challenge them, while 4.d3 settles for a passive setup.
sources: IM Kushager Krishnater, Dangerous System against the Sicilian: the Concept with 3.Bc4 (Modern Chess) | https://www.modern-chess.com/course/dangerous-system-against-the-sicilian-the-concept-with-3-bc4/64692/
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4
Andre Schulz, Beating the Sicilian with 3.Bc4 - seriously? (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/beating-the-sicilian-with-3-bc4

ideas.title: c3 and d4 against ...c5 and ...e5
ideas.text: Black's pawns on c5 and e5 hold d4. c3 prepares d4 to challenge them, the plan IM Krishnater uses against ...e5.

ideas.title: Qb3 hits f7 and b7
ideas.text: Once c3 is in, the queen can go to b3, joining the bishop against f7 and hitting b7, as in 5.Qb3.

ideas.title: Italian-style setup
ideas.text: d3, c3, castling and a rook to the e-file is the quiet 3.Bc4 plan. Against ...e5, an early d3 means d4 costs a second move.

habit.why: 4.d3 is passive: the d-pawn takes one step, so challenging Black's centre with d4 later costs another move. After 4...Be7 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.a4 Nf6 7.Bg5 Bg4 8.h3 Be6 Black has developed freely, the e6-bishop challenges yours and the game is level.

strays.text: The d-pawn takes one step, so challenging Black's centre costs another move.

taught.why: 4.c3 prepares d4 and opens b3 for your queen. After 4...Nf6 5.Qb3 Qc7 6.d4 Nc6 7.d5 Ne7 8.Qc2 you have hit f7 and b7, gained space with the d-pawn and pushed Black's knight back.

enforces.text: 4.c3 gets 6.d4 in, then 7.d5 gains space.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 blocks your c-pawn, so it can't support a d4 push against Black's c5 and e5 pawns. After 4...Be7 5.d3 the game is quiet and Black is comfortable.
alternatives.after: 4.c3 keeps the d4 break: after 6.d4 Nc6 7.d5 you gain space and push the knight back to e7.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.O-O is natural, but Black develops freely with 4...Be7 and ...Nf6. After 6.d3 O-O 7.Nc3 Nc6 you have no central break and 8...Nb4 hits your bishop.
alternatives.after: 4.c3 first prepares d4 and opens b3 for the queen: 5.Qb3 hits b7 and f7 before Black has castled.

2927847296126403|e7e6.headline: Take again on f3 before White wins the pawn back
2927847296126403|e7e6.why: 4...e6 does nothing about 5.fxe4, so White wins the pawn straight back and gets pawns on d4 and e4. After 5.fxe4 Bb4 6.a3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 e5 8.Bd3 Bg4 9.Nf3 material is level and White has the centre and the bishop pair. 4...exf3 takes again before White can play fxe4, so White has to recapture with 5.Nxf3 and stays a pawn down. After 5...g6 6.Bf4 Bg7 7.Qd2 O-O 8.h3 Be6 your king is safe and White's play rests on development and the open f-file.
2927847296126403|e7e6.principle: Accept the gambit and keep taking: 4...exf3 holds on to the extra pawn instead of letting White win it back with a free centre.

ideas.title: fxe4 wins the pawn back
ideas.text: White threatens 5.fxe4, regaining the pawn with pawns on d4 and e4. A quiet move like ...e6 does nothing against it.

ideas.title: Accept gambits, hit the centre
ideas.text: Take again with 4...exf3. White gets development and the f-file for the pawn, but never the big pawn centre.

ideas.title: The Bogoljubow ...g6
ideas.text: After 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 g6 your bishop goes to g7, eyes d4 and lets you castle fast. Kalinichenko's gambit guide rates it among the best replies.

habit.why: 4...e6 does nothing about 5.fxe4, so White wins the pawn straight back and gets pawns on d4 and e4. After 5.fxe4 Bb4 6.a3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 e5 8.Bd3 Bg4 9.Nf3 material is level and White has the centre and the bishop pair.

strays.text: A quiet move lets White regain the pawn with a free centre.

taught.why: 4...exf3 takes again before White can play fxe4, so White has to recapture with 5.Nxf3 and stays a pawn down. After 5...g6 6.Bf4 Bg7 7.Qd2 O-O 8.h3 Be6 your king is safe and White's play rests on development and the open f-file.

enforces.text: You take again, so White never rebuilds the pawn centre.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Bf5 guards e4 and keeps the extra pawn, the Vienna Defence. But after 5.fxe4 Nxe4 6.Qf3 Nxc3 7.bxc3 e6 8.Qxb7 White wins the material back on b7. Playable, though a more common move exists.
alternatives.after: 4...exf3 is the main line, 79% of master games: it removes the f3 pawn, so you never have to hold e4 against 5.fxe4 and 6.Qf3 tricks.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...e3 gives the pawn straight back, the Langeheinicke Defence. After 5.Bxe3 a6 6.Qd2 e6 7.O-O-O White develops easily and keeps the initiative; there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: The engine accepts 4...e3, but Wikipedia and gambit sites rate it one of Black's weaker choices. 4...exf3 keeps the extra pawn and still develops fast with 5.Nxf3 g6.

2927859860869340|f3g5.headline: After 3...d6, the queen covers g5; strike with 4.d4 instead.
2927859860869340|f3g5.why: With Black's e-pawn gone from e7, the queen on d8 sees g5, so 4.Ng5 just loses the knight to 4...Qxg5. 3...d6 is a passive move that blocks Black's own bishop and concedes space, and 4.d4 takes that space: after 4...exd4 5.Nxd4 White has a centralised knight, open lines and an easy lead in development.
2927859860869340|f3g5.principle: When the opponent shuts in a bishop with a passive pawn move, claim the centre with your d-pawn instead of launching a lone piece attack.

2939336997955700|b8c6.headline: Win back the c5-pawn with 3...e6 and the bishop
2939336997955700|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 lets White keep the extra pawn: 4.a3 and then 6.b4 support the c5-pawn with pawns, and Black has no easy way to regain it. 3...e6 opens the diagonal for the king's bishop so it can recapture: after 4.c4 Bxc5 Black has the pawn back with an active bishop.
2939336997955700|b8c6.principle: When a pawn of yours has been taken, prefer the developing move that also wins it back: here the e-pawn frees the bishop to recapture on c5.

2949088022019168|g7g6.headline: Take the free e4 pawn with 3...Nxe4
2949088022019168|g7g6.why: 3...g6 is too slow: 4.e5 dxe5 5.Nxe5 puts a knight next to f7 and threatens mate there. The best answer, 5...e6, shuts in your c8-bishop, and after 6.d4 Bg7 7.O-O O-O White has the freer game. 3...Nxe4 takes the pawn on e4, which nothing defended. After 4.d4 g6 5.Bd3 Nf6 6.c4 Bg7 7.Nc3 O-O White has some space for it, but you are a pawn up with a safe king.
2949088022019168|g7g6.principle: Count attackers and defenders: e4 is attacked once and defended by nothing, so take it.
sources: Jeremy Silman, A Pirc Quirk (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/a-pirc-quirk

ideas.title: Guard e4 before anything else
ideas.text: 3.Bc4 develops but leaves e4 with no defender, so 3...Nxe4 wins a pawn.

ideas.title: The bishop on c4 eyes f7
ideas.text: White's bishop aims at f7. If you play slowly, 4.e5 dxe5 5.Nxe5 adds a knight and threatens mate on f7.

ideas.title: White's e5 kick
ideas.text: Against a slow move, 4.e5 gains time on your knight and opens the way for 5.Nxe5.

ideas.title: Take a pawn that is really free
ideas.text: Grab e4 only when White can't win it back. Here nothing can: after 4.d4 g6 5.Bd3 Nf6 you are a pawn up.

habit.why: 3...g6 is too slow: 4.e5 dxe5 5.Nxe5 puts a knight next to f7 and threatens mate there. The best answer, 5...e6, shuts in your c8-bishop, and after 6.d4 Bg7 7.O-O O-O White has the freer game.

strays.idea: Take a pawn that is really free
strays.text: Nothing guarded e4, and 3...g6 lets White push it with tempo instead.

taught.why: 3...Nxe4 takes the pawn on e4, which nothing defended. After 4.d4 g6 5.Bd3 Nf6 6.c4 Bg7 7.Nc3 O-O White has some space for it, but you are a pawn up with a safe king.

enforces.text: White's 3.Bc4 left e4 unguarded, and you take it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Bg4 is sound: with your knight on f6 guarding g4, the usual trick against f7 doesn't win this bishop. But there is a stronger move here.
alternatives.after: 3...Nxe4 wins a pawn outright; 3...Bg4 only develops, and White gets 5.d4 and 6.d5 for free.
alternatives.idea: Take a pawn that is really free

2973368771887475|f3e5.headline: Kick the knight with 5.c3; 5.Nxe5 runs into 5...Qf6
2973368771887475|f3e5.why: 5.Nxe5 runs into 5...Qf6, which hits the e5 knight and threatens mate on f2. After 6.O-O Qxe5 you have lost the knight for the e5 pawn, and Black keeps an extra piece. 5.c3 kicks the b4 knight, so you gain time instead of a pawn: after 5...Nc6 6.d4 exd4 7.cxd4 Bb6 you have pawns on e4 and d4. That is the same position as the usual 4...Bxb4 5.c3 Bc5, the normal Evans centre for one pawn.
2973368771887475|f3e5.principle: Before grabbing a pawn, check what the opponent's queen can hit: here 5...Qf6 hits the e5 knight and f2 at once.

Bruce Pandolfini, The Winning Way (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%22Nxb4%22+%22Nxe5+Qf6%22

ideas.title: Watch the queen counter-hit
ideas.text: If your knight takes on e5, 5...Qf6 hits it and threatens mate on f2 at the same time.

ideas.title: Evans: the centre is the payment
ideas.text: You gave the b-pawn so that c3 and d4 come with tempo. 5.c3 kicks the knight, then 6.d4 builds your centre.

ideas.title: Black threatens ...d5
ideas.text: Black's next idea is 5...d5, hitting your c4 bishop and the e4 pawn to win a second pawn.

habit.why: 5.Nxe5 runs into 5...Qf6, which hits the e5 knight and threatens mate on f2. After 6.O-O Qxe5 you have lost the knight for the e5 pawn, and Black keeps an extra piece.

strays.text: The e5 knight is loose, and 5...Qf6 hits it with a mate threat.

taught.why: 5.c3 kicks the b4 knight, so you gain time instead of a pawn: after 5...Nc6 6.d4 exd4 7.cxd4 Bb6 you have pawns on e4 and d4. That is the same position as the usual 4...Bxb4 5.c3 Bc5, the normal Evans centre for one pawn.

enforces.idea: Evans: the centre is the payment
enforces.text: Kicking the knight, then 6.d4, gets your centre with tempo.

2977407816810866|a7a6.headline: After White castles, Bxc6 and Nxe5 is a real threat
2977407816810866|a7a6.why: With White castled, 4...a6 no longer holds e5: 5.Bxc6 removes its defender and 6.Nxe5 wins the pawn, because the old ...Qd4 counter fails now that the rook on f1 guards f2. 4...Nd4 attacks the bishop on b5 and takes the knight out of the exchange; after 5.Nxd4 Bxd4 Black recaptures with the bishop. Masters choose it in 43.4% of games.
2977407816810866|a7a6.principle: Ask what your opponent's last move threatens: castling made Bxc6 and Nxe5 work, so move the knight with a counterattack instead of a slow pawn move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5/4. O-O

3001047939008470|e7e5.headline: Count first: ...e5 here just drops a pawn
3001047939008470|e7e5.why: 5...e5 puts a pawn where the d4 pawn and the f3-knight both hit it, and nothing of yours defends it. After 6.dxe5 Nfd7 7.Nd4 Bg6 8.f4 White keeps the extra pawn on e5 and you never win it back. 5...e6 holds d5 and frees the f8-bishop, and it costs nothing because your light-squared bishop is already out on f5. If White chases the bishop with 6.Nh4, 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bh5 sidesteps it and the game stays balanced.
3001047939008470|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn, count who attacks and defends its square: e5 is hit by the d4 pawn and the f3-knight and guarded by nothing.
sources: Marin on Tromso R8 - Lasker's Copyright (GM Mihail Marin, ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/marin-on-tromso-r8-lasker-s-copyright

ideas.title: Loose ...e5 drops a pawn
ideas.text: The d4 pawn and the f3-knight both hit e5 and nothing of yours guards it, so 6.dxe5 wins a pawn and kicks your f6-knight.

ideas.title: Bishop out, then ...e6
ideas.text: Your bishop is already on f5, so ...e6 no longer shuts it in. It holds d5 and opens the f8-bishop.

ideas.title: Nh4 hunts the bishop
ideas.text: White can play 6.Nh4, chasing your f5-bishop to win the bishop pair. ...h6 gives the bishop a retreat on h7.

habit.why: 5...e5 puts a pawn where the d4 pawn and the f3-knight both hit it, and nothing of yours defends it. After 6.dxe5 Nfd7 7.Nd4 Bg6 8.f4 White keeps the extra pawn on e5 and you never win it back.

strays.text: e5 is attacked twice and defended by nothing.

taught.why: 5...e6 holds d5 and frees the f8-bishop, and it costs nothing because your light-squared bishop is already out on f5. If White chases the bishop with 6.Nh4, 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bh5 sidesteps it and the game stays balanced.

enforces.text: The bishop came out first, so ...e6 locks nothing in.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Nbd7 develops sensibly, but White starts chasing your bishop with 6.Nh4 Be4 7.f3 Bg6. Playable, though there is a more useful move.
alternatives.after: 5...e6 holds d5 and opens the f8-bishop first. Masters play it 58% of the time against 10.5% for 5...Nbd7; both are fine.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...h6 gives the f5-bishop a retreat on h7, so White's knight can't win the bishop pair. Masters prefer another move, but the engine rates this one just as highly.
alternatives.after: 5...e6 is the masters' choice (58% to 31%), while the engine rates the two the same. With 5...h6 you make the retreat first and play ...e6 a move later, as in 6.c4 e6.

3021266198007975|d8f6.headline: Develop with 5...Nf6; 5...Qf6 runs into 6.Nd5
3021266198007975|d8f6.why: 5...Qf6 brings the queen out early, and 6.Nd5 hits it and c7 at once. After 6...Qd8 7.c3 Bb6 8.d4 White has gained time for a big centre, and 10.Nxb6 takes your bishop pair. 5...Nf6 develops toward the centre, hits e4 and gets you ready to castle, as 6...O-O does in the line. After 6.a3 O-O 7.d3 a5 you have a normal slow Italian with the ...a5 plan Wesley So favours for Black.
3021266198007975|d8f6.principle: Bring the knights out before the queen: a queen on f6 takes the knight's square and gives White's knight a target.
sources: IM Roven Vogel reviews Wesley So's Modern Italian (ChessBase) | http://en.chessbase.com/post/roven-vogel-reviews-the-modern-italian-by-wesley-so
Souleidis and Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf
Giuoco Piano (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuoco_Piano

ideas.title: Knights before the queen
ideas.text: A knight on f6 develops, hits e4 and prepares castling. A queen there takes the knight's square and gives White a target.

ideas.title: White's knight jumps to d5
ideas.text: The c3 knight can jump to d5, hitting f6 and c7, and gain time for c3 and d4.

ideas.title: Give the bishop a retreat
ideas.text: White's knight can chase your c5 bishop from a4; ...a6 makes a7 a safe retreat.

ideas.title: Swap off the Italian bishop
ideas.text: ...Be6 offers to trade White's c4 bishop. It's safe here: the d8 queen covers g5, so after the trade White's knight can't reach e6 that way.

habit.why: 5...Qf6 brings the queen out early, and 6.Nd5 hits it and c7 at once. After 6...Qd8 7.c3 Bb6 8.d4 White has gained time for a big centre, and 10.Nxb6 takes your bishop pair.

strays.text: The queen takes the knight's square and becomes a target for 6.Nd5.

taught.why: 5...Nf6 develops toward the centre, hits e4 and gets you ready to castle, as 6...O-O does in the line. After 6.a3 O-O 7.d3 a5 you have a normal slow Italian with the ...a5 plan Wesley So favours for Black.

enforces.text: The knight develops, hits e4 and clears the way to castle.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...h6 keeps White's pieces off g5 and is sound, but 6.Na4 goes straight for your c5 bishop. A developing move is a touch more useful.
alternatives.after: 5...Nf6 develops a piece instead. The engine rates the two about equal, but after 5...h6 6.Na4 Qf6 the queen still comes out early.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Be6 offers to trade White's c4 bishop; after 6.Bxe6 fxe6 you get the half-open f-file and an extra guard on d5. It's sound, though 7.Na4 then chases your other bishop.
alternatives.after: 5...Nf6 develops the kingside first. After 5...Be6 6.Bxe6 fxe6 7.Na4 Bb6 White can win the bishop pair; both moves keep the balance.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...a6 gives your bishop a7 as a retreat against a knight on a4, and if 6.Nd5 you can trade it off with 7...Nxd5. It's sound; a developing move is a touch more useful.
alternatives.after: 5...Nf6 develops at once; 5...a6 is a useful waiting move, and both keep the balance. After 5...a6 6.Nd5 the knight still comes out with 6...Nf6.

3024364401435985|g8h6.headline: Grab the centre with d5 against the early queen
3024364401435985|g8h6.why: 2...Nh6 does nothing for the centre or for the pawn on e5, and after 3.d4 d5 4.dxe5 White has won it. 2...d5 takes the centre with a second pawn while White's queen sits in front of its own knight; after 3.Qg3 the queen has moved twice, and 3...Nc6 develops while guarding e5.
3024364401435985|g8h6.principle: An early queen blocks its own pieces and wastes time; answer it by taking the centre with pawns and developing, not with a knight on the rim.

3047838571696673|d7d5.headline: Develop with 2...Bc5 and aim at the d4 hole
3047838571696673|d7d5.why: 2...d5 is the Bavarian gambit, and the theory marks it as a mistake: 3.cxd5 wins a pawn. 2.c4 is slow and leaves White with a permanent hole on d4. 2...Bc5, the most common master reply, develops the bishop to a square that aims at d4 and f2.
3047838571696673|d7d5.principle: When your opponent's pawn moves leave a square that no pawn can cover, point your pieces at it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. c4

3047838571696673|d8g5.headline: Develop with 2...Bc5; an early queen just gets chased
3047838571696673|d8g5.why: 2...Qg5 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home, and White develops by attacking it: 3.Nf3 sends it back to e7, and Black has lost time. 2.c4 left a permanent hole on d4 and blocked White's own king's bishop, and 2...Bc5 exploits that: the bishop takes an active diagonal aimed at d4 and f2.
3047838571696673|d8g5.principle: An early queen sortie invites knights and bishops to come out with tempo; develop a minor piece toward the squares your opponent has weakened instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. c4

3078274341826662|f3e5.headline: Take back the d4 pawn; 6.Ne5 just drops a knight
3078274341826662|f3e5.why: 6.Ne5 puts the knight where the d6 pawn takes it, 6...dxe5, and 7.Qh5+ Kd7 8.Qxe5 wins back only one pawn. You are a knight for a pawn down, and after 8...Nc6 9.Qg3 Nf6 10.O-O Nxe4 Black takes your e4 pawn too. 6.Nxd4 wins back the pawn, which is attacked twice and defended by nothing, and puts the knight in the centre. After 6...Nf6 7.Bg5 e5 8.Nf5 it jumps to f5, a square Black's pawns no longer cover, and masters choose 6.Nxd4 in 96% of games.
3078274341826662|f3e5.principle: Count what covers a square before you land on it: e5 is taken by the d6 pawn, while d4 is attacked twice and defended by nothing.
sources: Sean Marsh, Chess Opening Basics: The Philidor Defense (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-philidor-defense/

ideas.title: Take back the d4 pawn
ideas.text: Black's pawn on d4 is attacked by your knight and queen and defended by nothing, so recapturing wins it back.

ideas.title: Hit the doubled e6 pawn
ideas.text: Black's doubled e-pawns are a target, so play fast: a knight on d4 eyes e6 and f5.

ideas.title: Knight jumps need a follow-up
ideas.text: With your light-squared bishop gone, nothing backs up a knight raid: 6.Ne5 dxe5 7.Qh5+ Kd7 wins one pawn for the knight.

habit.why: 6.Ne5 puts the knight where the d6 pawn takes it, 6...dxe5, and 7.Qh5+ Kd7 8.Qxe5 wins back only one pawn. You are a knight for a pawn down, and after 8...Nc6 9.Qg3 Nf6 10.O-O Nxe4 Black takes your e4 pawn too.

strays.text: No bishop backs up the knight, so the raid wins one pawn for a piece.

taught.why: 6.Nxd4 wins back the pawn, which is attacked twice and defended by nothing, and puts the knight in the centre. After 6...Nf6 7.Bg5 e5 8.Nf5 it jumps to f5, a square Black's pawns no longer cover, and masters choose 6.Nxd4 in 96% of games.

enforces.text: The knight regains the pawn and lands in the centre.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Qxd4 regains the pawn, but 6...Nc6 hits your queen and after 7.Qd3 Qd7 Black develops with tempo. A stronger move exists.
alternatives.after: 6.Nxd4 recaptures with a piece that belongs in the centre and keeps your queen safe from 6...Nc6. Masters prefer it, 96% to 4%.

3087437353600707|d1e2.headline: Kick the f6-knight with 7.e5 before Black can pin
3087437353600707|d1e2.why: 7.Qe2 lets Black play 7...Bg4, pinning your knight now that the f6-knight covers g4. After 8.Be3 Rc8 9.h3 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Black has traded off one of your attackers and stays a pawn up. 7.e5 hits the f6-knight before Black can pin or castle: after 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 9.O-O Be7 10.h3 the knight must go back and Black's d6 pawn is isolated. It is the masters' main move here (57%).
3087437353600707|d1e2.principle: You lead in development and Black's king is in the centre, so open the game now with 7.e5 instead of a quiet setup move that allows the pin.

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: e4-e5 hits the f6-knight and the d6 pawn and opens lines while Black's king is still on e8.

ideas.title: Bc4 eyes f7
ideas.text: With Black's e-pawn still on e7, your c4-bishop aims at f7, so opening the centre is risky for Black.

ideas.title: The ...Bg4 pin
ideas.text: With the f6-knight covering g4, Black can pin your f3-knight with a bishop on g4 and trade it off, freeing Black's game.

ideas.title: No autopilot setup
ideas.text: The usual setup with the queen on e2 and a rook on d1 doesn't fit every defence; check what Black is ready for first.

habit.why: 7.Qe2 lets Black play 7...Bg4, pinning your knight now that the f6-knight covers g4. After 8.Be3 Rc8 9.h3 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Black has traded off one of your attackers and stays a pawn up.

strays.text: The routine queen move gives Black time for 7...Bg4 and a trade on f3.

taught.why: 7.e5 hits the f6-knight before Black can pin or castle: after 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 9.O-O Be7 10.h3 the knight must go back and Black's d6 pawn is isolated. It is the masters' main move here (57%).

enforces.text: The pawn kicks the f6-knight before Black can pin your f3-knight.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is a good, natural move, played in 40% of master games. After 7...a6 8.Bf4 e6 Black reaches a solid setup; there's a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: 7.e5 is the masters' main choice (57%): it strikes before Black can set up with ...a6, ...Bg4 and ...e6. After 7.O-O a6 Black has time for that.

3087437353600707|f3g5.headline: 7.e5, not 7.Ng5: Black's 7...e6 shuts out the knight's target
3087437353600707|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 7...e6 shuts the c4-bishop off from f7 and the knight has nothing to hit. After 8.O-O Be7 9.Qe2 O-O 10.Nf3 it goes back home, two moves lost in a gambit where time is everything. 7.e5 hits the f6-knight while Black's king is still on e8, and 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qxd8 wins the queen. Black's best is 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 9.O-O Be7 10.h3, when the knight must retreat and the d6 pawn is isolated.
3087437353600707|f3g5.principle: Don't move the same piece twice without a target: after 7.Ng5 e6 the knight hits nothing and goes back, while 7.e5 hits the f6-knight.

ideas.title: Bc4 eyes f7
ideas.text: Your c4-bishop aims at f7: after 7.e5, 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qxd8 wins Black's queen.

ideas.title: ...e6 shuts out the bishop
ideas.text: One pawn move, ...e6, cuts your c4-bishop off from f7. Then a knight on g5 has nothing to attack.

ideas.title: The ...Bg4 pin
ideas.text: With the f6-knight covering g4, Black can pin your f3-knight with a bishop on g4 and trade it off, freeing Black's game.

habit.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 7...e6 shuts the c4-bishop off from f7 and the knight has nothing to hit. After 8.O-O Be7 9.Qe2 O-O 10.Nf3 it goes back home, two moves lost in a gambit where time is everything.

strays.text: One pawn move by Black makes the knight's trip pointless.

taught.why: 7.e5 hits the f6-knight while Black's king is still on e8, and 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qxd8 wins the queen. Black's best is 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 9.O-O Be7 10.h3, when the knight must retreat and the d6 pawn is isolated.

enforces.text: The pawn kicks the f6-knight and opens lines toward Black's king.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is a good, natural move, played in 40% of master games. After 7...a6 8.Bf4 e6 Black reaches a solid setup; there's a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: 7.e5 is the masters' main choice (57%): it strikes before Black can set up with ...a6, ...Bg4 and ...e6. After 7.O-O a6 Black has time for that.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qe2 allows 7...Bg4, pinning your knight now that the f6-knight covers g4. After 8.O-O e6 9.h3 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Black has traded off an attacker and is solid.
alternatives.after: 7.e5 hits the f6-knight first, so Black is busy answering threats instead of pinning and trading on f3.

3105714547729451|c8g4.headline: Hit e4 with 2...Nf6 instead of pinning early
3105714547729451|c8g4.why: 2...Bg4 commits your bishop before you have chosen a set-up, and 3.d4 gives White the full centre at once. In the line 3...e5 4.dxe5 Nc6 5.exd6 Qxd6 6.Be3 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 you are a pawn down for little. 2...Nf6 attacks e4, so White spends 3.Nc3 guarding it instead of grabbing more space. After 3...c5 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 you reach a Najdorf Sicilian, and masters choose 2...Nf6 62% of the time.
3105714547729451|c8g4.principle: Develop with a threat: a move that attacks e4 makes White react, while an early pin lets White build the centre for free.
sources: Sergio Trigo Urquijo, The Modernized Philidor Defense (Thinkers Publishing excerpt) | https://thinkerspublishing.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/PHILIDOR-DEFENSE.pdf

ideas.title: Guard e4 before anything else
ideas.text: 2...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White must spend a move guarding it, usually with 3.Nc3.

ideas.title: Keep your options open
ideas.text: The knight on f6 fits every set-up: a Pirc with ...g6, a Philidor with ...e5 or a Sicilian with ...c5.

ideas.title: An early pin gives White d4
ideas.text: After 2...Bg4 White plays 3.d4 at once and owns the centre, while your bishop has committed before you chose a set-up.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: You let White build the centre, then strike it from the side, as 3...c5 4.d4 cxd4 does after 3.Nc3.

habit.why: 2...Bg4 commits your bishop before you have chosen a set-up, and 3.d4 gives White the full centre at once. In the line 3...e5 4.dxe5 Nc6 5.exd6 Qxd6 6.Be3 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 you are a pawn down for little.

strays.idea: An early pin gives White d4
strays.text: The pin threatens nothing, so 3.d4 builds the centre for free.

taught.why: 2...Nf6 attacks e4, so White spends 3.Nc3 guarding it instead of grabbing more space. After 3...c5 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 you reach a Najdorf Sicilian, and masters choose 2...Nf6 62% of the time.

enforces.text: The knight hits e4, so White must defend it before building further.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2...e5 turns the game into a Philidor Defence, a different opening. After 3.d4 and 4.dxe5 Nxe4 5.Be3 White hits back in the centre and keeps an edge; masters play it only 5% of the time.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 hits e4 first and keeps both the Pirc and the Philidor open; with 2...e5 you have already chosen the Philidor.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2...g6 stays in the Modern, and masters play it 11% of the time. But it makes no threat, so White builds the centre with 3.d4 and 4.Be2 at no cost.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 forces White to guard e4 first, and you can still play ...g6 next. The engine marks 2...g6 a little worse even though masters use it.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2...e6 is passive: it shuts in your c8-bishop, and White builds a big centre with 3.d4, 5.c4 and 7.d5.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 develops with a threat to e4; 2...e6 attacks nothing and blocks your bishop.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2...c5 switches to an Open Sicilian, the masters' second choice here at 16%. The engine marks it a little worse, but it is a fine choice if you play the Sicilian.
alternatives.after: Both moves can reach the same Najdorf after 5.Nxd4 a6, as the lines show; 2...Nf6 also keeps the Pirc and Philidor open.

3119368342174684|e7e6.headline: Strike at e5 with d6 before it gets support
3119368342174684|e7e6.why: 3...e6 is slow: it lets White shore up the advanced pawn with 4.Nc3 and 5.f4, leaving Black cramped behind it. 3...d6 attacks e5 together with the bishop on g7 before it can be supported; after 4.exd6 Qxd6 the queen and bishop both bear on d4, and 5...c5 attacks White's centre again.
3119368342174684|e7e6.principle: When White pushes a centre pawn to the fifth rank early, hit it with a pawn at once, before other pawns arrive to support it.

3179485995949204|c1f4.headline: Kick the knight with 6.e5 instead of developing the bishop
3179485995949204|c1f4.why: 6.Bf4 develops but lets Black strike first with 6...c5, and after 7.Nc3 cxd4 8.Nxd4 d6 your d-pawn is traded off and Black is comfortable. The moment to kick the knight while it has no good square has passed. 6.e5 hits the knight while d7 and e8 are blocked, so it goes back to g8, and after 7.O-O c5 8.dxc5 bxc5 9.Na3 your knight heads for c4 with a big lead in space. Masters rarely play it (4%), but the engine rates it clearly best.
3179485995949204|c1f4.principle: A pawn that hits a knight with no good retreat gains time: 6.e5 sends it back to g8, while 6.Bf4 gives Black time for 6...c5.
sources: Welling & Basman, U Cannot Be Serious! (publisher excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/8423.pdf
Matthew Astle, The Offbeat Owen's (Chessable blog) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/owens-defense/
Owen's Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen%27s_Defence

ideas.title: e5 kicks the f6-knight
ideas.text: Now e5 leaves the knight no good square: d7 and e8 are blocked, so it must go back to g8 or to an exposed square.

ideas.title: Count attackers on e4
ideas.text: The f6-knight and b7-bishop hit e4; your bishop and queen guard it twice, so the pawn is safe and free to advance.

ideas.title: Black strikes back with ...c5
ideas.text: Given time, Black hits d4 with ...c5, as in 6.Bf4 c5 7.Nc3 cxd4.

habit.why: 6.Bf4 develops but lets Black strike first with 6...c5, and after 7.Nc3 cxd4 8.Nxd4 d6 your d-pawn is traded off and Black is comfortable. The moment to kick the knight while it has no good square has passed.

strays.text: 6...c5 hits d4 before your centre is secured.

taught.why: 6.e5 hits the knight while d7 and e8 are blocked, so it goes back to g8, and after 7.O-O c5 8.dxc5 bxc5 9.Na3 your knight heads for c4 with a big lead in space. Masters rarely play it (4%), but the engine rates it clearly best.

enforces.text: The knight returns to g8 and Black's development goes backwards.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: Castling is natural and masters choose it in 83% of games, but 6...O-O gives the f6-knight a retreat on e8, and Black's ...d5 follows, as in 7.c4 d5.
alternatives.after: The engine prefers 6.e5 at once, while the knight has no good square; masters castle far more often (83% to 4%).

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.c4 grabs more space, but after 6...d6 7.Nc3 O-O Black is castled and ready for 8...c5 against your centre.
alternatives.after: 6.e5 hits the knight before Black castles or plays ...d6, so it has to go back to g8. After 6.c4 d6 that chance is gone.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.c3 supports d4 but is quiet: 6...d6 gives Black time to cover the centre, and the knight later finds a route via d7 and f8 to g6.
alternatives.after: 6.e5 at once leaves the knight no good square; after 6.c3 d6 Black has prepared 7...Nfd7, so the push gains less.

3179485995949204|e1h1.headline: Kick the knight with 6.e5 before Black can castle
3179485995949204|e1h1.why: 6.O-O is natural and masters' usual move (83%), but Black castles too, and then the f6-knight can drop back to e8. After 6...O-O 7.c4 d5 8.cxd5 exd5 9.e5 Ne8 the push no longer costs Black time. 6.e5 hits the knight while d7 and e8 are blocked, so it goes back to g8, and after 7.O-O c5 8.dxc5 bxc5 9.Na3 your knight heads for c4 with a big lead in space. Masters rarely play it (4%), but the engine rates it clearly best.
3179485995949204|e1h1.principle: A pawn that hits a knight with no good retreat gains time: 6.e5 sends it back to g8, while castling lets Black free e8 for it.
sources: Welling & Basman, U Cannot Be Serious! (publisher excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/8423.pdf
Matthew Astle, The Offbeat Owen's (Chessable blog) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/owens-defense/

strays.text: After 6...O-O the knight gets e8, so e5 gains much less.

3191630614517678|f2f3.headline: Punish 2...Nh6 by developing 3.Nc3, not with f3
3191630614517678|f2f3.why: 3.f3 props up e4 but takes f3 from White's knight and doesn't hold: after 3...c6 4.d4 d5 5.Bb3 dxe4 Black wins a pawn. 2...Nh6 put Black's knight on the rim, away from the centre; 3.Nc3 simply develops, defends e4 and controls d5, and White keeps the lead in development.
3191630614517678|f2f3.principle: When your opponent puts a knight on the rim, just develop toward the centre; a pawn move like f3 needs a concrete reason and takes your knight's best square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4

3244175099892819|f7f6.headline: Take the centre with 1...d5 instead of 1...f6
3244175099892819|f7f6.why: 1...f6 does nothing about the centre or the g4-pawn, and it takes f6 away from your knight. After 2.d4 d5 3.h3 Nc6 4.Bg2 e6 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.Qd3 White has built a centre and the game is level. 1...d5 takes the centre and lets your c8-bishop eye the g4-pawn. After 2.c4 d4 3.Bg2 e5 4.d3 your pawns hold the centre and cxd5 is no longer possible; masters play 1...d5 67% of the time.
3244175099892819|f7f6.principle: Meet a flank opening by taking the centre it neglects.

ideas.title: Punish 1.g4 in the centre
ideas.text: 1.g4 does nothing for the centre and loosens White's kingside. Take the centre with ...d5, then ...c6 or ...e5.

ideas.title: The g4-pawn is a target
ideas.text: Once the d-pawn moves, your c8-bishop hits g4, and ...h5 can attack it too.

ideas.title: White's free centre
ideas.text: If you don't strike first, White builds a centre with d4, as in 1...f6 2.d4 d5 3.h3.

ideas.title: Gain space with ...d4
ideas.text: Against c4, ...d4 grabs space and sidesteps cxd5, as in 1...d5 2.c4 d4.

habit.why: 1...f6 does nothing about the centre or the g4-pawn, and it takes f6 away from your knight. After 2.d4 d5 3.h3 Nc6 4.Bg2 e6 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.Qd3 White has built a centre and the game is level.

strays.text: The f-pawn move does nothing in the centre, and 2.d4 takes it.

taught.why: 1...d5 takes the centre and lets your c8-bishop eye the g4-pawn. After 2.c4 d4 3.Bg2 e5 4.d3 your pawns hold the centre and cxd5 is no longer possible; masters play 1...d5 67% of the time.

enforces.text: Your pawns take d4 and e5 while White's g-pawn does nothing there.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 1...e5 is a strong central reply, and 2.Bg2 h5 attacks the g4-pawn at once. There is a slightly more popular move.
alternatives.after: 1...d5 and 1...e5 both punish 1.g4; the d-pawn move also lets the c8-bishop hit g4. Masters prefer 1...d5, 67% to 19%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 1...e6 is sound: after 3.d4 c5 you get a French-like centre. But it blocks your c8-bishop, and there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 1...d5 takes the centre at once and frees your c8-bishop to attack g4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 1...c5 is a reasonable reply: after 4.Nf3 Bxg4 5.Nc3 Qf5 you have won the g-pawn. There is a simpler move.
alternatives.after: 1...d5 takes the centre straight away; 1...c5 gets ...d5 in a move later and wins g4 with 4...Bxg4.

3244175099892819|g8f6.headline: Take the centre with 1...d5; 1...Nf6 gets kicked by g5
3244175099892819|g8f6.why: 1...Nf6 develops onto a square the g-pawn can hit, and 2.g5 Nh5 sends the knight to the rim. After 3.e4 g6 4.Nc3 c6 5.d4 d5 6.Be2 White has used the time for a big centre and hits the h5-knight again. 1...d5 takes the centre and lets your c8-bishop eye the g4-pawn. After 2.c4 d4 3.Bg2 e5 4.d3 your pawns hold the centre and cxd5 is no longer possible; masters play 1...d5 67% of the time.
3244175099892819|g8f6.principle: Meet a flank opening by taking the centre it neglects.

3249639623522672|c7c6.headline: Use the fork trick: 6...Nxe4 and 7...d5
3249639623522672|c7c6.why: 6...c6 is slow and lets White push 7.e5, kicking your knight to the passive e8 square. After 8.Re1 dxe5 9.Nxe5 Nd6 10.Bb3 White's pieces are the more active. 6...Nxe4 7.Nxe4 d5 hits bishop and knight at once, so you win the piece back. After 8.Bd3 dxe4 9.Bxe4 Nd7 10.c3 c5 material is level and you are already hitting d4; masters choose 6...Nxe4 36% of the time.
3249639623522672|c7c6.principle: Checks, captures and threats first: 6...Nxe4 works because 7...d5 forks two pieces and wins the material back.

ideas.title: The fork trick against Bc4
ideas.text: 6...Nxe4 7.Nxe4 d5 forks bishop and knight, so you win the piece back and free your game.

ideas.title: White's e5 kick
ideas.text: Slow moves let White push 7.e5 and drive your knight to a passive square like e8.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: You let White build e4 and d4, then hit them: here ...Nxe4, ...d5 and later ...c5 take the centre apart.

habit.why: 6...c6 is slow and lets White push 7.e5, kicking your knight to the passive e8 square. After 8.Re1 dxe5 9.Nxe5 Nd6 10.Bb3 White's pieces are the more active.

strays.text: 6...c6 gives White time for 7.e5, sending your knight back.

taught.why: 6...Nxe4 7.Nxe4 d5 hits bishop and knight at once, so you win the piece back. After 8.Bd3 dxe4 9.Bxe4 Nd7 10.c3 c5 material is level and you are already hitting d4; masters choose 6...Nxe4 36% of the time.

enforces.text: The pawn on d5 hits c4 and e4, so the piece comes back.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6...Bg4 pins the f3-knight, a normal Pirc idea that masters play 19% of the time. After 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 White has the bishop pair and gains space with 10.d5; the engine rates it a little worse.
alternatives.after: 6...Nxe4 frees your game at once with the fork trick; 6...Bg4 gives up the bishop pair for slower pressure on d4.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6...Nc6 develops and hits d4, but 7.d5 drives the knight back to b8 and White gains space. Masters play it 19% of the time; the engine is less keen.
alternatives.after: 6...Nxe4 gets play at once, while after 6...Nc6 7.d5 Nb8 your knight has spent two moves to go home.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6...Nbd7 takes d7 away from your f6-knight, so 7.e5 Ng4 8.h3 drives it to the edge at h6.
alternatives.after: 6...Nxe4 uses the knight to take a pawn before it can be kicked; after 6...Nbd7 7.e5 it ends up on h6.

3253136195144505|f7f6.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6; 3...f6 weakens your king and wastes time
3253136195144505|f7f6.why: 3...f6 is a third pawn move that takes the f6 square from your own knight and opens the diagonal from the bishop on c4 toward g8, so castling kingside becomes risky. After 4.d4 Nc6 5.Be3 White has a strong centre and a lead in development. 3...Nf6 develops toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e4, which gains time; after 4.Nc3 Be7 Black is ready to castle.
3253136195144505|f7f6.principle: With two pawn moves already played and the bishop on c4 eyeing your king, every extra pawn move costs time and loosens the king; develop a piece instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

3294566395905444|f1c4.headline: Punish 3...Bd6 with 4.Nxe5 and a pawn fork
3294566395905444|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 lets Black off the hook: after 4...Nc6 e5 is defended and the game is normal. 3...Bd6 puts the bishop beside the knight where White's centre pawns can reach them both, and 4.Nxe5 exploits it: after 4...Bxe5 5.d4 Bd6 6.e5 the pawn hits bishop and knight together, and after 6...Bb4 7.exf6 Qxf6 White has won back the piece and is a pawn up.
3294566395905444|f1c4.principle: When an enemy bishop and knight stand side by side within reach of your centre pawns, check the capture that clears the way for a pawn fork.

3294907482050607|f3g5.headline: Guard e4 with 4.Nc3 instead of moving the knight twice
3294907482050607|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight again, and 4...e6 covers f7 and blunts your bishop. After 5.d3 Be7 6.O-O O-O 7.Nc3 Nc6 8.Re1 a6 the g5-knight has no target and Black has the easier game. 4.Nc3 develops a new piece and guards e4 against 4...Nxe4. After 4...e6 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 a6 7.a4 you have an Open Sicilian with your bishop on c4 and a level game.
3294907482050607|f3g5.principle: Develop a new piece rather than moving one twice: 4.Nc3 guards e4 and develops, while 4.Ng5 spends a second knight move that 4...e6 answers.

ideas.title: Guard e4 first
ideas.text: 3...Nf6 attacks e4. 4.Nc3 or 4.d3 defends it; castling first allows 4...Nxe4.

ideas.title: No time for knight raids
ideas.text: 4.Ng5 moves a piece twice; 4...e6 covers f7 and the knight has nothing to hit.

ideas.title: Open Sicilian with Bc4
ideas.text: Pushing d4 can give an Open Sicilian with your bishop already on c4, as in 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4.

ideas.title: Italian-style setup
ideas.text: The quiet alternative from IM Krishnater's course: d3, castling and c3, later a rook to e1, a4 and the bishop back to b3.

habit.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight again, and 4...e6 covers f7 and blunts your bishop. After 5.d3 Be7 6.O-O O-O 7.Nc3 Nc6 8.Re1 a6 the g5-knight has no target and Black has the easier game.

strays.text: The knight jumps to g5, but 4...e6 leaves it nothing to hit.

taught.why: 4.Nc3 develops a new piece and guards e4 against 4...Nxe4. After 4...e6 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 a6 7.a4 you have an Open Sicilian with your bishop on c4 and a level game.

enforces.text: The knight defends e4 and develops in one move.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.d3 guards e4 and is the main line in IM Krishnater's course. After 4...e6 5.O-O Be7 6.a4 O-O 7.Bb3 you keep a solid Italian-style position. It's fully sound.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 also guards e4 but heads for an open game with d4; 4.d3 is the slower plan with c3 and a rook on e1. The engine rates them the same.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.O-O leaves e4 hanging: after 4...Nxe4 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 e6 you're a pawn down without enough for it.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 defends e4 first; you can castle later, once Black can no longer take the pawn.

3297019676720294|d8e7.headline: 5...Qg5 hits the knight on e5 and the g2 pawn at once
3297019676720294|d8e7.why: 5...Qe7 attacks only the knight, so 6.d4 gains time on your bishop. You get the pawn back with 6...Bb4+ 7.c3 Bd6 8.O-O Bxe5 9.dxe5 Qxe5, but White has castled, your dark-squared bishop is gone and after 10.Re1 White is well ahead in development. 5...Qg5 hits the e5 knight and g2 together, so White must deal with both at once. After 6.Ng4 d5 7.d4 Qxg4 8.Qxg4 Bxg4 9.dxc5 dxe4 material is level with the queens off.
3297019676720294|d8e7.principle: When you need a pawn back, use a move with two threats: 5...Qg5 hits the knight and g2, so White has no time for 6.d4.
sources: Andrew Kauffman, The Ruy Lopez Opening: How to Play It as White and Black (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/the-ruy-lopez-opening-how-to-play-it-as-white-and-black/

ideas.title: Bxc6 and Nxe5 is not yet a threat
ideas.text: With the d-file closed, the queen uses g5 instead: it hits the e5 knight and g2 at once, and you win the pawn back.

ideas.title: The c5 bishop is a target
ideas.text: Slow moves let 6.d4 hit your c5 bishop with tempo, and White keeps the extra pawn.

ideas.title: Open the c8 bishop with ...d5
ideas.text: After 6.Ng4, 6...d5 opens your c8 bishop onto the knight, and 7.d4 Qxg4 8.Qxg4 Bxg4 evens the material.

habit.why: 5...Qe7 attacks only the knight, so 6.d4 gains time on your bishop. You get the pawn back with 6...Bb4+ 7.c3 Bd6 8.O-O Bxe5 9.dxe5 Qxe5, but White has castled, your dark-squared bishop is gone and after 10.Re1 White is well ahead in development.

strays.idea: The c5 bishop is a target
strays.text: 6.d4 gains time on your bishop, and White castles first.

taught.why: 5...Qg5 hits the e5 knight and g2 together, so White must deal with both at once. After 6.Ng4 d5 7.d4 Qxg4 8.Qxg4 Bxg4 9.dxc5 dxe4 material is level with the queens off.

enforces.idea: Bxc6 and Nxe5 is not yet a threat
enforces.text: The double attack on e5 and g2 wins the pawn back by force.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5...Nf6 develops and hits e4, but White simply keeps the pawn: 6.d4 Be7 7.Nc3 pushes your bishop back and guards e4.
alternatives.after: 5...Qg5 regains the pawn by force with its double attack on e5 and g2. 5...Nf6 gives White time for 6.d4.
alternatives.idea: The c5 bishop is a target

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: The queen hits e5 and f2, but 6.d4 shuts the bishop's line with tempo, and after 6...Bb6 7.O-O f2 is safe and White stays a pawn up.
alternatives.after: 5...Qg5 hits targets that 6.d4 can't cover: the knight and g2.
alternatives.idea: The c5 bishop is a target

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...d6 kicks the knight, but after 6.Nf3 White is simply a healthy pawn up and you have no forcing way to win it back.
alternatives.after: 5...Qg5 wins the pawn back by force, because White must answer threats to the e5 knight and g2 at once.
alternatives.idea: Bxc6 and Nxe5 is not yet a threat

3303598185152393|d1d5.headline: Develop with 4.Nc3; the early 4.Qd5 just gets chased
3303598185152393|d1d5.why: 4.Qd5 brings your queen out with three minor pieces still at home, and Black develops by attacking it. After 4...Nc6 5.Bf4 Be6 6.Qd2 dxe5 7.Qxd8+ Rxd8 8.Bxe5 Nxe5 Black wins the pawn back and the queens are gone. 4.Nc3 develops and gives your queen a second guard, so the ...Bxf2+ tricks fail. After 4...Nc6 5.Bf4 Nge7 6.exd6 cxd6 you keep the extra pawn and develop smoothly.
3303598185152393|d1d5.principle: Keep the queen home while the minor pieces sleep: 4.Qd5 lets Black develop by attacking it, while 4.Nc3 develops and guards the queen.
sources: How to Play and Play Against the Englund Gambit (chess.com blog) | https://www.chess.com/blog/SavageOppress/how-to-play-and-play-against-the-englund-gambit-an-in-depth-guide

ideas.title: Derek Wu trap
ideas.text: 3...d6 sets the trap: after 4.exd6 Ne7, taking with 5.dxe7 loses your queen to 5...Bxf2+ and 6...Qxd1.

ideas.title: Nc3 defuses the f2 tricks
ideas.text: 4.Nc3 adds a second guard to your queen, so ...Bxf2+ deflections stop working and you keep the extra pawn.

ideas.title: Black develops by hitting your queen
ideas.text: An early queen on d5 is a target: 4...Nc6 and 5...Be6 develop with gain of time.

ideas.title: Take the pawn, keep e5
ideas.text: You're a pawn up; develop so e5 stays covered, as 5.Bf4 does, and swap on d6 only when it suits you.

habit.why: 4.Qd5 brings your queen out with three minor pieces still at home, and Black develops by attacking it. After 4...Nc6 5.Bf4 Be6 6.Qd2 dxe5 7.Qxd8+ Rxd8 8.Bxe5 Nxe5 Black wins the pawn back and the queens are gone.

strays.idea: Black develops by hitting your queen
strays.text: Every Black developing move comes with a hit on your queen.

taught.why: 4.Nc3 develops and gives your queen a second guard, so the ...Bxf2+ tricks fail. After 4...Nc6 5.Bf4 Nge7 6.exd6 cxd6 you keep the extra pawn and develop smoothly.

enforces.text: A second guard on your queen takes the sting out of ...Bxf2+.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.exd6 is the natural capture, but it walks into the Derek Wu trap: after 4...Ne7, 5.dxe7 loses your queen to 5...Bxf2+. Even without the trap, Black develops quickly.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 guards your queen first, so the trap can't work, and you take on d6 later on your terms, as with 6.exd6 cxd6.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.e3 blunts the c5-bishop but shuts in your c1-bishop, and after 4...Qe7 5.exd6 Bxd6 Black develops quickly with easy play.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 develops a piece and keeps the c1-bishop free for 5.Bf4, guarding e5.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.Bg5 develops with a hit on the queen, but after 4...Ne7 5.exd6 Nbc6 Black gets active pieces for the pawn.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 is more solid: it guards your queen against ...Bxf2+ tricks before you start chasing Black's pieces.

3324621583464853|c6e5.headline: Develop with 5...Bb4 instead of moving the c6 knight again
3324621583464853|c6e5.why: 5...Ne5 moves the knight a second time and puts it where White's pawns can chase it: 6.f4 kicks it back to c6 and 7.e5 sends the other knight home to g8, so White gains a lot of time. 5...Bb4 develops a bishop, pins the knight on c3 and prepares to castle. After 6.Bd2 O-O 7.Bd3 d5 Black strikes in the centre, the break that White's queen retreat 4.Qd1 allows.
3324621583464853|c6e5.principle: With both bishops still at home, a second knight move needs a concrete gain; this one has none and only gives White's pawns a target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Qxd4/3...Nc6

3337365835027440|d2d3.headline: Strike with 4.d4 and gain time on Black's early queen
3337365835027440|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is solid but gives Black time: 4...Be6 trades off your c4-bishop after 5.Bb3 Bxb3 6.axb3, and 6...Qd8 takes the queen home. You play 7.d4 a move later anyway, and Black has fixed the early-queen problem. 4.d4 hits e5 at once, so Black must react instead of developing. After 4...Nc6 5.d5 Nb8 6.Nc3 Qd8 both Black pieces are back home while you have three pieces out.
3337365835027440|d2d3.principle: When the opponent brings the queen out early, open the centre and gain time against it instead of playing a slow pawn move.
sources: Lessons - Philidor's Defence (Exeter Chess Club) | https://www.exeterchessclub.org.uk/content/lessons-philidors-defence

ideas.title: Claim the centre with d4
ideas.text: Against ...d6 your centre is better. 4.d4 hits e5 at once, while the slower d3 lets Black settle.

ideas.title: Gain time on the early queen
ideas.text: 3...Qf6 blocks the g8-knight. Developing with threats, like 4.Nc3 and 5.Nd5, sends the queen back and wins you time.

ideas.title: Philidor structure: solid but cramped
ideas.text: Black's d6-e5 chain is solid but passive: the f8-bishop has only e7, and Black's kingside pieces are slow to come out.

habit.why: 4.d3 is solid but gives Black time: 4...Be6 trades off your c4-bishop after 5.Bb3 Bxb3 6.axb3, and 6...Qd8 takes the queen home. You play 7.d4 a move later anyway, and Black has fixed the early-queen problem.

strays.text: The pawn stops on d3, and Black gets time to regroup.

taught.why: 4.d4 hits e5 at once, so Black must react instead of developing. After 4...Nc6 5.d5 Nb8 6.Nc3 Qd8 both Black pieces are back home while you have three pieces out.

enforces.text: 4.d4 hits e5 now and gains time against Black's queen.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Gain time on the early queen
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 is good: it develops and aims at 5.Nd5, hitting the queen, so 5...Qd8 sends it home. There is a slightly more direct move.
alternatives.after: Both are good, and 4.Nc3 reaches 6.d4 a move later. 4.d4 strikes e5 first and gains time on the queen at once.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.idea: Gain time on the early queen
alternatives.before: Castling is safe but slow: 4...Bg4 pins your f3-knight to the queen, and you spend 5.Be2 dealing with it.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 uses the move to hit e5 and gain time on the queen; castling can wait a move or two.

3350501418691275|a7a6.headline: Stop e4-e5 with 5...d6 before it kicks your knight
3350501418691275|a7a6.why: 5...a6 does nothing about e4-e5, and 6.e5 Ng8 sends your knight back home. After 7.Bf4 Ne7 8.Bd3 Ng6 9.Bg3 your knight has moved four times while White has space and a big lead in development. 5...d6 covers e5, so your knight stays on f6. After 6.g4 h6 7.Rg1 Nc6 8.Be3 Bd7 9.Be2 d5 you meet the Keres Attack with the central ...d5 break once your pieces are out.
3350501418691275|a7a6.principle: A piece a pawn can attack is a target: 5...d6 controls e5, while 5...a6 lets 6.e5 chase your knight home.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6

ideas.title: The e4-e5 kick
ideas.text: With your knight on f6 and no pawn on d6, e4-e5 drives it away: 6.e5 sends it back to g8.

ideas.title: Control e5 with ...d6
ideas.text: 5...d6 stops e4-e5 for good and gives a Scheveningen, the most common choice here (55% of master games).

ideas.title: White's Keres Attack
ideas.text: Against the Scheveningen, White's sharpest try is 6.g4, aiming g5 at your knight; Semkov names it, with White's f4 and queen-to-f3 system, as the Scheveningen's biggest problem.

habit.why: 5...a6 does nothing about e4-e5, and 6.e5 Ng8 sends your knight back home. After 7.Bf4 Ne7 8.Bd3 Ng6 9.Bg3 your knight has moved four times while White has space and a big lead in development.

strays.text: Without ...d6, nothing stops 6.e5 from kicking the knight.

taught.why: 5...d6 covers e5, so your knight stays on f6. After 6.g4 h6 7.Rg1 Nc6 8.Be3 Bd7 9.Be2 d5 you meet the Keres Attack with the central ...d5 break once your pieces are out.

enforces.text: The d6 pawn holds e5, so the f6-knight can't be kicked.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Bb4, the Pin Variation, hits e4 at once, but 6.e5 Nd5 7.Qg4 attacks g7 and 7...Kf8 costs you castling.
alternatives.after: 5...d6 stops 6.e5 before it happens. The pin works better when a knight on c6 is ready to meet e5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...Nc6 is the Sicilian Four Knights, played in 41% of master games and judged sound by Willis and Kotronias. The engine grades it lower: 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.e5 Nd5 8.Ne4 leaves you a dark-square hole that the e5 pawn and the e4-knight eye.
alternatives.after: 5...d6 is a little more popular (55% to 41%) and stops e4-e5 at once. Both are normal; the engine just prefers 5...d6.

3383188774541308|d8f6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qg5 forks the knight and g2.
3383188774541308|d8f6.why: 5...Qf6 attacks only the knight, and 6.Ng4 hits the queen while White keeps the pawn. 5...Qg5 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 together, and after 6.Ng4 h5 7.Ne3 Nxb5 8.Nxb5 Bxe3 Black wins a knight for a pawn.
3383188774541308|d8f6.principle: When a knight grabs a pawn, look for the queen move that attacks it and a second target at once; a double attack beats a single one.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

3400735200665154|g5e4.headline: Don't recapture on e4: 5.Bxf7+ comes first, with check
3400735200665154|g5e4.why: 5.Nxe4 walks into 5...d5, a pawn fork of your knight and c4 bishop. After 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Bd7 material is level, but Black has a free centre and easy development, and your attack is gone. 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 wins back the pawn with check, and Black's king can never castle. 6.d4 stops Black taking on g5, since your c1 bishop would recapture with check and win the queen; after 6...h6 7.Nxe4 Kxf7 8.d5 the king stays exposed.
3400735200665154|g5e4.principle: Look for checks before recaptures: 5.Bxf7+ forces Black's king to move, while the natural 5.Nxe4 runs into the 5...d5 fork.
sources: Jan Pinski, The Two Knights Defence (Everyman, 2004) | https://masterinchess.com/Media/2024/07/The%20Two%20Knights%20Defence.pdf

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: 5.Bxf7+ takes f7 with check: the king must go to e7, can never castle, and 6.d4 follows with tempo.

ideas.title: Black's counter-threats
ideas.text: Black's e4 knight hits your g5 knight and f2. A queen on h4 would add a second attacker on f2.

ideas.title: The skewer on g5
ideas.text: After 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 6.d4, taking on g5 fails: your c1 bishop recaptures with check and wins the queen behind the king.

ideas.title: Watch the d5 fork
ideas.text: If your knight takes on e4, the pawn jump to d5 forks it and the c4 bishop, and Black wins the piece back.

habit.why: 5.Nxe4 walks into 5...d5, a pawn fork of your knight and c4 bishop. After 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Bd7 material is level, but Black has a free centre and easy development, and your attack is gone.

strays.text: Recapturing on e4 lets 5...d5 fork knight and bishop.

taught.why: 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 wins back the pawn with check, and Black's king can never castle. 6.d4 stops Black taking on g5, since your c1 bishop would recapture with check and win the queen; after 6...h6 7.Nxe4 Kxf7 8.d5 the king stays exposed.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
enforces.text: The bishop takes with check, and the e4 knight can wait.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.Nxf7 forks queen and rook, but 5...Qh4 threatens mate on f2. After 6.Qe2 Nd4 7.g3 Nxe2 8.gxh4 Nd4 9.Nxh8 Nxc2+ Black forks back, and you have no edge.
alternatives.after: 5.Bxf7+ takes the same pawn with check, so Black never gets time for 5...Qh4, and the king can never castle.

3400735200665154|g5f7.headline: Take on f7 with the bishop and check, not the knight
3400735200665154|g5f7.why: 5.Nxf7 forks queen and rook, but 5...Qh4 hits f2 with the queen and the e4 knight and threatens mate. After 6.Qe2 Nd4 7.g3 Nxe2 8.gxh4 Nd4 9.Nxh8 Nxc2+ Black forks your king and rook, and you have no advantage left. 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 wins back the pawn with check, and Black's king can never castle. 6.d4 stops Black taking on g5, since your c1 bishop would recapture with check and win the queen; after 6...h6 7.Nxe4 Kxf7 8.d5 the king stays exposed.
3400735200665154|g5f7.principle: Check the opponent's threats before grabbing material, and prefer captures with check: 5.Bxf7+ moves the king before Black has time for 5...Qh4.
sources: Jan Pinski, The Two Knights Defence (Everyman, 2004) | https://masterinchess.com/Media/2024/07/The%20Two%20Knights%20Defence.pdf

ideas.title: The skewer on g5

ideas.title: Watch the d5 fork
ideas.text: If your knight takes on e4, the pawn jump to d5 forks it and the c4 bishop, and Black wins the piece back.

habit.why: 5.Nxf7 forks queen and rook, but 5...Qh4 hits f2 with the queen and the e4 knight and threatens mate. After 6.Qe2 Nd4 7.g3 Nxe2 8.gxh4 Nd4 9.Nxh8 Nxc2+ Black forks your king and rook, and you have no advantage left.

strays.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
strays.text: The knight takes without check, so Black strikes first with 5...Qh4.

taught.why: 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 wins back the pawn with check, and Black's king can never castle. 6.d4 stops Black taking on g5, since your c1 bishop would recapture with check and win the queen; after 6...h6 7.Nxe4 Kxf7 8.d5 the king stays exposed.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.Nxe4 takes the knight back, but 5...d5 forks your e4 knight and c4 bishop. After 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Black has a free centre and the better game.
alternatives.after: 5.Bxf7+ comes first, with check, and you take the e4 knight later with 7.Nxe4, when your bishop is no longer on c4 to be forked.

3408833361615716|e2e3.headline: A pawn up, develop with 3.Nc3 and guard your queen
3408833361615716|e2e3.why: 3.e3 blocks the c5-bishop's view of f2 but shuts in your c1-bishop. After 3...Nc6 4.Nf3 Qe7 5.Bd2 d6 6.exd6 Bxd6 7.Nc3 Nf6 your e5 pawn is gone and Black has developed every piece, so your extra pawn counts for much less. 3.Nc3 develops and gives your queen a second guard, so the ...Bxf2+ tricks fail. After 3...Nc6 4.Nf3 Nge7 5.Ne4 your knight hits the c5-bishop, and by 7...Kf8 Black has given up castling while you keep the extra pawn.
3408833361615716|e2e3.principle: A pawn up, develop quickly and with threats: 3.Nc3 brings out a piece, guards the queen against ...Bxf2+ tricks and heads for e4 to hit the c5-bishop.
sources: How to Play and Play Against the Englund Gambit (chess.com blog) | https://www.chess.com/blog/SavageOppress/how-to-play-and-play-against-the-englund-gambit-an-in-depth-guide

ideas.title: Take the pawn, keep e5
ideas.text: You're a pawn up. Develop so e5 stays guarded, as 3.Nf3 or 3.Bf4 does, and Black has to prove the gambit.

ideas.title: Nc3 defuses the f2 tricks
ideas.text: The c5-bishop eyes f2. With 3.Nc3 a second piece guards your queen, so the ...Bxf2+ deflection of the Derek Wu trap fails.

ideas.title: Derek Wu trap
ideas.text: After 3.Nf3 d6 4.exd6 Ne7, taking with 5.dxe7 loses your queen to 5...Bxf2+ and 6...Qxd1.

ideas.title: Hit the c5-bishop
ideas.text: Your knight can jump to e4 and attack the bishop, as in 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.Nf3 Nge7 5.Ne4, gaining more time.

habit.why: 3.e3 blocks the c5-bishop's view of f2 but shuts in your c1-bishop. After 3...Nc6 4.Nf3 Qe7 5.Bd2 d6 6.exd6 Bxd6 7.Nc3 Nf6 your e5 pawn is gone and Black has developed every piece, so your extra pawn counts for much less.

strays.text: Your c1-bishop is shut in, so nothing helps hold e5.

taught.why: 3.Nc3 develops and gives your queen a second guard, so the ...Bxf2+ tricks fail. After 3...Nc6 4.Nf3 Nge7 5.Ne4 your knight hits the c5-bishop, and by 7...Kf8 Black has given up castling while you keep the extra pawn.

enforces.text: A second guard on your queen takes the sting out of ...Bxf2+.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Nf3 is the most common move and guards e5, but it allows the Derek Wu trap: after 3...d6 4.exd6 Ne7, 5.dxe7 loses the queen to 5...Bxf2+. A slightly stronger move exists.
alternatives.after: 3.Nc3 guards your queen at once, so the trap never works; 3.Nf3 is fine as long as you don't take on e7.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Bf4 holds e5 with a piece, the standard Englund method: after 3...Ne7 4.e3 Ng6 5.Bg3 your bishop keeps guarding it. Another move is about as strong.
alternatives.after: 3.Nc3 and 3.Bf4 are close; 3.Nc3 also guards your queen against ...Bxf2+ tricks and prepares 5.Ne4 against the bishop.

3415269394174453|b2b4.headline: 5.d3 builds a quiet Pianissimo; 5.b4 just drops a pawn
3415269394174453|b2b4.why: 5.b4 offers a pawn, but after 5...Bxb4 your knight on c3 blocks the c-pawn, so there is no c3 and d4 to gain time on the bishop. In the line 6.Nd5 O-O 7.Nxb4 Nxb4 the pieces come off and you are simply a pawn down. 5.d3 guards e4 and keeps the position quiet; masters play it in 88% of games. In the line 5...a6 6.O-O d6 7.a4 h6 8.Ne2 you castle, gain queenside space and free your c-pawn for 9.c3.
3415269394174453|b2b4.principle: In a level position, don't throw in a pawn for an attack that isn't there: guard your centre, castle and build slowly.

ideas.title: The Pianissimo set-up
ideas.text: Build slowly: castle, gain space with a4 and reroute the c3 knight via e2, as in 7.a4 h6 8.Ne2.

ideas.title: Keep e4 guarded
ideas.text: Black's f6 knight hits e4. 5.d3 guards it with a pawn, so your pieces stay free.

ideas.title: No c3, no Evans Gambit
ideas.text: In the Evans Gambit, b4 is followed by c3 and d4. Here your knight blocks the c-pawn, so after 5.b4 Bxb4 nothing hits the bishop.

ideas.title: Ng5 hits f7 only when it hurts
ideas.text: With Black's bishop on c5, 5...O-O guards f7 at once, so a knight jump to g5 just moves a piece twice.

habit.why: 5.b4 offers a pawn, but after 5...Bxb4 your knight on c3 blocks the c-pawn, so there is no c3 and d4 to gain time on the bishop. In the line 6.Nd5 O-O 7.Nxb4 Nxb4 the pieces come off and you are simply a pawn down.

strays.text: Without a c3 push, the b4 pawn is lost for nothing.

taught.why: 5.d3 guards e4 and keeps the position quiet; masters play it in 88% of games. In the line 5...a6 6.O-O d6 7.a4 h6 8.Ne2 you castle, gain queenside space and free your c-pawn for 9.c3.

enforces.text: Guard e4, castle, and build slowly instead of forcing matters.

alternatives.label: sound

3415269394174453|f3e5.headline: The fork trick fails here; play the quiet 5.d3.
3415269394174453|f3e5.why: 5.Nxe5 Nxe5 6.d4 hopes to fork the knight and the bishop on c5, but the knight answers 6...Nxc4 by taking White's own bishop. After 7.dxc5 White has given a knight for a pawn. 5.d3 is the hallmark of the Giuoco Pianissimo: it defends e4, opens a line for the dark-squared bishop, and prepares a slow build-up.
3415269394174453|f3e5.principle: Before a capture that relies on a follow-up fork, check what your own loose pieces can be taken in reply.

3415269394174453|f3g5.headline: 5.d3 builds quietly; 5.Ng5 runs into 5...O-O
3415269394174453|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again to hit f7, but 5...O-O guards it with the rook and the attack is over. After 6.d3 Nd4 7.Nf3 the knight goes back, two moves wasted, and Black's knight sits on d4. 5.d3 guards e4 and keeps the position quiet; masters play it in 88% of games. In the line 5...a6 6.O-O d6 7.a4 h6 8.Ne2 you castle, gain queenside space and free your c-pawn for 9.c3.
3415269394174453|f3g5.principle: Don't move a piece twice in the opening unless it wins something; here castling makes the knight jump pointless.

3420590449456095|c1e3.headline: Pin the c6-knight with 6.Bb5 before it hits d4
3420590449456095|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 adds a defender to d4 but leaves the c3-knight pinned and the c6-knight free. After 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 O-O-O 9.O-O-O e5 10.d5 Nd4 Black's knight lands in the centre with active play. 6.Bb5 develops and pins the c6-knight to your king, so it can't take part in the fight for d4. After 6...Nd5 7.Rb1 a6 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 9.O-O Black's c-pawns are doubled and isolated, and you have castled.
3420590449456095|c1e3.principle: A pin ties a piece down: pin the knight that would attack d4, and Black's pressure on your centre loses its key piece.
sources: IM John Bartholomew, Main Line Scandinavian (Chessiverse) | https://chessiverse.com/resources/openings/main-line-scandinavian

ideas.title: Pin the c6-knight
ideas.text: 6.Bb5 pins the c6-knight to your king, so it can't join ...Bg4 and ...O-O-O against d4. It's the masters' top choice (48%).

ideas.title: Black's pressure on d4
ideas.text: Black's knight, a bishop on g4 and a rook after ...O-O-O can all hit d4; only your queen and f3-knight defend it.

ideas.title: The pin on c3
ideas.text: Black's queen on a5 pins your c3-knight to the king. A bishop on d2 breaks the pin; 6.Be3 does not.

ideas.title: Broken pawns for Black
ideas.text: If Black chases the bishop with ...a6, 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 leaves Black with doubled, isolated c-pawns.

habit.why: 6.Be3 adds a defender to d4 but leaves the c3-knight pinned and the c6-knight free. After 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 O-O-O 9.O-O-O e5 10.d5 Nd4 Black's knight lands in the centre with active play.

strays.text: The c6-knight stays free and lands on d4 in the end.

taught.why: 6.Bb5 develops and pins the c6-knight to your king, so it can't take part in the fight for d4. After 6...Nd5 7.Rb1 a6 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 9.O-O Black's c-pawns are doubled and isolated, and you have castled.

enforces.text: While the pin lasts, the c6-knight can't jump to d4 or e5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Bd2 breaks the pin on c3 and is the masters' second choice (33%). It's sound, but d4 needs watching: after 6...a6 7.Bc4 Nxd4 the c6-knight joins in with a tactic.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5 takes the c6-knight out of play first, so a trick like 7...Nxd4 can't happen while the pin lasts. Masters play 6.Bb5 in 48% of games, 6.Bd2 in 33%.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: After 6.Bc4 Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 O-O-O Black's pieces pile up on d4, and after 9.d5 Ne5 the knight hits your queen and bishop. Your edge is gone.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5 pins the c6-knight, so it can't join the attack on d4 or jump to e5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Be2 is too quiet: 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Bxf3 e5 lets Black strike at d4 at once.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5 pins the c6-knight, the piece that supports ...e5 and hits d4. Masters prefer it, 48% to 4%.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.d5 chases the knight, but after 6...Nb4 7.Bc4 e6 8.dxe6 Bxe6 9.Bxe6 fxe6 Black is developed and comfortable. Masters play it in 7% of games, but the engine doesn't like it.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5 develops a piece and keeps your pawn on d4, while 6.d5 spends a move and then trades it off.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.h3 stops ...Bg4 before it comes, so the f3-knight keeps guarding d4; after 6...a6 7.Bc4 b5 8.Bb3 Black gains queenside space. Sound, but another move does more.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5 develops and deals with the c6-knight directly, while 6.h3 spends a pawn move on prevention. Masters prefer 6.Bb5, 48% to 6%; the engine rates both close.

3420590449456095|f1d3.headline: Black is eyeing d4: pin the c6-knight with 6.Bb5
3420590449456095|f1d3.why: 6.Bd3 blocks your queen's guard of d4, leaving only the f3-knight to defend it. Black goes after that knight: 6...Bg4 7.Bd2 O-O-O 8.Nb5 Qb6 9.a4 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Nxd4 wins the pawn. 6.Bb5 develops and pins the c6-knight to your king, so it can't take part in the fight for d4. After 6...Nd5 7.Rb1 a6 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 9.O-O Black's c-pawns are doubled and isolated, and d4 is safe.
3420590449456095|f1d3.principle: Count the defenders before you develop: 6.Bd3 blocks the queen's guard of d4 just as Black lines up the knight, the g4-bishop and a rook against it.
sources: IM John Bartholomew, Main Line Scandinavian (Chessiverse) | https://chessiverse.com/resources/openings/main-line-scandinavian

3428826784804820|d7d5.headline: Against the Bishop's Opening, attack e4 with 2...Nf6.
3428826784804820|d7d5.why: The bishop on c4 already watches d5, so 2...d5 just gives up a pawn after 3.exd5. Black gets some activity, but not enough for the pawn. 2...Nf6 develops and attacks the pawn on e4, and it also covers h5, ruling out the early 3.Qh5 aimed at f7.
3428826784804820|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a pawn to a central square, count how many enemy pieces and pawns already attack it.

3428826784804820|d7d6.headline: Answer the Bishop's Opening with 2...Nf6, developing with a threat
3428826784804820|d7d6.why: 2...d6 overprotects a pawn that isn't attacked, since White has not played Nf3, and it shuts in Black's own king's bishop. 2...Nf6 develops with a threat to the pawn on e4, and it also controls h5, so White can't aim the queen at f7 with 3.Qh5. It is the choice in 83.2% of master games.
3428826784804820|d7d6.principle: When the e4-pawn is unprotected, develop the knight to f6 so your developing move also gains time by attacking it.
