3428826784804820|d8e7.headline: Against 2.Bc4, develop 2...Nf6 instead of the queen
3428826784804820|d8e7.why: 2...Qe7 guards e5 and f7 with the queen and blocks the bishop on f8 while all four minor pieces are still at home; White just develops with 3.Nf3 and 4.O-O and then strikes with 5.d4. 2...Nf6 develops the king's knight with an attack on e4 and takes h5 away from White's queen, ruling out 3.Qh5. Masters choose it in 83.2% of games.
3428826784804820|d8e7.principle: Meet early pressure with a developing move that attacks, not with the queen, which only blocks your own pieces and becomes a target.

3428826784804820|d8f6.headline: Develop with 2...Nf6, which attacks e4 and guards h5
3428826784804820|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home and takes the knight's natural square. White develops calmly, and in the engine line the knight jumps to d5 with 7.Nd5, gaining time on your queen. 2...Nf6, played in 83% of master games, develops while attacking the e4 pawn and controls h5, so the scholar's-mate idea 3.Qh5 is off the table.
3428826784804820|d8f6.principle: Bring the knights out first and let them do the defending; the queen on f6 blocks the knight and becomes a target.

3428826784804820|d8h4.headline: Answer 2.Bc4 with 2...Nf6, not an early queen raid
3428826784804820|d8h4.why: 2...Qh4 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home; after 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.Qe2 d6 5.Nf3 the knight hits the queen and it goes back with 5...Qd8, so Black has spent two moves for nothing. 2...Nf6 develops, attacks the pawn on e4 and controls h5, which rules out White's own queen raid. It is the master choice in 83% of games.
3428826784804820|d8h4.principle: An early queen only gives White targets to develop against with gain of time; bring out the knight that attacks e4 instead.

3428826784804820|f7f5.headline: Answer 2.Bc4 with 2...Nf6, not a risky f-pawn push
3428826784804820|f7f5.why: 2...f5 is the Calabrese Countergambit, a risky system that loosens Black's king before any piece is out, while the bishop on c4 already aims at f7. White opens lines with 3.d4 exd4 and gets active pieces, as in 4.Nh3 Nc6 5.Ng5. 2...Nf6 develops with an attack on e4 and covers h5, which rules out 3.Qh5; masters choose it in 83.2% of games.
3428826784804820|f7f5.principle: With White's bishop on c4 aiming at f7, keep the f-pawn home and develop the knight to f6, which also covers h5.

3428826784804820|f7f6.headline: Put the knight on f6, not the pawn
3428826784804820|f7f6.why: 2...f6 takes the g8-knight's best square and opens the diagonal from c4 to your king, while White calmly builds the centre with 3.d4 and develops with 4.Nf3 and 5.O-O. 2...Nf6 develops with an attack on the pawn on e4 and covers h5, so it fights for the centre and keeps White's queen out at the same time.
3428826784804820|f7f6.principle: The bishop on c4 already aims at f7 and g8, so never loosen that diagonal further; meet it with pieces, not pawn moves around your king.

3428826784804820|g8h6.headline: Knight to f6, not the rim: hit e4 and cover h5
3428826784804820|g8h6.why: 2...Nh6 puts the knight on the rim, where it neither attacks e4 nor contests d5, and White gets a free hand in the centre with 3.Nf3 and 4.d4. 2...Nf6 develops the same knight to its natural square, attacks the pawn on e4 and covers h5, so the scholar's-mate idea 3.Qh5 is off the table.
3428826784804820|g8h6.principle: A knight on f6 controls central squares and hits e4, while on h6 it controls nothing central; pick the square that fights for the middle.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6

3450965353871567|d8f6.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6, which also stops 4.Qg4
3450965353871567|d8f6.why: 3...Qf6 guards g7 against 4.Qg4, but it brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home and takes the best square from your knight. In the engine line the knight has to settle for 4...Ne7, and White's knight jumps to b5 with 6.Nb5 to go after c7. 3...Nf6 is the most popular move in master games: it develops toward the centre and covers g4, so the queen can't come there to attack g7.
3450965353871567|d8f6.principle: Meet a threat with a developing move when you can; the queen should stay home while the minor pieces are still undeveloped.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Bc5

3450965353871567|f7f6.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6; 3...f6 opens the king to checks.
3450965353871567|f7f6.why: 3...f6 weakens the squares around Black's king. After 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qh4 Black has a loose kingside, and the bishop on c4 eyes g8, so castling is uncomfortable. White was also threatening 4.Qg4 to win a pawn. 3...Nf6 develops the knight to its natural square, covers g4 and h5, and prepares to castle.
3450965353871567|f7f6.principle: When the bishop on c4 aims at your king's side, protect it by developing pieces, not by moving the f-pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Bc5

3451177064254537|d8b6.headline: Don't bring the queen out: strike with 6...d5 instead
3451177064254537|d8b6.why: 6...Qb6 brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home, and White simply castles and breaks. After 7.O-O Nf6 8.Nc3 Be7 9.d5 exd5 10.exd5 the c6 knight is driven off and the e-file opens with your king still on e8. 6...d5 hits the c4 bishop and the e4 pawn and rules out 7.d5 for good. After 7.exd5 exd5 8.Bb3 Bb4+ 9.Nc3 Nf6 you have an isolated d-pawn but free, quick development.
3451177064254537|d8b6.principle: Don't bring the queen out early: 6...Qb6 hits d4 but leaves three minor pieces at home while White castles and breaks with 9.d5.

3451177064254537|g8f6.headline: Hit the c4 bishop and e4 with 6...d5 before developing

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

ideas.title: White threatens d4-d5
ideas.text: 7.d5 would hit your c6 knight and e6 pawn; after 7...exd5 8.exd5 Ne5 9.Qe2 White wins a pawn.

ideas.title: Strike with ...d5
ideas.text: 6...d5 hits the c4 bishop and the e4 pawn at once and stops d4-d5 for good.

ideas.title: ...e6 blunts the c4 bishop
ideas.text: Your e6 pawn keeps the c4 bishop off f7 and prepares ...d5 with gain of time.

ideas.title: White's broad centre
ideas.text: Given time, White keeps pawns on d4 and e4, castles and pushes 8.e5 to cramp your d6 and e6 pawns.

habit.why: 6...Nf6 develops but lets White gain space: after 7.Qe2 Be7 8.e5 Nd5 the e5 pawn cramps your d6 and e6 pawns. White castles with 9.O-O and builds up with 10.Re1 and 11.Bd2 while your pieces have little room.

strays.text: The knight develops but lets White keep the big centre and push 8.e5.

taught.why: 6...d5 hits the c4 bishop and the e4 pawn and rules out 7.d5 for good. After 7.exd5 exd5 8.Bb3 Bb4+ 9.Nc3 Nf6 you have an isolated d-pawn but free, quick development.

enforces.text: The pawn hits the bishop and e4 together, gaining time.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6...a6 is a useful waiting move in many Sicilians, but here it ignores the centre: after 7.Nc3 Nf6 8.Bd3 Be7 9.O-O O-O 10.Bf4 White keeps the big centre and a free hand.
alternatives.after: 6...d5 challenges the centre at once and gains time on the c4 bishop instead of waiting.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6...Be7 is solid but passive: after 7.Bd3 a6 8.Nc3 Nf6 9.O-O O-O 10.Bf4 White keeps the broad e4/d4 centre.
alternatives.after: 6...d5 strikes at e4 and the bishop before White has finished developing.

3453954165498770|g7g6.headline: Hit the queen and e4 at once with 3...Nf6.
3453954165498770|g7g6.why: 3...g6 does chase the queen, but it develops nothing and ignores e4. After 4.Qd1 White has lost nothing, and Black has weakened the kingside. 3.Bb5 left the pawn on e4 without a defender, and 3...Nf6 attacks the queen on h5 and that pawn at the same time. After 4.Qd1 Nd4 5.a4 Nxe4 Black wins the pawn while developing.
3453954165498770|g7g6.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, chase it with a developing piece that also attacks something else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

3462820906204562|d7d6.headline: 4...Nd4 counterattacks; 4...d6 leaves Black cramped and passive.
3462820906204562|d7d6.why: 4...d6 shuts in the bishop on f8 and lets White open the centre with 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4, leaving Black cramped and a step behind. 4...Nd4 is the Rubinstein variation: the knight jumps to the centre, where it attacks the bishop on b5 and the knight on f3, and after 5.Nxd4 exd4 6.e5 dxc3 7.exf6 Qxf6 Black's pieces come alive.
3462820906204562|d7d6.principle: Answer a developing move with a centralising move that attacks something, rather than a pawn move that only defends.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6/4. Nc3

3464521704326894|e1h1.headline: Defend e4 with 4.d3 before castling
3464521704326894|e1h1.why: 4.O-O leaves e4 hanging, and after 4...Nxe4 White has to spend time getting the pawn back: 5.Bd5 Nf6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.Nxe5 Bc5 gives up the strong bishop and leaves Black with free, active development. 4.d3 simply defends e4 and opens the diagonal for the dark-squared bishop, leading to the calm Giuoco Pianissimo structure that masters choose in 74.6% of games.
3464521704326894|e1h1.principle: Before castling, check whether your e4-pawn is attacked and defended; protect it first, since castling can wait a move.

3472532178632675|f1b5.headline: 5...e5 left f7 weak: your bishop belongs on c4
3472532178632675|f1b5.why: 6.Bb5 pins a knight that is easy to cover, and the bishop no longer aims at f7. After 6...Be7 7.Qa4 Nf6 8.O-O d6 Black is developed, and 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.Qxc6+ Bd7 wins the pawn back only by handing Black the two bishops. 6.Bc4 aims at f7, which Black can no longer shield with ...e6 after 5...e5. If 6...Nf6, then 7.Ng5 hits f7 twice and 7...d5 8.exd5 wins the pawn back with Black's king still in the centre.
3472532178632675|f1b5.principle: Put the bishop where it hits a weakness: after ...e5 Black can no longer shield f7 with ...e6, so the bishop goes to c4, not b5.

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3

ideas.title: Aim at f7 and d5
ideas.text: 5...e5 means Black can't block the a2-g8 diagonal with ...e6. Your bishop belongs on c4 aiming at f7, with 7.Ng5 to follow.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black needs ...Nf6, ...Be7 and castling to make f7 safe. Wade calls 6...Be7 a mistake because your queen jumps to d5 against f7.

ideas.title: The d5 hole
ideas.text: After 5...e5 the d5 square is weak for good: Black's c-pawn is gone and the e-pawn can't go back to e6.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 block
ideas.text: Black shuts a c4 bishop with ...d5, but against 7.Ng5 it costs the pawn: 6.Bc4 Nf6 7.Ng5 d5 8.exd5.

habit.why: 6.Bb5 pins a knight that is easy to cover, and the bishop no longer aims at f7. After 6...Be7 7.Qa4 Nf6 8.O-O d6 Black is developed, and 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.Qxc6+ Bd7 wins the pawn back only by handing Black the two bishops.

strays.text: On b5 the bishop leaves the diagonal toward f7.

taught.why: 6.Bc4 aims at f7, which Black can no longer shield with ...e6 after 5...e5. If 6...Nf6, then 7.Ng5 hits f7 twice and 7...d5 8.exd5 wins the pawn back with Black's king still in the centre.

enforces.text: The bishop goes where ...e5 left f7 open, with 7.Ng5 next.

347661827882589|b8a6.headline: Play 3...e6 first; 3...Na6 lets White double your pawns.
347661827882589|b8a6.why: 3...Na6 guards c7 before it is threatened, and after 4.e3 Bf5 5.Bxa6 bxa6 White trades the bishop for the knight and leaves Black with doubled, isolated a-pawns. 3...e6 reinforces the centre and opens the dark-squared bishop; only after 4.Nb5 threatens the fork on c7 does Black play 4...Na6, and then ...c6 kicks the knight back so Black's knight can reroute via c7.
347661827882589|b8a6.principle: Make the useful developing move first and meet the c7 threat only once it exists, so your knight's placement answers White's actual choice.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3/2...d5/3. Bf4
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3/2...d5/3. Bf4/3...e6

3481634403483951|f7f6.headline: Trade on c4 so the knight has nothing to win on e6
3481634403483951|f7f6.why: White threatens 6.Nxe6 fxe6 7.Bxe6, trading on e6 and then taking the pawn. 5...f6 makes it worse: the f-pawn no longer guards e6, so 6.Nxe6 wins the bishop outright. 5...Bxc4 removes the bishop on c4 that backs up the attack, and after 6.dxc4 h6 7.Nf3 the knight has to retreat and Black is fine.
3481634403483951|f7f6.principle: The bishop on e6 is attacked twice, by the knight on g5 and the bishop on c4, and defended once, by the f7 pawn; remove an attacker rather than weaken the defender.

3516647903289485|f8d6.headline: Develop the g8-knight and meet e4 by trading
3516647903289485|f8d6.why: 6...Bd6 leaves d5 thin, so 7.e4 hits it and your f5-bishop at once, and after 7...Be6 8.d4 Ngf6 your centre is under fire. After 9.exd5 cxd5 10.Nb5 Bb8 11.dxe5 White is a pawn up and hits your f6-knight. 6...Ngf6 develops and adds a guard to d5, so 7.e4 dxe4 8.Nxe4 Nxe4 9.dxe4 just swaps a pair of knights. Your e5-pawn stays well placed, and 9...Be6 puts the bishop on a safe square.
3516647903289485|f8d6.principle: Develop the piece that guards the square White's break hits, then settle the centre by trading when White pushes e4.
sources: Two Ideas Against the KIA (GM Alex Colovic) | https://www.alexcolovic.com/2017/05/two-ideas-kia/
The Réti Opening: How to Play It as White and Black (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/the-reti-opening-how-to-play-as-white-and-black/
Réti Opening (IM Alberto Chueca) | https://www.albertochueca.com/blog/reti-opening-for-white-pieces/

ideas.title: White's e4 break
ideas.text: White plans 7.e4, hitting d5 and your f5-bishop at once. Keep d5 well covered so e4 only leads to trades.

ideas.title: Slav setup against d3
ideas.text: With d3 and no c4, your bishop can come out to f5, Slav-style. Then develop calmly and keep d5 covered; a knight on f6 helps most.

ideas.title: Take on e4 yourself
ideas.text: When White pushes e4, take on e4 and choose the structure yourself: after 7.e4 dxe4 8.Nxe4 Nxe4 9.dxe4 your e5-pawn stands firm.

ideas.title: Bishop on d6 is a target
ideas.text: A bishop on d6 runs into 8.d4 and 10.Nb5: after 10...Bb8 11.dxe5 your e5-pawn is gone.

habit.why: 6...Bd6 leaves d5 thin, so 7.e4 hits it and your f5-bishop at once, and after 7...Be6 8.d4 Ngf6 your centre is under fire. After 9.exd5 cxd5 10.Nb5 Bb8 11.dxe5 White is a pawn up and hits your f6-knight.

strays.text: The bishop leaves d5 thin, so 7.e4 and 8.d4 break open your centre.

taught.why: 6...Ngf6 develops and adds a guard to d5, so 7.e4 dxe4 8.Nxe4 Nxe4 9.dxe4 just swaps a pair of knights. Your e5-pawn stays well placed, and 9...Be6 puts the bishop on a safe square.

enforces.text: 7...dxe4 settles the centre on your terms and swaps knights.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6...Bb4 hits the c3-knight, but after 7.e4 dxe4 8.Nxe4 Bxe4 9.dxe4 Be7 you have given up the f5-bishop and moved the other bishop twice.
alternatives.after: 6...Ngf6 trades on e4 with the knight instead, 7.e4 dxe4 8.Nxe4 Nxe4, so you keep both bishops and lose no time.

3520598348324233|d2d3.headline: Punish the early queen: 3.Nc3 heads for d5 with tempo
3520598348324233|d2d3.why: 2...Qf6 brought the queen out early and took f6 away from Black's knight, and 3.d3 lets Black off with a pawn move instead of attacking it. 3.Nc3 develops and threatens 4.Nd5, centralising the knight with tempo on the queen. After 3...Nc6 4.Nd5 Qd8 the queen has gone back home and White is clearly ahead in development, with Bc4 and castling to follow.
3520598348324233|d2d3.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, develop your pieces to squares where they attack it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

3540159667319526|b7b6.headline: Develop with 5...Nc6; 5...b6 invites 6.dxc5 and 7.b4
3540159667319526|b7b6.why: 5...b6 develops nothing, and White uses the time: 6.dxc5 Bxc5 7.b4 chases the bishop, and after 7...Be7 8.Bb5+ Kf8 you have lost the right to castle. Blocking the check with a piece instead lets White take on d5 and hit your a8 rook down the long diagonal that ...b6 opened. 5...Nc6 develops and adds pressure on d4, so White usually pins it with 6.Bb5 before taking on c5. After 6...Bd6 7.dxc5 Bxc5 8.O-O Nf6 your pieces are out and you get an active isolated-pawn position, as in French Tarrasch lines.
3540159667319526|b7b6.principle: Develop a piece before moving more pawns: 5...Nc6 brings a knight out and presses d4, while 5...b6 only loosens your queenside.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...e6
The Alapin Variation (Matthew Astle, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/the-alapin-variation/

ideas.title: Develop toward d4
ideas.text: 5...Nc6 brings a piece out and hits d4, the pawn White's centre rests on. Pawn moves here only lose time.

ideas.title: Keep the tension on d4
ideas.text: Swapping with ...cxd4 frees White's pieces and leaves you an isolated d5 pawn to defend. Keep your c5 pawn pressing d4.

ideas.title: Watch the b5 check
ideas.text: Your king is still on e8 and the e-file is open, so White's bishop checks on b5 the moment you allow it.

ideas.title: White's dxc5 and b4
ideas.text: If nothing covers c5, White takes with 6.dxc5 and after 6...Bxc5 chases your bishop with 7.b4.

habit.why: 5...b6 develops nothing, and White uses the time: 6.dxc5 Bxc5 7.b4 chases the bishop, and after 7...Be7 8.Bb5+ Kf8 you have lost the right to castle. Blocking the check with a piece instead lets White take on d5 and hit your a8 rook down the long diagonal that ...b6 opened.

strays.text: A pawn move instead of a piece: c5 stays loose and your king stuck.

taught.why: 5...Nc6 develops and adds pressure on d4, so White usually pins it with 6.Bb5 before taking on c5. After 6...Bd6 7.dxc5 Bxc5 8.O-O Nf6 your pieces are out and you get an active isolated-pawn position, as in French Tarrasch lines.

enforces.text: The knight comes out and hits d4 at once, chosen in 70% of master games.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Nf6 is natural development and fine: after 6.Bd3 Be7 7.O-O O-O you have castled safely. Masters prefer another move here, though.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 is the masters' choice (70% to 13%) because the knight presses d4 at once. Both are sound; 5...Nf6 just lets White pick the moment for 10.dxc5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...c4 gives up the pressure on d4 and hands White a target: 6.b3 cxb3 7.axb3 opens the a-file, and 10.b4 later gains space.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 keeps your c5 pawn pressing d4, so White's centre stays under fire instead of being left alone.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5...cxd4 releases the tension and lets White develop with checks: 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Bxd7+ Qxd7 8.O-O and 9.Re1+ come while your king is still in the centre.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 keeps the tension and blocks the b5 diagonal in advance, so a bishop on b5 meets a knight, not your king.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5...Bd6 develops, but White checks first with 6.Bb5+, and after 7.dxc5 Bxc5 8.O-O a6 9.Re1+ Ne7 your king is stuck in the centre a while longer.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 first means 6.Bb5 is only a pin, and after 6...Bd6 you reach the same structure on your terms.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5...a6 stops the bishop check but costs a tempo in an open position: after 6.Bd3 and 7.O-O White is a move ahead in development.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 develops instead and is still fine against 6.Bb5, so you don't need a pawn move to prevent it.

3541436241248924|c4f7.headline: Bxf7+ with no follow-up just loses a bishop
3541436241248924|c4f7.why: 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives a bishop for one pawn, and no other piece can join in because Black's g4-bishop pins your f3 knight to the queen. After 6.h3 Bxf3 7.Qxf3+ Nf6 Black's king is safe and you are a piece down for a pawn. 5.c3 takes d4 from Black's knight and prepares 6.b4, the slow Steinitz plan with pawns on c3 and d3. After 5...Qd7 6.b4 Nf6 7.O-O Be7 8.h3 you have castled and gained queenside space, and Black's bishop must decide.
3541436241248924|c4f7.principle: f7 is defended by the king and attacked only by your bishop, and the f3 knight is pinned, so the capture just trades a bishop for a pawn.
sources: NM Jeremy Kane, Bad Trades Amateurs Make In Chess (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/bad-trades-amateurs-make-in-chess

ideas.title: Don't rush at f7
ideas.text: f7 is guarded by the king and only your bishop hits it. Take there only when another piece can follow up.

ideas.title: Black's pin on f3
ideas.text: The g4-bishop pins your f3 knight to the queen: if the knight moves, Black takes on d1.

ideas.title: The Steinitz c3 plan
ideas.text: Pawns on c3 and d3 are the Steinitz set-up: c3 takes d4 from Black's knight and prepares b4 and a later d4.

ideas.title: Question the g4-bishop
ideas.text: 3...Bg4 delays Black's castling and development; h3 asks the bishop to take on f3 or retreat.

habit.why: 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives a bishop for one pawn, and no other piece can join in because Black's g4-bishop pins your f3 knight to the queen. After 6.h3 Bxf3 7.Qxf3+ Nf6 Black's king is safe and you are a piece down for a pawn.

strays.text: Nothing backs up the bishop, so the check just loses a piece.

taught.why: 5.c3 takes d4 from Black's knight and prepares 6.b4, the slow Steinitz plan with pawns on c3 and d3. After 5...Qd7 6.b4 Nf6 7.O-O Be7 8.h3 you have castled and gained queenside space, and Black's bishop must decide.

enforces.text: Pawns on c3 and d3 keep ...Nd4 out and prepare b4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.h3 asks the bishop to decide, and after 5...Be6 6.Bb5 Bd7 7.O-O you keep a pleasant game. It is nearly as good as the best move.
alternatives.after: 5.c3 and 5.h3 are about equal: 5.c3 first takes d4 from the knight and prepares 6.b4, while 5.h3 settles the bishop question at once.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.O-O is sound, but 5...Qf6 adds pressure on the pinned knight, and the line ends 8.gxf3 with doubled pawns for you. A stronger move exists.
alternatives.after: 5.c3 first takes d4 from Black's knight and keeps your pawns intact; after 5.O-O Qf6 6.c3 Bxf3 Black trades into a quieter ending.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 allows 5...Nd4, a second attacker on the pinned f3 knight; after 6.Be3 c6 7.Bxd4 exd4 8.Nb1 your knight has to go back home.
alternatives.after: 5.c3 covers d4, so Black's knight can't land there and the pin on f3 stays harmless.

3557627017946811|b7b5.headline: Play 3...g6; 3...b5 just drops a pawn to 4.Bxb5+
3557627017946811|b7b5.why: 3...b5 just drops a pawn: 4.Bxb5+ takes it with check, and after 4...c6 5.Be2 you have nothing for it. Nothing supports the b-pawn yet, so White develops a pawn up. 3...g6 is the main Pirc move (49.1% of master games): ...Bg7 will aim at d4 and you castle soon. Against 4.Be3 you can play 4...a6 first and keep ...b5 for when it is supported.
3557627017946811|b7b5.principle: Don't push a pawn where it can simply be taken: expand only once the pawn is supported.
sources: The Pirc: Move by Move (GM Nigel Davies), publisher excerpt | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/7604.pdf
Pirc Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirc_Defence

Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense (Sean Marsh, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/

ideas.title: Prepare ...b5 with ...a6 or ...c6
ideas.text: ...b5 is a real Pirc plan, but only with ...a6 or ...c6 behind it. Here 4.Bxb5+ just takes the pawn with check.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: With 3...g6 and ...Bg7 your bishop aims at d4; later ...e5, or ...c6 and ...b5, hit White's centre.

ideas.title: Be3-Qd2-Bh6 attack
ideas.text: Against a bishop on e3 with a queen coming to d2, hold back castling and expand with ...a6 first, as in 4.Be3 a6.

ideas.title: Time ...e5 after ...Bg7 and castling
ideas.text: An early ...e5 lets White trade on e5 and then queens with 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8, and you lose the right to castle.

habit.why: 3...b5 just drops a pawn: 4.Bxb5+ takes it with check, and after 4...c6 5.Be2 you have nothing for it. Nothing supports the b-pawn yet, so White develops a pawn up.

strays.text: ...b5 without ...a6 or ...c6 first simply loses the pawn.

taught.why: 3...g6 is the main Pirc move (49.1% of master games): ...Bg7 will aim at d4 and you castle soon. Against 4.Be3 you can play 4...a6 first and keep ...b5 for when it is supported.

enforces.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
enforces.text: The fianchetto aims at d4 and prepares a later ...e5 or ...b5.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 3...c6 prepares ...Qa5 and ...e5, but 4.f4 grabs space at once. After 4...Qa5 5.Bd3 e5 6.Nf3 exd4 7.Nxd4 White's pieces are much more active.
alternatives.after: 3...g6 gets the bishop to g7 against d4 first. Masters do play 3...c6 (9.7%), but the engine clearly dislikes it here.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 3...Nbd7 aims for a Philidor with ...e5, but 4.f4 e5 5.Nf3 exd4 6.Qxd4 gives White a big lead and long castling with 8.O-O-O.
alternatives.after: 3...g6 develops the kingside and castles first. Masters play 3...Nbd7 in 6.9% of games, but the engine dislikes it against 4.f4.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...e5 strikes at d4 at once, and masters play it in 33.6% of games. The catch is that White can trade queens with 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8, and you can no longer castle.
alternatives.after: 3...g6 develops first and keeps ...e5 for later; the engine prefers it, though masters play both often.

3562880418201798|b8c6.headline: 1...c5 contests d4 with a pawn; 1...Nc6 doesn't stop 2.d4
3562880418201798|b8c6.why: 1...Nc6 lets White play 2.d4 and take the full centre, because the queen helps guard d4. After 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.c3 e6 White has more space, and masters almost never choose 1...Nc6. 1...c5 controls d4 with a pawn, so White must spend a move preparing the push; masters choose it in 46% of games. In the line 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 you trade a wing pawn for a centre pawn and gain time on the d4 knight.
3562880418201798|b8c6.principle: Fight for the centre from move one: a pawn on c5 or e5 stops White from setting up e4 and d4 for free.
sources: Andrew Martin: Nimzowitsch Defence 1.e4 Nc6 - Review (Markus Reinke, ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/andrew-martin-nimzowitsch-defence-1-e4-nc6-review

ideas.title: Control d4 with a pawn
ideas.text: 1...c5 and 1...e5 put a pawn on guard of d4, so White can't easily keep pawns on both e4 and d4.

ideas.title: A knight on c6 doesn't stop d4
ideas.text: After 1...Nc6, 2.d4 is safe because White's queen also guards d4. White gets the two-pawn centre for free.

ideas.title: Trade a wing pawn for a centre pawn
ideas.text: In the Sicilian, 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 swaps your c-pawn for White's d-pawn, leaving you two centre pawns to one and an open c-file.

habit.why: 1...Nc6 lets White play 2.d4 and take the full centre, because the queen helps guard d4. After 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.c3 e6 White has more space, and masters almost never choose 1...Nc6.

strays.text: The knight eyes d4, but White's queen covers it too.

taught.why: 1...c5 controls d4 with a pawn, so White must spend a move preparing the push; masters choose it in 46% of games. In the line 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 you trade a wing pawn for a centre pawn and gain time on the d4 knight.

enforces.text: The c-pawn guards d4, so White's centre push must be prepared.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 1...e5 is the classical reply: it claims a share of the centre, guards d4 and opens a diagonal for your bishop. It is fully sound, and masters play it in 24% of games; the card teaches a different, more popular reply.
alternatives.after: 1...c5 also controls d4 but unbalances the game, which is why masters choose it in 46% of games. 1...e5 is just as good and keeps the position more symmetrical.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 1...d5 hits e4 at once, but after 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qd8 White gains time on your queen and follows with 4.d4.
alternatives.after: 1...c5 fights for the centre without bringing your queen out early.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 1...e6, the French, is solid, but White takes the centre with 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 and your c8 bishop stays shut in for a while. The engine marks it an inaccuracy, though masters play it in 12% of games.
alternatives.after: 1...c5 hits d4 at once and leaves your light-squared bishop free. Both are respected defences; the engine simply prefers 1...c5 here.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 1...c6, the Caro-Kann, is solid, but White grabs space with 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.h4. The engine marks it an inaccuracy, though masters play it in 8% of games.
alternatives.after: 1...c5 contests d4 at once instead of preparing ...d5, and leads to sharper play. Masters use both; the engine prefers 1...c5.

3562880418201798|g8f6.headline: 1...c5 controls d4; 1...Nf6 invites White's pawns forward
3562880418201798|g8f6.why: 1...Nf6 attacks e4, but 2.e5 kicks the knight and White keeps gaining space with tempo: 2...Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4. IM Alberto Chueca rates White slightly better in this Four Pawns Attack, and Black must not drift into passivity. 1...c5 controls d4 with a pawn, so White must spend a move preparing the push; masters choose it in 46% of games. In the line 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 you trade a wing pawn for a centre pawn and gain time on the d4 knight.
3562880418201798|g8f6.principle: Fight for the centre from move one: a pawn on c5 or e5 stops White from setting up e4 and d4 for free.

3563738946985954|d1f3.headline: Retreat with 6.Nf3: f7 is covered, so the queen sortie fails
3563738946985954|d1f3.why: 6.Qf3 adds the queen to the f7 attack, but the h6 knight and the king already guard f7, and 6...Nd4 hits your queen and c2 at once. After 7.Qd1 Qf6 8.Nf3 Qg6 your queen is back home and Black has gained time. 6.Nf3 admits f7 is covered and brings the knight back to the slow plan. After 6...Ng4 7.O-O h6 8.c3 a5 9.Nbd2 you have the normal c3 set-up, and castling has covered the f2 pawn that 6...Ng4 eyed.
3563738946985954|d1f3.principle: An early queen becomes a target: with f7 covered, 6.Qf3 walks into 6...Nd4, while 6.Nf3 keeps building.
sources: Georgios Souleidis and Karsten Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (New in Chess), pp. 11-13 | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: 5.Ng5 only works when Black can't cover f7 in time. After 5...Nh6 it is covered, so go back with 6.Nf3 and build up.

ideas.title: Guard f7, chase the bishop
ideas.text: 5...Nh6 develops and guards f7. Black then hits whatever comes out early, as with 6...Nd4 or 6...Bg4.

ideas.title: An early queen is a target
ideas.text: With your b1 knight and c1 bishop at home, a queen on f3 or h5 gets hit: 6...Nd4 attacks it and c2 at once.

ideas.title: Slow Italian: build first
ideas.text: Castle, play c3 and keep d4 until it's prepared, as in 6.Nf3 Ng4 7.O-O h6 8.c3 a5 9.Nbd2.

habit.why: 6.Qf3 adds the queen to the f7 attack, but the h6 knight and the king already guard f7, and 6...Nd4 hits your queen and c2 at once. After 7.Qd1 Qf6 8.Nf3 Qg6 your queen is back home and Black has gained time.

strays.idea: An early queen is a target
strays.text: The queen comes out with two minor pieces at home and gets chased by 6...Nd4.

taught.why: 6.Nf3 admits f7 is covered and brings the knight back to the slow plan. After 6...Ng4 7.O-O h6 8.c3 a5 9.Nbd2 you have the normal c3 set-up, and castling has covered the f2 pawn that 6...Ng4 eyed.

enforces.text: With f7 covered, the knight goes back and you build up.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.O-O tucks your king away and keeps the knight on g5 for now, in the spirit of the slow plan. After 6...O-O 7.a4 Bg4 Black's pressure makes the knight decide anyway, so it's slightly less accurate.
alternatives.after: 6.Nf3 makes that decision at once, before 7...Bg4 can force it. In the 6.O-O line the knight goes back with 8.Nf3 anyway.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Qh5 also adds the queen to the f7 attack, but f7 is already covered, and 6...Bg4 7.Qh4 Nd4 lets Black develop by hitting your queen.
alternatives.after: 6.Nf3 keeps your queen home and returns to the slow plan; with f7 covered, a queen sortie only gives Black targets.
alternatives.idea: An early queen is a target

3586492073419954|g7g6.headline: In the Sozin, develop with 6...Be7 and castle
3586492073419954|g7g6.why: 6...g6 leaves d6 and f6 with no pawn cover, and 7.Bg5 pins your f6-knight to the queen. After 7...Nbd7 8.Qe2 h6 9.Be3 e5 you have moved the e-pawn twice and your king is still in the centre. 6...Be7 develops and gets castling ready, which is what the Sozin demands. After 7.Be3 a6 8.Bb3 b5 9.f3 O-O your king is safe and ...b5 has gained queenside space.
3586492073419954|g7g6.principle: Against the Sozin, get your king safe fast: 6...Be7 prepares castling, while 6...g6 spends a move and leaves d6 and f6 weak.
sources: Wikibooks: Sozin vs Scheveningen 6.Bc4 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...c5/2._Nf3/2...d6/3._d4/3...cxd4/4._Nxd4/4...Nf6/5._Nc3/5...e6/6._Bc4
David Vigorito, Playing the Najdorf (preview) | https://docslib.org/doc/3378894/playing-the-najdorf-david-vigorito

ideas.title: Pick one pawn setup
ideas.text: With ...e6 played, ...g6 leaves d6 and f6 without pawn cover. The Scheveningen setup wants ...Be7 and castling.

ideas.title: Castle before the attack
ideas.text: In the Sozin, delaying ...Be7 and castling invites a dangerous attack; 6...Be7 and 9...O-O get your king out of the centre.

ideas.title: The Sozin bishop
ideas.text: White's c4-bishop aims at e6 and f7. ...a6 and ...b5 push it back, as in 7.Be3 a6 8.Bb3 b5.

ideas.title: Bg5 pins the knight
ideas.text: After ...g6, 7.Bg5 pins your f6-knight to the queen, and you have to untangle with ...Nbd7 and ...h6.

habit.why: 6...g6 leaves d6 and f6 with no pawn cover, and 7.Bg5 pins your f6-knight to the queen. After 7...Nbd7 8.Qe2 h6 9.Be3 e5 you have moved the e-pawn twice and your king is still in the centre.

strays.text: ...g6 mixes a Dragon into the Scheveningen and leaves dark-square holes.

taught.why: 6...Be7 develops and gets castling ready, which is what the Sozin demands. After 7.Be3 a6 8.Bb3 b5 9.f3 O-O your king is safe and ...b5 has gained queenside space.

enforces.text: The bishop clears f8, and you castle before White's attack arrives.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6...a6 is sound (35% of master games): it prepares ...b5 to chase the c4-bishop, as after 7.Be3 b5 8.Bb3. One move is still a little more precise.
alternatives.after: 6...Be7 and 6...a6 usually reach the same position, as here after 9.f3 O-O; 6...Be7 gets castling ready first, as Wikibooks advises in the Sozin.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6...Nc6 is sound and leads to a Classical Sozin. White can answer with 8.Qe2 and 9.O-O-O, the sharp Velimirovic-style setup. A slightly more precise move exists.
alternatives.after: 6...Be7 is more common (55% to 9%) and gets castling ready at once; both are fine moves.

3598575371397628|b1c3.headline: Kick the knight with 3.e5; 3.Nc3 lets Black equalise
3598575371397628|b1c3.why: 3.Nc3 lets Black transpose into a comfortable open game with 3...e5, where Black's pieces develop freely, as in 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Bb4. 2...Nf6 put the knight where White's e-pawn can kick it, and 3.e5 exploits that: it gains space with tempo and drives the knight back to g8, then White takes the centre with 4.d4. Masters choose 3.e5 in 84.6% of games.
3598575371397628|b1c3.principle: When an enemy knight on f6 can be hit by your e-pawn, the push gains space and costs the knight time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3598575371397628|d2d3.headline: Push e5 and kick the knight
3598575371397628|d2d3.why: 3.d3 is passive: it holds e4 but gives Black an easy game, and after 3...e5 4.g3 Black has a free hand in the centre. 3.e5 attacks the knight on f6 and takes the pawn out of danger in one move; after 3...Ng8 4.d4 Black's pieces are back home while White owns the centre.
3598575371397628|d2d3.principle: A knight on f6 that your e-pawn can reach with one push is a target: kick it to gain space and time.

3598575371397628|d2d4.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 3.e5; 3.d4 drops the e4 pawn
3598575371397628|d2d4.why: 2...Nf6 attacks e4, and 3.d4 ignores it: 3...Nxe4 wins the pawn, and after 4.d5 Nb8 White has little for it. 3.e5, the master choice in 85% of games, gains space with tempo, and the knight retreats with 3...Ng8. After 4.d4 d6 White has a big centre and a lead in development.
3598575371397628|d2d4.principle: A knight on f6 that your e-pawn can reach is a target: push to gain space and time instead of leaving e4 to be taken.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3598575371397628|f1c4.headline: Kick the knight with 3.e5 instead of leaving e4 hanging
3598575371397628|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 leaves e4 undefended, and 3...Nxe4 simply takes it; after 4.d4 d5 Black keeps the extra pawn and blocks the bishop. 3.e5 punishes the knight's arrival on f6: the pawn gains space with tempo and drives the knight back to g8, after which White builds the centre with 4.d4. Masters play 3.e5 in 84.6% of games here.
3598575371397628|f1c4.principle: When a knight on f6 attacks your e-pawn and your pawn can advance with tempo, push it: you gain space and the knight loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3601332546328408|f3g5.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; 5.Ng5 just gets chased back
3601332546328408|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 aims at f7, but 5...O-O guards it, and after 6.d4 h6 the knight has to go back with 7.Nf3. Black uses the time for 7...Nxe4 8.Nxe4 d5, forking bishop and knight, and after 9.Bd3 dxe4 Black has freed the game. 5.O-O puts your king away first, the masters' choice in 55% of games. After 5...c5 6.d4 cxd4 7.Nxd4 O-O 8.Be2 you have an open game with free development and the bishop out of the fork's reach.
3601332546328408|f3g5.principle: Don't move the same piece twice in the opening without a concrete gain: 5.Ng5 goes out and back while Black castles and hits e4.
sources: A Pirc Quirk (IM Jeremy Silman, chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/a-pirc-quirk
Dejan Bojkov: Attacking with the Pirc - A Review (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/dejan-bojkov-attacking-with-the-pirc-a-review
Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense (Sean Marsh, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/

ideas.title: Castle before you attack
ideas.text: Get your king safe and keep d4 in hand. A knight raid on f7 does nothing once Black castles and the f8 rook guards it.

ideas.title: The fork trick against Bc4
ideas.text: With your bishop on c4 and knight on c3, ...Nxe4 then ...d5 forks bishop and knight, so Black wins the piece back.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Black lets you have e4 and d4 and hits them later with ...c5 and the g7 bishop. Castle, then build the centre with d4.

habit.why: 5.Ng5 aims at f7, but 5...O-O guards it, and after 6.d4 h6 the knight has to go back with 7.Nf3. Black uses the time for 7...Nxe4 8.Nxe4 d5, forking bishop and knight, and after 9.Bd3 dxe4 Black has freed the game.

strays.text: The knight goes out and back while Black castles and hits e4.

taught.why: 5.O-O puts your king away first, the masters' choice in 55% of games. After 5...c5 6.d4 cxd4 7.Nxd4 O-O 8.Be2 you have an open game with free development and the bishop out of the fork's reach.

enforces.text: King safe first, then 6.d4 opens the centre.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.d3 guards e4 with a pawn, so the ...Nxe4 and ...d5 trick is gone. It is a quiet set-up that masters use in 25% of games, but there is a more useful move.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O keeps the d-pawn free for 6.d4 and the full centre; after 5.d3 O-O 6.h3 c5 the game is level and quiet.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.d4 takes the full centre at once, and the engine rates it about as good as the top move. Black's usual answer is 6...Bg4, pinning your f3 knight and pressing on d4.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O plays d4 a move later, as in 5...c5 6.d4, once the king is safe. Masters prefer castling, 55% to 10%.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5.h3 does nothing about the fork trick: Black can take with 6...Nxe4, and 7.Nxe4 d5 wins the piece back, so Black is comfortable at once.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O spends the move on king safety and prepares 6.d4; 5.h3 spends it on a pawn move that doesn't stop 6...Nxe4.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: With no d-pawn behind it, 5.e5 just gets traded: after 5...dxe5 6.Nxe5 your centre pawn is gone without any space to show for it.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O keeps the e4 pawn and prepares 6.d4 to back it up; pushing e5 early hands Black an easy game.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

3610881811711296|d7d5.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6, not the Elephant Gambit
3610881811711296|d7d5.why: 2...d5 is the Elephant Gambit, and it is unsound: after 3.exd5 e4 4.Qe2 Black is a pawn down without enough to show for it, and in the game line 6.Nxe4 picks off the advanced pawn as well. 2...Nc6 develops a piece while defending e5 and controlling d4, which is why it is about five times more popular than everything else combined.
3610881811711296|d7d5.principle: When the knight on f3 attacks e5, defend it with a developing move instead of giving up a pawn for activity you don't have yet.

3610881811711296|d8f6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6, not the queen.
3610881811711296|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home and takes f6 away from the king's knight. White develops with gain of time, for example 3.Nc3 with the idea Nd5 hitting the queen, and Black falls behind. 2...Nc6 defends e5 while developing and also controls d4, which is why it is about five times more popular than everything else combined.
3610881811711296|d8f6.principle: Defend attacked pawns with developing pieces; a queen used as a defender becomes a target for White's next knight move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

3610881811711296|f7f5.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6; the Latvian gambit 2...f5 is unsound
3610881811711296|f7f5.why: 2...f5 leaves e5 hanging and opens the diagonal from h5 to your king: after 3.Nxe5 you can't grab e4 with 3...fxe4 because of 4.Qh5+, and in the engine line 3...Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3 White is simply better developed. The theory calls the gambit utterly unsound. 2...Nc6 is the main line, chosen in 86% of master games: it develops a piece, defends e5 and also controls d4.
3610881811711296|f7f5.principle: Answer an attack on e5 with a developing move that defends it, not with a pawn move that leaves the pawn loose and weakens your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

3610881811711296|f7f6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6; 2...f6 only seems to defend it
3610881811711296|f7f6.why: 2...f6 only seems to defend e5: 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn anyway, because 3...fxe5 runs into 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxe5+, forking the king and the rook on h8. It also takes f6 away from the knight and opens the diagonal to Black's king. 2...Nc6 develops a piece while defending e5 and controlling d4, and is played in 86% of master games.
3610881811711296|f7f6.principle: Defend a centre pawn with a developing piece, not with a pawn move that weakens your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6

3610881811711296|f8c5.headline: 2.Nf3 attacks e5: defend it with 2...Nc6 before developing elsewhere
3610881811711296|f8c5.why: 2...Bc5 develops but ignores the attack on e5, so 3.Nxe5 just wins a pawn. The theory calls this Busch-Gass gambit unsound: Black hopes for play with 3...Qh4, but gets no real compensation if White keeps their head. 2...Nc6, the main line and 86% of master games, develops the knight while defending e5 and controlling d4.
3610881811711296|f8c5.principle: Before choosing a developing move, check what your opponent's last move attacks: 2.Nf3 hit e5, so the developing move should also defend it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

3610881811711296|f8d6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6, not a bishop that blocks your d-pawn
3610881811711296|f8d6.why: 2...Bd6 defends e5 but blocks Black's d-pawn, so the queen's bishop stays shut in, and White can open the centre with 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4, aiming at f7 before Black is organised. 2...Nc6 develops a piece while defending e5 and controlling d4; it is about five times more popular than everything else combined.
3610881811711296|f8d6.principle: Defend attacked pawns with pieces developing toward the centre, without blocking the pawns that free your other pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

3610922251931051|c1d2.headline: The c3 knight is pinned: guard e4 with 4.Bd3
3610922251931051|c1d2.why: Black threatens 4...Qxe4+, and the c3 knight can't really defend e4 because the b4 bishop pins it. 4.Bd2 doesn't help: 4...Bxc3 5.Bxc3 Qxe4+ removes the defender and takes the pawn with check. 4.Bd3 develops a bishop that defends e4 directly, and in the engine line Black's queen has to go back with 5...Qd8 while White castles.
3610922251931051|c1d2.principle: A pinned piece is not a real defender; protect what it guards with a piece that is free to recapture.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4

3610922251931051|c1e3.headline: Defend e4 with a piece the pin can't remove
3610922251931051|c1e3.why: Black's queen attacks e4 and the bishop on b4 pins its only defender, the knight on c3: after 4.Be3 Bxc3+ 5.bxc3 Qxe4 the knight is gone and so is the pawn. 4.Bd3 develops a bishop that guards e4 directly, and after 4...d5 5.Nf3 White develops with an attack on the queen, which has to retreat with 5...Qd8.
3610922251931051|c1e3.principle: When a pinned piece is the only guard of a pawn, give the pawn a second defender that the pin can't take away.

3610922251931051|g2g3.headline: The c3 knight is pinned: guard e4 with 4.Bd3 first
3610922251931051|g2g3.why: The b4 bishop pins your c3 knight, so after 4.g3 the e4 pawn is loose: 4...Qxe4+ is check and hits the h1 rook. After 5.Qe2 Qxh1 Black has won the rook and keeps grabbing: 6.f3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qxg1. 4.Bd3 guards e4 with a piece that isn't pinned, so 4...Qxe4+ is off the table. Black's queen is now just exposed: after 4...d5 5.Nf3 Qd8 6.O-O it has gone home and you are ahead in development.
3610922251931051|g2g3.principle: A pinned piece defends nothing: before attacking the queen, check what the pinned c3 knight no longer guards.

ideas.title: Pinned knight, loose e4
ideas.text: The b4 bishop pins your c3 knight to the king, so it can't take back on e4. Count it out as a defender.

ideas.title: The ...Qxe4+ fork
ideas.text: Look for checks before chasing the queen: 4...Qxe4+ hits your king and the h1 rook at once.

ideas.title: Guard e4 with a free piece
ideas.text: Defend e4 with a piece that isn't pinned: the bishop on d3 develops and holds the pawn.

ideas.title: Chase the queen with tempo
ideas.text: Once e4 is safe, attacking the queen gains time: after 4...d5 5.Nf3 Qd8 it has gone back home.

habit.why: The b4 bishop pins your c3 knight, so after 4.g3 the e4 pawn is loose: 4...Qxe4+ is check and hits the h1 rook. After 5.Qe2 Qxh1 Black has won the rook and keeps grabbing: 6.f3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qxg1.

strays.text: 4.g3 forgets that the pinned knight can't take back on e4.

taught.why: 4.Bd3 guards e4 with a piece that isn't pinned, so 4...Qxe4+ is off the table. Black's queen is now just exposed: after 4...d5 5.Nf3 Qd8 6.O-O it has gone home and you are ahead in development.

enforces.idea: Guard e4 with a free piece
enforces.text: The d3 bishop holds e4, so the queen has nothing to take.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4.Nf3 attacks the queen but still drops e4 because of the pin: 4...Qxe4+ 5.Be2 leaves you a pawn down, with only some development for it.
alternatives.after: 4.Bd3 guards e4 first, so 5.Nf3 next hits the queen and costs you nothing.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 4.Bd2 tries to break the pin, but it's a move too slow: 4...Bxc3 5.Bxc3 Qxe4+ wins the pawn with check.
alternatives.after: 4.Bd3 defends e4 at once instead of spending a move on the pin, and Black's queen is left out of play.

361821916697346|f3g5.headline: Gain queenside space with 7.a4, not 7.Ng5
361821916697346|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 7...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 8.a4 a5 9.b5 Ne7 10.Qb3 Qe8 11.Nf3 the knight is back home and Black has castled for free. 7.a4 gains space and threatens a5 against the b6 bishop, so Black answers 7...a5. Then 8.b5 Ne7 9.O-O Ng6 10.Nbd2 follows Mestel-Pinter, a White win, and masters choose 7.a4 69% of the time.
361821916697346|f3g5.principle: When Black can castle and cover f7, use the move to gain space with your pawns instead of moving the f3 knight twice.
sources: Modern Italian Game (Exeter Chess Club) | https://www.exeterchessclub.org.uk/content/modern-italian-game
Souleidis and Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf
NM Jeremy Kane, Bad Trades Amateurs Make In Chess | https://www.chess.com/article/view/bad-trades-amateurs-make-in-chess

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: f7 is guarded by the king only until Black castles. After 7...O-O, taking on f7 gives two pieces for a rook and pawn.

ideas.title: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4
ideas.text: a4 gains queenside space and threatens a5 against the b6 bishop. Then castle and bring the b1 knight out via d2.

ideas.title: Push b5 only when it can't go to a5
ideas.text: After 7.a4 a5, 8.b5 kicks the c6 knight, and with a pawn on a5 it can't jump there to hit your bishop.

ideas.title: Don't move a piece twice
ideas.text: Your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. Moving the f3 knight again gives Black free time.

habit.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 7...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 8.a4 a5 9.b5 Ne7 10.Qb3 Qe8 11.Nf3 the knight is back home and Black has castled for free.

strays.text: Black castles, f7 is covered, and the knight has to go back.

taught.why: 7.a4 gains space and threatens a5 against the b6 bishop, so Black answers 7...a5. Then 8.b5 Ne7 9.O-O Ng6 10.Nbd2 follows Mestel-Pinter, a White win, and masters choose 7.a4 69% of the time.

enforces.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4
enforces.text: a4 gains space with a threat, then castle and develop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is a sound move that gets your king safe before play starts; after 7...Ne7 Black heads for ...Ng6. Masters choose a different move more often (69% to 20%).
alternatives.after: 7.a4 first threatens a5 against the bishop and forces 7...a5; 7.O-O usually comes back to the same plan after 7...Ne7 8.a4.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 7.Qb3 aims at f7, but 7...O-O covers it and Black gets ...a5 in. Once your queenside pawns advance, the queen on b3 becomes a target.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 uses the move for space and forces 7...a5, so 8.b5 kicks the knight without letting it reach a5; 7.Qb3 hits f7 just as Black is ready to castle.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.h3 takes g4 from Black's pieces, and the engine rates it fine. Souleidis' guideline is to wait with h3 until Black has castled, since it can invite ...g5-g4.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 does something on the queenside straight away, while 7.h3 waits; its line comes back to 10.a4 a5 11.b5 anyway.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Nbd2 starts the standard regrouping: the knight heads for f1 and g3, or c4. After 7...Ne7 Black also reroutes a knight toward g6.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 forces the issue on the queenside first; after 7.Nbd2 Black gets 7...Ne7 and 8...c6, and your bishop has to drop back with 9.Bb3.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

362391570447215|c5d4.headline: 4.d4 left e4 hanging: take it with 4...dxe4
362391570447215|c5d4.why: 4...cxd4 releases the tension when White's e4 pawn was simply hanging. After 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.Nxd4 Bd7 8.Qe2+ you have an isolated d5 pawn, a pinned knight and a king stuck in the centre. 4...dxe4 wins a pawn, because 4.d4 left e4 attacked once and defended zero times. After 5.Ne5 Nf6 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Nxd7 Nbxd7 8.O-O you keep the extra pawn and your pieces are out.
362391570447215|c5d4.principle: Check what is loose before releasing the tension: 4.d4 left e4 attacked and undefended, so take it.
sources: The Alapin Variation (Matthew Astle, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/the-alapin-variation/
Sicilian Defence, Alapin Variation (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilian_Defence,_Alapin_Variation

ideas.title: Take the loose e4 pawn
ideas.text: After 4.d4, e4 is attacked by your d5 pawn and defended by nothing, so 4...dxe4 wins it.

ideas.title: Keep the tension on d4
ideas.text: Swapping with ...cxd4 frees White's pieces and, after 5.exd5 exd5, leaves you an isolated d5 pawn to defend.

ideas.title: Watch the b5 check
ideas.text: Your king is still on e8, so once the centre opens 6.Bb5+ and 8.Qe2+ come with gain of time.

ideas.title: A French Advance if White pushes
ideas.text: After 4...Nc6 5.e5 the centre locks as in the French Advance, and 5...Bd7 6.Be2 Nge7 aims your pieces at d4.

habit.why: 4...cxd4 releases the tension when White's e4 pawn was simply hanging. After 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.Nxd4 Bd7 8.Qe2+ you have an isolated d5 pawn, a pinned knight and a king stuck in the centre.

strays.text: 4...cxd4 lets White rescue e4 by trading it off on d5.

taught.why: 4...dxe4 wins a pawn, because 4.d4 left e4 attacked once and defended zero times. After 5.Ne5 Nf6 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Nxd7 Nbxd7 8.O-O you keep the extra pawn and your pieces are out.

enforces.text: Count it: e4 is attacked once and defended by nothing.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: A French Advance if White pushes
alternatives.before: 4...Nc6 is solid: after 5.e5 Bd7 6.Be2 Nge7 you have a standard French Advance setup. There is a stronger move here, though.
alternatives.after: 4...dxe4 simply wins the pawn that 4.d4 left undefended; 4...Nc6 lets White push 5.e5 and keep everything.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...c4 gains queenside space and keeps the centre closed, which is playable. There is a more direct move.
alternatives.after: 4...dxe4 takes the pawn at once; 4...c4 gives up the pressure on d4 and only grabs e4 a move later with 5...dxe4.

3649736493107135|b7b6.headline: Castle now; ...b6 leaves you open to e5-e6
3649736493107135|b7b6.why: 5...b6 neither develops nor castles, and 6.e5 hits your f6 knight at once. With the d3 bishop blocking the d-file you have no queen trade, so 6...dxe5 7.dxe5 Nfd7 8.e6 fxe6 leaves your pawns broken and your king in the centre. 5...O-O is the standard move (85% of masters) and gets your king off e8. After 6.O-O Nc6 7.d5 Nb4 the knight hits the d3 bishop, and 8.Bc4 e6 strikes back at the centre.
3649736493107135|b7b6.principle: Castle before the centre opens: 5...O-O gets your king away before 6.e5 can rip into e6 and f7.
sources: Igor Smirnov, Beat the Pirc Defense with This Trap! | https://chess-teacher.com/beat-the-pirc-defense-with-this-trap/

ideas.title: Castle before the centre opens
ideas.text: After ...Bg7, castle at once. Your king leaves e8 before White can open lines with an e5 push.

ideas.title: Bd3 blocks the queen trade
ideas.text: With White's bishop on d3, the d-file is shut. If White pushes e5, you can't defuse it by trading queens.

ideas.title: The e6 thrust
ideas.text: If 6.e5 drives your knight to d7, then 8.e6 fxe6 breaks your pawns with your king still on e8.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then strike
ideas.text: You let White keep e4 and d4, then hit back: in the main line ...Nc6, ...Nb4 and ...e6 chip at the centre.

habit.why: 5...b6 neither develops nor castles, and 6.e5 hits your f6 knight at once. With the d3 bishop blocking the d-file you have no queen trade, so 6...dxe5 7.dxe5 Nfd7 8.e6 fxe6 leaves your pawns broken and your king in the centre.

strays.text: A pawn move while your king still sits on e8.

taught.why: 5...O-O is the standard move (85% of masters) and gets your king off e8. After 6.O-O Nc6 7.d5 Nb4 the knight hits the d3 bishop, and 8.Bc4 e6 strikes back at the centre.

enforces.text: King safe first; then ...Nc6 and ...e6 go after the centre.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...Bg4 pins the f3 knight to press d4, and masters choose it 12% of the time. The engine is less keen: after 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 White has the bishop pair and castles long with 10.O-O-O.
alternatives.after: 5...O-O is the main move (85% of masters): king safe first, and the c8 bishop is kept. 5...Bg4 is playable but hands White the two bishops.

3678353102233444|g8f6.headline: Recapture at once with 3...exd5 in the Exchange QGD
3678353102233444|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 lets White capture again: after 4.dxe6 Bxe6 White has taken two pawns for one. d5 is attacked twice and not defended, so 3...exd5 recaptures at once, keeps a pawn on d5 and opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop that 2...e6 had blocked.
3678353102233444|g8f6.principle: Recapture toward the centre straight away: the pawn on d5 holds your share of the centre and frees the bishop on c8.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6

3692429315258999|c4e2.headline: Ask the bishop with 6.h3 before Black wins e5 back
3692429315258999|c4e2.why: 6.Be2 doesn't stop 6...dxe5, so Black wins the pawn back at once, and after 7.Nbd2 Nf6 8.c3 a5 the game is level. It also moves your bishop a second time while the b1 knight and c1 bishop wait. 6.h3 asks the bishop first: after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 your queen comes out with a threat on f7. Black wins the pawn back only with 7...Nxe5 8.Qe2 Nxc4 9.Qxc4, giving up the c6 knight for your bishop while you stay ahead in development.
3692429315258999|c4e2.principle: Deal with the pin with tempo: 6.h3 makes the bishop decide while you're still a pawn up, instead of retreating your own bishop.
sources: Semi-Italian Opening (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-Italian_Opening

ideas.title: Ask the bishop with h3
ideas.text: 6.h3 makes the g4 bishop decide. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 your queen and c4 bishop threaten mate on f7.

ideas.title: Black wins e5 back
ideas.text: You're a pawn up only for now: Black threatens 6...dxe5, and a quiet move just lets it happen.

ideas.title: Develop, don't retreat
ideas.text: Your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. Moving the c4 bishop again with 6.Be2 hands Black the time.

habit.why: 6.Be2 doesn't stop 6...dxe5, so Black wins the pawn back at once, and after 7.Nbd2 Nf6 8.c3 a5 the game is level. It also moves your bishop a second time while the b1 knight and c1 bishop wait.

strays.text: The bishop moves twice and Black regains the pawn with 6...dxe5.

taught.why: 6.h3 asks the bishop first: after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 your queen comes out with a threat on f7. Black wins the pawn back only with 7...Nxe5 8.Qe2 Nxc4 9.Qxc4, giving up the c6 knight for your bishop while you stay ahead in development.

enforces.text: The bishop must decide, and 7.Qxf3 develops your queen with a threat.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.exd6 gives the pawn back on your terms: after 6...Bxd6 the centre is open and Black's 4...h6 was a lost move. It's sound, and 72% of club players choose it.
alternatives.after: The engine rates both moves the same. 6.h3 makes Black trade the c6 knight for your bishop to regain the pawn; after 6.exd6 Bxd6 you ask the bishop a move later with 7.h3 Bh5.

3699514865674152|d1e2.headline: Hit f7 at once with 7.Ng5 before Black castles
3699514865674152|d1e2.why: 7.Qe2 threatens nothing, so Black develops with 7...Be7, 8...d6 and 9...O-O, and f7 is covered for good. After 10.h3 Be6 Black has every piece out and still keeps the extra pawn. 7.Ng5 hits f7 twice, with knight and bishop, so Black blocks the bishop with 7...d5 and gives the pawn back. After 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 material is level, your d5 pawn hits the c6 knight and Black's king is still in the centre.
3699514865674152|d1e2.principle: After ...e5, f7 is guarded only by the king, so hit it at once with 7.Ng5 before Black castles; a quiet 7.Qe2 gives that time away.
sources: Benjamin Katz, Chess Bootcamp | https://books.google.com/books?id=l1SZEQAAQBAJ
Robert G. Wade, Playing Chess | https://books.google.com/books?id=3kbGN38YU9YC

ideas.title: Aim at f7 and d5
ideas.text: 5...e5 means Black can't block your c4 bishop with ...e6. Bishop and a knight jump to g5 both hit f7.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black needs ...Be7 and castling to make f7 safe. Quiet moves like 7.Qe2 or castling give Black exactly that time, and the pawn stays.

ideas.title: The d5 hole
ideas.text: After 5...e5 the d5 square is weak for good: Black's c-pawn is gone and the e-pawn can't go back to e6.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 block
ideas.text: Black shuts the c4 bishop with ...d5, but against 7.Ng5 it costs the pawn: 7...d5 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5.

habit.why: 7.Qe2 threatens nothing, so Black develops with 7...Be7, 8...d6 and 9...O-O, and f7 is covered for good. After 10.h3 Be6 Black has every piece out and still keeps the extra pawn.

strays.text: The queen move threatens nothing, so Black castles and keeps the pawn.

taught.why: 7.Ng5 hits f7 twice, with knight and bishop, so Black blocks the bishop with 7...d5 and gives the pawn back. After 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 material is level, your d5 pawn hits the c6 knight and Black's king is still in the centre.

enforces.text: Knight and bishop both hit f7, so Black must return the pawn.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: Castling is natural but threatens nothing. After 7...Be7 8.Bg5 d6 9.Bxf6 Bxf6 10.Nd5 O-O Black has castled, kept the pawn and has the two bishops.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 uses the move while Black's king is still in the centre: f7 is hit twice and 7...d5 gives the pawn back.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: The pin is slow: after 7...Be7 8.Bxf6 Bxf6 you've given up a bishop for the knight, and 9.Qd6 Qe7 10.Qd3 d6 only sends your queen back.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 makes a real threat against f7, so Black has no time for ...Be7 and castling and must return the pawn.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qb3 hits f7 too, but 7...Na5 attacks queen and bishop at once. After 8.Qa4 Nxc4 9.Qxc4 your best attacker is gone and f7 is safe.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 attacks f7 with a piece Black can't chase with tempo, so the c4 bishop stays and Black must play 7...d5 to block it.

3699514865674152|e1h1.headline: 7.Ng5 hits f7 and forces Black to give back the pawn
3699514865674152|e1h1.why: 7.O-O threatens nothing, so Black develops with 7...Be7 and castles soon, and f7 is safe. After 8.Bg5 d6 9.Bxf6 Bxf6 10.Nd5 O-O Black has the bishop pair and the extra pawn. 7.Ng5 threatens to take on f7, and Black's only decent answer, 7...d5, gives up a pawn: 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 hits the c6-knight. After 9...Nd4 10.O-O Be7 11.f4 material is level and Black's king is still in the centre.
3699514865674152|e1h1.principle: Attack f7 while only Black's king guards it: 7.Ng5 makes Black give back the pawn, while castling lets Black develop and castle first.
sources: IM Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf

ideas.title: Hit f7 early
ideas.text: After ...e5, f7 is guarded only by the king. Knight on g5 and the c4-bishop threaten to take there before Black can castle.

ideas.title: Use the d5 hole
ideas.text: After ...e5, d5 is a weak spot. If Black blocks the bishop with 7...d5, that pawn falls: 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black's king is still on e8. Quiet moves give Black time for ...Be7 and castling, and then f7 is safe.

ideas.title: Black hunts the c4-bishop
ideas.text: Black's c6-knight can jump to a5 to trade off your best attacking bishop, especially when it also hits a queen on b3.

habit.why: 7.O-O threatens nothing, so Black develops with 7...Be7 and castles soon, and f7 is safe. After 8.Bg5 d6 9.Bxf6 Bxf6 10.Nd5 O-O Black has the bishop pair and the extra pawn.

strays.text: Castling gives Black the move needed for 7...Be7 and castling.

taught.why: 7.Ng5 threatens to take on f7, and Black's only decent answer, 7...d5, gives up a pawn: 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 hits the c6-knight. After 9...Nd4 10.O-O Be7 11.f4 material is level and Black's king is still in the centre.

enforces.text: Knight and bishop hit f7 together, forcing Black to give back the pawn.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Bg5 pins the knight but makes no threat. After 7...Be7 8.Bxf6 Bxf6 9.Qd6 Qe7 10.Qd3 Black has the bishop pair and an easy game.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 makes a direct threat against f7, so Black has no time for 7...Be7 and has to give back the pawn with 7...d5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qb3 lines up on f7 and b7, but 7...Na5 hits the queen. After 8.Qa4 Nxc4 9.Qxc4 your best attacking bishop is gone.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 keeps the queen at home, so there is no 7...Na5 with tempo, and the threat on f7 leaves Black little better than 7...d5.

3708088433535320|f1b5.headline: Take the whole centre with d4 against 1...b6
3708088433535320|f1b5.why: 2.Bb5 develops the bishop to a square with no target: Black hits e4 with 2...Bb7 and chases the bishop with 3...a6 and 4...b5. 1...b6 lets White take the centre for free, and 2.d4 does so: both centre pawns stand side by side and both bishops are ready to come out.
3708088433535320|f1b5.principle: When the opponent's first move ignores the centre, occupy it with a second pawn before sending pieces to squares without a purpose.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4

3725666597101221|c2c3.headline: Develop with 3.Bb5; 3.c3 leaves e4 loose
3725666597101221|c2c3.why: 3.c3 prepares d4 but takes the c3 square from White's own knight, so the pawn on e4 is loose and Black can hit it at once with 3...d5 or 3...Nf6. 3.Bb5, the Ruy Lopez, is the master choice (65%): it develops, gets White ready to castle, and pressures the knight on c6 that defends e5.
3725666597101221|c2c3.principle: Develop a piece with pressure before spending a move on pawn preparation like c3.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5

3725666597101221|d2d3.headline: Develop with 3.Bb5 rather than the passive 3.d3
3725666597101221|d2d3.why: 3.d3 defends e4 before it is attacked and shuts in the bishop on f1, so Black takes free play in the centre, as in 3...Nf6 4.g3 d5. 3.Bb5, the Ruy Lopez, develops the bishop instead, gets White ready to castle, and puts pressure on the knight on c6, the defender of e5. Masters choose it in 65% of games.
3725666597101221|d2d3.principle: When nothing of yours is attacked, develop a piece that pressures the opponent rather than a pawn move that guards what is already safe.

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5

3726374757153429|f1c4.headline: Pin the e7 knight with 5.Bg5 before Black untangles
3726374757153429|f1c4.why: 5.Bc4 lets Black untangle at once with 5...Nec6, hitting your d4 knight. After 6.Nc3 Be7 7.Nd5 Nxd4 8.Qxd4 O-O the knights are traded, Black has castled and your bishop has nothing to hit on f7. 5.Bg5 pins the e7 knight to the queen on d8, so Black must spend 5...h6 before 6.Be3 Nec6 can follow. After 7.Nc3 Be7 8.Nd5 O-O 9.Nb5 your knights take over d5 and b5, and Black's knight has to go to a6 to guard c7.
3726374757153429|f1c4.principle: Develop with a threat when the opponent's pieces are tangled: 5.Bg5 makes Black spend 5...h6 before untangling.
sources: Philidor Defense: A Practical Guide (ChessMood) | https://chessmood.com/openings/philidor-defense

ideas.title: Pin the e7 knight
ideas.text: 5.Bg5 pins the e7 knight to the queen on d8, so Black must spend 5...h6 before the knight can move.

ideas.title: Black's cramped Philidor
ideas.text: Black's dark-squared bishop needs e7, and the knight stands there. Black needs extra moves to untangle and castle.

ideas.title: Black trades on d4
ideas.text: Black's knight heads for c6 to hit your d4 knight and trade it, easing the cramp, as in 5...Nec6 and 7...Nxd4.

ideas.title: Keep the space with active pieces
ideas.text: Your e4 pawn gives you space. Keep it with a knight on c3, bishops on g5 or f4, the queen on d2 and long castling.

habit.why: 5.Bc4 lets Black untangle at once with 5...Nec6, hitting your d4 knight. After 6.Nc3 Be7 7.Nd5 Nxd4 8.Qxd4 O-O the knights are traded, Black has castled and your bishop has nothing to hit on f7.

strays.text: The e7 knight moves freely, so Black untangles with 5...Nec6 at once.

taught.why: 5.Bg5 pins the e7 knight to the queen on d8, so Black must spend 5...h6 before 6.Be3 Nec6 can follow. After 7.Nc3 Be7 8.Nd5 O-O 9.Nb5 your knights take over d5 and b5, and Black's knight has to go to a6 to guard c7.

enforces.text: The pin costs Black a move, and your knights then take over d5 and b5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Keep the space with active pieces
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 is the club favourite (48.7%) and fully sound: it guards e4, and after 5...Nec6 6.Be3 Be7 7.Nd5 your pieces stay active. The app teaches another move, but the engine rates this one as good.
alternatives.after: 5.Bg5 is just as good and more forcing: the pin makes Black spend 5...h6 first. After 5.Nc3 Black plays 5...Nec6 at once, and you reach a similar position.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.Bd3 is passive: the bishop blocks the d-file, so your queen no longer guards the d4 knight, and Black sets up comfortably with 5...g6 6.Nc3 Bg7 7.Bf4 O-O.
alternatives.after: 5.Bg5 develops with a threat, so Black loses time on 5...h6; 5.Bd3 asks nothing of Black.

3729547871689507|f1c4.headline: Answer 1...Nc6 with 2.Nf3; a c4 bishop runs into ...d5
3729547871689507|f1c4.why: 2.Bc4 puts the bishop where Black's centre pawns can hit it: after 2...e6 3.d4 d5 4.exd5 exd5 it has to move again with 5.Bb3, and 6...Na5 chases it once more. 2.Nf3 develops the knight to its best square and is the most popular master move at 60%. If Black answers 2...e5 the game is a normal Open Game, and other replies leave Black's knight awkwardly placed.
3729547871689507|f1c4.principle: The knight's best square, f3, is clear already, while the bishop's depends on how Black's pawns settle; Black can still choose ...e6 and ...d5, which would hit a bishop on c4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3729547871689507|f2f4.headline: Develop the king's knight; save pawn moves for the centre
3729547871689507|f2f4.why: 2.f4 develops nothing, and after 2...d5 3.e5 d4 Black gains space and White's edge is gone. 2.Nf3 develops the knight to its most active square and invites 2...e5, a normal Open Game; if Black avoids it, the knight on c6 gets in the way of Black's usual pawn breaks.
3729547871689507|f2f4.principle: With no reason yet to commit pawns, bring the king's knight out first; its best square is already clear.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3747843569338814|d2d4.headline: After 3...Bc5, use the fork trick: 4.Nxe5 and 5.d4
3747843569338814|d2d4.why: 4.d4 loses a pawn after 4...exd4, and 5.Nd5 does not win it back. 4.Nxe5 takes the e5 pawn because the knight on c6 is not really defending it: after 4...Nxe5 5.d4 the pawn forks the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5, and White wins the piece back. Material stays level, but White gets the freer game and the centre.
3747843569338814|d2d4.principle: Look at captures first: e5 looks defended, but after the capture 5.d4 forks two pieces, so the defence is an illusion.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

3772385141189769|d2d4.headline: Prepare d4 with 2.Nf3 so a knight, not the queen, recaptures.
3772385141189769|d2d4.why: 2.d4 cxd4 leaves an awkward choice: 3.Qxd4 lets Black develop 3...Nc6 with tempo on the queen, and 3.Nf3 allows 3...e5, keeping the extra pawn. Playing 2.Nf3 first means that after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 White recaptures with the knight and keeps the tempo, and Black has no time to defend the d4 pawn.
3772385141189769|d2d4.principle: Prepare the central break so a knight recaptures on d4; a queen there is chased by ...Nc6.

3772385141189769|f1c4.headline: Play 2.Nf3 against the Sicilian; 2.Bc4 runs into ...e6 and ...d5.
3772385141189769|f1c4.why: 2.Bc4 aims at f7, but Black answers 2...e6 and later ...d5, blunting the bishop and gaining time on it with an easy central position. 2.Nf3 adds control of d4 and prepares 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4, opening the position while Black, whose 1...c5 did nothing for development, is still catching up.
3772385141189769|f1c4.principle: Against the Sicilian, put your pieces where they support the d4 break, not on squares Black can hit with a central pawn.

3772385141189769|f2f4.headline: Against the Sicilian, develop with 2.Nf3 and prepare d4
3772385141189769|f2f4.why: 2.f4 starts a kingside attack before White has developed, and Black answers by striking in the centre: after 2...e6 3.Nf3 d5 White has to commit with 4.Bb5+ Nd7 5.e5, and Black's position is fine. 2.Nf3 develops and prepares 3.d4; after the pawn trade White recaptures with the knight and gets open lines for both bishops and the queen. It is the choice in 83% of master games.
3772385141189769|f2f4.principle: 1...c5 does nothing for Black's development, so develop and open the centre with d4 rather than spend a move on a flank pawn.

3800718395256466|c6d5.headline: Retake with 7...Nxd5 so c6 still guards b5
3800718395256466|c6d5.why: 7...cxd5 removes the pawn that kept White's knight off b5, and 8.Nb5 threatens a fork on c7, so you must answer 8...Kd8. After 9.Ne5 Bg6 10.Nxa7 White's knight and the a1 rook have won the a7 pawn. 7...Nxd5 wins the pawn back and keeps the c6 pawn guarding b5, so the knight raid never starts. After 8.e4 Nxc3 9.exf5 Nd5 material is level and your structure is solid.
3800718395256466|c6d5.principle: In a queenless position weigh the differences: 7.axb3 opened the a-file at a7, so keep c6 covering b5 and recapture with the knight.
