ideas.title: Nb5 jumps at c7 and a7
ideas.text: If the c6 pawn leaves, 8.Nb5 threatens a fork on c7, and the a1 rook backs up a hit on a7.

ideas.title: Recapture with the knight here
ideas.text: After the queen trade on b3, 7...Nxd5 keeps the c6 pawn guarding b5, so White's knight has no way in.

ideas.title: Early ...Bf5 drops b7
ideas.text: With your bishop on f5, 5.Qb3 hit b7 and d5 together. That pressure is why the queens came off and you face this choice.

habit.why: 7...cxd5 removes the pawn that kept White's knight off b5, and 8.Nb5 threatens a fork on c7, so you must answer 8...Kd8. After 9.Ne5 Bg6 10.Nxa7 White's knight and the a1 rook have won the a7 pawn.

strays.idea: Nb5 jumps at c7 and a7
strays.text: The c6 pawn leaves, so 8.Nb5 threatens c7 and wins a7.

taught.why: 7...Nxd5 wins the pawn back and keeps the c6 pawn guarding b5, so the knight raid never starts. After 8.e4 Nxc3 9.exf5 Nd5 material is level and your structure is solid.

enforces.text: The c6 pawn stays, covering b5, so White's knight has no way in.

3815488023003540|b8c6.headline: Take on d4 before White's pawn can push to d5
3815488023003540|b8c6.why: 5...Nc6 leaves the c5 and d4 pawns facing each other, and 6.d5 gains space with a hit on the knight. After 6...Na5 7.O-O d6 8.c4 Nxc4 9.a4 Bd7 10.Nc3 you are a pawn up, but your knight is stuck on c4 and White's lead in development and pressure on b5 count for more. 5...cxd4 takes White's centre pawn before it can advance. After 6.a4 b4 7.Nxd4 Qc7 8.Bd3 Nf6 your b-pawn has gained space, your pieces develop freely and the game is level.
3815488023003540|b8c6.principle: Resolve pawn tension on your terms: 5...cxd4 trades your flank pawn for White's centre pawn, while 5...Nc6 lets 6.d5 gain space with tempo.
sources: The Bowlder Attack: Bold move or beginner's folly? (Matthew Astle, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/bowlder-attack/
countering 2. Bc4 in the Sicilian (chess.com forum) | https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess-openings/countering-2-bc4-in-the-sicilian
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

ideas.title: Settle the d4 tension
ideas.text: White's d4 pawn and your c5 pawn hit each other. Taking with 5...cxd4 clears the centre before White can push past.

ideas.title: White's d5 space grab
ideas.text: If the tension stays, the d-pawn advances, gains space and kicks a knight on c6, as in 6.d5 Na5.

ideas.title: Chase the bishop with ...a6 and ...b5
ideas.text: Your ...a6 and ...b5 gained space and drove the bishop back to e2. If White hits b5 with a4, push on, as in 6.a4 b4.

ideas.title: Kan-style setup
ideas.text: After 7.Nxd4 you have an Open Sicilian with ...e6, ...a6 and ...b5 already played: develop with 7...Qc7 and 8...Nf6.

habit.why: 5...Nc6 leaves the c5 and d4 pawns facing each other, and 6.d5 gains space with a hit on the knight. After 6...Na5 7.O-O d6 8.c4 Nxc4 9.a4 Bd7 10.Nc3 you are a pawn up, but your knight is stuck on c4 and White's lead in development and pressure on b5 count for more.

strays.text: The tension stays, so 6.d5 gains space and chases your knight.

taught.why: 5...cxd4 takes White's centre pawn before it can advance. After 6.a4 b4 7.Nxd4 Qc7 8.Bd3 Nf6 your b-pawn has gained space, your pieces develop freely and the game is level.

enforces.text: Trading on d4 removes the pawn that wanted to push to d5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...c4 releases the pressure on d4 instead of trading. After 6.b3 cxb3 7.axb3 Bb7 8.Bd3 Nf6 9.e5 Nd5 White's centre stays whole and your knight has been pushed around.
alternatives.after: 5...cxd4 removes White's d-pawn instead. The ...c4 push is a known trap when White's bishop retreats to b3, but here it stands on e2 and nothing is trapped.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Bb7 develops and eyes e4, a plan club players like against 2.Bc4. After 6.a4 the queenside opens up, as in 7.axb5 Bxe4 8.bxa6; it stays level, though a more precise move exists.
alternatives.after: 5...cxd4 settles the centre first, so 6.a4 can be met by 6...b4 and your queenside pawns stay. Both moves keep the game level.

3815955546086349|d8f6.headline: Take the centre with 2...d5; a queen on f6 is a target.
3815955546086349|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home, and White gains time on it: after 3.c4 c6 4.Bg2 the queen has to move again with 4...Qe6. 2.g3 is slow, and 2...d5 punishes it by building a full pawn centre, as in 3.d4 Nc6 4.Nf3 e4, where Black gains space with tempo on the knight.
3815955546086349|d8f6.principle: Against a slow flank setup like e3 and g3, occupy the centre with both pawns; that is worth more than an early queen sortie.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e3/1...e5

3842365322435851|b8c6.headline: Take the free pawn: 3...Nxe4 punishes 3.Nf3
3842365322435851|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 is a decent move, but it gives White time to cover e4 with 4.d3, and the game becomes a quiet Italian where Black's chance is gone. White's 3.Nf3 left the pawn on e4 attacked by your knight and defended by nothing. After 3...Nxe4 4.Nxe5 d5 Black's pawn attacks the bishop on c4 and takes the centre; the bishop retreats with 5.Be2 and Black develops with 5...Bd6.
3842365322435851|b8c6.principle: Every time your opponent moves, check what they left undefended: here the e4 pawn was hanging to the f6 knight.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3842365322435851|d7d5.headline: 3.Nf3 left e4 hanging: take it with 3...Nxe4
3842365322435851|d7d5.why: 3...d5 gives up a pawn for nothing: 4.exd5 takes it, and after 4...e4 5.Ne5 White's knight is active while Black is a pawn down. 3.Nf3 left the pawn on e4 attacked by the knight and defended by nothing, so 3...Nxe4 simply takes it. After 4.Nxe5 d5 Black hits the bishop on c4 and shuts it off from f7.
3842365322435851|d7d5.principle: Before each move, check what is loose: White's e4 pawn has no defender, so take it before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3842365322435851|d7d6.headline: 3.Nf3 left e4 undefended: take it with 3...Nxe4
3842365322435851|d7d6.why: 3...d6 defends e5 but passes up a free central pawn, and after 4.Nc3 White has covered e4 and the chance is gone. White's 3.Nf3 left the pawn on e4 attacked by your knight and defended by nothing. 3...Nxe4 takes it; White can only win back e5 with 4.Nxe5, and then 4...d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and builds a strong centre, with 5...Bd6 hitting the knight on e5 next.
3842365322435851|d7d6.principle: Check what is loose after every opponent move: White's third move developed a piece but left the e4 pawn hanging.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3842365322435851|f6h5.headline: 3.Nf3 left e4 hanging: take it with 3...Nxe4
3842365322435851|f6h5.why: 3...Nh5 moves the knight a second time to the rim and leaves e5 unprotected: 4.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and after 4...Qg5 5.Bxf7+ Kd8 6.Qxh5 the knight on h5 falls too. 3.Nf3 left e4 attacked and not defended at all, so 3...Nxe4 simply takes it, and after 4.Nxe5 d5 Black has a solid centre and easy development.
3842365322435851|f6h5.principle: Check what is loose on both sides before moving: White's e4 pawn was free, and taking it also gets your knight out of trouble.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3881559155902992|d7d5.headline: Guard e5 with 4...d6; 4...d5 just drops a pawn.
3881559155902992|d7d5.why: White threatens 5.Nxe5, and 4...d5 doesn't help: d5 is attacked by the e4 pawn, the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4, more times than Black can defend it, so 5.Nxd5 wins it. 4...d6 calmly defends e5 and opens the c8 bishop, and Black castles next, as in 5.O-O O-O.
3881559155902992|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a pawn into the centre, count: d5 is hit three times by White and covered only twice by Black.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Bc5

3903276797068408|a2a3.headline: Take the loose c5 pawn now with 7.dxc5
3903276797068408|a2a3.why: 7.a3 is a waiting move, and Black uses the time: 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Qb6 hits b2 and backs up the pressure on d4. After 9.Qe2 Nh6 10.Qb5 Nf5 the knight joins in against d4 and your e3 bishop. 7.dxc5 takes the loose pawn: taking back with the f8 bishop just loses it to your e3 bishop, and grabbing e5 lets a queen check on a4 win the g4 bishop. After 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 a6 9.Qg3 you are a pawn up and your pawns are intact.
3903276797068408|a2a3.principle: Black aims everything at d4, the base of your chain; when the pawn attacking it can be taken for free, take it instead of waiting.

ideas.title: Grab c5 when it hangs
ideas.text: After 6...e6, c5 is still attacked by d4 and guarded by nothing. 7.dxc5 takes it, and your e3 bishop guards the pawn on c5.

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: Black's c5 pawn and c6 knight hit d4, and the g4 bishop eyes its f3 guard. Later the queen and g8 knight join in.

ideas.title: Don't invite ...Bxf3
ideas.text: Your f3 knight guards d4. After 7...Bxf3, 8.gxf3 wrecks your kingside and 8.Qxf3 lets 8...Qb6 hit b2 anyway.

ideas.title: Black's knight eyes f5
ideas.text: Black's g8 knight heads for f5, where it hits d4 and your e3 bishop, as in 9...Nh6 and 10...Nf5.

habit.why: 7.a3 is a waiting move, and Black uses the time: 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Qb6 hits b2 and backs up the pressure on d4. After 9.Qe2 Nh6 10.Qb5 Nf5 the knight joins in against d4 and your e3 bishop.

strays.text: You wait, and the free pawn on c5 is never taken.

taught.why: 7.dxc5 takes the loose pawn: taking back with the f8 bishop just loses it to your e3 bishop, and grabbing e5 lets a queen check on a4 win the g4 bishop. After 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 a6 9.Qg3 you are a pawn up and your pawns are intact.

enforces.text: The c5 pawn was loose, and your e3 bishop guards it once taken.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 7.h3 invites 7...Bxf3, and 8.gxf3 Qb6 breaks up your kingside while the queen hits b2.
alternatives.after: 7.dxc5 takes the pawn instead of asking the bishop a question Black is glad to answer.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Be2 develops, but after 7...Nh6 8.Ng1 Bxe2 9.Nxe2 Nf5 10.Nd2 Qb6 Black's knight hits d4 and e3, and 11.Rb1 is spent guarding b2. Black won Vorotnikov-Guliev 1996 with this plan.
alternatives.after: 7.dxc5 takes the pawn and leaves no d4 pawn for Black's knight and queen to attack.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 7.Nbd2 lets 7...cxd4 8.cxd4 Bb4 pin the knight. After 9.Be2 Bxf3 10.Bxf3 Nge7 11.a3 Bxd2+ Black has traded off your knights and keeps d4 under fire.
alternatives.after: 7.dxc5 changes the structure before Black can play ...cxd4 and set up the pins.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Bb5 pins the c6 knight, but 7...Qb6 attacks your bishop and the b2 pawn at once, and 8.a4 a6 forces a decision about the bishop.
alternatives.after: 7.dxc5 takes the pawn at once. In the 7.Bb5 line you take on c5 only at move 9, when the queen on b6 backs it up and 9...Bxc5 wins it back.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

3903276797068408|h2h3.headline: Take on c5 with 7.dxc5 before Black liquidates
3903276797068408|h2h3.why: 7.h3 invites 7...Bxf3, and 8.gxf3 Qb6 leaves your kingside pawns broken while Black's queen hits b2. After 9.Qd2 O-O-O 10.f4 Kb8 11.Bd3 cxd4 Black is better, and 8.Qxf3 is no cure because 8...Qb6 hits b2 too. 7.dxc5 takes the loose pawn: taking back with the f8 bishop just loses it to your e3 bishop, and grabbing e5 lets a queen check on a4 win the g4 bishop. After 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 a6 9.Qg3 you are a pawn up and your pawns are intact.
3903276797068408|h2h3.principle: Look at captures before quiet moves: with the tension still there, 7.dxc5 simply takes a loose pawn.

alternatives.after: 7.dxc5 takes the pawn and leaves no d4 pawn for Black's knight and queen to attack.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 7.Nbd2 lets 7...cxd4 8.cxd4 Bb4 pin the knight. After 9.Be2 Bxf3 10.Bxf3 Nge7 11.a3 Bxd2+ Black has traded off your knights and keeps d4 under fire.
alternatives.after: 7.dxc5 changes the structure before Black can play ...cxd4 and set up the pins.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Bb5 pins the c6 knight, but 7...Qb6 attacks your bishop and the b2 pawn at once, and 8.a4 a6 forces a decision about the bishop.
alternatives.after: 7.dxc5 takes the pawn at once. In the 7.Bb5 line you take on c5 only at move 9, when the queen on b6 backs it up and 9...Bxc5 wins it back.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

3931450314873962|d2d3.headline: Black's bishop is gone: hit b7 and f7 with 6.Qb3
3931450314873962|d2d3.why: 6.d3 is solid but slow: Black gets time for 6...Be7, ...Nc6 and ...Qd7, and after 9.g4 h6 10.Be3 O-O-O Black's king is safe and b7 is covered. Your bishop pair counts for less once Black has caught up. 6.Qb3 hits b7 and lines up with the c4-bishop against f7, two targets at once, as in Morphy's Opera Game. After 6...d5 7.Qxb7 Nbd7 8.Bxd5 Rb8 9.Qa6 Nxd5 10.exd5 you have won the b7 and d5 pawns.
3931450314873962|d2d3.principle: When the opponent gives up the bishop that guards b7, hit the loose squares at once with a double attack instead of slow development.
sources: Opera Game (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_Game
Bobby Ang quoting GM Larry Kaufman, Beating the Philidor (BusinessWorld) | https://www.euvolution.com/prometheism-transhumanism-posthumanism/chess-engines/beating-the-philidor-businessworld-online/
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

ideas.title: Hit b7 with Qb3
ideas.text: Black traded the c8-bishop on f3, so nothing guards b7. 6.Qb3 attacks it from the queen's new square.

ideas.title: Queen and bishop against f7
ideas.text: 5...Nf6 shut the f-file between your queen and f7. On b3 the queen lines up behind the c4-bishop against f7 again.

ideas.title: Use the bishop pair
ideas.text: After 4...Bxf3 you have both bishops; quiet moves like 6.d3 let Black finish developing and that edge fades.

habit.why: 6.d3 is solid but slow: Black gets time for 6...Be7, ...Nc6 and ...Qd7, and after 9.g4 h6 10.Be3 O-O-O Black's king is safe and b7 is covered. Your bishop pair counts for less once Black has caught up.

strays.text: The slow pawn move gives Black time to cover b7 and f7.

taught.why: 6.Qb3 hits b7 and lines up with the c4-bishop against f7, two targets at once, as in Morphy's Opera Game. After 6...d5 7.Qxb7 Nbd7 8.Bxd5 Rb8 9.Qa6 Nxd5 10.exd5 you have won the b7 and d5 pawns.

enforces.text: The queen attacks b7 and f7 together, and one of them drops.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Nc3 develops but lets 6...Nc6 7.Ne2 Na5 chase your bishop, and after 10...Nxe4 Black wins the e4 pawn.
alternatives.after: 6.Qb3 makes threats on b7 and f7 first, so Black has no time for the ...Na5 hunt.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.O-O is natural, but 6...c6 and ...Be7 let Black cover up, and the weak squares on the queenside disappear.
alternatives.after: 6.Qb3 hits b7 and f7 before Black has time for 6...c6.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.g4 weakens your own kingside with no target; after 6...Nc6 7.c3 h6 8.d3 Qd7 Black castles long and is fine.
alternatives.after: 6.Qb3 attacks real targets on b7 and f7 instead of loosening your king.

3931450314873962|g2g4.headline: Black's b7 lost its defender: hit it with 6.Qb3
3931450314873962|g2g4.why: 6.g4 attacks nothing yet and loosens your own kingside, while b7 and f7 stay untouched. Black just develops with 6...Nc6, 8...Qd7 and 9...O-O-O, and after 10...d5 your lead in time is gone. 6.Qb3 hits b7 and lines up with the c4-bishop against f7, and Black cannot cover both. After 6...d5 7.Qxb7 Nbd7 8.Bxd5 you have won material and Black's queenside is loose.
3931450314873962|g2g4.principle: When the opponent trades off the bishop that guarded b7, look for a queen move that hits it before pushing pawns.
sources: Steven Craig Miller, Philidor's Defense (handout) | http://renaissanceknights.org/IL%20Scholastic/Handouts/Handouts%20PDFs/Philidor.pdf
Opera Game - Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera_game
Lessons - Philidor's Defence (Exeter Chess Club) | https://www.exeterchessclub.org.uk/content/lessons-philidors-defence

ideas.title: After ...Bxf3, hit b7 with Qb3
ideas.text: 4...Bxf3 gave up the bishop that guarded b7. 6.Qb3 hits b7 at once, and together with your c4-bishop also f7.

ideas.title: Use the time Black spent
ideas.text: 3...Bg4 and 4...Bxf3 spent two moves on a bishop that is now gone. A slow move lets Black catch up with ...Nc6 and castling.

ideas.title: Keep the bishop pair working
ideas.text: You have both bishops, but they need open lines. Quiet moves let Black's knights settle and your edge fades.

ideas.title: Black aims to castle long
ideas.text: Given time, Black plays ...Nc6, ...Qd7 and ...O-O-O, and the king is out of reach of your c4-bishop.

habit.why: 6.g4 attacks nothing yet and loosens your own kingside, while b7 and f7 stay untouched. Black just develops with 6...Nc6, 8...Qd7 and 9...O-O-O, and after 10...d5 your lead in time is gone.

strays.text: The pawn push leaves b7 and f7 alone while Black catches up.

taught.why: 6.Qb3 hits b7 and lines up with the c4-bishop against f7, and Black cannot cover both. After 6...d5 7.Qxb7 Nbd7 8.Bxd5 you have won material and Black's queenside is loose.

enforces.text: The queen hits b7, which lost its defender, and f7 with the bishop.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.d3 is solid but slow: Black finishes developing with 6...Be7, 7...Nc6 and 8...Qd7, then castles long. The time Black spent on the bishop trade is repaid.
alternatives.after: 6.Qb3 uses that time at once: it hits b7 and f7 before Black can cover them, and wins a pawn.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Nc3 develops, but 6...Nc6 and 7...Na5 chase your c4-bishop and trade it off with 8...Nxb3, so the bishop pair is gone.
alternatives.after: 6.Qb3 acts before Black's knights come out: b7 and f7 are hit at once, and you keep both bishops.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: Castling is safe, but Black uses the move for 6...c6, 8...Be7 and 9...O-O and is fully developed with no weak spots.
alternatives.after: 6.Qb3 first makes Black react: b7 and f7 are both hit, so you win a pawn before you castle.

3941407114211180|a2a3.headline: Castle first with 5.O-O, then strike with d4 and e5
3941407114211180|a2a3.why: 5.a3 spends a move that does nothing for your king. After 5...d6 6.d4 Bxd4 7.Nxd4 exd4 the pawn hits your c3 knight, and with your king on e1 the queen could take on e5 with check, so 8.Ne2 Be6 9.Bxe6 fxe6 leaves Black a pawn up. 5.O-O gets your king off the e-file, so the centre can open at once. After 5...d6 6.d4 Bxd4 7.Nxd4 exd4 8.e5 the queen must run, since taking on e5 lets a rook land on e1, and 8...Qg6 9.Bd3 Bf5 gives you strong play for the pawn.
3941407114211180|a2a3.principle: Castle before you open the centre: with your king on g1, the e5 push hits the queen instead of walking into a check.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6/3. Bc4 (Wikibooks) | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...e5/2._Nf3/2...Qf6/3._Bc4
Greco Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco_Defence

ideas.title: Castle, then play d4
ideas.text: With your king on g1, 6.d4 Bxd4 7.Nxd4 exd4 8.e5 hits the queen, and it can't take on e5 because a rook comes to e1.

ideas.title: Hit the early queen with tempo
ideas.text: The queen on f6 is a target: 8.e5 drives it away, as in 8...Qg6 9.Bd3, and you gain time for the pawn.

ideas.title: Watch the pins on your knights
ideas.text: Slow moves give Black time for ...d6 and ...Bg4, pinning your f3 knight while the queen also hits f3, as after 5.d3.

ideas.title: No time for slow pawn moves
ideas.text: 5.a3 spends the move your king needs. One tempo decides whether 8.e5 works, so every move now must develop or castle.

habit.why: 5.a3 spends a move that does nothing for your king. After 5...d6 6.d4 Bxd4 7.Nxd4 exd4 the pawn hits your c3 knight, and with your king on e1 the queen could take on e5 with check, so 8.Ne2 Be6 9.Bxe6 fxe6 leaves Black a pawn up.

strays.text: With your king still on e1, the e5 push no longer works.

taught.why: 5.O-O gets your king off the e-file, so the centre can open at once. After 5...d6 6.d4 Bxd4 7.Nxd4 exd4 8.e5 the queen must run, since taking on e5 lets a rook land on e1, and 8...Qg6 9.Bd3 Bf5 gives you strong play for the pawn.

enforces.text: Your king leaves e1, so 8.e5 later comes with tempo, not into a check.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5.d3 is slow and gives up the quick d4 break. After 5...d6 Black gets 6...Bg4, pinning your f3 knight, and the tactics after 7.Bg5 Qxg5 8.Bxf7+ Ke7 9.Nxg5 Bxd1 leave you only a small edge.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O keeps the d-pawn ready for 6.d4 in one step, and with your king safe 8.e5 hits the queen. After 5.d3 that break takes two moves.
alternatives.idea: Watch the pins on your knights

397857285398425|d5d4.headline: After 4.e5, hit the chain with 4...Nc6 instead of 4...d4
397857285398425|d5d4.why: 4...d4 pushes past the c3 knight and hands it the e4 square: after 5.Ne4 it eyes d6 and f6. Following 5...Nc6 6.d3 f5 7.exf6 Nxf6 8.g3 your d4 pawn is a target and White develops freely. 4...Nc6 develops and eyes d4, where White's chain will need support. After 5.Nf3 Bd7 6.d4 Nh6 7.Ne2 Qb6 8.c3 f6 your knights, queen and f-pawn all press on White's centre.
397857285398425|d5d4.principle: Attack a pawn chain with pieces and pawn breaks instead of pushing past it: 4...Nc6, ...Qb6 and ...f6 hit d4 and e5.
sources: Playing the Grand Prix Attack Against the Sicilian (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/grand-prix-attack/
How I play against the Closed Sicilian (IM Junta Ikeda) | https://juntaikeda.substack.com/p/how-i-play-against-the-closed-sicilian
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nc3/2...e6

ideas.title: Attack the e5/f4 chain
ideas.text: Your e6/d5 pawns face White's e5/f4 chain, French style: pressure it with 4...Nc6, 7...Qb6 and 8...f6.

ideas.title: Knight to f5
ideas.text: Your g8 knight heads for f5 via h6 or e7, where it presses on d4 and covers the kingside.

ideas.title: Don't hand over e4
ideas.text: 4...d4 lets the c3 knight jump to e4, eyeing d6 and f6; chasing it with ...f5 allows 7.exf6.

ideas.title: White's kingside space
ideas.text: 3.f4 and 4.e5 grab kingside space; White follows with 5.Nf3 and 6.d4 to support the chain.

habit.why: 4...d4 pushes past the c3 knight and hands it the e4 square: after 5.Ne4 it eyes d6 and f6. Following 5...Nc6 6.d3 f5 7.exf6 Nxf6 8.g3 your d4 pawn is a target and White develops freely.

strays.text: Pushing past the chain leaves e5 alone and gives White e4.

taught.why: 4...Nc6 develops and eyes d4, where White's chain will need support. After 5.Nf3 Bd7 6.d4 Nh6 7.Ne2 Qb6 8.c3 f6 your knights, queen and f-pawn all press on White's centre.

enforces.text: The knight is the first piece aimed at the d4 square.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Ne7 is the other master move (18%): the knight heads for f5, as in 5.Nf3 Nbc6 6.d4 Nf5, pressing on d4. It is sound and close to the best move.
alternatives.after: 4...Nc6 is the masters' choice (77%) and keeps the g8 knight free for h6 or e7; both plans aim at d4 and f5.

3987932696906099|d1f3.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; a queen on f3 only becomes a target.
3987932696906099|d1f3.why: 5.Qf3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and Black meets it with 5...Qf6, offering a trade, so White's queen has to retreat with 6.Qe2 having achieved nothing. 5.O-O tucks the king away first and prepares Re1 behind the e4 pawn, as in 5...Nf6 6.d3 c6 7.Re1, keeping the lead in development the trade on d4 gave White.
3987932696906099|d1f3.principle: With the knights traded, finish development and castle before bringing the queen out, so Black gets nothing to develop against.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxd4

399137672893272|f1b5.headline: Take the pawn with 4.exd5; 4.Bb5+ lets Black push ...d4.
399137672893272|f1b5.why: 4.Bb5+ c6 5.Be2 wastes time, and 5...d4 drives the knight back to b1, after which Black takes on e4 with 6...Nxe4 and has the active game. 3...d5 is a loose pawn break, and 4.exd5 wins the pawn and claims the centre. After 4...Bd6 Black spends a move defending e5, and White can still give the check 5.Bb5+ once it gains something.
399137672893272|f1b5.principle: Among forcing moves, look at captures before checks: a check that wins nothing only helps the opponent improve.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

399137672893272|f1c4.headline: Take the offered pawn with 4.exd5; c4 is covered by d5
399137672893272|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 puts the bishop where the d5 pawn takes it: 4...dxc4 wins a piece, and 5.Nxe5 gets back only a pawn. 3...d5 was a loose pawn push, and 4.exd5 simply takes it while claiming the centre. After 4...Bd6 5.Bb5+ c6 6.dxc6 Nxc6 White still has the extra pawn.
399137672893272|f1c4.principle: Before developing a piece, check which squares enemy pawns attack: the d5 pawn covers c4, and it is itself the loose target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

3996150506658750|f3g5.headline: Castle and hit e5: 6.O-O, not 6.Ng5
3996150506658750|f3g5.why: 6.Ng5 attacks f7 with the knight alone, since the d5 knight blocks your c4 bishop, and 6...f6 kicks it while guarding e5. After 7.Nc3 Bb4 8.Ne4 Nb6 9.Bb3 Bf5 that knight has moved three times, and Black develops with gain of time. 6.O-O gets your king safe and lets the rook join the fight for e5: after 6...Be7 7.Re1 f6 8.c3 Be6 9.d4 you strike in the centre. Masters choose 6.O-O 88% of the time; Emms says Black's early 4...d5 shouldn't really work because e5 can be hit so quickly.
3996150506658750|f3g5.principle: With Black's knight on d5 blocking your c4 bishop, f7 is no target: castle and pressure e5 instead of moving the f3 knight again.
sources: John Emms, Beating 1e4 e5 (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=inauthor:Emms+%22shouldn%27t+really+work%22
John Emms, Beating 1e4 e5: 4.d3 d5 5.exd5 Nxd5 6.O-O (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=inauthor:Emms+%22d3+d5%22+%22exd5+Nxd5%22+%22Ng5%22
Modern Italian Game (Exeter Chess Club) | https://www.exeterchessclub.org.uk/content/modern-italian-game
Souleidis and Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. d3

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: The d5 knight blocks your c4 bishop, so 6.Ng5 hits f7 with the knight alone, and 6...f6 sends it on its way.

ideas.title: Pressure e5: castle, then Re1
ideas.text: You haven't spent time on c3 or a bishop retreat to b3, so go after e5 at once: castle, then 7.Re1.

ideas.title: Black's ...f6 holds e5
ideas.text: One pawn move guards e5 and takes g5 from your knight and bishop. Black then develops with ...Bf5 or ...Be6.

ideas.title: Don't move a piece twice
ideas.text: Your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. Moving the f3 knight again gives Black free time.

habit.why: 6.Ng5 attacks f7 with the knight alone, since the d5 knight blocks your c4 bishop, and 6...f6 kicks it while guarding e5. After 7.Nc3 Bb4 8.Ne4 Nb6 9.Bb3 Bf5 that knight has moved three times, and Black develops with gain of time.

strays.text: Black covers f7 and kicks the knight with one pawn move.

taught.why: 6.O-O gets your king safe and lets the rook join the fight for e5: after 6...Be7 7.Re1 f6 8.c3 Be6 9.d4 you strike in the centre. Masters choose 6.O-O 88% of the time; Emms says Black's early 4...d5 shouldn't really work because e5 can be hit so quickly.

enforces.text: Castling first brings the rook to e1 against e5.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.Bxd5 gives up your Italian bishop for the knight, and 6...Qxd5 puts Black's queen on a strong central square. After 7.Nc3 Qd6 Black follows with 8...Bf5 and castles long, with the two bishops.
alternatives.after: 6.O-O keeps the bishop and puts pressure on e5 with 7.Re1, so Black's queen never gets a free central post.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.Bg5 develops, but 6...f6 hits the bishop at once and guards e5 too. After 7.Bd2 Bf5 8.Nh4 Be6 Black gains time and later trades your c4 bishop with 10...Bxc4.
alternatives.after: 6.O-O is a move Black can't kick, and 7.Re1 keeps e5 under pressure before Black finishes developing.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.h3 does nothing against e5, and Souleidis' guideline is to wait with h3 until Black has castled. After 6...Bf5 Black adds 7...Qd7 and castles long.
alternatives.after: Masters do play 6.h3 (5.5%), but 6.O-O (88%) spends the move on king safety and brings the rook to e1 against e5.

4040334401902569|c4e2.headline: Ask the bishop with 5.h3; 5.Be2 drops the d4 pawn
4040334401902569|c4e2.why: 5.Be2 breaks the pin but leaves d4 short of guards: 5...Bxf3 6.Bxf3 Nxd4 removes the defender and wins the pawn. It also moves your bishop a second time while your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. 5.h3 hits the bishop before Black can win d4: after 5...Bh5 6.d5 Nb8 your pawn gains space with tempo on the c6 knight and closes the centre. Black then gives up the bishop with 7.Be3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3, leaving you the bishop pair.
4040334401902569|c4e2.principle: Count who guards d4: once the f3 knight is traded off, 5.Be2 can't hold the pawn, so ask the bishop first with 5.h3.
sources: Semi-Italian Opening (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-Italian_Opening
Légal Trap (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9gal_Trap
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

ideas.title: Ask the bishop with h3
ideas.text: 5.h3 makes the g4 bishop decide now: take on f3 and hand you the bishop pair, or retreat and allow 6.d5 with tempo.

ideas.title: The pin hits d4
ideas.text: The g4 bishop pins your f3 knight to the queen, so it can't really guard d4: Black threatens 5...Nxd4, winning a pawn.

ideas.title: Keep d4 and your space
ideas.text: 3...d6 gave you more space. Keep the d4 pawn standing, by asking the bishop, adding c3 or pushing d5, rather than trading on e5.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: A bishop sacrifice on f7 pays only when a check or fork wins it back. Here 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 just gives a bishop for a pawn.

habit.why: 5.Be2 breaks the pin but leaves d4 short of guards: 5...Bxf3 6.Bxf3 Nxd4 removes the defender and wins the pawn. It also moves your bishop a second time while your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home.

strays.text: The bishop retreats instead of guarding d4, and 6...Nxd4 takes it.

taught.why: 5.h3 hits the bishop before Black can win d4: after 5...Bh5 6.d5 Nb8 your pawn gains space with tempo on the c6 knight and closes the centre. Black then gives up the bishop with 7.Be3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3, leaving you the bishop pair.

enforces.text: The bishop must decide now, and 6.d5 comes with tempo.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.dxe5 dxe5 saves the pawn but releases the tension: the centre turns symmetrical, your space is gone and Black's bishop stays active, as in 6.Nbd2 Bd6.
alternatives.after: 5.h3 keeps the d4 pawn and your space, and makes the bishop decide first. Only 6% of master games trade on e5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.d5 gains space and hits the c6 knight, but 5...Nd4 jumps into the hole and the pin stops you chasing it cheaply: 6.Qd3 Nxf3+ 7.gxf3 wrecks your kingside pawns.
alternatives.after: 5.h3 asks the bishop first; after 5...Bh5 6.d5 Nb8 the space gain sends Black's knight home. Masters choose 5.d5 in 11% of games, 5.h3 in 33%.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives a bishop for one pawn with no follow-up. Even after 7.Qxf3+ Nf6 Black's king is safe enough and Black stays a piece up.
alternatives.after: 5.h3 keeps all your pieces and makes the g4 bishop decide. A bishop check on f7 only works when a fork or a knight follows to win the material back.
alternatives.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.c3 shores up d4, so 5...Nxd4 no longer wins a pawn, and it's the most common master move (44%). The engine rates it a little lower: after 5...Nf6 6.d5 Nb8 7.Bd3 Black gets a solid set-up.
alternatives.after: Masters and the engine disagree here: masters prefer 5.c3 (44% to 33%), while the engine prefers 5.h3 because it makes the bishop decide at once instead of leaving the pin in place.

4040334401902569|d4e5.headline: Ask the bishop with 5.h3 instead of trading on e5
4040334401902569|d4e5.why: 5.dxe5 releases the tension: after 5...dxe5 the centre is symmetrical, your space is gone and the pin on f3 is still there. In 6.Nbd2 Bd6 7.h3 Bd7 8.c3 Nf6 Black's bishop just steps back and Black is comfortable. 5.h3 hits the bishop before Black can win d4: after 5...Bh5 6.d5 Nb8 your pawn gains space with tempo on the c6 knight and closes the centre. Black then gives up the bishop with 7.Be3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3, leaving you the bishop pair.
4040334401902569|d4e5.principle: When a pinning bishop is about to win a pawn, ask it to decide at once: 5.h3 keeps your d4 pawn and your space, 5.dxe5 gives them up.
sources: Semi-Italian Opening (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-Italian_Opening

ideas.text: A bishop sacrifice on f7 pays only when a check or fork wins it back. Here 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 just gives a bishop for a pawn.

habit.why: 5.dxe5 releases the tension: after 5...dxe5 the centre is symmetrical, your space is gone and the pin on f3 is still there. In 6.Nbd2 Bd6 7.h3 Bd7 8.c3 Nf6 Black's bishop just steps back and Black is comfortable.

strays.text: Trading on e5 gives back the space that 3...d6 handed you.

taught.why: 5.h3 hits the bishop before Black can win d4: after 5...Bh5 6.d5 Nb8 your pawn gains space with tempo on the c6 knight and closes the centre. Black then gives up the bishop with 7.Be3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3, leaving you the bishop pair.

enforces.text: The bishop must decide now, and 6.d5 comes with tempo.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.d5 gains space and hits the c6 knight, but 5...Nd4 jumps into the hole and the pin stops you chasing it cheaply: 6.Qd3 Nxf3+ 7.gxf3 wrecks your kingside pawns.
alternatives.after: 5.h3 asks the bishop first; after 5...Bh5 6.d5 Nb8 the space gain sends Black's knight home. Masters choose 5.d5 in 11% of games, 5.h3 in 33%.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives a bishop for one pawn with no follow-up. Even after 7.Qxf3+ Nf6 Black's king is safe enough and Black stays a piece up.
alternatives.after: 5.h3 keeps all your pieces and makes the g4 bishop decide. A bishop check on f7 only works when a fork or a knight follows to win the material back.
alternatives.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.c3 shores up d4, so 5...Nxd4 no longer wins a pawn, and it's the most common master move (44%). The engine rates it a little lower: after 5...Nf6 6.d5 Nb8 7.Bd3 Black gets a solid set-up.
alternatives.after: Masters and the engine disagree here: masters prefer 5.c3 (44% to 33%), while the engine prefers 5.h3 because it makes the bishop decide at once instead of leaving the pin in place.

4084843176360845|f8e8.headline: Use the fork trick: 6...Nxe4, then ...d5
4084843176360845|f8e8.why: 6...Re8 is too slow: 7.e5 hits your f6 knight, and after 7...d5 8.Bd3 Nh5 it sits on the rim while White keeps a big pawn centre. White then trades off your light-squared bishop with 10.Bb5 Bd7 11.Bxd7. 6...Nxe4 is the fork trick: after 7.Nxe4 d5 the pawn hits bishop and knight, so you win the piece back. 8.Bd3 dxe4 9.Bxe4 c5 then frees your game with level material.
4084843176360845|f8e8.principle: Look for forcing moves first: with White's bishop on c4, 6...Nxe4 7.Nxe4 d5 wins the piece back with a fork.
sources: Jeremy Silman, A Pirc Quirk | https://www.chess.com/article/view/a-pirc-quirk
Moshe Rachmuth, Dejan Bojkov: Attacking with the Pirc - A Review | https://en.chessbase.com/post/dejan-bojkov-attacking-with-the-pirc-a-review
Pirc Defence - Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirc_Defence

ideas.title: The fork trick against Bc4
ideas.text: With White's bishop on c4 and knight on c3, 6...Nxe4 7.Nxe4 d5 forks bishop and knight and wins the piece back.

ideas.title: The e5 push hits f6
ideas.text: White's main idea is e4-e5 against your f6 knight. Slow moves let 7.e5 drive it away.

ideas.title: Castled, so f7 is covered
ideas.text: With your king on g8, a bishop capture on f7 is met by the rook taking back, so the trick costs you nothing.

ideas.title: Free your game with c7-c5
ideas.text: After the trades, 9...c5 hits d4, which your g7 bishop already eyes down the long diagonal.

habit.why: 6...Re8 is too slow: 7.e5 hits your f6 knight, and after 7...d5 8.Bd3 Nh5 it sits on the rim while White keeps a big pawn centre. White then trades off your light-squared bishop with 10.Bb5 Bd7 11.Bxd7.

strays.text: A quiet rook move gives White time for 7.e5.

taught.why: 6...Nxe4 is the fork trick: after 7.Nxe4 d5 the pawn hits bishop and knight, so you win the piece back. 8.Bd3 dxe4 9.Bxe4 c5 then frees your game with level material.

enforces.text: Take on e4, then 7...d5 forks bishop and knight.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6...Bg4 pins the knight, but 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 gives White the bishop pair and brings the queen toward your king, with 11.O-O-O to follow.
alternatives.after: 6...Nxe4 is more active: the fork trick wins the piece back at once and frees your game, instead of giving up a bishop.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6...Nbd7 is too slow: 7.e5 Nb6 8.Bb3 pushes your knights around, and after 11.Bf4 White still has the e5 pawn.
alternatives.after: 6...Nxe4 acts before 7.e5 can come: the fork trick removes the e4 pawn and opens your g7 bishop's diagonal.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6...c6 is useful but slow: 7.e5 Nd5 8.exd6 Qxd6 opens the centre on White's terms, and after 10.h3 Bxf3 11.Qxf3 White has the two bishops.
alternatives.after: 6...Nxe4 uses the moment while e4 is weak. In Silman's lines with the bishop on c4, the e5 push is White's main idea against slow moves like this.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6...h6 makes the bishop decide, and after 7.Be3 the position is much the same, with a pawn move spent. There is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 6...Nxe4 at once is a little more accurate. After 6...h6 7.Be3 the same trick, 7...Nxe4 8.Nxe4 d5, still works.

4111926581298046|d6e5.headline: Against the Austrian e5, 5...Nfd7 keeps more tension
4111926581298046|d6e5.why: 5...dxe5 is playable (masters choose it 39% of the time), but it gives White the easier game. After 6.dxe5 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 Ng4 8.Ke1 the f4 pawn still guards e5, and 9.Nd5 Kd8 leaves your king stuck in the centre. 5...Nfd7 keeps the queens on and lets your g7 bishop press e5 (59% of masters). After 6.Nf3 c5 you strike at d4 from the side, and 7.dxc5 dxe5 8.fxe5 O-O leaves you castled in a level game.
4111926581298046|d6e5.principle: Attack a pawn chain at its base: after 5...Nfd7, c7-c5 hits d4, the pawn that holds up White's centre.
sources: James Vigus, Chess Developments: The Pirc (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-chess-developments-the-pirc.pdf
Robert Ramirez, Pirc vs Austrian Attack | https://www.chessissimple.com/_files/ugd/775286_68e8b5f08b2a4d649a461dd8ecdcb1c6.pdf
Sean Marsh, Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/

ideas.title: f4 backs up e5
ideas.text: With the f4 pawn behind it, e5 stays protected even after a queen trade, so ...Ng4 does not win it.

ideas.title: Meet e5 with ...Nfd7
ideas.text: In the Austrian, 5...Nfd7 is the usual answer: the knight steps back, the queens stay on, and your g7 bishop presses e5.

ideas.title: Bg7, castle, then c7-c5
ideas.text: Hit the base of White's centre with ...c5, as in 6.Nf3 c5, and castle soon after.

habit.why: 5...dxe5 is playable (masters choose it 39% of the time), but it gives White the easier game. After 6.dxe5 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 Ng4 8.Ke1 the f4 pawn still guards e5, and 9.Nd5 Kd8 leaves your king stuck in the centre.

strays.text: The queen trade works in the Classical, but f4 holds e5 here.

taught.why: 5...Nfd7 keeps the queens on and lets your g7 bishop press e5 (59% of masters). After 6.Nf3 c5 you strike at d4 from the side, and 7.dxc5 dxe5 8.fxe5 O-O leaves you castled in a level game.

enforces.text: The knight steps back, then c7-c5 hits d4.

4120112958252679|f6d7.headline: Trade queens on d1 first, then hit e5
4120112958252679|f6d7.why: 6...Nfd7 keeps the queens on and allows 7.e6 fxe6 8.Ng5, which breaks your pawns and hits e6. After 8...Ne5 9.Qxd8+ Kxd8 10.f4 h6 11.fxe5 both knights come off, and your king sits on d8 behind broken pawns. 6...Qxd1+ 7.Nxd1 trades queens on your terms, and your king can still castle. Then 7...Ng4 and 8...Nc6 gang up on the lone e5 pawn, and White has to give it back with 10.e6 fxe6.
4120112958252679|f6d7.principle: When an early e5 attacks your knight, make the forcing capture first: 6...Qxd1+ takes the queens off on your terms before the knight moves.
sources: Sean Marsh, Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/
Igor Smirnov, Beat the Pirc Defense with This Trap! | https://chess-teacher.com/beat-the-pirc-defense-with-this-trap/

ideas.title: Early e5: trade queens first
ideas.text: With no White pawn on d4 or f4, take the queens off with 6...Qxd1+. You keep castling rights and avoid a check on d8.

ideas.title: A lone e5 pawn is a target
ideas.text: Nothing guards e5 except the f3 knight. Once the queens are off, ...Ng4 and ...Nc6 both attack it.

ideas.title: Don't hand White the queen trade
ideas.text: If your knight moves first, White trades on d8 with check. Your king is stuck on d8 and White develops with tempo.

ideas.title: The e6 thrust
ideas.text: With your knight on d7, White pushes e5-e6. After 7.e6 fxe6 8.Ng5 your pawns are broken and e6 is hit.

habit.why: 6...Nfd7 keeps the queens on and allows 7.e6 fxe6 8.Ng5, which breaks your pawns and hits e6. After 8...Ne5 9.Qxd8+ Kxd8 10.f4 h6 11.fxe5 both knights come off, and your king sits on d8 behind broken pawns.

strays.text: The knight on d7 invites 7.e6, and your pawns fall apart.

taught.why: 6...Qxd1+ 7.Nxd1 trades queens on your terms, and your king can still castle. Then 7...Ng4 and 8...Nc6 gang up on the lone e5 pawn, and White has to give it back with 10.e6 fxe6.

enforces.text: Queens off first, then the knight jumps to g4 against e5.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.idea: Don't hand White the queen trade
alternatives.before: 6...Ng4 hits e5, but White trades first: 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 costs your castling rights, and 9.Rd1+ and 11.Nd5 come with tempo.
alternatives.after: 6...Qxd1+ makes the same knight jump work: after 7.Nxd1 Ng4 the queens are already gone, so no check on d8 and you can still castle.

4120112958252679|f6g4.headline: Trade queens before your knight jumps to g4
4120112958252679|f6g4.why: 6...Ng4 lets White trade queens with check: 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 and your king loses its castling rights. White develops with tempo, 8.Bf4 guards e5, and after 9.Rd1+ Bd7 10.Bb5 Kc8 11.Nd5 the knight jumps at c7 and e7. 6...Qxd1+ 7.Nxd1 trades queens on your terms, and your king can still castle. Then 7...Ng4 and 8...Nc6 gang up on the lone e5 pawn, and White has to give it back with 10.e6 fxe6.
4120112958252679|f6g4.principle: When an early e5 attacks your knight, make the forcing capture first: 6...Qxd1+ takes the queens off on your terms before the knight moves.
sources: Sean Marsh, Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/
Igor Smirnov, Beat the Pirc Defense with This Trap! | https://chess-teacher.com/beat-the-pirc-defense-with-this-trap/

ideas.text: With no White pawn on d4 or f4, take the queens off with 6...Qxd1+. You keep castling rights and avoid a check on d8.

ideas.title: A lone e5 pawn is a target

ideas.title: The e6 thrust
ideas.text: With your knight on d7, White pushes e5-e6. After 7.e6 fxe6 8.Ng5 your pawns are broken and e6 is hit.

habit.why: 6...Ng4 lets White trade queens with check: 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 and your king loses its castling rights. White develops with tempo, 8.Bf4 guards e5, and after 9.Rd1+ Bd7 10.Bb5 Kc8 11.Nd5 the knight jumps at c7 and e7.

strays.idea: Don't hand White the queen trade
strays.text: Moving the knight first lets 7.Qxd8+ come with check.

taught.why: 6...Qxd1+ 7.Nxd1 trades queens on your terms, and your king can still castle. Then 7...Ng4 and 8...Nc6 gang up on the lone e5 pawn, and White has to give it back with 10.e6 fxe6.

enforces.text: Queens off first, then the knight jumps to g4 against e5.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6...Nfd7 dodges the attack, but 7.e6 fxe6 8.Ng5 breaks your pawns and hits e6. After 10.f4 h6 11.fxe5 your king is stuck on d8.
alternatives.after: 6...Qxd1+ trades first and keeps e5 as a target. After 7.Nxd1 Ng4 White has to give the pawn back with 10.e6.

4138915868453329|b7b5.headline: Develop the bishop with 4...Bg4 before starting ...b5
4138915868453329|b7b5.why: 4...b5 starts the queenside before any piece is out, and 5.Bd3 b4 6.Ne2 simply chases the pawn while White keeps the centre. After 7.O-O e6 8.a3 bxa3 9.Rxa3 White's rook joins the game along the a-file. 4...Bg4 develops the bishop and pins the f3-knight, which guards d4; masters choose it 77% of the time. After 5.h3 Bxf3 6.Qxf3 e6 your position is solid, and 8...b5 comes once your pieces are out.
4138915868453329|b7b5.principle: Develop quickly: bring out a piece before starting a pawn advance on the wing.
sources: Sean Marsh, Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/
Pirc Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirc_Defence

ideas.title: ...Bg4 pin versus f7 tactics
ideas.text: Pinning the f3-knight puts pressure on d4. Here it is safe: no white bishop on c4 is aiming at f7.

ideas.title: Bishop out before ...e6
ideas.text: In ...c6 set-ups your c8-bishop comes out first, then ...e6 builds a solid centre, as in 6...e6 after 5.h3 Bxf3.

ideas.title: Develop before ...b5
ideas.text: Queenside expansion with ...b5 is a Czech Pirc plan, but before your pieces are out, 5.Bd3 b4 6.Ne2 just chases the pawn.

habit.why: 4...b5 starts the queenside before any piece is out, and 5.Bd3 b4 6.Ne2 simply chases the pawn while White keeps the centre. After 7.O-O e6 8.a3 bxa3 9.Rxa3 White's rook joins the game along the a-file.

strays.text: 4...b5 moves a pawn while your pieces still sit at home.

taught.why: 4...Bg4 develops the bishop and pins the f3-knight, which guards d4; masters choose it 77% of the time. After 5.h3 Bxf3 6.Qxf3 e6 your position is solid, and 8...b5 comes once your pieces are out.

enforces.text: The bishop gets out before ...e6 shuts it in.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4...Qa5 pins the c3-knight and prepares ...e5, a known Czech Pirc idea and the top club move. Here 5.Bd2 unpins, and after 6.Bc4 Qc7 your queen has moved twice; the engine calls it a mistake though masters play it 8% of the time.
alternatives.after: 4...Bg4 develops a minor piece and pressures d4, and masters choose it 77% of the time; 4...Qa5 spends queen moves instead.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4...g6 turns it into a Pirc with ...c6 included, played by masters 11% of the time, but the engine rates it a mistake here: after 5.h3 and 6.Be2 White keeps a comfortable centre.
alternatives.after: 4...Bg4 gets the bishop out before 5.h3 can take g4 away from it.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 4...Nbd7 takes d7 away from your f6-knight, so 5.e5 drives it off: after 5...Nd5 6.Nxd5 cxd5 7.Ng5 and 8.Qh5 White's pieces aim at your king.
alternatives.after: 4...Bg4 gets the bishop out first; 4...Nbd7 blocks it and takes the f6-knight's best retreat before 5.e5 comes.

4140088474015032|e7e5.headline: Finish the fianchetto with 2...Bg7; 2...e5 abandons the plan.
4140088474015032|e7e5.why: 2...e5 mixes two setups: after 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 White's queen sits in the centre, and the dark squares on Black's kingside, weakened by 1...g6, have no bishop to guard them. 2...Bg7 completes the fianchetto that 1...g6 prepared: Black lets White build a centre and undermines it later with ...d6 and ...Nf6, as in 2...Bg7 3.d4 d6 4.Nc3 Nf6.
4140088474015032|e7e5.principle: Complete the setup your first move committed to: after 1...g6, the bishop on g7 is the piece that makes that pawn move worthwhile.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6

4141510809291242|d7d5.headline: Develop with 1...Nf6; play ...d5 when a pawn can retake
4141510809291242|d7d5.why: 1...d5 lets White swap a wing pawn for your centre pawn with 2.cxd5, and no pawn can take back. After 2...Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 Nxc6 5.Nf3 Bg4 6.e3 you are a pawn down for some activity. 1...Nf6 develops and keeps every set-up open; it is the masters' most popular reply (28%). After 2.d4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 it becomes a Nimzo-Indian, where ...d5 can come later with the e6-pawn behind it.
4141510809291242|d7d5.principle: Play ...d5 against 1.c4 only when a pawn can take back on d5.
sources: The Ultimate English Opening (1.c4) Guide (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/the-ultimate-english-opening-1-c4-guide/
Chess Opening Theory/1. c4/1...d5 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._c4/1...d5

ideas.title: Prepare ...d5 so a pawn recaptures
ideas.text: Against 1.c4, play ...d5 only when a pawn can retake on d5, after ...e6 or ...c6.

ideas.title: c4 discourages ...d5
ideas.text: After 1...d5 2.cxd5 no pawn can take back, and a queen recapture gets chased by White's knight.

ideas.title: Keep your options open
ideas.text: 1...Nf6 develops and keeps every set-up open; after 2.d4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 it becomes a Nimzo-Indian.

habit.why: 1...d5 lets White swap a wing pawn for your centre pawn with 2.cxd5, and no pawn can take back. After 2...Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 Nxc6 5.Nf3 Bg4 6.e3 you are a pawn down for some activity.

strays.text: No pawn can retake on d5, so 2.cxd5 trades off your centre pawn.

taught.why: 1...Nf6 develops and keeps every set-up open; it is the masters' most popular reply (28%). After 2.d4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 it becomes a Nimzo-Indian, where ...d5 can come later with the e6-pawn behind it.

enforces.text: The knight develops and the d-pawn waits for pawn support.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 1...e5 is a sound Reversed Sicilian: White gets a Sicilian with an extra move, but after 2.g3 and 4.Nf3 e4 5.Nd4 d5 you have a fine centre. It is as good as any move here.
alternatives.after: 1...Nf6 and 1...e5 are both good; masters split almost evenly, 28% to 25%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 1...c5 is the Symmetrical English: you can copy White's set-up, though after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 White keeps a slight edge. There is a more flexible move.
alternatives.after: 1...Nf6 keeps more set-ups open, including a later ...c5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 1...e6 prepares ...d5 with pawn support, and after 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5 Be7 you reach a Queen's Gambit Declined. It is fully sound, as good as the move the drill wants.
alternatives.after: 1...e6 and 1...Nf6 often meet after 2.d4: both get ...d5 in only once a pawn can retake.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 1...c6 prepares ...d5 with pawn support, but after 4.e3 e6 5.Bd3 dxc4 6.Bxc4 your c8-bishop is shut in by ...e6.
alternatives.after: 1...Nf6 keeps more options; with 1...c6, get the c8-bishop out before ...e6.

4149741967394205|c1f4.headline: Knight to c3 first; Bf4 now lets Black take c4
4149741967394205|c1f4.why: 4.Bf4 leaves c4 unguarded and d5 free for Black's knight. After 4...dxc4 5.Qa4+ Nbd7 6.e3 Nd5 7.Bxc4 Nxf4 8.exf4 Black has the bishop pair and your pawns are doubled on the f-file. 4.Nc3 develops and adds a guard on d5, so Black's knight has no free jump there. After 4...c5 5.cxd5 cxd4 6.Qxd4 exd5 7.e4 Nc6 8.Bb5 your pieces come out fast and 8.Bb5 pins the c6-knight.
4149741967394205|c1f4.principle: Develop the knights first: 4.Nc3 covers d5, and the c1-bishop's square can be chosen later.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6
A Crash Course In Understanding 1.d4 (GM Max Illingworth, chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/blog/Illingworth/a-crash-course-in-understanding-1-d4

ideas.title: Win back c4, don't Bf4
ideas.text: An early 4.Bf4 does nothing for c4: 4...dxc4 takes it, and 5.Qa4+ spends a queen move to win it back.

ideas.title: ...Nd5 hits the bishop
ideas.text: With no knight on c3 covering d5, Black's knight jumps to d5 and hits a bishop on f4, as in 6...Nd5 7.Bxc4 Nxf4.

ideas.title: Nc3 controls d5
ideas.text: 4.Nc3 develops and adds a guard on d5. The c1-bishop can choose between f4 and g5 once the knight is out.

ideas.title: Catalan long diagonal
ideas.text: 4.g3 makes it a Catalan: if Black opens the long diagonal with ...dxc4, your g2-bishop becomes dangerous.

habit.why: 4.Bf4 leaves c4 unguarded and d5 free for Black's knight. After 4...dxc4 5.Qa4+ Nbd7 6.e3 Nd5 7.Bxc4 Nxf4 8.exf4 Black has the bishop pair and your pawns are doubled on the f-file.

strays.text: The bishop does nothing for c4, so 4...dxc4 costs you time.

taught.why: 4.Nc3 develops and adds a guard on d5, so Black's knight has no free jump there. After 4...c5 5.cxd5 cxd4 6.Qxd4 exd5 7.e4 Nc6 8.Bb5 your pieces come out fast and 8.Bb5 pins the c6-knight.

enforces.text: The knight guards d5 before the c1-bishop picks its square.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Bg5 pins the f6-knight and is a main line, but 4...dxc4 5.e4 b5 6.a4 c6 leads to sharp play over the c4 pawn. There is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 adds control of d5 and is played 62% of the time; 4.Bg5 is fine but invites 4...dxc4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.g3 turns the game into a Catalan: after 4...dxc4 5.Bg2 your bishop rakes the long diagonal and you win c4 back with 8.Qxc4. A main line, as good as any here.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 and 4.g3 are both main lines. Masters pick 4.Nc3 62% to 29%, while the engine rates 4.g3 at least as highly.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.e3 is solid and lets your f1-bishop guard c4, but it shuts in the c1-bishop; after 4...b6 5.Bd3 Bb7 Black develops easily. A good move, though a better one exists.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 keeps the c1-bishop free to come out later. 4.e3 is quieter, 4% of master games.

4149982820903367|e8h8.headline: Take 7...dxc4 before 8.Bxf6 and 9.Bxf5 strip d5
4149982820903367|e8h8.why: 7...O-O doesn't stop White's trick: 8.Bxf6 Bxf6 9.Bxf5 exf5 removes the knight and pulls your e-pawn off d5's defence. 10.cxd5 then wins a pawn, and after 10...Qb6 11.dxc6 Nxc6 you are simply a pawn down with doubled f-pawns. 7...dxc4 takes the target away before White can strip its defenders, and 8.Bxc4 costs the d3 bishop a second move. Then 8...h6 9.Bh4 Ne4 forces trades, and after 10.Nxe4 Bxe4 11.Bxe7 Qxe7 your position is free and level.
4149982820903367|e8h8.principle: Count the defenders of a centre pawn, including pieces your opponent can swap off, and release the tension before a routine move like castling.
sources: James Vigus, Play the Slav (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=Vigus+Slav+%22Bf4%22+%22dxc4%22+%22b5%22+%22Qb3%22

ideas.title: Bxf6 and Bxf5 strip d5
ideas.text: 8.Bxf6 removes the knight guarding d5, 9.Bxf5 exf5 pulls your e-pawn away, and 10.cxd5 wins the pawn.

ideas.title: Take c4 when it's loose
ideas.text: With White's bishop just on d3, 7...dxc4 removes the target, and 8.Bxc4 makes that bishop move twice.

ideas.title: Early ...Bf5 drops b7
ideas.text: Your f5 bishop left b7 without a defender; once d5 falls, the queen can come to b3 and hit both.

ideas.title: Trade pieces to free your game
ideas.text: After 8.Bxc4 h6 9.Bh4 Ne4, swaps on e4 and e7 ease your slightly cramped position.

habit.why: 7...O-O doesn't stop White's trick: 8.Bxf6 Bxf6 9.Bxf5 exf5 removes the knight and pulls your e-pawn off d5's defence. 10.cxd5 then wins a pawn, and after 10...Qb6 11.dxc6 Nxc6 you are simply a pawn down with doubled f-pawns.

strays.text: Castling ignores the two bishop swaps that strip d5 of defenders.

taught.why: 7...dxc4 takes the target away before White can strip its defenders, and 8.Bxc4 costs the d3 bishop a second move. Then 8...h6 9.Bh4 Ne4 forces trades, and after 10.Nxe4 Bxe4 11.Bxe7 Qxe7 your position is free and level.

enforces.text: The pawn trade removes d5 as a target and gains a tempo.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7...Bxd3 8.Qxd3 swaps off the f5 bishop, so the bishop trick on f5 that wins d5 is gone; it's the most common club choice. Sound, but there's an even more precise move.
alternatives.after: 7...dxc4 makes White's d3 bishop spend a move recapturing, so you gain a tempo and keep your bishop; 7...Bxd3 gives it up but is fine too.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 7...Bg6 keeps the bishop out of the trick, but after 8.Bxg6 hxg6 White has made the trade on their terms and your position is a little passive.
alternatives.after: 7...dxc4 removes the d5 target and makes White's bishop spend a move recapturing, so you gain time instead of losing it.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 7...Bg4 pins the f3 knight but leaves b7 loose: 8.Qb3 hits it, and after 9.Bxc4 Bxf3 10.gxf3 you have given the bishop for a knight.
alternatives.after: 7...dxc4 gains a tempo on the d3 bishop and keeps your bishop on f5, where it is safe once d5 is no longer a target.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.idea: Trade pieces to free your game
alternatives.before: 7...Ne4 trades pieces, but after 8.Bxe4 Bxe4 9.Nxe4 dxe4 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nd2 your pawn on e4 is cut off and becomes a target.
alternatives.after: 7...dxc4 8.Bxc4 h6 9.Bh4 Ne4 gets the same trades with your d-pawn swapped off, so you are left with no weak pawn on e4.

4150297190773573|e7e5.headline: Fianchetto first: an early ...e5 drops a pawn
4150297190773573|e7e5.why: 4...e5 loses a pawn: 5.dxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 trades off your queen, e5's only real guard, and costs your castling rights. Then 7.Bg5 Be7 8.Nxe5 picks up the pawn with your king still on d8. 4...Bg7 is the Classical main move (97% of masters): it develops and points the bishop at d4. After 5.Be2 O-O 6.O-O your king is safe, and the centre fight comes later, as with 6...Nc6 7.d5 Ne5.
4150297190773573|e7e5.principle: Develop and castle before you open the centre: 4...e5 now lets 6.Qxd8+ pull your king to d8 and the e5 pawn falls.

ideas.title: Develop first, ...e5 later
ideas.text: ...e5 is your main break, but only after ...Bg7 and castling. Played now, the queen trade on d8 costs you the e5 pawn.

ideas.title: The queen trade costs e5
ideas.text: After 5.dxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 your queen no longer guards e5, and 7.Bg5 and 8.Nxe5 win it.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then strike
ideas.text: You let White build pawns on e4 and d4, then hit them later. The g7 bishop will aim at d4.

habit.why: 4...e5 loses a pawn: 5.dxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 trades off your queen, e5's only real guard, and costs your castling rights. Then 7.Bg5 Be7 8.Nxe5 picks up the pawn with your king still on d8.

strays.text: The break comes before the bishop and king are ready.

taught.why: 4...Bg7 is the Classical main move (97% of masters): it develops and points the bishop at d4. After 5.Be2 O-O 6.O-O your king is safe, and the centre fight comes later, as with 6...Nc6 7.d5 Ne5.

enforces.text: Bishop out and king castled before any central break.

4164085910631465|c1g5.headline: Retake with 8.cxd4: the centre is what your pawns paid for
4164085910631465|c1g5.why: 8.Bg5 develops but leaves both centre pawns hanging: 8...dxc3 9.Nxc3 h6 10.Bh4 d6 and Black is two pawns up with no weaknesses. After 11.Nd5 Qd7 12.Rc1 O-O Black has castled and your attack has nothing to hit. 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and hits the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 costs Black a tempo. Then 9.Ng5 hits f7 twice, and after 9...d5 10.exd5 Na5 11.d6 Nxc4 12.Qa4+ c6 your queen wins back the piece on c4.
4164085910631465|c1g5.principle: In a gambit your pawns buy a centre and time, so take the centre when you can: 8.cxd4 restores pawns on e4 and d4 with gain of time.

ideas.title: Rebuild the centre with cxd4
ideas.text: Your pawns paid for c3 and d4. With your king castled, 8.cxd4 puts pawns back on e4 and d4 and hits the c5 bishop.

ideas.title: Quiet moves cost the centre
ideas.text: 8.Bg5 and other quiet moves leave d4 and c3 to Black. After 8...dxc3 9.Nxc3 you are two pawns down with no centre.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: Once 8.cxd4 has kicked the c5 bishop, 9.Ng5 joins the c4 bishop against f7, and Black must block with 9...d5.

ideas.title: Black's knight prepares ...d5
ideas.text: 7...Nge7 covers d5 and gets ready for ...d5, giving a pawn back so Black's pieces come out easily.

habit.why: 8.Bg5 develops but leaves both centre pawns hanging: 8...dxc3 9.Nxc3 h6 10.Bh4 d6 and Black is two pawns up with no weaknesses. After 11.Nd5 Qd7 12.Rc1 O-O Black has castled and your attack has nothing to hit.

strays.text: A developing move, but d4 and c3 are left to Black.

taught.why: 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and hits the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 costs Black a tempo. Then 9.Ng5 hits f7 twice, and after 9...d5 10.exd5 Na5 11.d6 Nxc4 12.Qa4+ c6 your queen wins back the piece on c4.

enforces.text: Pawns back on e4 and d4, with a tempo on the c5 bishop.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 8.Ng5 hits f7 at once, but 8...d5 9.exd5 Ne5 blocks and hits your bishop. A few moves later 12...Qxd1 trades the queens, and your attack is gone.
alternatives.after: 8.cxd4 first kicks the c5 bishop to b6, so when the knight jumps in with 9.Ng5 Black is a tempo behind. With Black's bishop retreated to a5 instead, the knight jump is a main try that roughly levels.

4164085910631465|c4f7.headline: No follow-up after the f7 sacrifice here: retake with 8.cxd4
4164085910631465|c4f7.why: 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives your bishop for one pawn, and no queen check follows because the d4 pawn and the e7 knight cover d5. After 9.cxd4 Bb6 10.d5 Na5 11.e5 d6 12.e6+ Kg8 Black is a whole piece up and the king is safe. 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and hits the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 costs Black a tempo. Then 9.Ng5 hits f7 twice, and after 9...d5 10.exd5 Na5 11.d6 Nxc4 12.Qa4+ c6 your queen wins back the piece on c4.
4164085910631465|c4f7.principle: A sacrifice on f7 needs a concrete follow-up; with no queen check to come, rebuild the centre with 8.cxd4 instead.

ideas.title: Rebuild the centre with cxd4
ideas.text: Your pawns paid for c3 and d4. With your king castled, 8.cxd4 puts pawns back on e4 and d4 and hits the c5 bishop.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: 8.Bxf7+ pays only when a check follows. Here the d4 pawn and the e7 knight stop any queen check on d5, so nothing follows.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: Once 8.cxd4 has kicked the c5 bishop, 9.Ng5 joins the c4 bishop against f7, and Black must block with 9...d5.

ideas.title: Black's knight prepares ...d5
ideas.text: 7...Nge7 covers d5 and gets ready for ...d5, giving a pawn back so Black's pieces come out easily.

habit.why: 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives your bishop for one pawn, and no queen check follows because the d4 pawn and the e7 knight cover d5. After 9.cxd4 Bb6 10.d5 Na5 11.e5 d6 12.e6+ Kg8 Black is a whole piece up and the king is safe.

strays.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
strays.text: No check follows on d5, so the bishop is simply lost.

taught.why: 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and hits the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 costs Black a tempo. Then 9.Ng5 hits f7 twice, and after 9...d5 10.exd5 Na5 11.d6 Nxc4 12.Qa4+ c6 your queen wins back the piece on c4.

enforces.text: Pawns back on e4 and d4, with a tempo on the c5 bishop.

alternatives.before: 8.Ng5 hits f7 at once, but 8...d5 9.exd5 Ne5 blocks and hits your bishop. A few moves later 12...Qxd1 trades the queens, and your attack is gone.
alternatives.after: 8.cxd4 first kicks the c5 bishop to b6, so when the knight jumps in with 9.Ng5 Black is a tempo behind. With Black's bishop retreated to a5 instead, the knight jump is a main try that roughly levels.

4175344914430296|e7e5.headline: Don't hang e5: play ...e6 and build the Slav set-up
4175344914430296|e7e5.why: 4...e5 puts a pawn where the f3-knight can take it, and nothing defends it: 5.Nxe5 wins it. After 5...Bd6 6.Nf3 you are a pawn down with nothing to show for it. 4...e6 backs up d5 and opens the way for the f8-bishop, as in 5.O-O Be7 6.Nbd2 h6. ...h6 gives the f5-bishop a retreat on h7 when White pushes e4 or chases it, and it is the masters' most common move here (43%).
4175344914430296|e7e5.principle: A pawn that steps into a knight's reach with no defender is simply lost: develop first, and push it once it is supported.

ideas.title: Nf3 takes loose pawns
ideas.text: The f3-knight hits e5 and g5. A pawn pushed there with no defender is simply taken, as in 4...e5 5.Nxe5.

ideas.title: Support ...e5 first
ideas.text: Strong players push ...e5 in these lines once a knight backs it up from d7 or c6.

ideas.title: Slav setup against d3
ideas.text: With d3 and no c4, your bishop can come out to f5, Slav-style. Follow with ...e6, ...Be7 and ...h6, keeping h7 as a retreat.

ideas.title: White's e4 break
ideas.text: White's plan is 6.Nbd2 and a later e4, hitting d5 and the f5-bishop. Keep d5 covered so e4 only leads to trades.

habit.why: 4...e5 puts a pawn where the f3-knight can take it, and nothing defends it: 5.Nxe5 wins it. After 5...Bd6 6.Nf3 you are a pawn down with nothing to show for it.

strays.text: Nothing defends e5, so 5.Nxe5 wins a clean pawn.

taught.why: 4...e6 backs up d5 and opens the way for the f8-bishop, as in 5.O-O Be7 6.Nbd2 h6. ...h6 gives the f5-bishop a retreat on h7 when White pushes e4 or chases it, and it is the masters' most common move here (43%).

enforces.text: Bishop out first, then ...e6, ...Be7 and ...h6: calm and solid.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4...Nf6 develops, but after 5.O-O the jump 6.Nh4 chases your bishop, and 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bh5 8.f4 Be7 9.g4 gains White kingside space with tempo.
alternatives.after: 4...e6 with ...h6 next keeps h7 ready as a retreat for the bishop. Masters play 4...Nf6 often (31%), but the engine prefers the ...e6 and ...h6 set-up.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4...Nd7 does nothing for d5, so after 6.Qe1 h6 7.e4 dxe4 8.dxe4 Bh7 White has pushed e4 and gained time on your bishop.
alternatives.after: 4...e6 prepares ...Be7 and ...Nf6, as in 7...Nf6, so d5 stays covered; with 4...Nd7 White gets 7.e4 in at once.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4...h6 makes room on h7 for the bishop, but after 6.c4 dxc4 7.d4 Nf6 8.Nbd2 Be7 9.Nxc4 White wins the pawn back and has the d4-pawn in the centre.
alternatives.after: 4...e6 develops first and keeps ...h6 for the right moment, as in 6.Nbd2 h6. Masters play 4...h6 18% of the time; the engine rates it a little lower.

4211428648959227|c5d4.headline: Take back on d5 with 4...exd5
4211428648959227|c5d4.why: 4...cxd4 leaves White's pawn on d5 alive and lets 5.Bb5+ in. After 5...Bd7 6.dxe6 fxe6 7.cxd4 your e6 pawn is isolated, your king is exposed and White is clearly better. 4...exd5 takes back at once and opens the diagonal for your c8-bishop; masters choose it 90% of the time. After 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.Bd3 Bd6 you develop quickly and the game is level.
4211428648959227|c5d4.principle: Fight for the centre: recapture on d5 with 4...exd5, while 4...cxd4 releases the tension and lets White's d5 pawn and 5.Bb5+ hurt you.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...e6

ideas.title: Recapture toward the centre
ideas.text: After 4.exd5, take back at once: 4...exd5 keeps a pawn in the centre and opens the diagonal for your c8-bishop.

ideas.title: Keep ...cxd4 for later
ideas.text: While White's c-pawn sits on c3, the knight can't use that square. Wikibooks notes Black usually delays ...cxd4 so as not to free it.

ideas.title: Check on the a4-e8 diagonal
ideas.text: With your d-pawn gone, the b5-e8 diagonal is open: an early ...cxd4 lets 5.Bb5+ in before you've developed.

ideas.title: Isolated d-pawn
ideas.text: After 4...exd5 you may end up with an isolated d-pawn, as in the French Tarrasch; in return your pieces come out quickly.

habit.why: 4...cxd4 leaves White's pawn on d5 alive and lets 5.Bb5+ in. After 5...Bd7 6.dxe6 fxe6 7.cxd4 your e6 pawn is isolated, your king is exposed and White is clearly better.

strays.text: You leave d5 alone, and White's pawn on d5 takes on e6.

taught.why: 4...exd5 takes back at once and opens the diagonal for your c8-bishop; masters choose it 90% of the time. After 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.Bd3 Bd6 you develop quickly and the game is level.

enforces.text: A pawn stays on d5 and your c8-bishop comes to life.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Qxd5 is sound: the queen is safe because the c3 pawn keeps White's knight off c3. After 5.Na3 Bd7 6.Nb5 the knight takes the long way round, and the game stays level.
alternatives.after: 4...exd5 is the masters' main move (90% to 10%): it frees your c8-bishop at the cost of a possible isolated d-pawn, while 4...Qxd5 avoids that pawn but brings your queen out early.

4215612887472399|b8c6.headline: Meet the Vienna Gambit with 3...d5, hitting back in the centre
4215612887472399|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 lets White play 4.fxe5, and after 4...Nxe5 5.d4 Ng6 6.e5 the white pawns chase both black knights, sending the one on f6 back to g8. 3...d5 is the correct counterstrike: it hits e4 at once, so after 4.fxe5 Nxe4 Black's knight lands on a strong central square and Black has active play.
4215612887472399|b8c6.principle: When White pushes the f-pawn against your e-pawn, counter in the centre against e4 rather than defending e5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. f4

4215612887472399|d7d6.headline: Meet the Vienna Gambit with 3...d5, striking back in the centre
4215612887472399|d7d6.why: 3...d6 is too slow: after 4.Nf3 Be7 5.fxe5 dxe5 6.Nxe5 White has won the e5 pawn, and 6...Nxe4 7.Nxe4 costs Black a knight. The theory says the correct move is 3...d5. It counterattacks e4 and leaves White almost forced to take with 4.fxe5, after which 4...Nxe4 puts your knight on a strong central square.
4215612887472399|d7d6.principle: When your opponent attacks your centre pawn with a flank pawn, counterattack theirs with a central pawn instead of defending passively.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. f4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. f4/3...d5

4215612887472399|f8c5.headline: Against the Vienna Gambit, strike back with 3...d5
4215612887472399|f8c5.why: 3...Bc5 lets 4.fxe5 hit the knight on f6, and with no good square it has to go home with 4...Ng8, leaving Black a pawn down and undeveloped. The theory gives 3...d5 as the correct reply: it counterattacks in the centre, and after 4.fxe5 Nxe4 the knight lands on a strong central square instead of retreating.
4215612887472399|f8c5.principle: When White attacks your e-pawn with f4, hit back in the centre so your knight gets e4 instead of being kicked home.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. f4

4237788959769826|c1e3.headline: Push 10.e5 before Black gets in ...d6
4237788959769826|c1e3.why: 10.Be3 puts the bishop where 10...Ng4 hits it, and after 11.Rac1 Nxe3 12.Qxe3 Black has the bishop pair. Black then plays 12...d6, and your e4-e5 break is off. 10.e5 hits the f6-knight before Black can play ...d6, and after 10...Ne8 11.Bf4 your e5 pawn cramps Black. The d7 pawn and c8-bishop are stuck facing your d1-rook, and Black's c7-queen, meant to stop this push, can't hold e5 alone.
4237788959769826|c1e3.principle: A pawn down for activity, you must attack or the edge fades: 10.e5 strikes now, while a quiet 10.Be3 lets Black play ...Ng4 and ...d6.
sources: IM Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf
