ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: e4-e5 kicks the f6-knight to e8 and cramps Black; the d7 pawn and c8-bishop stay stuck facing your d1-rook.

ideas.title: Bishop to f4
ideas.text: Your dark-squared bishop belongs on f4, backing the e5 pawn and eyeing d6, as in 11.Bf4.

ideas.title: Knight jumps to b5
ideas.text: 10.Nb5 hits the queen on c7 and eyes d6; it can come before the pawn push, as in 10.Nb5 Qd8 11.e5.

ideas.title: Black wants ...d6
ideas.text: Black's c7-queen guards e5. Given a quiet move, Black plays 10...Ng4 or ...d6, and your e5 push is gone.

habit.why: 10.Be3 puts the bishop where 10...Ng4 hits it, and after 11.Rac1 Nxe3 12.Qxe3 Black has the bishop pair. Black then plays 12...d6, and your e4-e5 break is off.

strays.text: A quiet bishop move gives Black time for 10...Ng4 and ...d6.

taught.why: 10.e5 hits the f6-knight before Black can play ...d6, and after 10...Ne8 11.Bf4 your e5 pawn cramps Black. The d7 pawn and c8-bishop are stuck facing your d1-rook, and Black's c7-queen, meant to stop this push, can't hold e5 alone.

enforces.text: The push kicks the f6-knight before Black gets in ...d6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 10.Nb5 is good: it hits the queen and eyes d6, and after 10...Qd8 Black's queen has gone back home. There's a slightly more direct move.
alternatives.after: Both share a plan: 10.Nb5 Qd8 11.e5 Ne8 12.Bf4 is the same push a move later. 10.e5 plays it at once, while Black's d-pawn is still at home.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 10.Bg5 runs into 10...h6: after 11.Nb5 Qb8 12.Bh4 d6 Black has completed the setup, and you later give up the bishop with 14.Bxf6.
alternatives.after: 10.e5 stops ...d6 from coming in comfort; after 10.Bg5 h6 Black gets ...d6 in, and your bishop ends up trading itself on f6.

4245409631012417|d4e5.headline: 5.Bg5 first: hit the queen, then take on e5
4245409631012417|d4e5.why: 5.dxe5 releases the tension before the queen has been hit. After 5...dxe5 6.Bg5 Qd6 7.Nxe5 Qxd1+ 8.Rxd1 you win a pawn, but the queens are off and Black's misplaced queen is no longer a target. 5.Bg5 develops with an attack on the queen, and after 5...Qg6 it no longer guards e5. 6.dxe5 wins a pawn, since taking back would open the d-file for mate on d8, and after 6...Bg4 7.Qd2 f6 8.exf6 Nxf6 9.O-O-O you are a pawn up and castled.
4245409631012417|d4e5.principle: Against an early queen, develop with threats to it before releasing the central tension.
sources: Greco Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco_Defence
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6 (Wikibooks) | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...e5/2._Nf3/2...Qf6

ideas.title: Hit the early queen with tempo
ideas.text: 5.Bg5 attacks the queen on f6. After 5...Qg6 it no longer guards e5, and 6.dxe5 wins a pawn.

ideas.title: Keep the queens on
ideas.text: Black's queen is the piece you gain time on. Trading it, as after 7...Qxd1+ in the 5.dxe5 line, throws that target away.

ideas.title: Keep the centre open
ideas.text: Open lines suit the side ahead in development. Releasing the tension with 5.dxe5 or closing it with 5.d5 lets Black catch up.

ideas.title: Keep the g8 knight shut out
ideas.text: The queen on f6 takes the g8 knight's best square. Each time you hit the queen, Black loses another move while that knight waits.

habit.why: 5.dxe5 releases the tension before the queen has been hit. After 5...dxe5 6.Bg5 Qd6 7.Nxe5 Qxd1+ 8.Rxd1 you win a pawn, but the queens are off and Black's misplaced queen is no longer a target.

strays.text: Swapping first lets Black trade queens with 7...Qxd1+.

taught.why: 5.Bg5 develops with an attack on the queen, and after 5...Qg6 it no longer guards e5. 6.dxe5 wins a pawn, since taking back would open the d-file for mate on d8, and after 6...Bg4 7.Qd2 f6 8.exf6 Nxf6 9.O-O-O you are a pawn up and castled.

enforces.idea: Hit the early queen with tempo
enforces.text: The bishop develops with a threat and drives the queen away from e5.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.d5 closes the centre and lets the queen drop back with 5...Qd8. Black then develops normally with 6...Nf6 and 7...Be7, castles with 9...O-O, and most of your lead is gone.
alternatives.after: 5.Bg5 keeps the centre open and hits the queen, which is how a lead in development turns into material.

4245409631012417|f1c4.headline: 5.Bg5 hits the queen first; 5.Bc4 allows the 5...Bg4 pin
4245409631012417|f1c4.why: 5.Bc4 ignores the queen and lets Black pin your f3 knight with 5...Bg4: the queen and bishop both hit f3, and that knight guards d4. In the line 6.Bg5 Bxf3 7.Qd2 Qg6 8.gxf3 exd4 your d-pawn is gone and your kingside pawns are broken. 5.Bg5 develops with an attack on the queen, and after 5...Qg6 it no longer guards e5. 6.dxe5 wins a pawn, since taking back would open the d-file for mate on d8, and after 6...Bg4 7.Qd2 f6 8.exf6 Nxf6 9.O-O-O you are a pawn up and castled.
4245409631012417|f1c4.principle: Against an early queen, develop with threats to it before the opponent's pieces catch up.
sources: Greco Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco_Defence
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6 (Wikibooks) | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...e5/2._Nf3/2...Qf6

ideas.title: Hit the early queen with tempo
ideas.text: 5.Bg5 attacks the queen on f6. After 5...Qg6 it no longer guards e5, and 6.dxe5 wins a pawn.

ideas.title: Watch the pins on your knights
ideas.text: Black's c8 bishop wants g4, pinning your f3 knight while the f6 queen also hits f3. That knight holds d4.

ideas.title: Keep the centre open
ideas.text: Open lines suit the side ahead in development. Releasing the tension with 5.dxe5 or closing it with 5.d5 lets Black catch up.

ideas.title: Keep the queens on
ideas.text: Black's queen is the piece you gain time on. Trading it, as after 7...Qxd1+ in the 5.dxe5 line, throws that target away.

habit.why: 5.Bc4 ignores the queen and lets Black pin your f3 knight with 5...Bg4: the queen and bishop both hit f3, and that knight guards d4. In the line 6.Bg5 Bxf3 7.Qd2 Qg6 8.gxf3 exd4 your d-pawn is gone and your kingside pawns are broken.

strays.idea: Watch the pins on your knights
strays.text: The bishop goes to c4 and leaves 5...Bg4 free to pin your knight.

taught.why: 5.Bg5 develops with an attack on the queen, and after 5...Qg6 it no longer guards e5. 6.dxe5 wins a pawn, since taking back would open the d-file for mate on d8, and after 6...Bg4 7.Qd2 f6 8.exf6 Nxf6 9.O-O-O you are a pawn up and castled.

enforces.idea: Hit the early queen with tempo
enforces.text: The bishop develops with a threat and drives the queen away from e5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.dxe5 dxe5 releases the tension: in the line you win the e5 pawn with 7.Nxe5, but 7...Qxd1+ 8.Rxd1 trades queens. Your lead in development counts for much less in an endgame.
alternatives.after: 5.Bg5 makes the queen move before you release the tension, so you win the e5 pawn and keep queens on, with Black's queen stuck on g6.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.d5 closes the centre and lets the queen drop back with 5...Qd8. Black then develops normally with 6...Nf6 and 7...Be7, castles with 9...O-O, and most of your lead is gone.
alternatives.after: 5.Bg5 keeps the centre open and hits the queen, which is how a lead in development turns into material.

4251014388407323|b8c6.headline: Answer 2.Nc3 with 2...d5 to stop e4.
4251014388407323|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 does nothing to control e4, so White plays 3.e4 and gets a big pawn centre, later gaining more space with 6.d5. 2.Nc3 is aimed at e4, and 2...d5 stops it: Black now controls e4 with knight and pawn, so 3.e4 would only be a pawn gambit. That is why 2...d5 is played in 82.9% of master games.
4251014388407323|b8c6.principle: When a knight move prepares e4, put a pawn on d5 so the square is covered twice before White can occupy it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3/2...d5

425955225904234|g7g6.headline: Against 5.f3, hit the knight with 5...e5 before c4
425955225904234|g7g6.why: 5...g6 spends a move without touching the d4-knight, and 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.Be3 gives White a Yugoslav-style setup where f3 is already played. After 7...h5 8.h3 h4 9.Bc4 Nh5 10.O-O White simply castles and keeps a comfortable game. 5...e5 hits the d4-knight before White can play c4 behind it. After 6.Nb3 Be7 7.c4 a5 8.Be3 O-O your ...a5 bothers the b3-knight and the game is level.
425955225904234|g7g6.principle: Develop with threats: 5...e5 attacks the d4-knight before White can play c4, while 5...g6 lets White set up at leisure.
sources: Wikipedia: Sicilian Defence | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilian_Defence
Wikibooks: 4...Nf6 and the Prins 5.f3 | https://en.wikibooks.org/w/index.php?title=Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...c5/2._Nf3/2...d6/3._d4/3...cxd4/4._Nxd4/4...Nf6&direct

ideas.title: White wants the Maroczy bind
ideas.text: 5.f3 holds e4 with a pawn and delays the c3-knight, so White can still play c4 and clamp down on d5.

ideas.title: Hit the knight with ...e5
ideas.text: 5...e5 attacks the d4-knight at once, before c4 is in, so White must spend a move on 6.Nb3.

ideas.title: Harass the b3-knight
ideas.text: After 6.Nb3 Be7 7.c4, your 7...a5 gets ready to chase the b3-knight further.

habit.why: 5...g6 spends a move without touching the d4-knight, and 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.Be3 gives White a Yugoslav-style setup where f3 is already played. After 7...h5 8.h3 h4 9.Bc4 Nh5 10.O-O White simply castles and keeps a comfortable game.

strays.text: The d4-knight stays put and White picks the setup.

taught.why: 5...e5 hits the d4-knight before White can play c4 behind it. After 6.Nb3 Be7 7.c4 a5 8.Be3 O-O your ...a5 bothers the b3-knight and the game is level.

enforces.text: The knight must move, so White has to spend time before c4.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...a6 is the club favourite (43%), but it allows 6.c4: White gets the Maroczy bind that 5.f3 was played for.
alternatives.after: 5...e5 hits the knight first, so White has to spend 6.Nb3 before 7.c4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Nc6 is sound (22% of master games): it develops and hits d4, and after 6.Nc3 White has blocked the c-pawn and given up the bind. There is a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: 5...e5 is the main line (58% to 22%). 5...Nc6 often reaches a similar structure after 6.Nc3 e5 7.Nb3 Be6 8.Nd5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...e6 aims for a Scheveningen, but with f3 already in, 6.Nc3 a6 7.Be3 h5 8.Qd2 gives White an English Attack setup for free.
alternatives.after: 5...e5 makes the d4-knight move at once instead of letting White build the attack setup at leisure.

426883407817076|c5b4.headline: Retreat the attacked bishop to b6, not into the open with 6...Bb4+
426883407817076|c5b4.why: 6...Bb4+ checks, but after 7.Nc3 the bishop stands where White's pieces and pawns can chase it: 9.Nd5, 10.Qa4 and 11.b4 hound it while White develops. 6...Bb6, the La Bourdonnais variation, retreats the attacked bishop to a safe diagonal at once, still pressing on the d4 pawn. Black then develops calmly with 7.Bb5 Bd7 8.Nc3 Nge7.
426883407817076|c5b4.principle: When a pawn attacks your bishop, retreat it to a square where pawns and pieces cannot keep chasing it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3

4292473947156740|e4d5.headline: Keep the tension: guard e4 with 4.Nbd2 instead of swapping
4292473947156740|e4d5.why: 4.exd5 exd5 releases the tension: Black's c6 pawn already backs d5 and the c8 bishop is free again. After 5.Bd3 Bd6 6.O-O Ne7 7.c4 h6 8.c5 Bc7 the position is symmetrical and your edge is small. 4.Nbd2 guards e4, so 4...dxe4 wins nothing, and with no knight on c3 Black can't swap it off and double your pawns. After 4...Nf6 5.Bd3 c5 6.e5 Nfd7 7.c3 Nc6 8.O-O you have a Closed Tarrasch with an extra move, because Black's c-pawn went to c5 in two steps.
4292473947156740|e4d5.principle: When a pawn of yours is attacked in the centre, keep the tension with a defending move rather than a swap that frees the opponent's pieces.
sources: Sam Collins: The French Advance Structure (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/sam-collins-the-french-advance-structure-050613
Wikibooks: Chess Opening Theory/1._e4/1...e6/2._d4/2...d5/3._Nd2 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...e6/2._d4/2...d5/3._Nd2

ideas.title: Answer ...d5 by keeping e4
ideas.text: Black's d5 pawn hits e4. Guard it with 4.Nbd2 or 4.Nc3, or push 4.e5; 4.exd5 just lets the tension go.

ideas.title: Nd2 Tarrasch, a move ahead
ideas.text: After 4.Nbd2 Nf6 5.Bd3 c5 6.e5 Nfd7 you reach a Closed Tarrasch, but Black's c-pawn took two steps to c5.

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: Once you push e5, Black hits d4 with ...c5 and ...Nc6, as in 6...Nfd7 7.c3 Nc6; c3 keeps d4 solid.

habit.why: 4.exd5 exd5 releases the tension: Black's c6 pawn already backs d5 and the c8 bishop is free again. After 5.Bd3 Bd6 6.O-O Ne7 7.c4 h6 8.c5 Bc7 the position is symmetrical and your edge is small.

strays.text: 4.exd5 gives up the tension and frees Black's c8 bishop.

taught.why: 4.Nbd2 guards e4, so 4...dxe4 wins nothing, and with no knight on c3 Black can't swap it off and double your pawns. After 4...Nf6 5.Bd3 c5 6.e5 Nfd7 7.c3 Nc6 8.O-O you have a Closed Tarrasch with an extra move, because Black's c-pawn went to c5 in two steps.

enforces.text: You get the Tarrasch structure with Black a full move behind.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain
alternatives.before: 4.e5 gains space and is the most popular club move here. After 4...c5 5.c3 Nc6 6.Bd3 Nge7 7.O-O cxd4 8.cxd4 Nf5 you have a normal Advance French, but there's a stronger move.
alternatives.after: Both keep e4 from being taken. 4.Nbd2 waits, keeps e5 in reserve and reaches a Tarrasch a move up if Black plays ...Nf6 and ...c5; 4.e5 commits the centre at once.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 guards e4, but 4...Bb4 pins the knight: after 5.e5 c5 6.a3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qa5 you get the bishop pair and space for doubled c-pawns. Good, but there's a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4.Nbd2 guards e4 without allowing the swap on c3 and the doubled pawns, and Black's c-pawn still needs two moves to reach c5.

4293527898658762|g1f3.headline: Take back with 4.cxd4 and keep two pawns in the centre
4293527898658762|g1f3.why: 4.Nf3 leaves the d4 pawn alone, and 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 turns the game into a Smith-Morra Gambit, with you a pawn down. After 5...Nc6 6.Bc4 a6 7.O-O b5 8.Bd3 Bb7 Black has a standard set-up, and the gambit gives you attacking chances but no real advantage. 4.cxd4 takes back and keeps two pawns in the centre; masters choose it 97% of the time. After 4...d5 5.e5 Ne7 6.Nf3 Nbc6 7.Nc3 Nf5 you have an Advance French where Black presses d4 and your pieces hold it.
4293527898658762|g1f3.principle: When your opponent captures in the centre, take back toward the centre unless you really mean to gambit.
sources: Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (sample, New in Chess) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf
Sam Collins: The French Advance Structure (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/sam-collins-the-french-advance-structure-050613

ideas.title: Take the full centre with d4
ideas.text: 4.cxd4 puts a pawn back on d4 next to e4: two pawns in the centre and nothing given away.

ideas.title: A gambit by accident
ideas.text: 4.Nf3 dxc3 5.Nxc3 is a Smith-Morra Gambit: development for a pawn. Fine if you mean it, not by accident.

ideas.title: Answer ...d5 by keeping e4
ideas.text: After 4...d5 your e4 pawn is attacked; 5.e5 steps forward, gains space and keeps it safe.

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: Then Black hits d4 with ...Ne7-f5 and ...Nc6, as in 5...Ne7 6.Nf3 Nbc6 7.Nc3 Nf5; 6.Nf3 guards it.

habit.why: 4.Nf3 leaves the d4 pawn alone, and 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 turns the game into a Smith-Morra Gambit, with you a pawn down. After 5...Nc6 6.Bc4 a6 7.O-O b5 8.Bd3 Bb7 Black has a standard set-up, and the gambit gives you attacking chances but no real advantage.

strays.idea: Take the full centre with d4
strays.text: 4.Nf3 gives up the pawn instead of taking back on d4.

taught.why: 4.cxd4 takes back and keeps two pawns in the centre; masters choose it 97% of the time. After 4...d5 5.e5 Ne7 6.Nf3 Nbc6 7.Nc3 Nf5 you have an Advance French where Black presses d4 and your pieces hold it.

enforces.idea: Take the full centre with d4
enforces.text: Taking back on d4 rebuilds your pawn centre for free.

4304063535539389|g7g6.headline: With ...a6 and ...Nc6 in, 7...e6 fits; ...g6 doesn't
4304063535539389|g7g6.why: 7...g6 lets 8.Nd5 jump in at once and attack your f6-knight. After 8...Nd7 9.Qd2 Bg7 10.f3 Nc5 11.c3 the knight sits on d5 and your ...a6 does little in a Dragon setup. 7...e6 covers d5 with a pawn and makes it a Scheveningen, where ...a6 and ...Nc6 belong. After 8.Qd2 Bd7 9.a3 Be7 10.Rg1 Nxd4 11.Qxd4 O-O you are castled and solid.
4304063535539389|g7g6.principle: Pick one pawn setup and stick to it: with ...a6 and ...Nc6 played, 7...e6 fits, while 7...g6 wastes ...a6 and gives up d5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...a6/6. Be2
David Vigorito, Playing the Najdorf (preview) | https://docslib.org/doc/3378894/playing-the-najdorf-david-vigorito
Semko Semkov, The Taimanov-Scheveningen Hybrid (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-the-taimanov-scheveningen-hybrid.pdf
John & Joshua Doknjas, Opening Repertoire: The Sicilian Najdorf (sample) | https://www.scacco.it/data/attachments/8688/najdorf-rep-chess.pdf

ideas.title: Pick one pawn setup
ideas.text: With ...a6 and ...Nc6 played, the Scheveningen setup with ...e6 fits. Switching to ...g6 turns ...a6 into a wasted move and weakens the dark squares.

ideas.title: White's d5 square
ideas.text: After ...g6, 8.Nd5 lands on d5 and hits your f6-knight. With ...e6 played, a pawn would cover d5.

ideas.title: White's kingside storm
ideas.text: Against the ...e6 setup White can storm with the g-pawn, as in 10.Rg1 and 12.g4.

habit.why: 7...g6 lets 8.Nd5 jump in at once and attack your f6-knight. After 8...Nd7 9.Qd2 Bg7 10.f3 Nc5 11.c3 the knight sits on d5 and your ...a6 does little in a Dragon setup.

strays.text: Mixing ...g6 into a ...a6 and ...Nc6 setup wastes time and leaves d5.

taught.why: 7...e6 covers d5 with a pawn and makes it a Scheveningen, where ...a6 and ...Nc6 belong. After 8.Qd2 Bd7 9.a3 Be7 10.Rg1 Nxd4 11.Qxd4 O-O you are castled and solid.

enforces.text: ...e6 completes a setup where every earlier move has a job.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7...e5 is a normal Najdorf-style choice (24% of master games): after 8.Nb3 Be6 you fight for d5 with your pieces. It does leave a hole on d5, and the engine rates one other move a little higher.
alternatives.after: 7...e6 is more common (64% to 24%) and keeps a pawn guarding d5; 7...e5 trades that for space and time on the knight. Both are normal, and the engine prefers 7...e6.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7...Bd7 develops but decides nothing about your pawns. After 8.f3 h5 9.h3 you are still undecided while White builds calmly.
alternatives.after: 7...e6 picks the setup at once: d5 is covered and your bishop can still go to d7 later, as after 8.Qd2 Bd7.

4324455140961344|d1e2.headline: Block 3...Qe5+ with a developing move: 4.Be2, not the queen.
4324455140961344|d1e2.why: 4.Qe2 offers a queen trade, and after 4...Qxe2+ 5.Bxe2 Black's misplaced queen is gone, so White can no longer gain time against it. 4.Be2 develops another piece while blocking the check, and the queen on e5 is in the way of Black's e-pawn and will probably have to move again, as in 4...c6 5.d4 Qc7.
4324455140961344|d1e2.principle: When checked, block with a piece you wanted to develop anyway, and keep your queen home so the opponent's early queen stays a target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

4386914372944806|b4b5.headline: Play 7.a4 first; 7.b5 sends Black's knight to a5
4386914372944806|b4b5.why: 7.b5 drives the knight to a5, where it hits your c4-bishop, and 8.Bb3 d5 lets Black break in the centre while your queenside push has cost time. After 9.Qe2 dxe4 10.dxe4 a6 11.bxa6 Rxa6 your b-pawn is gone and Black's rook joins the game. 7.a4 gains space and threatens a5 against the b6-bishop, so Black spends 7...a6 on a retreat square. Then 8.O-O h6 9.Nbd2 d6 10.Re1 Ba7 11.Nf1 is the slow Italian plan: castle and reroute the knight via d2 and f1.
4386914372944806|b4b5.principle: Ask what your push allows: 7.b5 hands the knight a5 with tempo on your bishop, while 7.a4 gains space without a gift.
sources: Souleidis & Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf
Chess Life (2002) | https://books.google.com/books?id=XGJLAAAAYAAJ
Nick de Firmian, Modern Chess Openings, 15th ed. | https://books.google.com/books?id=oC3GNWHyrl0C

ideas.title: a4 before b5
ideas.text: a4 gains queenside space and threatens a5 against the b6-bishop. Push b5 only once the a-pawn supports it.

ideas.title: b5 sends the knight to a5
ideas.text: Push b5 too soon and the c6-knight jumps to a5, hitting your c4-bishop; Black trades it or breaks with ...d5.

ideas.title: Build up, then d4
ideas.text: Castle, bring the queen's knight via d2 and f1 to g3, and push d4 only after that preparation.

ideas.title: Black breaks with ...d5
ideas.text: Black's freeing break is ...d5 against e4; a loose queenside push gives Black the time for it.

habit.why: 7.b5 drives the knight to a5, where it hits your c4-bishop, and 8.Bb3 d5 lets Black break in the centre while your queenside push has cost time. After 9.Qe2 dxe4 10.dxe4 a6 11.bxa6 Rxa6 your b-pawn is gone and Black's rook joins the game.

strays.text: Without a4 behind it, the b5-pawn just drives the knight to a5.

taught.why: 7.a4 gains space and threatens a5 against the b6-bishop, so Black spends 7...a6 on a retreat square. Then 8.O-O h6 9.Nbd2 d6 10.Re1 Ba7 11.Nf1 is the slow Italian plan: castle and reroute the knight via d2 and f1.

enforces.text: a4 gains space and makes Black spend a move on 7...a6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Castling is useful and masters play it in 20% of games. There is a slightly more ambitious move.
alternatives.after: Both moves fit the plan; 7.a4 (70% of masters) makes Black spend 7...a6 at once, and castling follows next move.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Bg5 pins the f6-knight, a sound choice (6% of masters); after 10.Bxf6 gxf6 Black's kingside pawns are broken. There is a slightly more useful move.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 keeps the bishop and goes on with the queenside plan, while 7.Bg5 aims at Black's king position instead.

4424038725631884|g1f3.headline: Your e2 bishop is pinned: hit the queen with 5.d4
4424038725631884|g1f3.why: Your e2 bishop is pinned by the queen on e5, so after 5.Nf3 Bxf3 you can't take back with it and must play 6.gxf3. Your kingside pawns are broken, and after 6...Nc6 7.Ne4 f5 Black is the one doing well. 5.d4 attacks the queen with a pawn and opens your c1 bishop; all 35 master games chose it. After 5...Bxe2 6.Ngxe2 the queen is still attacked, and 6...Qa5 7.b4 Qh5 chases her once more.
4424038725631884|g1f3.principle: When an early queen pins one of your pieces, attack the queen: the pin is gone once she has to move.
sources: Jeremy Silman, First Verbalize, Then Analyze (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/first-verbalize-then-analyze-plus-one-from-the-rule-books
John Elburg, review of Jovanka Houska's Starting Out: The Scandinavian | http://chessbooks.nl/elburg141.html
Scandinavian Defense Guide (Control The Center) | https://openings.controlthecenter.com/openings/scandinavian-defense/?side=white
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

ideas.title: Mind the pin on e2
ideas.text: Black's queen on e5 pins your e2 bishop to your king, so the bishop can't take back on f3.

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: Moves that hit the queen gain time: 5.d4 attacks her, and after 5...Bxe2 6.Ngxe2 she still has to move.

ideas.title: Black's bishop trade on e2
ideas.text: 4...Bg4 aims to swap off your e2 bishop. After 5.d4 Bxe2 6.Ngxe2 the swap just brings your knight out.

habit.why: Your e2 bishop is pinned by the queen on e5, so after 5.Nf3 Bxf3 you can't take back with it and must play 6.gxf3. Your kingside pawns are broken, and after 6...Nc6 7.Ne4 f5 Black is the one doing well.

strays.text: The pinned bishop can't recapture, so 5...Bxf3 breaks your pawns.

taught.why: 5.d4 attacks the queen with a pawn and opens your c1 bishop; all 35 master games chose it. After 5...Bxe2 6.Ngxe2 the queen is still attacked, and 6...Qa5 7.b4 Qh5 chases her once more.

enforces.idea: Develop with tempo on the queen
enforces.text: The pawn hits the queen, and the recapture on e2 brings out a knight.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5.f3 kicks the bishop and stops it from trading on e2, and 5...Bf5 6.g4 Bg6 keeps gaining time. But those pawn moves loosen your kingside while your king still stands on e1.
alternatives.after: 5.d4 hits the queen rather than the bishop, with no weakening pawn moves on the king's side. Every master game in the database chose it.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5.h3 asks the bishop to decide, and Black simply trades with 5...Bxe2. After 6.Ncxe2 Nf6 7.Nf3 Qa5 your knight has left c3 and Black develops in peace.
alternatives.after: 5.d4 makes the same trade come with a threat: after 5...Bxe2 6.Ngxe2 the queen is still attacked and must move again.

4444685778052974|e7e5.headline: Against 6.Bg5, play 6...e6 and keep d5 covered
4444685778052974|e7e5.why: 6...e5 gives up pawn control of d5 and f5, and 7.Nf5 jumps in at once. After 7...Nc6 8.Qf3 Bxf5 9.exf5 Be7 10.Bxf6 Bxf6 11.Bd3 White has traded off your d5 guards and owns the light squares. 6...e6 keeps a pawn guarding d5 and f5 and lets the bishop come to e7 to back up the f6-knight. After 7.Qd2 Be7 8.f3 b5 9.g4 h6 10.Be3 b4 your queenside play is already rolling.
4444685778052974|e7e5.principle: A square no pawn can guard becomes an outpost: after 6...e5 White trades on f6 and owns d5, so 6...e6 keeps a pawn on guard.

ideas.title: Choose ...e6, not ...e5
ideas.text: Vigorito's Najdorf plays ...e5 when it can, but ...e6 against 6.Bg5: the bishop can remove your f6-knight, a key guard of d5.

ideas.title: White takes over d5
ideas.text: After ...e5, White gives up the bishop on f6 and puts pieces on f5 and d5, as in 7.Nf5 and 10.Bxf6.

ideas.title: The threat on f6
ideas.text: 6.Bg5 threatens to take on f6: if only a pawn can take back, your f-pawns are doubled and your king's cover is broken.

ideas.title: Recapture with a piece
ideas.text: 6...e6 prepares ...Be7 and 6...Nbd7 brings a knight to d7, so a piece can take back on f6.

habit.why: 6...e5 gives up pawn control of d5 and f5, and 7.Nf5 jumps in at once. After 7...Nc6 8.Qf3 Bxf5 9.exf5 Be7 10.Bxf6 Bxf6 11.Bd3 White has traded off your d5 guards and owns the light squares.

strays.text: With the g5-bishop ready to take on f6, ...e5 hands d5 to White.

taught.why: 6...e6 keeps a pawn guarding d5 and f5 and lets the bishop come to e7 to back up the f6-knight. After 7.Qd2 Be7 8.f3 b5 9.g4 h6 10.Be3 b4 your queenside play is already rolling.

enforces.text: The e6 pawn guards d5, so trading on f6 wins White nothing there.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6...Nbd7 is a serious choice (19% of master games): the knight can retake on f6 and watches e5. The engine grades it lower after 7.Qe2 h6 8.Bh4 Qc7 9.O-O-O, where White aims for f4 and e5.
alternatives.after: 6...e6 is played four times as often (78% to 19%). 6...Nbd7 is still playable: Kuzmin argued its dubious reputation is undeserved.

4444685778052974|h7h6.headline: Against 6.Bg5, play 6...e6 so a piece can retake on f6
4444685778052974|h7h6.why: 6...h6 does nothing about the threat: 7.Bxf6 gxf6 doubles your f-pawns and opens your king. After 8.Qh5 Nc6 9.Nxc6 bxc6 10.Bc4 e6 11.O-O-O your pawns are broken on both wings and White has castled. 6...e6 lets the bishop come to e7, so a piece can retake on f6. After 7.Qd2 Be7 8.f3 b5 9.g4 h6 your ...h6 comes with the bishop already guarding f6, and 10.Be3 b4 gets your queenside going.
4444685778052974|h7h6.principle: Meet a pin threat by preparing a recapture: 6...e6 readies ...Be7, while 6...h6 lets 7.Bxf6 wreck your pawns.

4472366471003602|a2a3.headline: Hit b5 at once with 4.a4 before ...a6 props it up
4472366471003602|a2a3.why: 4.a3 doesn't touch b5, so Black supports it with 4...a6 and c4 stays protected. After 5.Nf3 e6 6.b3 cxb3 7.a4 Nf6 8.Nbd2 bxa4 Black keeps an extra pawn and your queenside is broken. 4.a4 attacks b5 at once, and 4...a6 fails to 5.axb5 because the a6 pawn is pinned to the a8-rook. After 4...c6 5.axb5 cxb5 6.Nc3 your knight hits b5 again and 7.d5 opens lines; masters choose 4.a4 98% of the time.
4472366471003602|a2a3.principle: Attack an overextended pawn chain at its base: 4.a4 hits b5, the pawn that holds c4.

ideas.title: a4 hits ...b5
ideas.text: The b5 pawn props up c4. 4.a4 attacks it at once, before Black can back it up with ...a6.

ideas.title: The pinned a-pawn
ideas.text: After 4.a4, 4...a6 fails to 5.axb5: the a6 pawn can't take back because your rook would take the a8-rook.

ideas.title: Overstretched queenside
ideas.text: Black's pawns on b5 and c4 stand far forward and need constant defence; 4.a4 and later 6.Nc3 keep hitting b5.

ideas.title: Slow moves let Black keep it
ideas.text: Against slow moves Black supports b5 with ...a6 and stays a clean pawn up, as after 4.a3 a6.

habit.why: 4.a3 doesn't touch b5, so Black supports it with 4...a6 and c4 stays protected. After 5.Nf3 e6 6.b3 cxb3 7.a4 Nf6 8.Nbd2 bxa4 Black keeps an extra pawn and your queenside is broken.

strays.text: a3 doesn't attack b5, so Black has time for ...a6.

taught.why: 4.a4 attacks b5 at once, and 4...a6 fails to 5.axb5 because the a6 pawn is pinned to the a8-rook. After 4...c6 5.axb5 cxb5 6.Nc3 your knight hits b5 again and 7.d5 opens lines; masters choose 4.a4 98% of the time.

enforces.text: 4.a4 strikes b5 before Black can back it up with ...a6.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.idea: Slow moves let Black keep it
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 attacks b5, but 4...a6 holds it, and after 5.Nf3 e6 the pawn can later kick your knight with ...b4.
alternatives.after: 4.a4 comes before ...a6, so Black can't prop up b5 that way and must play 4...c6.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.idea: Slow moves let Black keep it
alternatives.before: 4.Nf3 develops but is too slow: 4...a6 holds b5, and Black keeps the extra pawn with ...Bb7 to follow.
alternatives.after: 4.a4 straight away stops ...a6 from holding b5. One move later, after 4.Nf3 a6 5.a4 Bb7 6.axb5 axb5 7.Rxa8 Bxa8, Black keeps the pawn.

4491386101925356|c5c4.headline: Take toward the centre with 3...cxd4; 3...c4 just hangs
4491386101925356|c5c4.why: 3...c4 puts the pawn where nothing defends it, and 4.Bxc4 takes it while developing. After 4...d5 5.Bd3 dxe4 6.Bxe4 White is a clean pawn up with an open centre. 3...cxd4 trades your flank pawn for White's centre pawn, the trade 1...c5 was played for. After 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5.Nc3 Qc7 you are in a Taimanov, with two centre pawns and the half-open c-file.
4491386101925356|c5c4.principle: Fight for the centre: capture toward it with 3...cxd4 instead of pushing a flank pawn that can be taken.
sources: David Vigorito, Playing the Najdorf (preview) | https://docslib.org/doc/3378894/playing-the-najdorf-david-vigorito

ideas.title: Swap a flank pawn for a centre pawn
ideas.text: 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 leaves you two centre pawns to White's one and a half-open c-file for your rooks.

ideas.title: A pawn on c4 hangs
ideas.text: Nothing can defend a pawn on c4, so 4.Bxc4 takes it with a developing move.

ideas.title: Prepare ...d5, don't rush it
ideas.text: ...d5 is your freeing break, but played now 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5+ leaves an isolated, pinned pawn before you've castled.

ideas.title: White's d4-d5 push
ideas.text: Leave the d4 pawn standing and White can push it to d5, gaining space with tempo against a knight on c6.

habit.why: 3...c4 puts the pawn where nothing defends it, and 4.Bxc4 takes it while developing. After 4...d5 5.Bd3 dxe4 6.Bxe4 White is a clean pawn up with an open centre.

strays.idea: Swap a flank pawn for a centre pawn
strays.text: The c-pawn goes forward instead of taking on d4, and simply drops.

taught.why: 3...cxd4 trades your flank pawn for White's centre pawn, the trade 1...c5 was played for. After 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5.Nc3 Qc7 you are in a Taimanov, with two centre pawns and the half-open c-file.

enforces.idea: Swap a flank pawn for a centre pawn
enforces.text: You give the c-pawn for d4 and get two centre pawns to one.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 3...d5 opens the centre too early: after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5+ Nc6 6.O-O Nf6 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.Bg5 your isolated d5 pawn is pinned and attacked while you are behind in development.
alternatives.after: 3...cxd4 opens the c-file for you instead; ...d5 can come later, once your pieces are out and your king is safe.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 3...Nc6 lets White push 4.d5 with tempo, and after 4...Na5 5.d6 the pawn on d6 cramps you badly while the knight is stuck on a5.
alternatives.after: 3...cxd4 removes the d4 pawn, so there is no push to fear and the knight can come to c6 next.

4491386101925356|d7d5.headline: Trade first with 3...cxd4; save ...d5 for later
4491386101925356|d7d5.why: 3...d5 opens the centre before you have developed: 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5+ Nc6 leaves you an isolated d5 pawn and a pinned knight. After 6.O-O Nf6 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.Bg5 White's pieces all bear on d5 while your king is still on e8. 3...cxd4 trades your flank pawn for White's centre pawn, the trade 1...c5 was played for. After 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5.Nc3 Qc7 you are in a Taimanov, with two centre pawns and the half-open c-file.
4491386101925356|d7d5.principle: Don't open the centre while behind in development: trade 3...cxd4 first and save ...d5 for when your pieces are ready.
sources: David Vigorito, Playing the Najdorf (preview) | https://docslib.org/doc/3378894/playing-the-najdorf-david-vigorito

4499356755733709|d2d3.headline: Black retreated the queen: grab the centre with 4.d4
4499356755733709|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is timid: it lets Black take the centre with 4...Nc6 and 5...e5, after which White has nothing. Black's 3...Qd8 spent a move un-developing the queen, so White has a free hand; 4.d4 takes space in the centre and opens the bishop on c1, and it is the choice in 85% of master games. After 4...Nf6 5.Nf3 White develops smoothly and keeps the edge.
4499356755733709|d2d3.principle: When the opponent spends time un-developing, use it to put a second pawn in the centre, taking the squares Black's pieces need.

4513314094589663|b1c3.headline: After 7...dxc3, hit f7 with check and fork with the queen
4513314094589663|b1c3.why: 8.Nxc3 takes a pawn back but lets the c5 bishop off the hook: after 8...d6 it is guarded, and 9.Qb3 Na5 hits your queen and c4 bishop. After 10.Bxf7+ Kf8 11.Qa4 Kxf7 12.Qxa5 b6 you are still a pawn down and the game is only level. 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 9.Qd5+ is a double attack: the queen checks the king and hits the loose c5 bishop. After 9...Ke8 10.Qh5+ Kf8 11.Qxc5+ d6 12.Qxc3 you have won back the bishop and the c3 pawn, and Black's king can never castle.
4513314094589663|b1c3.principle: When Black grabs pawns instead of developing, look for checks first: 8.Bxf7+ and 9.Qd5+ use two checks to pick up the loose c5 bishop.

ideas.text: 8.Bxf7+ works here because 9.Qd5+ follows: the queen checks the king and hits the loose c5 bishop at the same time.

ideas.title: A third pawn costs time
ideas.text: 7...dxc3 grabs a third pawn instead of developing. Nunn calls it simply bad, because the checks on f7 and d5 come at once.

ideas.title: King in the centre: keep queens
ideas.text: After 8...Kxf7 Black's king can never castle. Keep the queens on and bring your pieces out while it has no safe home.

ideas.title: Moves that gain time
ideas.text: 8.Qb3 lines up with the c4 bishop against f7 and also hits b7, so Black must spend a move defending.

habit.why: 8.Nxc3 takes a pawn back but lets the c5 bishop off the hook: after 8...d6 it is guarded, and 9.Qb3 Na5 hits your queen and c4 bishop. After 10.Bxf7+ Kf8 11.Qa4 Kxf7 12.Qxa5 b6 you are still a pawn down and the game is only level.

strays.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
strays.text: The check on f7 and the queen fork on d5 are passed up.

taught.why: 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 9.Qd5+ is a double attack: the queen checks the king and hits the loose c5 bishop. After 9...Ke8 10.Qh5+ Kf8 11.Qxc5+ d6 12.Qxc3 you have won back the bishop and the c3 pawn, and Black's king can never castle.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
enforces.text: The bishop check comes first, so 9.Qd5+ arrives with check too.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 8.Qb3 lines up your queen with the c4 bishop against f7 and eyes b7, so Black has to defend, as with 8...Qf6. It's a good attacking move, but there is a stronger one.
alternatives.after: 8.Bxf7+ cashes in at once: the bishop check and 9.Qd5+ win back the c5 bishop. 8.Qb3 keeps a strong attack, but after 8...Qf6 9.Bg5 Qg6 10.Nxc3 you have won back only one pawn.

alternatives.label: blunder

alternatives.after: 8.Bxf7+ comes first, with check, so the king is pulled to f7 and 9.Qd5+ is check too. Black never gets the time to guard the c5 bishop.

4552034363865958|d7d5.headline: Cover b5 with 4...a6 before breaking with ...d5
4552034363865958|d7d5.why: 4...d5 opens the centre before you have developed: 5.Bb5+ Bd7 6.exd5 exd5 leaves you an isolated d-pawn. After 7.O-O Bc5 8.Re1+ Ne7 9.Nf5 your king is stuck on e8 and White adds pressure on the pinned e7-knight and g7. 4...a6, the Kan, takes b5 away from White's bishop and knights and keeps your setup flexible. After 5.c4 Nf6 6.Nc3 Bb4 7.Qf3 Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 d6 you hit e4 and White has doubled c-pawns.
4552034363865958|d7d5.principle: Keep the centre closed until your king is safe: 4...a6 covers b5 first, while 4...d5 opens lines with your king still on e8.

ideas.title: Prepare the ...d5 break
ideas.text: ...d5 is your freeing break, but played now 5.Bb5+ and 6.exd5 leave you an isolated d-pawn and your king stuck in the centre.

ideas.title: Knight jumps to b5 and d6
ideas.text: With ...e6 played, d6 has no pawn guard, so White's pieces eye b5 and then d6. A pawn on a6 takes b5 away.

ideas.title: Pressure on e4
ideas.text: In the Kan your pieces hit e4: after 5.c4 Nf6 6.Nc3 Bb4, 7...Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 also doubles White's c-pawns.

habit.why: 4...d5 opens the centre before you have developed: 5.Bb5+ Bd7 6.exd5 exd5 leaves you an isolated d-pawn. After 7.O-O Bc5 8.Re1+ Ne7 9.Nf5 your king is stuck on e8 and White adds pressure on the pinned e7-knight and g7.

strays.text: The break comes before development, so 5.Bb5+ and e-file checks hit your king.

taught.why: 4...a6, the Kan, takes b5 away from White's bishop and knights and keeps your setup flexible. After 5.c4 Nf6 6.Nc3 Bb4 7.Qf3 Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 d6 you hit e4 and White has doubled c-pawns.

enforces.idea: Knight jumps to b5 and d6
enforces.text: With b5 covered there is no bishop check and no knight raid on d6.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.idea: Knight jumps to b5 and d6
alternatives.before: 4...Nc6 is the Taimanov, a main line played in 37% of master games. The engine still grades it lower here, after 5.Nc3 and 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Bf4 d6 8.Qd2, where White eyes d6.
alternatives.after: Masters split almost evenly, 40% for 4...a6 and 37% for 4...Nc6, so this is the engine's preference more than a real error. 4...a6 rules out a knight jump to b5 at once and waits with the knights.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.idea: Knight jumps to b5 and d6
alternatives.before: 4...Nf6 hits e4 and is played in 22% of master games. After 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.e5 Nd5 8.Ne4 the knight has been kicked and you are left with a hole on d6.
alternatives.after: 4...a6 brings the knight out only once White has committed, as in 5.c4 Nf6, and keeps b5 covered for good. Masters play both, so the gap is the engine's view.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4...Bc5 develops with a threat to the knight, but after 5.Be3 Qb6 6.Na3 Qa5+ 7.Bd2 Qd8 your queen has moved three times and gone home.
alternatives.after: 4...a6 makes no early threat but wastes no time either. Even the book on 4...Bc5 admits Black scores only about 46% with it.

4559296915298785|f1d3.headline: Guard d4 with 6.Nf3 before your bishop blocks the queen
4559296915298785|f1d3.why: 6.Bd3 blocks your queen's guard of d4, so 6...Qxd4 takes the pawn. If 7.Bxf5, 7...Qe5+ forks your king and bishop, and after 8.Be4 Nxe4 Black is a pawn up. 6.Nf3 guards d4 a second time, and after 6...e6 7.Qb3 your queen hits b7, which Black's bishop no longer covers. After 7...Nc6 8.Be3 Bb4 9.Be2 you are developed with a firm centre.
4559296915298785|f1d3.principle: Before you develop a piece, count the defenders of the pawns behind it: a bishop can cut off the only guard.

ideas.title: Black targets d4
ideas.text: Black's queen eyes d4 down the open d-file, and only your queen guards it. Block that guard and 6...Qxd4 takes the pawn.

ideas.title: Knight to f3 first
ideas.text: 6.Nf3 develops and adds a guard to d4, so your bishop can come out next without dropping the pawn.

ideas.title: Hit b7 with Qb3
ideas.text: Black's bishop has left c8, so nothing guards b7. After 6.Nf3 e6, 7.Qb3 attacks it.

ideas.title: Watch the queen's checks
ideas.text: With your e-pawn gone, a queen on e5 checks your king. After 6.Bd3 Qxd4 7.Bxf5, 7...Qe5+ forks king and bishop.

habit.why: 6.Bd3 blocks your queen's guard of d4, so 6...Qxd4 takes the pawn. If 7.Bxf5, 7...Qe5+ forks your king and bishop, and after 8.Be4 Nxe4 Black is a pawn up.

strays.text: The bishop cuts your queen off from d4 before the knight guards it.

taught.why: 6.Nf3 guards d4 a second time, and after 6...e6 7.Qb3 your queen hits b7, which Black's bishop no longer covers. After 7...Nc6 8.Be3 Bb4 9.Be2 you are developed with a firm centre.

enforces.text: The knight guards d4, so your bishops can come out next.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Be3 guards d4, so nothing hangs, but the bishop commits early and Black develops easily with 6...Nbd7 and ...e6.
alternatives.after: 6.Nf3 guards d4 and keeps your options open, ready for 7.Qb3 against b7; the bishop can pick its square later.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Bg5 pins the knight but leaves d4 guarded only by your queen. After 6...e6 7.Bd3 h6 8.Bxf6 Qxf6 9.Bxf5 Qxf5 both your bishops are gone and Black's queen is active.
alternatives.after: 6.Nf3 adds a defender to d4 instead of giving up bishops for Black's minor pieces.

4572718139339834|c1a3.headline: Castle first: 8.Ba3 lets the e7 queen take e4 with check
4572718139339834|c1a3.why: 8.Ba3 attacks the queen, but she escapes with 8...Qxe4+, taking your loose centre pawn with check. After 9.Kd1 you can never castle, and you're three pawns down with no centre. 8.O-O takes your king off the e-file and unpins c3, so 9.cxd4 is possible at once. After 8...Bb6 9.cxd4 Nxd4 10.Nxd4 Bxd4 11.Nc3 you develop quickly, and the bishop still reaches a3 with 12.Ba3.
4572718139339834|c1a3.principle: Castle before you hunt with tempo moves: while your king is on the e-file, a loose pawn there can be taken with check.

ideas.text: The e7 queen hits e4, which nothing guards. While your king stands on e1, 8...Qxe4+ takes it with check.

ideas.title: Unpin, then rebuild the centre
ideas.text: The a5 bishop pins your c3 pawn. Once your king leaves e1, 9.cxd4 puts your pawns back on e4 and d4.

ideas.title: Ba3 comes later
ideas.text: A bishop on a3 keeps Black's king in the centre, but the sources play it only after castling, as with 12.Ba3 in the main line.

ideas.title: Hit f7 with tempo

habit.why: 8.Ba3 attacks the queen, but she escapes with 8...Qxe4+, taking your loose centre pawn with check. After 9.Kd1 you can never castle, and you're three pawns down with no centre.

taught.why: 8.O-O takes your king off the e-file and unpins c3, so 9.cxd4 is possible at once. After 8...Bb6 9.cxd4 Nxd4 10.Nxd4 Bxd4 11.Nc3 you develop quickly, and the bishop still reaches a3 with 12.Ba3.

enforces.text: With your king on g1, the c3 pawn is free to recapture with 9.cxd4.

alternatives.after: 8.O-O takes your king off the e-file first, so e4 never falls with check and 9.cxd4 rebuilds the centre.

4572718139339834|f3g5.headline: Castle with 8.O-O; a knight raid with 8.Ng5 meets 8...Nh6
4572718139339834|f3g5.why: 8.Ng5 moves the same knight again, and 8...Nh6 covers f7 with a developing move. After 9.O-O O-O 10.Nf3 Qxe4 the knight has gone back, e4 is gone, and you're still two pawns down with no centre. 8.O-O takes your king off the e-file and unpins c3, so 9.cxd4 is possible at once. 4589106906936820|f1c4.headline: After the slow 2...c6, take the centre with 3.d4
4589106906936820|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 points the bishop at e6, and 3...d5 hits it at once. After 4.Bd3 dxe4 5.Bxe4 Nf6 it is attacked again, and 6.Nc3 Nxe4 7.Nxe4 c5 trades it off and frees Black's game. 2...c6 is slow, so 3.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre. After 3...d5 4.Nbd2 your knight guards e4, and when Black spends a second move on the c-pawn with 5...c5, 6.e5 gains space.
4589106906936820|f1c4.principle: When the opponent makes a slow pawn move, use the time to put both centre pawns forward.
sources: French Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Defence
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3/2...d5

ideas.title: Take the full centre with d4
ideas.text: 2...c6 doesn't fight for the centre. 3.d4 puts a second pawn there before Black's ...d5 comes.

ideas.title: Bishop on c4 hits a wall
ideas.text: ...d5 is coming, and it hits a bishop on c4. After 3...d5 4.Bd3 dxe4 5.Bxe4 Nf6 the bishop gets chased again.

ideas.title: Answer ...d5 by keeping e4
ideas.text: After 3.d4 d5, guard e4 with 4.Nbd2, then push 6.e5 for space instead of letting Black take on e4.

ideas.title: Two moves for the c-pawn
ideas.text: In the 3.d4 line Black plays 5...c5 anyway, two moves for one pawn, so you are a move ahead of a normal French.

habit.why: 3.Bc4 points the bishop at e6, and 3...d5 hits it at once. After 4.Bd3 dxe4 5.Bxe4 Nf6 it is attacked again, and 6.Nc3 Nxe4 7.Nxe4 c5 trades it off and frees Black's game.

strays.idea: Bishop on c4 hits a wall
strays.text: The bishop runs into 3...d5 and is chased until it is traded.

taught.why: 2...c6 is slow, so 3.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre. After 3...d5 4.Nbd2 your knight guards e4, and when Black spends a second move on the c-pawn with 5...c5, 6.e5 gains space.

enforces.idea: Take the full centre with d4
enforces.text: Your two centre pawns arrive while Black spends time on the c-pawn.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 guards e4 and develops, so it's sound, with a stronger move available. After 3...d5 Black's 4...Bb4 pins the knight, and 7...Qa5 later hits your doubled c-pawns.
alternatives.after: 3.d4 takes the centre first, and after 3...d5 4.Nbd2 your knight guards e4 without the pin that 4...Bb4 puts on a knight on c3.

4603395450140279|g1f3.headline: 3...Nc6 didn't take the pawn: recapture with 4.cxd4
4603395450140279|g1f3.why: 4.Nf3 leaves d4 to Black, who accepts after all with 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3: now you're a real pawn down in a Morra. After 5...e6 6.Be2 Be7 7.Qa4 d6 8.e5 d5 Black has a solid setup, keeps the pawn and has blocked the centre. 4.cxd4 wins the pawn back and gives you pawns on e4 and d4; masters choose it 96% of the time. If Black hits back with 4...d5 5.exd5 Qxd5 6.Nf3 e5, then 7.Nc3 develops with a hit on the queen.
4603395450140279|g1f3.principle: When your opponent declines a gambit, take the pawn back and build the centre instead of offering it again.
sources: Bill Harvey, Quick Kills: Alapin Sicilian | https://books.google.com/books?id=4IicEQAAQBAJ
Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3

ideas.title: Take the free centre
ideas.text: 3...Nc6 neither takes on c3 nor defends d4. 4.cxd4 gets your pawn back and puts pawns on e4 and d4.

ideas.title: Don't gambit what you can take
ideas.text: 4.Nf3 lets Black accept after all: 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 leaves you a pawn down when the pawn was yours for free.

ideas.title: Black hits back with ...d5
ideas.text: After 4.cxd4 Black's try is 4...d5 5.exd5 Qxd5 6.Nf3. The queen is out early, and 7.Nc3 develops with a hit on her.

habit.why: 4.Nf3 leaves d4 to Black, who accepts after all with 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3: now you're a real pawn down in a Morra. After 5...e6 6.Be2 Be7 7.Qa4 d6 8.e5 d5 Black has a solid setup, keeps the pawn and has blocked the centre.

strays.text: Black takes on c3 after all, and you're simply a pawn down.

taught.why: 4.cxd4 wins the pawn back and gives you pawns on e4 and d4; masters choose it 96% of the time. If Black hits back with 4...d5 5.exd5 Qxd5 6.Nf3 e5, then 7.Nc3 develops with a hit on the queen.

enforces.text: You get the pawn back and two centre pawns side by side.

4670522513947528|h2h4.headline: Take first with 5.Bxf5 and double Black's f-pawns
4670522513947528|h2h4.why: 5.h4 lets Black make the swap on their terms: 5...Bxd3 6.Qxd3 leaves your light squares weak. After 6...c5 7.c3 Nc6 8.Nf3 Rc8 9.Qd1 cxd4 Black is already hitting d4, and the h-pawn push has done nothing. 5.Bxf5 exf5 doubles Black's f-pawns, and with c6, d5 and f5 on light squares Black has no bishop to cover the holes, e6 above all. After 6.Ne2 Na6 7.Nd2 Nc7 8.Nf3 h6 you build calmly and push 9.h4 later.
4670522513947528|h2h4.principle: Choose the exchange that leaves your opponent the weaknesses: take on f5 so Black's pawns are doubled, rather than letting Black take on d3.
sources: Jeremy Silman, Kt Maneuvers Against the Advance Caro-Kann (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/kt-maneuvers-against-the-advance-caro-kann?page=2

ideas.title: The light-squared bishop question
ideas.text: Black played ...e6 before swapping, so you choose the trade: 5.Bxf5 exf5 doubles Black's f-pawns.

ideas.title: Black's light-square holes
ideas.text: After 5...exf5 Black's pawns on c6, d5 and f5 sit on light squares with no light bishop to guard e6.

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: If Black takes on d3 instead, they hit d4 at once with ...c5 and ...Nc6, as in 6...c5 7.c3 Nc6.

habit.why: 5.h4 lets Black make the swap on their terms: 5...Bxd3 6.Qxd3 leaves your light squares weak. After 6...c5 7.c3 Nc6 8.Nf3 Rc8 9.Qd1 cxd4 Black is already hitting d4, and the h-pawn push has done nothing.

strays.text: 5.h4 lets Black trade bishops on d3, which helps Black.

taught.why: 5.Bxf5 exf5 doubles Black's f-pawns, and with c6, d5 and f5 on light squares Black has no bishop to cover the holes, e6 above all. After 6.Ne2 Na6 7.Nd2 Nc7 8.Nf3 h6 you build calmly and push 9.h4 later.

enforces.text: Taking first doubles Black's f-pawns instead of letting Black swap on d3.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.Nf3 develops, but 5...Bxd3 6.Qxd3 reaches the line IM Silman judges good for Black, and 6...c5 7.c3 Nc6 hits d4 at once.
alternatives.after: 5.Bxf5 makes the trade on your terms: 5...exf5 leaves doubled f-pawns, while after 5.Nf3 Black takes on d3 with a healthy structure.

4675628834516483|f1d3.headline: Keep the d-file open: 5.Be2, not 5.Bd3
4675628834516483|f1d3.why: 5.Bd3 blocks your queen's guard of d4, and nothing else defends the pawn. After 5...cxd4 6.cxd4 Nxd4 Black is simply a pawn up, and 7.Nf3 Nc6 8.O-O Bg4 gives you nothing for it. 5.Be2 develops off the d-file, so your queen keeps guarding d4; it is the masters' top choice at 46%. It also waits: after 5...a6 6.Nf3 Bg4 the knight isn't pinned to your queen, and 7.O-O e6 8.Nbd2 cxd4 9.cxd4 keeps d4 held.
4675628834516483|f1d3.principle: Black piles up on d4, so count its defenders before every move and never cut one off, as a bishop on d3 does.

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: Black's c5 pawn and c6 knight both attack d4. Once Black takes with ...cxd4 and you take back, a piece has to guard the pawn.

ideas.title: Don't block the queen's guard of d4
ideas.text: Your queen guards d4 down the d-file. A bishop on d3 cuts that line, and 5...cxd4 6.cxd4 Nxd4 wins the pawn.

ideas.title: Be2 before Nf3
ideas.text: 5.Be2 develops and waits for Black's c8 bishop to commit before 6.Nf3, so a later 6...Bg4 can't pin your knight to the queen.

ideas.title: ...Bg4 pins d4's defender
ideas.text: If your knight comes out first, 5.Nf3 cxd4 6.cxd4 Bg4 pins the piece that guards d4 and keeps the pressure on.

habit.why: 5.Bd3 blocks your queen's guard of d4, and nothing else defends the pawn. After 5...cxd4 6.cxd4 Nxd4 Black is simply a pawn up, and 7.Nf3 Nc6 8.O-O Bg4 gives you nothing for it.

strays.idea: Don't block the queen's guard of d4
strays.text: The bishop blocks the d-file, so d4 loses its only defender.

taught.why: 5.Be2 develops off the d-file, so your queen keeps guarding d4; it is the masters' top choice at 46%. It also waits: after 5...a6 6.Nf3 Bg4 the knight isn't pinned to your queen, and 7.O-O e6 8.Nbd2 cxd4 9.cxd4 keeps d4 held.

enforces.text: You develop, keep d4 guarded, and bring the knight out when a pin can't hurt.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Nf3 guards d4 and is sound, but there is a stronger move. Wikibooks gives 5...cxd4 6.cxd4 Bg4, pinning the knight that guards d4 and keeping up the pressure.
alternatives.after: 5.Be2 waits for Black's bishop first, so 6.Nf3 comes without a pin on your queen. Masters prefer 5.Be2, 46% to 17%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bb5 pins the c6 knight and keeps d4 safe, a solid choice, but there is a stronger move. After 5...cxd4 6.cxd4 Bf5 Black's light bishop develops freely.
alternatives.after: 5.Be2 waits for Black's bishop to commit instead of letting it out to f5 with no trouble; masters choose it 46% of the time, 5.Bb5 9%.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.f4 props up e5 but leaves your kingside pieces at home. After 5...cxd4 6.cxd4 Nh6 Black's knight heads for f5 and arrives with 9...Nf5 to hit d4.
alternatives.after: 5.Be2 develops a piece and keeps the queen's line to d4 open, while 5.f4 spends the move on a pawn.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Be3 adds a guard to d4 and is sound, but there is a stronger move. Wikibooks notes 5...Nh6, and after 6.Nf3 Nf5 7.Bf4 your bishop has to move again.
alternatives.after: 5.Be2 gives Black's knight no target on e3; masters prefer it, 46% to 12%.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

4701892040283773|b8c6.headline: When White plays 2.d4, take the pawn with 2...exd4
4701892040283773|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 defends e5 but lets White gain space with tempo: 3.d5 kicks the knight to e7, where it blocks your pieces, and after 3...Nce7 4.Nf3 d6 5.c4 White has a big space advantage. 2...exd4 removes White's centre pawn and is played in over 95% of master games. If White takes back with the queen, 3...Nc6 develops with tempo; after 3.Nf3 Bb4+ Black develops with check and has an easy game.
4701892040283773|b8c6.principle: When White offers a centre pawn trade, take it so White is left with one centre pawn and has to spend time winning the pawn back.

4701892040283773|d7d5.headline: Against 2.d4, take with 2...exd4 instead of leaving e5 hanging
4701892040283773|d7d5.why: 2...d5 leaves the pawn on e5 hanging: 3.dxe5 takes it, and copying with 3...dxe4 runs into 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8, an endgame where Black's king can no longer castle. 2...exd4 removes White's centre pawn at once and is played in 95% of master games. White then has to spend time getting the pawn back, and 3.Qxd4 lets Black develop 3...Nc6 with tempo on the queen.
4701892040283773|d7d5.principle: After 2.d4 your e5 pawn is attacked and loose, so settle the tension by capturing before you start anything new.

4701892040283773|d7d6.headline: Take 2...exd4; 2...d6 lets White trade queens and keep space.
4701892040283773|d7d6.why: 2...d6 is an inferior route into the Philidor: White can take 3.dxe5 and, after 3...dxe5 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8, Black has lost the right to castle, or simply transpose with 3.Nf3. 2...exd4 takes the pawn White offered and is chosen in 95.3% of master games; if White recaptures with the queen, Black develops ...Nc6 with tempo on it.
4701892040283773|d7d6.principle: When White opens the centre with a pawn offer, capture and keep it open on your terms; defending with a pawn just hands over space and time.

4701892040283773|d8h4.headline: Take with 2...exd4; the early 2...Qh4 just gets chased
4701892040283773|d8h4.why: 2...Qh4 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home: after 3.Nf3 Qxe4+ 4.Be2 Qf5 5.dxe5 Nc6 6.Nc3 d6 7.Nb5 White develops with gain of time while the queen keeps moving. 2...exd4 takes the pawn instead and is played in 95% of master games. White has to spend time getting it back, and 3.Qxd4 lets Black develop 3...Nc6 with tempo on the queen.
4701892040283773|d8h4.principle: Leave the queen at home and let White's queen be the early target: capture, then develop with tempo against it.

4701892040283773|f7f5.headline: Answer 2.d4 with 2...exd4, not a lunge with the f-pawn
4701892040283773|f7f5.why: 2...f5 leaves e5 attacked and loosens the pawns in front of your king. After 3.exf5 Black has to spend 3...Qe7 to hold e5, which blocks the bishop on f8, while White develops with 4.Nf3 and 5.Be2 and castles with 6.O-O. 2...exd4 removes White's centre pawn at once and is the master choice in over 95% of games; White then has to spend time getting the pawn back while you develop.
4701892040283773|f7f5.principle: With your king still in the centre and White opening lines, don't loosen the f-pawn; settle the centre with a capture and develop toward castling.

4701892040283773|f7f6.headline: Capture on d4; f6 doesn't hold e5
4701892040283773|f7f6.why: 2...f6 doesn't save the e5 pawn: after 3.dxe5 Black recaptures with the f-pawn, and 5.Bc4 then aims at a king whose diagonal you opened yourself. 2...exd4 simply wins the pawn White offered, so White must spend time getting it back, and after 3.Nf3 Bb4+ Black develops with check.
4701892040283773|f7f6.principle: When White strikes at e5 with the d-pawn, capture: trading keeps material level and opens lines for your pieces, while f6 only weakens your king.

4701892040283773|g8f6.headline: Take on d4 first; 2...Nf6 lets 3.dxe5 kick the knight
4701892040283773|g8f6.why: 2...Nf6 leaves e5 to be taken with 3.dxe5, which also hits the knight; it can grab 3...Nxe4, but 4.Qe2 attacks it again, and after 4...Nc5 5.Nc3 the knight has moved three times while White develops. 2...exd4 takes the pawn first and is played in 95% of master games. White has to spend time recovering it, and 3.Qxd4 lets Black develop 3...Nc6 with tempo on the queen.
4701892040283773|g8f6.principle: When a pawn attacks your centre pawn, look at the capture first: it settles the tension on your terms before you develop.

4722555415307870|d8g5.headline: Strike the centre with 2...d5; keep the queen home
4722555415307870|d8g5.why: 2...Qg5 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home, and White gains time on it: 3.d4 attacks e5 and opens the c1 bishop's diagonal toward g5, so the queen has to retreat with 3...Qe7. After 4.dxe5 Qxe5 5.Ne2 the queen has moved three times while White develops. 2...d5 uses the weakness of 1.f3: it opens lines for your pieces and takes on White's centre before White can develop.
4722555415307870|d8g5.principle: Develop pieces and hit the centre with pawns; an early queen just gives your opponent targets to develop against.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. f3/1...e5

473877128562412|b7b5.headline: Hit the bishop with 4...Na5 instead of hanging a pawn
473877128562412|b7b5.why: 4...b5 simply hangs a pawn: the bishop on c4 takes it with 5.Bxb5, and Black gets nothing for it. 4...Na5 attacks the bishop with a piece it can't capture, and in the line 5.Bd5 c6 6.Bxf7+ Kxf7 White ends up giving the bishop for a single pawn.
473877128562412|b7b5.principle: Attack an enemy bishop with a piece it cannot capture; a pawn sent toward it that nothing defends just becomes a free meal.

4756123934331352|d7d6.headline: 5.d3 opened the bishop's line to h6: counterattack with 5...Nd4
4756123934331352|d7d6.why: 5.d3 opened the diagonal of the c1 bishop, so the knight on h6 is hanging, and 5...d6 does nothing about it: 6.Bxh6 wins the knight and even sets up mate on f7. 5...Nd4 answers with a bigger threat, hitting the queen on f3 and the pawn on c2, so White has no time for Bxh6. After 6.Qd1 b5 7.Bd5 c6 8.c3 cxd5 9.cxd4 exd4 Black comes out a pawn up.
4756123934331352|d7d6.principle: Before a quiet move, look at White's forcing moves: 5.d3 uncovered 6.Bxh6, so reply with a forcing move of your own that attacks the queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...g6/4. Qf3

4781739738408769|b1c3.headline: 9.Qd5+ checks the king and wins the loose e5 knight
4781739738408769|b1c3.why: 9.Nbc3 develops but misses that the e5 knight is loose and Black's king is exposed. After 9...Kg8 10.O-O d6 11.f4 Nf7 the king is tucked away, the knight is safe, and material stays level. 9.Qd5+ checks the king and attacks the e5 knight, so after 9...Kg6 10.Qxe5 you are a whole piece up. Black's king stays exposed on g6, and 12.Qg3+ keeps chasing it.
4781739738408769|b1c3.principle: Look for checks that also hit a loose piece: 9.Qd5+ forks the king and the undefended e5 knight.

ideas.title: Forks with check
ideas.text: 9.Qd5+ checks the king and hits the e5 knight at once. Whichever way the king goes, 10.Qxe5 picks up the knight.

ideas.title: King in the centre: keep queens
ideas.text: Black's king on f7 has lost castling. Queen checks keep it on the run; slow moves let it hide on g8.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: 5.Bxf7+ paid off because checks follow it. Now the queen check on d5 is the follow-up that wins material.

habit.why: 9.Nbc3 develops but misses that the e5 knight is loose and Black's king is exposed. After 9...Kg8 10.O-O d6 11.f4 Nf7 the king is tucked away, the knight is safe, and material stays level.

strays.text: The queen check on d5 that wins the knight is missed.

taught.why: 9.Qd5+ checks the king and attacks the e5 knight, so after 9...Kg6 10.Qxe5 you are a whole piece up. Black's king stays exposed on g6, and 12.Qg3+ keeps chasing it.

enforces.text: The queen checks the king and wins the e5 knight.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 9.Qh5+ also wins material: Black has to block with 9...Ng6, and 10.Qf5+ Kg8 11.Qxg6 picks up the knight. It works, but another move wins the piece more directly.
alternatives.after: 9.Qd5+ wins the e5 knight in one move. 9.Qh5+ wins a piece too, but needs 10.Qf5+ and 11.Qxg6 to collect it.
alternatives.idea: King in the centre: keep queens

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 9.O-O is natural, but it gives Black time for 9...d5, kicking your e4 knight and freeing the c8 bishop. Black gets organised, and material stays level.
alternatives.after: 9.Qd5+ uses the moment while the king is exposed and the e5 knight loose. After 9.O-O d5 that check is no longer possible.
alternatives.idea: King in the centre: keep queens

4842782731159492|a7a6.headline: White's castling left e4 hanging: take it with 4...Nxe4
4842782731159492|a7a6.why: 4...a6 is too slow: 5.Bxc6 dxc6 6.Nxe5 removes the defender of e5 and wins the pawn, and Black has nothing in return. Castling left e4 attacked and undefended, so 4...Nxe4, the Open Berlin, takes it; when White wins back e5 it is only a trade of pawns, as in 5.d4 Nd6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.dxe5.
4842782731159492|a7a6.principle: Before a quiet move, check what is loose on both sides: White's e4 pawn hangs now, and your e5 pawn will too once its defender is taken.

4844296345294265|g4g5.headline: Develop with 7.Nc3; pushing g5 attacks nothing
4844296345294265|g4g5.why: 7.g5 attacks nothing, since no knight stands on f6, and it gives up the f5 and h5 squares for good. After 7...Na5 8.Bb5+ c6 9.Ba4 b5 10.Bb3 Bh5 Black's bishop is back pinning your knight, and 11.Nbd2 Nxb3 takes your bishop. 7.Nc3 develops a piece, guards e4 against the g6 bishop and covers d5. After 7...Na5 8.Qe2 Nf6 9.a3 Nxc4 10.dxc4 you give the bishop for a knight, but your pieces are coming out and your kingside has no new holes.
4844296345294265|g4g5.principle: Only push pawns that free pieces or fight for the centre: 7.g5 attacks nothing and leaves holes, while 7.Nc3 develops.

ideas.title: Develop, don't push
ideas.text: With the pin gone after 6...Bg6, bring out new pieces: 7.Nc3 covers d5 and guards e4, which the g6 bishop now eyes.

ideas.title: Black's bishop wants h5
ideas.text: Push the g-pawn again and the g6 bishop drops back to h5, pinning your f3 knight on squares your pawns no longer guard.

ideas.title: Chase the bishop
ideas.text: Black's knight heads for a5 to trade off your c4 bishop; checking on b5 just chases your bishop further.

ideas.title: Lock in the bishop with h4
ideas.text: 7.h4 threatens h5, trapping the g6 bishop. After 7...h5, 8.g5 gains space without leaving new holes.

habit.why: 7.g5 attacks nothing, since no knight stands on f6, and it gives up the f5 and h5 squares for good. After 7...Na5 8.Bb5+ c6 9.Ba4 b5 10.Bb3 Bh5 Black's bishop is back pinning your knight, and 11.Nbd2 Nxb3 takes your bishop.

strays.text: Another pawn move attacks nothing and weakens f5 and h5.

taught.why: 7.Nc3 develops a piece, guards e4 against the g6 bishop and covers d5. After 7...Na5 8.Qe2 Nf6 9.a3 Nxc4 10.dxc4 you give the bishop for a knight, but your pieces are coming out and your kingside has no new holes.

enforces.text: A knight comes out and guards e4 instead of another pawn move.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Ng5 hits f7, but 7...h6 drives the knight straight back with 8.Nf3, and 8...h5 then attacks your g4 pawn. Black gains the time.
alternatives.after: 7.Nc3 brings out a new piece instead of moving the knight twice, and it guards e4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.h4 threatens h5, trapping the g6 bishop, so Black answers 7...h5; then 8.g5 gains space without leaving holes. It's sound, and the engine rates it almost level with its first choice.
alternatives.after: 7.Nc3 develops first; 7.h4 is the consistent pawn follow-up. Both are fine, and in the 7.h4 line Black's knight still trades off your bishop with 9...Nxc4.
alternatives.idea: Lock in the bishop with h4

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 7.Bg5 develops with an attack on the queen, but after 7...Be7 the bishop has nothing to do and drops back with 8.Bd2. Black then plays ...h5 against your g4 pawn.
alternatives.after: 7.Nc3 develops to a square where the piece stays, guarding e4 and d5; 7.Bg5 costs a move when it has to retreat.

4845873281403230|d7d5.headline: Against 3.b3, develop with 3...Nc6 before ...d5 opens the e-file
4845873281403230|d7d5.why: 3...d5 opens the centre before you have developed: after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5+ Nc6 6.Nf3 Nf6 7.O-O Bd6 your d-pawn is isolated and your king is still on e8. Then 8.Bxc6+ doubles your c-pawns. 3...Nc6 develops first, so ...d5 can come later with support. After 4.Bb5 Nge7 5.Nf3 a6 6.Bxc6 Nxc6 you take back with a knight, keep a healthy pawn structure and have the two bishops.
4845873281403230|d7d5.principle: Keep the centre closed until you can castle: 3...Nc6 develops, while 3...d5 opens the e-file with your king on e8.
sources: Playing the Grand Prix Attack Against the Sicilian (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/grand-prix-attack/

ideas.title: Develop before ...d5
ideas.text: Bring out 3...Nc6 and 4...Nge7 first; ...d5 then comes with support, not as a lone pawn.

ideas.title: Checks on e2 and b5
ideas.text: If the centre opens now, 5.Bb5+ comes before you can castle and pins your c6 knight.

ideas.title: Knight on e7 recaptures
ideas.text: After 4.Bb5 Nge7 the knight backs up c6, so 6.Bxc6 Nxc6 leaves you no doubled pawns.

ideas.title: White's b2 bishop
ideas.text: 3.b3 prepares 6.Bb2 down the long diagonal; in the 3...a6 line you contest it with 4...b5 and 5...Bb7.

habit.why: 3...d5 opens the centre before you have developed: after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5+ Nc6 6.Nf3 Nf6 7.O-O Bd6 your d-pawn is isolated and your king is still on e8. Then 8.Bxc6+ doubles your c-pawns.

strays.text: The centre opens while your pieces are still at home.

taught.why: 3...Nc6 develops first, so ...d5 can come later with support. After 4.Bb5 Nge7 5.Nf3 a6 6.Bxc6 Nxc6 you take back with a knight, keep a healthy pawn structure and have the two bishops.

enforces.text: 4...Nge7 backs up c6, so 6.Bxc6 costs you nothing.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...a6 is the most common club reply: it prepares 4...b5 and 5...Bb7 to contest the long diagonal against White's b3 setup. It is sound, but there is a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: 3...Nc6 develops a piece at once and meets 4.Bb5 with 4...Nge7, while 3...a6 spends the move on queenside space. Both are fine.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Nf6 hits e4: after 4.e5 Nd5 5.Bb2 Nxc3 6.dxc3 White's queenside pawns are doubled. It is sound, though the knight has to move twice.
alternatives.after: 3...Nc6 develops without letting White gain time with 4.e5, and keeps ...d5 for later.

4846046788305631|c8e6.headline: In the Philidor, control d4 with 3...c5 before developing
4846046788305631|c8e6.why: 3...Be6 puts the bishop where White's knight can hit it: in the line 4.d4 Nd7 5.Ng5 the knight attacks e6, the centre opens with 5...exd4 6.Qxd4, and White later takes the bishop with 8.Nxe6. 3...c5 takes control of d4, so White cannot easily crack open the centre, and Black develops calmly with 4...Be7 and 5...Nf6.
4846046788305631|c8e6.principle: Ask where White wants to break: d4 is the main lever against the Philidor, so cover it before putting a bishop where Ng5 can reach it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6

4846046788305631|f7f5.headline: Keep it closed: 3...c5 stops d4, while 3...f5 opens your king
4846046788305631|f7f5.why: 3...f5 opens lines while Black is behind in development: after 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe4 Nf6 6.Nxf6+ gxf6 Black's kingside pawns are broken and 7.Bc4 aims at the weakened squares around the king. 3...c5 does the opposite: it takes control of d4, so White cannot blow open the centre with d4, the critical plan against 2...d6. Black then develops calmly with 4...Be7 and 5...Nf6.
4846046788305631|f7f5.principle: When behind in development, keep the centre closed: control d4 with a pawn rather than opening the f-file in front of your own king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...d6

4867591183206233|b8c6.headline: Develop with 2...Nf6; 2...Nc6 gets kicked by d4-d5
4867591183206233|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 blocks your c-pawn, and after 3.d4 e5 4.d5 the knight is pushed back with 4...Nce7. White gains space and develops with 5.a4 and 6.Bc4 while your knight has moved twice. 2...Nf6 develops toward the centre and eyes e4; it is the most common master move (43.5%). After 3.d4 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 you get a solid Philidor set-up, and your c-pawn stays free for 6...c6.
4867591183206233|b8c6.principle: Develop knights toward the centre without blocking the pawns you will need to hit back at White's centre.

ideas.title: The c6 knight runs into d5
ideas.text: After 3.d4 e5 4.d5 the c6 knight is kicked back to e7. It also blocked your c-pawn.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Pirc plan: let White build e4 and d4, then hit them with ...e5 or ...c5. A knight on f6 keeps both breaks free.

ideas.title: Knight to f6 first
ideas.text: 2...Nf6 develops toward the centre and eyes e4, steering into a main Pirc or Philidor after 3.d4.

habit.why: 2...Nc6 blocks your c-pawn, and after 3.d4 e5 4.d5 the knight is pushed back with 4...Nce7. White gains space and develops with 5.a4 and 6.Bc4 while your knight has moved twice.

strays.idea: The c6 knight runs into d5
strays.text: The knight blocks the c-pawn and gets kicked by 4.d5.

taught.why: 2...Nf6 develops toward the centre and eyes e4; it is the most common master move (43.5%). After 3.d4 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 you get a solid Philidor set-up, and your c-pawn stays free for 6...c6.

enforces.text: Develops, eyes e4 and keeps the c-pawn free.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2...e5 claims the centre at once and leaves White more choices. The engine rates it a little worse, though after 3.d4 the game usually becomes a normal Philidor.
alternatives.after: The gap is small: 2...Nf6 keeps your options open, and masters still play 2...e5 in 15.9% of games.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2...g6 heads for the Modern, and masters play it in 31.3% of games. The engine still rates it a little worse: after 3.d4 Bg7 4.Be3 White takes the centre freely.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 hits e4 at once; the engine prefers it, but masters' practice disagrees and 2...g6 is a main choice.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2...c6 is slow: after 3.d4 e5 4.f4 White gets f4 in for free and a big centre, while your knights are still at home.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 develops first and keeps f4 from coming for free; ...c6 can come later, as in 6...c6 of the main line.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2...c5 turns the game into a Sicilian with d6 already played. After 3.Nf3 e5 4.Bc4 you have a hole on d5 for White's pieces.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 keeps your pawns flexible and develops; ...c5 or ...e5 can follow once White commits.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

4870221886044145|e1h1.headline: 5...e6 shut out your bishop: guard e4 with 6.Bd3 first
4870221886044145|e1h1.why: 6.O-O leaves e4 with no defender, and the b7 bishop takes it: 6...Bxe4. The e6 pawn blocks your c4 bishop from f7, so there is no trick to win it back, and after 7.d5 Nf6 8.dxe6 dxe6 9.Qxd8+ Kxd8 10.Ng5 Ke7 you are simply a pawn down. 6.Bd3 moves the bishop that 5...e6 blunted to a square where it guards e4. After 6...d6 7.O-O Ne7 8.Re1 the rook adds a second defender and you keep a comfortable centre.
4870221886044145|e1h1.principle: After every move, quiet ones too, ask what it changed: 5...e6 blocked your bishop's path to f7, so e4 needs a real defender before you castle.

ideas.title: Black's bishop hits e4
ideas.text: The b7 bishop aims at e4, and with your pawn on c3 no knight can guard it from c3.

ideas.title: Guard e4 before anything else
ideas.text: Defend e4 first, with 6.Bd3, 6.Qe2 or 6.Nbd2, and castle after.

ideas.title: The f7 trick is gone
ideas.text: With the e6 pawn in the way, your c4 bishop no longer reaches f7, so no sacrifice there wins e4 back.

ideas.title: Bishop to d3, not c4
ideas.text: Against ...e6 set-ups the bishop belongs on d3: it guards e4 and no pawn blunts it.

habit.why: 6.O-O leaves e4 with no defender, and the b7 bishop takes it: 6...Bxe4. The e6 pawn blocks your c4 bishop from f7, so there is no trick to win it back, and after 7.d5 Nf6 8.dxe6 dxe6 9.Qxd8+ Kxd8 10.Ng5 Ke7 you are simply a pawn down.

strays.text: Castling leaves e4 hanging to the b7 bishop.

taught.why: 6.Bd3 moves the bishop that 5...e6 blunted to a square where it guards e4. After 6...d6 7.O-O Ne7 8.Re1 the rook adds a second defender and you keep a comfortable centre.

enforces.text: The blunted bishop now guards e4, so castling comes safely next.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.e5 takes the pawn out of the b7 bishop's reach, but 6...d6 hits back, and after 7.O-O dxe5 8.Nxe5 Bxe5 9.dxe5 Qxd1 10.Rxd1 the queens are off and your edge is almost gone.
alternatives.after: 6.Bd3 keeps the pawn on e4, guarded, so your centre and the queens stay on the board.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Nbd2 guards e4 from d2, standing in for the knight that can't reach c3. After 6...d6 7.O-O Nf6 you keep a small edge, but one move keeps more.
alternatives.after: 6.Bd3 guards e4 and leaves the knight free to follow with 10.Nbd2; in the 6.Nbd2 line the bishop is chased with 8.Bb5+ c6 9.Be2.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.d5 blocks the b7 bishop's diagonal with a pawn, but Black just develops with 6...Nf6 7.Bg5 h6 8.Bxf6 Qxf6, and the d5 pawn can become a target.
alternatives.after: 6.Bd3 guards e4 and keeps your pawns side by side on d4 and e4; after 6.d5 that pawn needs looking after.

4876809165764258|c8g4.headline: Answer 5.d4 with 5...exd4: that pawn attacks your c5 bishop
4876809165764258|c8g4.why: 5...Bg4 pins the f3 knight but leaves your bishop hanging, and 6.dxc5 takes it. The counter 6...Qf6 fails to 7.Bg5 Qxg5 8.Nxg5 Bxd1 9.Rxd1, and White stays a piece up. 5...exd4 removes the pawn that attacks your bishop, so it keeps its place on c5. After 6.Nxd4 Ne7 7.Bg5 O-O you have castled with an active bishop, and masters played 5...exd4 in all 30 of their games here.
4876809165764258|c8g4.principle: Before starting your own plan, check what the last move threatens: 5.d4 attacks your bishop, so 5...exd4 comes before any pin.
