ideas.title: Answer d4 by taking on d4
ideas.text: 5.d4 hits your c5 bishop and e5 at once. 5...exd4 removes the attacker and keeps the bishop on its diagonal.

ideas.title: The c5 bishop is a target
ideas.text: With your bishop on c5, White's d4 push gains time on it. Ignore it and 6.dxc5 takes the bishop.

ideas.title: A pin is no defence
ideas.text: 5...Bg4 pins the f3 knight, but that does nothing about the d4 pawn, which still takes on c5.

habit.why: 5...Bg4 pins the f3 knight but leaves your bishop hanging, and 6.dxc5 takes it. The counter 6...Qf6 fails to 7.Bg5 Qxg5 8.Nxg5 Bxd1 9.Rxd1, and White stays a piece up.

strays.idea: Answer d4 by taking on d4
strays.text: The d4 pawn stays, and 6.dxc5 wins your bishop.

taught.why: 5...exd4 removes the pawn that attacks your bishop, so it keeps its place on c5. After 6.Nxd4 Ne7 7.Bg5 O-O you have castled with an active bishop, and masters played 5...exd4 in all 30 of their games here.

enforces.idea: Answer d4 by taking on d4
enforces.text: Taking the attacker saves the c5 bishop.

4879166842565878|c1g5.headline: Take back first: 8.cxd4 before you develop the bishop
4879166842565878|c1g5.why: 8.Bg5 develops but leaves d4 alone, and 8...f6 blunts the bishop. After 9.cxd4 Nxd4 10.Nxd4 fxg5 the pieces come off, Black is still two pawns up, and your bishop and centre are gone. 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and gains a tempo on the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 follows. Then 9.h3 stops the pin on your f3 knight, and after 9...Na5 10.Bd3 Ne7 11.Nc3 you have a full centre for the pawn.
4879166842565878|c1g5.principle: Fight for the centre first in a gambit: 8.cxd4 puts pawns back on e4 and d4, while 8.Bg5 lets Black keep them.

ideas.title: Rebuild the centre with cxd4
ideas.text: With your king castled, 8.cxd4 puts pawns back on e4 and d4 and hits the c5 bishop. This is the Evans main line.

ideas.title: Quiet moves cost the centre
ideas.text: 8.Bg5 develops but leaves d4 to Black, and 8...f6 simply blunts the bishop. You stay two pawns down with no centre.

ideas.title: Black wants the pin on f3
ideas.text: Black's c8 bishop wants g4 to pin your f3 knight, which guards d4. That is why 9.h3 comes in the main line.

ideas.title: Black gives a pawn back
ideas.text: 7...d6 guards the c5 bishop and lets you retake on d4. Nunn says Black should give one pawn back this way: Black stays a pawn up and develops.

habit.why: 8.Bg5 develops but leaves d4 alone, and 8...f6 blunts the bishop. After 9.cxd4 Nxd4 10.Nxd4 fxg5 the pieces come off, Black is still two pawns up, and your bishop and centre are gone.

strays.text: Development is fine, but here it lets Black keep d4.

taught.why: 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and gains a tempo on the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 follows. Then 9.h3 stops the pin on your f3 knight, and after 9...Na5 10.Bd3 Ne7 11.Nc3 you have a full centre for the pawn.

enforces.text: Pawns back on e4 and d4, with a tempo on the bishop.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 8.Qb3 aims at f7 before you have won anything back. 8...Qe7 guards f7, and after 9.Bd5 d3 Black's pawn wedges into your camp while you are still two pawns down.
alternatives.after: 8.cxd4 takes a pawn back first and kicks the c5 bishop. The queen trip to b3 can wait until your centre stands.

4879166842565878|f1e1.headline: Take back on d4 at once: 8.cxd4 is the Evans main line
4879166842565878|f1e1.why: 8.Re1 leaves the c3 and d4 pawns to Black, and 8...Bg4 pins the f3 knight that guards d4. After 9.e5 d5 10.Be2 dxc3 11.Nxc3 Nge7 Black is two pawns up and well developed. 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and gains a tempo on the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 follows. Then 9.h3 stops the pin on your f3 knight, and after 9...Na5 10.Bd3 Ne7 11.Nc3 you have a full centre for the pawn.
4879166842565878|f1e1.principle: In a gambit the pawns buy a centre and time: take the centre back with 8.cxd4 before making quiet moves.

4886445385944472|c2c3.headline: Take on e5 and keep c3 for your knight

ideas.title: Settle the d4 tension
ideas.text: Black's pawn and knight both hit d4, so you must push, capture or defend it before 3...Nxd4.

ideas.title: Make the knight pay
ideas.text: Black's knight came out early; the best replies make it move again, as after 3.dxe5 Nxe5 and 5.f4.

ideas.title: Keep c3 for your knight
ideas.text: Your knight belongs on c3, guarding e4 and d5. A pawn there leaves e4 loose.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 break
ideas.text: Against slow set-ups Black frees the game with ...d5, as after 3.c3 d5.

habit.why: 3.c3 lets Black strike with 3...d5 at your e4 pawn, which no piece defends. After 4.dxe5 Be6 5.exd5 Qxd5 you can't chase the queen with Nc3, and after 6.Nf3 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 O-O-O+ your king is stuck in the middle and the game is level.

strays.text: The pawn takes the knight's square, so nothing guards e4 against 3...d5.

taught.why: 3.dxe5 captures first, and after 3...Nxe5 the knight stands in the centre with nothing defending it. 4.Nc3 develops onto the square 3.c3 would have taken, and after 4...Bc5 5.f4 Nc6 the knight is back on c6 while your pawns on e4 and f4 hold the centre.

enforces.text: Black's knight spends three moves to end up back on c6 while you gain space.

4886445385944472|c2c3.principle: A knight in the centre with no pawn to protect it is a target: 5.f4 gains space and sends it back, while 3.c3 attacks nothing.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.d5 gains space and sends the knight on a long trip, 3...Nce7 4.Nf3 Ng6, and 5.h4 threatens to kick it again.
alternatives.after: 3.dxe5 is just as good but keeps the game open: you chase the knight with 4.Nc3 Bc5 5.f4 instead of playing on the wings around a locked centre. Masters prefer it, 43% to 31%.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.Nf3 turns the game into a sound Scotch Game, but after 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.Bd3 d5 your knight has moved three times only to be swapped off, and the position is level.
alternatives.after: 3.dxe5 keeps your e4 pawn alone in the centre and your knight on c3 guards d5, so Black gets no easy ...d5 and your small edge stays.

4907156095699170|c8f5.headline: Nothing guards f5: develop with 3...Nf6, not 3...Bf5
4907156095699170|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 puts the bishop where White's d3 bishop attacks it, and nothing defends f5 because your e-pawn hasn't moved. 4.Bxf5 simply wins a whole bishop. 3...Nf6 develops toward the centre and controls e4. The bishop still comes out next, as in 4.Nf3 Bg4, on a square White doesn't control.
4907156095699170|c8f5.principle: Before putting a piece on a new square, check whether it is attacked there and whether you can recapture.

ideas.title: Nothing guards f5
ideas.text: White's d3 bishop covers f5, and with your e-pawn still on e7 nothing defends it: 3...Bf5 4.Bxf5 wins a piece.

ideas.title: Develop the knight first
ideas.text: 3...Nf6 develops and controls e4, and waits to see where the bishop will be safe.

ideas.title: Bring the bishop out to g4
ideas.text: Your c8 bishop can still develop, just not to f5: after 3...Nf6 4.Nf3 Bg4 nothing can take it.

ideas.title: Don't shut in the c8 bishop
ideas.text: A pawn on e6 is solid but locks the c8 bishop behind your pawns; get the bishop out first when you can.

habit.why: 3...Bf5 puts the bishop where White's d3 bishop attacks it, and nothing defends f5 because your e-pawn hasn't moved. 4.Bxf5 simply wins a whole bishop.

strays.text: The bishop lands on a square White attacks and you can't retake on.

taught.why: 3...Nf6 develops toward the centre and controls e4. The bishop still comes out next, as in 4.Nf3 Bg4, on a square White doesn't control.

enforces.idea: Bring the bishop out to g4
enforces.text: The bishop develops a move later, on a safe square.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.idea: Don't shut in the c8 bishop
alternatives.before: 3...e6 is solid and aims for ...c5 later, but it shuts your c8 bishop in behind the e6 pawn.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 develops first and keeps the bishop's road to g4 open, as in 4.Nf3 Bg4.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 3...g6 aims for ...Bg7 and sidesteps the bishop problem; after 4.c4 you get a sound but slightly slower Grünfeld-style set-up.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 develops a piece at once and keeps both bishops flexible, with ...Bg4 next.

4920065110243890|c2c3.headline: Don't gambit here: 3.dxe5 simply wins the loose pawn
4920065110243890|c2c3.why: 3.c3 offers a gambit against a move that already drops a pawn, and Black takes with 3...exd4. After 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.cxd4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Nxc6 dxc6 material is level and the free pawn is gone. 3.dxe5 takes the free pawn and moves your d-pawn out of the c5 pawn's reach, so the 3...cxd4 threat is gone too. If Black wins it back with 3...d6 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Bb5 Be6 6.Bf4 dxe5, then 7.Bxc6+ bxc6 wrecks Black's pawns and e5 drops again.
4920065110243890|c2c3.principle: When a loose pawn can be taken by the very pawn that is under attack, take it: you win material and remove the target at once.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4

ideas.title: Take the loose pawn
ideas.text: 2...e5 leaves e5 attacked by your d4 pawn and defended by nothing. Taking it also moves your pawn out of the c5 pawn's reach.

ideas.title: Black's threat: ...cxd4
ideas.text: Black's c5 pawn attacks d4, so 3...cxd4 is threatened. Your d4 pawn must move or be defended.

ideas.title: Don't gambit what you can take
ideas.text: 3.c3 offers a pawn when e5 was free: after 3...exd4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.cxd4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 material is level.

ideas.title: Don't close the centre for free
ideas.text: 3.d5 stops the threat but locks the pawns. Black's e5 pawn is then safe for good, and Black develops calmly behind it.

habit.why: 3.c3 offers a gambit against a move that already drops a pawn, and Black takes with 3...exd4. After 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.cxd4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Nxc6 dxc6 material is level and the free pawn is gone.

strays.idea: Don't gambit what you can take
strays.text: You offer a pawn when Black's e5 pawn was yours for free.

taught.why: 3.dxe5 takes the free pawn and moves your d-pawn out of the c5 pawn's reach, so the 3...cxd4 threat is gone too. If Black wins it back with 3...d6 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Bb5 Be6 6.Bf4 dxe5, then 7.Bxc6+ bxc6 wrecks Black's pawns and e5 drops again.

enforces.text: You win the pawn and dodge the threat on d4 in one move.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 3.d5 stops 3...cxd4 but locks the centre. After 3...Nf6 4.Nd2 Be7 5.a4 d6 Black sets up calmly behind the closed pawns and your big edge shrinks.
alternatives.after: 3.dxe5 also stops the threat and wins a pawn, keeping a much larger edge than the closed centre after 3.d5.
alternatives.idea: Don't close the centre for free

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 3.dxc5 lets Black recapture with a developing move, 3...Bxc5, and the bishop hits f2 at once. After 4.Nc3 Nf6 Black is comfortably developed.
alternatives.after: 3.dxe5 takes the loose pawn and keeps it, while 3.dxc5 Bxc5 only helps Black develop.

alternatives.after: 3.dxe5 removes your d-pawn from danger and wins a pawn instead of losing one.

4947710214196192|b1c3.headline: Guard your extra e5 pawn with 3.Nf3
4947710214196192|b1c3.why: 3.Nc3 develops but leaves e5 to the d6-pawn: 3...dxe5 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8 wins your extra pawn back and swaps queens. Black's king can no longer castle, but you keep only a small edge instead of a clean extra pawn. 3.Nf3 guards e5, so a swap there no longer works: your knight would take back on e5 and you stay a pawn up. In the line 3...h6 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nc3 g5 6.Bg3 g4 7.Bh4 Black has to loosen the kingside to chase your pieces, still a pawn down.

ideas.title: Guard e5 with Nf3
ideas.text: The d6-pawn attacks your extra pawn on e5. 3.Nf3 defends it with a developing move, so the pawn stays yours.

ideas.title: Loose e5 means a queen swap
ideas.text: If e5 is loose, 3...dxe5 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8 swaps queens and Black has the pawn back; losing castling is a small price.

ideas.title: Black wants fast development
ideas.text: The gambit is about time: Black aims for ...Nc6, ...Bg4, ...Qe7 and long castling. Opening lines with exd6 helps that plan.

enforces.text: The knight defends e5 and keeps the queens on the board.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: Taking a second pawn is the old main line and still good for you, but after 3...Bxd6 Black gets the quick development and open lines the gambit is after, as 4.Nc3 Nc6 5.Nb5 Nf6 shows.
alternatives.after: 3.Nf3 keeps the extra pawn without opening lines for Black. Sources agree 3.exd6 is objectively better for you, but Black gets real practical chances.

494920144507383|c6d4.headline: Develop the last knight with 5...Nf6, don't move one twice
494920144507383|c6d4.why: 5...Nd4 moves the knight again while the g8 knight and c8 bishop are still at home, and it achieves nothing: 6.Na4 hits the bishop on c5, and after 6...Qe7 7.Nxc5 dxc5 8.Nxd4 cxd4 Black has traded off the bishop and handed White the bishop pair. 5...Nf6 is the most common master move (46%), developing toward the centre and getting ready to castle in this slow, manoeuvring Italian.
494920144507383|c6d4.principle: In a quiet opening, bring out a new piece each move; moving one twice only pays when it wins something concrete.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

4965498870244384|c1f4.headline: Take on d5 now: Black's recapturing piece becomes a target
4965498870244384|c1f4.why: 4.Bf4 does nothing for c4, and 4...dxc4 takes it at once. After 5.e3 e5 6.Nxe5 Bb4+ 7.Nd2 Nxe5 8.Bxe5 b5 you win back a pawn on e5, but Black's pieces are active, ...b5 holds c4 and your edge is gone. 4.cxd5 makes Black recapture on d5 with a piece, and 4...Qxd5 5.Nc3 hits the queen at once. After 5...Qd6 6.e4 e5 7.d5 Nb8 you have the full centre and Black's knight has gone back home.
4965498870244384|c1f4.principle: When the opponent guards d5 with pieces instead of a pawn, exchange on d5 and gain time by hitting whatever recaptures.

ideas.title: cxd5 against loose d5
ideas.text: Black guards d5 with knights, not a pawn. 4.cxd5 forces a piece to recapture, and 5.Nc3 or 6.e4 then hits it with tempo.

ideas.title: Big centre with tempo
ideas.text: After 4.cxd5 Qxd5 5.Nc3 the queen must move again, and 6.e4 gives you the full pawn centre.

ideas.title: Take c4 and strike ...e5
ideas.text: Against slow moves Black takes on c4 and hits your centre with ...e5, as after 4.Bf4 dxc4 5.e3 e5.

ideas.title: ...Ne4 hits a bishop on g5
ideas.text: A bishop on g5 can be hit by the f6-knight jumping to e4, as after 4.Bg5 Ne4.

habit.why: 4.Bf4 does nothing for c4, and 4...dxc4 takes it at once. After 5.e3 e5 6.Nxe5 Bb4+ 7.Nd2 Nxe5 8.Bxe5 b5 you win back a pawn on e5, but Black's pieces are active, ...b5 holds c4 and your edge is gone.

strays.text: A slow bishop move gives Black time to take on c4.

taught.why: 4.cxd5 makes Black recapture on d5 with a piece, and 4...Qxd5 5.Nc3 hits the queen at once. After 5...Qd6 6.e4 e5 7.d5 Nb8 you have the full centre and Black's knight has gone back home.

enforces.text: Black's recapturing queen becomes a target for 5.Nc3 and 6.e4.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 is natural, but it gives Black time to back up d5 with 4...e6, a solid Queen's Gambit Declined after 5.Bg5 Be7 6.e3 O-O. Black is comfortable.
alternatives.after: 4.cxd5 forces Black to recapture with a piece before ...e6 can support d5. Masters split 54.5% to 36.4% between the two, in only 22 games.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.e3 guards c4 but shuts in your c1-bishop, and after 4...e6 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.Bd2 dxc4 7.Bxc4 O-O Black has an easy game.
alternatives.after: 4.cxd5 uses the moment while d5 has no pawn behind it: Black's recapturing piece gets hit by 5.Nc3 and 6.e4.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4.Bg5 runs into 4...Ne4, hitting the bishop. In the main line Black wins your bishop for a knight, and after 7.gxf3 your kingside pawns are wrecked.
alternatives.after: 4.cxd5 settles the centre on your terms instead of putting a bishop where a knight can hit it.

497056438217906|b8c6.headline: Challenge d4 with the c-pawn before playing Nc6
497056438217906|b8c6.why: 5...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, Black's natural lever against d4, and lets White take the whole centre with 6.Nc3 and 7.e4. 5...c5 strikes at d4 straight away, the standard freeing move in the Queen's Gambit Accepted; the knight still reaches c6 later, as in 6.O-O a6 7.a4 Nc6.
497056438217906|b8c6.principle: In queen's-pawn openings, challenge d4 with the c-pawn before putting a knight in front of it.

4975913143337329|a2a3.headline: Hit f7 with 5.Ng5; 5.a3 allows the centre fork trick
4975913143337329|a2a3.why: 5.a3 is a slow pawn move that leaves e4 loose: 5...Nxe4 6.Nxe4 d5 is the centre fork trick, hitting the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4 and winning the piece back with a free game for Black. 4...d6 was passive, and 5.Ng5 punishes it by lining up knight and bishop against f7. Black has to block with 5...d5, and 6.exd5 wins a pawn.
4975913143337329|a2a3.principle: With the bishop on c4 aimed at f7, a knight jump to g5 doubles the attack on the square only the king defends.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

4975913143337329|c4d5.headline: Hit f7 with the knight when Black skips Be7
4975913143337329|c4d5.why: 5.Bd5 moves the bishop a second time for no gain, and after 5...Nd4 6.Bc4 it has to go back, so Black has gained time. 4...Nc6 left f7 guarded only by the king, and 5.Ng5 attacks it with knight and bishop; Black has to block with 5...d5, and 6.exd5 wins a pawn.
4975913143337329|c4d5.principle: With a bishop on c4 and f7 defended only by the king, bringing a knight to g5 adds a second attacker and forces concessions.

4975913143337329|d2d3.headline: 4...d6 left f7 weak: hit it with 5.Ng5
4975913143337329|d2d3.why: 5.d3 lets Black hunt the bishop with 5...Na5: in the engine line 6.Bd5 c6 leaves it to give itself up with 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7, a bishop for a pawn. Black's 4...d6 was passive and left f7 guarded only by the king, while the c4 bishop already aims at it. 5.Ng5 adds the knight to that attack, and after 5...d5 6.exd5 White wins a pawn.
4975913143337329|d2d3.principle: When f7 is defended only by the king and your bishop already aims at it, add a second attacker before making quiet moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

4981514382355858|b8c6.headline: Take the pawn with 3...dxc3, or decline properly; 3...Nc6 does neither
4981514382355858|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 lets White recapture with 4.cxd4, so White has the ideal pawns on e4 and d4 without giving anything. After 4...d5 5.exd5 Qxd5 6.Nf3 e5 7.Nc3 your queen is hit in the centre and White develops with gain of time. 3...dxc3 4.Nxc3 takes the pawn, the masters' main choice (55%), and leaves you a pawn up against White's lead in development. With 4...Nc6 5.Nf3 e6 6.Be2 Be7 7.O-O d6 you build a solid setup and the game is level.
4981514382355858|b8c6.principle: Accept a gambit only if you can consolidate: 3...dxc3 takes the pawn and develops after, while 3...Nc6 gives White the centre for free.

ideas.title: White's free centre
ideas.text: If you neither take on c3 nor hit the centre, 4.cxd4 gives White pawns on e4 and d4 at no cost.

ideas.title: Take the pawn, know a setup
ideas.text: 3...dxc3 4.Nxc3 is the main line: a pawn up, you must finish ...Nc6, ...e6, ...d6 before White's lead tells.

ideas.title: Hit the centre when declining
ideas.text: Good declines strike at once: 3...Nf6 hits e4 and 3...d5 hits the centre, heading for a 2.c3 Sicilian.

ideas.title: Morra setup: fast development, open files
ideas.text: For the pawn White gets quick development and open c- and d-files: knights to c3 and f3, bishop to c4, castling, queen to e2.

habit.why: 3...Nc6 lets White recapture with 4.cxd4, so White has the ideal pawns on e4 and d4 without giving anything. After 4...d5 5.exd5 Qxd5 6.Nf3 e5 7.Nc3 your queen is hit in the centre and White develops with gain of time.

strays.text: 4.cxd4 gives White pawns on e4 and d4 without paying a pawn.

taught.why: 3...dxc3 4.Nxc3 takes the pawn, the masters' main choice (55%), and leaves you a pawn up against White's lead in development. With 4...Nc6 5.Nf3 e6 6.Be2 Be7 7.O-O d6 you build a solid setup and the game is level.

enforces.idea: Take the pawn, know a setup
enforces.text: You take the pawn, then develop with ...Nc6, ...e6 and ...d6.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...d3 gives the pawn back so that White's c3 pawn blocks the knight's best square. But after 4.Bxd3 d6 5.c4 White clamps d5 with pawns on c4 and e4 and keeps a small edge.
alternatives.after: 3...dxc3 keeps the extra pawn and is the main line. 3...d3 is a quieter decline that masters use in 13% of games, though White keeps a pleasant space edge.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Nf6 is a good decline: it hits e4 at once, and after 4.e5 Nd5 5.cxd4 d6 you reach an Alapin-type position without the Morra's attack. Engines slightly prefer another move.
alternatives.after: Both are good: accepting keeps a pawn but means facing White's development, while 3...Nf6 avoids the gambit (25% of masters games).

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...d5 hits the centre at once: after 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.cxd4 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bg4 you develop quickly in an Alapin-type position. It is sound, though not the main choice.
alternatives.after: 3...dxc3 wins a pawn and is far more popular (55% against 5%); 3...d5 is a sound way to avoid the Morra's attack.

4997272018450256|c5b4.headline: Escape the pawn fork with 5...Bd6, guarding the knight
4997272018450256|c5b4.why: 5.d4 forks the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5. 5...Bb4 saves the bishop but leaves the knight hanging, so 6.dxe5 wins a piece. 5...Bd6 saves the bishop and guards the knight at once; after 6.dxe5 Bxe5 Black has the piece back and material is level. Masters play it in 99.3% of games.
4997272018450256|c5b4.principle: When a pawn forks two pieces, find the retreat that moves one and protects the other, so nothing is left loose.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

4997272018450256|c5d4.headline: d4 is guarded by the queen: retreat the bishop, don't capture
4997272018450256|c5d4.why: 5...Bxd4 takes the forking pawn, but 6.Qxd4 recaptures and the queen hits your e5 knight from the centre. After 6...d6 7.Be3 Nf6 8.O-O-O White has the bishop pair and a big lead in development. 5...Bd6 steps out of the fork and still guards the knight on e5. After 6.dxe5 Bxe5 material is level and you keep both bishops; masters play 5...Bd6 99.3% of the time.
4997272018450256|c5d4.principle: Before capturing, count: d4 is guarded by White's queen, so taking there just trades your best bishop for a pawn.

ideas.title: The fork trick
ideas.text: 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 5.d4 hits your c5 bishop and e5 knight at once; only one move saves both.

ideas.title: Retreat to d6, guarding e5
ideas.text: 5...Bd6 leaves the fork and guards the knight; after 6.dxe5 Bxe5 material is level. Masters play it 99% of the time.

ideas.title: Keep the dark-squared bishop
ideas.text: Taking on d4 gives up your dark-squared bishop: 6.Qxd4 centralises the queen against e5, and White keeps both bishops.

ideas.title: White keeps the better centre
ideas.text: Even after 6.dxe5 Bxe5 White has the extra centre pawn and can hit your bishop with 9.f4.

habit.why: 5...Bxd4 takes the forking pawn, but 6.Qxd4 recaptures and the queen hits your e5 knight from the centre. After 6...d6 7.Be3 Nf6 8.O-O-O White has the bishop pair and a big lead in development.

strays.text: Your dark-squared bishop goes for a pawn, and the queen lands on d4.

taught.why: 5...Bd6 steps out of the fork and still guards the knight on e5. After 6.dxe5 Bxe5 material is level and you keep both bishops; masters play 5...Bd6 99.3% of the time.

enforces.text: The bishop leaves the fork and still guards e5.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5...Bb4 pins the c3 knight but leaves e5 to be taken: after 6.dxe5 Qe7 7.Bd2 Qxe5 8.f4 Qc5 9.Qg4 your queen is chased while White develops and castles long.
alternatives.after: 5...Bd6 saves the bishop and the knight in one move, so your queen never has to come out. Masters play 5...Bb4 in under 1% of games.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5...Bb6 saves the bishop but drops the knight: after 6.dxe5 Qe7 7.Bf4 Qc5 8.Qd2 White guards e5, stays a pawn up and develops while your queen wanders.
alternatives.after: 5...Bd6 steps out of the fork on a square that still guards e5, so nothing is lost.

4997272018450256|d8f6.headline: Against the fork, retreat the bishop where it still guards the knight
4997272018450256|d8f6.why: 5...Qf6 guards the knight but not the bishop, so 6.dxc5 takes it for nothing. After 6...Ne7 7.f4 N5c6 your knights are pushed back, and White, up material, develops and castles long. 5...Bd6 steps out of the fork and still guards the knight on e5. After 6.dxe5 Bxe5 material is level, which is why masters play 5...Bd6 99.3% of the time.
4997272018450256|d8f6.principle: When a pawn forks two pieces, look for the one move that saves both: put the attacked piece where it protects the other.

5001203520556314|c8f5.headline: Against the Queen's Gambit, support d5 with 2...c6
5001203520556314|c8f5.why: 2...Bf5 leaves d5 without pawn support, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn, and to get it back Black has to give the bishop for a knight with 3...Bxb1 4.Rxb1 and bring the queen out with 4...Qxd5. 2...c6, the Slav, supports d5 with a pawn, so Black can recapture with a pawn after cxd5 and keep control of e4, while the light-squared bishop stays free to come out later.
5001203520556314|c8f5.principle: Against the Queen's Gambit, keep a pawn on d5 controlling e4: support it with the c- or e-pawn before developing the bishop.

5001203520556314|e7e5.headline: Support d5 with 2...c6, the Slav, instead of gambiting e5
5001203520556314|e7e5.why: 2...e5 gives up a pawn after 3.dxe5; the d4 wedge of the Albin Countergambit gives Black some play, but masters choose it in under 1% of games and White can return the pawn later for a positional edge. 2...c6, the Slav, is the most common master reply (50%): it supports d5 with the c-pawn so that cxd5 can be met by a pawn recapture, and unlike ...e6 it leaves the bishop on c8 free to develop.
5001203520556314|e7e5.principle: When White attacks your d5 pawn, keep a pawn there by supporting it, rather than giving up a centre pawn.

5001203520556314|g8f6.headline: Defend d5 with a pawn: 2...c6.
5001203520556314|g8f6.why: 2...Nf6 doesn't stop 3.cxd5, which costs Black a pawn. If the knight takes back with 3...Nxd5, 4.e4 chases it away and White gets the whole centre. 2...c6, the Slav, supports d5 with a pawn, so a pawn can recapture and keep control of e4. Unlike ...e6, it does this without locking in the bishop on c8.
5001203520556314|g8f6.principle: Against the Queen's Gambit, defend d5 with a pawn so that a pawn, not a piece, recaptures there.

505062396368968|b1c3.headline: Take the free pawn with 2.dxe5 before developing
505062396368968|b1c3.why: 2.Nc3 develops but leaves d4 to 2...exd4, and after 3.Qxd4 Nc6 your queen is chased. Black gains more time with 4.Qd3 Bc5 5.Be3 Nb4, and the gambit has cost Black nothing. 2.dxe5 takes the pawn 1...e5 left undefended, and Black must spend time trying to win it back. After 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 your knight guards e5; masters play 2.dxe5 in 90.4% of games, and the theory calls it White's best answer.
505062396368968|b1c3.principle: When the opponent offers an unsound gambit pawn you can keep, take it first; developing instead lets Black swap it off with gain of time.

ideas.title: Take the pawn, keep e5
ideas.text: 1...e5 offers a pawn nothing defends. 2.dxe5 takes it and 3.Nf3 guards it; 90.4% of masters accept, as the gambit is considered unsound.

ideas.title: Englund: watch the ...Qb4+ fork
ideas.text: Black's trick is ...Qe7 and ...Qb4+, hitting b2 and a bishop on f4. After 4.Bf4 Qb4+, block with 5.Bd2; never answer 5...Qxb2 with 6.Bc3.

ideas.title: Declining gives an even game
ideas.text: Moves like 2.Nc3, 2.e3, 2.c4 or 2.d5 let Black off the hook: Black swaps on d4 or develops freely, and the game is level.

ideas.title: Black develops by hitting your queen
ideas.text: Taking back on d4 with the queen lets ...Nc6 hit it, so Black develops with gain of time, as after 2...exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6.

habit.why: 2.Nc3 develops but leaves d4 to 2...exd4, and after 3.Qxd4 Nc6 your queen is chased. Black gains more time with 4.Qd3 Bc5 5.Be3 Nb4, and the gambit has cost Black nothing.

strays.text: You leave the free e5 pawn, and Black trades it off with gain of time.

taught.why: 2.dxe5 takes the pawn 1...e5 left undefended, and Black must spend time trying to win it back. After 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 your knight guards e5; masters play 2.dxe5 in 90.4% of games, and the theory calls it White's best answer.

enforces.text: You win a pawn and guard it with 3.Nf3.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2.d5 keeps the position closed and gives up the free pawn: after 2...Nf6 3.a3 Bc5 Black develops quickly and the game is level.
alternatives.after: 2.dxe5 wins a pawn and makes Black prove the gambit; 2.d5 throws that away for a closed, level game.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.idea: Black develops by hitting your queen
alternatives.before: 2.c4 allows 2...exd4, and after 3.Qxd4 Nc6 your queen is chased while Black develops with gain of time.
alternatives.after: 2.dxe5 grabs the pawn without exposing your queen; after 2.c4 exd4 the gambit has cost Black nothing.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2.e3 lets Black swap pawns: 2...exd4 3.exd4 d5 is a level, symmetrical French Exchange structure instead of an extra pawn for you.
alternatives.after: 2.dxe5 keeps the extra pawn; 2.e3 gives it back at once.

505062396368968|e2e4.headline: Take the Englund pawn with 2.dxe5; don't give your own
505062396368968|e2e4.why: 2.e4 lets 2...exd4 take your d4 pawn, so instead of winning a pawn you are the one gambiting, in a Centre Game. After 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nbd2 Nc6 Black develops with check and an extra pawn, and the game is about level. 2.dxe5 takes the pawn 1...e5 left undefended, and Black must spend time trying to win it back. After 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 your knight guards e5; masters play 2.dxe5 in 90.4% of games, and the theory calls it White's best answer.
505062396368968|e2e4.principle: When the opponent offers an unsound gambit pawn you can keep, take it and develop, instead of offering a pawn of your own.

ideas.title: Take the pawn, keep e5
ideas.text: 1...e5 offers a pawn nothing defends. 2.dxe5 takes it and 3.Nf3 guards it; 90.4% of masters accept, as the gambit is considered unsound.

ideas.title: Englund: watch the ...Qb4+ fork
ideas.text: Black's trick is ...Qe7 and ...Qb4+, hitting b2 and a bishop on f4. After 4.Bf4 Qb4+, block with 5.Bd2; never answer 5...Qxb2 with 6.Bc3.

ideas.title: Declining gives an even game
ideas.text: Moves like 2.e4, 2.e3, 2.c4 or 2.d5 let Black off the hook: Black swaps on d4 or develops freely, and the game is level.

ideas.title: Black develops by hitting your queen
ideas.text: Taking back on d4 with the queen lets ...Nc6 hit it, so Black develops with gain of time, as after 2.c4 exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6.

habit.why: 2.e4 lets 2...exd4 take your d4 pawn, so instead of winning a pawn you are the one gambiting, in a Centre Game. After 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nbd2 Nc6 Black develops with check and an extra pawn, and the game is about level.

strays.text: You leave e5 alone and offer your own d4 pawn instead.

taught.why: 2.dxe5 takes the pawn 1...e5 left undefended, and Black must spend time trying to win it back. After 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 your knight guards e5; masters play 2.dxe5 in 90.4% of games, and the theory calls it White's best answer.

enforces.text: You win a pawn and guard it with 3.Nf3.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2.d5 keeps the position closed and gives up the free pawn: after 2...Nf6 3.a3 Bc5 Black develops quickly and the game is level.
alternatives.after: 2.dxe5 wins a pawn and makes Black prove the gambit; 2.d5 throws that away for a closed, level game.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.idea: Black develops by hitting your queen
alternatives.before: 2.c4 allows 2...exd4, and after 3.Qxd4 Nc6 your queen is chased while Black develops with gain of time.
alternatives.after: 2.dxe5 grabs the pawn without exposing your queen; after 2.c4 exd4 the gambit has cost Black nothing.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2.e3 lets Black swap pawns: 2...exd4 3.exd4 d5 is a level, symmetrical French Exchange structure instead of an extra pawn for you.
alternatives.after: 2.dxe5 keeps the extra pawn; 2.e3 gives it back at once.

505062396368968|g1f3.headline: Take the Englund pawn: 2.dxe5.
505062396368968|g1f3.why: 2.Nf3 lets Black push 2...e4 and kick the knight, which has to retreat with 3.Nfd2, and Black gains space. 1...e5 offers a pawn that is attacked once and defended by nothing, and 2.dxe5 simply wins it. The Englund Gambit is unsound, and after 2.dxe5 Black has to work to find compensation.
505062396368968|g1f3.principle: When the opponent offers an unsound gambit, take the pawn and make them prove the compensation.

5083117640380754|b8c6.headline: Answer 3.c3 by hitting e4 at once: 3...Nf6
5083117640380754|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 doesn't touch e4, so White plays 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 and has the ideal two-pawn centre that 3.c3 was played for. After 5...Nf6 6.Nc3 d5 7.e5 Ne4 8.Bd3 you have spent an extra tempo on ...d5 and White leads in development. 3...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White has to look after it before playing d4: 4.Be2 prepares castling and a queen check on a4 if you grab the pawn. After 4...g6 5.O-O Bg7 6.Re1 O-O you are fully developed by the time 8.d4 comes.
5083117640380754|b8c6.principle: Contest the centre White is building: 3.c3 prepares d4, so attack e4 with 3...Nf6 before the pawns arrive.

ideas.title: Hit e4 with ...Nf6 early
ideas.text: 3...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White has to look after it before playing d4.

ideas.title: White wants two centre pawns
ideas.text: 3.c3 prepares d4, so White can retake with the c-pawn and keep pawns on d4 and e4.

ideas.title: No Nc3 for White
ideas.text: The c3 pawn takes the knight's square, so White can't simply guard e4 with a knight.

ideas.title: White's d4-d5 push
ideas.text: Without pressure on e4, White plays d4 and then pushes on to d5, gaining space with tempo.

habit.why: 3...Nc6 doesn't touch e4, so White plays 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 and has the ideal two-pawn centre that 3.c3 was played for. After 5...Nf6 6.Nc3 d5 7.e5 Ne4 8.Bd3 you have spent an extra tempo on ...d5 and White leads in development.

strays.text: No threat to e4, so White plays d4 at once and keeps two centre pawns.

taught.why: 3...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White has to look after it before playing d4: 4.Be2 prepares castling and a queen check on a4 if you grab the pawn. After 4...g6 5.O-O Bg7 6.Re1 O-O you are fully developed by the time 8.d4 comes.

enforces.text: The knight develops with a threat, so White can't play d4 at once.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...e6 doesn't hit e4, so White plays 4.d4 and then pushes: 4...Nc6 5.d5 exd5 6.exd5 Nce7 7.c4 gains space with tempo and cramps you.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 attacks e4 first, so White has no time for that free advance in the centre.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...e5 lets the centre open with White better developed: after 4.d4 exd4 5.cxd4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Nc6 7.Bc4 your d6 pawn is a target.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 develops with a threat to e4 instead of a pawn move that opens the centre for White's pieces.

5083117640380754|e7e6.why: 3...e6 doesn't touch e4, so White plays 4.d4 for free, and after 4...Nc6 5.d5 exd5 6.exd5 Nce7 7.c4 the d5 pawn cramps you. Your knight is pushed back to e7 and White has a clear space edge. 3...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White has to look after it before playing d4: 4.Be2 prepares castling and a queen check on a4 if you grab the pawn. After 4...g6 5.O-O Bg7 6.Re1 O-O you are fully developed by the time 8.d4 comes.
5083117640380754|e7e6.principle: Contest the centre White is building: 3.c3 prepares d4, so attack e4 with 3...Nf6 before the pawns arrive.

ideas.title: Hit e4 with ...Nf6 early
ideas.text: 3...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White has to look after it before playing d4.

ideas.title: White wants two centre pawns
ideas.text: 3.c3 prepares d4, so White can retake with the c-pawn and keep pawns on d4 and e4.

ideas.title: No Nc3 for White
ideas.text: The c3 pawn takes the knight's square, so White can't simply guard e4 with a knight.

ideas.title: White's d4-d5 push
ideas.text: Without pressure on e4, White plays d4 and then pushes on to d5, gaining space with tempo.

habit.why: 3...e6 doesn't touch e4, so White plays 4.d4 for free, and after 4...Nc6 5.d5 exd5 6.exd5 Nce7 7.c4 the d5 pawn cramps you. Your knight is pushed back to e7 and White has a clear space edge.

strays.text: No pressure on e4, so White gets d4 and then d5 for free.

taught.why: 3...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White has to look after it before playing d4: 4.Be2 prepares castling and a queen check on a4 if you grab the pawn. After 4...g6 5.O-O Bg7 6.Re1 O-O you are fully developed by the time 8.d4 comes.

enforces.text: The knight develops with a threat, so White can't play d4 at once.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...Nc6 develops but doesn't hit e4: 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 gives White the ideal two-pawn centre, and breaking it with ...d5 later costs you an extra tempo.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 makes White deal with e4 before d4, so you never face the full centre a tempo down.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...e5 lets the centre open with White better developed: after 4.d4 exd4 5.cxd4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Nc6 7.Bc4 your d6 pawn is a target.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 develops with a threat to e4 instead of a pawn move that opens the centre for White's pieces.

5092403403866739|b8c6.headline: Take on d4 with 4...cxd4: 4...Nc6 drops the c5 pawn
5092403403866739|b8c6.why: 4...Nc6 ignores the attack on c5: after 5.dxc5, taking back at once allows a queen trade with check on d8 that leaves you badly behind. In the line 5...a6 6.Bf4 e5 7.Bg5 f6 8.Be3 dxc5 9.Qxd8+ you spend pawn moves to win the pawn back, and White is far ahead in development. 4...cxd4 trades your wing pawn for White's centre pawn, the normal Sicilian swap. After 5.Nxd4 a6 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Be2 Be7 you have a sound Scheveningen setup; watch for White's 8.g4.
5092403403866739|b8c6.principle: Check what is loose: 4.d4 attacks c5, so take on d4 before you develop.
sources: Move Order Tricks in the 2.Nc3 Sicilian! (GM Max Illingworth) | https://www.chess.com/blog/Illingworth/move-order-tricks-in-the-2-nc3-sicilian-1
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Nc3

ideas.title: White hits c5
ideas.text: 4.d4 attacks your c5 pawn; if you don't take, 5.dxc5 wins it or drags your king into the centre.

ideas.title: Trade c5 for d4
ideas.text: Swapping your wing pawn for White's centre pawn leaves you two centre pawns, d6 and e6, against White's one.

ideas.title: Scheveningen setup
ideas.text: With pawns on d6 and e6, develop with 5...a6, 6...Nf6 and 7...Be7, then castle.

ideas.title: White's g4 push
ideas.text: In this structure White often throws in 8.g4 to gain kingside space and chase your f6 knight.

habit.why: 4...Nc6 ignores the attack on c5: after 5.dxc5, taking back at once allows a queen trade with check on d8 that leaves you badly behind. In the line 5...a6 6.Bf4 e5 7.Bg5 f6 8.Be3 dxc5 9.Qxd8+ you spend pawn moves to win the pawn back, and White is far ahead in development.

strays.text: The knight develops but leaves c5 to 5.dxc5.

taught.why: 4...cxd4 trades your wing pawn for White's centre pawn, the normal Sicilian swap. After 5.Nxd4 a6 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Be2 Be7 you have a sound Scheveningen setup; watch for White's 8.g4.

enforces.text: Taking on d4 gives White no target and keeps your centre pawns.

5100201113541958|b2b3.headline: Develop with tempo: 4.Nc3 hits the queen on d5
5100201113541958|b2b3.why: 4.b3 neither develops nor attacks the queen, so Black gets 4...Bg4 in and 5.Nc3 comes a move late: 5...Qe6+ checks down the open e-file. After 6.Qe2 Qf6 7.Qe4 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Qxf3 your kingside pawns end up doubled and Black is more comfortable. 4.Nc3 develops and attacks the queen at once, and masters choose it 93% of the time. After 4...Qd8 5.d4 Nf6 6.a3 e6 7.Bb5 Bd7 8.Qe2 Black's queen is back home while you have a pawn on d4 and your pieces out.
5100201113541958|b2b3.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, develop with a move that attacks her, so you gain a move while she retreats.
sources: Markus Reinke, Andrew Martin: Nimzowitsch Defence review (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/andrew-martin-nimzowitsch-defence-1-e4-nc6-review
Wisnewski; Tartakower on 4.Nc3 (Google Books snippets) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%22Nc6+2.Nf3+d5+3.exd5+Qxd5+4.Nc3%22
Davide Nastasio, Get nasty with the Nimzowitsch Defence (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/newsroom/post/review-the-nasty-nimzowitsch-defence?page=0
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

ideas.title: Gain time on early black pieces
ideas.text: Black's queen on d5 is exposed: 4.Nc3 develops and attacks it, so Black spends a move retreating with 4...Qd8.

ideas.title: Black develops with ...Bg4 and ...O-O-O
ideas.text: Given time, Black brings the bishop to g4 against your f3-knight and castles long, as in 4...Bg4 5.O-O O-O-O.

ideas.title: Nimzowitsch: Black targets d4
ideas.text: Once your pawn reaches d4, Black's queen and c6-knight hit it and ...e5 adds more, as in 4.d4 e5.

habit.why: 4.b3 neither develops nor attacks the queen, so Black gets 4...Bg4 in and 5.Nc3 comes a move late: 5...Qe6+ checks down the open e-file. After 6.Qe2 Qf6 7.Qe4 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Qxf3 your kingside pawns end up doubled and Black is more comfortable.

strays.idea: Gain time on early black pieces
strays.text: The queen on d5 is left alone, so Black develops freely with 4...Bg4.

taught.why: 4.Nc3 develops and attacks the queen at once, and masters choose it 93% of the time. After 4...Qd8 5.d4 Nf6 6.a3 e6 7.Bb5 Bd7 8.Qe2 Black's queen is back home while you have a pawn on d4 and your pieces out.

enforces.idea: Gain time on early black pieces
enforces.text: The queen must move again, so you develop with gain of time.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.d4 claims the centre but doesn't attack the queen, so Black hits d4 at once with 4...e5, followed by 5...Bb4 and 7...e4. After 8.Ne5 Nxe5 pieces come off and the game is level.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 hits the queen first, so Black has no time for ...e5, and you can still play 5.d4 next. Starting with 4.d4 gives Black's queen a free move.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Be2 develops quietly but leaves the queen on d5 alone, so Black plays 4...Bg4 and castles long: after 5.O-O O-O-O 6.h3 Bh5 Black's pieces are active and the game is level.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 develops with a threat to the queen, so Black spends a move on it. After 4.Be2 Bg4 Black gets ...Bg4 and ...O-O-O in for free.

513248652268614|c1e3.headline: Strike with 10.Nb5 before Black plays ...a6
513248652268614|c1e3.why: 10.Be3 attacks nothing: from e3 the bishop doesn't press d6 or back e4-e5. After 10...O-O 11.Rac1 Qb8 12.h3 Bd7 13.g4 Be8 Black is castled and solid, and you are simply a pawn down. 10.Nb5 jumps in while ...a6 hasn't been played, hitting the queen on c7 and the d6 pawn. After 10...Qb8 11.Bf4 e5 12.Bg5 O-O 13.Bxf6 Bxf6 14.Nxd6 you win the pawn back and keep your pieces active.
513248652268614|c1e3.principle: With a lead in development, act before the opponent catches up: 10.Nb5 hits the queen and d6 now, while 10.Be3 lets Black castle and keep the pawn.
sources: Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (sample) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf

ideas.title: Morra: pawn for development
ideas.text: For the pawn your knights, bishop, queen and rooks are all out. Use that lead before Black castles and consolidates.

ideas.title: Knight jumps to b5 and d6
ideas.text: Without ...a6, b5 is free: a knight there hits the queen on c7 and the d6 pawn at once.

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: Your dark bishop belongs on f4 or g5, pressing d6 and backing e4-e5. From e3 it does neither.

ideas.title: No slow moves
ideas.text: A pawn down, quiet moves like 12.h3 and 14.a3 give Black time to castle, tuck pieces away and keep the pawn.

habit.why: 10.Be3 attacks nothing: from e3 the bishop doesn't press d6 or back e4-e5. After 10...O-O 11.Rac1 Qb8 12.h3 Bd7 13.g4 Be8 Black is castled and solid, and you are simply a pawn down.

strays.text: A quiet bishop move gives Black time to castle and keep the pawn.

taught.why: 10.Nb5 jumps in while ...a6 hasn't been played, hitting the queen on c7 and the d6 pawn. After 10...Qb8 11.Bf4 e5 12.Bg5 O-O 13.Bxf6 Bxf6 14.Nxd6 you win the pawn back and keep your pieces active.

enforces.idea: Knight jumps to b5 and d6
enforces.text: The knight gains time on the queen and wins back the d6 pawn.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 10.Bf4 presses d6 and is Langrock's recommended move against this setup, as well as the club favourite (47%). Here, after 10...a6 11.Rac1 O-O Black castles and is close to keeping the pawn, so the engine prefers a sharper move.
alternatives.after: 10.Nb5 uses the one moment ...a6 hasn't been played. Langrock's 10.Bf4 lines mostly have ...a6 in already; here the knight jump comes first, and the bishop follows with 11.Bf4.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 10.Bg5 puts the bishop on one of its usual squares, pinning the f6-knight. But after 10...Qb8 11.Rac1 O-O Black is castled before your 12.e5 dxe5 break comes.
alternatives.after: 10.Nb5 forces matters first; the bishop still reaches g5 later, as in 11.Bf4 e5 12.Bg5.

5136765216062701|f1c4.headline: Against ...e6 and ...Ne7, push 5.h4 or put the bishop on d3
5136765216062701|f1c4.why: 5.Bc4 puts the bishop where Black's d-pawn hits it in one move: 5...d5 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bd3, and you have spent two moves to reach d3. After 7...O-O 8.O-O Bf5 9.Re1 Bxd3 Black swaps that bishop off and most of your edge is gone. 5.h4 gains kingside space before Black has castled, a push also seen in Hippo lines. After 5...h6 6.Be3 d6 7.Bd3 your bishop goes straight to d3, guarding e4, and you keep your full edge.
5136765216062701|f1c4.principle: Develop a piece straight to the square where it will stay: a pawn push that chases it costs you the move back, as 5.Bc4 d5 shows.
sources: GM Max Illingworth, The Mad Dog Attack vs. the Modern (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/blog/Illingworth/the-mad-dog-attack-vs-the-modern
GM Igor Stohl, Carlsen and his hippopotamus (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/carlsen-and-his-hippopotamus
IM Andrew Martin, The Hippopotamus system of defence (ChessBase) | https://shop.chessbase.com/en/products/martin_hippopotamus
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...g6/2._d4/2...Bg7

ideas.title: Bishop to d3, not c4
ideas.text: With Black's pawn on e6, ...d5 hits a bishop on c4. On d3 it guards e4 and stays put.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 break
ideas.text: The e6 pawn prepares ...d5, attacking e4 and anything on c4, as in 5.Bc4 d5.

ideas.title: The h-pawn against the Hippo
ideas.text: h4 gains kingside space before Black castles. The cost is the g4 square, as in 9...Ng4.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Black lets you keep pawns on e4 and d4, then hits them with ...c5 or ...d5, the g7 bishop aiming at d4.

habit.why: 5.Bc4 puts the bishop where Black's d-pawn hits it in one move: 5...d5 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bd3, and you have spent two moves to reach d3. After 7...O-O 8.O-O Bf5 9.Re1 Bxd3 Black swaps that bishop off and most of your edge is gone.

strays.text: On c4 the bishop is a target for 5...d5 and must move again.

taught.why: 5.h4 gains kingside space before Black has castled, a push also seen in Hippo lines. After 5...h6 6.Be3 d6 7.Bd3 your bishop goes straight to d3, guarding e4, and you keep your full edge.

enforces.text: The h-pawn takes kingside space while the bishop waits for d3.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bd3 puts the bishop on its best square at once: it guards e4 and ...d5 won't hit it. A good move, though the engine slightly prefers another.
alternatives.after: 5.h4 and 5.Bd3 reach the same set-up: the 5.Bd3 line plays 7.h4 anyway. The engine just prefers starting the kingside play first.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
alternatives.before: 5.e5 gains space but gives Black a chain to hit: 5...d6 6.Bd3 c5 attacks it at once, and after 7.O-O cxd4 8.cxd4 dxe5 9.dxe5 your space is gone.
alternatives.after: 5.h4 keeps your pawns on e4 and d4 and gains space on the wing instead, so ...d6 and ...c5 have no fixed chain to hit.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bg5 develops, but 5...h6 6.Be3 sends the bishop back, so you have spent an extra move. Playable, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: In the 5.h4 line the bishop reaches e3 in one move, 6.Be3, and your h-pawn has already taken space.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Be3 is solid development, and after 5...d6 6.Bd3 Nd7 7.Qe2 O-O you have a good set-up. A slightly stronger move exists.
alternatives.after: Both lines put the bishop on d3 and the queen on e2; 5.h4 starts the kingside play first, while in the 5.Be3 line Black has castled by 7...O-O.

5143411063260921|d8b6.headline: Guard d5 with 7...e6; 7...Qb6 drops it to 8.Nxd5
5143411063260921|d8b6.why: 7...Qb6 covers b7 but takes the only guard off d5: 8.Nxd5, and the b3-queen protects the knight, so a queen trade just leaves you a pawn down. After 8...Qa5+ 9.Nc3 White is a clean pawn up and your kingside pawns are still broken. 7...e6 guards d5 with a pawn and opens the f8-bishop, giving up b7 to finish your development. After 8.e4 Bxe4 9.Qxb7 Nd7 10.Bb5 Rc8 you have taken a pawn back, your rook uses the open c-file, and the game is level.
5143411063260921|d8b6.principle: Count before you move a defender: the queen on d8 is d5's only guard against the b3-queen and c3-knight, so 7...Qb6 leaves it to be taken.
sources: Konstantin Sakaev, Complete Slav I (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-complete-slav-i.pdf

Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3

ideas.title: ...Qb6 runs into Nxd5
ideas.text: Your queen is d5's only guard. Once it leaves for b6, 8.Nxd5 takes the pawn, with the b3-queen covering the knight.

ideas.title: Early ...Bf5 drops b7
ideas.text: With your bishop gone from c8, 7.Qb3 hits b7 while the c3-knight presses d5; you can't keep both pawns cheaply.

ideas.title: Guard d5 with a pawn
ideas.text: 7...e6 holds d5 with a pawn and frees your f8-bishop; if White takes b7, you gain time and use the open c-file.

ideas.title: Lines open on your king
ideas.text: Your king is still on e8, so after 7...Qd7, 8.e4 and 9.Bb5 open the centre against it fast.

habit.why: 7...Qb6 covers b7 but takes the only guard off d5: 8.Nxd5, and the b3-queen protects the knight, so a queen trade just leaves you a pawn down. After 8...Qa5+ 9.Nc3 White is a clean pawn up and your kingside pawns are still broken.

strays.text: The queens face off, and 8.Nxd5 takes the unguarded pawn.

taught.why: 7...e6 guards d5 with a pawn and opens the f8-bishop, giving up b7 to finish your development. After 8.e4 Bxe4 9.Qxb7 Nd7 10.Bb5 Rc8 you have taken a pawn back, your rook uses the open c-file, and the game is level.

enforces.text: A pawn holds d5, so only b7 is on offer, and it buys time.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 7...Qd7 guards b7 and d5 but blocks your development, and 8.e4 dxe4 9.Bb5 Nc6 10.d5 opens lines on your uncastled king; by 12.dxc6 White wins a piece.
alternatives.after: 7...e6 defends d5 with a pawn and leaves your queen free; after 8.e4 Bxe4 9.Qxb7 Nd7 10.Bb5 Rc8 you have counterplay instead of a pinned knight.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7...Nc6 develops but leaves both pawns loose: after 8.e3 e5 9.Nf3 Bg7 10.Qxb7 Bd7 11.Nxd5 White has taken two pawns, and your activity doesn't quite make up for them.
alternatives.after: 7...e6 keeps d5 covered by a pawn, so White can win only b7, and you take the e4 pawn back in the 8.e4 Bxe4 line.

5165721780484766|d2d3.headline: Claim the centre with 2.d4 instead of the quiet 2.d3
5165721780484766|d2d3.why: 2.d3 is a quiet King's Indian Attack set-up, and after 2...d5 you must guard e4 straight away. The natural 3.Nf3 runs into 3...dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1: the queens are off and your king has lost the right to castle. 2.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre and frees both bishops; it's the choice in nearly 90% of master games. After 2...d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4 c5 6.Nf3 Nc6 you have space and a big pawn centre.
5165721780484766|d2d3.principle: Occupy the centre with pawns when your opponent lets you: 2.d4 takes the second central square for free.
sources: Neil McDonald, The King's Indian Attack: Move by Move (sample, New in Chess) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/7277.pdf

ideas.title: Take the full centre with d4
ideas.text: 1...e6 prepares ...d5 against e4. 2.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre and frees both bishops.

ideas.title: Answer ...d5 by keeping e4
ideas.text: After 2.d4 d5 your e4 pawn is attacked: 3.Nc3 guards it, and 4.e5 gains space and kicks the f6 knight.

ideas.title: The ...Qxd1+ queen swap
ideas.text: In a d3 set-up, if the centre opens with 3...dxe4 4.dxe4, then 4...Qxd1+ swaps queens and your king can't castle.

ideas.title: Black: break with ...d5 and ...c5
ideas.text: Black's plan is ...d5 at once, then ...c5 against d4, as in 5...c5 after 2.d4.

habit.why: 2.d3 is a quiet King's Indian Attack set-up, and after 2...d5 you must guard e4 straight away. The natural 3.Nf3 runs into 3...dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1: the queens are off and your king has lost the right to castle.

strays.idea: Take the full centre with d4
strays.text: 2.d3 keeps your centre small and gives Black an easy game.

taught.why: 2.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre and frees both bishops; it's the choice in nearly 90% of master games. After 2...d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4 c5 6.Nf3 Nc6 you have space and a big pawn centre.

enforces.idea: Take the full centre with d4
enforces.text: Two pawns in the centre, and both bishops free to develop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Take the full centre with d4
alternatives.before: 2.Nf3 develops and is sound, but after 2...d5 3.exd5 exd5 you get an Exchange French where Black's pieces come out freely. There's a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 2.d4 claims the centre at once. McDonald notes that after 2.Nf3 d5 a quiet d3 runs into a queen swap, so 2.Nf3 usually just reaches an Exchange French with 4.d4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Take the full centre with d4
alternatives.before: 2.Nc3 develops and often transposes: after 2...c5 3.Nge2 d5 you still have to settle the centre. Sound, but there's a more direct move.
alternatives.after: 2.d4 claims the centre at once; 2.Nc3 often reaches a similar French after 4.d4, by a slower road.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.idea: Take the full centre with d4
alternatives.before: 2.Bc4 aims at a wall: 2...d5 hits the bishop, and after 3.exd5 exd5 4.Be2 it has moved twice while Black is comfortable.
alternatives.after: 2.d4 builds the centre first, so your bishop goes out once the pawns have settled.

5165721780484766|e4e5.headline: Build the two-pawn centre before advancing
5165721780484766|e4e5.why: 2.e5 advances a pawn with no support, and Black undermines it with 2...c5 and 4...d6, so White ends up trading it off with 5.exd6 without gaining anything. 2.d4 builds the two-pawn centre and opens both bishops; after 2...d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 the pawn advances only once d4 stands behind it.
5165721780484766|e4e5.principle: Occupy the centre with both pawns first; a lone advanced pawn is easy to undermine.

5165721780484766|f1c4.headline: Build the centre with 2.d4 before the bishop comes out
5165721780484766|f1c4.why: 2.Bc4 points the bishop at the e6 pawn, and 2...d5 hits it with tempo. After 3.exd5 exd5 4.Be2 Nf6 5.Nf3 Bd6 the bishop has moved twice and Black has a free, comfortable position. 2.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre and frees both bishops; it's the choice in nearly 90% of master games. After 2...d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4 c5 6.Nf3 Nc6 you have space and a big pawn centre.
5165721780484766|f1c4.principle: Settle the centre before placing the bishop: on c4 it runs into 2...d5 and has to move again.

5165721780484766|f2f4.headline: Against the French, build the two-pawn centre with 2.d4
5165721780484766|f2f4.why: 2.f4 spends the move on a flank pawn and does nothing about the coming 2...d5; after 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 c5 Black has traded off your e-pawn and strikes at the centre with an easy game. 2.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre and opens lines for the bishop and queen, which is what White plays almost every time here. The f-pawn can still come later, as in 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4, once the centre is fixed and the pawn supports e5.
5165721780484766|f2f4.principle: When Black's first move only prepares ...d5, occupy the centre with a second pawn so you have something to meet it with.

5169185492904926|c8f5.headline: Knight to f6 first: ...Bf5 lets Qb3 hit b7
5169185492904926|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 takes away b7's only defender, and 4.Qb3 hits it at once, so 4...Qc7 has to guard it. After 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.Nc3 e6 7.d3 Nc6 8.Bf4 your queen is hit again and White is better developed. 3...Nf6 develops and adds a guard to d5 without loosening b7. After 4.Nf3 g6 5.b3 Bg7 6.Bb2 O-O you have a solid fianchetto, and masters choose this move 87% of the time.
5169185492904926|c8f5.principle: Knights before bishops: here the c8-bishop is b7's only guard, so bring the knight out first.

ideas.title: Bishop c8 guards b7
ideas.text: Your c8-bishop is b7's only guard. Once it goes to f5, 4.Qb3 hits b7 at once.

ideas.title: Fianchetto plus c4 hits d5
ideas.text: The g2-bishop and the c4-pawn both aim at d5. Back it up rather than let White win it cheaply.

ideas.title: Knight first, bishop later
ideas.text: Develop ...Nf6 first: it guards d5 and keeps the bishop's choice open for later.

ideas.title: Mirror the fianchetto
ideas.text: After 3...Nf6 4.Nf3 g6 5.b3 Bg7 your bishop matches White's on the long diagonal.

habit.why: 3...Bf5 takes away b7's only defender, and 4.Qb3 hits it at once, so 4...Qc7 has to guard it. After 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.Nc3 e6 7.d3 Nc6 8.Bf4 your queen is hit again and White is better developed.

strays.text: The bishop leaves b7 unguarded, and 4.Qb3 forces the awkward 4...Qc7.

taught.why: 3...Nf6 develops and adds a guard to d5 without loosening b7. After 4.Nf3 g6 5.b3 Bg7 6.Bb2 O-O you have a solid fianchetto, and masters choose this move 87% of the time.

enforces.text: The knight guards d5 now; the bishop can pick its square later.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...e6 is sound: it backs up d5, and after 4.d4 dxc4 5.Nf3 b5 you hold the pawn for now. But it shuts in your c8-bishop, and there is a more flexible move.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 guards d5 without blocking the bishop. Masters choose it 87% of the time, against 3% for 3...e6.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 3...dxc4 gives up your centre pawn: 4.Na3 g6 5.Nxc4 wins it back, and your d-pawn has been traded for White's c-pawn.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 keeps the d5-pawn and adds a guard to it, so White's c4 gains nothing.

5184811817876652|e1h1.headline: Answer the attack on e4 with 6.e5, not castling
5184811817876652|e1h1.why: 6.O-O doesn't guard e4, which the f6-knight and b7-bishop both attack, so 6...Nxe4 wins a centre pawn. After 7.Re1 Nf6 8.h4 O-O Black is a pawn up and safely castled. 6.e5 attacks the knight instead of defending the pawn, and 6...Ng4 7.Na3 Qc8 8.h3 Nh6 drives it to the edge. Your pawn on e5 cramps Black, and you castle with 10.O-O once the knight is gone from the centre.
5184811817876652|e1h1.principle: Count attackers and defenders before a quiet move: e4 is hit twice and guarded once, so 6.e5 moves it out of danger with gain of time.
sources: Owen's Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen%27s_Defence

ideas.title: Count attackers on e4
ideas.text: The f6-knight and b7-bishop hit e4 twice; only your d3-bishop guards it, so a quiet move drops the pawn to 6...Nxe4.

ideas.title: e5 kicks the f6-knight
ideas.text: e5 pushes past the attack and the knight must leave f6; after 6...Ng4, 8.h3 sends it to h6.

ideas.title: Secure e4 before castling
ideas.text: Castling doesn't guard e4. Deal with the attack first, then castle, as with 6.e5 and 10.O-O later.

habit.why: 6.O-O doesn't guard e4, which the f6-knight and b7-bishop both attack, so 6...Nxe4 wins a centre pawn. After 7.Re1 Nf6 8.h4 O-O Black is a pawn up and safely castled.

strays.text: Castling leaves e4 to 6...Nxe4.

taught.why: 6.e5 attacks the knight instead of defending the pawn, and 6...Ng4 7.Na3 Qc8 8.h3 Nh6 drives it to the edge. Your pawn on e5 cramps Black, and you castle with 10.O-O once the knight is gone from the centre.

enforces.text: The knight ends up on h6, far from the centre.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Nbd2 guards e4, but the knight is passive there, and after 6...d6 7.O-O O-O 8.Re1 Nbd7 Black has a comfortable game.
alternatives.after: 6.e5 gains space and drives the knight to the rim instead of tying a knight to e4's defence.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Qe2 guards e4, but 6...d6 lets Black meet your pawn push by taking, and after 8...Bxf3 9.Qxf3 Nd5 the knight finds a fine central square.
alternatives.after: 6.e5 at once, before ...d6, leaves the knight no good square; a move later Black is ready to take on e5 and use d5.

5200406229951823|e1f2.headline: Step aside with 6.Kf1: no knight check, and the rook falls
5200406229951823|e1f2.why: 6.Kxf2 lets Black start a king hunt with 6...Nxe4+: after 7.Ke3 Qh4 8.g3 Nxg3 9.hxg3 Qd4+ 10.Kf3 you are two pieces up, but your king stands in the open. Quintiliano judges that too risky, and the other king moves are no better, one ending in perpetual check. 6.Kf1 avoids the knight check and still attacks the f2 bishop, so after 6...Qe7 7.Nxh8 you win the rook. Black fights on with 7...d5 8.exd5 Nd4, and after 9.d6 Qxd6 10.Nf7 Qe7 you are well ahead in material, but Black has real counterplay and you must play very precisely.
5200406229951823|e1f2.principle: When your king has to move, pick the square where the opponent's pieces can't give check with tempo.

ideas.title: Kf1: out of reach of checks
ideas.text: On f1 your king can't be checked by a knight landing on e4, and the f2 bishop is still attacked.

ideas.title: Collect the rook
ideas.text: Your f7 knight forks the d8 queen and h8 rook; after 6.Kf1 Qe7 7.Nxh8 you are a rook up.

ideas.title: Black's king hunt
ideas.text: After 6.Kxf2 Nxe4+ Black drags your king out, and the queen joins with 7...Qh4.

habit.why: 6.Kxf2 lets Black start a king hunt with 6...Nxe4+: after 7.Ke3 Qh4 8.g3 Nxg3 9.hxg3 Qd4+ 10.Kf3 you are two pieces up, but your king stands in the open. Quintiliano judges that too risky, and the other king moves are no better, one ending in perpetual check.

strays.text: Taking the bishop with the king allows 6...Nxe4 with check.

taught.why: 6.Kf1 avoids the knight check and still attacks the f2 bishop, so after 6...Qe7 7.Nxh8 you win the rook. Black fights on with 7...d5 8.exd5 Nd4, and after 9.d6 Qxd6 10.Nf7 Qe7 you are well ahead in material, but Black has real counterplay and you must play very precisely.

enforces.idea: Kf1: out of reach of checks
enforces.text: The king sidesteps the checks, and the h8 rook falls next.

5214612586178464|d2d3.headline: Castle before ...d5 opens the centre
5214612586178464|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is solid but slow, and 4...d5 attacks your bishop straight away. After 5.Bb3 dxe4 6.dxe4 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 the queens are gone and your king has lost the right to castle. 4.O-O puts your king safe before the centre opens; masters choose it 69% of the time. After 4...d5 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5 Bd6 7.d4 you pin the c6-knight and hit Black's c5 pawn, and the game is level.
5214612586178464|d2d3.principle: Castle before the centre opens: ...d5 is coming, and 4.O-O makes sure the open d-file can't cost you castling, as it does after 4.d3 and 6...Qxd1+.

ideas.title: Castle, then prepare d4
ideas.text: Castle first, then strike with d4 when it helps, as with 7.d4 once the centre has opened.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 hits your bishop
ideas.text: With ...e6 in, ...d5 comes next and attacks the c4-bishop with gain of time.

ideas.title: Bb5 against ...Nc6
ideas.text: When ...d5 opens the a4-e8 diagonal, the bishop goes to b5 and pins the c6-knight, as with 6.Bb5.

habit.why: 4.d3 is solid but slow, and 4...d5 attacks your bishop straight away. After 5.Bb3 dxe4 6.dxe4 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 the queens are gone and your king has lost the right to castle.

strays.text: The slow pawn move lets ...d5 open the d-file before you castle.

taught.why: 4.O-O puts your king safe before the centre opens; masters choose it 69% of the time. After 4...d5 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5 Bd6 7.d4 you pin the c6-knight and hit Black's c5 pawn, and the game is level.

enforces.text: King safe first, then 7.d4 strikes at Black's centre.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.d4 opens the game at once: after 4...cxd4 5.Nxd4 Nf6 6.Nc3 Qc7 you're in an Open Sicilian with your bishop on c4. Sound, though masters seldom choose it.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O keeps d4 for later and meets 4...d5 with 5.exd5; masters prefer it, 69% to 2%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 develops and guards e4 against ...d5. After 4...Nf6 5.Bb5 Qc7 your bishop has moved twice, and 6...Nd4 puts Black's knight on a strong square.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O is the masters' main move (69% to 12%): it gets your king safe before the centre opens.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.c3 prepares d4, but 4...d5 comes first: after 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5 Bd6 7.d4 Nf6 Black's pieces are well placed and the game is level.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O reaches a similar structure with your king already safe; masters play it in 69% of games and 4.c3 almost never.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Qe2 makes ...d5 harder for now, since exd5 exd5 would open the e-file towards Black's king. After 4...Be7 the game stays level; masters choose it in 14% of games.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O is the masters' main move (69% to 14%); 4.Qe2 is sound too, a known Bowdler line of its own.

5215145015608227|c8f5.headline: Develop a knight first: 4...Bf5 runs into Qb3
5215145015608227|c8f5.why: 4...Bf5 leaves b7 unguarded, and 5.Qb3 hits b7 and d5, so your queen has to go to 5...Qc8. After 6.Nc3 e6 7.d3 Nc6 8.e4 dxe4 9.dxe4 White gains time on the bishop and is better developed. 4...Nc6 develops a piece while the c8-bishop still guards b7. After 5.d4 Bf5 6.Nf3 Nf6 7.Nc3 e6 the bishop comes out a move later, with both knights developed and d5 well covered.
5215145015608227|c8f5.principle: Knights before bishops: the c8-bishop guards b7, so a knight comes out before ...Bf5.

ideas.title: Bishop c8 guards b7
ideas.text: Your c8-bishop is b7's only guard. After 4...Bf5 5.Qb3 hits b7 and d5, and your queen must go to c8.

ideas.title: Fianchetto plus c4 hits d5
ideas.text: With the c-file open, the g2-bishop and a knight on c3 press on d5, and 5.Qb3 adds b7.

ideas.title: Knight first, bishop later
ideas.text: Develop ...Nc6 or ...Nf6 first, then ...Bf5, as in 4...Nc6 5.d4 Bf5.

habit.why: 4...Bf5 leaves b7 unguarded, and 5.Qb3 hits b7 and d5, so your queen has to go to 5...Qc8. After 6.Nc3 e6 7.d3 Nc6 8.e4 dxe4 9.dxe4 White gains time on the bishop and is better developed.

strays.text: With the bishop gone, 5.Qb3 hits b7 and forces 5...Qc8.

taught.why: 4...Nc6 develops a piece while the c8-bishop still guards b7. After 5.d4 Bf5 6.Nf3 Nf6 7.Nc3 e6 the bishop comes out a move later, with both knights developed and d5 well covered.

enforces.text: Knight out first; the bishop follows with 5...Bf5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nf6 is sound: it develops and guards d5, and after 6.d4 Bf5 the bishop comes out a move later. The move the drill wants is just as good.
alternatives.after: 4...Nc6 and 4...Nf6 reach the same structure after 5.Nf3 Nc6 6.d4 Bf5: both keep the bishop on c8 until a knight is out.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...e6 is sound and holds d5, but it shuts in your c8-bishop, and after 8.O-O O-O 9.Ne5 White is a little more active.
alternatives.after: 4...Nc6 keeps the bishop's road open so it can still come to f5, as in 5.d4 Bf5.

5231539809808326|e6e5.headline: Recapture 4...Qxd5; 4...e5 drops a pawn to 5.Nxe5
5231539809808326|e6e5.why: 4...e5 leaves the pawn on a square the f3 knight attacks and nothing defends, so 5.Nxe5 takes it. After 5...Qxd5 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Nxd7 Nxd7 8.O-O you have won back d5 but are a clean pawn down. 4...Qxd5 wins the pawn back at once, and with c3 taken by a pawn White has no Nc3 to chase your queen. After 5.Na3 Nf6 6.d4 Nc6 7.Be3 cxd4 8.Nb5 Qd7 9.Nbxd4 White's knight needed three moves to get into play while you developed freely.
5231539809808326|e6e5.principle: Count attackers and defenders: d5 is attacked twice and defended by nothing, so recapture before pushing past it.

ideas.title: Win back the d5 pawn
ideas.text: White's pawn on d5 is attacked twice, by your queen and e6 pawn, and defended by nothing. Take it back first.

ideas.title: No Nc3 for White
ideas.text: The c3 pawn takes the knight's square, so a queen on d5 can't be hit with tempo the way it is after an early Nc3.

ideas.title: Watch the b5 check
ideas.text: Your king is still on e8, so White's bishop checks on b5 as soon as the e-file or the a4-e8 diagonal opens.

habit.why: 4...e5 leaves the pawn on a square the f3 knight attacks and nothing defends, so 5.Nxe5 takes it. After 5...Qxd5 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Nxd7 Nxd7 8.O-O you have won back d5 but are a clean pawn down.

strays.text: Pushing past d5 instead of recapturing hands White the e5 pawn.

taught.why: 4...Qxd5 wins the pawn back at once, and with c3 taken by a pawn White has no Nc3 to chase your queen. After 5.Na3 Nf6 6.d4 Nc6 7.Be3 cxd4 8.Nb5 Qd7 9.Nbxd4 White's knight needed three moves to get into play while you developed freely.

enforces.text: The queen recaptures safely, since no white knight can reach c3.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4...exd5 is common (41% of master games), but White checks at once: 5.Bb5+ Bd7 6.Qe2+ Qe7 7.O-O Qxe2 8.Bxe2 trades queens and leaves you slightly worse.
alternatives.after: 4...Qxd5 keeps the e6 pawn blocking the e-file checks, and no Nc3 can hit the queen. Masters play both (58% to 41%), but the engine clearly prefers the queen recapture.

5254169560142503|c1d2.headline: Ignore the pin and hit f7 with 7.Ng5
5254169560142503|c1d2.why: 7.Bd2 meets the pin passively and does nothing about f7: after 7...Nf6 8.O-O O-O Black has castled with an extra pawn. Black can later trade bishops with 11...Bxd2, and every trade helps the side with more material. 7.Ng5 threatens to take on f7 and fork queen and rook, so Black must answer 7...Nh6, putting the knight on the rim. After 8.O-O O-O 9.Qh5 your pieces bear down on Black's kingside.
5254169560142503|c1d2.principle: Attack f7 while only Black's king guards it; the pin on c3 can wait, because trading on c3 costs Black the dark-squared bishop.
sources: IM Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf
Morra Gambit Accepted (ianchessgambits) | http://www.ianchessgambits.com/morra-gambit-accepted.html

ideas.title: Hit f7 early
ideas.text: After ...e5, f7 is guarded only by the king. A knight on g5 and the c4-bishop threaten it before Black can castle.

ideas.title: Ignore the pin
ideas.text: The b4-bishop pins your c3-knight, but trading on c3 gives up Black's dark-squared bishop, so you need not spend a move on it.

ideas.title: Use the d5 hole
ideas.text: With ...e5 played, no black pawn can cover d5. Your c3-knight can land there later, as in 10.Nd5.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black's king is still on e8. Passive moves let Black castle and keep the extra pawn.

habit.why: 7.Bd2 meets the pin passively and does nothing about f7: after 7...Nf6 8.O-O O-O Black has castled with an extra pawn. Black can later trade bishops with 11...Bxd2, and every trade helps the side with more material.

strays.text: A quiet unpinning move lets Black castle by move 8.

taught.why: 7.Ng5 threatens to take on f7 and fork queen and rook, so Black must answer 7...Nh6, putting the knight on the rim. After 8.O-O O-O 9.Qh5 your pieces bear down on Black's kingside.

enforces.text: The knight joins the bishop against f7 and sends Black's knight to h6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is good: it ignores the pin, since trading on c3 would give up Black's dark-squared bishop, and gets your king safe. Most club players (53%) castle here, but there's a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: Both are good. 7.Ng5 forces 7...Nh6 at once, while 7.O-O Nf6 8.Ng5 O-O 9.Qb3 brings the same pressure on f7 a move later, after Black has castled.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qb3 hits f7 at once, but 7...Qe7 covers it and your c3-knight stays pinned. Even after you grab f7 with 9.Bxf7+ Kf8, 10...Nd4 drives your queen back to d1.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 makes the bigger threat, a fork on f7, so Black must answer 7...Nh6 at once instead of developing with gain of time.

5265791031076490|b5d7.headline: Guard the bishop with 7.Qe2 and hit e5; keep the extra pawn
5265791031076490|b5d7.why: 7.Bxd7+ trades your only developed piece, and 7...Qxd7 develops Black's queen with pressure on d5. Black castles long and wins back the pawn: 8.O-O O-O-O 9.d4 Nxd5. 7.Qe2 guards the b5-bishop against 7...Bxb5 and attacks e5, so Black spends 7...Bd6 on defending it; masters play it 96% of the time. Only then 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 9.Nc3 c6 10.dxc6 Nxc6 11.d3 keeps you a pawn up with easy development.
5265791031076490|b5d7.principle: Defend with a move that also attacks: 7.Qe2 guards the b5-bishop and hits e5, so Black spends time on defence instead of winning d5 back.
sources: Tim Harding, Two Knights Defence without Tears, Part 2 | https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/tim-harding-two-knights-defence-part-ii/250495309

ideas.title: Keep the extra pawn
ideas.text: After 5.exd5 you are a pawn up. Black develops fast to win d5 back, so keep it covered and never hand it back.

ideas.title: Keep your active bishop
ideas.text: 6.Bb5+ was virtually forced, and the b5-bishop is your only developed piece. Do not trade it off for nothing.

ideas.title: Black gains time on your pieces
ideas.text: Black develops by hitting things: ...Na5 chased your bishop, and now 7...Bxb5 threatens to win it.

ideas.title: Qe2 hits e5
ideas.text: 7.Qe2 guards b5 and attacks e5, so Black must spend a move defending the pawn.

habit.why: 7.Bxd7+ trades your only developed piece, and 7...Qxd7 develops Black's queen with pressure on d5. Black castles long and wins back the pawn: 8.O-O O-O-O 9.d4 Nxd5.

strays.text: The trade gives Black time to castle long and win back d5.

taught.why: 7.Qe2 guards the b5-bishop against 7...Bxb5 and attacks e5, so Black spends 7...Bd6 on defending it; masters play it 96% of the time. Only then 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 9.Nc3 c6 10.dxc6 Nxc6 11.d3 keeps you a pawn up with easy development.

enforces.text: The queen defends b5 and attacks e5 in one move.

5269510306588935|f1c4.headline: Kick the knight with 6.e5 before Black can support it
5269510306588935|f1c4.why: 6.Bc4 is natural, but it lets Black play 6...Nc6, so after 7.e5 Ng4 the knight hits your e5 pawn. After 8.Qe2 d5 9.exd6 Bxd6 10.O-O O-O Black has developed freely and kept the extra pawn. 6.e5 kicks the knight before Black can support it, and it has no good square, so it goes back with 6...Ng8. After 7.Bc4 d5 8.exd6 Bxd6 9.O-O you are well ahead in development.
5269510306588935|f1c4.principle: A knight on f6 that a pawn can hit is a target: 6.e5 gains space and time now, before 6...Nc6 gives the knight support.
sources: IM Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf
Mayhem in the Morra, reviews (polishchess.com) | https://www.polishchess.com/-kartapdf-192.html
