ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: e4-e5 kicks the f6-knight at once; with no knight on c6 yet, nothing of Black's hits e5.

ideas.title: Black's knight on c6 changes it
ideas.text: Once a knight is on c6, e4-e5 can be met by a knight jump to g4 hitting e5, as in 7.e5 Ng4.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: A pawn down, you must use your lead now. Quiet moves let Black develop, castle and keep the pawn.

ideas.title: Trades help the extra pawn
ideas.text: A pawn up, Black is happy to trade pieces; after a quiet pin Black can swap off with a knight on d5.

habit.why: 6.Bc4 is natural, but it lets Black play 6...Nc6, so after 7.e5 Ng4 the knight hits your e5 pawn. After 8.Qe2 d5 9.exd6 Bxd6 10.O-O O-O Black has developed freely and kept the extra pawn.

strays.text: Waiting a move lets Black's knight reach c6 and cover e5 first.

taught.why: 6.e5 kicks the knight before Black can support it, and it has no good square, so it goes back with 6...Ng8. After 7.Bc4 d5 8.exd6 Bxd6 9.O-O you are well ahead in development.

enforces.text: The pawn kicks the f6-knight back to g8 for free.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.Bg5 pins the knight, but after 6...h6 7.Bh4 Nc6 Black is developing, and later 9...Nd5 10.Nxd5 exd5 trades pieces. Trades help the side with the extra pawn.
alternatives.after: 6.e5 hits the knight at once instead of pinning it, so Black loses time going back instead of developing.

5284557229021992|d3d4.headline: Castle first; 7.d4 takes away e4's only pawn guard.
5284557229021992|d3d4.why: The pawn on d3 is what protects e4. After 7.d4 exd4 8.exd4 Nxe4 the knight on f6 takes the pawn, and White's king is still in the centre. 7.O-O tucks the king away and puts the rook on the half-open f-file that the earlier recapture opened. White can prepare central play after that.
5284557229021992|d3d4.principle: Before pushing a pawn, check what it was defending, and get your king safe before opening the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. d3/4...Bc5

5286148894410756|d3c2.headline: Release the tension with 7.dxc5; don't move the bishop twice
5286148894410756|d3c2.why: 7.Bc2 moves the bishop a second time while your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. After 7...cxd4 8.cxd4 Nb4 9.O-O Nxc2 10.Qxc2 Rc8 Black has swapped off that bishop and taken the c-file; masters almost never play 7.Bc2 (0.4%). 7.dxc5 removes the pawn that attacks d4 before Black can take there; it is the masters' top choice at 51%. After 7...Bxc5 8.O-O a5 9.Qe2 you are castled, your e5 pawn still cramps Black, and 10.Nbd2 and 11.Nb3 chase the c5 bishop.
5286148894410756|d3c2.principle: With your b1 knight and c1 bishop still at home, a second bishop move must win something; here it only gives Black time and the c-file.
sources: French Defense: Advance Variation, Milner-Barry Gambit (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/french-defense/advance-variation/milner-barry-gambit/
Nick Visel, Chessable Course Review: The Supercharged Milner-Barry Gambit (Nick Plays Chess) | https://www.nickplayschess.com/p/chessable-course-review-the-supercharged
Robert Ris, Fast and Furious: The Improved Milner-Barry Gambit (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/robert-ris-fast-and-furious-the-improved-milner-barry-gambit
Lukas Köpl, Review: Mastering the French Advance Main Line by Jan Werle (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/newsroom/post/review-jan-werle-french-advance?page=0

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: Black's c5 pawn and c6 knight hit d4, and the b6 queen joins once the c-pawn takes. 7...cxd4 is a real threat.

ideas.title: Don't block the queen's guard of d4
ideas.text: Your d3 bishop cuts the queen off from d4. Moving it again to c2 costs a move, and 8...Nb4 then swaps it off.

ideas.title: Release the tension with dxc5
ideas.text: 7.dxc5 removes the pawn that hits d4. After 7...Bxc5 8.O-O your e5 pawn still cramps Black and you are castled.

ideas.title: The Milner-Barry gambit
ideas.text: Giving up d4 on purpose is the Milner-Barry: after 7.O-O cxd4 8.Re1 you keep e5 and develop fast for the pawn.

habit.why: 7.Bc2 moves the bishop a second time while your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. After 7...cxd4 8.cxd4 Nb4 9.O-O Nxc2 10.Qxc2 Rc8 Black has swapped off that bishop and taken the c-file; masters almost never play 7.Bc2 (0.4%).

strays.idea: Don't block the queen's guard of d4
strays.text: You fix the blocked d-file with a second bishop move, and 8...Nb4 trades it off.

taught.why: 7.dxc5 removes the pawn that attacks d4 before Black can take there; it is the masters' top choice at 51%. After 7...Bxc5 8.O-O a5 9.Qe2 you are castled, your e5 pawn still cramps Black, and 10.Nbd2 and 11.Nb3 chase the c5 bishop.

enforces.text: The pawn that hit d4 is gone, and you keep e5 and castle next.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is the Milner-Barry idea: after 7...cxd4 8.Re1 you give up d4 to keep e5 and attack. It's sound, but there is a calmer, stronger move.
alternatives.after: 7.dxc5 keeps material level and still lets you castle next move. Masters split almost evenly, 51% to 48%, and the engine slightly prefers 7.dxc5.

5414391277109696|b1c3.headline: Bishop on g4 is loose: 5.Bxf7+ and 6.Ng5+ win it back
5414391277109696|b1c3.why: 5.Nc3 develops but lets the chance pass: after 5...e6 your bishop no longer reaches f7. After 6.Be3 Nc6 7.Qd2 Bxf3 8.gxf3 Black's mistake on move 4 goes unpunished and you keep only a small edge. 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ moves the knight with check and uncovers your queen on the g4 bishop, so 6...Ke8 7.Qxg4 wins the piece back. Even after 7...Bxd4 levels the material, Black can no longer castle and 8.Qe6 plants your queen next to the stuck king, a large advantage.
5414391277109696|b1c3.principle: Early on only the king guards f7: when a bishop sacrifice there is followed by a knight check that uncovers your queen on a loose piece, play it.
sources: Bill Wall, 700 Opening Traps (archive.org) | https://archive.org/stream/700OpeningTraps/700%20Opening%20Traps_djvu.txt
GM Max Illingworth, The Mad Dog Attack vs. the Modern (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/blog/Illingworth/the-mad-dog-attack-vs-the-modern

ideas.title: The f7 and g4 trick
ideas.text: 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ moves the knight with check and opens your queen's line to the g4 bishop.

ideas.title: Loose bishop on g4
ideas.text: Nothing defends the g4 bishop; only your f3 knight stands between it and your queen on d1.

ideas.title: Black closes f7 with ...e6
ideas.text: If you wait, ...e6 shuts your bishop out of f7, as after 5.Nc3 e6, and the trick is gone.

ideas.title: King stuck in the centre
ideas.text: After 6...Ke8 7.Qxg4 Black can't castle, and 8.Qe6 with the g5 knight keeps aiming at f7.

habit.why: 5.Nc3 develops but lets the chance pass: after 5...e6 your bishop no longer reaches f7. After 6.Be3 Nc6 7.Qd2 Bxf3 8.gxf3 Black's mistake on move 4 goes unpunished and you keep only a small edge.

strays.text: 5...e6 blocks your bishop's path to f7 and the trick is gone.

taught.why: 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ moves the knight with check and uncovers your queen on the g4 bishop, so 6...Ke8 7.Qxg4 wins the piece back. Even after 7...Bxd4 levels the material, Black can no longer castle and 8.Qe6 plants your queen next to the stuck king, a large advantage.

enforces.text: The knight check uncovers your queen on the loose g4 bishop.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: After 5.h3 Bxf3 6.Qxf3 e6 Black has swapped off your f3 knight and closed the centre, and you keep only a small edge. A much bigger chance was on offer.
alternatives.after: 5.Bxf7+ needs the f3 knight for 6.Ng5+; after 5.h3 Bxf3 that knight is gone, and the trick with it.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: Castling is natural, but after 5...e6 6.c3 Nf6 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Black is safely developed and you keep only a small edge. Black's move 4 goes unpunished.
alternatives.after: After 5.O-O e6 the e6 pawn blocks your bishop's path to f7, so 5.Bxf7+ had to come at once.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.c3 supports d4, but after 5...e6 6.O-O Nf6 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Black is safely developed and you keep only a small edge. Black's move 4 goes unpunished.
alternatives.after: 5.Bxf7+ comes first because 5...e6 would block your bishop's path to f7 and end the trick.

5414391277109696|c2c3.headline: Punish 4...Bg4 at once with 5.Bxf7+ while g4 is loose
5414391277109696|c2c3.why: 5.c3 does nothing about the loose bishop on g4, and after 5...e6 the pawn blocks your bishop's path to f7. After 6.O-O Nf6 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 O-O Black has castled into a normal Modern and your chance is gone. 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ forces the king to move, and 7.Qxg4 takes the bishop back. Even after 7...Bxd4 8.Qe6 Nc6 9.c3, Black can't castle and your queen and knight stand right next to the king.
5414391277109696|c2c3.principle: f7 is Black's weak point before castling: with your bishop aimed at it, check whether Bxf7+ wins something before making a quiet move.
sources: Bill Wall, 700 Opening Traps (archive.org) | https://archive.org/stream/700OpeningTraps/700%20Opening%20Traps_djvu.txt

ideas.title: ...Bg4 pin versus f7 tactics
ideas.text: Pinning the f3-knight is normal, but with your bishop on c4 and Black uncastled, 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ and 7.Qxg4 win the bishop back.

ideas.title: Strike before ...Nf6 or ...e6
ideas.text: The trick works only now: ...Nf6 would guard g4 and ...e6 would block your bishop, so a quiet move lets it slip.

ideas.title: Black's king stuck in the centre
ideas.text: After 5...Kxf7 Black can never castle. Even when 7...Bxd4 wins a pawn back, 8.Qe6 keeps your queen and knight next to the king.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Black's g7-bishop aims at d4. Against quiet moves Black keeps the pin or trades with ...Bxf3 and gets a normal Modern.

habit.why: 5.c3 does nothing about the loose bishop on g4, and after 5...e6 the pawn blocks your bishop's path to f7. After 6.O-O Nf6 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 O-O Black has castled into a normal Modern and your chance is gone.

strays.text: 5.c3 gives Black time for ...e6 and ...Nf6, which kill the trick.

taught.why: 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ forces the king to move, and 7.Qxg4 takes the bishop back. Even after 7...Bxd4 8.Qe6 Nc6 9.c3, Black can't castle and your queen and knight stand right next to the king.

enforces.text: 6.Ng5+ comes with check and opens your queen's path to g4.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.h3 puts the question to the bishop, but Black simply trades with 5...Bxf3 6.Qxf3 e6, and then the pin is gone and the e6 pawn shields f7.
alternatives.after: 5.Bxf7+ strikes while the bishop on g4 is loose; after 5.h3 Bxf3 that bishop is off the board and the trick goes with it.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.O-O is natural, but it gives Black time for 5...e6, which shields f7; after 7.Re1 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Black has a normal game.
alternatives.after: 5.Bxf7+ works only while f7 is open and g4 is loose; after 5.O-O e6 your bishop no longer reaches f7.

After 7.d5 Nf6 8.dxe6 fxe6 9.e5 Nd5 Black has a normal game and your chance is gone. 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ forces the king to move, and 7.Qxg4 takes the bishop back. strays.text: Black trades on f3 at once, and the f7 trick disappears.

taught.why: 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ forces the king to move, and 7.Qxg4 takes the bishop back. Even after 7...Bxd4 8.Qe6 Nc6 9.c3, Black can't castle and your queen and knight stand right next to the king.

enforces.text: 6.Ng5+ comes with check and opens your queen's path to g4.

alternatives.after: 5.Bxf7+ works only while f7 is open and g4 is loose; after 5.O-O e6 your bishop no longer reaches f7.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.c3 supports d4 but ignores the loose bishop on g4; after 5...e6 6.O-O Nf6 Black has covered both f7 and g4.
alternatives.after: 5.Bxf7+ hits while nothing covers f7 or g4; 5.c3 gives Black the two moves needed to fix both.

5431389031817647|c6e5.headline: Bring out a new piece that attacks e4
5431389031817647|c6e5.why: 4...Ne5 moves the knight a second time while three minor pieces are still at home, and 5.f4 chases it straight back with 5...Nc6, so White gains two moves for free. 4...Nf6 develops a new piece and attacks the pawn on e4 at once; theory calls this the Schmidt variation, where White usually trades with 5.Nxc6 bxc6.
5431389031817647|c6e5.principle: When the opponent's knight stands in the centre, develop a new piece with a threat rather than moving a knight that is already out.

5431389031817647|d7d6.headline: Seize the initiative with 4...Nf6 against e4
5431389031817647|d7d6.why: 4...d6 is passive: it shuts in the bishop on f8 and lets White develop freely with 5.Nc3, 6.Bf4, 7.Qd2 and 8.O-O-O. Wikibooks stresses that Black has a chance to take the initiative here that should not be wasted. 4...Nf6 develops the knight with immediate pressure on the pawn on e4, so White has to spend the next move dealing with it, usually 5.Nxc6 bxc6.
5431389031817647|d7d6.principle: Develop with a threat when you can: a knight that attacks a centre pawn gains time because White must answer it.

5459128121989910|g7g5.headline: Take the free pawn with 3...Nxe4
5459128121989910|g7g5.why: 3...g5 offers a pawn and ignores the free one on e4: after 4.fxg5 Nxe4 you only win back the material, and 5.d3 Nc5 6.d4 Ne6 chases your knight around. Your kingside is loosened while White builds a big centre. 3...Nxe4 takes a centre pawn that nothing defends. After 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.d4 g6 6.Be3 Bg7 7.Qd2 O-O you are a pawn up with a normal Pirc set-up.
5459128121989910|g7g5.principle: Undefended pawns are where to strike: e4 is attacked by your knight and guarded by nothing, so take it before setting up.

ideas.title: Grab e4 if White neglects it
ideas.text: Your f6-knight hits e4, and 3.Nf3 left it unguarded, with no knight on c3 yet. 3...Nxe4 simply wins a pawn.

ideas.title: e5 kicks the f6-knight
ideas.text: If you leave e4 alone, White pushes it and kicks your knight, as in 3...g6 4.e5 Nfd7.

ideas.title: Fianchetto after the grab
ideas.text: Take the pawn first; ...g6 and ...Bg7 still follow, as in 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.d4 g6 6.Be3 Bg7.

habit.why: 3...g5 offers a pawn and ignores the free one on e4: after 4.fxg5 Nxe4 you only win back the material, and 5.d3 Nc5 6.d4 Ne6 chases your knight around. Your kingside is loosened while White builds a big centre.

strays.idea: Grab e4 if White neglects it
strays.text: e4 was free to take; 3...g5 gives a pawn instead.

taught.why: 3...Nxe4 takes a centre pawn that nothing defends. After 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.d4 g6 6.Be3 Bg7 7.Qd2 O-O you are a pawn up with a normal Pirc set-up.

enforces.idea: Grab e4 if White neglects it
enforces.text: The knight takes e4 and returns to f6, a clean pawn up.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...g6 is normal Pirc development and keeps a playable game, but there's a far stronger move. After 4.e5 Nfd7 5.d4 c5 White gains space and your knight has moved twice.
alternatives.after: 3...Nxe4 is much stronger: it takes a free pawn, and ...g6 still follows, as in 5.d4 g6. After 3...g6 4.e5 the pawn is gone for good.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Bg4 develops and pins the f3-knight, a sound idea, but a much stronger move is available. After 4.h3 Bxf3 5.Qxf3 e6 White has the bishop pair and a solid centre.
alternatives.after: 3...Nxe4 wins a pawn outright; 3...Bg4 leaves e4 alone, and after 4.h3 Bxf3 you also give up a bishop for the knight.
alternatives.idea: Grab e4 if White neglects it

5459128121989910|g7g6.headline: Take the free pawn with 3...Nxe4 before fianchettoing
5459128121989910|g7g6.why: 3...g6 is normal Pirc development, but it leaves the free e4 pawn alone and lets 4.e5 kick your knight to d7. After 5.d4 c5 6.Bc4 cxd4 7.Qxd4 dxe5 8.Nxe5 White's pieces aim at f7 and you never got the pawn. 3...Nxe4 takes a centre pawn that nothing defends. After 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.d4 g6 6.Be3 Bg7 7.Qd2 O-O you are a pawn up with a normal Pirc set-up.
5459128121989910|g7g6.principle: Undefended pawns are where to strike: e4 is attacked by your knight and guarded by nothing, so take it before your usual set-up.

5465976377681862|d8f6.headline: Take the knight: 4...Nxe5, then meet the fork with 5...Bd6.
5465976377681862|d8f6.why: The knight on e5 is attacked once and defended by nothing, and 4...Qf6 only attacks it. After 5.Ng4 it escapes with gain of time on the queen, and Black is a pawn down. 4...Nxe5 wins the knight. White gets the material back with 5.d4, but after 5...Bd6 6.dxe5 Bxe5 the material is level again.
5465976377681862|d8f6.principle: When a piece is free to take, take it with a minor piece rather than attacking it with the queen.

5477278678228721|c1f4.headline: Win back c4 with 4.e3; 4.Bf4 lets Black keep it
5477278678228721|c1f4.why: 4.Bf4 does nothing to win back c4, so Black holds it with 4...b5 5.a4 c6. After 6.axb5 cxb5 7.Nc3 Qb6 8.b3 e5 Black's queen and e-pawn hit d4, and the extra pawn is still there. 4.e3 opens the f1 bishop's path to c4, and after 4...c5 5.Bxc4 the pawn is back with a piece developed. You castle next with 6.O-O, the plan masters choose 80% of the time.
5477278678228721|c1f4.principle: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, free the king's bishop to win back c4 before Black can prop it up with ...b5.

Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. e3

ideas.title: Win back c4, don't Bf4
ideas.text: Black can rarely keep the c4 pawn: 4.e3 and 5.Bxc4 win it back with a developing move. 4.Bf4 does nothing for c4.

ideas.title: a4 against ...b5
ideas.text: If Black props up c4 with ...b5, hit it at once with a4; a3 is too slow.

ideas.title: Bf4 leaves d4 loose
ideas.text: With your c1 bishop on f4, ...Qb6 and ...e5 can gang up on d4, as in 7.Nc3 Qb6 8.b3 e5.

ideas.title: Keep the bigger centre
ideas.text: Once c4 is back you have the bigger centre: develop and castle, as in 5.Bxc4 e6 6.O-O.

habit.why: 4.Bf4 does nothing to win back c4, so Black holds it with 4...b5 5.a4 c6. After 6.axb5 cxb5 7.Nc3 Qb6 8.b3 e5 Black's queen and e-pawn hit d4, and the extra pawn is still there.

strays.text: The bishop develops but leaves the c4 pawn in Black's hands.

taught.why: 4.e3 opens the f1 bishop's path to c4, and after 4...c5 5.Bxc4 the pawn is back with a piece developed. You castle next with 6.O-O, the plan masters choose 80% of the time.

enforces.text: One pawn move frees the bishop that takes back c4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 is the Two Knights gambit: after 4...a6 5.e4 b5 you get a big centre but can't expect to win c4 back. Sound, but there's a calmer, more common move.
alternatives.after: 4.e3 simply wins c4 back with 5.Bxc4, while 4.Nc3 a6 5.e4 b5 leaves you a pawn down for central play. Masters prefer 4.e3, 80% to 14%.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.g3 aims the bishop at c4 from g2, but it's slow: after 4...Nc6 5.Nc3 e5 Black hits d4, and the queens come off with Black still holding c4.
alternatives.after: 4.e3 opens the f1 bishop's path to c4 in one move and guards d4, so ...e5 doesn't come with tempo.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Qa4+ wins c4 back at once with 5.Qxc4, but after 4...Nc6 Black develops while chasing your queen, as in 5...Be6 6.Qa4 Bd7 7.Qb3. Sound, though Black gets easy equality.
alternatives.after: 4.e3 regains c4 with a bishop that develops instead of a queen that gets chased. Masters prefer it, 80% to 5%.

5482220977229606|g7g6.headline: Stop e4 with 2...d5 while the c-pawn is blocked
5482220977229606|g7g6.why: 2...g6 does nothing about e4, so 3.e4 d6 4.d4 gives White the full centre. After 4...Bg7 5.Be3 O-O 6.Qd2 White has a free hand and a ready-made set-up. 2...d5 puts a pawn in the centre and, with the f6-knight, holds e4, so White can't build the big centre. After 3.d4 a6 4.e3 Nbd7 5.Bd3 c5 you have your share of the centre, the move masters play 77% of the time.
5482220977229606|g7g6.principle: Claim the centre while White's c-pawn is blocked, so White can't build a full pawn centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3/2...d5 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._d4/1...Nf6/2._Nc3/2...d5
The Ultimate English Opening (1.c4) Guide (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/the-ultimate-english-opening-1-c4-guide/

ideas.title: Stop e4 with ...d5
ideas.text: With White's knight on c3, ...d5 at once is good: the d5-pawn and the f6-knight hold e4.

ideas.title: White's big centre
ideas.text: Given time, White plays e4 and d4, as in 2...g6 3.e4 d6 4.d4, and takes the whole centre.

ideas.title: Prepare ...d5 so a pawn recaptures
ideas.text: Against c4 you prepare ...d5; here the c3-knight blocks the c-pawn, so nothing can swap off your d-pawn.

habit.why: 2...g6 does nothing about e4, so 3.e4 d6 4.d4 gives White the full centre. After 4...Bg7 5.Be3 O-O 6.Qd2 White has a free hand and a ready-made set-up.

strays.text: Without ...d5, 3.e4 and 4.d4 give White both centre squares.

taught.why: 2...d5 puts a pawn in the centre and, with the f6-knight, holds e4, so White can't build the big centre. After 3.d4 a6 4.e3 Nbd7 5.Bd3 c5 you have your share of the centre, the move masters play 77% of the time.

enforces.text: The d5-pawn and the f6-knight both hold e4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...Nc6 develops, and after 3.d4 you get a solid game, as in 4.Bf4 Bf5 5.e3 e6. But it blocks your c-pawn, and there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 2...d5 claims the centre at once; with 2...Nc6 you reach a similar game after 3.d4 d5, but White had the choice.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...e6 lets White play 3.e4, and after 4.e5 Nfd7 you get a French where your knight has been pushed back.
alternatives.after: 2...d5 stops e4 outright, so you don't have to accept a French.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...c5 is sound: after 3.e4 d6 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 you get a Najdorf Sicilian, a fine opening if you know it.
alternatives.after: 2...d5 keeps e4 out, while 2...c5 lets White push 3.e4 and reach an open Sicilian.

5530528877961804|f3d4.headline: Pin the e4 pawn with 4.Qe2 instead of retreating the knight
5530528877961804|f3d4.why: 4.Nd4 moves the knight a second time and gives back the d5 pawn: 4...Qxd5 wins it while hitting the knight again. After 5.Nb5 Qd7 6.N5c3 Nc6 7.d3 exd3 8.Bxd3 Nb4 your knight has made four moves to reach c3 and your edge is gone. 4.Qe2 pins the e4 pawn to Black's king on e8, so it cannot take your knight, and 5.d3 attacks it again. After 4...Nf6 5.d3 Qxd5 6.Nc3 Bb4 7.Nd2 Bxc3 8.bxc3 Nc6 the e4 pawn is attacked three times and defended twice, so you win it and stay a pawn up.
5530528877961804|f3d4.principle: When a pawn attacks your piece, look for a pin on that pawn before retreating: after 4.Qe2 the capture 4...exf3 is illegal.
sources: GM Avetik Grigoryan, Elephant Gambit: The Refutation (ChessMood) | http://chessmood.com/blog/elephant-gambit-the-refutation
Matthew Astle, The Ultimate Elephant Gambit Opening Guide (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/elephant-gambit/
Michael Goeller, Elephant Gambit (C40) Bibliography | https://kenilworthian.blogspot.com/2012/12/elephant-gambit-c40-bibliography_12.html

ideas.title: Pin the e4 pawn
ideas.text: 4.Qe2 pins the e4 pawn to Black's king on e8, so 4...exf3 is illegal and your knight is safe.

ideas.title: Win the e4 pawn
ideas.text: With the pawn pinned, 5.d3 and your knights attack it again. Black struggles to hold it, and you keep the advantage.

ideas.title: Black's ...Qxd5 with tempo
ideas.text: If your knight retreats, 4...Qxd5 wins back the pawn and hits the knight again, and Black takes over the initiative.

habit.why: 4.Nd4 moves the knight a second time and gives back the d5 pawn: 4...Qxd5 wins it while hitting the knight again. After 5.Nb5 Qd7 6.N5c3 Nc6 7.d3 exd3 8.Bxd3 Nb4 your knight has made four moves to reach c3 and your edge is gone.

strays.text: The retreat lets 4...Qxd5 regain the pawn and chase your knight again.

taught.why: 4.Qe2 pins the e4 pawn to Black's king on e8, so it cannot take your knight, and 5.d3 attacks it again. After 4...Nf6 5.d3 Qxd5 6.Nc3 Bb4 7.Nd2 Bxc3 8.bxc3 Nc6 the e4 pawn is attacked three times and defended twice, so you win it and stay a pawn up.

enforces.text: The pin saves the knight without moving it, and the e4 pawn falls later.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Ng1 saves the knight by undeveloping it, and 4...Qxd5 wins the pawn back. After 5.d4 exd3 6.Qxd3 Qe6+ 7.Be3 Bc5 Black's pieces come out faster.
alternatives.after: 4.Qe2 keeps the knight on f3 and the pawn pinned. GM Grigoryan notes that 4...Qxd5 then costs Black the e4 pawn.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Ne5 keeps the knight central, but 4...Qxd5 wins the pawn back, and after 5.d4 exd3 6.Nxd3 Nc6 Black develops quickly. Masters play it 14.5% of the time, but the engine rates it clearly worse.
alternatives.after: 4.Qe2 is the masters' main choice (75.4%) and the engine's: the pin saves the knight and keeps your extra pawn, which 4.Ne5 gives back.

5540647116069974|f1c4.headline: Take the centre with 4.d4 before developing the bishop
5540647116069974|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 develops, but the bishop is a target once Black plays ...d5: after 4...Nf6 5.e5 d5 it has to go back with 6.Bf1, and 6...d4 7.exf6 dxc3 leads to a messy, level game. Without a pawn on d4 you have also given up your share of the centre. 4.d4 takes the centre with pawns and reaches a main Owen position, chosen in 88% of master games. After 4...Bb4 5.Bd3 Nf6 6.Nd2 your pieces keep e4 safe despite the pin, and 6...c5 7.dxc5 even wins a pawn.
5540647116069974|f1c4.principle: Black has given you the centre, so occupy it with pawns first: 4.d4 sets up e4 and d4, while 4.Bc4 puts a bishop where ...d5 hits it.
sources: Dejan Bojkov, The English Defence (ChessBase) | https://shop.chessbase.com/en/products/bojkov_the_english_defence
Matthew Astle, The Offbeat Owen's (Chessable blog) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/owens-defense/
Owen's Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen%27s_Defence

ideas.title: Take the centre with pawns
ideas.text: Black has handed you the centre, so put a second pawn on d4 before the bishops come out.

ideas.title: ...d5 hits a bishop on c4
ideas.text: With ...e6 in, ...d5 gains time against a bishop on c4, as in 4...Nf6 5.e5 d5.

ideas.title: Black strikes back with ...c5
ideas.text: After 4.d4 Black pins your c3-knight with 4...Bb4 and hits d4 with 6...c5; 5.Bd3 and 6.Nd2 keep e4 covered.

ideas.title: Count attackers on e4
ideas.text: Once ...Nf6 comes, the knight and b7-bishop hit e4. Your c3-knight guards it, but a pin from b4 takes that guard away.

habit.why: 4.Bc4 develops, but the bishop is a target once Black plays ...d5: after 4...Nf6 5.e5 d5 it has to go back with 6.Bf1, and 6...d4 7.exf6 dxc3 leads to a messy, level game. Without a pawn on d4 you have also given up your share of the centre.

strays.text: The bishop comes out before d4, and ...d5 chases it.

taught.why: 4.d4 takes the centre with pawns and reaches a main Owen position, chosen in 88% of master games. After 4...Bb4 5.Bd3 Nf6 6.Nd2 your pieces keep e4 safe despite the pin, and 6...c5 7.dxc5 even wins a pawn.

enforces.text: Pawns on e4 and d4 claim the centre Black gave you.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.d3 gives up a big centre: after 4...Nf6 5.e5 Nd5 6.Ne4 d6 Black's knight sits well on d5 and Black is comfortable.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 claims the centre at once; with 4.d3 you later play 7.d4 anyway, a move down.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.a3 stops ...Bb4 pinning your c3-knight, but without a pawn in the centre it's slow, and after 4...Nf6 5.e5 Nd5 Black is fine.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 takes the centre first and meets the pin with 5.Bd3 and 6.Nd2. Masters choose it 88% of the time, 4.a3 under 6%.

5580466240815728|c8f5.headline: Knight to f6 first: 3...Bf5 hands b7 to 5.Qb3
5580466240815728|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 takes the only guard off b7, so 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 at once. After 5...Nf6 6.Qxb7 Nbd7 7.Nc3 Rb8 8.Qxa7 you are two pawns down. 3...Nf6 guards d5 and covers e4, keeping the bishop at home until it's safe. After 4.e3 Bg4 5.h3 Bxf3 6.Qxf3 Nbd7 the bishop comes out once e3 has shut in White's c1-bishop, at the cost of the bishop pair; masters pick 3...Nf6 in 91.7% of games.
5580466240815728|c8f5.principle: Knights before bishops: in the Slav the knight on f6 guards d5 and covers e4, while the c8-bishop waits until a queen on b3 no longer wins b7.
sources: Tartakower, The Hypermodern Game of Chess (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%223...Bf5%22+%224.cxd5+cxd5+5.Qb3%22

ideas.title: Early ...Bf5 drops b7
ideas.text: Once the bishop leaves c8, 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 together and wins a pawn.

ideas.title: Knight to f6 before ...Bf5
ideas.text: 3...Nf6 guards d5 and covers e4. The bishop comes out once a queen on b3 no longer wins anything, for example after White's 4.e3.

ideas.title: Ne5 hits an early ...Bg4
ideas.text: A bishop on g4 can be hit by the knight from e5, as after 3...Bg4 4.Ne5 Bc8, costing you two moves.

habit.why: 3...Bf5 takes the only guard off b7, so 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 at once. After 5...Nf6 6.Qxb7 Nbd7 7.Nc3 Rb8 8.Qxa7 you are two pawns down.

strays.text: The bishop leaves c8, and 5.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 together.

taught.why: 3...Nf6 guards d5 and covers e4, keeping the bishop at home until it's safe. After 4.e3 Bg4 5.h3 Bxf3 6.Qxf3 Nbd7 the bishop comes out once e3 has shut in White's c1-bishop, at the cost of the bishop pair; masters pick 3...Nf6 in 91.7% of games.

enforces.text: d5 gets its guard first; the bishop comes out after 4.e3.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...e6 guards d5 and often transposes to Semi-Slav lines, but it shuts in your c8-bishop. After 4.e3 and 5.b3 White develops calmly and keeps a small edge.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 keeps the bishop's road open and covers e4. Masters still play 3...e6 in 6.7% of games; the engine just prefers 3...Nf6.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...Bg4 has the same flaw as ...Bf5 and adds another: 4.Ne5 hits the bishop, and after 4...Bc8 you have spent two moves to go back home.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 develops a piece that stays put; the bishop waits until 4.e3, when ...Bg4 is a normal line.

5588080788603958|c7c6.headline: Take the e4 pawn: White can't win it back quickly
5588080788603958|c7c6.why: 2...c6 declines the pawn and turns the game into a Caro-Kann, so White closes the centre and grabs space with 3.e5 Bf5 4.h4 h5 5.c4. It's playable, but you give up a free pawn and have to know Caro-Kann lines. 2...dxe4 takes a pawn that nothing defends, and White can't win it back at once. After 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bf5 5.Bxf6 exf6 6.Qe2 Nc6 7.O-O-O White has development and open lines, but you're still a pawn up.
5588080788603958|c7c6.principle: Accept a gambit when the opponent can't win the pawn back quickly: 2...dxe4 takes material and makes White prove the compensation.
sources: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit - Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackmar-Diemer_Gambit

Defending Against Gambits (GM Bryan Smith, chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/defending-against-gambits

ideas.title: Accept gambits, hit the centre
ideas.text: Nothing defends e4, and White has no quick way to win it back after 2...dxe4. Masters take it three times out of four.

ideas.title: White's gambit play
ideas.text: For the pawn White wants fast development and open lines, then long castling, as in 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5.

ideas.title: Declining changes the opening
ideas.text: 2...c6 turns the game into a Caro-Kann and 2...e6 into a French. Both are playable, but White gains space with 3.e5.

habit.why: 2...c6 declines the pawn and turns the game into a Caro-Kann, so White closes the centre and grabs space with 3.e5 Bf5 4.h4 h5 5.c4. It's playable, but you give up a free pawn and have to know Caro-Kann lines.

strays.text: You turn down a pawn that White can't win back quickly.

taught.why: 2...dxe4 takes a pawn that nothing defends, and White can't win it back at once. After 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bf5 5.Bxf6 exf6 6.Qe2 Nc6 7.O-O-O White has development and open lines, but you're still a pawn up.

enforces.text: You bank the pawn and make White prove the compensation.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...e6 is a sound French Defence: after 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4 c5 White has space and you hit back at d4. There is a stronger move here, though.
alternatives.after: 2...dxe4 wins a pawn instead of steering into French theory. Masters take the pawn 75% of the time, against 14% for 2...e6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...Nf6 lets White gain space with 3.e5 Nfd7, a French-like centre where you still need ...e6 and ...c5. Playable, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 2...dxe4 takes the pawn before White can push past your knight with 3.e5. Masters almost never play 2...Nf6 (1%).

5588080788603958|c8e6.headline: Accept the Blackmar-Diemer pawn with 2...dxe4
5588080788603958|c8e6.why: 2...Be6 blocks Black's e-pawn and walks into 3.exd5 Bxd5 4.c4, which kicks the bishop again, so White gains time and a broad centre. 2.e4 left e4 attacked and undefended; 2...dxe4 accepts the gambit and wins a pawn, and White has no way to win it back at once. Masters choose it in 74.8% of games.
5588080788603958|c8e6.principle: Accept a gambit when the pawn is free and you can develop normally afterwards, as with ...Nf6 and ...Bf5 here.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. e4
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. e4/2...dxe4

5588080788603958|e7e5.headline: Accept the Blackmar-Diemer pawn with 2...dxe4; 2...e5 just drops one
5588080788603958|e7e5.why: 2...e5 leaves Black's own e-pawn hanging and reaches the Beyer Gambit by transposition: 3.dxe5 takes it, and 3...dxe4 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8 leaves Black's king stuck in the centre. 2.e4 offered a pawn that nothing defends, and 2...dxe4 takes it; masters accept in 75% of games. White's compensation is development, so Black's job is to develop soundly, as in 3.Nc3 Nf6.
5588080788603958|e7e5.principle: Take a gambit pawn when you can develop normally afterwards, rather than offering a pawn of your own back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. e4
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. e4/2...e5
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. e4/2...dxe4

5641703819423939|c8f5.headline: 4.f3 leaves c4 loose: take it instead of ...Bf5
5641703819423939|c8f5.why: 4...Bf5 puts the bishop where White's pawns can hit it: 5.g4 Bc8 6.g5 Nh5 7.e4 sends it home, pushes your knight to the rim and gives White a big centre with gain of time. Meanwhile the free pawn on c4 stays where it was. 4...dxc4 takes the pawn 4.f3 left undefended, and f3 has cost White a move that develops nothing. After 5.a4 Nd5 6.e4 Nxc3 7.bxc3 b5 your c6 pawn backs up b5 and you are a pawn up.
5641703819423939|c8f5.principle: Accept the pawn when you can hold it: after 4.f3 nothing guards c4, and ...b5 backed by c6 keeps it, while a bishop on f5 only gives White's g-pawn a target.

ideas.title: Take c4 when it's loose
ideas.text: 4.f3 leaves c4 attacked and undefended. 4...dxc4 grabs it, and your c6 pawn backs up ...b5 to hold it.

ideas.title: Accept gambits, hit the centre
ideas.text: f3 aims at a big centre with e4. Taking material at once beats slow moves that let White build it for free.

ideas.title: f3 and g4 chase the bishop
ideas.text: With f3 in, 5.g4 hits a bishop on f5, and 6.g5 kicks the f6-knight too, gaining space with tempo.

habit.why: 4...Bf5 puts the bishop where White's pawns can hit it: 5.g4 Bc8 6.g5 Nh5 7.e4 sends it home, pushes your knight to the rim and gives White a big centre with gain of time. Meanwhile the free pawn on c4 stays where it was.

strays.text: You leave the free c4 pawn and walk into White's g-pawn.

taught.why: 4...dxc4 takes the pawn 4.f3 left undefended, and f3 has cost White a move that develops nothing. After 5.a4 Nd5 6.e4 Nxc3 7.bxc3 b5 your c6 pawn backs up b5 and you are a pawn up.

enforces.text: c4 had no defender, and ...b5 backed by c6 holds the extra pawn.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...e6 is solid: after 5.cxd5 Nxd5 6.e4 Nxc3 7.bxc3 c5 you strike at White's big centre at once. There is a stronger move here, though.
alternatives.after: 4...dxc4 wins a pawn instead of letting White build the e4-d4 centre with 5.cxd5 and 6.e4; 4...e6 attacks that centre only afterwards.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...g6 is fine: after 5.cxd5 Nxd5 6.e4 Nxc3 7.bxc3 Bg7 your bishop presses White's centre, Grünfeld style. There's still a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4...dxc4 grabs the loose pawn before White gets 6.e4 in for free; with 4...g6 you fight the centre later instead of taking material now.

5651959838826145|f7f6.headline: In the Scotch Gambit, develop with 4...Nf6 and hit e4.
5651959838826145|f7f6.why: 4...f6 does nothing to hold the pawn on d4: 5.Nxd4 Nxd4 6.Qxd4 wins it back at once. It also takes the f6 square from the knight and weakens the diagonal the bishop on c4 aims along toward f7. 4...Nf6 is the most played move: it develops and attacks the pawn on e4, so White has to spend time before recovering the pawn, as in 5.e5 d5 6.Bb5 Ne4.
5651959838826145|f7f6.principle: When you are a pawn up against a lead in development, develop with threats instead of making pawn moves that loosen your king.

5687709244296283|e4e5.headline: Guard e4 with 5.Re1; 5.e5 just gets hit by 5...Ng4
5687709244296283|e4e5.why: 5.e5 pushes the attacked pawn into the knight's path: 5...Ng4 hits it at once and eyes f2. After 6.Re1 d6 7.exd6 Bxd6 the pawn is gone and Black's pieces are active; with no ...d5 played, there was never a pawn chain to cramp. 5.Re1 defends e4 indirectly: if 5...Nxe4 6.Rxe4 d5 forks rook and bishop, then 7.Bxd5 Qxd5 8.Nc3 hits the queen and the material is level again. Masters choose it in 81% of games, keeping a flexible centre with d4 still to come.
5687709244296283|e4e5.principle: Meet the threat to e4 with a developing move: 5.Re1 guards it and activates a rook, while 5.e5 only gives the knight a target.
sources: How I play against the Closed Sicilian (Junta Ikeda) | https://juntaikeda.substack.com/p/how-i-play-against-the-closed-sicilian
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

ideas.title: Black threatens ...Nxe4
ideas.text: 4...Nf6 hits your e4 pawn, which nothing defends yet, so 5...Nxe4 is a real threat to deal with first.

ideas.title: Defend e4 with the rook
ideas.text: 5.Re1 guards e4 indirectly: 5...Nxe4 6.Rxe4 d5 7.Bxd5 Qxd5 8.Nc3 wins the material back and hits the queen.

ideas.title: Castle, then fight ...d5
ideas.text: ...e6 blunts your c4 bishop and prepares ...d5 with gain of time. Develop and be ready to meet it rather than lunging forward.

ideas.title: The knight jumps to g4
ideas.text: After 5.e5 Ng4 the knight hits e5 and eyes f2, and ...d6 then knocks the pawn off.

habit.why: 5.e5 pushes the attacked pawn into the knight's path: 5...Ng4 hits it at once and eyes f2. After 6.Re1 d6 7.exd6 Bxd6 the pawn is gone and Black's pieces are active; with no ...d5 played, there was never a pawn chain to cramp.

strays.text: Pushing the pawn instead of guarding it lets the knight jump to g4 with tempo.

taught.why: 5.Re1 defends e4 indirectly: if 5...Nxe4 6.Rxe4 d5 forks rook and bishop, then 7.Bxd5 Qxd5 8.Nc3 hits the queen and the material is level again. Masters choose it in 81% of games, keeping a flexible centre with d4 still to come.

enforces.text: Taking on e4 now costs Black the knight, and 8.Nc3 hits the queen.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.d3 is sound: it guards e4 directly and opens your c1 bishop, but after 5...d5 6.Bb5 Black takes space. There is a more active choice.
alternatives.after: 5.Re1 is the masters' move (81% to 9%): the rook joins the game and d2-d4 stays possible, where 5.d3 settles for a smaller centre.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 develops and is sound: 5...Nxe4 6.Nxe4 d5 is the fork trick to regain the piece, and after 7.Bb5 dxe4 8.Ne5 play is balanced.
alternatives.after: Both allow the ...d5 fork, but after 5.Re1 the reply 8.Nc3 hits Black's queen and your rook is already active. Masters chose 5.Re1 in 81% of games.

57158813525553|f1d3.headline: The c5 pawn is loose: take it with 5.dxc5
57158813525553|f1d3.why: 5.Bd3 lets the free pawn go and offers Black the swap of light bishops. After 5...Bxd3 6.Qxd3 e6 the f8 bishop guards c5, and when you finally take with 9.dxc5, 9...Nxc5 recaptures and hits your queen. 4...Bf5 left c5 attacked by your d4 pawn and defended by nothing, so 5.dxc5 wins a pawn. After 5...a6 6.Nf3 e6 7.b4 you hold the extra pawn, and the knight on f3 guards e5.
57158813525553|f1d3.principle: After each opponent move, check what it left undefended: 4...Bf5 left c5 loose, and taking it comes before developing.

ideas.title: Grab c5 when it hangs
ideas.text: 4...Bf5 leaves the c5 pawn attacked by d4 and guarded by nothing. 5.dxc5 takes it, and 7.b4 holds it.

ideas.title: Keep e5 guarded after dxc5
ideas.text: Taking on c5 removes d4's support of your e5 pawn, so guard it with 6.Nf3.

ideas.title: The light-squared bishop question
ideas.text: Black wants a French without the bad bishop. 5.Bd3 Bxd3 6.Qxd3 e6 hands it over: Black's problem piece is traded.

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: Given time, Black covers c5 with ...e6 and ...Nc6, and the c5 pawn starts hitting d4, as after 5.Nf3 e6 6.Be2 Nc6.

habit.why: 5.Bd3 lets the free pawn go and offers Black the swap of light bishops. After 5...Bxd3 6.Qxd3 e6 the f8 bishop guards c5, and when you finally take with 9.dxc5, 9...Nxc5 recaptures and hits your queen.

strays.text: The c5 pawn was free, and after 6...e6 it is guarded.

taught.why: 4...Bf5 left c5 attacked by your d4 pawn and defended by nothing, so 5.dxc5 wins a pawn. After 5...a6 6.Nf3 e6 7.b4 you hold the extra pawn, and the knight on f3 guards e5.

enforces.text: You take the pawn before 5...e6 can cover it, and 7.b4 keeps it.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.Nf3 develops, but it gives Black time to cover c5: after 5...e6 the f8 bishop guards it, and 6.Be2 Nc6 starts the usual pressure on d4.
alternatives.after: 5.dxc5 takes the pawn before ...e6 can guard it; one move later the chance is gone.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bb5+ is sound: after 5...Bd7 6.Bxd7+ Nxd7 7.e6 fxe6 Black's pawns are broken, though the push costs you a pawn. There is a simpler, stronger move.
alternatives.after: 5.dxc5 just wins a pawn. In the 5.Bb5+ line 6...Nxd7 guards c5, and you sacrifice a pawn with 7.e6 for a better structure instead.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5.f4 adds a pawn to e5 but develops nothing and ignores c5: after 5...e6 the pawn is guarded, and 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.Be2 Qb6 piles up on d4.
alternatives.after: 5.dxc5 cashes in on the loose c5 pawn at once; 5.f4 spends the move on a pawn push that wasn't needed.
alternatives.idea: Hit the d4 base of the chain

5811727298789441|f6g4.headline: Take on e5 first and keep your knight on f6
5811727298789441|f6g4.why: 9...Ng4 takes the knight off the kingside while d4 still guards e5, so it attacks nothing. 10.h3 Nh6 11.h4 leaves it on the rim and White's h-pawn rolls on, as in 13.h5 g5 14.Nxg5. 9...dxe5 removes the pawn that attacks f6 and opens the d-file. After 10.Nxe5 Qd6 11.h4 Nbd7 12.Nxd7 Bxd7 your knight still guards h5, so 13.h5 Nxh5 wins a pawn.
5811727298789441|f6g4.principle: When White attacks on the wing, hit back in the centre: 9...dxe5 opens the d-file and keeps your f6 knight home to guard the king.
sources: Nigel Davies, The Pirc: Move by Move (excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/7604.pdf

ideas.title: Take on e5 first
ideas.text: Capture 9...dxe5 before moving the knight. It removes the pawn that hits f6 and opens the d-file for your queen.

ideas.title: White's Bh6 and h-pawn attack
ideas.text: Your g7 bishop is already traded off. White's next step is h4-h5 to open the h-file at your king.

ideas.title: Keep a knight on f6
ideas.text: With the bishop gone, the f6 knight is your king's best defender. It watches h5, so moving it away invites the h-pawn.

habit.why: 9...Ng4 takes the knight off the kingside while d4 still guards e5, so it attacks nothing. 10.h3 Nh6 11.h4 leaves it on the rim and White's h-pawn rolls on, as in 13.h5 g5 14.Nxg5.

strays.text: The defender leaves and gets kicked to h6 by 10.h3.

taught.why: 9...dxe5 removes the pawn that attacks f6 and opens the d-file. After 10.Nxe5 Qd6 11.h4 Nbd7 12.Nxd7 Bxd7 your knight still guards h5, so 13.h5 Nxh5 wins a pawn.

enforces.text: The capture comes first, and the knight stays home on f6.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 9...Nfd7 takes the last defender off the kingside. With your g7 bishop gone, 10.h4 h5 11.g4 rips your king open, and 14.hxg6 breaks through.
alternatives.after: 9...dxe5 keeps the knight on f6, where it watches h5. In that line 13.h5 is simply met by 13...Nxh5.

5850892143506287|b1c3.headline: Block with 5.Bd2; 5.Nc3 still leaves the f4 bishop hanging
5850892143506287|b1c3.why: 5.Nc3 blocks the check but leaves the f4 bishop unguarded, and 5...Qxf4 takes it. You can win the rook with 6.Nd5 Qe4 7.Nxc7+ Kd8 8.Nxa8, but the knight is stuck in the corner, 8...Nxe5 wins back the pawn, and your edge is gone. 5.Bd2 blocks with the attacked bishop itself and hits the queen on b4, so nothing hangs. After 5...Qe7 6.Nc3 Nxe5 7.e4 Black has the pawn back, but you lead in development and hold the centre.
5850892143506287|b1c3.principle: A queen check often hits a second target: block with the attacked piece, or make sure it is guarded.

ideas.text: 4...Qb4+ checks your king and also hits b2 and the f4 bishop. A block that leaves the bishop loose drops it.

ideas.title: Block and hit the queen
ideas.text: 5.Bd2 moves the attacked bishop into the check line, so nothing hangs and the queen must move again.

ideas.title: Nc3 after ...Qxb2, never Bc3
ideas.text: If Black grabs b2 after 5.Bd2, develop with 6.Nc3. 6.Bc3?? walks into a bishop check from b4 and mate on c1.

ideas.title: Keep the extra pawn
ideas.text: After 2.dxe5 you are a pawn up. Black's gambit lives on tricks to win it back, so block safely and develop.

habit.why: 5.Nc3 blocks the check but leaves the f4 bishop unguarded, and 5...Qxf4 takes it. You can win the rook with 6.Nd5 Qe4 7.Nxc7+ Kd8 8.Nxa8, but the knight is stuck in the corner, 8...Nxe5 wins back the pawn, and your edge is gone.

strays.text: The knight blocks the check, but the f4 bishop still hangs.

taught.why: 5.Bd2 blocks with the attacked bishop itself and hits the queen on b4, so nothing hangs. After 5...Qe7 6.Nc3 Nxe5 7.e4 Black has the pawn back, but you lead in development and hold the centre.

enforces.text: The bishop leaves the queen's line and attacks it, so Black loses time.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.Nbd2 blocks the check, but nothing guards the f4 bishop, so 5...Qxf4 wins a piece. After 6.g3 Qb4 you have nothing for it.
alternatives.after: 5.Bd2 blocks with the bishop itself and hits the queen, so nothing is left loose.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.c3 attacks the queen, but it simply takes the f4 bishop. After 5...Qxf4 6.g3 Qf5 7.Bg2 Nxe5 you are a piece down and the e5 pawn is gone too.
alternatives.after: 5.Bd2 blocks the check and takes the bishop off the fourth rank in one move, so the queen has nothing to grab.

5859332280044982|b8c6.headline: Meet 1.d4 with 1...Nf6, the most flexible reply
5859332280044982|b8c6.why: 1...Nc6 is the rare Mikenas defence: the knight blocks Black's c-pawn and stands in front of White's d-pawn, so 2.d5 kicks it at once and after 2...Ne5 3.Nc3 White gains space and time. 1...Nf6 is the Indian defence: it develops, controls e4 and keeps every pawn setup open, so Black can fight for the centre later on their own terms. Masters choose it in 60.9% of games.
5859332280044982|b8c6.principle: Against 1.d4, stop White's second centre pawn: a knight on f6 controls e4 so White cannot simply play it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6

5859332280044982|e7e5.headline: Develop with 1...Nf6 instead of giving a pawn with 1...e5
5859332280044982|e7e5.why: 1...e5 gives a pawn, and after 2.dxe5 the Englund Gambit is considered unsound: careful play leaves White a pawn up for little. After 2...d5 3.Nf3 Ne7 4.Bf4 you are simply a pawn down with no attack to show for it. 1...Nf6 develops a knight and controls e4, so White can't build a two-pawn centre for free. After 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 you are in a solid Queen's Indian, and masters choose 1...Nf6 in 61% of games.
5859332280044982|e7e5.principle: Answer 1.d4 with a move that develops and controls e4, so White can't build a big centre for free.

ideas.title: Control e4 first
ideas.text: 1.d4 aims for e4 next and a big two-pawn centre. 1...Nf6 or 1...d5 stops that at once.

ideas.title: Gambits need compensation
ideas.text: A gambit pawn should buy a lead or an attack. The Englund is considered unsound and almost never appears at top level.

ideas.title: White keeps the pawn
ideas.text: After 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4, your ...Qb4+ trick only works if White blocks badly; careful play keeps the pawn.

ideas.title: Stay flexible with 1...Nf6
ideas.text: 1...Nf6 keeps your pawns uncommitted: after 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 you are in a Queen's Indian, bishop heading for b7.

habit.why: 1...e5 gives a pawn, and after 2.dxe5 the Englund Gambit is considered unsound: careful play leaves White a pawn up for little. After 2...d5 3.Nf3 Ne7 4.Bf4 you are simply a pawn down with no attack to show for it.

strays.text: You give a pawn, and White keeps it with simple development.

taught.why: 1...Nf6 develops a knight and controls e4, so White can't build a two-pawn centre for free. After 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 you are in a solid Queen's Indian, and masters choose 1...Nf6 in 61% of games.

enforces.text: The knight develops and stops White's e4 in one move.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 1...d5 takes the centre with a pawn and stops White's e4; after 2.c4 e6 you have a solid Queen's Gambit Declined. Sound, though another move is a little more flexible.
alternatives.after: 1...Nf6 also controls e4 but develops a piece and keeps your pawns uncommitted. Masters choose it 61% to 26%, and the engine rates the two close.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 1...e6 lets White take the centre with 2.e4, and after 2...d5 you are in a French Defence. Fine if you play the French; otherwise it hands White a big centre.
alternatives.after: 1...Nf6 stops e4 at once, so White doesn't get the two-pawn centre for free.

5860472034319888|e7e6.headline: 3.Bg5 left e4 undefended: take it with 3...Nxe4
5860472034319888|e7e6.why: 3...e6 ignores the loose e4 pawn and gives White time to guard it with 4.Nc3. After 4...Be7 5.f4 White has a big pawn centre for free and later gains space with 7.e5. 3.Bg5 left e4 with no defender, and 3...Nxe4 also hits the g5 bishop, so White spends 4.Be3 saving it. You are a pawn up and finish your set-up with 4...g6, 5...Nf6 and 6...Bg7.
5860472034319888|e7e6.principle: After every White move, ask whether e4 is still defended: the pawn your f6 knight attacks is often left loose.

ideas.title: Guard e4 before anything else
ideas.text: Your f6 knight attacks e4, and White normally guards it at once, usually with a knight on c3. 3.Bg5 does not guard it.

ideas.title: Take a pawn that is really free
ideas.text: Before an autopilot ...e6 or ...g6, check if e4 is free. Here the knight on e4 would also hit the g5 bishop.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: In the Pirc you let White have the centre and hit it later. That only works if White has to spend moves holding it.

habit.why: 3...e6 ignores the loose e4 pawn and gives White time to guard it with 4.Nc3. After 4...Be7 5.f4 White has a big pawn centre for free and later gains space with 7.e5.

strays.idea: Take a pawn that is really free
strays.text: A routine move instead of taking the pawn White left hanging.

taught.why: 3.Bg5 left e4 with no defender, and 3...Nxe4 also hits the g5 bishop, so White spends 4.Be3 saving it. You are a pawn up and finish your set-up with 4...g6, 5...Nf6 and 6...Bg7.

enforces.idea: Take a pawn that is really free
enforces.text: e4 had no defender, so the pawn is truly free.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...g6 is a normal Pirc move, and after 4.Nc3 it becomes a Byrne-type line where White plays 5.Qd2 and long castling. It is sound, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 3...Nxe4 wins a pawn for nothing; 3...g6 lets 4.Nc3 guard e4 and White keeps the full centre.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Nbd7 heads for a Philidor set-up, with 4.Nc3 e5 striking at d4. It is solid, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 3...Nxe4 grabs the pawn first; 3...Nbd7 lets 4.Nc3 guard it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...h6 asks the bishop at once. After 4.Bxf6 exf6 you have the bishop pair but doubled f-pawns, and White keeps the centre.
alternatives.after: 3...Nxe4 wins a pawn and hits the g5 bishop; 3...h6 lets White trade on f6 and keep e4.

5864435021787537|d2d3.headline: Open the centre with 4.d4 against Black's misplaced queen
5864435021787537|d2d3.why: 3...c6 spent another pawn move and left Black further behind in development, with the queen exposed on f6. 4.d3 is too quiet: in the engine line Black gets time for 4...d6 and 6...Nf6 and catches up. 4.d4 opens the centre while you lead: after 4...exd4 5.Bg5 your bishop develops by attacking the queen, and 6.Nxd4 regains the pawn with more pieces in play.
5864435021787537|d2d3.principle: When you are ahead in development and your opponent's queen is out, open lines so your pieces can attack it with gain of time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

5864435021787537|f1c4.headline: Open the centre with 4.d4 while Black's queen sits on f6
5864435021787537|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 is a natural developing move, but 3...c6 already covers d5, so the bishop has no quick target. In the line 4...Bb4 5.O-O d6 6.d4 Bg4 Black pins both your knights while developing, and your lead shrinks. 4.d4 opens the centre while Black has only the queen out. After 4...exd4 5.Bg5 the bishop hits the queen, and 5...Qd6 6.Nxd4 wins the pawn back with three pieces in play against one.
5864435021787537|f1c4.principle: Open the centre when you lead in development; an early queen is easiest to hit in an open position.

ideas.title: Open the centre with d4
ideas.text: Your knights are out and Black's only developed piece is the queen. 4.d4 opens lines while you lead in development.

ideas.title: Hit the early queen with tempo
ideas.text: After 4.d4 exd4 5.Bg5 your bishop hits the queen on f6, and you take back on d4 a move later.

ideas.title: Watch the pins on your knights
ideas.text: Black's bishops want b4 and g4 to pin your knights, as in 4...Bb4 and 6...Bg4 after 4.Bc4.

ideas.title: Keep the g8 knight shut out
ideas.text: The queen on f6 takes the g8 knight's best square. Each time you hit the queen, Black loses another move while that knight waits.

habit.why: 4.Bc4 is a natural developing move, but 3...c6 already covers d5, so the bishop has no quick target. In the line 4...Bb4 5.O-O d6 6.d4 Bg4 Black pins both your knights while developing, and your lead shrinks.

strays.text: A bishop move lets Black develop before the centre opens.

taught.why: 4.d4 opens the centre while Black has only the queen out. After 4...exd4 5.Bg5 the bishop hits the queen, and 5...Qd6 6.Nxd4 wins the pawn back with three pieces in play against one.

enforces.text: The centre opens while Black's only developed piece is the queen.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 4.d3 is slow: after 4...d6 5.Bg5 Qe6 the queen simply steps aside, Black develops with 6...Nf6, and your lead in development shrinks.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 opens lines at once, so 5.Bg5 later hits the queen with tempo and you regain the pawn with a clear lead in development.

5876653910199998|c8e6.headline: When a pawn hits the bishop on c5, move it: 5...Bb6
5876653910199998|c8e6.why: 5.d4 attacks the bishop on c5 with a pawn, and 5...Be6 doesn't deal with it: after 6.Bxe6 fxe6 7.dxc5 White trades bishops and then takes the c5 bishop, a whole piece. 5...Bb6 simply saves the bishop. If White takes 6.dxe5, Black develops with 6...Bg4, pinning the knight on f3, and 7...Nf6; 5...exd4 is also fine.
5876653910199998|c8e6.principle: Look at White's captures first: 6.dxc5 takes a bishop, so any move that ignores it loses a piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3

5887905008267832|c2c4.headline: Give the pawn back with 3.d4 and take the centre
5887905008267832|c2c4.why: 3.c4 props up the pawn, but 3...c6 hits it again, and after 4.d4 cxd5 it is gone and you are in a Caro-Kann Panov-Botvinnik. That is a level game: you have given the pawn back anyway, on Black's terms. 3.d4 gives back d5 at once and takes the centre; after 3...Nxd5 4.Nf3 you have space and easy development. If 4...Bf5, 5.Nh4 hits the bishop, and by 7.Bg2 Bb5 it has moved three times while your pieces came out.
5887905008267832|c2c4.principle: Rather than spend moves holding a pawn the opponent will win back, return it and take the centre.

ideas.title: Return the pawn, take the centre
ideas.text: Don't cling to the d5 pawn. 3.d4 gives it back but grabs the centre and opens lines for your queen and c1-bishop.

ideas.title: Black undermines d5
ideas.text: If you hold d5 with 3.c4, Black hits it with 3...c6 or 3...e6 and wins it back or gets a fast gambit.

ideas.title: Squeeze with Nf3 and c4
ideas.text: After 3...Nxd5 you usually follow with 4.Nf3 and c4, kicking the knight; Black can end up cramped.

ideas.title: No tempo on the queen
ideas.text: After 3.Nc3 Nxd5 and a knight trade, Black's queen reaches d5 without being chased: a better version of 2...Qxd5 for Black.

habit.why: 3.c4 props up the pawn, but 3...c6 hits it again, and after 4.d4 cxd5 it is gone and you are in a Caro-Kann Panov-Botvinnik. That is a level game: you have given the pawn back anyway, on Black's terms.

strays.idea: Return the pawn, take the centre
strays.text: Holding d5 only invites 3...c6, and the pawn falls anyway.

taught.why: 3.d4 gives back d5 at once and takes the centre; after 3...Nxd5 4.Nf3 you have space and easy development. If 4...Bf5, 5.Nh4 hits the bishop, and by 7.Bg2 Bb5 it has moved three times while your pieces came out.

enforces.idea: Return the pawn, take the centre
enforces.text: The d-pawn claims the centre, and you develop while Black's bishop wanders.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 develops, but after 3...Nxd5 4.Nf3 g6 5.Nxd5 Qxd5 Black's queen reaches d5 without losing time. That is a better version of the 2...Qxd5 lines for Black.
alternatives.after: 3.d4 takes the centre first, so you don't end up trading knights on d5 and handing Black a free central queen. Masters play 3.d4 in 53% of games, 3.Nc3 in 4%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Nf3 is a flexible developing move, and after 3...Nxd5 it often transposes to the main lines, with 7.c4 later kicking the knight. It's sound, though there's a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: The two often meet: 3.Nf3 Nxd5 4.d4 is the same position as 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3. Masters play 3.d4 almost four times as often (53% to 14%).

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Return the pawn, take the centre
alternatives.before: 3.Bb5+ is another way to keep the pawn: after 3...Bd7 4.Bc4 Bg4 5.f3 Bc8 you hold d5 for now, as in Alexandria-Gaprindashvili. It's sound, though there's a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 3.d4 doesn't spend bishop moves holding d5; it gives the pawn back and takes the centre. Masters choose 3.d4 in 53% of games, 3.Bb5+ in 15%.

5887905008267832|f1c4.headline: Give the pawn back with 3.d4 and take the centre
5887905008267832|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 does nothing to stop 3...Nxd5, so Black wins the pawn back with a knight in the centre. After 4.d4 Bf5 5.Nf3 e6 6.O-O Be7 7.Bd3 Bxd3 your bishop has moved twice only to be traded off. 3.d4 gives back d5 at once and takes the centre; after 3...Nxd5 4.Nf3 you have space and easy development. If 4...Bf5, 5.Nh4 hits the bishop, and by 7.Bg2 Bb5 it has moved three times while your pieces came out.
5887905008267832|f1c4.principle: If the pawn is lost anyway, give it back in the way that takes the centre, not with a piece that will be chased.

5915229736017859|c5d4.headline: 4.d4 left e4 undefended: take it with 4...dxe4
5915229736017859|c5d4.why: 4...cxd4 lets White push 5.e5, and the pawns on e5 and f4 close the centre with your c8 bishop shut in behind e6. After 5...Nc6 6.Nbd2 Nh6 7.Nb3 White goes after your d4 pawn, and the free pawn on e4 is gone. 4...dxe4 takes a pawn that 4.d4 left undefended, and White's knight has to move. After 5.Nfd2 f5 6.Nb3 cxd4 7.Nxd4 Nc6 you are a clean pawn up with easy development.
5915229736017859|c5d4.principle: Check what is loose before releasing tension: 4.d4 left e4 attacked and undefended, so 4...dxe4 wins a pawn, while 4...cxd4 lets White close the centre with 5.e5.
sources: Shaun Sedice, Playing the Grand Prix Attack (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/grand-prix-attack/

ideas.title: Strike with ...d5
ideas.text: Against an early f4, ...e6 and ...d5 hit e4 at once. With no knight on c3, 4.d4 left the e4 pawn without a defender.

ideas.title: Don't free White's centre
ideas.text: Taking on d4 only frees White's game. Keep the pawns tense and take on e4 when it is loose.

ideas.title: French pawn chain
ideas.text: If White pushes e5 with f4 behind it, the centre closes and your c8 bishop is shut in behind e6.

habit.why: 4...cxd4 lets White push 5.e5, and the pawns on e5 and f4 close the centre with your c8 bishop shut in behind e6. After 5...Nc6 6.Nbd2 Nh6 7.Nb3 White goes after your d4 pawn, and the free pawn on e4 is gone.

strays.text: It releases the tension and lets White close the centre with 5.e5.

taught.why: 4...dxe4 takes a pawn that 4.d4 left undefended, and White's knight has to move. After 5.Nfd2 f5 6.Nb3 cxd4 7.Nxd4 Nc6 you are a clean pawn up with easy development.

enforces.text: Your d-pawn takes the loose e4 pawn.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nc6 develops and adds pressure on d4. After 5.e5 Qb6 you hit d4 the French way, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4...dxe4 wins a pawn because 4.d4 left e4 undefended. After 4...Nc6 5.e5 the centre closes and that chance is gone.

591532767997359|c6d4.headline: Develop the other knight: 3...Nf6, the Four Knights
591532767997359|c6d4.why: 3...Nd4 moves the same knight twice with three minor pieces still at home, and it takes the defender away from e5: 4.Nxe5 simply wins the pawn. 3...Nf6 develops toward the centre and attacks e4, entering the Four Knights Game; masters choose it 92% of the time. Against 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4, Black develops with 5...Bb4, pinning the knight on c3.
591532767997359|c6d4.principle: With three pieces still undeveloped, a second knight move must win something; here it gives up the e5 pawn instead.

591532767997359|d7d6.headline: Mirror White with 3...Nf6: the Four Knights is the main line
591532767997359|d7d6.why: 3...d6 is passive: it shuts in your f8 bishop and gives White a free hand in the centre. In the engine line 4.d4 Nf6 5.d5 Ne7 White gains space and pushes your knight back, then plays 6.Bg5 to add pressure. 3...Nf6, played in 92% of master games, enters the Four Knights: the theory notes that none of the ways to break the symmetry are appealing, so develop the knight and keep the bishop free to come out in one move later.
591532767997359|d7d6.principle: When both of your knights have obvious squares, develop them before committing pawns that block your bishops.

591532767997359|f7f5.why: 3...f5 loosens Black's king while White is ready to strike in the centre: the line 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe5 Bb4 6.Qh5+ shows how the open diagonal toward e8 is exploited. 3...Nf6 puts the knight on its best square and enters the quiet but sound Four Knights Game, chosen in 92.2% of master games.
591532767997359|f7f5.principle: Don't open lines toward your own uncastled king: an early f-pawn push loosens the diagonal from h5 to e8.

5925543013863182|e7e5.headline: Don't hang e5: develop with 2...Nf6
5925543013863182|e7e5.why: 2...e5 puts a pawn where the f3-knight can take it, and nothing defends it: 3.Nxe5 wins it. After 3...Nf6 4.g3 c5 5.Bg2 Bd6 6.Nf3 you are a pawn down with no real compensation. 2...Nf6 develops and hits e4, the square White wants for a pawn. After 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.c4 O-O you have a safe fianchetto, and masters choose this move 45% of the time.
5925543013863182|e7e5.principle: Develop first; a pawn pushed into a knight's reach with no defender is simply lost.

ideas.text: Against d3 set-ups strong players push ...e5 once a knight backs it up, as 2...Nc6 prepares.

ideas.title: Keep e4 covered
ideas.text: A knight on f6 hits e4, so White can't push e4 for free.

ideas.title: Mirror the fianchetto
ideas.text: After 2...Nf6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 your bishop matches White's on the long diagonal.

habit.why: 2...e5 puts a pawn where the f3-knight can take it, and nothing defends it: 3.Nxe5 wins it. After 3...Nf6 4.g3 c5 5.Bg2 Bd6 6.Nf3 you are a pawn down with no real compensation.

strays.text: Nothing guards e5, so 3.Nxe5 wins a clean pawn.

taught.why: 2...Nf6 develops and hits e4, the square White wants for a pawn. After 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.c4 O-O you have a safe fianchetto, and masters choose this move 45% of the time.

enforces.text: Your bishop goes to g7 to match White's on g2.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...Nc6 is sound and prepares ...e5 properly; after 3.Bf4 and 4.d4 Bf5 White turns it into a London-type game. There is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: Both are fine: 2...Nf6 is the masters' most common move (45% to 13%), and 2...Nc6 is the way to prepare ...e5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...c5 grabs space, and after 3.e4 e6 4.g3 Bd6 you face a King's Indian Attack against a French-type set-up. It is sound; there is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 keeps the centre flexible, while 2...c5 lets 3.e4 come and commits you to a French-type structure.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...e6 is solid, and after 3.e4 c5 4.Qe2 Be7 you have a French-type set-up against the King's Indian Attack. There is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 hits e4 first, while 2...e6 lets 3.e4 come at once.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...g6 is sound, but after 3.e4 dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1 the queens come off early. There is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 keeps e4 covered first and goes for the same fianchetto with 3...g6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...c6 is a solid Slav-style set-up, but after 3.Nbd2 g6 4.e4 Bg7 5.e5 White grabs space in the centre. There is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 hits e4, so White can't push 4.e4 and 5.e5 so easily.

5945701382218233|d4c5.headline: Push past c5 with 2.d5 instead of swapping your centre pawn
5945701382218233|d4c5.why: 2.dxc5 gives up your centre pawn for a wing pawn, and 2...e6 wins it straight back: after 3.e4 Bxc5 Black has a bishop out and a pawn more in the centre. Then 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.O-O d6 gives Black an easy, equal game. 2.d5 keeps your pawn in the centre and takes c6 and e6 from Black's pieces. In the line 2...Nf6 3.Nc3 e6 4.e4 d6 5.Bb5+ Bd7 6.Bc4 you have pawns on d5 and e4, more space and free development.
5945701382218233|d4c5.principle: Don't swap a centre pawn for a wing pawn: 2.d5 keeps your d-pawn and gains space, while 2.dxc5 lets 2...e6 win the pawn back with an easy game.
sources: Benoni Defense - Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benoni_Defense
Charlie Morton, The Old Benoni Defense (Wholesale Chess) | https://www.wholesalechess.com/blogs/chess-openings/the-old-benoni-defense
Anton Shuravin, Benoni Defense (ChessDoctrine) | https://chessdoctrine.com/chess-openings/queens-pawn/benoni-defense/
