ideas.title: Gain space with d5
ideas.text: Pushing past the c5-pawn keeps your centre pawn, gains space and cramps Black: from d5 it takes c6 and e6 from Black's pieces.

ideas.title: ...e6 wins c5 back
ideas.text: After dxc5, ...e6 opens the f8-bishop onto c5, so Black regains the pawn while developing. Holding it with b4 fails to an a-pawn strike.

ideas.title: Quiet moves allow ...cxd4
ideas.text: Against slow moves like 2.Nf3, 2.e3 or 2.c3, Black simply takes on d4 and gains time or reaches an easy, symmetrical game.

habit.why: 2.dxc5 gives up your centre pawn for a wing pawn, and 2...e6 wins it straight back: after 3.e4 Bxc5 Black has a bishop out and a pawn more in the centre. Then 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.O-O d6 gives Black an easy, equal game.

strays.text: The capture hands Black the centre instead of cramping them.

taught.why: 2.d5 keeps your pawn in the centre and takes c6 and e6 from Black's pieces. In the line 2...Nf6 3.Nc3 e6 4.e4 d6 5.Bb5+ Bd7 6.Bc4 you have pawns on d5 and e4, more space and free development.

enforces.text: The pawn advances past c5 and cramps Black's position.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: This lets Black swap the c-pawn for your d-pawn: after 2...cxd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 your queen is hit and must move again with 4.Qa4.
alternatives.after: 2.d5 keeps the d-pawn out of reach and gains space. After 2.Nf3 cxd4 Black trades a wing pawn for your centre pawn and gains time on your queen.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: Solid, but Black takes on d4: after 2...cxd4 3.exd4 the centre turns symmetrical and your extra tempo means little.
alternatives.after: 2.d5 keeps an unbalanced centre with more space. Masters play it 76% of the time, against 7.5% for 2.e3.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: Supporting d4 lets Black develop freely: after 2...Nf6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Bf4 Be7 5.e3 Nh5 your bishop is already being chased, and you lack a clear plan.
alternatives.after: 2.d5 grabs space at once. Masters play 2.c3 in 8% of games, but the engine rates it clearly below 2.d5: avoiding the Benoni doesn't refute it.

5965252915693730|b8c6.headline: Take the King's Gambit pawn while ...Qh4+ still works
5965252915693730|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 develops, but after 3.Nf3 White covers h4, so the ...Qh4+ reply disappears and fxe5 becomes a real threat; in the line 3...exf4 4.d4 g5 5.d5 White gains time on the knight. 2...exf4 takes the undefended pawn at once, while ...Qh4+ is still a threat, so White must deal with it before building the centre. Masters accept in 67.3% of games.
5965252915693730|b8c6.principle: Accept a gambit pawn when it is free and your reply comes with a threat; waiting lets White cover the weakness first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4

5965252915693730|d7d6.headline: The King's Gambit pawn is free: take it with 2...exf4
5965252915693730|d7d6.why: 2...d6 declines passively and lets White develop and choose when to take on e5, as in 3.d3 Nc6 4.Nf3 g6 5.fxe5 Nxe5. 2.f4 offers a pawn that is attacked and not defended at all; 2...exf4 takes it, and now ...Qh4+ is a real threat that White has to spend time on. Masters accept in 67.3% of games.
5965252915693730|d7d6.principle: Take a gambit pawn when it costs you nothing and your position stays sound; then White must prove the compensation.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...d6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4

5965252915693730|f7f5.headline: Take the f4 pawn instead of offering your own
5965252915693730|f7f5.why: 2...f5 is the old Panteldakis Countergambit and simply loses a pawn to 3.exf5, which also opens the diagonal to Black's king and gives White the threat of Qh5+. 2...exf4 takes the undefended pawn instead, and the threat of ...Qh4+ makes White spend time on the king rather than on attack. Masters accept in 67.3% of games.
5965252915693730|f7f5.principle: Answer a gambit by taking the free pawn, not by opening lines toward your own king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...f5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4

5981569862362187|b1c3.headline: 4...d6 left f7 weak: hit it with 5.Ng5
5981569862362187|b1c3.why: 5.Nc3 lets Black go after your bishop with 5...Na5: in the engine line it ends with 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7, and White only wins the knight back with 8.b4 and 9.bxa5. Black's 4...d6 was a slip that left f7 defended only by the king, with the c4 bishop already aiming at it. 5.Ng5 adds a second attacker, and after 5...d5 6.exd5 White wins a pawn.
5981569862362187|b1c3.principle: When f7 is defended only by the king and your bishop already aims at it, add a second attacker before making quiet moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. d3

6004567141016616|c1f4.headline: 1...b6 ignores the centre, so take it with 2.e4
6004567141016616|c1f4.why: 2.Bf4 lets Black take e4 away from you: after 2...Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3 d5 the knight, the b7-bishop and the d5-pawn all cover e4. You never get a second pawn in the centre, and most of your opening edge is gone. 2.e4 puts pawns on e4 and d4 at once, reaching an Owen's Defence that IM Palliser calls quite pleasant for White; masters choose it 56% of the time. After 2...e6 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 Be7 6.Qe2 d5 your bishop and queen guard e4 and the c3-pawn keeps d4 firm.
6004567141016616|c1f4.principle: When your opponent's first move ignores the centre, put a second pawn there before developing the bishops.
sources: Palliser, Play 1 d4; Gonzalez, The English Defence (Google Books snippets) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%221.d4+b6+2.c4%22+English+Defence
Matthew Astle, The Offbeat Owen's (Chessable blog) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/owens-defense/
Jose Gonzalez, Opening Repertoire: The English Defence (excerpt) | https://www.scacco.it/data/attachments/11733/opening-repertoire-the-english-defence.pdf
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...b6

ideas.title: Take the centre with pawns
ideas.text: Black has handed you the centre, so put a second pawn on e4 before the bishops come out.

ideas.title: Count attackers on e4
ideas.text: Black's b7-bishop and a knight on f6 aim at e4. Guard it with 4.Bd3, then add a second guard with 6.Qe2.

ideas.title: Black strikes back with ...c5
ideas.text: Black hits your pawn centre with ...c5 and ...d5, as in 4...c5 and 6...d5; 5.c3 keeps d4 firm.

habit.why: 2.Bf4 lets Black take e4 away from you: after 2...Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3 d5 the knight, the b7-bishop and the d5-pawn all cover e4. You never get a second pawn in the centre, and most of your opening edge is gone.

strays.text: The bishop comes out before e4, and 2...Nf6 makes e4 hard to play.

taught.why: 2.e4 puts pawns on e4 and d4 at once, reaching an Owen's Defence that IM Palliser calls quite pleasant for White; masters choose it 56% of the time. After 2...e6 3.Nf3 Bb7 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 Be7 6.Qe2 d5 your bishop and queen guard e4 and the c3-pawn keeps d4 firm.

enforces.text: Pawns on e4 and d4 claim the centre 1...b6 left free.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2.c4 is the standard Queen's Gambit-style reply and sound: after 2...Nf6 3.f3 g6 Black heads for a King's Indian setup. There's a more direct move, though.
alternatives.after: 2.e4 claims the centre a move sooner; with 2.c4 you need 3.f3 before 4.e4. Masters play 2.e4 in 56% of games and 2.c4 in 28%.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2.Nf3 is solid but gives up a big pawn centre: after 2...Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.g3 Bb4+ 5.Bd2 Bxd2+ 6.Qxd2 Ba6 it's a Queen's Indian where Black is comfortable.
alternatives.after: 2.e4 takes the Owen's centre for free, which 2.Nf3 gives up. Masters still play 2.Nf3 in 11% of games, so the engine is harsher on it than practice.

6047686001480310|e4e5.headline: Against 3...e6, develop and keep it open; don't play 4.e5
6047686001480310|e4e5.why: 4.e5 closes the centre and gives Black a French-style game where ...c5 strikes at the base of White's pawn chain; after 4...c5 5.dxc5 Bxc5 Black's bishop develops actively. 3...e6 shuts in Black's light-squared bishop and wastes the move ...c6 that a French player would use for ...c5, so White should keep the position open: 4.Bd3 develops and offers the d4-pawn, and after 4...dxe4 5.Nxe4 Qxd4 6.Nf3 White gains time on the queen and castles with a clear lead in development.
6047686001480310|e4e5.principle: When your opponent's setup locks in a bishop and spends moves on pawns, keep lines open and develop quickly rather than closing the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3

6065829209254937|f1c4.headline: Guard e4 with 4.Bd3: Black's b7 bishop is already aiming at it
6065829209254937|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 leaves e4 with no defender, so 4...Bxe4 wins a clean pawn. After 5.Nc3 Bxf3 6.Qxf3 Nc6 Black is a pawn up, and your c4 bishop just bites on the e6 pawn. 4.Bd3 develops and guards e4, which is why masters choose it 95% of the time. After 4...c5 5.c3 Nf6 6.Qe2 d5 7.e5 Nfd7 8.Bf4 you keep both centre pawns, and Black's own d5 pawn blocks the b7 bishop.
6065829209254937|f1c4.principle: Before developing a piece, check what the opponent attacks: 4.Bd3 develops and guards e4, while 4.Bc4 leaves it loose.
sources: Matthew Astle, The Offbeat Owen's: 1.e4 b6 (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/owens-defense/
Wikibooks: Chess Opening Theory/1._e4/1...e6/2._d4/2...b6/3._Nf3/3...Bb7 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...e6/2._d4/2...b6/3._Nf3/3...Bb7

ideas.title: The long-diagonal bishop
ideas.text: Black's b7 bishop aims at e4 and d5. Leave e4 unguarded and 4...Bxe4 takes it.

ideas.title: Guard e4 against ...b6 lines
ideas.text: Your light bishop belongs on d3, where it guards e4, with the queen behind it as in 6.Qe2.

ideas.title: Hit the d4 base of the chain
ideas.text: Black hits d4 with ...c5; 4...c5 5.c3 keeps a pawn ready to take back on d4.

ideas.title: Answer ...d5 by keeping e4
ideas.text: When Black adds ...d5, push past it: 6...d5 7.e5 gains space and sends the f6 knight to d7.

habit.why: 4.Bc4 leaves e4 with no defender, so 4...Bxe4 wins a clean pawn. After 5.Nc3 Bxf3 6.Qxf3 Nc6 Black is a pawn up, and your c4 bishop just bites on the e6 pawn.

strays.text: The bishop on c4 doesn't guard e4, so 4...Bxe4 wins it.

taught.why: 4.Bd3 develops and guards e4, which is why masters choose it 95% of the time. After 4...c5 5.c3 Nf6 6.Qe2 d5 7.e5 Nfd7 8.Bf4 you keep both centre pawns, and Black's own d5 pawn blocks the b7 bishop.

enforces.text: The bishop on d3, then 6.Qe2, keeps e4 safe from the b7 bishop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 guards e4 and is sound, but 4...Bb4 pins the knight Nimzo-Indian style, so e4 will need another defender soon. There's a simpler move.
alternatives.after: 4.Bd3 guards e4 with a piece that can't be pinned and leaves c3 for a pawn, as in 5.c3. Masters prefer it 95% to 4%; 4.Nc3 often comes back to it with 5.Bd3.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.d5 gains space, but after 4...Nf6 5.dxe6 dxe6 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 the queens are off early. The b7 bishop and f6 knight both hit e4, so you spend 8.f3 guarding it.
alternatives.after: 4.Bd3 keeps the centre pawns side by side and the queens on, so your space lasts and the b7 bishop stays blocked.

6104332673881535|d7d6.headline: Against 2.c3, hit e4 with 2...Nf6 while White can't play Nc3

ideas.title: White wants two centre pawns
ideas.text: 2.c3 prepares 3.d4, so White can retake with the c-pawn and keep pawns on d4 and e4.

ideas.title: No Nc3 for White
ideas.text: The c3 pawn takes the knight's square: White can't guard e4 with Nc3 or chase your pieces from d5.

ideas.title: Strike the centre at once
ideas.text: Black's best replies, 2...Nf6 and 2...d5, both hit e4 straight away; slow moves hand White the full centre.

ideas.title: Chip at the e5 pawn
ideas.text: After 3.e5 Nd5 the advanced pawn becomes a target for ...cxd4 and ...d6.

habit.why: 2...d6 attacks nothing, so White plays 3.d4 and gets the full centre for free. After 3...Nf6 4.Bd3 cxd4 5.cxd4 White has pawns on d4 and e4 and a lasting space edge.

strays.text: 2...d6 makes no threat, so 2.c3 gets exactly what it was played for.

taught.why: 2...Nf6 attacks e4, and with no Nc3 available White usually pushes 3.e5. After 3...Nd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 d6 you hit the e5 pawn and the chances are equal.

enforces.text: The knight hits e4 and then sits safely on d5, since no white knight can reach c3.

6104332673881535|d7d6.principle: Contest the centre your opponent is building: 2.c3 prepares 3.d4, so attack e4 with 2...Nf6 now instead of letting White set up pawns on d4 and e4.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 2...Nc6 develops but lets White play 3.d4, and after 3...cxd4 4.cxd4 White has the two-pawn centre. It's the most common club move here, but rare among masters.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 gives White no free 3.d4: after 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 d6 you are already attacking the centre.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 2...e6 is solid, but after 3.d4 d5 4.e5 you're in an Advance French, with your light-squared bishop shut in behind the e6 pawn.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 keeps it a Sicilian: after 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 d6 the e5 pawn is under attack and your c8-bishop's diagonal stays open.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...d5 hits back in the centre: after 3.exd5 Qxd5 your queen stands well because no white knight can hit it from c3. It's the old main line, played in a third of master games.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 is more popular with masters (45% to 33%) and fully level, while 2...d5 opens the centre and often leads to isolated-pawn middlegames or an early queen trade.

sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3

After 3...Nd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 d6 you hit the e5 pawn and the chances are equal.

612982152772711|d1b3.headline: Castle first with 7.O-O; 7.Qb3 walks into 8...Na5
612982152772711|d1b3.why: 7.Qb3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and 7...Qe7 covers f7. After 8.O-O Na5 9.Qb5 Nxc4 10.Qxc4 you have lost your Italian bishop and are still pawns down for little. 7.O-O tucks your king away and leaves Black to deal with your centre. After 7...d3 8.e5 Be7 9.Qb3 Kf8 10.Bxf7 you win a pawn back and Black's king has lost castling.
612982152772711|d1b3.principle: Don't bring the queen out early while minor pieces are at home; castle first, and the queen move gains force later.

ideas.title: Castle, then rebuild the centre
ideas.text: 7.cxd4 at once allows 7...Bb4+. Castling first gets your king safe and keeps the recapture for later.

ideas.title: Qb3 needs the right moment
ideas.text: Queen on b3 and bishop on c4 aim at f7, but too early 7...Qe7 covers it and 8...Na5 chases both pieces.

ideas.title: Kick the d6 bishop with e5
ideas.text: Once you have castled, e4-e5 hits the d6 bishop with tempo, as in 7.O-O d3 8.e5, and 9.Qb3 then aims at f7.

ideas.title: ...Na5 chases the bishop
ideas.text: Black's c6 knight can jump to a5 to hit your c4 bishop and a queen on b3, as in 7.Qb3 Qe7 8.O-O Na5.

habit.why: 7.Qb3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and 7...Qe7 covers f7. After 8.O-O Na5 9.Qb5 Nxc4 10.Qxc4 you have lost your Italian bishop and are still pawns down for little.

strays.text: 7...Qe7 covers f7 and 8...Na5 chases queen and bishop.

taught.why: 7.O-O tucks your king away and leaves Black to deal with your centre. After 7...d3 8.e5 Be7 9.Qb3 Kf8 10.Bxf7 you win a pawn back and Black's king has lost castling.

enforces.idea: Kick the d6 bishop with e5
enforces.text: After castling, 8.e5 hits the d6 bishop with tempo.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.cxd4 rebuilds your centre but allows a check: 7...Bb4+ 8.Nbd2 Nf6 9.d5 Ne7, and Black castles with a sound extra pawn.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O gets the king out of the check first; the recapture can wait, and meanwhile 8.e5 can hit the d6 bishop.

612982152772711|f3g5.headline: Castle first with 7.O-O; 7.Ng5 runs into 7...Ne5
612982152772711|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight again with two minor pieces still at home, and 7...Ne5 covers f7 while hitting your bishop. After 8.Bb3 h6 9.Nf3 Nxf3+ 10.Qxf3 Qf6 the knight has moved three times only to be traded, and Black is still pawns up. 7.O-O tucks your king away and leaves Black to deal with your centre. After 7...d3 8.e5 Be7 9.Qb3 Kf8 10.Bxf7 you win a pawn back and Black's king has lost castling.
612982152772711|f3g5.principle: Don't move the same piece twice in the opening without a real target; castle and develop first.

enforces.text: After castling, 8.e5 hits the d6 bishop with tempo.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.cxd4 rebuilds your centre but allows a check: 7...Bb4+ 8.Nbd2 Nf6 9.d5 Ne7, and Black castles with a sound extra pawn.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O gets the king out of the check first; the recapture can wait, and meanwhile 8.e5 can hit the d6 bishop.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 7.Qb3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces at home: 7...Qe7 covers f7, and 8...Na5 then hits queen and bishop. 9.Qb5 Nxc4 10.Qxc4 costs you the Italian bishop.
alternatives.after: With 7.O-O first, the queen comes to b3 later with 9.Qb3, after 8.e5 has pushed the bishop to e7, and then 10.Bxf7 wins a pawn back.

6180716488927123|d7d6.headline: Hit the loose e4 pawn with 3...d5 against the Ponziani
6180716488927123|d7d6.why: 3...d6 defends e5, which was not really threatened, hems in the bishop on f8, and lets White play 4.d4 for a big two-pawn centre; Wikibooks calls it passive. 3.c3 took the c3 square from White's knight, so the pawn on e4 is loose, and 3...d5 strikes at it at once. If White takes on d5, Black's queen recaptures without Nc3 to chase it.
6180716488927123|d7d6.principle: Strike at the centre pawn your opponent can no longer defend easily: with c3 played, e4 has lost its natural knight defender.

6180716488927123|f7f5.headline: Against the Ponziani, hit e4 with 3...d5.
6180716488927123|f7f5.why: 3...f5, the Ponziani Countergambit, gives up a pawn after 4.exf5 and loosens Black's own king. It is thought to give White an advantage when White knows the theory. 3.c3 left e4 loose and took c3 away from White's knight. 3...d5 attacks e4, and if 4.exd5 Qxd5 the queen is safe because White cannot chase it with Nc3.
6180716488927123|f7f5.principle: When the opponent's opening leaves a centre pawn loose, attack it with a centre pawn, not with a flank pawn that weakens your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3

6180716488927123|f8c5.headline: Against the Ponziani, hit e4 at once with 3...d5.
6180716488927123|f8c5.why: 3...Bc5 ignores what 3.c3 is for: White plays 4.d4, gaining time on the bishop, and after 4...exd4 5.cxd4 Bb6 owns a two-pawn centre. 3...d5 attacks the pawn on e4, which is loose because c3 has taken the knight's natural square. If 4.exd5 Qxd5, White has no Nc3 to chase the queen away, so Black gets a free hand in the centre.
6180716488927123|f8c5.principle: When White spends a move on c3 to prepare d4, strike at the centre before d4 arrives, aiming at the pawn that c3 left without a knight's support.

6186919355194995|f1c4.headline: Take the full centre with 3.d4 against a passive ...e6
6186919355194995|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 walks into 3...d5, which hits the bishop and the e4 pawn at once. After 4.exd5 exd5 5.Be2 your bishop has moved twice and Black develops freely. 3.d4 takes the full centre while Black's set-up is passive. After 3...Nf6 4.Bd3 your bishop guards e4, and after 5.c4 e5 6.Nc3 g6 7.d5 you have a big space edge.
6186919355194995|f1c4.principle: Fight for the centre: when Black sets up passively, take the full centre with your pawns.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Black lets you build the centre and hopes to hit it later, so take it now: 3.d4 puts pawns on e4 and d4.

ideas.title: Modern ...e6 set-ups: bishop to d3
ideas.text: Against ...e6 your bishop belongs on d3, where it guards e4. On c4 it gets hit by ...d5.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 break
ideas.text: With ...e6 in, Black is ready for ...d5, hitting e4; against a bishop on c4 it also gains a move.

habit.why: 3.Bc4 walks into 3...d5, which hits the bishop and the e4 pawn at once. After 4.exd5 exd5 5.Be2 your bishop has moved twice and Black develops freely.

strays.text: On c4 the bishop is a target for 3...d5.

taught.why: 3.d4 takes the full centre while Black's set-up is passive. After 3...Nf6 4.Bd3 your bishop guards e4, and after 5.c4 e5 6.Nc3 g6 7.d5 you have a big space edge.

enforces.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
enforces.text: You take e4 and d4 before Black can challenge them.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 develops and guards e4, a sound move. After 3...c5 and 5.Nxd4 a6 the game becomes an Open Sicilian; there is a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: 3.d4 takes the centre at once and keeps Black in a passive set-up; 3.Nc3 lets Black switch to a Sicilian with 3...c5.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

6196978325404138|b8c6.headline: Challenge the London with 3...c5 before ...Nc6.
6196978325404138|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, so Black gives up the ...c5 break and lets White build the London setup in peace. After 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.c4 White even takes over the initiative. 3...c5 is the most common reply: it strikes at d4 and challenges the bishop's setup. The knight still comes to c6 afterwards, as in 3...c5 4.Nf3 Nc6.
6196978325404138|b8c6.principle: Against a solid pawn centre, put your c-pawn to work before your queen's knight blocks it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Bf4/2...Nf6/3. e3

6230854239967859|c2c3.headline: Break the pin with 5.Be2 before ...Bxf3 costs you d4
6230854239967859|c2c3.why: 5.c3 guards d4 with a pawn but leaves the f3-knight pinned, so Black keeps piling on: 5...e5 6.Be2 O-O-O 7.h3 Bh5 8.O-O exd4 9.cxd4 Nxd4 wins your d4 pawn. It also spends a move while your f1-bishop is still at home. 5.Be2 develops and breaks the pin, so 5...Bxf3 can be met by the bishop, which hits the queen; masters choose it 88% of the time. After 5...O-O-O 6.Be3 e5 7.Nc3 Qa5 your bishop guards d4, the knight gains time on the queen, and 8.Nxe5 Bxe2 9.Qxe2 Nxe5 trades off Black's pressure.
6230854239967859|c2c3.principle: When a bishop pins the knight that guards your centre pawn, break the pin by developing a piece in between; a pawn move leaves the pin.

ideas.title: Nimzowitsch: Black targets d4
ideas.text: The c6-knight and d5-queen hit d4, and the g4-bishop pins its guard on f3; ...e5 and ...O-O-O add more pressure.

ideas.title: Break the pin with Be2
ideas.text: A bishop on e2 unpins the f3-knight: if Black takes on f3, the bishop retakes, hits the queen and keeps your pawns whole.

ideas.title: Gain time on early black pieces
ideas.text: Black's queen on d5 is exposed: a knight on c3 develops and attacks it, as in 7.Nc3 Qa5 or 5.Nc3 Qh5.

habit.why: 5.c3 guards d4 with a pawn but leaves the f3-knight pinned, so Black keeps piling on: 5...e5 6.Be2 O-O-O 7.h3 Bh5 8.O-O exd4 9.cxd4 Nxd4 wins your d4 pawn. It also spends a move while your f1-bishop is still at home.

strays.text: The pawn guards d4 but the pin stays, so ...e5 and ...O-O-O pile up.

taught.why: 5.Be2 develops and breaks the pin, so 5...Bxf3 can be met by the bishop, which hits the queen; masters choose it 88% of the time. After 5...O-O-O 6.Be3 e5 7.Nc3 Qa5 your bishop guards d4, the knight gains time on the queen, and 8.Nxe5 Bxe2 9.Qxe2 Nxe5 trades off Black's pressure.

enforces.text: With the pin gone, 5...Bxf3 no longer wrecks your pawns or wins d4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Gain time on early black pieces
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 develops with a hit on the queen. But the pin stays: after 5...Qh5 6.Bb5 e6 7.Bf4 O-O-O 8.Bxc6 bxc6 9.Qd3 Bxf3 your kingside pawns get split. A more popular move exists.
alternatives.after: 5.Be2 removes the pin first, so a capture on f3 is answered by a piece; masters prefer it 88% to 9%. 5.Nc3 gains time on the queen but leaves tactical tricks for both sides.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Be3 adds a guard to d4, so it is sound. But the f3-knight stays pinned, and after 5...e5 6.Nc3 Bb4 Black keeps hitting your centre. There's a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 5.Be2 deals with the pin first, and the other bishop can still come to e3 next, as in 6.Be3. With 5.Be3 first, 6...Bb4 and 7...exd4 break up your centre.

6239823014560158|e2e4.headline: Develop with 3.Bf4; 3.e4 gives away a pawn
6239823014560158|e2e4.why: 3.e4 pushes a pawn that nothing defends: after 3...dxe4 the knight on f3 is attacked, and 4.d5 Nb4 5.Nfd2 Nf6 6.Nc3 Nfxd5 leaves Black a clean pawn up. 3.Bf4 is the most common master move (34%): it develops the bishop to an active square before 4.e3 closes its diagonal, as in 3...Bg4 4.e3 e6 5.c4.
6239823014560158|e2e4.principle: Before pushing a pawn into contact, count who defends it: e4 is hit by Black's d5 pawn and covered by nothing of yours.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nc6

6251023477722752|c1e3.headline: Bishop to c4 and castle: the classic plan against ...Bf5
6251023477722752|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 puts the bishop where it does nothing against ...Bf5, and after 6...e6 7.Bd3 Bxd3 8.Qxd3 your king's bishop is traded off before you've castled. Black goes on with 8...c6 9.O-O-O Qa5, and your e3-bishop later drops back with 10.Bd2. 6.Bc4 takes an active diagonal and lets you castle at once with 7.O-O; Jaenisch and Staunton already gave this bishop move against ...Bf5 and ...e6, with White better. After 7...c6 8.Nh4 Bg6 9.Nxg6 hxg6 you have the bishop pair.
6251023477722752|c1e3.principle: Develop the kingside pieces first so you can castle: the king's bishop has an obvious active square on c4, while the queen's bishop can wait.
sources: John Emms, Discovering Chess Openings (2006) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%22Qd8%22+%22Nf6+5.Nf3+Bf5+6.Bc4%22

IM Alberto Chueca, Scandinavian Defense | https://www.albertochueca.com/blog/scandinavian-defense/

ideas.title: Kingside pieces first
ideas.text: Your f1-bishop has a good square on c4 and clears the way to castle; the c1-bishop can wait until its job is clear.

ideas.title: Hunt the f5 bishop
ideas.text: Black's bishop on f5 is a target: a knight on e5 with g4 and h4, or 8.Nh4 Bg6 9.Nxg6, which wins you the bishop pair.

ideas.title: Bishop out before ...e6/...c6
ideas.text: Black got the bishop to f5 before playing ...e6 and ...c6, so it stands outside the solid pawn wall.

habit.why: 6.Be3 puts the bishop where it does nothing against ...Bf5, and after 6...e6 7.Bd3 Bxd3 8.Qxd3 your king's bishop is traded off before you've castled. Black goes on with 8...c6 9.O-O-O Qa5, and your e3-bishop later drops back with 10.Bd2.

strays.text: The c1-bishop comes out first, and the f1-bishop gets swapped off.

taught.why: 6.Bc4 takes an active diagonal and lets you castle at once with 7.O-O; Jaenisch and Staunton already gave this bishop move against ...Bf5 and ...e6, with White better. After 7...c6 8.Nh4 Bg6 9.Nxg6 hxg6 you have the bishop pair.

enforces.text: Castle first, then 8.Nh4 trades your knight for the f5-bishop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Bd3 develops and offers to swap Black's active bishop: after 6...Bxd3 7.Qxd3 c6 8.Bg5 e6 9.O-O-O you are castled quickly. Masters play it in 22% of games, but another move keeps more.
alternatives.after: 6.Bc4 keeps pieces on and wins the bishop pair with 8.Nh4 instead of swapping bishops. Masters choose 6.Bc4 in 37% of games, 6.Bd3 in 22%.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Bg5 pins the f6-knight, but after 6...e6 7.Bd3 h6 8.Bh4 Bxd3 Black gains time on your bishop and still trades off your f1-bishop.
alternatives.after: 6.Bc4 develops the king's bishop and castles first; the c1-bishop chooses its square later.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Bf4 eyes c7, but the queen on d8 guards it. After 6...e6 7.Bd3 Bxd3 8.Qxd3 Bd6 Black challenges your bishop at once.
alternatives.after: 6.Bc4 heads for castling, and 8.Nh4 then goes after the f5-bishop instead of letting it trade itself off.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Ne5 is a top move too: the knight eyes f7 and backs up h4 and g4 against the f5-bishop, as in 6...Be6 7.h4. Masters play it in 33% of games.
alternatives.after: Masters pick 6.Bc4 (37%) and 6.Ne5 (33%) almost equally and the engine rates them alike. 6.Bc4 develops a new piece first, and the knight jump to e5 often follows in the same plan.

6277794409955082|b7c6.headline: Recapture 4...dxc6 to open lines for queen and bishop
6277794409955082|b7c6.why: After 4...bxc6 the d-pawn still blocks Black's queen and bishop, and the e5 pawn has no tactical cover, so 5.d4 exd4 6.Qxd4 lets White's queen take over the centre; Wikibooks gives White a small advantage. 4...dxc6 is the main move: it opens lines for the queen and the bishop on c8, and the pawn on e5 is defended by a trick, since Nxe5 runs into ...Qd4, forking the knight and the pawn on e4.
6277794409955082|b7c6.principle: Recapture in the way that opens lines for your undeveloped pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6

6280706797964752|c2c3.headline: Add a second guard to e4 with 4.Qe2, not 4.c3
6280706797964752|c2c3.why: 4.c3 props up d4, but e4 is attacked twice by the f6-knight and b7-bishop and guarded once. 4...Nxe4 wins the pawn, and after 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.O-O d6 Black is a pawn up with a solid position. 4.Qe2 adds a second guard to e4 and stands behind the pawn ready to support e5; masters play it in 69% of games. After 4...e6 5.Nf3 d5 6.e5 Nfd7 the knight is pushed back, and 7.Ng5 Be7 8.Qh5 g6 makes Black loosen the kingside.
6280706797964752|c2c3.principle: e4 is attacked twice and defended once, so add a defender first: 4.Qe2 holds it, while 4.c3 supports d4 instead.

ideas.title: Count attackers on e4
ideas.text: The f6-knight and b7-bishop hit e4 twice; your d3-bishop guards it once. Add a second guard: 4.Qe2, 4.Nc3, 4.Nd2 or 4.f3.

ideas.title: e5 kicks the f6-knight
ideas.text: With the queen behind it and the g1-knight out, e5 drives the knight back, as in 5.Nf3 d5 6.e5 Nfd7.

ideas.title: Black strikes back with ...c5
ideas.text: Black lets you have the centre, then hits d4 with ...c5 and e4 with ...d5.

habit.why: 4.c3 props up d4, but e4 is attacked twice by the f6-knight and b7-bishop and guarded once. 4...Nxe4 wins the pawn, and after 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.O-O d6 Black is a pawn up with a solid position.

strays.text: The pawn guards d4, not e4, so 4...Nxe4 wins it.

taught.why: 4.Qe2 adds a second guard to e4 and stands behind the pawn ready to support e5; masters play it in 69% of games. After 4...e6 5.Nf3 d5 6.e5 Nfd7 the knight is pushed back, and 7.Ng5 Be7 8.Qh5 g6 makes Black loosen the kingside.

enforces.text: The queen is the second guard, so e4 holds.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 adds a second guard to e4 while developing, and after 4...e6 5.h4 the engine grabs kingside space. Fine, but masters prefer another move.
alternatives.after: 4.Qe2 also guards e4, keeps c3 free for a pawn and stands behind a later e5. Masters prefer it, 69% to 8%; both hold the pawn.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.f3 holds e4 with a pawn, but it takes the f3 square from your knight, and 4...Nc6 hits d4 with a lot of central tension. A better move exists.
alternatives.after: 4.Qe2 guards e4 without blocking your knight, so 5.Nf3 comes next and e5 stays possible.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nd2 guards e4 solidly and masters play it in 20% of games, but it also lets Black build a centre, and the game is nearly equal. A more active move exists.
alternatives.after: 4.Qe2 is the main line (69%): the queen backs up e5, which kicks the f6-knight. 4.Nd2 is more solid but blocks your c1-bishop.

After 4...e6 5.Nf3 d5 6.e5 Nfd7 the knight is pushed back, and 7.Ng5 Be7 8.Qh5 g6 makes Black loosen the kingside.

6285819280081780|d2d3.headline: Castle first, then open the centre against the early queen
6285819280081780|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is safe but passive: it spends a move on a one-square pawn push, and after 4...Nc6 5.Nc3 Nge7 Black has caught up in development and the chance to punish the early queen is gone. 4.O-O gets the king safe and keeps the d-pawn free to go two squares. After 4...d6 5.Nc3 Ne7 6.d4 White strikes in the centre while Black's king is still uncastled and the queen on f6 is exposed; after 6...Bxd4 7.Nxd4 exd4 8.Nb5 the knight jumps in.
6285819280081780|d2d3.principle: White is ahead in development and Black's queen came out early, so castle and open the centre quickly before Black catches up.

6309463160940467|e1h1.headline: Hit f7 with 7.Qb3 before Black plays ...Nc6
6309463160940467|e1h1.why: Castling lets Black finish the setup with 7...Nc6. After 8.Ng5 Ne5 9.Qb3 Nxc4 10.Qxc4 Nh6 Black's knight has traded off your c4 bishop and f7 is safe. 7.Qb3 lines up queen and bishop on f7 and threatens to take it with check, while Black's knight is still on b8. After 7...Nh6 8.Bxh6 Bxh6 9.Bxf7+ Kf8 you take f7 with check and Black's king can no longer castle.
6309463160940467|e1h1.principle: f7 is guarded only by Black's king, so add a second attacker while you can: 7.Qb3 joins the c4 bishop before ...Nc6 and ...Ne5 can trade it off.

ideas.title: Hit f7 with the queen
ideas.text: Your c4 bishop aims at f7, guarded only by the king. The queen on b3 adds a second attacker, threatening to take f7 with check.

ideas.title: Strike before ...Nc6
ideas.text: Black hasn't played ...Nc6 yet. Once it comes, ...Ne5 can trade off your c4 bishop and the pressure on f7 is gone.

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: Against the fianchetto, e5 blocks the g7 bishop. With ...d6 already in, Black answers ...Nh6 and the pawns just get traded.

ideas.title: Gambit pawn buys time
ideas.text: You are a pawn down for quick development. Use it on threats now, or Black finishes the setup and keeps the pawn.

habit.why: Castling lets Black finish the setup with 7...Nc6. After 8.Ng5 Ne5 9.Qb3 Nxc4 10.Qxc4 Nh6 Black's knight has traded off your c4 bishop and f7 is safe.

strays.text: It gives Black time for 7...Nc6, and the f7 pressure fades.

taught.why: 7.Qb3 lines up queen and bishop on f7 and threatens to take it with check, while Black's knight is still on b8. After 7...Nh6 8.Bxh6 Bxh6 9.Bxf7+ Kf8 you take f7 with check and Black's king can no longer castle.

enforces.text: Queen and bishop together hit f7 before ...Nc6 and ...Ne5 can help.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.e5 hits d6, but 7...Nh6 and castling follow. After 9.exd6 Qxd6 10.Qxd6 exd6 the queens are off and your attacking chances with them.
alternatives.after: 7.Qb3 uses the missing knight on c6: f7 falls with check (9.Bxf7+ Kf8). The push only trades pawns and queens.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Ng5 adds a second attacker on f7, but 7...Nh6 covers it and Black castles. After 8.O-O O-O 9.h3 Nc6 your knight on g5 has nothing to do.
alternatives.after: 7.Qb3 hits f7 from far away, so 7...Nh6 doesn't hold it: 8.Bxh6 Bxh6 9.Bxf7+ takes the pawn anyway.

6359291933074994|d7d5.headline: In the Vienna, prepare ...d5 with 2...Nf6 first
6359291933074994|d7d5.why: 2...d5 comes too early: the knight on c3 and the e4 pawn both attack d5, so 3.Nxd5 simply wins a pawn, and after 3...Nf6 4.Nxf6+ Qxf6 your queen is out early as well. 2...Nf6 develops, attacks e4 and adds a guard to d5, so ...d5 becomes possible later, for instance as the answer to f4. Masters choose it in 72% of games.
6359291933074994|d7d5.principle: Before pushing ...d5, count: Nc3 and the e4 pawn attack it twice and only the queen defends it, so add a defender with the knight first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6

6359291933074994|f7f5.headline: Don't open your own kingside; develop the knight to f6
6359291933074994|f7f5.why: 2...f5 is a King's Gambit reversed with White's queen knight already out: after 3.exf5 Black is a pawn down with a loosened kingside and less development. 2...Nf6 develops a knight, attacks e4 and contests d5, and prepares to meet White's f4 with a counter-strike in the centre.
6359291933074994|f7f5.principle: Opening lines near your own king only pays when you lead in development; here White is ahead, so Black develops first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...f5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6

6363157341111651|d1e2.headline: Block the queen check with a bishop, not your queen
6363157341111651|d1e2.why: 4.Qe2 blocks the check with the queen, so Black trades with 5...Qxe2+ and the early queen trip costs Black nothing. 3...Qe6+ is a common amateur try that achieves little: 4.Be2 blocks with a developing piece, and the queen on e6 blocks Black's e-pawn and will have to move again, as in 4...Nf6 5.Nf3 Qd6. White gains time for 6.d4 and castling.
6363157341111651|d1e2.principle: When an early queen checks you, block with a developing piece so the queen, not you, has to spend another move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

6375481783376729|g1f3.headline: Take first with 3.dxc5 and make Black's queen win it back
6375481783376729|g1f3.why: 3.Nf3 allows 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4, the trade Black wanted, and after 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 a6 it is a normal Najdorf. Masters play 3.Nf3 most often (43%) and it is fully playable, but the chance to punish 2...d6 is gone. 3.dxc5 makes Black win the pawn back with the queen: after 3...Qa5+ 4.Nc3 Qxc5 5.Be3 Qa5 she has moved three times. Then 6.Qd5 Qxd5 7.Nxd5 Kd8 trades queens, and Black's king gives up castling to stop a knight fork on c7.
6375481783376729|g1f3.principle: Take on c5 so Black can only win the pawn back with the queen, then develop with tempo on her.
sources: Joel Johnson, Positional Attacks | https://books.google.com/books?id=7H14BgAAQBAJ
Jef Kaan, Better Chess Openings | https://books.google.com/books?id=3jFlCQAAQBAJ

ideas.title: The c-for-d trade
ideas.text: Trading Black's c-pawn for your d-pawn is the point of 1...c5. After 2...d6 you choose: allow 3...cxd4 or prevent it.

ideas.title: Take on c5 first
ideas.text: 3.dxc5 makes Black spend queen moves to get the pawn back: 3...Qa5+ 4.Nc3 Qxc5.

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: With Black's queen on c5, 5.Be3 hits her, and 6.Qd5 forces a trade that costs Black castling after 7.Nxd5 Kd8.

habit.why: 3.Nf3 allows 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4, the trade Black wanted, and after 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 a6 it is a normal Najdorf. Masters play 3.Nf3 most often (43%) and it is fully playable, but the chance to punish 2...d6 is gone.

strays.text: Black gets the trade 1...c5 aims for and an ordinary Open Sicilian.

taught.why: 3.dxc5 makes Black win the pawn back with the queen: after 3...Qa5+ 4.Nc3 Qxc5 5.Be3 Qa5 she has moved three times. Then 6.Qd5 Qxd5 7.Nxd5 Kd8 trades queens, and Black's king gives up castling to stop a knight fork on c7.

enforces.text: Black has to spend queen moves to get the pawn back.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.d5 is a good move: it avoids the c-for-d trade and gains space, with Benoni-like play after 3...g6 4.c4 Nf6. A more forcing move is available.
alternatives.after: 3.dxc5 is more forcing, since Black's queen must win the pawn back while you develop. Masters play 3.d5 (20%) almost as often as 3.dxc5 (27%).

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.c3 is slow: Black doesn't have to take, and after 3...Nf6 4.Bd3 g6 5.h3 cxd4 6.cxd4 e5 7.d5 Black develops freely while you've spent moves on pawns.
alternatives.after: 3.dxc5 makes Black react: the pawn comes back only with queen moves that you meet with 4.Nc3 and 5.Be3.

6379793223839|c7c6.headline: Take back with 2...Qxd5; the 2...c6 gambit gives too little
6379793223839|c7c6.why: 2...c6 offers a pawn, and after 3.dxc6 Nxc6 4.Nf3 e5 5.Nc3 Nf6 6.Bb5 White develops normally and stays a pawn up. Your quick development isn't enough: theory calls the gambit inferior, and masters almost never play it (0.1%). 2...Qxd5 takes the pawn back at once. White gains a tempo with 3.Nc3, but after 3...Qd6 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 c6 your queen is safe and the game is level and solid; 70% of master games go this way.
6379793223839|c7c6.principle: Win back a pawn when it only costs a tempo; a gambit without enough compensation just leaves you a pawn down.
sources: Scandinavian Defense: Blackburne-Kloosterboer Gambit (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/scandinavian-defense/blackburne-kloosterboer-gambit/

ideas.title: Win back d5 at once
ideas.text: Nothing defends White's pawn on d5, and taking it back is your first job.

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: After 2...Qxd5, 3.Nc3 hits your queen and she must move again, usually to a5, d6 or d8.

ideas.title: Keep the queen safe
ideas.text: Pick a square where she can't be hit again; on d6, play ...c6 soon to stop a knight jump to b5, as with 5...c6.

ideas.title: Grab the gambit pawn, not the centre
ideas.text: Against 2...c6, White takes a second pawn with 3.dxc6, develops and keeps the extra pawn.

habit.why: 2...c6 offers a pawn, and after 3.dxc6 Nxc6 4.Nf3 e5 5.Nc3 Nf6 6.Bb5 White develops normally and stays a pawn up. Your quick development isn't enough: theory calls the gambit inferior, and masters almost never play it (0.1%).

strays.text: You leave White's d5 pawn alone and end up a pawn down.

taught.why: 2...Qxd5 takes the pawn back at once. White gains a tempo with 3.Nc3, but after 3...Qd6 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 c6 your queen is safe and the game is level and solid; 70% of master games go this way.

enforces.text: You restore material at once and accept losing a tempo for it.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2...Nf6 is the Modern Scandinavian, 29.5% of master games: you win d5 back with the knight, as in 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3 Bf5 5.Bd3, where White keeps a little more space. Masters treat it as fully respectable, though the engine here rates it lower.
alternatives.after: 2...Qxd5 is the main line, preferred 70% to 30% by masters: it takes the pawn at once, and the tempo White gains with 3.Nc3 costs you little.

6423991710179470|e1h1.headline: Before castling, punish 5...Bg4 with 6.Ne5 and the f7 threat
6423991710179470|e1h1.why: 6.O-O is a natural developing move, but after 6...e6 Black blocks your c4-bishop's path to f7, and 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 c6 leaves you only a small edge. You castled one move too early and let the chance on f7 go. 6.Ne5 steps out of the pin and threatens mate on f7, while your queen now hits the g4-bishop. Black has to give up the bishop with 6...Be6 7.Bxe6 fxe6, and after 8.Qf3 you keep a large advantage; in Balode-Sondore, Riga 1965, Black retreated the bishop to h5 instead and was mated on f7.
6423991710179470|e1h1.principle: Before a quiet move like castling, look for a forcing move: a knight jump that threatens mate on f7 comes first, and castling can wait.

ideas.title: Ne5 and the f7 point
ideas.text: With your bishop on c4, 6.Ne5 adds a second attacker to f7, which only the king defends: the bishop takes on f7 with mate.

ideas.title: Two threats at once
ideas.text: The knight jump also uncovers your queen against the g4-bishop. Black's only good answer is 6...Be6, which saves the bishop and covers f7.

ideas.title: Black's ...e6 shuts the door
ideas.text: Give Black one quiet move and ...e6 or a trade on f3 ends the trick: a pawn on e6 blocks your bishop's path to f7.

ideas.title: Doubled e-pawns
ideas.text: After 6...Be6 7.Bxe6 fxe6 Black has doubled e-pawns and a loose king, the structure Alekhine also reached in this line.

habit.why: 6.O-O is a natural developing move, but after 6...e6 Black blocks your c4-bishop's path to f7, and 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 c6 leaves you only a small edge. You castled one move too early and let the chance on f7 go.

strays.text: Castling gives Black time for ...e6, and f7 is safe again.

taught.why: 6.Ne5 steps out of the pin and threatens mate on f7, while your queen now hits the g4-bishop. Black has to give up the bishop with 6...Be6 7.Bxe6 fxe6, and after 8.Qf3 you keep a large advantage; in Balode-Sondore, Riga 1965, Black retreated the bishop to h5 instead and was mated on f7.

enforces.text: Knight on e5 and bishop on c4 hit f7, which only the king guards.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.h3 is the usual answer to ...Bg4, but here 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 c6 lets Black swap off and settle, and your big edge is gone. Black's last move had a flaw you could punish right now.
alternatives.after: 6.Ne5 steps out of the pin with a mate threat on f7, while 6.h3 lets Black trade the knight before it can jump. The 15th-century Scachs d'amor game also went 6.h3 Bxf3 7.Qxf3.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.d3 is solid but slow: after 6...e6 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 c6 Black's position is sound and your big edge is gone. Black's last move had a flaw you could punish right now.
alternatives.after: 6.Ne5 strikes before Black gets ...e6 in; once a pawn on e6 blocks your bishop, the chance on f7 is gone.

6423991710179470|h2h3.headline: Punish 5...Bg4 with 6.Ne5: mate on f7 is threatened
6423991710179470|h2h3.why: 6.h3 is the standard answer to ...Bg4, already played in the 15th-century Scachs d'amor game, but here 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 c6 8.Ne2 e6 lets Black swap off and shut your bishop out of f7. A big advantage shrinks to a small one. 6.Ne5 steps out of the pin and threatens mate on f7, while your queen now hits the g4-bishop. Black has to give up the bishop with 6...Be6 7.Bxe6 fxe6, and after 8.Qf3 you keep a large advantage; in Balode-Sondore, Riga 1965, Black retreated the bishop to h5 instead and was mated on f7.
6423991710179470|h2h3.principle: With your bishop aimed at f7, check whether only the king defends it: a knight jump that adds a second attacker can win on the spot.

ideas.title: Two threats at once

ideas.title: Black's ...e6 shuts the door

ideas.title: Doubled e-pawns

Black has to give up the bishop with 6...Be6 7.Bxe6 fxe6, and after 8.Qf3 you keep a large advantage; in Balode-Sondore, Riga 1965, Black retreated the bishop to h5 instead and was mated on f7.

enforces.text: Knight on e5 and bishop on c4 hit f7, which only the king guards.

6438780653454793|g7g6.headline: 3.d4 left e4 hanging: take it with 3...Nxe4
6438780653454793|g7g6.why: 3...g6 turns down a free pawn: White guards e4 with 4.Nc3 and gets a normal Pirc with 5.Be3 and 6.Qd2. Wikibooks says White has nothing better than that, so you passed up a pawn for an ordinary game. 3...Nxe4 wins the e4 pawn, and after 4.Bd3 Nf6 5.c4 White's lead in development is not thought to be enough for it. You keep the pawn by finishing with 5...g6, 6...Bg7 and 7...O-O.
6438780653454793|g7g6.principle: After every White move, ask whether e4 is still defended; take a pawn that is really free.
sources: A Pirc Quirk (IM Jeremy Silman, chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/a-pirc-quirk

ideas.title: Guard e4 before anything else
ideas.text: 3.d4 leaves e4 with no defender. White usually guards it first, as 4.Nc3 does after 3...g6; here 3...Nxe4 just takes it.

ideas.title: Take a pawn that is really free
ideas.text: Wikibooks calls this Roscher Gambit unsound: after 3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 Nf6 5.c4 White's lead in development is not enough.

ideas.title: Keep the pawn, then castle
ideas.text: After taking, bring the knight back to f6, then play ...g6, ...Bg7 and castle to keep the extra pawn.

habit.why: 3...g6 turns down a free pawn: White guards e4 with 4.Nc3 and gets a normal Pirc with 5.Be3 and 6.Qd2. Wikibooks says White has nothing better than that, so you passed up a pawn for an ordinary game.

strays.idea: Take a pawn that is really free
strays.text: A routine fianchetto instead of taking the pawn White left loose.

taught.why: 3...Nxe4 wins the e4 pawn, and after 4.Bd3 Nf6 5.c4 White's lead in development is not thought to be enough for it. You keep the pawn by finishing with 5...g6, 6...Bg7 and 7...O-O.

enforces.idea: Take a pawn that is really free
enforces.text: e4 had no defender, so the pawn is really free.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...c6 prepares ...Qa5 in Czech style and is sound: after 4.Nc3 g6 5.Be3 Bg7 6.Qd2 Qa5 you get a normal game. There is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 3...Nxe4 wins a pawn first; 3...c6 lets 4.Nc3 guard it, and White keeps the centre.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 3...Bg4 pins the f3 knight but ignores the centre: 4.h3 Bh5 5.Nc3 e6 6.g4 Bg6 gains kingside space with tempo on your bishop.
alternatives.after: 3...Nxe4 wins a pawn; 3...Bg4 lets 5.Nc3 guard e4 and lets White chase the bishop with 6.g4.

6457800965205690|d8f6.headline: Block the bishop's line to f7 with 4...d5, not the queen
6457800965205690|d8f6.why: 4...Qf6 brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home, and it becomes a target: after 5.Nf3 Be7 6.d4 Qf5 7.d5 White develops and gains space while the queen keeps moving. 4...d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and cuts it off from f7, supports the knight on e4 and frees the c8 bishop. After 5.Be2 Bd6 6.Nf3 O-O Black is comfortably developed.
6457800965205690|d8f6.principle: Meet pressure on f7 with a pawn move that blocks and attacks, not by bringing the queen out where White develops against it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

6457800965205690|e4g5.headline: Strike back with 4...d5; 4...Ng5 loses time and a pawn.
6457800965205690|e4g5.why: 4...Ng5 moves the knight again with three minor pieces still at home, and after 5.d4 d5 6.Bxg5 Qxg5 7.Bxd5 White has won a pawn and leads in development. 4...d5 claims the centre and attacks the bishop on c4, so Black catches up with gain of time; after 5.Be2 Bd6 6.Nf3 O-O Black's pieces come out freely.
6457800965205690|e4g5.principle: Answer with a pawn move that attacks a piece and opens lines for your own, instead of moving the same knight yet again.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

6457800965205690|f7f6.headline: Hit the c4 bishop with 4...d5; 4...f6 opens your king
6457800965205690|f7f6.why: 4...f6 kicks the e5 knight but opens the diagonal from h5 to your king: after 5.Qh5+ g6 6.Nxg6 Qe7 the knight goes on to take your rook with 7.Nxh8+. 4...d5 is the theory's answer to 4.Nxe5: it gives Black a strong grip on the centre with the e4 knight already there, and attacks the c4 bishop so White has to move it to a worse square.
6457800965205690|f7f6.principle: Answer an attack with a central move that hits something, so your opponent has to respond instead of attacking you.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Bc4/3...Nxe4

6474108653422325|g2g4.headline: Castle with 4.O-O instead of lunging with 4.g4
6474108653422325|g2g4.why: 4.g4 defends nothing and loosens your kingside. After 4...Nf6 the knight hits e4 and g4 at once, and 5.h3 Nxe4 leaves you a pawn down with holes around your king. 4.O-O tucks your king away, and 5.Re1 guards e4 before ...Nf6 can win it. After 4...c5 5.Re1 Nf6 6.h3 O-O 7.d3 your centre is solid and your bishop still eyes f7; masters castle here in 53.8% of games.
6474108653422325|g2g4.principle: Castle and cover your centre before pushing flank pawns: 4.g4 leaves e4 and your king loose, while 4.O-O and 5.Re1 look after both.

ideas.title: f7 is the target

ideas.title: Black closes f7 with ...e6
ideas.text: ...e6 shuts your bishop out of f7, as after 4.Ng5 e6, so an early knight raid achieves nothing.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Black answers slow set-ups by hitting your centre with ...c5, as in 4.O-O c5.

habit.why: 4.g4 defends nothing and loosens your kingside. After 4...Nf6 the knight hits e4 and g4 at once, and 5.h3 Nxe4 leaves you a pawn down with holes around your king.

strays.text: 4.g4 adds a second target for 4...Nf6 and leaves e4 to fall.

taught.why: 4.O-O tucks your king away, and 5.Re1 guards e4 before ...Nf6 can win it. After 4...c5 5.Re1 Nf6 6.h3 O-O 7.d3 your centre is solid and your bishop still eyes f7; masters castle here in 53.8% of games.

enforces.text: Castling lets the rook guard e4 from e1 at once.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Ng5 attacks f7 with only two pieces, and 4...e6 shuts your bishop out and covers it. After 5.d4 Nf6 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.Bb5 the knight soon goes back home with 8.Nf3.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O develops and keeps the f7 ideas for when Black slips, while 4.Ng5 runs into 4...e6 and costs two knight moves.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
alternatives.before: 4.d4 takes the centre and reaches the Mad Dog set-up GM Illingworth covers: 4...Nf6 5.Qe2 prepares the sharp 6.e5. Good, though masters more often choose another move.
alternatives.after: Masters prefer 4.O-O (53.8% to 25.6%) and a quiet game with 5.Re1 and 7.d3; 4.d4 is sharper, aiming for 6.e5. The engine rates them equal.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
alternatives.before: 4.d3 guards e4 but is passive: after 4...Nf6 5.a4 Black gets 6...c5 and 7...Nc6 with easy equality.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O keeps both d3 and d4 open for later, so you can still take the centre; 4.d3 commits to a slow set-up at once.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it
alternatives.before: 4.c3 prepares d4, but after 4...Nf6 5.Qe2 c5 Black strikes back, and 7.d4 cxd4 8.cxd4 d5 frees the game.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O gets your king safe first; in the 4.c3 line Black's 8...d5 hits e4 while your king is still in the centre.

6499681702415085|d8h4.headline: Against 2.Qh5, defend e5 with 2...Nc6, never offer queens
6499681702415085|d8h4.why: 2...Qh4 puts the queen where nothing defends it, so 3.Qxh4 simply wins it. 2.Qh5 attacks e5 and eyes f7; 2...Nc6 defends e5 while developing, and Black can later gain time by attacking the exposed queen. Masters choose it in 89.6% of games.
6499681702415085|d8h4.principle: Before putting your queen next to the enemy queen, check what defends the square: nothing covers h4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

6499681702415085|g7g6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6 before you chase the queen
6499681702415085|g7g6.why: 2...g6 attacks the queen but leaves e5 hanging: 3.Qxe5+ checks the king and hits the rook on h8 at the same time, so Black loses the rook in the corner. 2...Nc6 defends e5 while developing the knight to its most active square. If White follows with 3.Bc4, Black answers 3...g6 and 4...Nf6, blocking the queen's view of f7 and gaining time on it.
6499681702415085|g7g6.principle: The queen on h5 already attacks the e5 pawn, so cover that loose pawn first; only then gain time by attacking the queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...g6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

6499681702415085|g8h6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6; 2...Nh6 drops it with check.
6499681702415085|g8h6.why: White's queen attacks e5 as well as f7, and 2...Nh6 guards neither: 3.Qxe5+ wins the pawn with check, and after 3...Qe7 4.Qxe7+ Bxe7 Black is simply a pawn down. 2...Nc6 defends e5 and develops the knight to its best square. Against 3.Bc4, Black then gains time on the queen with ...g6 and ...Nf6.
6499681702415085|g8h6.principle: Against an early queen, first make sure everything it attacks is defended, then develop with gain of time against it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

6508411408913645|f8c5.headline: Defend e5 with 3...Nc6; the bishop move leaves it hanging
6508411408913645|f8c5.why: 3...Bc5 leaves e5 undefended, and 4.Nxe5 takes it. Black can regain the pawn with 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4, but that costs the dark-squared bishop and White develops quickly with 7.Bd3. 3...Nc6 protects e5 with a developing move and reaches the Four Knights Game, Black's most common answer here.
6508411408913645|f8c5.principle: Once White's knight is on f3, check whether e5 is defended before anything else, and protect it with a piece that also develops.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

6510830178396203|b2b4.headline: 7.Qb3 hits the d5 knight twice and wins e5 through a pin
6510830178396203|b2b4.why: 7.b4 grabs queenside space, but with the centre open it just becomes a target: 7...Be7 8.O-O O-O 9.Re1 Bf6 10.a4 Ndxb4 wins the pawn. The d5 knight stays active and you have nothing for it. 7.Qb3 attacks the d5 knight a second time, and 7...Na5 hits queen and bishop. Then 8.Qa4+ Nc6 pins the knight to the king, and 9.Nxe5 wins the e5 pawn.
6510830178396203|b2b4.principle: Make moves that create threats: 7.Qb3 hits the d5 knight twice, and after 8.Qa4+ the pinned c6 knight can't guard e5.
sources: Evan's Gambit (How To Play It, Attack It, And Counter It), Simplify Chess | https://www.simplifychess.com/evans-gambit/index.html

ideas.title: Line up Qb3 with the bishop
ideas.text: 7.Qb3 joins the c4 bishop against the d5 knight, attacking it twice, with f7 behind it.

ideas.title: Pin the c6 knight
ideas.text: After 7...Na5 8.Qa4+ Nc6 the knight is pinned to the king, so 9.Nxe5 wins the pawn it was guarding.

ideas.title: ...Na5 chases the bishop
ideas.text: Black's c6 knight can jump to a5 to hit your queen and c4 bishop, as in 7...Na5. Answer it with a check.

ideas.title: Loose pawns become targets
ideas.text: With the centre open and the d5 knight active, a pawn on b4 is easy to hit: 9...Bf6 and 10...Ndxb4 win it.

habit.why: 7.b4 grabs queenside space, but with the centre open it just becomes a target: 7...Be7 8.O-O O-O 9.Re1 Bf6 10.a4 Ndxb4 wins the pawn. The d5 knight stays active and you have nothing for it.

strays.text: The b4 pawn is loose, and Black wins it with 10...Ndxb4.

taught.why: 7.Qb3 attacks the d5 knight a second time, and 7...Na5 hits queen and bishop. Then 8.Qa4+ Nc6 pins the knight to the king, and 9.Nxe5 wins the e5 pawn.

enforces.text: 8.Qa4+ pins the c6 knight, so it can no longer guard e5.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: Castling is natural but gives Black time for 7...Nb6, which kicks your bishop off its diagonal; after 8.Bb5 Bd6 9.d4 O-O the game is level.
alternatives.after: 7.Qb3 uses the moment while the d5 knight can be hit twice; after castling Black retreats it with tempo and the chance is gone.
alternatives.idea: Line up Qb3 with the bishop

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 7.h3 stops a bishop pin on g4 but is too slow: 7...Nb6 kicks your bishop, and 8.Bb3 Qf6 develops with pressure on your f3 knight.
alternatives.after: 7.Qb3 makes a threat instead of a waiting move, and wins the e5 pawn after 8.Qa4+ and 9.Nxe5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qe2 hits e5, but 7...Be6 calmly covers d5; after 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Qxe5 Qd7 10.Bxd5 Qxd5 11.Qxd5 Bxd5 the queens are off and Black's bishop pair makes up for the pawn.
alternatives.after: 7.Qb3 attacks the d5 knight twice and wins e5 with the queens still on, which keeps your edge.
alternatives.idea: Line up Qb3 with the bishop

6511980734057505|h2h3.headline: Settle the centre with 5.cxd5 before ...cxd4 hits your loose pieces
6511980734057505|h2h3.why: 5.h3 ignores the centre: after 5...cxd4 your king's diagonal is open, so ...Qa5+ is coming, and retaking with the knight leaves c4 to ...dxc4 because the f1-bishop can't guard it. In the line 6.a3 Qa5+ 7.Qd2 Nc6 8.Qxa5 Nxa5 9.Nxd4 Nxc4 Black wins your c4 pawn. 5.cxd5 releases the tension before ...cxd4 can hit your king's diagonal or c4. After 5...Nxd5 6.Bg5 Be7 7.Bxe7 Qxe7 8.dxc5 Qxc5 9.e3 pieces come off and the game is level and safe.
6511980734057505|h2h3.principle: Ask what Black wants, here ...cxd4 and ...Qa5+, and deal with it: 5.cxd5 or 5.e3 does, while 5.h3 does nothing about it.
sources: Queen's Gambit Declined - Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen%27s_Gambit_Declined

ideas.title: Settle the centre first
ideas.text: c4 and d4 are both attacked and your king's diagonal is open. cxd5 releases the tension before ...cxd4 can hit you.

ideas.title: The a5-e1 diagonal
ideas.text: Without 5.e3 or 5.Nc3, ...cxd4 opens the way for ...Qa5+ or ...Bb4+, and the queen check can win your c4 pawn.

ideas.title: e3 shuts the diagonal
ideas.text: e3 blocks the a5-e1 diagonal, lets you retake on d4 with a pawn and lets the f1-bishop guard c4.

habit.why: 5.h3 ignores the centre: after 5...cxd4 your king's diagonal is open, so ...Qa5+ is coming, and retaking with the knight leaves c4 to ...dxc4 because the f1-bishop can't guard it. In the line 6.a3 Qa5+ 7.Qd2 Nc6 8.Qxa5 Nxa5 9.Nxd4 Nxc4 Black wins your c4 pawn.

strays.text: h3 leaves c4 and d4 under fire and your king's diagonal open.

taught.why: 5.cxd5 releases the tension before ...cxd4 can hit your king's diagonal or c4. After 5...Nxd5 6.Bg5 Be7 7.Bxe7 Qxe7 8.dxc5 Qxc5 9.e3 pieces come off and the game is level and safe.

enforces.text: Taking on d5 ends the tension before Black can use ...cxd4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: The natural move: it shuts the a5-e1 diagonal and lets you retake on d4 with a pawn, as in 5...cxd4 6.exd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3. The engine slightly prefers another move.
alternatives.after: 5.cxd5 and 5.e3 are close. 5.cxd5 trades pieces at once, while 5.e3 keeps more tension and gives a Tarrasch-like centre after 6.exd4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: It develops and blocks the a5-e1 diagonal on c3; after 5...cxd4 6.Nxd4 you retake with a piece. The engine slightly prefers another move.
alternatives.after: Both are fine. 5.cxd5 settles the centre first, while 5.Nc3 keeps the tension and more pieces on, as in 6...Nbd7 7.Qa4 Bc5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Releasing the tension this way is fine: after 5...Bxc5 6.e3 you reach a standard structure with your bishop on f4. The engine slightly prefers another move.
alternatives.after: Both release the tension. 5.cxd5 trades bishops at once; after 5.dxc5 Bxc5 6.e3 O-O 7.a3 dxc4 8.Bxc4 Qxd1+ the queens come off instead.

6545901527067225|d4e5.headline: Develop against the early queen with 4.Nc3; keep the tension
6545901527067225|d4e5.why: 4.dxe5 dxe5 trades your central pressure for a level centre, because with the queen on f6 Black's d-pawn can safely recapture. After 5.Nc3 Bd6 6.Bg5 Qe6 Black's bishop has d6, the queen stands safely, and more than half your edge is gone. 4.Nc3 develops and keeps the tension, with 5.Bg5 coming and the knight eyeing d5, both against the queen on f6. After 4...Nc6 5.Bg5 Qg6 6.h4 f6 7.h5 Qf7 Black's queen has made three moves and the f6 pawn blocks Black's kingside.
6545901527067225|d4e5.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, keep the position tense and develop pieces that attack it, gaining time with each move.
sources: Lessons: Philidor's Defence (Exeter Chess Club) | https://www.exeterchessclub.org.uk/content/lessons-philidors-defence
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4

ideas.title: Keep the d4/e5 tension
ideas.text: dxe5 usually works because ...dxe5 drops the queen on d8. With Black's queen on f6 that pin is gone, so keep the tension.

ideas.title: Gain time on the queen
ideas.text: The early queen on f6 is a target: 4.Nc3 eyes d5 and 5.Bg5 hits the queen, each move developing with tempo.

ideas.title: Black's cramped Philidor set-up
ideas.text: 3...Qf6 takes the g8-knight's best square, and the f8-bishop has only e7. Trading on e5 frees d6 for it.

habit.why: 4.dxe5 dxe5 trades your central pressure for a level centre, because with the queen on f6 Black's d-pawn can safely recapture. After 5.Nc3 Bd6 6.Bg5 Qe6 Black's bishop has d6, the queen stands safely, and more than half your edge is gone.

strays.text: The trade lets Black's d-pawn recapture and frees d6 for the bishop.

taught.why: 4.Nc3 develops and keeps the tension, with 5.Bg5 coming and the knight eyeing d5, both against the queen on f6. After 4...Nc6 5.Bg5 Qg6 6.h4 f6 7.h5 Qf7 Black's queen has made three moves and the f6 pawn blocks Black's kingside.

enforces.text: 5.Bg5 and 6.h4 chase the queen while you develop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Bg5 hits the queen at once and gains a tempo, as the Exeter lesson suggests: after 4...Qe6 you follow with 6.Qd2 and 7.O-O-O. A slightly stronger move exists.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 keeps 4.Bg5 in reserve and eyes d5 with the knight, so the queen can be hit from two sides; the engine rates the two moves nearly the same.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4.d5 closes the centre, so e5 is safe and the queen simply goes home: 4...Qd8 5.c4 a5 and Black has lost no time.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 keeps the d4 pawn pressing on e5, so Black's queen stays a target instead of retreating for free.

6574951213252263|e7e5.headline: Against the Austrian, fianchetto first: ...e5 just loses a pawn
6574951213252263|e7e5.why: 4...e5 loses a pawn: after 5.dxe5 your knight is hit, and taking back only trades queens before the f-pawn retakes and hits f6 again. So 5...Nh5 6.Nf3 leaves you a pawn down with your knight on the rim. 4...Bg7 is the main move (99% of masters): it develops and aims the bishop at d4 and e5. After 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Bd3 Nc6 your king is safe and you hit the centre later, here with 7...Nb4 and 8...d5.
6574951213252263|e7e5.principle: Develop before you strike: against pawns on d4, e4 and f4, 4...Bg7 and castling come before any central break.
sources: Sean Marsh, Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/
James Vigus, Chess Developments: The Pirc (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-chess-developments-the-pirc.pdf
Pirc Defence, Austrian Attack - Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirc_Defence,_Austrian_Attack

ideas.title: f4 backs up e5
ideas.text: With a pawn on f4, White can retake on e5 with a pawn and hit your f6 knight. An early ...e5 drops a pawn.

ideas.title: Bg7, castle, then c7-c5
ideas.text: Against the Austrian, play ...Bg7 and castle first. Your break comes later, usually with c7-c5 against d4.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then strike
ideas.text: You let White build pawns on d4, e4 and f4, then attack them from the side. White hopes the big centre holds.

habit.why: 4...e5 loses a pawn: after 5.dxe5 your knight is hit, and taking back only trades queens before the f-pawn retakes and hits f6 again. So 5...Nh5 6.Nf3 leaves you a pawn down with your knight on the rim.

strays.text: The f4 pawn makes this break lose a pawn.

taught.why: 4...Bg7 is the main move (99% of masters): it develops and aims the bishop at d4 and e5. After 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Bd3 Nc6 your king is safe and you hit the centre later, here with 7...Nb4 and 8...d5.

enforces.text: Bishop out and king castled before any central break.

6589282572039958|b8c6.headline: Attack e4 with 2...Nf6 instead of 2...Nc6
6589282572039958|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 puts the knight where a pawn can hit it: 3.d5 Nb8 sends it home and White gains space. After 4.Be3 g6 5.Qd2 Bg7 6.Nc3 White develops freely while you have lost two moves. 2...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White guards it with 3.Nc3 instead of gaining space. After 3...e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 you reach a solid Philidor set-up, and masters choose 2...Nf6 83% of the time.
6589282572039958|b8c6.principle: Develop with threats: 2...Nf6 makes White defend e4, while 2...Nc6 hands White a free 3.d5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4 (Wikibooks) | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...d6/2._d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6 (Wikibooks) | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...d6/2._d4/2...Nf6

ideas.title: Guard e4 before anything else
ideas.text: 2...Nf6 hits e4, and since the e-pawn can't safely advance yet, White usually spends a move guarding it with 3.Nc3.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: You let White keep e4 and d4, then hit them from the side, here with 3...e5 after 3.Nc3.

ideas.title: White gains space with d5
ideas.text: A knight on c6 can be kicked: 3.d5 sends it back to b8 and White gains space for free.

habit.why: 2...Nc6 puts the knight where a pawn can hit it: 3.d5 Nb8 sends it home and White gains space. After 4.Be3 g6 5.Qd2 Bg7 6.Nc3 White develops freely while you have lost two moves.

strays.text: The knight on c6 invites 3.d5, which gains space with tempo.

taught.why: 2...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White guards it with 3.Nc3 instead of gaining space. After 3...e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 you reach a solid Philidor set-up, and masters choose 2...Nf6 83% of the time.

enforces.text: The knight hits e4, so White must defend it first.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2...g6 prepares ...Bg7 against d4 and leads to the Modern Defence, played by masters 14% of the time. The engine marks it a mistake here because White develops freely with 4.Be3 and 5.Qd2.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 makes White answer a threat to e4; 2...g6 lets White pick a set-up, here the 4.Be3 and 5.Qd2 plan.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2...e6 is passive: White builds a big centre with 4.Bd3 and 5.c4, and 7.d5 gains even more space.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 develops with a threat to e4; 2...e6 makes none and gives White time for 5.c4.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2...c6 makes no threat, so White develops freely with 3.Nf3 and 4.Nc3 and grabs queenside space with 5.a4 and 7.a5.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 attacks e4 at once; 2...c6 attacks nothing, so White has time for a4 and a5.

6593387168284860|b1c3.headline: Push 4.e5: kick the knight, then take back on c4
6593387168284860|b1c3.why: 4.Nc3 defends e4 but lets Black strike at d4 with 4...e5. After 5.Nf3 exd4 6.Qxd4 Qxd4 7.Nxd4 Bc5 8.Ndb5 Na6 the queens are off, c4 still isn't won back and Black is comfortable. 4.e5 hits the f6-knight, and after 4...Nd5 5.Bxc4 you've won the pawn back with more space. After 5...Nb6 6.Bd3 Nc6 7.Ne2 your e5 pawn cramps Black; masters choose 4.e5 93% of the time.
6593387168284860|b1c3.principle: Chase an undefended knight with a pawn: 4.e5 gains space and sends the f6-knight away before you win back c4.
sources: Queen's Gambit Accepted - Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Gambit_Accepted
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. e4 (Wikibooks) | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._d4/1...d5/2._c4/2...dxc4/3._e4
Queen's Gambit Accepted: Central Variation, Alekhine System (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/queens-gambit-accepted/central-variation-alekhine-system/
QGA 3.e4 Nf6 4.e5 Nd5 snippets (Seirawan, Chess Duels; Kasparov) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=Queen%27s+Gambit+Accepted+%223+e4%22+%22Nf6%22+%224+e5%22+%22Nd5%22+%22Bxc4%22

ideas.title: e4-e5 kicks the f6 knight
ideas.text: Black has no d-pawn left to take on e5, so 4.e5 drives the knight from f6 with tempo and gains space.

ideas.title: Win back c4
ideas.text: Black can rarely keep c4: after 4.e5 Nd5 5.Bxc4 you have the pawn back and more space.

ideas.title: Black's ...e5 strike
ideas.text: Given a free move, Black hits d4 with ...e5, as after 4.Nc3 e5 5.Nf3 exd4, and trades queens.

ideas.title: e4 needs a defender
ideas.text: The f6-knight attacks e4 and nothing guards it, so 4.Bxc4 drops it to 4...Nxe4.

habit.why: 4.Nc3 defends e4 but lets Black strike at d4 with 4...e5. After 5.Nf3 exd4 6.Qxd4 Qxd4 7.Nxd4 Bc5 8.Ndb5 Na6 the queens are off, c4 still isn't won back and Black is comfortable.

strays.text: You guard e4 instead of pushing it, so Black gets ...e5 in.

taught.why: 4.e5 hits the f6-knight, and after 4...Nd5 5.Bxc4 you've won the pawn back with more space. After 5...Nb6 6.Bd3 Nc6 7.Ne2 your e5 pawn cramps Black; masters choose 4.e5 93% of the time.

enforces.text: 4.e5 gains space with tempo, then 5.Bxc4 regains the pawn.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Bxc4 wins back the pawn but leaves e4 with no defender. After 4...Nxe4 5.Nf3 g6 6.O-O Bg7 Black has taken a pawn and stands well.
alternatives.after: 4.e5 moves the attacked pawn forward with tempo, so 5.Bxc4 wins c4 back without dropping e4.

6601544122617741|c2c4.headline: Take the gambit pawn with 3.dxc6, then just develop
6601544122617741|c2c4.why: 3.c4 holds d5 only for a moment: 3...Nf6 4.Nc3 cxd5 5.d4 wins the pawn back in a Panov-Botvinnik structure. After 6.Nf3 Bg4 7.cxd5 Nxd5 Black has easy development and pressure on d4. 3.dxc6 takes a second pawn, and after 3...Nxc6 4.Nf3 e5 5.Nc3 Nf6 you simply develop. 6.Bb5 pins the c6 knight, and after 7.d4 e4 you are a pawn up with your pieces out.
6601544122617741|c2c4.principle: Accept a gambit pawn when you can simply develop afterwards; propping up the old one just hands it back.
sources: Scandinavian Defense: Blackburne-Kloosterboer Gambit (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/scandinavian-defense/blackburne-kloosterboer-gambit/
Marek Soszynski, Double Trouble Scandinavian Style | https://books.google.com/books?id=TS8WEQAAQBAJ
Scandinavian Defense (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_Defense

ideas.title: Grab the gambit pawn
ideas.text: Black offers a second pawn. Take it with 3.dxc6, then develop normally, as with 4.Nf3, 5.Nc3 and 6.Bb5.

ideas.title: Black wins back d5
ideas.text: If you don't take, the pawn comes back: after 3.c4 Nf6 4.Nc3 cxd5 it is a Panov-Botvinnik structure.

ideas.title: Development for a pawn
ideas.text: After 3.dxc6 Nxc6 4.Nf3 e5 Black gets quick development. The gambit is thought unsound: develop and stay a pawn up.

ideas.title: Pin with Bb5
ideas.text: In the main line 6.Bb5 pins the c6 knight to Black's king, because Black's d-pawn is gone.

habit.why: 3.c4 holds d5 only for a moment: 3...Nf6 4.Nc3 cxd5 5.d4 wins the pawn back in a Panov-Botvinnik structure. After 6.Nf3 Bg4 7.cxd5 Nxd5 Black has easy development and pressure on d4.

strays.text: Propping up d5 fails; 4...cxd5 takes the pawn back anyway.

taught.why: 3.dxc6 takes a second pawn, and after 3...Nxc6 4.Nf3 e5 5.Nc3 Nf6 you simply develop. 6.Bb5 pins the c6 knight, and after 7.d4 e4 you are a pawn up with your pieces out.

enforces.text: You take the pawn and develop; Black's activity doesn't make up for it.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 develops but doesn't hold d5: after 3...cxd5 4.d4 Nc6 Black has the pawn back in a Caro-Kann Exchange-type position.
alternatives.after: 3.dxc6 keeps you a pawn up; 3.Nc3 lets Black regain it at once with 3...cxd5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.d4 lets Black take back with 3...cxd5, which is exactly a Caro-Kann Exchange: the pawn is returned for nothing.
alternatives.after: 3.dxc6 keeps the extra pawn. Masters played 3.d4 in a quarter of these 32 games, but 3.dxc6 (69%) is both their main choice and the engine's.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.Nf3 allows 3...cxd5, and after 4.d4 Nf6 Black has regained the pawn with a normal game.
alternatives.after: 3.dxc6 banks a second pawn instead; after 3.Nf3 cxd5 the gambit has done its job for Black.

6601544122617741|d2d4.headline: Take the gambit pawn with 3.dxc6, then just develop
6601544122617741|d2d4.why: 3.d4 leaves d5 to 3...cxd5, so the pawn is simply back and Black has no worries. After 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.c4 Nf6 6.Nc3 Bg4 Black's pieces are out and pressing on d4. 3.dxc6 takes a second pawn, and after 3...Nxc6 4.Nf3 e5 5.Nc3 Nf6 you simply develop. 6.Bb5 pins the c6 knight, and after 7.d4 e4 you are a pawn up with your pieces out.
6601544122617741|d2d4.principle: Accept a gambit pawn when you can simply develop afterwards; declining hands the material back for nothing.
sources: Scandinavian Defense: Blackburne-Kloosterboer Gambit (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/scandinavian-defense/blackburne-kloosterboer-gambit/
Scandinavian Defense (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_Defense

ideas.title: Grab the gambit pawn
ideas.text: Black offers a second pawn. Take it with 3.dxc6, then develop normally, as with 4.Nf3, 5.Nc3 and 6.Bb5.

ideas.title: Black wins back d5
ideas.text: If you don't take, 3...cxd5 wins the pawn back; after 3.d4 cxd5 you are simply in a Caro-Kann Exchange.

ideas.title: Development for a pawn
ideas.text: After 3.dxc6 Nxc6 4.Nf3 e5 Black gets quick development. The gambit is thought unsound: develop and stay a pawn up.

ideas.title: Pin with Bb5
ideas.text: In the main line 6.Bb5 pins the c6 knight to Black's king, because Black's d-pawn is gone.

habit.why: 3.d4 leaves d5 to 3...cxd5, so the pawn is simply back and Black has no worries. After 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.c4 Nf6 6.Nc3 Bg4 Black's pieces are out and pressing on d4.

strays.text: You turn down a free pawn and reach an ordinary Caro-Kann Exchange.

taught.why: 3.dxc6 takes a second pawn, and after 3...Nxc6 4.Nf3 e5 5.Nc3 Nf6 you simply develop. 6.Bb5 pins the c6 knight, and after 7.d4 e4 you are a pawn up with your pieces out.

enforces.text: You take the pawn and develop; Black's activity doesn't make up for it.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 develops but doesn't hold d5: after 3...cxd5 4.d4 Nc6 Black has the pawn back in a Caro-Kann Exchange-type position.
alternatives.after: 3.dxc6 keeps you a pawn up; 3.Nc3 lets Black regain it at once with 3...cxd5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.Nf3 allows 3...cxd5, and after 4.d4 Nf6 Black has regained the pawn with a normal game.
alternatives.after: 3.dxc6 banks a second pawn instead; after 3.Nf3 cxd5 the gambit has done its job for Black.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 3.c4 holds d5 only for a moment: after 3...Nf6 4.Nc3 cxd5 5.d4 you reach a Panov-Botvinnik structure with level material.
alternatives.after: 3.dxc6 is what masters play (69% of games); 3.c4 gives the pawn back by a slower route.

6606016440769341|g5f7.headline: Black has castled: f7 is guarded twice, so don't sacrifice
6606016440769341|g5f7.why: 6.Nxf7 runs into 6...Rxf7 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7, and you have given two minor pieces for a rook and pawn while Black's king stays safe. After 8.h3 Kg8 9.f4 Be6 10.O-O exf4 Black's extra piece counts and you are clearly worse. 6.a3 is a quiet, useful move: it gives your bishop a2 against ...Na5 or ...b5 before the knight goes back. After 6...Nc6 7.Nf3 d5 8.exd5 Nxd5 9.h3 the game is level and your pieces are intact.
6606016440769341|g5f7.principle: f7 is attacked twice and defended twice by rook and king, so the captures only swap two minor pieces for a rook and pawn; count before you sacrifice.
sources: NM Jeremy Kane, Bad Trades Amateurs Make In Chess (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/bad-trades-amateurs-make-in-chess
Philidor Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philidor_Defence
