ideas.title: Don't rush at f7
ideas.text: With Black castled, rook and king guard f7: 6.Nxf7 Rxf7 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives two minor pieces for rook and pawn.

ideas.title: Bring the knight back
ideas.text: Once Black castles, the knight on g5 has no target; Black is fine here. Bring it back, as with 7.Nf3.

ideas.title: Keep the bishop safe
ideas.text: 6.a3 gives your c4-bishop a retreat on a2, out of reach of ...Na5, ...b5 or ...d5.

habit.why: 6.Nxf7 runs into 6...Rxf7 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7, and you have given two minor pieces for a rook and pawn while Black's king stays safe. After 8.h3 Kg8 9.f4 Be6 10.O-O exf4 Black's extra piece counts and you are clearly worse.

strays.text: Rook and king guard f7, so you give two pieces for a rook.

taught.why: 6.a3 is a quiet, useful move: it gives your bishop a2 against ...Na5 or ...b5 before the knight goes back. After 6...Nc6 7.Nf3 d5 8.exd5 Nxd5 9.h3 the game is level and your pieces are intact.

enforces.text: The bishop gets a2 to retreat to before Black can hit it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.O-O is sound: your king gets safe and the knight returns with 7.Nf3, and after 7...b5 8.Bb3 the game stays level. A slightly better move exists.
alternatives.after: 6.a3 makes room for the bishop before ...b5 hits it; the engine rates the two moves almost the same.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Nc3 develops and keeps the game level, but after 6...Nc6 7.Nf3 Na5 8.Bb3 Black's knight comes for your bishop. A slightly better move exists.
alternatives.after: 6.a3 lets the bishop retreat to a2, out of the knight's reach; after 6.Nc3 Black gets 10...Nxb3 and the bishop pair.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.h4 is an attacking gesture with no follow-up: 6...h6 kicks the knight, and your h-pawn has only loosened your king.
alternatives.after: 6.a3 is the useful quiet move; 6.h4 commits a pawn and still needs 7.a3 afterwards.

6613050291850908|f6g4.headline: Take on e5 first; the knight jump comes later
6613050291850908|f6g4.why: 5...Ng4 moves the knight again, and with d4 guarding e5 it attacks nothing. After 6.h3 Nh6 7.Bf4 your knight sits on the rim while White keeps the e5 pawn and develops freely. 5...dxe5 removes the pawn that attacks f6 before it can cramp you. After 6.Nxe5 O-O 7.Be3 c5 you finish developing and hit d4 too, and the game is about level.
6613050291850908|f6g4.principle: Meet an early e5 in the centre: 5...dxe5 takes away the pawn that hits f6, instead of moving the knight a second time.
sources: Sean Marsh, Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/
Igor Smirnov, Beat the Pirc Defense with This Trap! | https://chess-teacher.com/beat-the-pirc-defense-with-this-trap/

ideas.title: Early e5: trade queens first
ideas.text: Answer 5.e5 with 5...dxe5. If White retakes with the d-pawn, you trade queens on d1 and the knight hits e5 from g4.

ideas.title: A lone e5 pawn is a target
ideas.text: While d4 guards e5, a knight on g4 attacks nothing and gets kicked by 6.h3. Take away the d4 support first.

ideas.title: The e5 push hits f6
ideas.text: 5.e5 threatens 6.exf6. Moving the knight lets White keep the cramping pawn, and after 6.h3 Nh6 your knight is on the rim.

habit.why: 5...Ng4 moves the knight again, and with d4 guarding e5 it attacks nothing. After 6.h3 Nh6 7.Bf4 your knight sits on the rim while White keeps the e5 pawn and develops freely.

strays.idea: A lone e5 pawn is a target
strays.text: With d4 still guarding e5, the knight has nothing to hit.

taught.why: 5...dxe5 removes the pawn that attacks f6 before it can cramp you. After 6.Nxe5 O-O 7.Be3 c5 you finish developing and hit d4 too, and the game is about level.

enforces.text: Capture on e5 first, so the pawn never gets settled there.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Nfd7 is sound: the knight steps aside and your g7 bishop now presses e5. After 6.Qe2 and 7...Nb6 the knight is a bit passive, though, and there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 5...dxe5 is stronger: it removes the e5 pawn at once. After 6.Nxe5 O-O 7.Be3 c5 you develop quickly and hit d4.

6621416387177535|d7d6.headline: Question the Spanish bishop with 3...a6 instead of pinning yourself
6621416387177535|d7d6.why: 3...d6 defends a pawn that was not really at risk and pins Black's own knight on c6 against the king, so after 4.d4 Black must either give up the centre with 4...exd4 or defend passively with ...Bd7. 3...a6, the Morphy defence, puts the question to the bishop at once: after 4.Ba4 Nf6 Black develops normally and can end the pressure on the knight with ...b5 when needed.
6621416387177535|d7d6.principle: When a bishop on b5 eyes your knight on c6, keep it from turning into a real pin: question the bishop with the a-pawn rather than locking the pin with d6.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...d6

6621416387177535|f7f6.headline: Question the bishop with 3...a6; e5 doesn't need ...f6
6621416387177535|f7f6.why: 3...f6 guards a pawn that wasn't hanging, takes the f6 square from your knight and weakens your king's diagonal. White just opens the centre with 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4, and after 5...Nge7 6.Be3 White develops freely while your knight sits on e7. 3...a6 makes the bishop decide: take on c6 or retreat. After 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O b5 6.Bb3 Bc5 your knight sits on f6 and the bishop no longer presses on c6; 71% of masters choose 3...a6.
6621416387177535|f7f6.principle: A pawn move in the opening should free a piece or gain time; one that takes your knight's best square only creates a weakness.
sources: IM Jeremy Silman, Readers' Games, Questions and Comments, Part 3 (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/readersrsquo-games-questions-and-comments-part-3?page=2

ideas.title: Bxc6 and Nxe5 is not yet a threat
ideas.text: e5 isn't hanging: after 4.Bxc6 dxc6 5.Nxe5 Qd4 you win the pawn back, so it needs no extra guard.

ideas.title: Weakening pawn moves invite punishment
ideas.text: 3...f6 doesn't develop, takes f6 from your g8 knight and weakens the diagonal to your king.

ideas.title: Put the question to the bishop
ideas.text: 3...a6 makes the bishop take or retreat. After 4.Ba4 Nf6 you can end the pressure with 5...b5 when you like.

ideas.title: Develop fast and open the centre
ideas.text: Against a weakening move White develops and opens lines with d4, as in 3...f6 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4.

habit.why: 3...f6 guards a pawn that wasn't hanging, takes the f6 square from your knight and weakens your king's diagonal. White just opens the centre with 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4, and after 5...Nge7 6.Be3 White develops freely while your knight sits on e7.

strays.text: It guards nothing that needed guarding and takes f6 from your knight.

taught.why: 3...a6 makes the bishop decide: take on c6 or retreat. After 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O b5 6.Bb3 Bc5 your knight sits on f6 and the bishop no longer presses on c6; 71% of masters choose 3...a6.

enforces.idea: Put the question to the bishop
enforces.text: The bishop must take or retreat, and your knight keeps f6.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...d6 holds e5 solidly but passively: after 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Bd7 you have given up the centre and stay a bit cramped.
alternatives.after: 3...a6 needs no guard for e5 because of the 5...Qd4 trick, and keeps the f8 bishop free. Masters choose it 71% of the time, 3...d6 0.4%.
alternatives.idea: Bxc6 and Nxe5 is not yet a threat

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Nf6, the Berlin, develops and hits e4, since e5 isn't really in danger. It is solid and played by 20% of masters; one move is more popular still.
alternatives.after: 3...a6 first asks the bishop's intention and keeps 5...b5 in reserve. Masters choose it 71% of the time, the Berlin 20%; the engine rates both about equal.
alternatives.idea: Bxc6 and Nxe5 is not yet a threat

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...Bc5 develops actively but does nothing about the long-term pressure on e5, and White's c3 and d4 can hit the bishop: 4.c3 Nf6 5.O-O O-O 6.d4 Bb6.
alternatives.after: 3...a6 forces the bishop's decision first. With 3...Bc5 your bishop becomes a target for 4.c3 and 6.d4.
alternatives.idea: Bxc6 and Nxe5 is not yet a threat

6658785597570768|f7f6.headline: Block the mate with a knight: 3...Nf6, not ...f6.
6658785597570768|f7f6.why: White threatens 4.Qxf7#. 3...f6 stops it but takes the knight's best square and leaves the king stuck: after 4.Ne2 Bc5 5.Qg3 Black plays 5...Kf8 and gives up castling. 3...Nf6 blocks the queen's path to f7 with a developing move. Black stays ready to castle.
6658785597570768|f7f6.principle: When the queen and the bishop on c4 aim at f7, defend by developing a piece into the queen's path, not by moving the f-pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nc6

6658785597570768|g8h6.headline: Block the mate threat with 3...Nf6, the knight's central square
6658785597570768|g8h6.why: White threatens 4.Qxf7#, and both knight moves stop it, but 3...Nh6 puts the knight on the edge, where it guards f7 and little else. 3...Nf6 blocks the queen's line to f7, develops toward the centre and attacks e4. The queen on f3 also takes that square from White's own knight, so after 4.Ne2 Black is comfortable.
6658785597570768|g8h6.principle: When you have to parry a threat, pick the defence that also develops toward the centre: a knight on f6 blocks the queen and fights for e4 and d5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qf3

666558173554|g5f7.headline: Kick the knight with 6.c3; 6.Nxf7 just loses a piece
666558173554|g5f7.why: 6.Nxf7 gives a knight for a pawn: after 6...Kxf7 there is no queen check on f3, because the d4-knight covers that square. Black's king is safe enough, and 7.a4 Bd6 8.d3 Rf8 leaves you a piece down with no attack. 6.c3 attacks the d4-knight, which has few safe squares; masters choose it 94% of the time. After 6...b5 7.Bf1 Nxd5 8.Nxf7 Kxf7 9.cxd4 exd4 10.Qf3+ the same sacrifice works, because the d4-knight is gone and the queen check arrives.
666558173554|g5f7.principle: Chase a centralised knight with a pawn when it has few retreats: 6.c3 makes it decide before you think about f7.
sources: John Emms, First Steps: 1 e4 e5 | https://books.google.com/books?id=0VSZEQAAQBAJ

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: The Fried Liver sacrifice on f7 works because a queen check on f3 follows. Here the d4-knight covers f3, so it loses a piece.

ideas.title: Kick the d4-knight with c3
ideas.text: The d4-knight has few retreats. A pawn on c3 attacks it, and it is often traded off or lost.

ideas.title: Keep the extra pawn
ideas.text: After 5.exd5 you are a pawn up. Pushing it to d6 just gives it back.

ideas.title: Black gains time on your pieces
ideas.text: ...b5 can deflect your bishop, and ...h6 or ...Bg4 kicks and pins your knight; Black plays for time, not the pawn.

habit.why: 6.Nxf7 gives a knight for a pawn: after 6...Kxf7 there is no queen check on f3, because the d4-knight covers that square. Black's king is safe enough, and 7.a4 Bd6 8.d3 Rf8 leaves you a piece down with no attack.

strays.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
strays.text: No queen check follows, so the sacrifice only loses a piece.

taught.why: 6.c3 attacks the d4-knight, which has few safe squares; masters choose it 94% of the time. After 6...b5 7.Bf1 Nxd5 8.Nxf7 Kxf7 9.cxd4 exd4 10.Qf3+ the same sacrifice works, because the d4-knight is gone and the queen check arrives.

enforces.text: The pawn kick removes the knight that was guarding f3.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.d6 gives the extra pawn straight back: 6...Qxd6 develops Black's queen, and after 7.d3 Nd5 Black's knight heads for e6 to trade off your g5-knight. The engine finds it playable, but there is a better move.
alternatives.after: 6.c3 hits the knight first and keeps the pawn. Masters choose it 94% of the time against 3% for 6.d6, and sources call 6.d6 inferior.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.O-O ignores the d4-knight: 6...h6 7.Nf3 Bg4 pins your knight, and after the trades on f3 Black wins back d5 with 10...Qxd5.
alternatives.after: 6.c3 kicks the knight before ...Bg4 can add to the pressure on f3, so it must decide at once.
alternatives.idea: Black gains time on your pieces

6673250859790786|e7e6.headline: Take the second pawn: 4...cxb2 leaves White too little
6673250859790786|e7e6.why: 4...e6 lets White play 5.Nxc3, winning back the pawn while developing a knight. After 5...a6 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.O-O you are in a normal Morra, one pawn up instead of two. 4...cxb2 5.Bxb2 makes White pay a second pawn for the bishop's long diagonal, which Wikibooks and other sources call too much. Then 5...e6 6.Nf3 Na6 7.Nc3 Nc5 blunts the c4-bishop and gets your pieces out with two extra pawns.
6673250859790786|e7e6.principle: Accept a gambit when you can consolidate: 4...cxb2 5.Bxb2 e6 leaves you two pawns up with a safe position, while 4...e6 hands back the c3 pawn.
sources: Morra Gambit Accepted (ianchessgambits) | http://www.ianchessgambits.com/morra-gambit-accepted.html

ideas.title: Take the second pawn
ideas.text: 4...cxb2 5.Bxb2 leaves you two pawns up; Wikibooks calls that too much material for White's compensation.

ideas.title: Blunt the c4-bishop with ...e6
ideas.text: After the bishop recaptures, 5...e6 shuts the c4-bishop off from f7 and opens a path for your f8-bishop.

ideas.title: Danish-style attack
ideas.text: As in the Danish Gambit, White trades pawns for fast development and two bishops aimed at f7 and g7.

ideas.title: White's threat: 5.Nxc3
ideas.text: Your c3 pawn is loose: 5.Nxc3 wins it back while developing, and the game turns into a normal Morra.

habit.why: 4...e6 lets White play 5.Nxc3, winning back the pawn while developing a knight. After 5...a6 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.O-O you are in a normal Morra, one pawn up instead of two.

strays.text: You leave the c3 pawn to be taken and give back material.

taught.why: 4...cxb2 5.Bxb2 makes White pay a second pawn for the bishop's long diagonal, which Wikibooks and other sources call too much. Then 5...e6 6.Nf3 Na6 7.Nc3 Nc5 blunts the c4-bishop and gets your pieces out with two extra pawns.

enforces.text: You take what's offered and stay two pawns up.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nc6 develops and is fine: after 5.Nxc3 a6 6.Nf3 b5 7.Bd3 White has the pawn back and normal Morra play. There is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4...cxb2 keeps two extra pawns. 4...Nc6 and 4...e6 both let White reach the normal Morra with 5.Nxc3.

6730545248551000|c4f7.headline: No sacrifice on f7 without a follow-up: build with 4.c3
6730545248551000|c4f7.why: 4.Bxf7+ Kxf7 5.Nxe5+ Nxe5 gives two pieces for two pawns, and the fork 6.d4 wins only one back: after 6...Bxd4 7.Qxd4 d6 you're a piece for a pawn down. This is the Jerome Gambit, which Wikipedia calls unsound. 4.c3 adds a guard to d4 so your d-pawn can go there, and opens the way for your queen to b3. After 4...Nf6 5.d3 a6 6.O-O d6 7.a4 you have the modern slow Italian, with a2 ready as your bishop's retreat.
6730545248551000|c4f7.principle: Sacrifice on f7 only when a concrete follow-up wins the material back; otherwise build the centre.
sources: Souleidis and Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf

ideas.title: Build with c3, then d4
ideas.text: Black guards d4 three times, you twice. c3 adds a guard so d4 can follow, and opens a path for your queen to b3.

ideas.title: Slow build: d3, castle, a4
ideas.text: Masters often add d3, castle and play a4, giving the bishop a2 as a retreat; d4 waits until it is prepared.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: f7 is guarded only by the king, but a sacrifice there needs a concrete follow-up. Here there is none, so it just loses material.

ideas.title: Count e5's defenders
ideas.text: The c6 knight guards e5. One attacker against one defender means taking it with the knight gives a piece for a pawn.

habit.why: 4.Bxf7+ Kxf7 5.Nxe5+ Nxe5 gives two pieces for two pawns, and the fork 6.d4 wins only one back: after 6...Bxd4 7.Qxd4 d6 you're a piece for a pawn down. This is the Jerome Gambit, which Wikipedia calls unsound.

strays.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
strays.text: The king is drawn out, but nothing follows and Black keeps the extra piece.

taught.why: 4.c3 adds a guard to d4 so your d-pawn can go there, and opens the way for your queen to b3. After 4...Nf6 5.d3 a6 6.O-O d6 7.a4 you have the modern slow Italian, with a2 ready as your bishop's retreat.

enforces.text: The pawn adds a guard on d4, preparing d4 now or later.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.d3 guards e4 and keeps a quiet, solid game: the Giuoco Pianissimo. It's sound, but masters choose another move more than three times as often.
alternatives.after: 4.c3 and 4.d3 often meet: 4.d3 Nf6 5.c3 d6 6.O-O reaches the same slow set-up. 4.c3 first keeps an early d4 possible.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.O-O gets your king safe and keeps every plan open; after 4...Nf6 5.d3 d6 you reach a quiet set-up. Masters play it in 19.9% of games, but one move is more popular still.
alternatives.after: 4.c3 starts the centre plan at once; after 4.O-O Nf6 5.d3 d6 6.c3 play usually reaches the same slow structures.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 develops and guards e4; after 4...Nf6 5.d3 you get a quiet Four Knights set-up. It's common in club games but rare among masters (1.6%).

6730545248551000|d2d4.headline: Prepare d4 with 4.c3 before pushing it
6730545248551000|d2d4.why: Black controls d4 three times and White only twice, so 4.d4 just loses the pawn: after 4...Nxd4 5.Be3 Qf6 6.Bxd4 exd4 Black is a pawn up. 4.c3 adds a third guard to d4, so White can follow with d4 and build a two-pawn centre. It is the classical plan in the Giuoco Piano and the master choice in 55% of games.
6730545248551000|d2d4.principle: Before pushing to a contested square, count: d4 is covered by the knight on c6, the bishop on c5 and the e5 pawn, so add a supporter with c3 first.

6730545248551000|f3e5.headline: The c6 knight guards e5: build with 4.c3 instead
6730545248551000|f3e5.why: The c6 knight guards e5, so 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 just gives a knight for a pawn, and the e5 knight then hits your c4 bishop. After 5.Be2 Ng6 6.d4 Bb6 Black is simply a piece up. 4.c3 adds a guard to d4 so your d-pawn can go there, and opens the way for your queen to b3. 6730545248551000|f3g5.headline: The d8 queen covers g5: build with 4.c3 instead
6730545248551000|f3g5.why: The d8 queen sees g5 along the open diagonal, so 4.Ng5 simply hangs the knight to 4...Qxg5. Even after 5.O-O Qh4 6.d4 you have nothing for the piece. 4.c3 adds a guard to d4 so your d-pawn can go there, and opens the way for your queen to b3. After 4...Nf6 5.d3 a6 6.O-O d6 7.a4 you have the modern slow Italian, with a2 ready as your bishop's retreat.
6730545248551000|f3g5.principle: A second move with a developed knight needs a square it can safely reach; with the queen covering g5, prepare d4 instead.

6739498744433180|c1g5.headline: Push 4.e5 now; the f6 knight has nowhere good to go
6739498744433180|c1g5.why: 4.Bg5 lets Black strike first with 4...d5, and after 5.Bxf6 exf6 6.exd5 O-O 7.g3 Re8+ Black has the bishop pair and a rook check on the open e-file. The chance to push e5 with tempo is gone. 4.e5 hits the f6 knight before Black can play ...d6 or ...d5, and after 4...Ng8 it is back home. You then develop with 5.Bf4 and 6.Qd2, castle long with 7.O-O-O and push 8.g4 with a big space edge.
6739498744433180|c1g5.principle: When nothing controls e5, a knight on f6 is a target: push the e-pawn with tempo before ...d5 or ...d6 arrives.

ideas.title: e4-e5 kicks the f6 knight
ideas.text: With no black pawn on d6, 4.e5 hits the f6 knight with tempo. It has to go back to g8 or out to h5.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 strike
ideas.text: Give Black one quiet move and ...d5 hits e4 first, as after 4.Bg5 d5 or 4.Nf3 d5.

ideas.title: ...d6 before ...Bg7
ideas.text: Black skipped ...d6, the Pirc move that covers e5. That move-order slip is why the push works right now.

ideas.title: Space first, then develop
ideas.text: After 4.e5 Ng8, develop with 5.Bf4 and 6.Qd2, then castle long and push g4 with a big space edge.

habit.why: 4.Bg5 lets Black strike first with 4...d5, and after 5.Bxf6 exf6 6.exd5 O-O 7.g3 Re8+ Black has the bishop pair and a rook check on the open e-file. The chance to push e5 with tempo is gone.

strays.text: A developing move, but it lets 4...d5 stop the push for good.

taught.why: 4.e5 hits the f6 knight before Black can play ...d6 or ...d5, and after 4...Ng8 it is back home. You then develop with 5.Bf4 and 6.Qd2, castle long with 7.O-O-O and push 8.g4 with a big space edge.

enforces.text: The pawn gains space and sends the knight back to g8.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4.Nf3 is natural, but it gives Black time for 4...d5, and then the knight can jump to e4 instead of being kicked home.
alternatives.after: 4.e5 comes first, before ...d5 is in, so the knight has to retreat to g8 and you gain space with tempo.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Be3 is a reasonable set-up, but after 4...c6 5.f4 d6 Black's pawn guards the push square and the f6 knight is safe for good.
alternatives.after: 4.e5 uses the moment before ...d6: the knight goes back to g8 and you develop with 5.Bf4 and 6.Qd2.

6739498744433180|g1f3.why: 4.Nf3 is natural, but it gives Black time for 4...d5, and after 5.e5 Ne4 the knight lands on a strong square instead of going home. After 7.Bd3 Nxc3 8.bxc3 c5 Black has doubled your c-pawns and hits your centre. 4.e5 hits the f6 knight before Black can play ...d6 or ...d5, and after 4...Ng8 it is back home. You then develop with 5.Bf4 and 6.Qd2, castle long with 7.O-O-O and push 8.g4 with a big space edge.

6748390364152037|d2d3.headline: Retreat with 9.Nf3; 9.d3 hangs the knight to 9...hxg5
6748390364152037|d2d3.why: 8...h6 attacks your g5 knight, and 9.d3 only lets the c1 bishop recapture: 9...hxg5 10.Bxg5 leaves you a pawn for a piece. Black's rook also gets the open h-file, and 10...Nb7 11.Bf3 Qc7 brings Black's pieces out. 9.Nf3 saves the knight with tempo on the e5 pawn; it's the classical main line, chosen in about half of master games. After 9...e4 10.Ne5 Bd6 11.d4 exd3 12.Nxd3 O-O you keep the extra pawn and the better structure, though Black is ahead in development.
6748390364152037|d2d3.principle: Check what's loose before each move: 8...h6 attacks your undefended g5 knight, so it has to move now.
sources: Tim Harding, Two Knights Defence without Tears, Part 2 (The Kibitzer) | https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/tim-harding-two-knights-defence-part-ii/250495309

ideas.title: Retreat the knight in time
ideas.text: 8...h6 attacks your g5 knight. Pull it back the moment it's hit: 9.Nf3 with tempo on e5, or 9.Nh3.

ideas.title: Keep the extra pawn
ideas.text: You're a pawn up since 5.exd5. Don't hand it back; Black's isolated a- and c-pawns are a lasting plus.

ideas.title: Black develops with tempo
ideas.text: Black's compensation is time: ...Na5, ...h6 and ...e4 all kick your pieces while Black develops.

habit.why: 8...h6 attacks your g5 knight, and 9.d3 only lets the c1 bishop recapture: 9...hxg5 10.Bxg5 leaves you a pawn for a piece. Black's rook also gets the open h-file, and 10...Nb7 11.Bf3 Qc7 brings Black's pieces out.

strays.text: The knight stays on g5 and 9...hxg5 wins it for a pawn.

taught.why: 9.Nf3 saves the knight with tempo on the e5 pawn; it's the classical main line, chosen in about half of master games. After 9...e4 10.Ne5 Bd6 11.d4 exd3 12.Nxd3 O-O you keep the extra pawn and the better structure, though Black is ahead in development.

enforces.text: The knight leaves g5 at once and hits e5 on the way.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 9.Nh3, the Steinitz Variation, saves the knight and keeps your f-pawn free to come to f4 later. Masters choose it in 49% of games; it's fully sound.
alternatives.after: The engine rates both retreats equally. 9.Nf3 hits e5, and after 9...e4 10.Ne5 the knight sits in the centre; 9.Nh3 keeps f4 free and can come back via 12.Ng1.

6756346848148721|d7d5.headline: Don't open with 2...d5: play 2...d6 and develop first
6756346848148721|d7d5.why: 2...d5 opens the centre before you have developed, and after 3.exd5 you can't recapture well: 3...Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains time on the queen. Leaving the pawn with 3...Nf6 4.Bb5+ Bd7 5.Bxd7+ Qxd7 6.c4 lets White simply keep it. 2...d6 frees your c8 bishop and covers e5, so your knight can come to f6 safely. After 3.d4 Nf6 4.Nc3 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 you are in a Najdorf with two centre pawns to White's one.
6756346848148721|d7d5.principle: Don't open the centre while behind in development: 2...d6 prepares your pieces, while 2...d5 opens lines only White is ready to use.
sources: David Vigorito, Playing the Najdorf (preview) | https://docslib.org/doc/3378894/playing-the-najdorf-david-vigorito

ideas.title: White gains time on your queen
ideas.text: After 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the knight hits your queen, and 4...Qd8 leaves you behind in development.

ideas.title: Prepare ...d5, don't rush it
ideas.text: ...d5 is the Sicilian's freeing break, but it needs preparation. Played before your pieces are out, it costs a pawn or time.

ideas.title: ...d6 keeps e5 covered
ideas.text: 2...d6 controls e5, so your knight can come to f6 without being kicked by e4-e5, and it frees the c8 bishop.

ideas.title: Swap a flank pawn for a centre pawn
ideas.text: After 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 you have two centre pawns to White's one and a half-open c-file.

habit.why: 2...d5 opens the centre before you have developed, and after 3.exd5 you can't recapture well: 3...Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains time on the queen. Leaving the pawn with 3...Nf6 4.Bb5+ Bd7 5.Bxd7+ Qxd7 6.c4 lets White simply keep it.

strays.text: The break comes before a single piece is out, and it drops a pawn.

taught.why: 2...d6 frees your c8 bishop and covers e5, so your knight can come to f6 safely. After 3.d4 Nf6 4.Nc3 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 you are in a Najdorf with two centre pawns to White's one.

enforces.text: A quiet pawn move that makes f6 safe for the knight and frees c8.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.idea: Swap a flank pawn for a centre pawn
alternatives.before: 2...Nc6 is a main line, played in 27% of master games, leading to the Sveshnikov, Taimanov or Classical. The engine rates it a shade below the top choice, a tiny difference.
alternatives.after: Both are main lines: 2...d6 is the most played (46% to 27%) and keeps e5 covered. The engine's gap between them is small, so pick one and learn it.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2...e6 is a main line too (23% of master games): it opens the f8 bishop, covers d5 and prepares ...d5 for later, as in the Kan and Taimanov.
alternatives.after: 2...d6 is more popular (46% to 23%) and keeps the c8 bishop free, while 2...e6 usually sends it to b7. Masters play both; the engine's gap is small.

6773809115680684|d1d5.headline: 7.Qb3 hits f7 too, and keeps your queen out of the centre
6773809115680684|d1d5.why: 7.Qd5 hits f7, but 7...Qe7 defends it, and the queen in the centre soon has to retreat with 8.Qd3. After 8...Qd8 9.O-O Nf6 Black has developed and you have spent two queen moves for nothing. 7.Qb3 lines up queen and bishop against f7, so Black must defend at once with 7...Qe7, which boxes in the f8-bishop. After 8.O-O d6 9.Nd5 your knight hits the queen from the d5 hole, and Black is still far from castling.
6773809115680684|d1d5.principle: Attack f7 while only the king guards it, but from a square that keeps your queen out of the centre: 7.Qb3, not 7.Qd5, where 7...Qe7 holds and the queen soon has to retreat.

ideas.title: Hit f7 early
ideas.text: After ...e5, f7 is guarded only by the king. Queen on b3 and the c4-bishop hit it before Black can castle.

ideas.title: Use the d5 hole
ideas.text: With the c-pawn gone and the e-pawn on e5, no black pawn can cover d5. Your knight lands there with tempo, as in 9.Nd5.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black's king is still on e8 and 6...h6 guarded nothing. Moves that lose time give Black time to develop, castle and keep the pawn.

ideas.title: The ...Bg4 pin
ideas.text: Given time, Black plays ...d6 and 8...Bg4, pinning and then trading your f3-knight, one of your main attackers.

habit.why: 7.Qd5 hits f7, but 7...Qe7 defends it, and the queen in the centre soon has to retreat with 8.Qd3. After 8...Qd8 9.O-O Nf6 Black has developed and you have spent two queen moves for nothing.

strays.text: Your queen sits on the square your knight wants, and has to leave.

taught.why: 7.Qb3 lines up queen and bishop against f7, so Black must defend at once with 7...Qe7, which boxes in the f8-bishop. After 8.O-O d6 9.Nd5 your knight hits the queen from the d5 hole, and Black is still far from castling.

enforces.text: The queen joins the c4-bishop against f7 before Black can castle.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is natural, and most club players (60%) castle here, but it makes no threat. After 7...d6 8.b4 Bg4 9.h3 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Nf6 Black has traded off your knight and caught up.
alternatives.after: 7.Qb3 forces 7...Qe7 at once, boxing in Black's f8-bishop. You castle a move later with 8.O-O, and 9.Nd5 follows with tempo.

6773809115680684|d1e2.headline: 7.Qe2 makes no threat; 7.Qb3 hits f7 right away
6773809115680684|d1e2.why: 7.Qe2 develops but threatens nothing, and with ...e5 already played there is no e4-e5 break for it to support. Black simply plays 7...Nf6 8.O-O Be7 9.Be3 O-O and is a pawn up with a safe king. 7.Qb3 lines up queen and bishop against f7, so Black must defend at once with 7...Qe7, which boxes in the f8-bishop. After 8.O-O d6 9.Nd5 your knight hits the queen from the d5 hole, and Black is still far from castling.
6773809115680684|d1e2.principle: With Black's king in the centre and f7 guarded only by the king, put the queen where it attacks f7 (7.Qb3), not on e2 where it only waits.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black's king is still on e8. The usual setup with the queen on e2 backs an e4-e5 break, and with ...e5 played there is none.

ideas.text: Given time, Black plays ...d6 and 8...Bg4, pinning and then trading your f3-knight, one of your main attackers.

6773809115680684|e1h1.why: 7.O-O is natural but makes no threat, so Black gets time to develop: 7...d6 8.b4 Bg4 pins your knight. After 9.h3 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Nf6 Black is a pawn up, nearly developed, and the chance against f7 is gone. 7.Qb3 lines up queen and bishop against f7, so Black must defend at once with 7...Qe7, which boxes in the f8-bishop. After 8.O-O d6 9.Nd5 your knight hits the queen from the d5 hole, and Black is still far from castling.
6773809115680684|e1h1.principle: With Black's king in the centre and f7 guarded only by the king, attack it at once with 7.Qb3 instead of a quiet move that lets Black develop.

6790604267482997|e2f3.headline: Let g2 go: develop with 5.Nf3, not 5.Bf3
6790604267482997|e2f3.why: 5.Bf3 guards g2 by moving the bishop a second time while your g1 knight and c1 bishop wait at home. After 5...e5 6.Qe2 Nc6 7.Bxc6+ Qxc6 8.Qxe5+ you grab a pawn only by giving up that bishop for a knight, and Black's two bishops and quick development make up for it. 5.Nf3 develops and simply lets the g2 pawn go: after 5...Qxg2 6.Rg1 Qh3 you have four pieces out and the open g-file, while Black has only the queen. If Black declines with 5...Qb6, then 6.d4 Nf6 7.Ne5 keeps you well ahead in development.
6790604267482997|e2f3.principle: When the opponent's queen goes pawn-hunting, keep developing: every extra queen move adds to your lead.
sources: Scandinavian Defense (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_Defense

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: Black's queen has already moved three times. Bring out new pieces, 5.Nf3 then 6.d4, and gain more time on her.

ideas.title: Black's queen eyes g2
ideas.text: 4...Qg6 threatens 5...Qxg2. It wins a pawn, but only with yet another queen move.

ideas.title: Let g2 go
ideas.text: After 5.Nf3 Qxg2 6.Rg1 Qh3 you have four pieces out and a rook on the open g-file, while Black has only the queen.

ideas.title: Don't move a piece twice
ideas.text: Your g1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home; moving the e2 bishop again gives back the time 3.Nc3 and 4.Be2 gained.

habit.why: 5.Bf3 guards g2 by moving the bishop a second time while your g1 knight and c1 bishop wait at home. After 5...e5 6.Qe2 Nc6 7.Bxc6+ Qxc6 8.Qxe5+ you grab a pawn only by giving up that bishop for a knight, and Black's two bishops and quick development make up for it.

strays.text: The bishop moves again while your g1 knight still waits at home.

taught.why: 5.Nf3 develops and simply lets the g2 pawn go: after 5...Qxg2 6.Rg1 Qh3 you have four pieces out and the open g-file, while Black has only the queen. If Black declines with 5...Qb6, then 6.d4 Nf6 7.Ne5 keeps you well ahead in development.

enforces.text: The pawn is bait: taking it costs Black more queen moves.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5.g3 guards g2 with a pawn move instead of a piece and loosens the light squares around your king. After 5...Bf5 6.d4 Nc6 Black develops freely and most of your lead is gone.
alternatives.after: 5.Nf3 spends the move on a piece instead: the g2 pawn is bait, and taking it costs Black more queen moves while you develop.

6819507096459648|f7f6.headline: Develop with 4...Be7 and castle; no more pawn moves
6819507096459648|f7f6.why: 4...f6 is another pawn move with Black's kingside pieces still at home: it takes f6 from the knight and loosens the king, while White just keeps building with 5.d4. 4...Be7 develops the bishop that 3...d6 shut in and prepares ...Nf6 and castling, as in 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Nc3 O-O.
6819507096459648|f7f6.principle: With White already castled and your centre under pressure, bring out the kingside pieces and castle before making more pawn moves near your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

6819507096459648|g8f6.headline: Play 4...Be7 first so 5.Ng5 doesn't hit f7
6819507096459648|g8f6.why: 4...Nf6 lets White's knight jump to g5 and attack f7 together with the c4 bishop: after 5.Ng5 d5 6.exd5 White wins a pawn. 4...Be7 develops the bishop that 3...d6 shut in and covers g5 for now. In the engine line the knight comes to f6 only after White's f3 knight has left for d4, and Black castles next.
6819507096459648|g8f6.principle: With an enemy bishop on c4 aiming at f7, don't let a knight land on g5 until f7 has extra cover.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

6820108232337383|f1c4.headline: Take the free e5 pawn with 3.Nxe5, as masters do
6820108232337383|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 ignores e5 and leaves your own e4 pawn hanging: 3...Nxe4 takes it, and after 4.Nxe5 d5 Black hits your bishop and frees the game. Material is level, and after 5.Be2 Bd6 6.Nf3 O-O Black is the one with easy play. 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn first, and Black can't take back at once because of the e-file pin. After 3...d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 you reach the main line with easy development, and Black's e4-knight becomes a target.
6820108232337383|f1c4.principle: When the opponent counterattacks instead of defending, check whether you can simply take what was left loose before developing on autopilot.

ideas.title: Take the free e5 pawn
ideas.text: 2...Nf6 counterattacks instead of defending e5, so 3.Nxe5 simply takes it; 68% of masters do.

ideas.title: Your e4 pawn is loose too
ideas.text: 3.Bc4 leaves e4 hanging: 3...Nxe4 grabs it, and 4.Nxe5 d5 hits your bishop with gain of time.

ideas.title: Petrov symmetry and the e4-knight
ideas.text: Black must first chase your knight with 3...d6 4.Nf3; only then is 4...Nxe4 safe. You hit back with 5.d4 and quick development.

ideas.title: Punish 3...Nxe4 with 4.Qe2
ideas.text: If Black grabs at once with 3...Nxe4, 4.Qe2 pins along the e-file; 4...Nf6?? 5.Nc6+ wins the queen.

habit.why: 3.Bc4 ignores e5 and leaves your own e4 pawn hanging: 3...Nxe4 takes it, and after 4.Nxe5 d5 Black hits your bishop and frees the game. Material is level, and after 5.Be2 Bd6 6.Nf3 O-O Black is the one with easy play.

strays.text: The bishop comes out, but e5 stays loose and e4 hangs.

taught.why: 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn first, and Black can't take back at once because of the e-file pin. After 3...d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 you reach the main line with easy development, and Black's e4-knight becomes a target.

enforces.text: The knight takes the pawn that 2...Nf6 left undefended.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 is a sound sideline: it guards e4 and invites 3...Nc6, a Four Knights. It doesn't press Black, and there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 3.Nxe5 is the main line (68% of masters) and takes the pawn at once; 3.Nc3 (11%) keeps it simple but lets Black defend e5.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 3.d3 is solid and harder to crack than it looks, but after 3...Nc6 and 4...d5 Black has the easier game.
alternatives.after: 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn Black left loose; 3.d3 (2% of masters) gives Black time to defend it and strike with 4...d5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.d4, the Steinitz attack, is a good choice of 19% of masters: after 3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 you develop quickly and hit the e4-knight. There is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: Both are good. 3.Nxe5 (68%) takes the pawn at once; 3.d4 often reaches similar positions with Black's knight on e4.

6833062692676193|b1c3.headline: Against the Alekhine, kick the knight with 2.e5
6833062692676193|b1c3.why: 2.Nc3 defends e4 but lets Black switch to a normal open game with 2...e5. After 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5.Nxd4 exd4 6.e5 dxc3 it is a level Four Knights, and Black has escaped the Alekhine's usual problems. 2.e5 kicks the knight and takes space, and masters choose it 85% of the time. After 2...Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.d4 d6 5.exd6 exd6 6.Nc3 Nc6 Black's knight has moved three times and you have pawns on c4 and d4.
6833062692676193|b1c3.principle: A knight on f6 that a pawn can attack is a target: kick it and gain space and time.

ideas.title: Gain time on early black pieces
ideas.text: 1...Nf6 brought a knight out early: 2.e5 kicks it, and 3.c4 and 4.d4 take space while chasing it again.

ideas.title: Your e4 pawn is attacked
ideas.text: The f6-knight hits e4, so push it or defend it. 2.Nf3 does neither, and 2...Nxe4 wins a pawn.

ideas.title: Black wants your pawns to overextend
ideas.text: Black invites your pawns forward to undermine them later, starting with ...d6 against e5, as in 4...d6 5.exd6.

ideas.title: 2...e5 turns it into a Vienna
ideas.text: If you don't kick the knight, Black can switch to an ordinary open game with ...e5, a Vienna or Four Knights.

habit.why: 2.Nc3 defends e4 but lets Black switch to a normal open game with 2...e5. After 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.Bb5 Nd4 5.Nxd4 exd4 6.e5 dxc3 it is a level Four Knights, and Black has escaped the Alekhine's usual problems.

strays.idea: Gain time on early black pieces
strays.text: Nothing kicks the f6-knight, so Black calmly plays 2...e5.

taught.why: 2.e5 kicks the knight and takes space, and masters choose it 85% of the time. After 2...Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.d4 d6 5.exd6 exd6 6.Nc3 Nc6 Black's knight has moved three times and you have pawns on c4 and d4.

enforces.idea: Gain time on early black pieces
enforces.text: Each pawn move kicks the knight again, so you gain time and space.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 2.Nf3 leaves e4 hanging: after 2...Nxe4 3.d4 g6 4.c4 Bg7 Black is a clean pawn up. As a gambit it gives too little for the pawn.
alternatives.after: 2.e5 answers the attack on e4 by kicking the knight; 2.Nf3 just drops the pawn to 2...Nxe4.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.idea: Gain time on early black pieces
alternatives.before: 2.d3 guards e4 but shuts in your f1-bishop, and Black develops freely: after 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 Bc5 5.Bg2 d6 you have a passive King's Indian Attack setup.
alternatives.after: 2.e5 makes Black's knight move again; 2.d3 takes no space and lets Black set up comfortably with 2...e5 and 4...Bc5. Masters play 2.d3 only 2% of the time.

6833062692676193|d1f3.headline: Against Alekhine's, chase the knight with 2.e5
6833062692676193|d1f3.why: 2.Qf3 guards e4 with the queen, but it takes f3 from White's knight and becomes a target: in the line 2...Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bd3 Nd4 Black hits it, and 5.Qg3 has to move it again. 2.e5 is played in 84.9% of master games: it attacks the knight on f6, gains space and makes it move, usually with 2...Nd5, where 3.c4 kicks it once more.
6833062692676193|d1f3.principle: A knight that attacks your centre pawn from f6 can be chased with e5, gaining space and time instead of defending passively.

6833062692676193|d2d3.headline: Kick the knight with 2.e5 and take space.
6833062692676193|d2d3.why: 2.d3 saves the pawn on e4 but shuts in the bishop on f1, and after 2...e5 Black has an easy, equal game. 1...Nf6 put a knight where White's e-pawn can attack it. 2.e5 gains space with tempo: the knight has to move, usually to d5, and after 3.c4 Nb6 4.d4 White builds a big centre. Masters play it 85% of the time.
6833062692676193|d2d3.principle: When an enemy knight stands in front of your centre pawns, push a pawn to gain space and time by chasing it.

6833062692676193|f2f3.headline: Answer 1...Nf6 with 2.e5, not 2.f3.
6833062692676193|f2f3.why: 2.f3 protects e4 but takes the f3 square from the knight and weakens the king. After 2...e5 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6 Black develops while chasing White's queen. 1...Nf6 put a knight where the e-pawn can hit it, and 2.e5 does exactly that: the knight must move, usually to d5. After 3.c4 Nb6 4.d4 White builds a big centre.
6833062692676193|f2f3.principle: When an enemy knight sits in front of your centre pawns, kick it with a pawn rather than defending with a pawn move that weakens your king.

6833062692676193|f2f4.headline: Against the Alekhine, 2.e5 gains space and kicks the knight
6833062692676193|f2f4.why: 2.f4 ignores the attack on e4, and 2...Nxe4 wins the pawn outright. 2.e5 is the main move: it gains space and kicks the knight, usually to d5, where 3.c4 chases it again and White keeps taking central space with tempo. Masters choose 2.e5 in 84.9% of games.
6833062692676193|f2f4.principle: When a knight on f6 attacks your e-pawn, the pawn advance that hits the knight defends nothing and attacks something, so it gains time.

6849990694088956|b2b4.headline: Don't give a pawn: 3...Bc5 lets you take one with 4.Nxe5
6849990694088956|b2b4.why: 4.b4 gives a pawn for nothing: 4...Bxb4 takes it, and the bishop now eyes your c3-knight, which guards e4. After 5.Nxe5 O-O 6.Nc4 Re8 Black's rook hits e4, and 8...Bxc3 removes its defender. 4.Nxe5 takes a pawn nothing defends, and your c3-knight keeps e4 covered. Black's best is 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4, getting the pawn back but giving you the bishop pair after 7.Bd3.
6849990694088956|b2b4.principle: Before offering a pawn, check what the opponent left undefended: here 3...Bc5 drops e5.

ideas.text: Black's best try, 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4, regains the pawn but hands you both bishops.

Black's best is 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4, getting the pawn back but giving you the bishop pair after 7.Bd3.

ideas.title: Take the free e5 pawn
ideas.text: 3...Bc5 doesn't defend e5, and your c3-knight guards e4, so 4.Nxe5 simply wins a pawn.

ideas.title: Black wins it back at a price
ideas.text: Black's best try, 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4, regains the pawn but hands you both bishops.

ideas.title: Guard f2 against ...Bc5 and ...Ng4
ideas.text: The c5-bishop already aims at f2. If Black gives up e5 for open lines, a knight jump to g4 adds a second attacker; h3 stops it.

ideas.title: Black's easy development
ideas.text: If you leave e5 alone, Black defends it or castles and brings a rook to e8 against your e4 pawn.

habit.why: 4.d4 offers to trade your d-pawn for e5 instead of just taking it. After 4...exd4 5.Nxd4 O-O Black develops easily, the c5-bishop eyes your knight, and 6...Re8 hits e4.

strays.text: You trade pawns on d4 instead of winning one on e5.

taught.why: 4.Nxe5 takes a pawn nothing defends, and your c3-knight keeps e4 covered. Black's best is 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4, getting the pawn back but giving you the bishop pair after 7.Bd3.

enforces.text: The knight takes the undefended pawn while c3 guards e4.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4.Bc4 develops, but 4...d6 defends e5 for good, and after 5.d3 c6 the game is quiet and level.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxe5 takes the pawn before 4...d6 can defend it; your bishops still come out, with the pair after 6.dxc3.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4.h3 stops a knight jump to g4 that isn't a threat yet, and 4...d6 defends e5 for good. After 5.Bc4 O-O Black is comfortable.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxe5 takes the pawn before 4...d6 can defend it; h3 matters only once Black has given up e5 and aims at f2.

6849990694088956|f1c4.headline: 3...Bc5 leaves e5 loose: take it with 4.Nxe5
6849990694088956|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 develops but leaves e5 alone, and 4...d6 defends it for good. After 5.d3 c6 6.h3 O-O the game is a quiet, level Italian-type position and the free pawn is gone. 4.Nxe5 takes a pawn nothing defends, and your c3-knight keeps e4 covered. Black's best is 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4, getting the pawn back but giving you the bishop pair after 7.Bd3.
6849990694088956|f1c4.principle: Before developing on autopilot, check what the opponent left undefended: here 3...Bc5 drops e5.

6850591830216347|g8h6.headline: Develop the knight to f6, toward the centre.
6850591830216347|g8h6.why: From h6 the knight controls none of the central squares, so 6.Nd5 lands on d5 with no knight to challenge it. 5...Nf6 develops toward the centre: it attacks e4, covers d5 and lets Black castle. After 6.Na4 a6 7.Nxc5 dxc5 Black has a comfortable game.
6850591830216347|g8h6.principle: Put your knights where they control the centre, normally f6 and c6; a knight on the edge leaves central squares to the opponent.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nc6

6863144374799225|f3d4.headline: Hit the queen with 5.Bg5 before taking back on d4
6863144374799225|f3d4.why: 5.Nxd4 is natural but leaves the queen alone, so Black gets a free move: 5...Bb4 pins your c3 knight. Black then develops with 6...Ne7 and 7...O-O, and your lead in development melts away. 5.Bg5 develops and attacks the queen, so Black must move it again before anything else. After 5...Qd6 6.Nxd4 you have won the pawn back with three pieces out, while Black has only the queen in play.
6863144374799225|f3d4.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, develop with threats against it before making a quiet recapture.
sources: Greco Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco_Defence

ideas.title: Hit the early queen with tempo
ideas.text: Black's queen on f6 is a target. 5.Bg5 develops while attacking it, so Black must spend the reply moving the queen again.

ideas.title: Watch the pins on your knights
ideas.text: After a plain recapture on d4, 5...Bb4 pins your c3 knight and Black catches up in development.

ideas.title: Keep the queens on
ideas.text: Black's queen is the piece you gain time on. Trading it, as after 5.Qxd4 Qxd4, throws that target away.

ideas.title: Keep the g8 knight shut out
ideas.text: The queen on f6 takes the g8 knight's best square. Each time you hit the queen, Black loses another move while that knight waits.

habit.why: 5.Nxd4 is natural but leaves the queen alone, so Black gets a free move: 5...Bb4 pins your c3 knight. Black then develops with 6...Ne7 and 7...O-O, and your lead in development melts away.

strays.idea: Hit the early queen with tempo
strays.text: The recapture leaves the f6 queen in peace, so Black develops freely.

taught.why: 5.Bg5 develops and attacks the queen, so Black must move it again before anything else. After 5...Qd6 6.Nxd4 you have won the pawn back with three pieces out, while Black has only the queen in play.

enforces.idea: Hit the early queen with tempo
enforces.text: The bishop comes out with a threat, and d4 is taken back a move later.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5.Qxd4 offers a queen trade: after 5...Qxd4 6.Nxd4 Bc5 Black's misplaced queen is gone and the bishop develops with tempo on your knight. Your lead shrinks to a small edge in an early endgame.
alternatives.after: 5.Bg5 keeps queens on and gains a move on Black's queen before you take back on d4. That queen is your best target, so don't trade it off.

6886380190448217|f3d5.headline: The d5 knight is loose: take it with the bishop, with check
6886380190448217|f3d5.why: 8.Qxd5+ wins the knight but brings your queen into the centre with two minor pieces still at home. After 8...Ke8 9.Bb5 Bd7 10.Nc3 Rd8 Black develops with gain of time, the queen on f6 hits f2, and most of your advantage is gone. 8.Bxd5+ wins the same knight with check and keeps your queen on f3, facing Black's. After 8...Be6 9.Bxc6 bxc6 10.Qxc6 you win a pawn too, and your queen hits the a8 rook.
6886380190448217|f3d5.principle: Check what is loose: the d5 knight has no defender, so take it with a minor piece and keep your queen out of reach.

ideas.title: Take the loose knight with the bishop
ideas.text: 7...Qf6 leaves the d5 knight attacked twice and defended by nothing. 8.Bxd5+ wins it with check.

ideas.title: Keep the queens on
ideas.text: Black's king on f7 can't castle; that is your attack. Keep your queen on f3, because trading queens lets the king walk to safety.

ideas.title: Take off the defenders
ideas.text: Once your bishop reaches d5, taking on c6 removes Black's other knight and 10.Qxc6 picks up a pawn.

ideas.title: Black wants trades and tempo
ideas.text: Black's queen offers a trade on f3 and hits f2 once your queen leaves. A queen in the centre gives Black free moves.

habit.why: 8.Qxd5+ wins the knight but brings your queen into the centre with two minor pieces still at home. After 8...Ke8 9.Bb5 Bd7 10.Nc3 Rd8 Black develops with gain of time, the queen on f6 hits f2, and most of your advantage is gone.

strays.idea: Take the loose knight with the bishop
strays.text: Takes with the queen, which then gets chased around the centre.

taught.why: 8.Bxd5+ wins the same knight with check and keeps your queen on f3, facing Black's. After 8...Be6 9.Bxc6 bxc6 10.Qxc6 you win a pawn too, and your queen hits the a8 rook.

enforces.idea: Take the loose knight with the bishop
enforces.text: A minor piece takes, with check, and the queen stays on f3.

6931592131044425|c6d4.headline: Develop the bishop instead of moving the knight again
6931592131044425|c6d4.why: 3...Nd4 moves the knight a second time while three minor pieces are still at home; after 4.Nxd4 exd4 5.O-O and 6.Re1 White is ahead in development, and the pawn on d4 falls to 7.c3 and 8.cxd4. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, develops the bishop to its best diagonal and keeps control of d4 and g5, ready for ...Nf6 and castling.
6931592131044425|c6d4.principle: With three minor pieces still at home, each move should bring a new one out; a second knight move needs a concrete gain.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nc6/3. Nf3

6931592131044425|f7f5.headline: Develop before touching the f-pawn in the Italian
6931592131044425|f7f5.why: 3...f5 opens the diagonal from c4 toward your king while you are undeveloped, and after 4.d4 exd4 5.Ng5 Ne5 6.Qxd4 Qe7 7.Bxg8 White wins a knight. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, develops the bishop to its best diagonal, keeps control of g5 until Black is ready to castle and adds a third guard to d4, so White's central break needs preparation.
6931592131044425|f7f5.principle: Against a bishop on c4, bring out a minor piece before moving the f-pawn; pawn moves near the king only weaken f7 and the diagonal toward g8.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4

6931592131044425|f7f6.headline: Develop a piece against the Italian; don't spend a move on ...f6
6931592131044425|f7f6.why: 3...f6 guards e5, which the knight on c6 already defends, and in exchange it takes the f6 square from Black's own knight and loosens the king. White opens the centre with 4.d4 exd4 5.O-O and develops quickly while Black's kingside is still at home. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, develops the bishop to an active diagonal, adds control of d4 and gets Black ready to castle.
6931592131044425|f7f6.principle: When a pawn is already protected by a piece, defending it again with a pawn only costs time and a good square for your knight.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4

6931592131044425|g8h6.headline: Develop toward the centre with 3...Bc5, not a knight on the rim
6931592131044425|g8h6.why: 3...Nh6 puts the knight on the edge, where it neither pressures e4 nor helps fight for the centre. In the engine line White plays 5.d4 and the knight has to move again with 6...Ng4, and after 7.Bb3 Nxd4 8.Qxd4 White's queen dominates the centre. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, puts the bishop on its most active diagonal and keeps the queen's control of g5, so 4...Nf6 and castling follow safely.
6931592131044425|g8h6.principle: Bring each piece to a square that fights for the centre; a knight on the rim controls half as much and usually has to move again.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|c8e6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qd4 wins the pawn back.
6936096123661830|c8e6.why: 5...Be6 develops but lets White keep the extra pawn: 6.Nf3 retreats the knight, and Black has nothing for it. 5.Nxe5 left the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 loose. 5...Qd4 attacks both and threatens mate on f2 with the bishop on c5, so after 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black regains the pawn with check.
6936096123661830|c8e6.principle: When you are a pawn down after a trade, look for a forcing queen move that hits two loose targets before you develop quietly.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|d8e7.headline: Punish 5.Nxe5 with 5...Qd4, hitting knight, pawn and f2
6936096123661830|d8e7.why: 5...Qe7 gives White time: 6.d4 defends the knight and takes the centre, and after 6...Bb4+ 7.c3 Black has nothing to show for the lost pawn. 5...Qd4 is a multiple attack: it hits the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 and, with the bishop on c5, threatens mate on f2. After 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black has the pawn back, and after 7.Qe2 Qxe2+ 8.Kxe2 White's king is stuck in the centre.
6936096123661830|d8e7.principle: With your bishop on c5 already aiming at f2, a queen move to d4 can add a mating threat to attacks on loose pieces in the centre.

6936096123661830|d8f6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qd4 hits the knight, e4 and f2 at once
6936096123661830|d8f6.why: 5...Qf6 hits e5 and f2, but 6.d4 blocks the bishop's line to f2 and attacks it, so your threats vanish. After 6...Bd6 7.Nc4 b5 8.Nxd6+ cxd6 White keeps the extra pawn and has your good bishop too. 5...Qd4 attacks the knight and e4 and threatens mate on f2, so White must retreat with 6.Nd3. After 6...Qxe4+ 7.Qe2 Qxe2+ 8.Kxe2 Bd4 you have the pawn back, the queens are off and White's king has lost castling.
6936096123661830|d8f6.principle: After a knight grabs e5, check what it left loose: one queen move to d4 hits the knight, e4 and f2 together.
sources: Andrew Kauffman, The Ruy Lopez Opening: How to Play It as White and Black (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/the-ruy-lopez-opening-how-to-play-it-as-white-and-black/

ideas.title: Bxc6 and Nxe5 is not yet a threat
ideas.text: White hasn't castled, so f2 is weak: a queen on d4 hits the e5 knight, e4 and f2, and you win the pawn back.

ideas.title: The c5 bishop is a target
ideas.text: Give White a spare move and 6.d4 hits your bishop and shuts its line to f2, so the extra pawn stays.

ideas.title: Castling ends the trick
ideas.text: Once White castles, the f1 rook guards f2 and the queen trick no longer works. Strike before that happens.

habit.why: 5...Qf6 hits e5 and f2, but 6.d4 blocks the bishop's line to f2 and attacks it, so your threats vanish. After 6...Bd6 7.Nc4 b5 8.Nxd6+ cxd6 White keeps the extra pawn and has your good bishop too.

strays.idea: The c5 bishop is a target
strays.text: 6.d4 hits your bishop with tempo and White keeps the pawn.

taught.why: 5...Qd4 attacks the knight and e4 and threatens mate on f2, so White must retreat with 6.Nd3. After 6...Qxe4+ 7.Qe2 Qxe2+ 8.Kxe2 Bd4 you have the pawn back, the queens are off and White's king has lost castling.

enforces.idea: Bxc6 and Nxe5 is not yet a threat
enforces.text: One queen move hits the knight, e4 and f2 before White castles.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Nf6 develops and hits e4, but White keeps the pawn with 6.Qe2 and later 7.Nd3. It is playable; a more forcing move exists.
alternatives.after: 5...Qd4 wins the pawn back at once with three threats. After 5...Nf6 6.Qe2 White stays a pawn up for a while.
alternatives.idea: Bxc6 and Nxe5 is not yet a threat

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Qe7 wins the pawn back: 6.d4 Bb4+ 7.c3 Bd6 8.O-O Bxe5 9.dxe5 Qxe5. But you give up your dark-squared bishop and trail in development; there is a sharper move.
alternatives.after: 5...Qd4 regains the pawn while threatening mate on f2 and keeps both bishops. 5...Qe7 lets 6.d4 gain time on the c5 bishop.
alternatives.idea: The c5 bishop is a target

6936096123661830|f7f6.headline: Answer 5.Nxe5 with 5...Qd4, forking the knight and e4.
6936096123661830|f7f6.why: 5...f6 opens the e8-h5 diagonal: 6.Qh5+ g6 7.Nxg6 hxg6 8.Qxh8 and Black loses a rook and a pawn for a knight. 5.Nxe5 took a pawn but left the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 loose. 5...Qd4 attacks both and threatens mate on f2 with the bishop on c5, so after 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black wins the pawn back with check.
6936096123661830|f7f6.principle: When the opponent grabs a pawn with a piece, look for a queen move that attacks the piece, a loose pawn and f2 together.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|g8f6.headline: Fork with 5...Qd4 before White can protect e4.
6936096123661830|g8f6.why: 5...Nf6 attacks e4 only once, and 6.Qe2 defends it, so White keeps the extra pawn. 5.Nxe5 left the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 loose. 5...Qd4 hits both and threatens mate on f2 with the bishop on c5. After 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black wins the pawn back with check.
6936096123661830|g8f6.principle: When you can attack two loose targets and threaten mate in one move, do that before a single attack the opponent can parry.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

695832176392433|g7g6.headline: Kick the pinning bishop with h6
695832176392433|g7g6.why: The bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6 to your queen, and 6...g6 does nothing about it: 7.Nd5 adds a second attacker, and after 7...Nxd5 8.Bxd8 Black has given the queen for a knight. 6...h6 puts the question to the bishop at once; after 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 the pin is gone, and 8.Nd5 is met by 8...Qd8.
695832176392433|g7g6.principle: When a bishop pins your f6-knight to the queen, challenge it with the h-pawn before White can bring another attacker to d5.

6967288124345715|g1f3.headline: Defend e4 with 3.d3; 3.Nf3 leaves it hanging
6967288124345715|g1f3.why: 3.Nf3 leaves e4 undefended, and 3...Nxe4 takes it; after 4.Nxe5 d5 the pawn hits the bishop and Black has the easier game. 3.d3 defends e4 with a pawn and opens the diagonal for the queen's bishop. It is the main line, played in 86.4% of master games.
6967288124345715|g1f3.principle: When the knight on f6 attacks your e4-pawn, defend it before developing elsewhere, ideally with a move that also frees a piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6

6980672627372882|d7d5.headline: Develop with 4...Nf6; ...d5 here just drops a pawn
6980672627372882|d7d5.why: 4...d5 opens the centre before Black is ready, and 5.exd5 wins a pawn, since d5 is hit by the pawn on e4, the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4. 4...Nf6 develops toward the centre, attacks e4 and prepares castling; masters choose it in 82.9% of games.
6980672627372882|d7d5.principle: Before pushing ...d5 here, count: White's pawn, knight and bishop all hit d5, so develop the knight first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6980672627372882|f7f6.headline: In the Giuoco Piano, bring out 4...Nf6, not the f-pawn
6980672627372882|f7f6.why: 4...f6 develops nothing, takes the f6 square from Black's own knight and weakens the light squares near Black's king, which White's bishop on c4 already aims at. 4...Nf6 develops the last kingside piece, adds pressure on e4 and gets Black ready to castle; masters choose it in 82.9% of games.
6980672627372882|f7f6.principle: With White's pieces out and aimed at your king, finish developing so you can castle; a pawn move like f6 has no concrete reason.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6994580878022218|b7b6.headline: Develop and clear the centre with 5...cxd4, not 5...b6
6994580878022218|b7b6.why: 5...b6 spends a move on a pawn while your kingside pieces wait. After 6.Nc3 Nf6 7.Be3 c4 8.a3 b5 9.Ne5 White's knight lands on e5, and after 9...b4 10.axb4 your queenside pawns are loose. 5...cxd4 settles the centre, and after 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 you have traded White's active bishop and developed quickly. Your d5 pawn is isolated, but with fewer pieces on the board it is less of a target.
6994580878022218|b7b6.principle: Develop before you push side pawns: 5...cxd4 settles the centre and gets your pieces out, while 5...b6 spends a move that White's 7.Be3 and 8.a3 punish.
sources: Shaun Sedice, Playing the Grand Prix Attack (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/grand-prix-attack/
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. f4

ideas.title: Keep a pawn in the centre
ideas.text: Your pawn on d5 is your share of the centre. Keep it supported by pieces: ...Nf6 and ...Nc6 cover it.

ideas.title: Bb5 against d5
ideas.text: White's plan against your d5 pawn is a bishop check from b5 and piece pressure. Develop fast and trade pieces, as with 7...Bd7.

ideas.title: Develop before pawn moves
ideas.text: With your king still on e8, bring out pieces first. Slow pawn moves like ...b6 let White develop with threats on your queenside.

habit.why: 5...b6 spends a move on a pawn while your kingside pieces wait. After 6.Nc3 Nf6 7.Be3 c4 8.a3 b5 9.Ne5 White's knight lands on e5, and after 9...b4 10.axb4 your queenside pawns are loose.

strays.text: A pawn move instead of a piece, and it loosens your queenside.

taught.why: 5...cxd4 settles the centre, and after 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 you have traded White's active bishop and developed quickly. Your d5 pawn is isolated, but with fewer pieces on the board it is less of a target.

enforces.text: You meet the check with 7...Bd7 and trade White's bishop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
alternatives.before: 5...Nf6 is a sound developing move: the knight guards d5 and prepares castling. There is a slightly more accurate move.
alternatives.after: 5...Nf6 usually transposes: 6.Nc3 cxd4 7.Nxd4 Nc6 reaches a similar position. Both are fine.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
alternatives.before: 5...Nc6 develops and adds pressure on d4. After 6.Nc3 Nf6 7.Be3 your pieces are ready; it's a fine choice, though not the most accurate.
alternatives.after: Similar plans: in the line 7...cxd4 8.Bxd4 Be7 9.Qd3 O-O 10.O-O-O White castles long, while 5...cxd4 at once lets you trade White's bishop after 7.Bb5+ Bd7.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
alternatives.before: 5...c4 gains queenside space and avoids an isolated pawn. White answers 6.b3 cxb3 7.axb3 and gets the open a-file, so it's fine but not the most accurate.
alternatives.after: 5...cxd4 keeps your pawns flexible; after 5...c4 6.b3 White undermines the chain at once and the a-file opens for White's rook.

7050462614834999|c1b2.headline: Hit b7 and f7 with 9.Qb3 while Black's bishop is away
7050462614834999|c1b2.why: 9.Bb2 points the bishop at your own d4-pawn and makes no threat. Black gets 9...Nf6, and after 10.h3 Bh5 11.d5 Bxf3 12.Qxf3 Ne5 the knight hits your queen and bishop while you are still a pawn down. With the bishop gone from c8, 9.Qb3 hits b7 and f7 at once. After 9...Bxf3 10.Qxf3 the queen recaptures along the third rank, so your kingside pawns stay intact and you keep the bishop pair.
7050462614834999|c1b2.principle: Make threats while you are a pawn down: 9.Qb3 attacks b7 and f7, while 9.Bb2 lets Black develop in peace.

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Be7

ideas.title: The centre is the payment
ideas.text: You are a pawn down for the e4-d4 centre and quicker development. Keep the centre and make moves that create threats.

ideas.title: Qb3 hits f7 and b7
ideas.text: With Black's light bishop gone from c8, a queen on b3 attacks b7 and joins the c4-bishop against f7.

ideas.title: Black trades your knight
ideas.text: The g4-bishop pins your f3-knight; Black wants to take it, then use e5 for a knight.

habit.why: 9.Bb2 points the bishop at your own d4-pawn and makes no threat. Black gets 9...Nf6, and after 10.h3 Bh5 11.d5 Bxf3 12.Qxf3 Ne5 the knight hits your queen and bishop while you are still a pawn down.

strays.text: A quiet move: no threat, so Black finishes developing for free.

taught.why: With the bishop gone from c8, 9.Qb3 hits b7 and f7 at once. After 9...Bxf3 10.Qxf3 the queen recaptures along the third rank, so your kingside pawns stay intact and you keep the bishop pair.

enforces.text: The double attack makes Black give up the g4-bishop for your knight.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 9.h3 asks the g4-bishop to decide at once and keeps a good game. There is a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: 9.Qb3 hits b7 and f7 right away; after 9.h3 Bh5 10.Qb3 you reach the same idea a move later.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 9.Nbd2 blocks your c1-bishop and makes no threat: 9...Nf6 10.h3 Bh5 and Black castles in time with 11...O-O, then trades on f3.
alternatives.after: 9.Qb3 makes threats on b7 and f7 first, so Black must trade on f3 at once instead of developing.

7062831770535036|c1e3.headline: Push 7.d5 first and keep Black's knight off c6
7062831770535036|c1e3.why: 7.Be3 lets Black develop with 7...Nc6, hitting your d4 pawn. After 8.d5 O-O-O 9.Nf4 Qxd1+ 10.Rxd1 Ne5 the queens are off, the knight is centralised and most of your lead is gone. 7.d5 takes c6 and e6 from Black's knights before 7...Nc6 can hit d4, so after 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 the b8 knight has to go to d7. After 8...Nbd7 9.Be3 O-O-O 10.O-O-O you keep the queens on, more space, and 11.Nf4 to hit the queen again.
7062831770535036|c1e3.principle: With a lead in development and the opponent's king in the centre, gain central space at once rather than make quiet moves.
sources: Jeremy Silman, First Verbalize, Then Analyze (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/first-verbalize-then-analyze-plus-one-from-the-rule-books
Scandinavian Defense Guide (Control The Center) | https://openings.controlthecenter.com/openings/scandinavian-defense/?side=white

ideas.title: Push d5 while you lead
ideas.text: Black's king is still on e8 and the queen is offside on h5. Push 7.d5 before Black is ready for it.

ideas.title: Take c6 and e6 from the knights
ideas.text: A pawn on d5 controls c6 and e6, so Black's b8 knight must go to d7 or a6 instead.

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: The queen on h5 is still a target: your e2 knight can hit her from f4, as in 11.Nf4 Qg4.

ideas.title: Black's pressure on d4
ideas.text: Given time, 7...Nc6 and ...O-O-O hit your d4 pawn, and 9...Qxd1+ can trade queens.

habit.why: 7.Be3 lets Black develop with 7...Nc6, hitting your d4 pawn. After 8.d5 O-O-O 9.Nf4 Qxd1+ 10.Rxd1 Ne5 the queens are off, the knight is centralised and most of your lead is gone.

strays.text: 7...Nc6 hits d4 and lets Black trade queens with check.

taught.why: 7.d5 takes c6 and e6 from Black's knights before 7...Nc6 can hit d4, so after 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 the b8 knight has to go to d7. After 8...Nbd7 9.Be3 O-O-O 10.O-O-O you keep the queens on, more space, and 11.Nf4 to hit the queen again.

enforces.text: The pawn gains space while Black's queen is offside on h5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is safe and the most common club move (74%), but it gives Black time for 7...e6 and 9...c6. Black's pawns are then ready for any central push, and the knight jumps in with 10...Nb4.
alternatives.after: 7.d5 comes before ...e6 and ...c6: it takes c6 and e6 from the knights while Black's queen is still offside on h5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Bf4 is one of the best moves here: the bishop takes an active diagonal and hits c7, so Black has to guard it with 7...Na6, putting the knight on the edge.
alternatives.after: 7.d5 and 7.Bf4 are about equally strong. 7.d5 takes c6 and e6 from the knights at once; 7.Bf4 develops first and pushes 8.d5 next move.

7062831770535036|e1h1.headline: Grab space with 7.d5 before Black builds ...e6 and ...c6
7062831770535036|e1h1.why: 7.O-O is safe, but it gives Black time for 7...e6 and later 9...c6. After 8.Bf4 Na6 9.Qd3 c6 10.d5 Nb4 Black's pawns are ready for your d5 push and the knight jumps in on b4, so much of your lead is gone. 7.d5 takes c6 and e6 from Black's knights before 7...Nc6 can hit d4, so after 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 the b8 knight has to go to d7. After 8...Nbd7 9.Be3 O-O-O 10.O-O-O you keep the queens on, more space, and 11.Nf4 to hit the queen again.
7062831770535036|e1h1.principle: With a lead in development and the opponent's king in the centre, gain central space at once rather than make quiet moves.
sources: Jeremy Silman, First Verbalize, Then Analyze (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/first-verbalize-then-analyze-plus-one-from-the-rule-books

7121051583391236|f3c3.headline: Don't retreat: 6.Qb3 hits b7, which nothing guards
7121051583391236|f3c3.why: 6.Qc3 only hits e5, and 6...Nd7 covers it while developing. After 7.d3 Ne7 8.Be3 c6 Black finishes development with 10...Be7, and your queen move has gained nothing. 6.Qb3 hits the undefended b7 pawn while your bishop keeps Black's queen tied to f7. Black's best is 6...b6, weakening the long diagonal, and after 7.Nc3, 8.O-O and 9.Nd5 you are well ahead in development.
7121051583391236|f3c3.principle: When the opponent's light-squared bishop is gone and its queen is out early, attack the loose b7 pawn with gain of time instead of retreating.
sources: Steven Craig Miller, Philidor's Defense (handout) | http://renaissanceknights.org/IL%20Scholastic/Handouts/Handouts%20PDFs/Philidor.pdf

ideas.title: After ...Bxf3, hit b7 with Qb3
ideas.text: 4...Bxf3 gave up the bishop that guarded b7. 6.Qb3 hits b7, and with your c4-bishop keeps Black's queen tied to f7.

ideas.title: Black's queen guards f7
ideas.text: 5...Qf6 covers f7 against your bishop, but the queen blocks the g8-knight and has to keep watching f7.

ideas.title: Use the time Black spent
ideas.text: 3...Bg4, 4...Bxf3 and 5...Qf6 cost Black time while both knights sit at home. A quiet move lets them catch up.

ideas.title: Keep the bishop pair working
ideas.text: You have both bishops; keep the queens on and the play open. A retreat or a queen trade leaves only a level game.

habit.why: 6.Qc3 only hits e5, and 6...Nd7 covers it while developing. After 7.d3 Ne7 8.Be3 c6 Black finishes development with 10...Be7, and your queen move has gained nothing.

strays.text: The queen goes after e5, which is easily covered, and b7 stays safe.

taught.why: 6.Qb3 hits the undefended b7 pawn while your bishop keeps Black's queen tied to f7. Black's best is 6...b6, weakening the long diagonal, and after 7.Nc3, 8.O-O and 9.Nd5 you are well ahead in development.

enforces.text: The queen hits b7 and keeps Black's queen tied to f7.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.Qxf6 trades your best piece and lets Black recapture 6...Nxf6 with a developing move. Black's early-queen problem is gone, and after 7.d3 c6 the endgame is level.
alternatives.after: 6.Qb3 keeps the queens on and hits b7, while Black's queen stays tied to f7 and the knights sit at home.

7127830528967939|e7e6.headline: Push 3...d4: shut the g2-bishop out, don't wall in yours
7127830528967939|e7e6.why: 3...e6 shuts in your c8-bishop, the piece that hits g4, and lets White play 4.d4 and 5.Nf3 for free. After 5...Ngf6 6.g5 Ne4 7.h4 Bd6 8.Nc3 White's kingside pawns have become useful and the game is level. 3...d4 gains space and keeps your centre pawn out of reach of cxd5, and your c8-bishop still covers b7. After 4.h3 h5 5.g5 e5 6.Nf3 e4 7.Ng1 Bf5 your pawns drive White's knight back home and your bishop comes out.
7127830528967939|e7e6.principle: When the opponent's opening neglects the centre, grab space there and block their best piece.
