ideas.title: Castle before opening the centre
ideas.text: Your king is still in the middle and Black is ahead in development. Castle first; open the centre with c4 later.

ideas.title: Guard g2
ideas.text: With the light bishops traded, Black's queen on d5 eyes g2. If you ignore it, 6...Qxg2 7.Rg1 Qxh2 takes two pawns.

ideas.title: Nothing guards c4
ideas.text: c4 attacks the queen, but no white piece covers that square, so 6...Qxc4 takes the pawn and hits your e2 knight.

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: Once 7.Nd2 covers c4, 8.c4 gains space with tempo on the queen, as in the main line.

habit.why: 6.c4 hits the queen, but nothing guards c4, so 6...Qxc4 wins a pawn and attacks your knight on e2. After 7.Na3 Qa6 8.Qb3 Nc6 9.Nb5 O-O-O Black is a pawn up, castled, while your king is still in the centre.

strays.text: You open the centre while your king is still on e1.

taught.why: 6.O-O puts your king on g1, where it guards g2 against ...Qxg2. Then 7.Nd2 covers c4, so 8.c4 Qd6 gains space with tempo on the queen.

enforces.text: Castling defends g2, and c4 follows once the square is covered.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.Nbc3 develops with tempo on the queen but leaves g2 unguarded: 6...Qxg2 7.Rg1 Qh3 wins a pawn, and with the rook gone from h1 you can no longer castle short.
alternatives.after: 6.O-O guards g2 first; masters castle here in 97% of games. The knight can come out later.

7782133965544018|f1c4.headline: Against 2...c6, take the free e5 pawn with 3.Nxe5
7782133965544018|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 leaves the loose e5 pawn alone and lets Black play 3...d5, the move 2...c6 prepared, with a hit on your bishop. After 4.Bb3 a5 5.a3 Nf6 6.Nc3 a4 7.Ba2 Bd6 Black has the centre and has pushed your bishop back to a2, and most of your edge is gone. 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn that nothing defends, and 2...c6 has taken the c6 square from Black's knight, so Black has little to show for it. After 3...Nf6 4.Bc4 d5 5.exd5 Bd6 6.d4 cxd5 7.Bb3 Nc6 you keep the extra pawn and develop; just don't play 4.d3, which loses to 4...Qa5+.
7782133965544018|f1c4.principle: After each opponent move, check what was left undefended: a centre pawn next to your knight with no guard is usually a free pawn.
sources: GM Petrov: Surprise Repertoire for Black after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3, Video 3: 2...Bc5 (ICC) | https://www.chessclub.com/videos/gm-petrov-surprise-repertoire-for-black-after-1.e4-e5-2.nf3-video-3-2...bc5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...c6 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...e5/2._Nf3/2...c6
King's Pawn Game: Gunderam Gambit (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/kings-pawn-game/gunderam-gambit/
Gunderam Gambit (ppqty) | https://ppqty.com/gunderam-gambit/

ideas.title: Take the undefended e5 pawn
ideas.text: Your knight attacks e5 and nothing defends it. Take it first with 3.Nxe5, then deal with Black's tries.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 break
ideas.text: 2...c6 prepares ...d5. Against a slow move like 3.Bc4, 3...d5 hits your bishop and Black gets the centre for free.

ideas.title: Watch for ...Qa5+
ideas.text: After 3.Nxe5 Nf6, Black's queen can check on a5 and hit your knight on e5, so a careless 4.d3 loses to 4...Qa5+.

ideas.title: No ...Nc6 for Black
ideas.text: 2...c6 took c6 from Black's queen knight, so it can't chase your queen after 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4.

habit.why: 3.Bc4 leaves the loose e5 pawn alone and lets Black play 3...d5, the move 2...c6 prepared, with a hit on your bishop. After 4.Bb3 a5 5.a3 Nf6 6.Nc3 a4 7.Ba2 Bd6 Black has the centre and has pushed your bishop back to a2, and most of your edge is gone.

strays.text: A normal developing move lets the gambit off the hook.

taught.why: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn that nothing defends, and 2...c6 has taken the c6 square from Black's knight, so Black has little to show for it. After 3...Nf6 4.Bc4 d5 5.exd5 Bd6 6.d4 cxd5 7.Bb3 Nc6 you keep the extra pawn and develop; just don't play 4.d3, which loses to 4...Qa5+.

enforces.text: You take the pawn first and handle Black's tries afterwards.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.d4 is strong: after 3...exd4 4.Qxd4 your queen stands in the centre, and 2...c6 has taken c6 from the knight that would chase it. The engine rates it as highly as any move here.
alternatives.after: Both moves are strong: 3.Nxe5 simply wins a pawn, while 3.d4 plays for fast development, and the queens can come off after 5.Nc3 Qb6 6.Bf4 Qxd4.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 develops and stops ...d5 for now, but it leaves the loose e5 pawn: after 3...d6 Black has guarded it and the chance is gone.
alternatives.after: 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn while it is loose; after 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4 Nd7 you have only a normal development lead.

7803977633029211|c8e6.headline: Guard f7 with 6...Nh6; 6...Be6 loses to 7.Bxe6 fxe6 8.Nxe6
7803977633029211|c8e6.why: 6...Be6 lets White trade on e6: 7.Bxe6 fxe6 8.Nxe6 wins a pawn and forks your queen and the c5 bishop. After 8...Bxf2+ 9.Kf1 Qd7 10.Qg4 your kingside falls apart, as 11.Nxg7+ shows. 6...Nh6 develops your last minor piece and adds a defender to f7. If 7.Qh5 you castle with 7...O-O so the rook guards f7 too, and 8...Na5 and 9...Nxc4 later remove the Italian bishop.
7803977633029211|c8e6.principle: When a knight and bishop both aim at f7, guard it with a developing move before starting your own plans.
sources: Souleidis and Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf
IM Roven Vogel reviews Wesley So's Modern Italian (ChessBase) | http://en.chessbase.com/post/roven-vogel-reviews-the-modern-italian-by-wesley-so
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nc6/3. Nf3

ideas.title: White's attack on f7
ideas.text: The g5 knight and c4 bishop both hit f7, and White threatens 7.Qh5 to add the queen.

ideas.title: Guard f7 with a piece
ideas.text: A knight on h6 covers f7, and castling then adds the rook, as in 6...Nh6 7.Qh5 O-O.

ideas.title: Swap off the Italian bishop
ideas.text: Trading White's c4 bishop is a good plan, as 8...Na5 and 9...Nxc4 do in the main line. 6...Be6 fails here: 7.Bxe6 fxe6 lets the knight into e6.

habit.why: 6...Be6 lets White trade on e6: 7.Bxe6 fxe6 8.Nxe6 wins a pawn and forks your queen and the c5 bishop. After 8...Bxf2+ 9.Kf1 Qd7 10.Qg4 your kingside falls apart, as 11.Nxg7+ shows.

strays.text: Here 7...fxe6 opens e6 to the g5 knight, so the trade backfires.

taught.why: 6...Nh6 develops your last minor piece and adds a defender to f7. If 7.Qh5 you castle with 7...O-O so the rook guards f7 too, and 8...Na5 and 9...Nxc4 later remove the Italian bishop.

enforces.text: The knight on h6 covers f7 and clears the way to castle.

7827708463373629|c2c3.headline: Block with 5.Nc3; 5.c3 hands b2 and c3 to the queen
7827708463373629|c2c3.why: 5.c3 blocks the check with a pawn, and 5...Qxb2 takes the b2 pawn at once. After 6.Nbd2 Qxc3 the queen eats c3 as well, so Black has the gambit pawn back plus one more. 5.Nc3 blocks with a developing move and keeps the d-file open for your queen. After 5...Qa5 6.Qd5 Bb4 7.Qxa5 Bxa5 the queens come off and you keep the extra pawn.
7827708463373629|c2c3.principle: Block a check with a piece you want to develop anyway, not a pawn move that gives the queen new targets.
sources: Anton Shuravin, Englund Gambit: Traps, Best Lines (ChessDoctrine) | https://chessdoctrine.com/chess-openings/queens-pawn/englund-gambit/
Michael Tam, Queen Sacrifice! Englund Gambit Line (chess.com blog) | https://www.chess.com/blog/vitualis/queen-sacrifice-amazing-englund-gambit-line
Englund Gambit - Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Englund_Gambit
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. dxe5

ideas.title: Watch the ...Qb4+ fork
ideas.text: 4...Qb4+ checks your king and eyes b2, which lost its guard when your bishop left c1. Block in a way that keeps b2 safe.

ideas.title: Develop while you block
ideas.text: 5.Nc3 blocks with a piece you want out anyway, and it keeps the d-file open for 6.Qd5.

ideas.title: Keep the extra pawn
ideas.text: After 2.dxe5 you are a pawn up. Black's plan is to win it back with ...Qxb2 or ...Nxe5, so don't hand it over.

habit.why: 5.c3 blocks the check with a pawn, and 5...Qxb2 takes the b2 pawn at once. After 6.Nbd2 Qxc3 the queen eats c3 as well, so Black has the gambit pawn back plus one more.

strays.text: The pawn block hands the queen two pawns, the whole point of the gambit.

taught.why: 5.Nc3 blocks with a developing move and keeps the d-file open for your queen. After 5...Qa5 6.Qd5 Bb4 7.Qxa5 Bxa5 the queens come off and you keep the extra pawn.

enforces.text: The knight blocks, develops, and leaves the d-file open for 6.Qd5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bd2 blocks and hits the queen, and after 5...Qe7 you lead in development, though Black soon wins the pawn back with ...Nxe5. Sound, but there's a move that keeps the pawn.
alternatives.after: 5.Nc3 develops a new piece instead of moving the bishop twice, and after 5...Qa5 6.Qd5 you keep the extra pawn rather than allowing 6...Nxe5.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5.Nbd2 blocks the check, but the knight shuts your queen off the d-file. After 5...h6 6.Bh4 Nxe5 Black wins the gambit pawn back with an easy game.
alternatives.after: 5.Nc3 also blocks, but leaves the d-file open, so after 5...Qa5 6.Qd5 you trade queens and keep the extra pawn.

7832135918552384|d2d3.headline: Black gives you the centre: take it with 2.d4
7832135918552384|d2d3.why: 2.d3 declines the centre Black offers, and after 2...c5 3.g3 Nc6 4.Bg2 Bg7 Black has a comfortable, level game. One quiet move has given away your opening edge. 2.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre while Black hasn't contested it, and 95.1% of masters play it. After 2...d6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Be3 c6 5.Qd2 you have space and quick development, and Black must work to undermine your centre.
7832135918552384|d2d3.principle: When the opponent lets you build a two-pawn centre, build it: 2.d4 takes space and frees your pieces before Black can challenge it.
sources: Modern Defense (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Defense
How to Beat the Modern Defense (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/modern-defense/how-to-beat/

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...g6/2._d4

ideas.title: Take the centre Black offers
ideas.text: 1...g6 lets you set up pawns on e4 and d4; 2.d4 does it at once, as 95.1% of masters do.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Black plans to hit your centre later, with the g7 bishop aiming at d4 and pawn levers like ...c5.

ideas.title: Black's ...c5 against slow moves
ideas.text: If you don't play d4, 2...c5 grabs control of d4 and Black gets an easy Sicilian-style game.

ideas.title: Be3, Qd2 and Bh6
ideas.text: With d4 in, 4.Be3 and 5.Qd2 prepare to trade the g7 bishop from h6; Black answers with ...c6 and 5...b5.

habit.why: 2.d3 declines the centre Black offers, and after 2...c5 3.g3 Nc6 4.Bg2 Bg7 Black has a comfortable, level game. One quiet move has given away your opening edge.

strays.text: 2.d3 leaves d4 to Black's 2...c5 instead of taking it.

taught.why: 2.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre while Black hasn't contested it, and 95.1% of masters play it. After 2...d6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Be3 c6 5.Qd2 you have space and quick development, and Black must work to undermine your centre.

enforces.text: Pawns on e4 and d4 give you space and open lines for your pieces.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2.Nf3 develops, but lets Black choose a Sicilian with 2...c5, and after 3.c3 d5 4.e5 Nc6 you get an Alapin-like game. Sound, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 2.d4 takes the centre before Black can answer with ...c5; masters choose it 95.1% of the time, 2.Nf3 0.8%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2.Bc4 aims at f7, but 2...c5 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.c3 e6 cuts the bishop off and Black gets a comfortable game. Sound, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 2.d4 takes space first; after 2.Bc4 the bishop runs into ...e6 and your d-pawn waits until 6.d4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2.Nc3 is sound, but 2...c5 turns the game into a Sicilian where Black develops comfortably. There is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 2.d4 sets up the centre before Black's ...c5 arrives; masters play it 95.1% of the time to 2.5% for 2.Nc3.

7832135918552384|f2f4.headline: Take the full centre with 2.d4 when Black allows it
7832135918552384|f2f4.why: 2.f4 doesn't develop anything and leaves d4 unsupported: Black strikes with 2...d5, and after 3.e5 c5 4.d4 cxd4 White has lost a pawn. 1...g6 is a hypermodern move that lets White build a classical centre and hopes to undermine it later. 2.d4, played in 95% of master games, accepts the invitation: two pawns in the centre, more space, and lines open for both bishops.
7832135918552384|f2f4.principle: When your opponent doesn't contest the centre, occupy it with both centre pawns before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4

7839204652261332|f1c4.headline: Against the Caro-Kann, put a second pawn in the centre
7839204652261332|f1c4.why: 2.Bc4 aims the bishop where 2...d5 hits it, so after 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bb3 it has moved twice and Black has traded the c-pawn for your e-pawn. Black then develops with 4...Nf6 and 5...Bg4 and has the easier game. 2.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre, the move 80% of masters play. After 2...d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.g4 you gain space and chase the bishop, though pushes like 6.h4 h5 can make your own pawns targets.
7839204652261332|f1c4.principle: If the opponent's first move doesn't stop d4, claim the centre with pawns first; bring bishops out once you know which squares enemy pawns will hit.

ideas.title: Take the full centre with d4
ideas.text: 1...c6 does nothing against d4, so put a second pawn in the centre with 2.d4 before Black's 2...d5 arrives.

ideas.title: Bishop on c4 hits a wall
ideas.text: 1...c6 prepares ...d5, which hits a bishop on c4. After 2...d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bb3 the bishop has moved twice.

ideas.title: Answer ...d5 by keeping e4
ideas.text: After 2.d4 d5 Black hits e4. 3.e5 gains space and keeps your central pawn instead of swapping it.

ideas.title: Black trades c-pawn for e-pawn
ideas.text: After exd5 cxd5 Black has swapped a side pawn for your central one and develops freely, as with 4...Nf6 and 5...Bg4.

habit.why: 2.Bc4 aims the bishop where 2...d5 hits it, so after 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bb3 it has moved twice and Black has traded the c-pawn for your e-pawn. Black then develops with 4...Nf6 and 5...Bg4 and has the easier game.

strays.idea: Bishop on c4 hits a wall
strays.text: The bishop comes out before d4, and 2...d5 blunts it.

taught.why: 2.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre, the move 80% of masters play. After 2...d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.g4 you gain space and chase the bishop, though pushes like 6.h4 h5 can make your own pawns targets.

enforces.idea: Take the full centre with d4
enforces.text: Pawns on d4 and e4 claim the centre before 2...d5 can challenge it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Take the full centre with d4
alternatives.before: 2.Nf3 develops and allows the Two Knights after 2...d5 3.Nc3, where Black develops solidly with 3...Bg4 and 4...e6. It is sound, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 2.d4 takes the centre at once; after 2.Nf3 you often play 5.d4 later anyway, as in 4.Be2 e6 5.d4. Club players pick 2.Nf3 in 31% of games, masters in 5%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2.Nc3 guards e4 with a knight ahead of 2...d5 and keeps the Two Knights open. It is sound, but there is a more direct move.
alternatives.after: 2.d4 claims the centre at once. 2.Nc3 often transposes: 2...d5 3.d4 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6 is the Classical main line.

7839204652261332|f2f4.headline: Against the Caro-Kann, put the second pawn on d4
7839204652261332|f2f4.why: 2.f4 doesn't defend e4 against 2...d5, and after 3.d3 dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1 the queens are gone and your king has lost the right to castle. 1...c6 neither makes a threat nor controls d4, so 2.d4 builds a two-pawn centre; it is the choice in over 80% of master games. After 2...d5 3.e5 White gains space and Black has to find a home for the bishop with 3...Bf5.
7839204652261332|f2f4.principle: When the opponent's first move doesn't contest d4, occupy it: two centre pawns give your pieces room and take squares from Black's.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6

7896021651424943|f1e2.headline: Against 3...Bg4, open the centre at once with 4.d4.
7896021651424943|f1e2.why: 4.Be2 is too slow: Black answers 4...Nc6 and sets up comfortably with no pressure on e5. The Philidor is a passive defence whose pawn on d6 blocks Black's own bishop, and the main plan against it is the d4 break. 4.d4 strikes at e5 at once; after 4...Nc6 5.Bb5 exd4 6.Qxd4 White's queen is centralised and Black has given up the centre.
7896021651424943|f1e2.principle: When the opponent's setup is passive, open the centre with d4 while your pieces are the more active ones.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6

7902974846795865|b4b5.headline: Play 8.a4 first; 8.b5 sends Black's knight to a5
7902974846795865|b4b5.why: 8.b5 drives the knight to a5, where it hits your c4-bishop, and 9.Nxe5 doesn't help: 9...Qe8 hits the knight at once. After 10.Ng4 Nxg4 11.Qxg4 Nxc4 12.dxc4 d6 Black has your bishop, your c-pawns are doubled and the c8-bishop now hits your queen. 8.a4 gains space and threatens a5 against the b6-bishop, so Black spends 8...a6 on a retreat. After 9.Nbd2 d6 10.Re1 Be6 11.Bxe6 fxe6 you have built up calmly and left Black with doubled e-pawns.
7902974846795865|b4b5.principle: Ask what your push allows: 8.b5 hands the knight a5 with tempo on your bishop, while 8.a4 gains space without a gift.

ideas.title: a4 before b5
ideas.text: a4 gains queenside space and threatens a5 against the b6-bishop. Push b5 only once the a-pawn supports it.

ideas.title: b5 sends the knight to a5
ideas.text: Push b5 too soon and the c6-knight jumps to a5, hitting your c4-bishop; Black can trade it off.

ideas.title: Build up, then d4
ideas.text: Bring the queen's knight via d2 and f1 to g3, and push d4 only after that preparation.

ideas.title: Black trades with ...Be6
ideas.text: Black often plays ...Be6 to trade your c4-bishop; taking on e6 leaves Black with doubled e-pawns.

habit.why: 8.b5 drives the knight to a5, where it hits your c4-bishop, and 9.Nxe5 doesn't help: 9...Qe8 hits the knight at once. After 10.Ng4 Nxg4 11.Qxg4 Nxc4 12.dxc4 d6 Black has your bishop, your c-pawns are doubled and the c8-bishop now hits your queen.

strays.text: Without a4 behind it, the b5-pawn just drives the knight to a5.

taught.why: 8.a4 gains space and threatens a5 against the b6-bishop, so Black spends 8...a6 on a retreat. After 9.Nbd2 d6 10.Re1 Be6 11.Bxe6 fxe6 you have built up calmly and left Black with doubled e-pawns.

enforces.text: a4 gains space and makes Black spend 8...a6 on the bishop.

7908463020324267|b8c6.headline: Hit e4 with 4...Nf6 before White gets in c4
7908463020324267|b8c6.why: 4...Nc6 attacks nothing, so White has time for 5.c4, putting pawns on c4 and e4 that clamp the d5 square. After 5...Nf6 6.Nc3 g6 7.f3 White holds the Maroczy bind and freeing your game with a pawn to d5 becomes very hard. 4...Nf6 attacks e4, so White has no time for 5.c4 and defends with 5.Nc3, which blocks the c-pawn. After 5...a6 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 you are in a Najdorf, the choice of 99.5% of masters at move 4.
7908463020324267|b8c6.principle: Develop with threats: 4...Nf6 attacks e4, so White must defend it instead of setting up the Maroczy bind with 5.c4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4

ideas.title: Hit e4 with ...Nf6 early
ideas.text: 4...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White must spend the next move defending it, usually with 5.Nc3.

ideas.title: White wants the Maroczy bind
ideas.text: With pawns on c4 and e4, White clamps d5 and freeing your game with a pawn to d5 becomes very hard.

ideas.title: Nc3 blocks the c-pawn
ideas.text: Once 5.Nc3 guards e4, the knight stands in front of the c-pawn, so the c4 clamp is off for now.

ideas.title: The d5 hole after ...e5
ideas.text: An early ...e5, before ...Nf6 and ...a6, leaves d5 weak and lets the d4 knight jump to f5.

habit.why: 4...Nc6 attacks nothing, so White has time for 5.c4, putting pawns on c4 and e4 that clamp the d5 square. After 5...Nf6 6.Nc3 g6 7.f3 White holds the Maroczy bind and freeing your game with a pawn to d5 becomes very hard.

strays.text: No pressure on e4, so White has a free move for 5.c4.

taught.why: 4...Nf6 attacks e4, so White has no time for 5.c4 and defends with 5.Nc3, which blocks the c-pawn. After 5...a6 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 you are in a Najdorf, the choice of 99.5% of masters at move 4.

enforces.text: The knight develops with a threat, and White must spend 5.Nc3 on e4.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4...e5 kicks the knight, but you haven't prepared it: 5.Bb5+ Nd7 6.Nf5 puts the knight on a fine square and d5 becomes a lasting hole.
alternatives.after: 4...Nf6 first makes White commit with 5.Nc3, and then ...e5 comes once ...a6 has covered b5: 5...a6 6.Be3 e5.

7908463020324267|g7g6.headline: Play 4...Nf6 first: 4...g6 leaves e4 alone and White free
7908463020324267|g7g6.why: 4...g6 puts no pressure on e4, so White can choose freely: 5.c4 for the Maroczy bind, or 5.Be3 Nf6 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.f3 and 8.Qd2. That is a Yugoslav Attack setup against the Dragon, with White's pieces placed before you have any counterplay. 4...Nf6 attacks e4, and 5.c4 would just drop the pawn to 5...Nxe4. So White defends with 5.Nc3, blocking the c-pawn, and after 5...a6 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 you are in a Najdorf.
7908463020324267|g7g6.principle: Develop with threats: 4...Nf6 attacks e4, so White must defend it instead of choosing a setup freely.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4

habit.why: 4...g6 puts no pressure on e4, so White can choose freely: 5.c4 for the Maroczy bind, or 5.Be3 Nf6 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.f3 and 8.Qd2. That is a Yugoslav Attack setup against the Dragon, with White's pieces placed before you have any counterplay.

enforces.text: The knight develops with a threat, and White must spend 5.Nc3 on e4.

alternatives.after: 4...Nf6 forces 5.Nc3 first, so the c-pawn is blocked and the bind is off; the knight can still come to c6 later.

7917889477711464|c6d4.headline: Develop the other knight; 4...Nd4 leaves e5 hanging.
7917889477711464|c6d4.why: 4...Nd4 moves the same knight again and stops guarding e5, so 5.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and after 5...Qf6 6.Bxf7+ Kd8 7.Bxg8 White's bishop on c4 also strikes at f7. 4...Nf6 develops a new piece to a good square where it pressures e4, controls d5 and prepares to castle. That calm setup is what the slow Giuoco Pianissimo calls for.
7917889477711464|c6d4.principle: In a quiet opening, bring out the pieces still at home rather than moving a developed piece again and abandoning what it guards.

7917889477711464|f7f6.headline: Knight to f6: develop and castle, don't play f6
7917889477711464|f7f6.why: 4...f6 takes the king knight's best square and weakens the diagonal from c4 toward g8; after 5.Nh4 g6 6.O-O Black ends up moving the king with ...Kf8 instead of castling. 4...Nf6 develops the knight to a good square where it pressures e4, controls d5 and prepares to castle kingside, and masters choose it in 91.7% of games.
7917889477711464|f7f6.principle: In the quiet Italian, finish developing and castle; a pawn move that blocks a knight and loosens the king costs more than it supports e5.

7920350690808360|f8c5.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6; 3...Bc5 runs into 4.d4
7920350690808360|f8c5.why: White wants 4.d4 anyway, and 3...Bc5 makes it stronger: the theory notes the pawn takes the centre, gains time on the bishop and opens the c1 bishop to win back the f4 pawn. After 4.d4 Be7 5.Bxf4 the gambit pawn is gone. 3...Nf6, the Schallopp defence, develops and attacks e4; if White pushes 4.e5, the theory recommends 4...Nh5 to keep defending f4.
7920350690808360|f8c5.principle: Don't put a piece where a pawn can attack it with gain of time; develop to squares where your piece attacks something instead.

7994400733701852|d7d5.headline: Develop with 3...Nc6 and go after the c4 bishop
7994400733701852|d7d5.why: 3...d5 opens the centre while d5 is hit by the c4-bishop and, after 4.exd5 exd5, by the queen too. 5.Qxd5 wins the pawn and threatens mate on f7, so after 5...Qe7+ 6.Ne2 Nc6 7.Nc3 Be6 8.Qd3 you are simply a pawn down. 3...Nc6 develops and heads for e5, where the knight hits both the queen and the c4-bishop. After 4.Ne2 Ne5 5.Qc3 Nxc4 6.Qxc4 Nf6 you have both bishops and White's queen has moved three times.
7994400733701852|d7d5.principle: Count attackers before you push: d5 is hit by the bishop and, once the e-pawns trade, the queen, so develop with 3...Nc6 instead of losing the pawn to 5.Qxd5.

ideas.title: ...Nc6 before ...d5
ideas.text: Develop before you push ...d5. With the c4-bishop and the queen both aiming at d5, an early 3...d5 just drops the pawn.

ideas.title: Hunt the c4 bishop
ideas.text: The bishop is White's best piece. 3...Nc6 and 4...Ne5 hit it and the queen together; ...a6 and ...b5 chase it too.

ideas.title: Queen and bishop aim at d5 and f7
ideas.text: 3.Qf3 joins the c4-bishop: both aim at d5, and the queen also eyes f7. Once the e-pawns are traded, 5.Qxd5 also threatens mate on f7.

habit.why: 3...d5 opens the centre while d5 is hit by the c4-bishop and, after 4.exd5 exd5, by the queen too. 5.Qxd5 wins the pawn and threatens mate on f7, so after 5...Qe7+ 6.Ne2 Nc6 7.Nc3 Be6 8.Qd3 you are simply a pawn down.

strays.text: The pawn goes to d5 before any piece can defend it.

taught.why: 3...Nc6 develops and heads for e5, where the knight hits both the queen and the c4-bishop. After 4.Ne2 Ne5 5.Qc3 Nxc4 6.Qxc4 Nf6 you have both bishops and White's queen has moved three times.

enforces.text: 4...Ne5 attacks queen and bishop, and you trade off the bishop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...a6 prepares ...b5 to chase the bishop, as in 4.d3 b5 5.Bb3 Bb7, and it's a sound choice. There is a more forcing one.
alternatives.after: 3...Nc6 goes after the bishop at once: 4...Ne5 hits it and the queen together, and 5...Nxc4 takes it. 3...a6 is also fine, just slower.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Nf6 develops and hits e4, so your ...d5 later comes with support, as in 5...d5. It's sound, but after 7.Bb5 and 8.Bxc6+ your c-pawns end up doubled.
alternatives.after: 3...Nc6 heads for e5 to win the bishop. Both moves develop before ...d5 and keep the game level.

8013895061699550|d5d6.headline: Keep the pawn: 7.Qe2 hits e5, don't push 7.d6
8013895061699550|d5d6.why: 7.d6 hands back your extra pawn: 7...Nxd6 takes it back and hits the c4-bishop. After 8.Be2 h6 9.Nf3 e4 10.Ne5 Qe7 Black's pieces chase yours and Black is the one pressing. 7.Qe2 attacks e5 and keeps the d5-pawn, so Black has to defend instead of recovering material. After 7...Nd6 8.Bb3 Be7 9.d3 you stay a pawn up with a solid position.
8013895061699550|d5d6.principle: You took Black's pawn, so consolidate: 7.Qe2 keeps it and makes Black defend, while 7.d6 just gives it back.

ideas.title: Keep the extra pawn
ideas.text: You are a pawn up on d5. Pushing it to d6 gives it back for nothing; keep it and develop.

ideas.title: Qe2 hits e5
ideas.text: 7.Qe2 attacks the e5-pawn, so Black must spend moves defending it instead of winning material back.

ideas.title: Retreat the knight in time
ideas.text: When ...h6 hits the g5-knight, pull it back to f3; after ...e4 it can jump on to e5.

ideas.title: Black gains time on your pieces
ideas.text: Black's knight hits your bishop from d6, and ...h6 and ...e4 drive your knight back; Black wants time, not just the pawn.

habit.why: 7.d6 hands back your extra pawn: 7...Nxd6 takes it back and hits the c4-bishop. After 8.Be2 h6 9.Nf3 e4 10.Ne5 Qe7 Black's pieces chase yours and Black is the one pressing.

strays.text: The push gives the pawn back and develops Black's knight.

taught.why: 7.Qe2 attacks e5 and keeps the d5-pawn, so Black has to defend instead of recovering material. After 7...Nd6 8.Bb3 Be7 9.d3 you stay a pawn up with a solid position.

enforces.text: The queen attacks e5, so Black defends instead of winning the pawn back.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: Castling is natural, but 7...h6 8.Nf3 e4 kicks your knight twice and Black gets active play for the pawn. There is a slightly more useful move.
alternatives.after: 7.Qe2 makes Black deal with e5 first. Nelson's engine check still rates 7.O-O as good for White.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.d4 opens the centre with your king on e1: after 7...exd4 8.O-O Nxd5 9.Re1+ Be7 Black has the pawn back, and you need a wild 10.g4 to keep going.
alternatives.after: 7.Qe2 keeps the centre closed and the d5-pawn guarded, so you never need a gamble like 11.Nxh7.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 7.Qf3 brings the queen out where Black gains time on it: 7...Nd6 hits the bishop, 8.Bd3 Bg4 hits the queen, and after 9.Qg3 h6 Black wins the d5-pawn back with the better game.
alternatives.after: 7.Qe2 also attacks e5, but after 7...Nd6 8.Bb3 the queen is not hit, and you stay a pawn up.
alternatives.idea: Black gains time on your pieces

8021519334015813|d2d3.headline: Take e5 with 4.Nxe5 before moving your d-pawn
8021519334015813|d2d3.why: 4.d3 pins your own c3-knight to the king, and 4...d5 frees Black's game at once. After 5.exd5 Nxd5 6.Bd2 O-O Black has easy play, and you never won the e5 pawn. 4.Nxe5 takes a pawn nothing defends, while your c3-knight still guards e4. Black usually wins it back with 4...O-O 5.Be2 Re8 6.Nd3 Bxc3 7.dxc3 Nxe4, but you keep the bishop pair and a slightly better game after 8.O-O.
8021519334015813|d2d3.principle: Don't move a pawn that unpins nothing and creates a pin: with ...Bb4 out, a d-pawn move pins c3, so take the loose e5 pawn instead.

ideas.title: Take the free e5 pawn
ideas.text: e5 is undefended and your c3-knight guards e4, so 4.Nxe5 is the main move, played in 67% of master games.

ideas.title: Moving the d-pawn pins c3
ideas.text: With the bishop on b4, any d-pawn move pins your c3-knight to the king, and e4 loses its only defender.

ideas.title: Black can't grab e4 at once
ideas.text: After 4.Nxe5, the grab 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 Nxe4? loses to 6.Qg4, forking the e4-knight and g7, so Black castles first.

ideas.title: Give the pawn back on your terms
ideas.text: After 4...O-O, the main line 5.Be2 Re8 6.Nd3 Bxc3 7.dxc3 Nxe4 8.O-O returns the pawn but leaves you both bishops.

habit.why: 4.d3 pins your own c3-knight to the king, and 4...d5 frees Black's game at once. After 5.exd5 Nxd5 6.Bd2 O-O Black has easy play, and you never won the e5 pawn.

strays.text: The d-pawn move pins c3, and Black frees the game with 4...d5.

taught.why: 4.Nxe5 takes a pawn nothing defends, while your c3-knight still guards e4. Black usually wins it back with 4...O-O 5.Be2 Re8 6.Nd3 Bxc3 7.dxc3 Nxe4, but you keep the bishop pair and a slightly better game after 8.O-O.

enforces.text: The knight takes e5 while c3 still guards e4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Bc4 is fine and the second most popular master move (19%): after 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 d6 you have the bishop pair and open lines. There is a more direct move.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxe5 (67% of masters) takes a pawn first; after 4.Bc4 the reply 5...d6 defends e5 and the pawn is gone.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.a3 asks the bishop at once: after 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 O-O you have the bishop pair and an open d-file. It's sound, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxe5 wins e5 first and still gets the bishop pair later; 4.a3 gets the bishops but never the pawn.

8021519334015813|d2d4.headline: 4.d4 pins your knight and drops e4: take e5 instead
8021519334015813|d2d4.why: 4.d4 pins your c3-knight to the king, so e4 loses its defender and 4...Nxe4 takes it. After 5.Qd3 d5 6.dxe5 O-O Black develops fast, and 7...Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 Re8 doubles your c-pawns with your king still in the centre. 4.Nxe5 takes a pawn nothing defends, while your c3-knight still guards e4. Black usually wins it back with 4...O-O 5.Be2 Re8 6.Nd3 Bxc3 7.dxc3 Nxe4, but you keep the bishop pair and a slightly better game after 8.O-O.
8021519334015813|d2d4.principle: Check what a pawn move unguards before playing it: with ...Bb4 out, 4.d4 pins c3 and leaves e4 loose, while 4.Nxe5 wins a pawn.

ideas.title: Take the free e5 pawn
ideas.text: e5 is undefended and your c3-knight guards e4, so 4.Nxe5 is the main move, played in 67% of master games.

ideas.title: Moving the d-pawn pins c3
ideas.text: With the bishop on b4, any d-pawn move pins your c3-knight to the king, and e4 loses its only defender.

ideas.title: Black can't grab e4 at once
ideas.text: After 4.Nxe5, the grab 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 Nxe4? loses to 6.Qg4, forking the e4-knight and g7, so Black castles first.

ideas.title: Give the pawn back on your terms
ideas.text: After 4...O-O, the main line 5.Be2 Re8 6.Nd3 Bxc3 7.dxc3 Nxe4 8.O-O returns the pawn but leaves you both bishops.

habit.why: 4.d4 pins your c3-knight to the king, so e4 loses its defender and 4...Nxe4 takes it. After 5.Qd3 d5 6.dxe5 O-O Black develops fast, and 7...Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 Re8 doubles your c-pawns with your king still in the centre.

strays.text: 4.d4 pins c3, so e4 falls to 4...Nxe4.

taught.why: 4.Nxe5 takes a pawn nothing defends, while your c3-knight still guards e4. Black usually wins it back with 4...O-O 5.Be2 Re8 6.Nd3 Bxc3 7.dxc3 Nxe4, but you keep the bishop pair and a slightly better game after 8.O-O.

enforces.text: The knight takes e5 while c3 still guards e4.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.d3 also pins your own c3-knight, and 4...d5 frees Black at once: after 5.exd5 Nxd5 6.Bd2 O-O Black has easy play.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxe5 takes a pawn and keeps the d-pawn home, so c3 still guards e4. Masters play 4.d3 in 6% of games.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Bc4 is fine and the second most popular master move (19%): after 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 d6 you have the bishop pair and open lines. There is a more direct move.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxe5 (67% of masters) takes a pawn first; after 4.Bc4 the reply 5...d6 defends e5 and the pawn is gone.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.a3 asks the bishop at once: after 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 O-O you have the bishop pair and an open d-file. It's sound, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxe5 wins e5 first and still gets the bishop pair later; 4.a3 gets the bishops but never the pawn.

8041898991527130|d1e2.headline: In the Exchange French, play 4.d4, not an early queen check
8041898991527130|d1e2.why: 4.Qe2+ is met by 4...Be7, which blocks the check and develops, while your queen shuts in the f1 bishop. After 5.d4 Nf6 6.Qd1 the queen goes home, and 6...O-O 7.Bd3 Re8 8.O-O Bg4 leaves Black ahead in development. 4.d4 puts a pawn in the centre and opens your c1 bishop; masters choose it 97% of the time. After 4...Nf6 5.Bd3 c5 6.c3 you develop normally, though the symmetrical position is comfortable for Black too.
8041898991527130|d1e2.principle: A queen check that the opponent blocks with a developing move only helps them; develop the minor pieces first.
sources: French Defense: Knight Variation (Chess Openings Lab) | https://www.chessopeningslab.com/openings/french-defense/knight-variation/

ideas.title: The queen check helps Black
ideas.text: 4.Qe2+ is blocked by 4...Be7, a developing move. Your queen then shuts in the f1 bishop and goes back with 6.Qd1.

ideas.title: Claim the centre with d4
ideas.text: 4.d4 puts a pawn in the centre and opens your c1 bishop. Masters play it 97% of the time.

ideas.title: Black's c8 bishop is free
ideas.text: After the swap on d5, Black's c8 bishop is no longer locked behind e6, so Black develops easily, as with 8...Bg4.

ideas.title: A knight on c3 gets kicked
ideas.text: Black's d5 pawn can advance and hit a knight on c3, sending it back with 5.Nb1.

habit.why: 4.Qe2+ is met by 4...Be7, which blocks the check and develops, while your queen shuts in the f1 bishop. After 5.d4 Nf6 6.Qd1 the queen goes home, and 6...O-O 7.Bd3 Re8 8.O-O Bg4 leaves Black ahead in development.

strays.text: Black blocks with a developing move, and your queen has to go back.

taught.why: 4.d4 puts a pawn in the centre and opens your c1 bishop; masters choose it 97% of the time. After 4...Nf6 5.Bd3 c5 6.c3 you develop normally, though the symmetrical position is comfortable for Black too.

enforces.text: A centre pawn and an open diagonal for your c1 bishop, with no lost time.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 develops, but Black's d5 pawn advances and kicks the knight back with 5.Nb1. After 5...Nc6 6.Bb5 Ne7 Black has gained space and time.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 stops the d5 pawn from advancing; masters play it 97% of the time, 4.Nc3 0.4%.
alternatives.idea: A knight on c3 gets kicked

8076559324931644|b1c3.headline: Punish 2...f6 with 3.Nxe5: the pawn on f6 can't defend e5
8076559324931644|b1c3.why: 2...f6 only seems to defend e5, and 3.Nc3 lets Black get away with it and develop normally. 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn, because 3...fxe5 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxe5+ forks the king and the rook on h8. Black's best try is 3...Qe7, and after 4.Nf3 White keeps a big lead in development; don't play 4.Qh5+ there, since 4...g6 leaves the queen with nowhere to go.
8076559324931644|b1c3.principle: Look at captures first and check what forcing reply follows: here the weakened diagonal to Black's king makes the capture safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6/3. Nxe5

8144277447096351|f1c4.headline: After ...Bxf3, hit b7 at once with 6.Qb3
8144277447096351|f1c4.why: 6.Bc4 threatens mate on f7, but 6...Qf6 defends f7 and offers a queen trade. After 7.Qb3 Nd7 8.Qxb7 Rb8 9.Qa6 Qxa6 10.Bxa6 Nc5 the queens are off, Black's pieces are active and you keep much less of your edge. 6.Qb3 hits b7 at once, and with your bishop coming to c4 it also eyes f7, so Black gets no time for ...Qf6. After 6...Nd7 7.Be3 Bc5 8.Bxc5 Nxc5 9.Qb5+ Nd7 10.Qxb7 you win the pawn with queens on, and GM Larry Kaufman rates 6.Qb3 above Morphy's 6.Bc4.
8144277447096351|f1c4.principle: When the opponent gives up a bishop, hit the squares it guarded at once: 6.Qb3 attacks b7 before Black can organise ...Qf6.
sources: Bobby Ang quoting GM Larry Kaufman, Beating the Philidor (BusinessWorld) | https://www.euvolution.com/prometheism-transhumanism-posthumanism/chess-engines/beating-the-philidor-businessworld-online/

ideas.title: Hit b7 with Qb3
ideas.text: Black traded the c8-bishop on f3, so nothing guards b7 any more. 6.Qb3 attacks it at once.

ideas.title: Queen and bishop against f7
ideas.text: With your bishop on c4, the queen on f3 or b3 adds a second attacker on f7, the pattern of Morphy's Opera Game.

ideas.title: Black's ...Qf6 defence
ideas.text: Black's usual answer to threats on f7 is ...Qf6, covering f7. Don't give Black time for it.

ideas.title: Use the bishop pair
ideas.text: After 4...Bxf3 you have both bishops and a lead in development; quick threats make them count before Black catches up.

habit.why: 6.Bc4 threatens mate on f7, but 6...Qf6 defends f7 and offers a queen trade. After 7.Qb3 Nd7 8.Qxb7 Rb8 9.Qa6 Qxa6 10.Bxa6 Nc5 the queens are off, Black's pieces are active and you keep much less of your edge.

strays.text: 7.Qb3 comes a move late, once Black's queen already covers f7.

taught.why: 6.Qb3 hits b7 at once, and with your bishop coming to c4 it also eyes f7, so Black gets no time for ...Qf6. After 6...Nd7 7.Be3 Bc5 8.Bxc5 Nxc5 9.Qb5+ Nd7 10.Qxb7 you win the pawn with queens on, and GM Larry Kaufman rates 6.Qb3 above Morphy's 6.Bc4.

enforces.text: The queen reaches b7 before Black's queen can offer a trade.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Nc3 develops but threatens nothing, so Black covers f7 in time: 6...Nd7 7.Bd2 Qf6 8.O-O-O and Black has caught up.
alternatives.after: 6.Qb3 makes a threat on b7 right away, so Black has no time for ...Qf6 and you keep the initiative.

8151329472450239|d2d3.headline: Against 3...g6, strike with 4.d4 before ...Bg7
8151329472450239|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is passive: it lets Black finish the fianchetto with 4...Bg7, and the bishop then guards e5. After 5.Ng5 Nh6 f7 is covered and most of your edge is gone. 4.d4 strikes at e5 before the bishop reaches g7, so Black has to hold it with the queen, 4...Qe7. After 5.Nc3 c6 6.a4 Bg4 7.Bg5 you develop with gain of time, hitting the queen on e7.
8151329472450239|d2d3.principle: Against a slow ...g6, claim the centre with d4 at once, before the fianchetto bishop arrives to guard e5.
sources: Lessons: Philidor's Defence (Exeter Chess Club) | https://www.exeterchessclub.org.uk/content/lessons-philidors-defence
Sean Marsh, Chess Opening Basics: The Philidor Defense (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-philidor-defense/
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

ideas.title: Claim the centre with d4
ideas.text: Black's 2...d6 set-up is solid but cramped: play 4.d4 rather than the passive 4.d3, while Black is still slow.

ideas.title: Hit e5 before ...Bg7
ideas.text: 4.d4 hits e5 while Black's bishop is still on f8, so Black must hold it with the queen, 4...Qe7.

ideas.title: Black's fianchetto plan
ideas.text: After ...Bg7 the bishop guards e5 and Black heads for a Larsen-style set-up, the riskier but active Exchange Philidor.

ideas.title: Don't rush at f7
ideas.text: Jumping at f7 achieves nothing here: after 4.d3 Bg7 5.Ng5 Nh6 the knight on h6 covers f7.

habit.why: 4.d3 is passive: it lets Black finish the fianchetto with 4...Bg7, and the bishop then guards e5. After 5.Ng5 Nh6 f7 is covered and most of your edge is gone.

strays.text: The pawn stops on d3 and gives up your space edge.

taught.why: 4.d4 strikes at e5 before the bishop reaches g7, so Black has to hold it with the queen, 4...Qe7. After 5.Nc3 c6 6.a4 Bg4 7.Bg5 you develop with gain of time, hitting the queen on e7.

enforces.text: The pawn hits e5 while Black's bishop is still on f8.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.O-O gives Black time for 4...Bg7, and after 6...d3 Black's pawn lodges deep in your camp.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 comes before ...Bg7, so e5 is attacked while no bishop covers it; castling can wait.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 develops but lets Black fianchetto with 4...Bg7, and the game heads for a Larsen-style Exchange Philidor with Black's set-up complete.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 forces the issue on e5 before the bishop reaches g7, so you keep more of your edge.

8153210382746448|f6g4.headline: Answer 4.e5 with 4...dxe5, not a knight retreat
8153210382746448|f6g4.why: 4...Ng4 moves the knight again to hit e5, which d4 still guards. 5.h3 Nh6 sends it to the rim, and White develops with 6.Bf4 and 7.Nf3 while your knight is offside. 4...dxe5 removes the pawn that attacked the knight, and after 5.dxe5 Qxd1+ 6.Nxd1 the queens are off and e5 stands alone. 6...Nd5 centralises the knight and 7...Bg7 aims at e5, so White has to keep defending it.
8153210382746448|f6g4.principle: When a pawn attacks your developed piece, first look for a capture that removes the attacker instead of retreating to a worse square.
sources: Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense (Sean Marsh, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/
Beat the Pirc Defense with This Trap! (GM Igor Smirnov) | https://chess-teacher.com/beat-the-pirc-defense-with-this-trap/
Pirc Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pirc_Defence

ideas.title: Early e5 push: trade queens
ideas.text: Take on e5 first. After 4...dxe5 5.dxe5 Qxd1+ the queens are off and the e5 pawn has lost its d4 support.

ideas.title: Don't retreat the f6 knight first
ideas.text: Moving the f6 knight lets White keep e5, gain time on the knight, or push e5-e6 to break your pawns.

ideas.title: e5 without support is a target
ideas.text: 4.e5 comes before f4 backs it up. Once d4 is traded off, your g7 bishop and knights can pile up on e5.

habit.why: 4...Ng4 moves the knight again to hit e5, which d4 still guards. 5.h3 Nh6 sends it to the rim, and White develops with 6.Bf4 and 7.Nf3 while your knight is offside.

strays.idea: Don't retreat the f6 knight first
strays.text: The knight moves twice and ends up on the rim at h6.

taught.why: 4...dxe5 removes the pawn that attacked the knight, and after 5.dxe5 Qxd1+ 6.Nxd1 the queens are off and e5 stands alone. 6...Nd5 centralises the knight and 7...Bg7 aims at e5, so White has to keep defending it.

enforces.text: Capture first, trade queens, then go after the lone e5 pawn.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nfd7 is the standard Pirc retreat against e5 and holds for now. But 6.e6 fxe6 breaks your pawns and 7.h4 gives White active play; there is a cleaner answer.
alternatives.after: 4...dxe5 removes the pawn before it can reach e6 and trades queens; 4...Nfd7 lets White keep the spearhead on e5.
alternatives.idea: Don't retreat the f6 knight first

8186436489067117|b5e2.headline: Play 8.d3: free the c1-bishop and keep the pin on c6
8186436489067117|b5e2.why: 8.Be2 moves the bishop again and drops the pin, and 8...h6 leaves the g5-knight short of squares: f3 runs into ...e4, and the c6-knight covers e5. After 9.Nh3 Bxh3 10.gxh3 Qc8 11.d3 Qxh3 Black has the pawn back and your kingside is wrecked. 8.d3 opens the c1-bishop, covers e4 against ...e4 and keeps the b5-bishop pinning c6. If 8...Qd5, 9.Bxc6+ Qxc6 10.O-O Bd6 11.Qf3 and you stay a clean pawn up.
8186436489067117|b5e2.principle: With a pawn in hand, bring out a new piece (8.d3 frees the c1-bishop) instead of moving the b5-bishop a second time.
sources: Tim Harding, Two Knights Defence without Tears, Part 2 | https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/tim-harding-two-knights-defence-part-ii/250495309
Wilhelm Steinitz, The Modern Chess Instructor | https://books.google.com/books?id=SJFXDwAAQBAJ
Todd Bardwick, Chess Openings: An Overview of Standard Variations | https://books.google.com/books?id=QME6EQAAQBAJ

ideas.title: Keep the extra pawn
ideas.text: You are still a pawn up after 7.dxc6 Nxc6. Develop the rest of your pieces without giving Black time to win it back.

ideas.title: Keep your active bishop
ideas.text: The b5-bishop pins the c6-knight. Moving it again costs time; take on c6 only when that wins time, as after 8...Qd5.

ideas.title: Retreat the knight in time
ideas.text: ...h6 and ...e4 will hit the g5-knight, and with the c6-knight covering e5 it has few good squares.

ideas.title: Black gains time on your pieces
ideas.text: Black wants ...h6 and ...e4 to drive your knight back, and develops with gain of time for the pawn.

habit.why: 8.Be2 moves the bishop again and drops the pin, and 8...h6 leaves the g5-knight short of squares: f3 runs into ...e4, and the c6-knight covers e5. After 9.Nh3 Bxh3 10.gxh3 Qc8 11.d3 Qxh3 Black has the pawn back and your kingside is wrecked.

strays.text: With e5 covered, ...h6 sends your knight to h3, where it gets taken.

taught.why: 8.d3 opens the c1-bishop, covers e4 against ...e4 and keeps the b5-bishop pinning c6. If 8...Qd5, 9.Bxc6+ Qxc6 10.O-O Bd6 11.Qf3 and you stay a clean pawn up.

enforces.text: You develop without weakening anything and stay a clean pawn up.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 8.Qf3 brings the queen out early. After 8...Be7 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.O-O O-O Black catches up in development, and your extra pawn counts for little.
alternatives.after: 8.d3 develops a pawn and frees the c1-bishop instead of the queen, so ...Ng4 and ...Be7 don't gain time on anything.
alternatives.idea: Black gains time on your pieces

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Back to c4 aims at f7 again: after 8...Bc5 9.Bxf7+ Ke7 a sharp fight starts. A calmer move is a little stronger.
alternatives.after: 8.d3 keeps the pin on c6 and the extra pawn without the complications of 9.Bxf7+.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Castling is fine: after 8...h6 9.Nf3 e4 10.Re1 the rook hits the e-pawn and your knight finds e5. There is a slightly more useful move.
alternatives.after: 8.d3 first covers e4 and frees the c1-bishop, so Black's ...e4 push can't kick your knight.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Taking on c6 doubles Black's pawns and keeps your extra pawn, but it gives up the pin for nothing yet. Keeping the tension is a little better.
alternatives.after: 8.d3 keeps the choice: you take on c6 only when it wins time, as in 8...Qd5 9.Bxc6+.

8211444126196396|c1f4.headline: 5.e3 guards d4 and opens the bishop's road to c4
8211444126196396|c1f4.why: 5.Bf4 does nothing for d4 or c4, so after 5...a6 your try to win c4 back with 6.Nd2 blocks the queen's guard of d4. 6...Qxd4 picks up a second pawn, and after 7.e3 Qc5 Black is two pawns up. 5.e3 guards d4 for good and opens the f1 bishop's path to c4. If Black holds on with 5...b5, 6.a4 c6 7.Bd2 hits the queenside at once and breaks the pin.
8211444126196396|c1f4.principle: Pick the pawn move that does two jobs: 5.e3 guards the centre pawn and frees the bishop that wins back c4.
sources: Max Illingworth, A Crash Course in Understanding 1.d4 (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/blog/Illingworth/a-crash-course-in-understanding-1-d4

Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nc3

ideas.title: Win back c4, don't Bf4
ideas.text: Black can rarely keep the c4 pawn: 5.e3 and then the bishop takes on c4. 5.Bf4 does nothing for c4.

ideas.title: Bf4 leaves d4 loose
ideas.text: Only your queen and f3 knight guard d4. Move the knight and it falls, as in 5.Bf4 a6 6.Nd2 Qxd4.

ideas.title: a4 against ...b5
ideas.text: If Black props up c4 with ...b5, hit it at once with a4, as in 5.e3 b5 6.a4.

ideas.title: The pin on c3
ideas.text: 4...Bb4 pins your c3 knight, and ...Bxc3+ can double your c-pawns; 5.Bd2 breaks the pin.

habit.why: 5.Bf4 does nothing for d4 or c4, so after 5...a6 your try to win c4 back with 6.Nd2 blocks the queen's guard of d4. 6...Qxd4 picks up a second pawn, and after 7.e3 Qc5 Black is two pawns up.

strays.text: The bishop develops, but d4 is guarded only by pieces that need to move.

taught.why: 5.e3 guards d4 for good and opens the f1 bishop's path to c4. If Black holds on with 5...b5, 6.a4 c6 7.Bd2 hits the queenside at once and breaks the pin.

enforces.text: e3 guards d4 and frees the bishop that takes back c4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.e4 grabs the centre; after 5...b5 6.a4 c6 7.Be2 Black holds c4 for now while you take space. Masters play it 25% of the time, but there's a slightly safer move.
alternatives.after: 5.e3 guards d4 for good and opens the f1-c4 diagonal, so you aim to win c4 back rather than gamble on the centre. Masters split 36% for 5.e3, 25% for 5.e4.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5.Bg5 develops but does nothing for d4 or c4: after 5...Ne7 6.Qa4+ Nbc6 7.Bxe7 Qxe7 you have given the bishop for a knight and still need to win c4 back.
alternatives.after: 5.e3 handles both problems at once: it guards d4 and lets the f1 bishop recapture on c4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bd2 breaks the pin, so ...Bxc3 no longer doubles your pawns, and your queen keeps d4 covered. It's as good as anything here.
alternatives.after: 5.e3 and 5.Bd2 are equally good and often meet: 5.Bd2 Nf6 6.e3 c5 7.Bxc4 reaches the same plan of guarding d4 and taking back c4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Qa4+ aims to win c4 back with the queen, but after 5...Nc6 6.a3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qd5 Black's queen guards c4 and your c-pawns are doubled.
alternatives.after: 5.e3 wins c4 back with a bishop and keeps your pawns intact. Masters prefer it, 36% to 14%.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5.g3 is a Catalan-style plan to win c4 back later from g2, but it's slow: after 7.a3 Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 c5 Black hits your weakened centre.
alternatives.after: 5.e3 guards d4 right away and brings the f1 bishop straight to c4.

8224292196866816|b8c6.headline: Support d5 with 3...e6; 3...Nc6 lets White take the centre
8224292196866816|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, so after 4.cxd5 Nxd5 Black has no pawn left on d5: 5.Bb5 pins the knight, and 7.Bxc6+ Qxc6 8.e4 lets White take the centre with gain of time on the queen. 3...e6 supports d5 with a pawn, so cxd5 can be answered by a pawn recapture, and it opens the bishop on f8 for development, as in 4.Nc3 Be7.
8224292196866816|b8c6.principle: When White attacks your d5 pawn with c4, support it with a pawn so you keep a foothold in the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5

826798325202564|c2c3.headline: The d4 pawn is undefended: take it with 4.Nxd4
826798325202564|c2c3.why: 4.c3 gives up a pawn that had no defender at all. After 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 Nc6 6.Be2 d6 7.O-O Nf6 Black has developed calmly and keeps the extra pawn. 4.Nxd4 regains the pawn with a developing move and gives a normal Open Sicilian. After 4...Nc6 5.Nc3 Qc7 6.Be3 a6 7.Qf3 you are in the sharp main-line Taimanov with material level.
826798325202564|c2c3.principle: Loose pawns drop off: nothing guards d4, so 4.Nxd4 takes it back with a developing move instead of gambiting it with 4.c3.
sources: Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (sample) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf
Semko Semkov, The Taimanov-Scheveningen Hybrid (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-the-taimanov-scheveningen-hybrid.pdf

ideas.title: Take back the d4 pawn
ideas.text: Nothing guards d4, and your knight and queen both hit it. 4.Nxd4 wins it back and develops; 99.7% of masters play it.

ideas.title: Morra: pawn for development
ideas.text: After 4.c3 dxc3 5.Nxc3 you're in a Smith-Morra, a pawn down for development. Black answers ...Nc6, ...d6, ...Nf6 and ...Be7 and keeps it.

ideas.title: Queen out, knight hits it
ideas.text: Taking with the queen invites ...Nc6, which attacks it and gains Black a move, as in 4.Qxd4 Nc6 5.Qd1.

habit.why: 4.c3 gives up a pawn that had no defender at all. After 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 Nc6 6.Be2 d6 7.O-O Nf6 Black has developed calmly and keeps the extra pawn.

strays.text: The undefended pawn was yours for free; now you're a pawn down.

taught.why: 4.Nxd4 regains the pawn with a developing move and gives a normal Open Sicilian. After 4...Nc6 5.Nc3 Qc7 6.Be3 a6 7.Qf3 you are in the sharp main-line Taimanov with material level.

enforces.text: The knight recaptures and develops in one move.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.Qxd4 takes the pawn back but brings the queen out early. After 4...Nc6 5.Qd1 it has gone home again, and after 6.Bd3 d5 Black develops freely.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxd4 recaptures with a piece that wants to stand in the centre anyway, so 4...Nc6 gains Black no time.

8290697107627463|f6d5.headline: Trade queens with check first, then win the e5 pawn
8290697107627463|f6d5.why: 4...Nd5 saves the knight but lets White keep the e5 pawn and gain time: 5.Bc4 hits the knight, and after 5...c6 6.Nc3 e6 7.Qe2 you are cramped. You pass up the queen trade with check that wins e5. 4...Qxd1+ forces 5.Kxd1, so White can no longer castle and the threat to your knight is gone. Then 5...Ng4 hits the undefended e5 pawn, and 6.Ke1 Nxe5 leaves you a clean pawn up.
8290697107627463|f6d5.principle: Look at checks and captures first: 4...Qxd1+ removes the threat to your knight and gives you time to win the loose e5 pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense (Sean Marsh, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/
Beat the Pirc Defense with This Trap! (GM Igor Smirnov) | https://chess-teacher.com/beat-the-pirc-defense-with-this-trap/

ideas.title: Early e5 push: trade queens
ideas.text: After White's unsupported e5 and dxe5, trade queens on d1 with check: after 4...Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1 White's king can no longer castle.

ideas.title: Hit the loose e5 pawn
ideas.text: With the d4 pawn gone, nothing guards e5. 5...Ng4 attacks it and 6...Nxe5 wins it.

ideas.title: Don't retreat the f6 knight first
ideas.text: Moving the knight first leaves your queen on d8 to be taken with check, or lets e5-e6 break your pawns.

ideas.title: White's threat: Qxd8+ and exf6
ideas.text: White threatens 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8 6.exf6, trading queens with check and then taking your knight.

habit.why: 4...Nd5 saves the knight but lets White keep the e5 pawn and gain time: 5.Bc4 hits the knight, and after 5...c6 6.Nc3 e6 7.Qe2 you are cramped. You pass up the queen trade with check that wins e5.

strays.text: The queens stay on, and the e5 pawn survives with White developing fast.

taught.why: 4...Qxd1+ forces 5.Kxd1, so White can no longer castle and the threat to your knight is gone. Then 5...Ng4 hits the undefended e5 pawn, and 6.Ke1 Nxe5 leaves you a clean pawn up.

enforces.text: Queens off with check, then 5...Ng4 wins e5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nfd7 is the usual Pirc retreat against e5 and saves the knight. Here, though, 5.e6 fxe6 breaks your pawns and 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 strands your king; you can do better.
alternatives.after: 4...Qxd1+ trades queens on your terms and wins e5; 4...Nfd7 lets White trade on d8 later and keep your king in the centre.
alternatives.idea: Don't retreat the f6 knight first

8290697107627463|f6g4.headline: Swap queens with 4...Qxd1+ before moving the knight
8290697107627463|f6g4.why: 4...Ng4 leaves your queen to be taken with check: 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8, and you can no longer castle. White then guards e5 with 6.Nf3 and 7.Bf4, so the pawn you were aiming at holds. 4...Qxd1+ trades queens with check, and after 5.Kxd1 White's king can no longer castle. Then 5...Ng4 hits e5 and f2, and after 6.Ke1 Nxe5 you have won a pawn.
8290697107627463|f6g4.principle: Checks, captures and threats first: 4...Qxd1+ is a forcing capture that removes White's 5.Qxd8+ before you move the knight.
sources: Sean Marsh, Chess Opening Basics: The Pirc Defense (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/chess-opening-basics-the-pirc-defense/
Igor Smirnov, Beat the Pirc Defense with This Trap! (Remote Chess Academy) | https://chess-teacher.com/beat-the-pirc-defense-with-this-trap/

ideas.title: Early e5 push: trade queens
ideas.text: Against an e5 push with nothing behind it, take on e5 and swap queens on d1 before moving your f6-knight.

ideas.title: Mind the queen on d8
ideas.text: Your f6-knight is attacked and the queens face each other on the open d-file: if the knight moves, 5.Qxd8+ comes with check.

ideas.title: White needs f4 behind e5
ideas.text: Marsh: e5 needs a pawn on f4 behind it. Here it has none, so after the queen trade 5...Ng4 and 6...Nxe5 win it.

habit.why: 4...Ng4 leaves your queen to be taken with check: 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8, and you can no longer castle. White then guards e5 with 6.Nf3 and 7.Bf4, so the pawn you were aiming at holds.

strays.text: The knight moves first, so White trades queens and your king loses castling.

taught.why: 4...Qxd1+ trades queens with check, and after 5.Kxd1 White's king can no longer castle. Then 5...Ng4 hits e5 and f2, and after 6.Ke1 Nxe5 you have won a pawn.

enforces.text: With no pawn on f4, the e5 pawn falls to 6...Nxe5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nfd7 keeps your queen covered and eyes e5, but 5.e6 fxe6 breaks your pawns, and 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 still costs you castling. There is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4...Qxd1+ removes the d-file danger first and then wins e5 with 5...Ng4; after 4...Nfd7 White strikes first with 5.e6.

8292354532353769|d2d3.headline: Trade on d4 and win the overextended pawn
8292354532353769|d2d3.why: 4.d3 lets Black trade with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3, so the double knight move becomes a harmless exchange and White's edge is gone. 4.Nxd4 removes the knight instead: after 4...exd4 the pawn on d4 is cut off, and 5.O-O, 6.Re1 and 7.c3 win it with 8.cxd4. Avoid the bait 4.Nxe5, which runs into 4...Qg5.
8292354532353769|d2d3.principle: The opponent's knight trip cost time; trade it off, castle and open the centre while you lead in development.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxd4

8292354532353769|f3e5.headline: Trade with 4.Nxd4; 4.Nxe5 walks into 4...Qg5
8292354532353769|f3e5.why: 4.Nxe5 walks into 4...Qg5, which hits the e5 knight and g2 at once, and saving the knight with 5.Nxf7 loses to 5...Qxg2. After 5.O-O Qxe5 you are a knight down for a pawn. 4.Nxd4 trades off the knight Black moved twice, and after 4...exd4 5.O-O Nf6 6.Re1 d6 7.c3 you go after the d4 pawn. 8.cxd4 wins it and leaves you a pawn up with a lead in development.
8292354532353769|f3e5.principle: When your opponent moves a piece twice to set a trap, don't grab the bait: check what is left loose, trade the piece off and keep your lead.
sources: Modern Chess Openings, 15th ed. (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%223...Nd4%22+%224.Nxd4%22+%22Qg5%22
Blackburne Shilling Gambit (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Game,_Blackburne_Shilling_Gambit

ideas.title: Watch the queen counter-hit
ideas.text: If your knight takes on e5, 4...Qg5 hits it and g2 at once. Saving it with 5.Nxf7 loses to 5...Qxg2.

ideas.title: Punish the twice-moved knight
ideas.text: 3...Nd4 moves a knight twice and leaves e5 bait. 4.Nxd4 trades it off and leaves you ahead in development.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: After 4.Nxd4 exd4 5.O-O, a careless 5...Bc5 allows 6.Bxf7+ Kxf7 7.Qh5+ and 8.Qxc5+, picking up the loose bishop.

ideas.title: Black wants ...Nxf3+
ideas.text: If your knight stays on f3, 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3 swaps Black's offside knight for your good one.

habit.why: 4.Nxe5 walks into 4...Qg5, which hits the e5 knight and g2 at once, and saving the knight with 5.Nxf7 loses to 5...Qxg2. After 5.O-O Qxe5 you are a knight down for a pawn.

strays.text: The e5 knight is loose, and the queen hits it and g2.

taught.why: 4.Nxd4 trades off the knight Black moved twice, and after 4...exd4 5.O-O Nf6 6.Re1 d6 7.c3 you go after the d4 pawn. 8.cxd4 wins it and leaves you a pawn up with a lead in development.

enforces.text: You trade the knight off on your terms and keep your lead.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.c3 kicks the knight, but Black just trades with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3, swapping the offside knight for your good one. After 5...Nf6 6.d4 d6 Black's development problems are gone.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxd4 does the trading on your terms: Black has to take back with a pawn, and 4...exd4 leaves a target on d4. Silman rates 4.c3 good for White, but it lets Black off lightly.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.d3 guards e4 but lets Black trade with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3. After 5...Nf6 6.Be3 d6 7.Nc3 Be7 Black has caught up in development.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxd4 trades the knight before Black can swap it for yours, and the pawn left on d4 becomes a target for 7.c3 and 8.cxd4.

8292354532353769|f3g5.headline: Against 3...Nd4, trade knights with 4.Nxd4; 4.Ng5 drops a piece.
8292354532353769|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 puts the knight where the queen on d8 can simply take it: 4...Qxg5, and the knight that moved twice is gone. 3...Nd4 is the Blackburne Shilling gambit, a trap that only works if White grabs e5 with 4.Nxe5, and its knight is misplaced. 4.Nxd4 exd4 trades it off and drags Black's pawn away from e5, and after 5.O-O Nf6 6.Re1 White ends up a pawn ahead with 8.cxd4.
8292354532353769|f3g5.principle: Before moving a piece, check whether it lands on a square an enemy piece already covers; g5 is on the diagonal of Black's queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxd4

8297553024226585|f3g5.headline: Castle first: 5.O-O, not 5.Ng5
8297553024226585|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 5...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 6.O-O Na5 7.Nc3 Nxc4 8.dxc4 h6 9.Nf3 Black has the two bishops and your knight is back where it started. 5.O-O gets your king safe and keeps every option for the build-up. After 5...d6 6.a3 O-O 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.h3 Bh5 9.Nd5 your knight takes a strong central square; masters choose 5.O-O 79% of the time.
8297553024226585|f3g5.principle: When Black can simply castle to cover f7, don't move the f3 knight twice: castle and build up.
sources: NM Jeremy Kane, Bad Trades Amateurs Make In Chess | https://www.chess.com/article/view/bad-trades-amateurs-make-in-chess

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: f7 is guarded by the king only until Black castles. After 5...O-O, taking on f7 gives two pieces for a rook and pawn.

ideas.title: Castle, then build slowly
ideas.text: Black's set-up is solid, with nothing to attack yet. Castle, then build up with c3 or the knight to c3, as masters do.

ideas.title: Black: chase the bishop
ideas.text: Black wants to swap off your c4 bishop with ...Na5 and get the two bishops.

ideas.title: Don't move a piece twice
ideas.text: Your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. Moving the f3 knight again gives Black free time.

habit.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 5...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 6.O-O Na5 7.Nc3 Nxc4 8.dxc4 h6 9.Nf3 Black has the two bishops and your knight is back where it started.

strays.text: Black castles, f7 is covered, and the knight has to go back.

taught.why: 5.O-O gets your king safe and keeps every option for the build-up. After 5...d6 6.a3 O-O 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.h3 Bh5 9.Nd5 your knight takes a strong central square; masters choose 5.O-O 79% of the time.

enforces.text: King safe first, then the pieces come out.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 develops a new piece and is a good move: after 5...d6 6.a4 and Black's 7...Bg4, 8.h3 Bh5 9.Nd5 puts your knight in the centre. Masters prefer another move by far, though.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O is the masters' choice (79%) and often reaches the same set-up, since 7.Nc3 follows in its main line. Castling first just keeps your king safe before play starts.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.c3 is the slow Italian set-up, preparing d4 for later. Once you spend a tempo on c3, though, 5...d5 is well timed: after 6.exd5 Nxd5 Black follows with 7...Bg4 and is comfortable.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O keeps the king safe first and doesn't yet invite ...d5; Emms notes that ...d5 is harder to justify before White has spent time on c3.

8308599203837326|e4f5.headline: Answer 3...f5 with 4.d4: hit e5, don't grab on f5
8308599203837326|e4f5.why: 4.exf5 lets 4...e4 kick your knight, and after 5.Nd4 Nf6 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.d4 d5 8.Be2 Bxf5 Black has the pawn back, a big centre and your bishop pushed back. Wikibooks calls 4.exf5 a common beginner mistake. 4.d4 hits e5 before Black is developed: after 4...fxe4 5.Nxe5 d5 6.Bb5 your knight is strong on e5 and the bishop pins c6. Wikipedia rates 4.d4 a clear advantage for White.
8308599203837326|e4f5.principle: When Black loosens the centre with an early ...f5, strike the centre at once with 4.d4 instead of grabbing the pawn.
sources: Tim Harding, Counter Gambits | https://books.google.com/books?id=iJarwg3VQowC
The Rousseau Gambit, Chessnote | https://www.chessnote.io/blog/rousseau-gambit-opening-guide
Rousseau Gambit, Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Game,_Rousseau_Gambit

ideas.title: Strike back with d4
ideas.text: ...f5 loosens Black's centre and king. 4.d4 hits e5 at once and opens lines before Black is developed.

ideas.title: Taking on f5 frees Black
ideas.text: After exf5, Black's centre rolls with gain of time: ...e4 kicks your knight and ...Bxf5 later wins the pawn back.

ideas.title: Aim at the loose king
ideas.text: With the f-pawn gone, your c4-bishop eyes g8 and the king's side; Wikibooks says to attack there with this bishop.

ideas.title: Keep the light bishop
ideas.text: Wikibooks warns that trades involving your light-squared bishop help Black: it is your best attacker against the king.

habit.why: 4.exf5 lets 4...e4 kick your knight, and after 5.Nd4 Nf6 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.d4 d5 8.Be2 Bxf5 Black has the pawn back, a big centre and your bishop pushed back. Wikibooks calls 4.exf5 a common beginner mistake.

strays.text: The pawn grab hands Black ...e4 and ...d5 with tempo.

taught.why: 4.d4 hits e5 before Black is developed: after 4...fxe4 5.Nxe5 d5 6.Bb5 your knight is strong on e5 and the bishop pins c6. Wikipedia rates 4.d4 a clear advantage for White.

enforces.text: You attack e5 instead of defending e4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.d3 holds e4 solidly and gives a reversed King's Gambit Declined, a good choice. There is a more forcing option.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 asks more of Black: after 4...fxe4 5.Nxe5 Wikibooks calls it an improved Latvian Gambit for White. 4.d3 is a solid second choice, though Black can later push the f-pawn to f4.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 doesn't hold e4: 4...fxe4 hits your knight, and after 5.Bxg8 exf3 6.Bd5 fxg2 7.Bxg2 Qh4 you are a pawn down with your king's cover gone.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 attacks e5 instead of defending e4, so 4...fxe4 costs Black the e5-pawn: 5.Nxe5.

8341087684859850|g5f7.headline: 6.Qh5 keeps the f7 attack without giving up a piece
8341087684859850|g5f7.why: 6.Nxf7 gives a knight for a pawn, and after 6...Kxf7 7.Qf3+ Ke6 8.O-O c6 Black's king holds in the centre. IM Silman calls it a fun attack, but you must keep pressing a piece down and you keep much less of your edge. 6.Qh5 threatens mate on f7, with the queen and the g5 knight both on f7, so Black's best reply weakens the kingside with 6...g6. Then 7.Qf3 hits f7 and the d5 knight, and after 7...Be6 8.Nc3 c6 9.Nxe6 fxe6 you keep the pressure without giving up material.
8341087684859850|g5f7.principle: f7 is guarded only by the king; with Black's knight gone from f6, bring the queen to h5 as a second attacker instead of sacrificing.
sources: IM Jeremy Silman, The Fried Liver's Identical Twin (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/the-fried-livers-identical-twin
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

ideas.title: Don't rush at f7
ideas.text: 6.Nxf7 Kxf7 gives a knight for a pawn. IM Silman shows Black's king holding on e6, so you must keep attacking a piece down.

ideas.title: Two attackers on f7
ideas.text: Your knight on g5 already hits f7. 6.Qh5 adds the queen and threatens mate there, since Black's knight left f6.

ideas.title: Hit f7 and d5 together
ideas.text: Your c4-bishop hits the d5 knight. A queen on f3 adds a second attacker on d5 and also hits f7.

ideas.title: A Fried Liver twin
ideas.text: IM Silman calls this a twin of the Two Knights 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5 Nxd5 and judges 5...Nxd5 unplayable for Black.

habit.why: 6.Nxf7 gives a knight for a pawn, and after 6...Kxf7 7.Qf3+ Ke6 8.O-O c6 Black's king holds in the centre. IM Silman calls it a fun attack, but you must keep pressing a piece down and you keep much less of your edge.

strays.text: You give up a knight when a queen move keeps all the pressure.

taught.why: 6.Qh5 threatens mate on f7, with the queen and the g5 knight both on f7, so Black's best reply weakens the kingside with 6...g6. Then 7.Qf3 hits f7 and the d5 knight, and after 7...Be6 8.Nc3 c6 9.Nxe6 fxe6 you keep the pressure without giving up material.

enforces.text: Queen and knight together threaten mate on f7.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Qf3 is IM Silman's key move: 6...Qxg5 7.Bxd5 hits f7 and b7, but after 7...Qg6 8.Bxb7 Bxb7 9.Qxb7 Qc6 Black hangs on.
alternatives.after: Silman mentions 6.Qh5 only in passing, but the engine rates it higher: it forces 6...g6 first, and only then 7.Qf3 hits f7 and d5.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.d3 is too slow: 6...f6 kicks your knight and shuts f7, and by the line's 10.Be6 Na6 your attack has run out and the game is level.
alternatives.after: 6.Qh5 makes a threat at once, so Black has no time for 6...f6.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.d4 opens the centre, but 6...c6 holds d5, and after 7.dxe5 Be7 8.Nf3 O-O Black is safely castled.
alternatives.after: 6.Qh5 hits f7 before Black can castle, so the king never reaches safety this easily.

8342193165505706|d7d6.headline: Play 4...a6 and keep ...d5 a one-step break
8342193165505706|d7d6.why: 4...d6 is passive: the d-pawn stops on d6, so ...d5 against the bishop now costs a second move. After 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Be3 a6 8.Qe2 Qc7 9.Nxc6 White has a free Open Sicilian with every piece developing easily. 4...a6, the masters' choice in 49% of games, prepares ...b5 against the bishop and keeps ...d5 in reserve. After 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Qc7 7.Nxc6 dxc6 8.a4 White spends a move stopping ...b5, and the d-file is open for your rook and queen.
8342193165505706|d7d6.principle: Make only the pawn moves you need: 4...a6 prepares ...b5 against the bishop, while 4...d6 makes the ...d5 break cost an extra move.
sources: The Bowlder Attack: Bold move or beginner's folly? (Matthew Astle, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/bowlder-attack/
Anton Shuravin, Bowdler Attack (ChessDoctrine) | https://chessdoctrine.com/chess-openings/kings-pawn/bowdler-attack/

countering 2. Bc4 in the Sicilian (chess.com forum) | https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess-openings/countering-2-bc4-in-the-sicilian

ideas.title: Keep ...d5 in one step
ideas.text: With ...e6 played, ...d5 hits the c4-bishop with tempo, as in the Wikibooks line 5.O-O d5. After ...d6 that break takes two moves.

ideas.title: Chase the bishop with ...a6 and ...b5
ideas.text: ...a6 takes b5 away from White's pieces and prepares ...b5 to drive the bishop off its diagonal.

ideas.title: Open Sicilian with Bc4
ideas.text: After 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 you're in an Open Sicilian against a bishop on c4, where your e6 pawn already blunts it.

habit.why: 4...d6 is passive: the d-pawn stops on d6, so ...d5 against the bishop now costs a second move. After 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Be3 a6 8.Qe2 Qc7 9.Nxc6 White has a free Open Sicilian with every piece developing easily.

strays.text: The d-pawn stops on d6, so ...d5 now costs an extra move.

taught.why: 4...a6, the masters' choice in 49% of games, prepares ...b5 against the bishop and keeps ...d5 in reserve. After 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Qc7 7.Nxc6 dxc6 8.a4 White spends a move stopping ...b5, and the d-file is open for your rook and queen.

enforces.text: ...b5 is ready, so White must spend 8.a4 to stop it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nf6 develops and prepares ...d5; the Wikibooks and Chessable line 5.O-O d5 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bb3 is comfortable for Black. The engine rates it as good as anything here.
alternatives.after: 4...a6 is the masters' slight favourite (49% to 40%) and keeps ...b5 ready, while 4...Nf6 aims for a quick ...d5. Both are fully sound.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4...Nge7 blocks your f8-bishop, and after 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 and 7.Bg5 the knight is pinned to your queen. After 7...Nxd4 8.Qxd4 White's pieces are the more active.
alternatives.after: 4...a6 keeps f6 for the knight and your f8-bishop free, and prepares ...b5 against the bishop.

8358083107211199|g7g6.headline: Develop with a threat: 4...Nbd7 hits the e5 knight
8358083107211199|g7g6.why: 4...g6 is slow and lets 5.Bc4 aim at f7, threatening mate there. You block with 5...e6, and after 6.d4 Bg7 7.O-O O-O White has more space and easy development. 4...Nbd7 develops and attacks the knight on e5, so White retreats with 5.Nc4. Then 5...e5 claims the centre, and after 6.Be2 Bc5 7.O-O O-O your pieces are out quickly.
8358083107211199|g7g6.principle: Develop with threats: a developing move that attacks a piece gains time, while a slow pawn move gives White time to aim at f7.

ideas.title: Develop with a threat
ideas.text: 4...Nbd7 brings a piece out and attacks the knight on e5, so White must spend a move on it, as in 5.Nc4.

ideas.title: The bishop on c4 eyes f7
ideas.text: With a knight on e5, a bishop on c4 threatens mate on f7, as 5.Bc4 does after 4...g6.

ideas.title: Claim the centre with ...e5
ideas.text: After 5.Nc4 e5 you get a pawn in the centre and develop fast with ...Bc5 and castling.

habit.why: 4...g6 is slow and lets 5.Bc4 aim at f7, threatening mate there. You block with 5...e6, and after 6.d4 Bg7 7.O-O O-O White has more space and easy development.

strays.idea: The bishop on c4 eyes f7
strays.text: 4...g6 does nothing about f7, so 5.Bc4 comes with a threat.

taught.why: 4...Nbd7 develops and attacks the knight on e5, so White retreats with 5.Nc4. Then 5...e5 claims the centre, and after 6.Be2 Bc5 7.O-O O-O your pieces are out quickly.

enforces.text: The knight comes out and hits e5, so White loses time.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...e6 is solid and covers f7 in advance; after 5.d4 you can trade off the e5 knight with 7...Nxe5. There is a slightly more active move.
alternatives.after: 4...Nbd7 hits the knight at once and lets 5...e5 follow, a share of the centre; 4...e6 is more passive.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Qd5 attacks the knight, but the queen comes out early: after 5.d4 Nc6 6.Nxc6 Qxc6 7.Na3 White gains time chasing it. Playable, but there is a better move.
alternatives.after: 4...Nbd7 attacks the knight with a minor piece, so your queen isn't chased as after 7.Na3 and 8.Nc4.

8378513320650736|e1h1.headline: e4 is hit twice: add a defender with 5.Qe2
8378513320650736|e1h1.why: After 4...Nf6, e4 is hit by the b7 bishop and the f6 knight and guarded only by your d3 bishop. 5.O-O ignores that, and 5...Nxe4 wins a pawn; 6.c4 Nf6 7.Nc3 gets your pieces out but not the pawn back. 5.Qe2 adds a second guard to e4; masters play it 63% of the time. After 5...d5 6.e5 Nfd7 7.c3 c5 8.Be3 the knight has been pushed off f6 and you have a French-type space edge.
8378513320650736|e1h1.principle: Two attackers against one defender: add a defender or move the pawn before anything else, castling included.
sources: Matthew Astle, The Offbeat Owen's: 1.e4 b6 (Chessable blog) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/owens-defense/
Owen's Defence (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen%27s_Defence
