ideas.title: Black's pieces hit e4
ideas.text: The b7 bishop and f6 knight both attack e4, and only your d3 bishop defends it. Black threatens 5...Bxe4.

ideas.title: Guard e4 against ...b6 lines
ideas.text: Against the b7 bishop your light bishop belongs on d3, backed by the queen: 5.Qe2 guards e4 a second time.

ideas.title: Gain space with e5
ideas.text: Once e4 is held, 5...d5 6.e5 Nfd7 kicks the knight and gives you a French-type space edge.

ideas.title: ...Bb4 pins a c3 knight
ideas.text: If a knight on c3 guards e4, 5...Bb4 pins it and the defence fails again.

habit.why: After 4...Nf6, e4 is hit by the b7 bishop and the f6 knight and guarded only by your d3 bishop. 5.O-O ignores that, and 5...Nxe4 wins a pawn; 6.c4 Nf6 7.Nc3 gets your pieces out but not the pawn back.

strays.text: You castle while e4 is attacked twice and defended once.

taught.why: 5.Qe2 adds a second guard to e4; masters play it 63% of the time. After 5...d5 6.e5 Nfd7 7.c3 c5 8.Be3 the knight has been pushed off f6 and you have a French-type space edge.

enforces.text: The queen holds e4, and 6.e5 then gains space with tempo.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 guards e4, but 5...Bb4 pins the knight and the guard is gone again; after 6.Nd2 O-O your f3 knight has had to drop back to hold e4.
alternatives.after: 5.Qe2 guards e4 with a piece Black can't pin, so ...Bb4 achieves nothing. Masters play 5.Qe2 63% of the time, 5.Nc3 about 1%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.e5 pushes past the attack and is sound; masters play it 17.5% of the time. But after 5...Ne4 Black's knight sits in the centre, and 6...f5 props it up.
alternatives.after: 5.Qe2 guards e4 first, so 5...d5 6.e5 sends the knight back to d7 instead of letting it land on e4. Masters prefer it, 63% to 17.5%.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.Bg5 pins the knight, but 5...h6 6.Bxf6 Qxf6 makes you give up the bishop pair just to remove an attacker of e4.
alternatives.after: 5.Qe2 holds e4 without giving up a bishop; masters play it 63% of the time, 5.Bg5 under 1%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Nbd2 guards e4 with a knight and is sound, but there is a stronger move. After 5...d6 6.O-O Be7 7.Re1 O-O 8.e5 Nfd7 9.c3 dxe5 Black has a solid game.
alternatives.after: Both moves guard e4. Masters prefer 5.Qe2, 63% to 18%, and after 5...d5 6.e5 it gives you a French-type space edge.

8399621132422899|b1c3.headline: Start with a centre pawn to free your pieces
8399621132422899|b1c3.why: 1.Nc3 is sensible but blocks the c-pawn, and it doesn't stop 1...d5, which threatens 2...d4 to kick the knight and gain space. 1.e4 claims the centre and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop at once, and with a pawn on e4 Black can't push a pawn there to chase a knight from f3.
8399621132422899|b1c3.principle: Begin by putting a pawn in the centre: it controls key squares and frees your pieces, while an early knight in front of the c-pawn can be chased.
sources: Chess Opening Theory
Chess Opening Theory/1. Nc3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4

8399621132422899|e2e3.headline: Start with a centre pawn: 1.e4 claims the centre
8399621132422899|e2e3.why: 1.e3 is not a mistake, but the theory calls it passive: it lets Black take over the centre with ...e5 and ...d5, and the pawn on e3 shuts in your queenside bishop, so White's first-move edge is gone. 1.e4 puts a pawn in the centre, opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, and keeps a black pawn off e4, so your knight can go to f3 without being kicked. It is the most popular first move at every level (45.5% of master games); 1.d4, 1.Nf3 and 1.c4 are good too.
8399621132422899|e2e3.principle: The opening is a race for development and control of the centre, so the first move should put a pawn on a central square and open lines for your pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory
Chess Opening Theory/1. e3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4

8399621132422899|g2g3.headline: Start with 1.e4: put a pawn in the centre at once
8399621132422899|g2g3.why: 1.g3 doesn't touch the centre; it only prepares to fianchetto the bishop, so Black takes central space for free with 1...e5 and gets an easy game. 1.e4 occupies the centre, controls d5 and f5, and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop at the same time. It is the most popular first move among masters, played in 45.5% of their games.
8399621132422899|g2g3.principle: On move one, a central pawn move both claims space and frees your pieces, so it does two jobs where a flank pawn move does neither.
sources: Chess Opening Theory
Chess Opening Theory/1. g3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4

8399621132422899|g2g4.headline: Start with 1.e4: take the centre, not the flank
8399621132422899|g2g4.why: 1.g4, Grob's Attack, is considered one of the worst first moves: it does nothing for the centre and loosens White's kingside, and after 1...d5 Black takes the centre while the g4-pawn becomes a target. 1.e4 controls d5 and f5, opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, and is the most popular first move at every level, played in 45.5% of master games.
8399621132422899|g2g4.principle: The first moves should fight for the central squares and free your pieces; a flank pawn move does neither.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4

8425508266792292|f6g4.headline: Take back the bishop on c6 first.
8425508266792292|f6g4.why: The bishop on c6 is attacked twice and defended by nothing, yet 4...Ng4 leaves it there. After 5.Ba4 it escapes and White keeps the knight it captured, and 6.exf5 even adds a pawn. 4...dxc6 wins the bishop back and opens the c8 bishop's diagonal, and Black is fine in the reference line.
8425508266792292|f6g4.principle: After every capture, look first at recapturing: count what attacks the capturing piece before making any other plan.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6

8425508266792292|f8d6.headline: Recapture on c6 before anything else.
8425508266792292|f8d6.why: 4...Bd6 develops but ignores the bishop on c6, which is attacked twice and defended by nothing. After 5.Ba4 the bishop retreats and White stays a whole piece up, and 5...Nxe4 only wins back a pawn. 4...dxc6 takes back the bishop and frees the c8 bishop, so the position is level again.
8425508266792292|f8d6.principle: When the opponent has just captured, recapture before developing; a developing move cannot make up for a missing piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6

8432999302569785|c2c3.headline: Recapture with 4.Nxd4 instead of gambiting with 4.c3
8432999302569785|c2c3.why: 4.c3 offers a pawn your knight could take back for free. After 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 e6 6.Be2 d6 7.O-O Be7 Black finishes developing and keeps the extra pawn. 4.Nxd4 wins the pawn back at once and gives a normal Open Sicilian. After 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6 7.Nd5 your knight lands on the d5 square that ...e5 left without a pawn guard.
8432999302569785|c2c3.principle: Only gambit a pawn when you get something you couldn't have for free: 4.Nxd4 regains it with a developing move, so 4.c3 just hands Black a pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...cxd4

ideas.title: Morra: pawn for development
ideas.text: 4.c3 dxc3 5.Nxc3 is a Smith-Morra: a pawn for quick development. Black can calmly answer with ...e6, ...d6 and ...Be7.

ideas.title: Black hits e4 with ...Nf6

strays.text: 4.c3 gives away a pawn your knight could recapture for nothing.

8432999302569785|f1c4.headline: Take the d4 pawn back with 4.Nxd4
8432999302569785|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 leaves the d4 pawn alone, so you are simply a pawn down. After 4...Nf6 5.Qe2 d5 6.exd5 Nxd5 7.h3 Bf5 8.O-O Ndb4 Black's pieces are out and the knight and bishop both hit c2. 4.Nxd4 wins the pawn back at once and gives a normal Open Sicilian. After 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6 7.Nd5 your knight lands on the d5 square that ...e5 left without a pawn guard.
8432999302569785|f1c4.principle: Count attackers and defenders: d4 is hit twice and guarded once, so 4.Nxd4 simply wins the pawn back.

843339252523142|d2d4.headline: Kick the b4 knight before opening the centre
843339252523142|d2d4.why: 10.d4 gives Black time: 10...Qf6 hits your queen, and after 11.Qe2 Kd7 12.dxe5 Qg6 13.O-O Kc7 Black's king is safe. The b4 knight still guards d5, so 14.Nxd5+ Nxd5 wins nothing and Black's extra piece counts. 10.a3 hits the b4 knight, and 10...Na6 takes it away from d5. Then 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.d4 opens the centre, and with d5 pinned, 12...e4 13.Qxe4+ and 14.Qxd5+ win two pawns with check.
843339252523142|d2d4.principle: Your compensation is the exposed king: remove its defenders before opening the centre, or the king walks to safety.

8455496353401048|c1g5.headline: 7.Ng5 hits f7 now; 7...d5 just drops a pawn
8455496353401048|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 pins the knight but threatens nothing, so Black answers 7...Be7 8.O-O O-O and f7 is safe. Black keeps the extra pawn and your lead in development is gone. 7.Ng5 threatens to take on f7 with knight or bishop, and Black has no comfortable way to cover it. The best try, 7...d5, loses a pawn to 8.Nxd5, and after 8...Be6 9.Nxe6 fxe6 10.Nxf6+ Qxf6 Black also has doubled e-pawns.
8455496353401048|c1g5.principle: Attack f7 while only Black's king guards it: 7.Ng5 forces the issue before Black can play ...Be7 and castle.

ideas.text: After ...e5, f7 is guarded only by the king. Knight on g5 and the c4-bishop threaten it before Black can castle.

ideas.text: With ...e5 played, no black pawn can hold d5. Your e4 pawn, c3-knight and c4-bishop all hit it, so 7...d5 loses a pawn to 8.Nxd5.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black's king is still on e8. Quiet moves give Black time for ...Be7 and castling, and then f7 is safe.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 freeing push
ideas.text: Black would like ...d5 to block your c4-bishop and free the game, even at the cost of the extra pawn, as in 7.Qb3 d5.

habit.why: 7.Bg5 pins the knight but threatens nothing, so Black answers 7...Be7 8.O-O O-O and f7 is safe. Black keeps the extra pawn and your lead in development is gone.

strays.text: The pin gives Black time to castle, and the f7 target disappears.

taught.why: 7.Ng5 threatens to take on f7 with knight or bishop, and Black has no comfortable way to cover it. The best try, 7...d5, loses a pawn to 8.Nxd5, and after 8...Be6 9.Nxe6 fxe6 10.Nxf6+ Qxf6 Black also has doubled e-pawns.

enforces.text: Knight and bishop hit f7 together while Black's king is still on e8.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is natural but makes no threat. Black plays 7...Be7 and castles next, and f7 is no longer a target.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 uses the move while Black's king is still in the centre; castling first gives Black exactly the time needed to make f7 safe. About a third of club players castle here.

alternatives.after: With 7.Ng5, 7...d5 8.Nxd5 Be6 9.Nxe6 fxe6 leaves Black with doubled e-pawns and no free development; after 7.Qb3 d5 Black develops with checks and threats.

8465086871106005|f1d3.headline: Against the Philidor, strike with 3.d4 before developing the bishop
8465086871106005|f1d3.why: 3.Bd3 blocks White's own d-pawn, so White gives up the d4 break and Black develops at leisure, as in 3...Nf6 4.O-O Be7 5.Re1 O-O. 3.d4 is the main line, played in 88.8% of master games: it attacks e5 again and threatens to crack the centre open, and since the d6-pawn is pinned to the queen, Black can't comfortably recapture after dxe5 and must trade or defend at once.
8465086871106005|f1d3.principle: When Black defends e5 with a pawn, attack it again with your d-pawn before developing pieces that would block it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4

8471347538789945|c2c3.headline: Guard e4 with 3.Bd3; 3.c3 leaves it hanging
8471347538789945|c2c3.why: 3.c3 supports d4, but nothing guards e4 against the b7-bishop, and 3...Bxe4 wins a centre pawn. After 4.c4 e6 5.Nc3 Bb7 Black is simply a pawn up with a sound position. 3.Bd3 guards e4 and develops a piece, and masters choose it in 69% of games. In the engine line 3...d6 4.f4 e5 5.c3 Nf6 6.Nf3 you keep a broad pawn centre with your pieces ready behind it.
8471347538789945|c2c3.principle: Count who attacks your pawns before a quiet move: the b7-bishop hits e4, and 3.c3 guards d4 instead, so 3.Bd3 comes first.
sources: Welling & Basman, U Cannot Be Serious! (publisher excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/8423.pdf

ideas.title: Count attackers on e4
ideas.text: The b7-bishop already hits e4. Guard it with a piece, as 3.Bd3, 3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2 do, or 3...Bxe4 wins a pawn.

ideas.title: Guard e4, then build the centre
ideas.text: With e4 held by 3.Bd3, the knight, c-pawn and queen follow, and a later e5 can gain space.

ideas.title: Black strikes back with ...c5
ideas.text: Black hands you the centre, then hits d4 with ...c5, as in 3.Nd2 e6 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3, where c3 holds it.

ideas.title: Punish ...f5 with Qh5+
ideas.text: After 3.Bd3, the greedy 3...f5? is a known mistake: 4.exf5 Bxg2 5.Qh5+ g6 6.fxg6 wins for you.

habit.why: 3.c3 supports d4, but nothing guards e4 against the b7-bishop, and 3...Bxe4 wins a centre pawn. After 4.c4 e6 5.Nc3 Bb7 Black is simply a pawn up with a sound position.

strays.text: The pawn guards d4, not e4, so the bishop takes e4.

taught.why: 3.Bd3 guards e4 and develops a piece, and masters choose it in 69% of games. In the engine line 3...d6 4.f4 e5 5.c3 Nf6 6.Nf3 you keep a broad pawn centre with your pieces ready behind it.

enforces.idea: Guard e4, then build the centre
enforces.text: The bishop holds e4 first; 5.c3 comes later, with nothing hanging.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Nc3 guards e4 with a developing move and is the club favourite; after 3...e6 your knight holds the pawn. Good, but there's a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 3.Bd3 is the main line (69% of master games to 23%) and keeps c3 free for a pawn to support d4. With 3.Nc3 the knight can later be pinned.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.d5 blocks the b7-bishop and gains space, but commits the pawn early: 3...Nf6 and 4...c6 undermine it, and after 6...cxd5 7.exd5 your centre is thinner.
alternatives.after: 3.Bd3 keeps both centre pawns side by side and develops a piece. Masters play it in 69% of games and 3.d5 in under 1%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.Nd2 guards e4 and keeps c3 free for a pawn; after 3...e6 and 4...c5, 5.c3 keeps your centre. Solid, but a more active move exists.
alternatives.after: 3.Bd3 brings out the bishop that 3.Nd2 still has to develop with 4.Bd3, and leaves your c1-bishop's diagonal open.

8471347538789945|g1f3.headline: Guard e4 with 3.Bd3 before developing the knight
8471347538789945|g1f3.why: 3.Nf3 develops but leaves e4 to the b7-bishop, and 3...Bxe4 wins a centre pawn for free. After 4.Nc3 Bb7 5.d5 Nf6 you have a bit more space but are simply a pawn down. 3.Bd3 guards e4 and develops a piece, and masters choose it in 69% of games. In the engine line 3...d6 4.f4 e5 5.c3 Nf6 6.Nf3 you keep a broad pawn centre with your pieces ready behind it.
8471347538789945|g1f3.principle: Before a developing move, count who attacks your pawns: the b7-bishop hits e4, so 3.Bd3 guards it first and the knight comes out later.

848566465308848|c8e6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qd4 forks the knight and the e4 pawn.
848566465308848|c8e6.why: 5...Be6 leaves White simply a pawn up: after 6.d3 the e4 pawn is defended and the chance is gone. 5...Qd4 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 at once, and after 6.Nf3 Qxe4+ 7.Qe2 Black has the pawn back. This ...Qd4 fork is the standard answer when White takes on c6 and grabs e5 without first defending e4.
848566465308848|c8e6.principle: After White trades on c6 and takes on e5, check what is undefended: the knight and the e4 pawn can both be hit by one queen move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6

8493377761529667|g8f6.headline: Challenge the g4 pawn with 2...h5 before putting a knight on f6
8493377761529667|g8f6.why: 2...Nf6 walks into White's plan: the theory notes that 2.Bg2 keeps the g-pawn ready to kick a knight on f6, and after 3.g5 Nh5 the knight sits on the rim and is later taken by 6.Bxh5. 2...h5 attacks the g4 pawn at once. After 3.gxh5 d5 Black takes the centre and White's kingside is left without its g-pawn.
8493377761529667|g8f6.principle: Don't develop a knight where an advancing pawn can kick it; first deal with the pawn that would chase it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...e5

853185718049302|d4e5.headline: Keep the tension: develop with 5.Be3, don't trade on e5
853185718049302|d4e5.why: 5.dxe5 dxe5 gives up the tension: e5 is solid again and the d6 square opens for Black's bishop, 6.Nc3 Bd6. After 7.Nd5 Qg6 Black's queen escapes and most of your advantage is gone. 5.Be3 develops and keeps the d4 pawn pressing on e5, so Black still has to solve that problem. After 5...Nc6 6.Nc3 Bg4 7.d5 Nb8 8.Nb5 Qd8 9.Nxa7 Black's pieces are driven home and you win a pawn.
853185718049302|d4e5.principle: When Black spends the opening on an early queen and pawn moves, keep the central tension and develop instead of trading it off.
sources: Lessons: Philidor's Defence (Exeter Chess Club) | https://www.exeterchessclub.org.uk/content/lessons-philidors-defence

ideas.title: Keep the d4/e5 tension
ideas.text: Don't release it with 5.dxe5: after 5...dxe5 the e5 pawn is solid again. Develop and leave Black with the e5 problem.

ideas.title: Gain time on the queen
ideas.text: Black's queen came out early and blocks the g8-knight. Bring out 5.Be3 and 6.Nc3, then 7.d5 and 8.Nb5 push Black back.

ideas.title: Black's cramped Philidor set-up
ideas.text: Black's d6-e5 chain is solid but passive: the f8-bishop has only e7. Trading on e5 would free d6 for it.

habit.why: 5.dxe5 dxe5 gives up the tension: e5 is solid again and the d6 square opens for Black's bishop, 6.Nc3 Bd6. After 7.Nd5 Qg6 Black's queen escapes and most of your advantage is gone.

strays.text: The trade settles e5 and hands Black's bishop the d6 square.

taught.why: 5.Be3 develops and keeps the d4 pawn pressing on e5, so Black still has to solve that problem. After 5...Nc6 6.Nc3 Bg4 7.d5 Nb8 8.Nb5 Qd8 9.Nxa7 Black's pieces are driven home and you win a pawn.

enforces.text: Each developing move adds a threat while Black's pieces go back.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.O-O is sound: your king is safe and the tension stays, as in 5...c6 6.a4 Ne7 7.Nc3. A stronger developing move exists.
alternatives.after: 5.Be3 brings another piece toward the centre first; in its line 7.d5 and 8.Nb5 win a pawn, while 5.O-O gives Black time for 5...c6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 develops, keeps the tension and eyes d5, where the knight would hit the queen on f6. The engine rates it as strong as any move here.
alternatives.after: 5.Be3 and 5.Nc3 are equally good and usually meet: each line brings the other piece out next, then plays 7.d5.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5.d5 closes the centre, so e5 is no longer under pressure, and 5...Qg6 hits e4 and g2 at once. After 6.Nc3 Be7 7.Rg1 f5 Black has active play.
alternatives.after: 5.Be3 keeps the d4 pawn pressing on e5 and pushes 7.d5 only when it gains time against the c6 knight.

8545457925751746|d2d3.headline: Develop with 4.Nc3 so Black's ...d5 costs more pawn moves
8545457925751746|d2d3.why: 4.d3 lets Black play the move 3...c6 prepared: 4...d5 hits your bishop, and after 5.exd5 cxd5 6.Bb3 Nc6 Black has a full pawn centre. The time Black lost on ...f6 and ...c6 is made up, and by 8.Re1 Qd7 your edge is gone. 4.Nc3 develops and adds a second guard to d5, so after 4...d5 5.exd5 Black can't simply recapture and spends 5...b5 6.Bb3 b4 7.Ne2 chasing your pieces. Only 7...cxd5 wins the pawn back, and 8.d4 strikes at the centre while Black's king is still uncastled.
8545457925751746|d2d3.principle: Black's ...f6 and ...c6 cost time, so answer with pieces and central breaks while you lead in development, not with quiet pawn moves.
sources: Jeremy Silman, Readers' Games, Questions and Comments, Part 3 (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/readersrsquo-games-questions-and-comments-part-3?page=2

ideas.title: Punish weakening pawn moves
ideas.text: ...f6 and ...c6 develop nothing, and ...f6 opens the a2-g8 diagonal toward Black's king. Answer with pieces and central breaks, not slow moves.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 break
ideas.text: 3...c6 prepares ...d5, hitting your bishop and taking the centre. After 4.d3 d5 5.exd5 cxd5 Black gets it for free.

ideas.title: Add a guard to d5
ideas.text: With a knight on c3, d5 is hit twice, so after 4...d5 5.exd5 Black needs 5...b5 and 6...b4 to win the pawn back.

ideas.title: Open the centre with d4
ideas.text: Black's king is still in the middle. Strike with d4 to open lines, as in 8.d4 in the main line.

habit.why: 4.d3 lets Black play the move 3...c6 prepared: 4...d5 hits your bishop, and after 5.exd5 cxd5 6.Bb3 Nc6 Black has a full pawn centre. The time Black lost on ...f6 and ...c6 is made up, and by 8.Re1 Qd7 your edge is gone.

strays.text: A quiet pawn move lets 4...d5 come with a hit on your bishop.

taught.why: 4.Nc3 develops and adds a second guard to d5, so after 4...d5 5.exd5 Black can't simply recapture and spends 5...b5 6.Bb3 b4 7.Ne2 chasing your pieces. Only 7...cxd5 wins the pawn back, and 8.d4 strikes at the centre while Black's king is still uncastled.

enforces.text: The knight makes ...d5 cost Black two extra pawn moves.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.d4 opens the centre while Black's king is uncastled: after 4...d5 5.exd5 cxd5 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Bxd7+ Qxd7 8.dxe5 lines open up. A slightly stronger move exists.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 develops first and makes ...d5 cost Black more pawn moves; 4.d4 opens up at once but swaps off your active bishop. Both keep a clear edge.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.O-O is natural but slow: 4...d5 hits your bishop, and after 5.exd5 cxd5 6.Bb3 Nc6 Black has the full pawn centre.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 adds a guard to d5, so the same break costs Black extra pawn moves like 5...b5 and 6...b4.

8567362508613525|d2d4.headline: Push 6.a4 at the b6 bishop; 6.d4 drops a pawn
8567362508613525|d2d4.why: 6.d4 exd4 just loses a pawn: taking back with the c-pawn leaves d4 under fire from Black's b6 bishop and c6 knight. In the card's line 7.Qb3 Qe7 8.O-O Nf6 9.a4 a6 10.a5 Ba7 you play on a pawn down with too little for it. 6.a4 threatens a5 against the b6 bishop, so Black spends 6...a6 and later 8...Ba7. Meanwhile you castle, play 8.d3 and 9.Nbd2, and keep a small edge without giving a pawn.
8567362508613525|d2d4.principle: Your b4 and c3 pawns give you queenside space, so play there with a4 instead of opening the centre before your pieces are out.

ideas.title: a4-a5 against the b6 bishop
ideas.text: a4 threatens a5 against the b6 bishop, so Black spends a move on ...a6 and later retreats the bishop to a7.

ideas.title: Build first: d3, castle, d2 knight
ideas.text: Castle, play d3 and bring the b1 knight to d2; push d4 only after that preparation, not while it just loses a pawn.

ideas.title: Black holds e5 and declines the tempo
ideas.text: 4...Bb6 and 5...d6 keep e5 firm instead of taking b4, so you get no c3 and d4 with tempo. The bishop also eyes f2.

habit.why: 6.d4 exd4 just loses a pawn: taking back with the c-pawn leaves d4 under fire from Black's b6 bishop and c6 knight. In the card's line 7.Qb3 Qe7 8.O-O Nf6 9.a4 a6 10.a5 Ba7 you play on a pawn down with too little for it.

strays.idea: Build first: d3, castle, d2 knight
strays.text: Opens the centre before your pieces are ready, and the pawn is lost.

taught.why: 6.a4 threatens a5 against the b6 bishop, so Black spends 6...a6 and later 8...Ba7. Meanwhile you castle, play 8.d3 and 9.Nbd2, and keep a small edge without giving a pawn.

enforces.text: Gains queenside space with a threat, before any central break.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Qb3 lines up with the c4 bishop against f7, and 6...Qf6 defends it. It is sound, but there is a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: 6.a4 gains space first and keeps the queen home; after 6.Qb3 Qf6 play returns to the a-pawn and d3 plan, and the queen goes back with 10.Qd1.
alternatives.idea: Build first: d3, castle, d2 knight

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Castling is sound: it keeps the quiet plan with d3 and the b1 knight to d2, and often reaches the same position. One move is slightly more useful first.
alternatives.after: 6.O-O Nf6 7.a4 a6 8.d3 usually transposes; 6.a4 just puts the question to the b6 bishop first.
alternatives.idea: Build first: d3, castle, d2 knight

8573734277279845|g8f6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6; 2...Nf6 hits the queen but drops e5.
8573734277279845|g8f6.why: White threatens 3.Qxe5+, and 2...Nf6 attacks the queen without stopping it: 3.Qxe5+ Be7 wins the pawn with check. 2...Nc6 develops the knight and guards e5, and the queen on h5 remains a target that Black later gains time on, as in 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.Qd1.
8573734277279845|g8f6.principle: Before attacking the queen, check White's own forcing moves: a capture with check on e5 comes first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e3/1...e5

8583587100088489|c6d4.headline: Defend e5 with 5...d6; 5...Nd4 lets 6.Nxe5 take a pawn.
8583587100088489|c6d4.why: 5...Nd4 removes e5's only defender, so 6.Nxe5 takes the pawn, and White's knight and bishop then combine against f7, as in 8.Nxf7 Rxf7 9.Bxf7+. 5...d6 defends e5 with a pawn and opens Black's light-squared bishop, keeping the solid Giuoco structure.
8583587100088489|c6d4.principle: Before moving a piece, check what it was defending: the knight on c6 is the only guard of the e5 pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. O-O

8640031168129389|f3g5.headline: Castle, then build the centre with c3 and d4
8640031168129389|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight again and 4...e6 covers f7, so after 5.d3 h6 6.Nf3 the knight is back and 6...d5 hits your bishop. 7.Bb3 dxe4 8.dxe4 Qxd1+ then trades queens and your king must take back, losing the right to castle. 4.O-O tucks your king away first, the masters' most common move here (36%). After 4...Nf6 5.Re1 g6 6.c3 Bg7 7.d4 cxd4 8.cxd4 you have pawns on d4 and e4 and a comfortable game.
8640031168129389|f3g5.principle: Don't move a piece twice in the opening: 4.O-O brings your king to safety, while 4.Ng5 spends two moves on a knight that has to retreat.
sources: Bowdler Attack - An Advanced Study Guide (Chess Klub) | https://chessklub.com/bowdler-attack/

ideas.title: Castle, then prepare d4
ideas.text: Castle, then build c3 and d4 to get two centre pawns, as in 7.d4 cxd4 8.cxd4.

ideas.title: No time for knight raids
ideas.text: 4.Ng5 moves a piece twice and hits only f7, which one move, 4...e6, covers. The knight then has to go back.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 hits your bishop
ideas.text: ...e6 prepares ...d5 against the c4-bishop, as with 6...d5 once the knight has retreated.

ideas.title: Italian-style setup
ideas.text: The quiet plan: d3, c3, castling and a rook on e1, keeping the bishop with a4 or a retreat to b3 (Wikibooks).

habit.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight again and 4...e6 covers f7, so after 5.d3 h6 6.Nf3 the knight is back and 6...d5 hits your bishop. 7.Bb3 dxe4 8.dxe4 Qxd1+ then trades queens and your king must take back, losing the right to castle.

strays.text: The knight goes to g5 and back, and ...d5 comes with tempo.

taught.why: 4.O-O tucks your king away first, the masters' most common move here (36%). After 4...Nf6 5.Re1 g6 6.c3 Bg7 7.d4 cxd4 8.cxd4 you have pawns on d4 and e4 and a comfortable game.

enforces.text: Castle, guard e4 with 5.Re1, then 7.d4 builds the centre.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 develops and guards e4, but it blocks your c-pawn, so the c3 and d4 plan is gone. After 4...e5 5.d3 Be7 the game turns slow and closed.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O keeps c3 free for the pawn, so 7.d4 cxd4 8.cxd4 gives you two centre pawns.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.c3 goes straight for d4, but after 4...Nf6 5.d4 cxd4 6.cxd4 Nxe4 7.d5 Ne5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 you've given up the e4 pawn for activity. It's playable; masters choose it 35% of the time.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O first lets 5.Re1 guard e4 before d4 comes. Masters play the two moves about equally (36% and 35%).

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.d3 guards e4 and leads to the quiet Italian-style setup with 6.Re1, 7.c3 and 8.a4. It's solid, though there are more active choices.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O keeps the d-pawn free to reach d4 in one step, as in 7.d4, instead of d3 and a slow build-up. Masters prefer it, 36% to 16%.

8645343577179290|g7g6.headline: Shut the c4 bishop with 7...e6 before e5 opens lines
8645343577179290|g7g6.why: 7...g6 leaves the c4 bishop aiming at f7, and 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.e5 opens lines at once: taking on e5 runs into a bishop check on f7 that wins your queen. After 9...Ng4 10.Re1 d5 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.Bxd5 the bishop hits your a8 rook and f7, and White comes out ahead. 7...e6 shuts the bishop's diagonal toward f7, so the e5 push no longer comes with a trick. After 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.Re1 e5 10.Bf1 White's bishop has to retreat and the game stays roughly level.

ideas.title: Shut the bishop with ...e6
ideas.text: Against the c4 bishop Black almost always plays ...e6: it closes the bishop's line to f7 and covers d5.

ideas.title: The Magnus Smith trap
ideas.text: After ...g6, 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.e5 hits your f6 knight. Taking on e5 loses your queen to a bishop check on f7.

ideas.title: Don't mix in ...g6
ideas.text: With ...a6 and ...Nc6 played, ...g6 costs another move and weakens the dark squares while your king is still in the centre.

ideas.title: Holes on d5 and f5
ideas.text: ...e5 kicks the d4 knight but leaves d5 and f5 for White's knights; 8.Nf5 jumps straight in.

habit.why: 7...g6 leaves the c4 bishop aiming at f7, and 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.e5 opens lines at once: taking on e5 runs into a bishop check on f7 that wins your queen. After 9...Ng4 10.Re1 d5 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.Bxd5 the bishop hits your a8 rook and f7, and White comes out ahead.

strays.text: The c4 bishop keeps its aim at f7 while e5 opens lines.

taught.why: 7...e6 shuts the bishop's diagonal toward f7, so the e5 push no longer comes with a trick. After 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.Re1 e5 10.Bf1 White's bishop has to retreat and the game stays roughly level.

enforces.text: The e6 pawn blocks the c4 bishop's line to f7.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7...e5 kicks the knight but leaves holes on d5 and f5, and 8.Nf5 jumps into one. After 8...Be6 9.Bb3 g6 10.Nh6 the knight stops you castling short.
alternatives.after: 7...e6 closes the bishop's line to f7 without giving White's knight f5; after 7...e5 the c4 bishop still hits f7.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7...Nxd4 8.Qxd4 brings White's queen to a strong central square. After 9.Be2 Be7 10.Rd1 Qc7 you're solid, just a little passive.
alternatives.after: 7...e6 shuts the bishop at once and keeps your knight on c6, where it eyes d4 and e5.

8671130214522057|b1a3.headline: Your c4 bishop is attacked: save it with check
8671130214522057|b1a3.why: 6.Na3 does nothing about 6...Nxc4 and drops a knight to 6...Bxa3. After 7.Bb5+ c6 8.dxc6 bxc6 9.Bd3 Bd6 10.b4 Bxb4 you are a piece down. 6.Bb5+ moves the bishop out of the knight's reach with check, so Black has no time for 6...Nxc4. After 6...c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 8.Bd3 Nd5 9.Nf3 you stay a pawn up while Black gets active play for it; masters choose it in 97.6% of games.
8671130214522057|b1a3.principle: When a piece is attacked, look first for a move that saves it with check, so the opponent must answer you.

ideas.title: Save the bishop with check
ideas.text: 5...Na5 attacks your c4 bishop. 6.Bb5+ moves it with check, so Black must answer before taking anything.

ideas.title: Keep the extra pawn
ideas.text: 5.exd5 left you a pawn up. Don't hand it back with a queen move or by trading your only developed bishop.

ideas.title: Black gains time on your pieces
ideas.text: For the pawn Black develops with tempo: 5...Na5 hits the bishop, then ...h6 and ...e4 chase your g5 knight back.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: With Black's knight on a5, not d5, a knight sacrifice on f7 has no queen fork to follow; it just loses a piece.

habit.why: 6.Na3 does nothing about 6...Nxc4 and drops a knight to 6...Bxa3. After 7.Bb5+ c6 8.dxc6 bxc6 9.Bd3 Bd6 10.b4 Bxb4 you are a piece down.

strays.text: Leaves the c4 bishop attacked and puts the knight where a bishop takes it.

taught.why: 6.Bb5+ moves the bishop out of the knight's reach with check, so Black has no time for 6...Nxc4. After 6...c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 8.Bd3 Nd5 9.Nf3 you stay a pawn up while Black gets active play for it; masters choose it in 97.6% of games.

enforces.text: The bishop escapes with check, so 6...Nxc4 never comes.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.Qe2 doesn't stop 6...Nxc4, and after 7.Qxc4 Qxd5 Black has the pawn back and the bishop pair.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5+ saves the bishop with check, so you keep the extra pawn; masters choose it in 97.6% of games.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.Bb3 Nxb3 7.axb3 gives up your bishop, then 7...h6 8.Nf3 e4 chases the knight and 10...Qxd5 wins the pawn back.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5+ keeps your bishop and the pawn: the check means Black has no time for 6...Nxc4.
alternatives.idea: Black gains time on your pieces

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.d3 lets you take back with the pawn if the knight takes on c4, but you give up the bishop pair, and 6...h6 7.Nf3 e4 gains space; 10...Nxd5 regains the pawn.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5+ keeps both bishops and the pawn. Masters prefer it 97.6% to 2.4%, and Harding calls 6.d3 hardly in keeping with White's aggressive start.

8671130214522057|d1e2.headline: Your queen move doesn't save the bishop; a check does
8671130214522057|d1e2.why: 6.Qe2 doesn't stop 6...Nxc4, and after 7.Qxc4 Qxd5 Black has the pawn back. 8.Qxd5 Nxd5 leaves Black with the bishop pair and the easier game. 6.Bb5+ moves the bishop out of the knight's reach with check, so Black has no time for 6...Nxc4. After 6...c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 8.Bd3 Nd5 9.Nf3 you stay a pawn up while Black gets active play for it; masters choose it in 97.6% of games.
8671130214522057|d1e2.principle: Deal with the threat first, with a check if you can: 6...Nxc4 is coming, and a queen move doesn't stop it.

8673706909167185|c1a3.headline: Castle first with 8.O-O; 8.Ba3 lets Black grab c3 and block
8673706909167185|c1a3.why: 8.Ba3 leaves the c3 pawn pinned, so Black takes a third pawn with 8...dxc3. After 9.O-O Nge7 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nxc3 d6 your bishop is traded off, Black can castle, and you're two pawns down. 8.O-O unpins c3 and gets your king safe, so Black has to deal with the d4 pawn at once. After 8...d3 9.e5 Qg6 10.Rd1 Nge7 11.Bxd3 you win a pawn back with tempo on the queen, and 12.Ba3 follows.
8673706909167185|c1a3.principle: In the Evans, castle before your tempo moves: 8.O-O unpins c3, and only then do e5 and Ba3 hit something.

ideas.title: Unpin, then rebuild the centre
ideas.text: The a5 bishop pins your c3 pawn. Once your king leaves e1, c3 can take on d4, so Black must react, as 8...d3 does.

ideas.title: Kick the queen first
ideas.text: A queen on f6 is a target: e4-e5 hits it with tempo, as in 9.e5 Qg6, and takes f6 from Black's knight.

ideas.title: Ba3 comes later
ideas.text: A bishop on a3 keeps Black's king in the centre, but played now, 8...dxc3 and 9...Nge7 blunt it. The main line plays 12.Ba3.

ideas.title: Greed needs a spare tempo
ideas.text: Taking a third pawn on c3 right after you castle runs into 9.e5 and a dangerous initiative; after a wasted move like 8.Ba3 it is safe.

habit.why: 8.Ba3 leaves the c3 pawn pinned, so Black takes a third pawn with 8...dxc3. After 9.O-O Nge7 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nxc3 d6 your bishop is traded off, Black can castle, and you're two pawns down.

strays.text: Before castling, the bishop is blocked and traded off by 9...Nge7.

taught.why: 8.O-O unpins c3 and gets your king safe, so Black has to deal with the d4 pawn at once. After 8...d3 9.e5 Qg6 10.Rd1 Nge7 11.Bxd3 you win a pawn back with tempo on the queen, and 12.Ba3 follows.

enforces.text: With your king off e1, c3 can take on d4, so Black must react.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 8.Bg5 hits the queen, but 8...Qg6 steps away, eyeing e4 and your g5 bishop, and after 9...Bb6 Black keeps both extra pawns. It develops a piece but gains no real time.
alternatives.after: 8.O-O unpins c3 first, so Black must react to the d4 pawn, and 9.e5 then kicks the queen with real effect.

8692601699406729|d7d5.headline: Develop with 5...Qc7 before the ...d5 break
8692601699406729|d7d5.why: 5...d5 opens the e-file before you have developed, and 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bb5 pins your c6-knight. After 7...Bd7 8.Nxd5 White has simply won the d5 pawn. 5...Qc7 develops the queen to a safe square that covers d6 and e5, keeping ...d5 for later. After 6.Be3 a6 7.Qf3 b5 8.Qg3 Ne5 your queenside play is under way and you have given nothing away.
8692601699406729|d7d5.principle: Develop before you open the centre: 5...Qc7 brings out a piece and guards d6, while 5...d5 opens lines that cost a pawn.

ideas.title: Prepare the ...d5 break
ideas.text: ...d5 frees your game later, but now 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bb5 pins your c6-knight and White's c3-knight hits d5.

ideas.title: Knight jumps to b5 and d6
ideas.text: With ...e6 played, d6 has no pawn guard: White's knights eye b5 and then d6, the Taimanov's soft spot.

ideas.title: Queen to c7 first
ideas.text: 5...Qc7 puts the queen on a safe square covering d6 and e5. If 6.Ndb5 hits it, it drops back to b8.

ideas.title: Queenside first
ideas.text: The Taimanov plan is ...Qc7, ...a6 and ...b5 before the kingside pieces, as in 6.Be3 a6 7.Qf3 b5.

habit.why: 5...d5 opens the e-file before you have developed, and 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bb5 pins your c6-knight. After 7...Bd7 8.Nxd5 White has simply won the d5 pawn.

strays.text: The break comes before your pieces, and the d5 pawn simply drops.

taught.why: 5...Qc7 develops the queen to a safe square that covers d6 and e5, keeping ...d5 for later. After 6.Be3 a6 7.Qf3 b5 8.Qg3 Ne5 your queenside play is under way and you have given nothing away.

enforces.text: The queen guards d6 and e5 before White's knights can use them.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.idea: Knight jumps to b5 and d6
alternatives.before: 5...a6 keeps White's knights off b5, and 17% of masters play it. But it invites 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Qf3, and the engine grades it lower.
alternatives.after: 5...Qc7 develops a piece and covers d6 and e5 first; ...a6 can still follow, as after 6.Be3 a6.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...Nf6 is the Sicilian Four Knights, which Willis judges sound. After 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.e5 Nd5 8.Ne4 your knight is kicked and you are left with a hole on d6.
alternatives.after: 5...Qc7 controls e5 before the knight comes out, so there is no 7.e5 kick. Masters prefer it, 66% to 8%.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...Bb4 pins the c3-knight, but with no knight on f6 it hits nothing. 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Qd4 attacks the bishop and g7, and 7...Bf8 goes home.
alternatives.after: 5...Qc7 develops without becoming a target; the bishop can wait to go to e7 or b4 later.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.idea: Knight jumps to b5 and d6
alternatives.before: 5...Bc5 develops, but 6.Ndb5 Nf6 7.Bf4 aims at c7 and d6. After 8.Bc7 Qe7 9.Bd6 Bxd6 10.Qxd6 White's queen sits on d6.
alternatives.after: 5...Qc7 guards c7 and d6 itself, so 6.Ndb5 only hits the queen, which drops back to b8.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...d6 heads for a Scheveningen and stops any knight landing on d6. But 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Qd2 Be7 8.f3 gives White an English Attack setup against your king.
alternatives.after: 5...Qc7 keeps ...d6 in reserve: Semkov's repertoire plays the Scheveningen setup later, once White has committed.

8692601699406729|g8e7.headline: Cover d6 with 5...Qc7; 5...Nge7 allows 6.Ndb5
8692601699406729|g8e7.why: 5...Nge7 cuts your f8-bishop off from d6, so 6.Ndb5 threatens 7.Nd6 mate. After 6...Ng6 7.Nd6+ Bxd6 8.Qxd6 Qe7 9.Qxe7+ Kxe7 you have lost your dark-squared bishop and the right to castle. 5...Qc7 develops the queen to a safe square that covers d6 and e5, so no knight can land on d6. After 6.Be3 a6 7.Qf3 b5 8.Qg3 Ne5 your queenside play is under way and you have given nothing away.
8692601699406729|g8e7.principle: Ask what your opponent wants first: White wants Ndb5 and Nd6, so 5...Qc7 covers d6, while 5...Nge7 blocks the bishop that guards it.

alternatives.before: 5...Bc5 develops, but 6.Ndb5 Nf6 7.Bf4 aims at c7 and d6. After 8.Bc7 Qe7 9.Bd6 Bxd6 10.Qxd6 White's queen sits on d6.
alternatives.after: 5...Qc7 guards c7 and d6 itself, so 6.Ndb5 only hits the queen, which drops back to b8.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...d6 heads for a Scheveningen and stops any knight landing on d6. But 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Qd2 Be7 8.f3 gives White an English Attack setup against your king.
alternatives.after: 5...Qc7 keeps ...d6 in reserve: Semkov's repertoire plays the Scheveningen setup later, once White has committed.

8698679373330427|c8f5.headline: 3.Bf4 leaves c4 hanging: take it with 3...dxc4
8698679373330427|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 ignores the free pawn on c4 and gives White a target. After 4.Nc3 Qb6 5.Qd2 Nf6 6.f3 h6 7.e3 e6 8.g4 White has guarded b2 and c4, then gains kingside space by chasing your bishop. 3...dxc4 takes the pawn 3.Bf4 left alone, while the f1-bishop is still shut in by the e2 pawn. After 4.g3 Nf6 5.Nf3 Nd5 6.Bd2 b5 your c6 pawn backs up b5 and you keep the extra pawn; masters take on c4 in 45.2% of games.
8698679373330427|c8f5.principle: When a pawn is left undefended and you can support it afterwards, take it: in the Slav the c6 pawn already backs up ...b5.
sources: James Vigus, Play the Slav, Introduction (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=Vigus+%22Play+the+Slav%22+%22dxc4%22+%22reinforced+with%22+%22b5%22

Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6

ideas.title: Take c4 when it's loose
ideas.text: 3.Bf4 leaves c4 attacked and undefended. 3...dxc4 wins it, and ...b5, backed by c6, or ...Nd5 helps keep it.

ideas.title: f3 and g4 chase the bishop
ideas.text: A bishop on f5 gives White a target: in the 3...Bf5 line, 6.f3 and 8.g4 gain kingside space by chasing it.

ideas.title: e3 closes the c4 window
ideas.text: Once White plays e3, the f1-bishop guards c4. That is why 3...Nf6 4.e3 Bf5 is playable but wins nothing.

habit.why: 3...Bf5 ignores the free pawn on c4 and gives White a target. After 4.Nc3 Qb6 5.Qd2 Nf6 6.f3 h6 7.e3 e6 8.g4 White has guarded b2 and c4, then gains kingside space by chasing your bishop.

strays.text: The free c4 pawn stays, and the bishop becomes a target.

taught.why: 3...dxc4 takes the pawn 3.Bf4 left alone, while the f1-bishop is still shut in by the e2 pawn. After 4.g3 Nf6 5.Nf3 Nd5 6.Bd2 b5 your c6 pawn backs up b5 and you keep the extra pawn; masters take on c4 in 45.2% of games.

enforces.text: c4 had no defender, and ...b5 backed by c6 holds it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Nf6 is a natural, sound reply: after 4.e3 Bf5 5.Nc3 Qb6 your bishop is out and b7 is covered. But there's a stronger move here.
alternatives.after: 3...dxc4 grabs the pawn before 4.e3 covers it; 3...Nf6 is the calmer choice and nearly as popular with masters, 41.9% to 45.2%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...e6 is solid, and after 4.e3 Bd6 5.Bg3 you challenge White's active bishop. But it shuts in your c8-bishop, and there's a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 3...dxc4 wins a pawn while c4 is loose; 3...e6 lets 4.e3 cover it and leaves your bishop behind the pawns.

8700918547269120|e2e3.headline: Kick the early bishop with 4.Ne5 instead of the quiet 4.e3
8700918547269120|e2e3.why: 4.e3 is solid but gives Black time to finish the setup with 4...e6. After 5.h3 Bh5 6.Qb3 Qb6 b7 is covered and the bishop stands well outside Black's pawn chain. 4.Ne5 hits the bishop at once, and after 4...Bc8 it is back home, two moves wasted. You spend the time on 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.e4, and after 6...dxe4 7.Nc3 Nd7 8.Bb5 your pieces come out fast while Black is still undeveloped.
8700918547269120|e2e3.principle: When the opponent develops a piece where you can attack it, hit it at once: every retreat is a move you get to spend on the centre.
sources: Jef Kaan, Better Chess Openings (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=Kaan+%22Better+Chess+Openings%22+%22Bg4%22+%224.Ne5%22
Konstantin Sakaev, Complete Slav I (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-complete-slav-i.pdf
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3

ideas.title: Ne5 hits an early ...Bg4
ideas.text: 4.Ne5 attacks the bishop at once; after 4...Bc8 Black has spent two moves on it, and you use the time in the centre.

ideas.title: Early ...Bg4 drops b7
ideas.text: With Black's bishop gone from c8, b7 is loose; a queen on b3 can hit it, together with d5 after cxd5 cxd5.

ideas.title: Spend the tempi in the centre
ideas.text: Ahead in time, open lines with 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.e4, even giving a pawn to get your pieces out fast.

habit.why: 4.e3 is solid but gives Black time to finish the setup with 4...e6. After 5.h3 Bh5 6.Qb3 Qb6 b7 is covered and the bishop stands well outside Black's pawn chain.

strays.text: You leave the bishop on g4 and let Black finish developing.

taught.why: 4.Ne5 hits the bishop at once, and after 4...Bc8 it is back home, two moves wasted. You spend the time on 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.e4, and after 6...dxe4 7.Nc3 Nd7 8.Bb5 your pieces come out fast while Black is still undeveloped.

enforces.text: The bishop goes back to c8, and you get two free moves.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 develops and adds pressure on d5. After 4...Bxf3 5.gxf3 Nf6 6.Rg1 you get the bishop pair and an open g-file, though there's a more forcing move.
alternatives.after: 4.Ne5 makes the bishop retreat at once; 4.Nc3 is about as good but lets Black trade it for your knight with 4...Bxf3.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.h3 asks the bishop to decide, and Black answers 4...Bxf3 5.gxf3 dxc4, grabbing c4 while your pawns are loosened.
alternatives.after: 4.Ne5 attacks the bishop without leaving a knight on f3 to take, so Black can't trade it off and grab c4.

8706009982340637|b2b3.headline: Claim the centre with 5.d4; 5.b3 opens a1 to a queen check
8706009982340637|b2b3.why: 5.b3 opens the long diagonal, and 5...Qe5+ checks your king and hits the rook on a1. After 6.Be2 Qxa1 you are a whole rook down. 5.d4 takes the centre and puts a pawn on the e5-a1 diagonal, then 6.Be3 and 7.Nf3 develop. If Black gives a pawn with 6...e5, after 8.dxe5 Qxd1+ 9.Kxd1 O-O-O+ the queens are off and you keep the extra pawn.
8706009982340637|b2b3.principle: Before each move, check what the opponent's queen can reach: one pawn move can open a line to a loose rook.
sources: Savielly Tartakower, The Hypermodern Game of Chess | https://books.google.com/books?id=MJFXDwAAQBAJ
Eric Schiller, Gambit Openings Repertoire for Black | https://books.google.com/books?id=WSEYAQAAMAAJ
Max Illingworth, Chess Grandmaster's Favourite Gambit vs. 1.e4! (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/blog/Illingworth/chess-grandmasters-favourite-gambit-vs-1-e4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6

ideas.title: Watch the queen's checks
ideas.text: With your e-pawn gone, Black's queen can check on e5. 5.b3 opens the diagonal to a1, so 5...Qe5+ forks king and rook.

ideas.title: No tempo on the queen
ideas.text: Black's queen reached d5 by a knight trade, not with you chasing it, so Black gets an easy game.

ideas.title: Claim the centre with d4
ideas.text: 5.d4 takes the centre, covers e5 and opens your c1-bishop, ready for 6.Be3 and 7.Nf3.

ideas.title: Trade off the active queen
ideas.text: 5.Qf3 offers a queen trade; after 5...Be6 6.Bd3 Qxf3 7.Nxf3 Black's best piece is gone and the game is quiet.

habit.why: 5.b3 opens the long diagonal, and 5...Qe5+ checks your king and hits the rook on a1. After 6.Be2 Qxa1 you are a whole rook down.

strays.text: The pawn move opens a1 to a queen check on e5.

taught.why: 5.d4 takes the centre and puts a pawn on the e5-a1 diagonal, then 6.Be3 and 7.Nf3 develop. If Black gives a pawn with 6...e5, after 8.dxe5 Qxd1+ 9.Kxd1 O-O-O+ the queens are off and you keep the extra pawn.

enforces.text: The pawn takes the centre and covers e5 against a queen check.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Nf3 develops and covers e5 against a queen check. It's sound, and the most common club move, but there's a stronger one.
alternatives.after: 5.d4 takes the centre first; after 5.Nf3 Nc6 6.d4 Bg4 Black pins your knight and presses on d4. Masters prefer 5.d4, 38% to 22%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Qf3 offers a queen trade, and after 5...Be6 6.Bd3 Qxf3 7.Nxf3 Black's lead in development fades. Sound, though there's a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 5.d4 keeps the queens on and takes the centre; 5.Qf3 heads for a quiet, level ending. Masters choose the two about equally, 38% and 35%.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5.d3 is solid but passive: it shuts in your f1-bishop and doesn't contest the centre. After 5...Nc6 6.Nf3 Bf5 7.Be2 e5 Black takes the centre instead.
alternatives.after: 5.d4 takes the space that 5.d3 gives up and keeps the f1-bishop's diagonal open.

8716466597702343|b1c3.headline: Take the gambit pawn: 3.dxe6 keeps you a pawn up
8716466597702343|b1c3.why: 3.Nc3 develops but lets Black recapture with 3...exd5, and after 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 Bd6 material is level in a symmetrical French Exchange structure. Even 6.Nb5 O-O 7.Nxd6 Qxd6 only wins the bishop pair, not the pawn. 3.dxe6 removes the attacker and takes a second pawn; after 3...Bxe6 Black's only gain is a developed bishop. Then 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.d4 gives you a solid centre and easy development while you stay a clean pawn up.
8716466597702343|b1c3.principle: When a gambit gives too little for the pawn, take it and develop rather than hand it straight back.
sources: Scandinavian Defense (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_Defense

ideas.title: Grab the gambit pawn, not the centre
ideas.text: Against 2...e6, take a second pawn with 3.dxe6. Other moves let Black win d5 back with an easy game.

ideas.title: Black wins d5 back
ideas.text: Black's e-pawn hits d5 and nothing defends it, so 3...exd5 would make material level.

ideas.title: Develop and keep the pawn
ideas.text: After 3...Bxe6, develop with 4.Nf3 and 5.d4 and castle; Black has too little for the pawn.

ideas.title: Symmetry lets Black off
ideas.text: 3.Nc3 exd5 4.d4 gives a French Exchange structure: level material and symmetrical pawns, so your edge is gone.

habit.why: 3.Nc3 develops but lets Black recapture with 3...exd5, and after 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 Bd6 material is level in a symmetrical French Exchange structure. Even 6.Nb5 O-O 7.Nxd6 Qxd6 only wins the bishop pair, not the pawn.

strays.text: Developing doesn't defend d5, so 3...exd5 makes material level.

taught.why: 3.dxe6 removes the attacker and takes a second pawn; after 3...Bxe6 Black's only gain is a developed bishop. Then 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.d4 gives you a solid centre and easy development while you stay a clean pawn up.

enforces.idea: Grab the gambit pawn, not the centre
enforces.text: Taking keeps the extra pawn; 2...e6 gives Black too little for it.

8716466597702343|c2c4.headline: Take the second pawn with 3.dxe6; 3.c4 doesn't hold d5
8716466597702343|c2c4.why: 3.c4 keeps a pawn for now, but after 3...exd5 4.cxd5 it stands alone on d5 and Black develops with 4...Nf6 5.Bb5+ Nbd7 6.Nf3 Be7 7.O-O O-O. The d5 pawn is about to fall to Black's knights, and your edge is gone. 3.dxe6 removes the attacker and takes a second pawn; after 3...Bxe6 Black's only gain is a developed bishop. Then 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.d4 gives you a solid centre and easy development while you stay a clean pawn up.
8716466597702343|c2c4.principle: When a gambit gives too little for the pawn, take it and develop rather than hand it straight back.

8733953429179306|c6e5.headline: Don't move the knight twice; develop with 4...Nf6
8733953429179306|c6e5.why: 4...Ne5 moves the knight a second time with three minor pieces still at home, and after 5.Qg3 it has to go back with 5...Nc6, so Black has spent two moves for nothing; 6.Bd2 d5 7.exd5 then leaves Black a pawn down. 4...Nf6 develops the other knight toward the centre and pressures e4, and Black continues with ...Bc5 and castling.
8733953429179306|c6e5.principle: Attacking a queen that can simply step aside with tempo is not worth a second knight move; bring out a new piece instead.

8751595729469873|c1a3.headline: Kick the queen first: 9.e5, then 10.Nxc3 and 11.Ba3
8751595729469873|c1a3.why: 9.Ba3 aims at e7 and f8, but 9...Nge7 blocks the diagonal at once. After 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nxc3 O-O Black has castled, your dark-squared bishop is gone, and you're still two pawns down. 9.e5 hits the queen, so after 9...Qg6 10.Nxc3 you win back a pawn with gain of time, and Black's knight can no longer use f6. Wikipedia gives 10...Nge7 11.Ba3 as a very dangerous initiative for White.
8751595729469873|c1a3.principle: Develop with threats: 9.e5 kicks the queen before you recapture, while a quiet 9.Ba3 gives Black time to block and castle.

ideas.title: Kick the queen first
ideas.text: 9.e5 hits the f6 queen and takes f6 away from Black's g8 knight, so you win back c3 with tempo.

ideas.title: Ba3 comes later
ideas.text: A bishop on a3 keeps Black's king in the centre, but played now 9...Nge7 blocks it. The sources play 11.Ba3 only after 9.e5 Qg6 10.Nxc3.

ideas.title: Greed needs a spare tempo
ideas.text: Black grabbed a third pawn with 8...dxc3. Sources rate this Compromised Defence as a very dangerous initiative for you, if you keep gaining time.

ideas.title: Development is your compensation
ideas.text: You're three pawns down for time and open lines, so every move should develop or hit something.

habit.why: 9.Ba3 aims at e7 and f8, but 9...Nge7 blocks the diagonal at once. After 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nxc3 O-O Black has castled, your dark-squared bishop is gone, and you're still two pawns down.

strays.text: Played before the queen is kicked, the bishop is blocked by 9...Nge7.

taught.why: 9.e5 hits the queen, so after 9...Qg6 10.Nxc3 you win back a pawn with gain of time, and Black's knight can no longer use f6. Wikipedia gives 10...Nge7 11.Ba3 as a very dangerous initiative for White.

enforces.text: The pawn hits the queen, so 10.Nxc3 comes with a tempo gained.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 9.Bg5 develops with a hit on the queen, and after 9...Qg6 10.Nxc3 you win back a pawn. It's the most common club move here, and the engine rates it about as good as the move the sources give.
alternatives.after: The engine sees 9.e5 and 9.Bg5 as about equal, but the sources give 9.e5, which also takes f6 from Black's knight. After 9.Bg5 Qg6 10.Nxc3 Bxc3 11.Qxc3 Nf6 that knight gets f6.

877042167833906|c1f4.headline: Take the centre with 5.e4 instead of a slow Bf4
877042167833906|c1f4.why: 5.Bf4 doesn't help win back c4, so Black plays 5...b5 to keep it. After 6.a4 b4 7.Na2 Nc6 8.e3 Na5 your knight is offside on a2 and the a5-knight guards c4. 5.e4 takes the centre at once, and 5...b5 is met by 6.e5 Nd5 7.a4, kicking the knight and hitting b5. After 7...e6 8.axb5 you've won material back and kept more space.
877042167833906|c1f4.principle: Fight for the centre: 5.e4 takes it at once, where a bishop move leaves c4 to Black.

ideas.title: Win back c4, don't Bf4
ideas.text: An early 5.Bf4 does nothing for c4 and gives Black time for ...b5. Play 5.e4 or 5.e3 to win the pawn back instead.

ideas.title: e4-e5 kicks the f6 knight
ideas.text: After 5.e4 b5, 6.e5 drives the knight from f6 to d5 with tempo, since Black has no d-pawn left to take on e5.

ideas.title: a4 hits ...b5
ideas.text: When Black plays ...b5, a4 hits it at once: after 5.e4 b5 6.e5 Nd5 7.a4 e6 8.axb5 you win material back.

ideas.title: ...b4 kicks the knight
ideas.text: With your knight on c3, ...b5-b4 can chase it away from the centre, as in 5.Bf4 b5 6.a4 b4 7.Na2.

habit.why: 5.Bf4 doesn't help win back c4, so Black plays 5...b5 to keep it. After 6.a4 b4 7.Na2 Nc6 8.e3 Na5 your knight is offside on a2 and the a5-knight guards c4.

strays.text: The bishop move leaves Black time to hold c4 with ...b5.

taught.why: 5.e4 takes the centre at once, and 5...b5 is met by 6.e5 Nd5 7.a4, kicking the knight and hitting b5. After 7...e6 8.axb5 you've won material back and kept more space.

enforces.text: 6.e5 gains time on the knight and 7.a4 hits b5.

alternatives.after: 5.e4 takes the centre at once and meets ...b5 with 6.e5 and 7.a4; 5.a4 is the quieter main alternative.

alternatives.label: sound

alternatives.after: 5.e4 takes more space: 6.e5 hits the f6-knight, so ...b5 costs Black time instead of you.

8832130732345993|f1d3.headline: Kick the knight with 4.e5 instead of leaving d4 to fall
8832130732345993|f1d3.why: 4.Bd3 blocks your queen's defence of d4: after 4...dxe4 5.Nxe4 Qxd4 Black simply takes the d-pawn. 3...Nf6 put the knight where your e-pawn can reach it, and 4.e5 punishes that: the pawn gains space and sends the knight back to g8, so Black's last move was wasted. The game turns into an Advance Caro-Kann with a closed centre, which Black was probably hoping to avoid.
8832130732345993|f1d3.principle: A knight on f6 in front of your e-pawn is a target: push the pawn to gain space and send the knight back.

8832130732345993|f2f3.headline: Gain space with 4.e5; 4.f3 doesn't hold e4.
8832130732345993|f2f3.why: Black threatens 4...dxe4, winning a pawn, and 4.f3 doesn't stop it: after 4...dxe4 5.fxe4 e5 Black hits the centre, and once the queens come off with 6.dxe5 Qxd1+ 7.Nxd1 Nxe4 Black's knight on e4 is active and White's kingside is loosened by the f-pawn. 4.e5 claims the centre and attacks the knight on f6, which has to go back with 4...Ng8, and White develops comfortably with 5.Bd3.
8832130732345993|f2f3.principle: When an enemy knight on f6 sits in front of your e-pawn, advance the pawn to gain space and drive the knight back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4

8849788781204745|g7g6.headline: 7...g6 hangs the h8 rook; block the diagonal with 7...Nf6
8849788781204745|g7g6.why: 7...g6 opens the long diagonal from White's queen on d4 to your h8 rook, and 8.Qxh8 simply takes it. After 8...Nf6 9.Bh6 Kd7 10.Qxf8 Qxf8 11.Bxf8 Rxf8 you are a whole rook down. 7...Nf6 develops and blocks the queen's diagonal towards h8, so the rook is safe. After 8.Bg5 e6 9.Qd3 Be7 10.O-O-O Qa5 11.Bh4 O-O you have castled, with your two bishops against White's active pieces.
8849788781204745|g7g6.principle: Before each move, check what becomes loose: moving the g-pawn leaves the h8 rook open to the queen on d4.

ideas.title: Queen on d4 eyes h8
ideas.text: White's queen looks down the long diagonal at g7 and h8; once your g-pawn moves, the h8 rook hangs.

ideas.title: Block the diagonal with ...Nf6
ideas.text: 7...Nf6 develops and shuts the d4-h8 diagonal before anything else on your kingside moves.

ideas.title: Your bishop pair
ideas.text: White gave up the b5 bishop for your knight; your two bishops are the long-term answer to White's active queen.

ideas.title: Solid ...e6 against the pin
ideas.text: After 8.Bg5, the solid 8...e6 and 9...Be7 is the recommended setup; an early ...e5 leaves a hole on d5.

habit.why: 7...g6 opens the long diagonal from White's queen on d4 to your h8 rook, and 8.Qxh8 simply takes it. After 8...Nf6 9.Bh6 Kd7 10.Qxf8 Qxf8 11.Bxf8 Rxf8 you are a whole rook down.

strays.text: The g-pawn moves while the queen's diagonal to h8 is still open.

taught.why: 7...Nf6 develops and blocks the queen's diagonal towards h8, so the rook is safe. After 8.Bg5 e6 9.Qd3 Be7 10.O-O-O Qa5 11.Bh4 O-O you have castled, with your two bishops against White's active pieces.

enforces.text: The knight closes the d4-h8 diagonal before the kingside pawns move.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7...e5 hits the queen at once, and after 8.Qd3 Be7 9.O-O h6 10.Be3 you are fine. The cost is a hole on d5, and White's knight heads for f5 with 11.Nh4 and 12.Nf5.
alternatives.after: 7...Nf6 develops first and keeps the e-pawn flexible, so no squares are weakened yet. Masters choose it 82% of the time, 7...e5 only 5%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7...e6 is solid and usually transposes to the main line, with the d6/e6 pawn wall recommended against 8.Bg5. It is fully sound.
alternatives.after: 7...Nf6 and 7...e6 usually meet after 8.Bg5; developing the knight first also shuts the queen's diagonal straight away.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 7...h6 stops 8.Bg5 before you commit, but it costs a tempo: after 8.Qd3 e5 9.Nd2 the knight heads for c4 and e3 with 10.Nc4 and 11.Ne3, eyeing d5.
alternatives.after: 7...Nf6 develops instead of spending a pawn move; masters choose it 82% of the time against 7% for 7...h6.

8865411260070790|g8f6.headline: Avoid 3...Nf6 4.e5: hit the centre with 3...c5 first
8865411260070790|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 lets White kick the knight straight back home with 4.e5 Ng8, and in the engine line White plays 5.d4 and keeps building with extra space. The theory explains why: in this setup Black needs ...d6 first to prevent e5. 3...c5 fights for d4 instead, and after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 Nc6 Black develops with a half-open c-file, and 6...Nf6 comes safely.
8865411260070790|g8f6.principle: Don't put a knight on f6 while White can push e5 and chase it; control the centre first so the knight can't be kicked.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6

8877803564094104|d2d3.headline: Stop 6...Ng4 first: 6.h3 keeps f2 safe and your pawn
8877803564094104|d2d3.why: 6.d3 doesn't stop 6...Ng4, which hits f2 twice, so 7.Be3 is forced. Then 7...Nxe3 8.fxe3 Bxe3 wins the pawn back, and Black has both bishops while your f-pawn is gone. 6.h3 takes g4 away from the knight, so f2 is safe from that attack. After 6...Qd4 7.Qf3 guards f2 and e4, and 8.d3 and 9.Nd1 untangle your pieces with the extra pawn still yours.
8877803564094104|d2d3.principle: Ask what your opponent threatens before making your own move: here 6...Ng4 hits f2 twice, so take g4 away first.

ideas.title: Guard f2 against ...Bc5 and ...Ng4
ideas.text: The c5-bishop aims at f2, and 6...Ng4 would add a second attacker while your king is its only defender.

ideas.title: Take g4 away with h3
ideas.text: 6.h3 stops the knight jump. After 6...Qd4, 7.Qf3 guards f2 and e4, and 8.d3 follows with the extra pawn kept.

ideas.title: The open d-file
ideas.text: After 5...dxc6 Black's queen sees down the d-file: 6...Qd4 hits f2 and e4, and a pawn on d4 just drops.

ideas.title: Don't castle into the attack
ideas.text: Castling short early walks into queen and knight attacks on f2 and h2; keep the king in the centre until g4 is covered.

habit.why: 6.d3 doesn't stop 6...Ng4, which hits f2 twice, so 7.Be3 is forced. Then 7...Nxe3 8.fxe3 Bxe3 wins the pawn back, and Black has both bishops while your f-pawn is gone.

strays.text: 6.d3 opens your bishop but leaves f2 to 6...Ng4.

taught.why: 6.h3 takes g4 away from the knight, so f2 is safe from that attack. After 6...Qd4 7.Qf3 guards f2 and e4, and 8.d3 and 9.Nd1 untangle your pieces with the extra pawn still yours.

enforces.text: 6.h3 takes g4 from the knight before it can hit f2.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.Bc4 develops but ignores f2: 6...Ng4 hits it twice, and after 7.Rf1 Qf6 8.Qe2 Nxh2 Black wins a pawn back with a strong attack.
alternatives.after: 6.h3 deals with the knight first; the bishop can come out once g4 is covered. Castling after 6.Bc4 runs into a well-known mating attack.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.Be2 doesn't stop 6...Qd4, which hits f2 and e4 at once: after 7.O-O Nxe4 Black has the pawn back with active pieces.
alternatives.after: 6.h3 meets 6...Qd4 with 7.Qf3, guarding both f2 and e4, and no knight can come to g4.

8877803564094104|d2d4.headline: Don't push into the open d-file: 6.h3 keeps your pawn
8877803564094104|d2d4.why: 6.d4 puts a pawn on the open d-file, where 6...Bxd4 takes it with the queen's backing. Your extra pawn is gone, and after 7.f3 Qd6 Black's pieces are active while your kingside is loosened. 6.h3 takes g4 away from the knight, so f2 is safe from that attack. After 6...Qd4 7.Qf3 guards f2 and e4, and 8.d3 and 9.Nd1 untangle your pieces with the extra pawn still yours.
8877803564094104|d2d4.principle: Ask what your opponent threatens before making your own move: here 6...Ng4 hits f2 twice, so take g4 away first.

8979060161382028|e4e5.headline: Guard e4 with 3.Nc3; 3.e5 just gets traded off
8979060161382028|e4e5.why: 3.e5 has no d-pawn behind it, so 3...dxe5 4.Nxe5 trades your centre pawn away. Then 4...Nbd7 and 5...b5 chase your knight around while Black develops. 3.Nc3 guards e4 with a developing move and keeps every plan open. After 3...c5 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 you get an Open Sicilian, a Najdorf by another move order; masters choose 3.Nc3 in 82.6% of games.
8979060161382028|e4e5.principle: Defend an attacked centre pawn with a developing piece, so the defence also brings a new piece into play.

ideas.title: Guard e4 before anything else
ideas.text: Black's f6 knight attacks e4. 3.Nc3 guards it while developing; Black takes it if you leave it alone.

ideas.title: An early e5 just gets traded
ideas.text: With no d4 pawn behind it, e5 is simply taken: 3...dxe5 4.Nxe5 Nbd7, and Black develops while chasing your knight.

ideas.title: Give the centre, then undermine it
ideas.text: Black lets you have e4 and d4 and attacks them later. Guard e4 first, then take the full centre with d4.

habit.why: 3.e5 has no d-pawn behind it, so 3...dxe5 4.Nxe5 trades your centre pawn away. Then 4...Nbd7 and 5...b5 chase your knight around while Black develops.

strays.idea: An early e5 just gets traded
strays.text: The push trades your centre pawn and your knight gets chased.

taught.why: 3.Nc3 guards e4 with a developing move and keeps every plan open. After 3...c5 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 you get an Open Sicilian, a Najdorf by another move order; masters choose 3.Nc3 in 82.6% of games.

enforces.text: The knight guards e4 and develops in one move.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 3.Bc4 develops but leaves e4 unguarded: 3...Nxe4 wins a pawn, and after 4.d4 Nf6 5.O-O g6 you have nothing for it.
alternatives.after: 3.Nc3 guards e4 first; the bishop can come out later.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.d3 holds e4 with a pawn and leads to a King's Indian Attack after 3...g6 4.g3, which Wikibooks marks equal. Solid, but there is a more ambitious move.
alternatives.after: 3.Nc3 keeps the d-pawn free for 4.d4 and the full centre; 3.d3 gives that space up.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.c3 prepares d4 so you can take back with a pawn. Black has no problems after 3...c5 4.Be2 g6, and a more active move exists.
alternatives.after: 3.Nc3 develops a piece while guarding e4; after 3.c3 Black equalises easily with 3...c5.
alternatives.idea: Give the centre, then undermine it

8979060161382028|f1c4.headline: Guard e4 with 3.Nc3; 3.Bc4 just drops the pawn
8979060161382028|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 develops but leaves e4 with no defender, so 3...Nxe4 wins a pawn. After 4.d4 Nf6 5.O-O g6 6.Re1 Bg7 7.Bf1 you have spent moves chasing the knight and are still a pawn down. 3.Nc3 guards e4 with a developing move and keeps every plan open. After 3...c5 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 you get an Open Sicilian, a Najdorf by another move order; masters choose 3.Nc3 in 82.6% of games.
8979060161382028|f1c4.principle: Defend an attacked centre pawn with a developing piece, so the defence also brings a new piece into play.

8999636484543636|g8f6.headline: Guard e5 with 4...Nc6; 4...Nf6 blocks the g7 bishop
8999636484543636|g8f6.why: The g7 bishop is the only thing guarding e5, and 4...Nf6 cuts it off, so 5.Nxe5 wins the pawn. 4...Nc6 develops the knight toward the centre and defends e5 directly, so your pawn holds and the bishop keeps watching the long diagonal.
8999636484543636|g8f6.principle: Count the defenders of a pawn before every move: a move that blocks the only defender's line leaves the pawn hanging.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6

922389477039223|d2d3.headline: Cover d4 with 4.Ne2 before Black's knight jumps in.
922389477039223|d2d3.why: Black threatens 4...Nd4, winning a pawn, and 4.d3 doesn't stop it: the knight hits the queen on f3, and after 5.Qd1 White has lost time while Black gains space with ...d5. 4.Ne2 develops the knight and covers d4, so White continues calmly with d3 and Nbc3, as in 4...Na5 5.d3 d6 6.Nbc3.
922389477039223|d2d3.principle: Ask which square the opponent's knight wants next to attack your early queen, and develop a piece that covers it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nc6

950795499557785|f7f6.headline: Release the tension with 4...exd4, then develop the knight
950795499557785|f7f6.why: White threatens 5.dxe5, and 4...f6 holds e5 at a cost: it takes f6 from the g8 knight and opens the diagonal from c4 toward your king. In the engine line White castles, plays 7.dxe5 dxe5 anyway and lands a knight on d5 with 8.Nd5. 4...exd4 trades the attacked pawn off; after 5.Nxd4 Nf6 your knight develops to its natural square and the f8 bishop comes out next.
950795499557785|f7f6.principle: Defend a centre pawn with pieces or trade it off; a defending pawn move like ...f6 blocks your own development and weakens your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

953559814433764|g8f6.headline: Cover f7 before you chase the queen
953559814433764|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 attacks the queen but does nothing for f7, which only your king guards. White answers 4.Qxf7#, Scholar's Mate on the spot. 3...g6 blocks the queen's line to f7 and attacks it, so White has to move the queen again. After 4.Qf3 Nf6 5.Ne2 Bg7 6.Nbc3 O-O you have developed and castled with f7 safe; masters play 3...g6 93% of the time.
953559814433764|g8f6.principle: When a queen and a bishop both aim at f7, the king is its only defender, so cover f7 before making any attacking move.

ideas.title: Scholar's Mate on f7
ideas.text: White's queen and c4 bishop both aim at f7, which only your king guards: 4.Qxf7# is threatened.

ideas.title: Cover f7 before you develop
ideas.text: Stop the mate first with 3...g6 or 3...Qe7; only then develop with ...Nf6 and ...Bg7.

ideas.title: Hit the queen with tempo
ideas.text: 3...g6 blocks the queen's line and attacks it, so White spends a move: 4.Qf3, and 4...Nf6 shuts f7 off.

ideas.title: Keep f6 for the knight
ideas.text: A queen on f6 guards f7 but takes the g8 knight's best square, so the knight must go to e7.

habit.why: 3...Nf6 attacks the queen but does nothing for f7, which only your king guards. White answers 4.Qxf7#, Scholar's Mate on the spot.

strays.text: You develop first, and f7 falls with mate.

taught.why: 3...g6 blocks the queen's line to f7 and attacks it, so White has to move the queen again. After 4.Qf3 Nf6 5.Ne2 Bg7 6.Nbc3 O-O you have developed and castled with f7 safe; masters play 3...g6 93% of the time.

enforces.text: 3...g6 shields f7 and chases the queen in one move.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Qf6 covers f7 and holds, but the queen takes f6 from your knight, which must go to e7 after 4.Nc3 Bc5 5.Nf3 Nge7. A more flexible move exists.
alternatives.after: 3...g6 defends f7 while attacking the queen and keeps f6 for the knight. Masters prefer it 93% to 2%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Qe7 guards f7 and e5, and Kasparov chose it against Woody Harrelson; it blocks your f8 bishop for now. A move that also gains time is more common.
alternatives.after: 3...g6 also gains time on the queen and opens g7 for your bishop. Masters play it 93% of the time, 3...Qe7 4.5%.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Nh6 guards f7 with a developing move and holds. But the knight sits on the rim, far from the centre; a better move exists.
alternatives.after: 3...g6 does the job with tempo and lets the knight go to f6 next; 3...Nh6 leaves it on the edge.

953559814433764|g8h6.headline: Block the mate and attack the queen with g6
953559814433764|g8h6.why: 3...Nh6 does stop 4.Qxf7#, but it puts the knight on the rim, where it neither controls the centre nor gains time, and White keeps a comfortable game with 4.Nc3. 3...g6 blocks the mate and attacks the queen at the same time; White has to move it again with 4.Qf3, and Black develops with 4...Nf6 and ...Bg7.
953559814433764|g8h6.principle: Meet an early queen attack with a move that both defends and hits the queen, so the defence also wins time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6/3. Bc4

956431266193433|d2d3.headline: Hit the e5 queen with 5.Nf3, not a quiet pawn move
956431266193433|d2d3.why: 5.d3 attacks nothing, so Black develops at leisure with 5...Bg4 and trades off your light-squared bishop: 6.Be3 Bxe2 7.Qxe2 Nf6. Black's queen was your target, but after 8.f4 Qa5 she is safe and your lead is gone. 5.Nf3 develops a piece and attacks the queen on e5 at once. After 5...Qd6 6.d4 e6 7.Nb5 Qd8 she is back home, while you have three pieces out and a pawn on d4.
956431266193433|d2d3.principle: Against an early queen, choose developing moves that attack it; a quiet pawn move gives the opponent time to catch up.

ideas.text: 5.Nf3 develops and hits the queen on e5; after 5...Qd6 6.d4 e6 7.Nb5 she is chased back to d8.

ideas.title: Mind the pin on e2
ideas.text: The queen on e5 pins your e2 bishop to your king; it can't move until she leaves the e-file.

ideas.title: Black's bishop trade on e2
ideas.text: Given time, Black plays 5...Bg4 and swaps off your e2 bishop, as after 6.Be3 Bxe2 7.Qxe2.

habit.why: 5.d3 attacks nothing, so Black develops at leisure with 5...Bg4 and trades off your light-squared bishop: 6.Be3 Bxe2 7.Qxe2 Nf6. Black's queen was your target, but after 8.f4 Qa5 she is safe and your lead is gone.

strays.idea: Develop with tempo on the queen
strays.text: A pawn move that hits nothing gives Black a free move.

taught.why: 5.Nf3 develops a piece and attacks the queen on e5 at once. After 5...Qd6 6.d4 e6 7.Nb5 Qd8 she is back home, while you have three pieces out and a pawn on d4.

enforces.idea: Develop with tempo on the queen
enforces.text: Each move that hits the queen brings out another piece.

961430540554751|c1e3.headline: Ask the g4 bishop at once: 6.h3 before Black develops
961430540554751|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 leaves the c3-knight pinned, since the bishop stands off the a5-e1 diagonal, and it gives Black a free move. After 6...Nf6 7.h3 Bh5 8.g4 Bg6 the bishop escapes to g6 instead of being traded for your knight. 6.h3, the choice in 84% of master games, makes the bishop decide now. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 Nd7 8.Bd2 e6 9.O-O-O you have both bishops, an active queen and no pin on c3.
961430540554751|c1e3.principle: A bishop that a pawn can attack is a target: hit it with the h-pawn right away, before Black's development lets it retreat for free.

ideas.title: Ask the Bg4 question with h3
ideas.text: h3 makes the g4-bishop decide now: after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you have the bishop pair and your queen is already active.

ideas.title: Bd2, long castling, pawn storm
ideas.text: Then 8.Bd2 unpins the c3-knight and 9.O-O-O follows; if the bishop retreats instead, g4 chases it to g6.

ideas.title: The pin on c3
ideas.text: Black's queen on a5 pins your c3-knight to the king. A bishop on d2 breaks the pin; 6.Be3 does not.

ideas.title: Bishop out before ...e6/...c6
ideas.text: Black's bishop came out before ...e6. Given a free move, it can dodge the h3 push via h5 to g6, as in 8...Bg6.

habit.why: 6.Be3 leaves the c3-knight pinned, since the bishop stands off the a5-e1 diagonal, and it gives Black a free move. After 6...Nf6 7.h3 Bh5 8.g4 Bg6 the bishop escapes to g6 instead of being traded for your knight.

enforces.idea: Ask the Bg4 question with h3
enforces.text: Black must trade on f3 or retreat right now.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Be2 answers the pin passively: after 6...Nd7 7.Nd2 Bxe2 8.Qxe2 Black trades the bishop on its own terms and develops calmly.
alternatives.after: 6.h3 forces the bishop to decide while that still costs Black something; masters choose it in 84% of games and 6.Be2 in 5%.
alternatives.idea: Ask the Bg4 question with h3

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Bd2 breaks the pin on c3 with a developing move, and after 6...e6 you still have the bishop question to settle. It's fully sound, though masters favour another move.
alternatives.after: Both work: 6.Bd2 e6 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 reaches the same kind of position. Settling the bishop first is the masters' main choice (84%).

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Bc4 develops actively, but after 6...Nf6 Black's queen can swing to h5 to keep the pin on f3, and your bishop drops back with 8.Be2. Masters play it in 11% of games.
alternatives.after: 6.h3 settles the bishop before Black can back it up with ...Qh5. Masters prefer it, 84% to 11%.
alternatives.idea: Ask the Bg4 question with h3

962560137426404|a7a6.headline: Use the centre fork trick: 4...Nxe4 beats slow moves like ...a6
962560137426404|a7a6.why: 4...a6 spends a move on the edge while White's pieces are ready: 5.Ng5 threatens to win a pawn on f7, and in the game line 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 White opens the centre with Black a step behind. 4...Nxe4 is the centre fork trick: after 5.Nxe4 d5 the pawn forks knight and bishop, and Black regains the piece with 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4, having removed White's centre pawn and equalised.
962560137426404|a7a6.principle: Check forcing moves before quiet ones: with White's bishop on c4 and knight on c3 both within reach of a pawn push, a capture on e4 sets up a fork.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Nc3

962560137426404|d7d6.headline: Use the fork trick 4...Nxe4; 4...d6 allows 5.Ng5 on f7
962560137426404|d7d6.why: 4...d6 does nothing for f7, so 5.Ng5 attacks it twice and 5...d5 6.exd5 follows. You can't take back on d5 without dropping f7, and after 6...Na5 7.Bb5+ c6 8.dxc6 bxc6 you are a pawn down. 4...Nxe4 removes White's centre pawn, and 5.Nxe4 d5 forks bishop and knight. After 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Bd6 you have the piece back and a free game; masters play it in 57% of games.
962560137426404|d7d6.principle: f7 is your weak point: a passive move like 4...d6 lets 5.Ng5 hit it, so strike first with the fork trick.
