ideas.title: The fork trick
ideas.text: 4...Nxe4 5.Nxe4 d5 hits bishop and knight at once, so you win the piece back and gain a share of the centre.

ideas.title: Ng5 hits f7 only when it hurts
ideas.text: The c4 bishop already hits f7. A passive move lets 5.Ng5 attack it a second time before you can castle.

ideas.title: Free the game
ideas.text: The fork trick ends with 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Bd6: White's e4 pawn is gone and your pieces come out easily.

habit.why: 4...d6 does nothing for f7, so 5.Ng5 attacks it twice and 5...d5 6.exd5 follows. You can't take back on d5 without dropping f7, and after 6...Na5 7.Bb5+ c6 8.dxc6 bxc6 you are a pawn down.

strays.text: A timid pawn move gives up the chance to hit back with ...d5.

taught.why: 4...Nxe4 removes White's centre pawn, and 5.Nxe4 d5 forks bishop and knight. After 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Bd6 you have the piece back and a free game; masters play it in 57% of games.

enforces.text: The knight takes on e4, and 5...d5 wins the piece back with a fork.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Bc5 develops and avoids complications, leading to a quiet Giuoco Pianissimo after 5.d3. It is sound, but there is a more active option.
alternatives.after: 4...Nxe4 is the masters' main move (57% to 33%) and frees your game at once; Wikibooks calls it the best move here, with White then fighting for equality.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Bb4 develops, but after 5.Nd5 O-O 6.c3 White gains time on the bishop, though the game stays roughly level. There is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4...Nxe4 uses the fork trick to free your game at once; 4...Bb4 lets White gain time with 5.Nd5 and 6.c3.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4...h6 stops 5.Ng5 but spends a move on the flank. White strikes in the centre with 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 and later 8.e5, chasing your f6 knight.
alternatives.after: 4...Nxe4 uses the move to break with 5...d5 instead of guarding g5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Be7 is sound and takes the sting out of knight jumps to g5 by covering the kingside. It is a little passive, and a more active move exists.
alternatives.after: 4...Nxe4 strikes at once; after 4...Be7 5.d4 the same fork trick still works a move later with 5...Nxe4 6.Nxe4 d5.

962560137426404|d8e7.headline: Use the fork trick 4...Nxe4 to take White's centre pawn
962560137426404|d8e7.why: 4...Qe7 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home and shuts in the f8 bishop. In the engine line White develops around it and hits the queen with 9.Nd5. 4...Nxe4 is only a temporary sacrifice: after 5.Nxe4 d5 the pawn forks knight and bishop, and 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 leaves Black with the piece back and a good foothold in the centre.
962560137426404|d8e7.principle: Look at captures before quiet moves: a capture on e4 is safe when a pawn fork wins the piece back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

962560137426404|h7h6.headline: Use the fork trick 4...Nxe4 instead of the slow 4...h6
962560137426404|h7h6.why: 4...h6 stops 5.Ng5 but spends a move on a pawn that neither develops nor fights for the centre. White uses the time to open the centre with 5.d4, and in the engine line 8.e5 hits your f6 knight. 4...Nxe4 is only a temporary sacrifice: after 5.Nxe4 d5 the pawn forks knight and bishop, and 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 leaves Black with the piece back and a good foothold in the centre.
962560137426404|h7h6.principle: Prefer a forcing move that fights for the centre over a pawn move that only prevents something.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

966581453995947|c8g4.headline: Win the pawn back with 6...Bxf2+ and 7...Qd4+
966581453995947|c8g4.why: 6...Bg4 puts the bishop on a square the e5 knight covers, and 7.Nxg4 simply takes it. 6...Bxf2+ uses forcing moves instead: after 7.Kxf2 Qd4+ the queen checks the king and hits the e5 knight, and 8.Kf1 Qxe5 regains the pawn. White's king has also lost the right to castle.
966581453995947|c8g4.principle: When your opponent's pieces are loose, look at checks first: a check that also attacks an undefended piece often wins material back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

966581453995947|d8d4.headline: Check first with 6...Bxf2+, then fork with 7...Qd4.
966581453995947|d8d4.why: Here the knight on c3 guards e4, so 6...Qd4 only threatens the knight, and 7.Nd3 covers f2 and attacks the bishop on c5, leaving Black a pawn down. 6...Bxf2+ drags the king out first: after 7.Kxf2 Qd4+ the queen checks the king and hits the knight on e5 at once, and 8...Qxe5 wins a pawn. White's king also loses the right to castle.
966581453995947|d8d4.principle: When a quiet attack can be parried, look for a check that sets up the same attack with tempo.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

972282943199495|g1f3.headline: 3...d6 declines the gambit: take back with 4.cxd4
972282943199495|g1f3.why: 4.Nf3 leaves d4 to Black, who accepts after all with 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3: now you're a real pawn down in a Morra. After 5...Nc6 6.Bc4 e6 7.O-O a6 8.Qe2 Be7 Black has a sound ...e6/...a6 setup and keeps the pawn. 4.cxd4 wins the pawn back and gives you pawns on e4 and d4; masters choose it 98.7% of the time. If Black strikes with 4...d5, then 5.exd5 Nf6 6.Bb5+ Nbd7 7.Nc3 keeps the extra pawn while you develop with check.
972282943199495|g1f3.principle: When your opponent declines a gambit, take the pawn back and build the centre instead of offering it again.
sources: Nikolai Kalinichenko, The Club Player's Modern Guide to Gambits | https://books.google.com/books?id=xAS1DwAAQBAJ
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3

ideas.title: Take the free centre
ideas.text: 3...d6 neither takes on c3 nor defends d4. 4.cxd4 gets your pawn back and puts pawns on e4 and d4.

ideas.title: Don't gambit what you can take
ideas.text: 4.Nf3 lets Black accept after all: 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 leaves you a pawn down when the pawn was yours for free.

ideas.title: Black hits back with ...d5
ideas.text: After 4.cxd4 Black's try is 4...d5, but 5.exd5 Nf6 6.Bb5+ Nbd7 7.Nc3 keeps your extra pawn on d5.

habit.why: 4.Nf3 leaves d4 to Black, who accepts after all with 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3: now you're a real pawn down in a Morra. After 5...Nc6 6.Bc4 e6 7.O-O a6 8.Qe2 Be7 Black has a sound ...e6/...a6 setup and keeps the pawn.

strays.text: Black takes on c3 after all, and you're simply a pawn down.

taught.why: 4.cxd4 wins the pawn back and gives you pawns on e4 and d4; masters choose it 98.7% of the time. If Black strikes with 4...d5, then 5.exd5 Nf6 6.Bb5+ Nbd7 7.Nc3 keeps the extra pawn while you develop with check.

enforces.text: You get the pawn back and two centre pawns side by side.

977859217629606|e4e5.headline: Bring the rook to e1 before you push e5
977859217629606|e4e5.why: 11.e5 pushes before the pawn is supported, and 11...d6 hits your queen and the e5 pawn at once. After 12.Qb5 a6 13.Qb3 dxe5 the pawn is gone and Black's c8 bishop is free. 11.Re1 lines up on the e-file against the king on e8 and gets e5 ready with support. After 11...d6 12.Qb5 Bd7 13.Qb3 Qe7 14.Nxc3 you win back the c3 pawn while Black's king is still stuck in the centre.
977859217629606|e4e5.principle: Open lines when you lead in development, but prepare the break: 11.Re1 aims at the king first, while 11.e5 at once just loses the pawn to 11...d6.
sources: John Nunn, GM tutorial: Learn to play the Evans Gambit (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/john-nunn-learn-to-play-the-evans-gambit
Evans Gambit (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_Gambit
Jeremy Silman, Blindfold Chess, the Fried Liver Attack, and Playing Multiple Openings (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/playing-multiple-openings-and-the-fried-liver-attack?page=2

ideas.title: King in the centre: keep queens
ideas.text: Black's king on e8 can never castle. Open lines toward it: 11.Re1 puts a rook on the e-file before any pawn push.

ideas.title: Moves that gain time
ideas.text: e5 would kick the f6 knight, but it only works when nothing is left loose. Here 11...d6 hits your queen and the pawn.

ideas.title: Win back c3 by developing
ideas.text: Black's c3 pawn can't be held. Take it with the knight, bringing a piece out, rather than spending another queen move.

habit.why: 11.e5 pushes before the pawn is supported, and 11...d6 hits your queen and the e5 pawn at once. After 12.Qb5 a6 13.Qb3 dxe5 the pawn is gone and Black's c8 bishop is free.

strays.text: The push leaves the e5 pawn loose to 11...d6.

taught.why: 11.Re1 lines up on the e-file against the king on e8 and gets e5 ready with support. After 11...d6 12.Qb5 Bd7 13.Qb3 Qe7 14.Nxc3 you win back the c3 pawn while Black's king is still stuck in the centre.

enforces.idea: King in the centre: keep queens
enforces.text: The rook takes the e-file toward the king before any pawn push.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 11.Nxc3 is simple and strong: it wins back the c3 pawn and develops a piece, and Black's king still can't castle.
alternatives.after: 11.Nxc3 is accepted too, and the engine rates it level with 11.Re1. 11.Re1 aims the rook at the king first and takes back on c3 a few moves later.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 11.Qxc3 wins the pawn back but spends another queen move. After 11...d6 Black develops, and the king walks to safety via 13...Kf7 and 14...Kg6.
alternatives.after: 11.Re1 brings a new piece into play and keeps the e-file pressure. The c3 pawn can be taken later with the knight, as 14.Nxc3 shows.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 11.Bg5 pins the knight but leaves c3 alone: after 11...d6 12.Qxc3 Be6 Black develops, and 14.Bxf6 gxf6 opens the g-file for Black's rook.
alternatives.after: 11.Re1 adds a piece to the attack instead of trading your bishop for the knight, and keeps the pressure on the king on e8.
alternatives.idea: King in the centre: keep queens

983258444083142|b1c3.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 7.e5 while you lead in development
983258444083142|b1c3.why: 7.Nc3 develops but gives Black the time it needs: 7...d6 8.Bf4 Be7 9.O-O-O O-O and Black has caught up. The lead you got from 3...h6 is gone and the f6 knight stays where it is. 7.e5 is protected by your queen and drives the knight to the rim with 7...Nh7. After 8.Nc3 c6 9.Ne4 Qb6 10.Nd6+ Bxd6 11.Qxd6 your queen sits on d6 and Black's queenside pieces are still at home.
983258444083142|b1c3.principle: When you lead in development, make moves that gain time, like a pawn push that kicks a piece, instead of quiet ones.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6
Italian game 3...h6 (chess.com forum) | https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess-openings/italian-game-3h6

ideas.title: Punish the slow 3...h6
ideas.text: 3...h6 cost Black a tempo and you are ahead in development. Use the lead before Black catches up with 7...d6, 8...Be7 and 9...O-O.

ideas.title: Gain time on the f6 knight
ideas.text: 7.e5 is protected by your queen and kicks the knight. After 7...Nh7 it sits offside, and your knight heads for d6 via 9.Ne4.

ideas.title: Black's freeing pawn moves
ideas.text: Quiet moves give Black time to free the c8 bishop, with 7.Nc3 d6 or 7.O-O d5, and then castle.

ideas.title: A queen on d6
ideas.text: In the 7.e5 line, 10.Nd6+ Bxd6 11.Qxd6 plants your queen on d6, blocking the d7 pawn while Black's queenside stays at home.

habit.why: 7.Nc3 develops but gives Black the time it needs: 7...d6 8.Bf4 Be7 9.O-O-O O-O and Black has caught up. The lead you got from 3...h6 is gone and the f6 knight stays where it is.

strays.idea: Gain time on the f6 knight
strays.text: A quiet developing move lets the f6 knight stay and Black catch up.

taught.why: 7.e5 is protected by your queen and drives the knight to the rim with 7...Nh7. After 8.Nc3 c6 9.Ne4 Qb6 10.Nd6+ Bxd6 11.Qxd6 your queen sits on d6 and Black's queenside pieces are still at home.

enforces.idea: Gain time on the f6 knight
enforces.text: The pawn push kicks the knight offside to h7 and keeps your lead.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: Castling is safe but quiet, and it allows 7...d5: after 8.exd5 Be7 9.Re1 O-O Black has freed the c8 bishop and caught up.
alternatives.after: 7.e5 makes Black spend the move on the knight instead of on 7...d5, and the knight ends up offside on h7.

987839445230107|e7e6.headline: Hit White's two-pawn centre at once with 3...e5
987839445230107|e7e6.why: 3...e6 is too slow: White takes back the pawn with 4.Bxc4 and keeps a broad pawn centre without having lost any time. 3...e5 attacks White's centre at once and opens the dark-squared bishop's diagonal. White has to answer 4.Nf3, because 4.Bxc4 is met by 4...Qxd4 and 4.dxe5 by 4...Qxd1, both forcing queen trades that suit Black.
987839445230107|e7e6.principle: When White builds a two-pawn centre, strike at it with your own centre pawn at once instead of preparing slowly.

987839445230107|f7f6.headline: Strike back at White's centre with e5
987839445230107|f7f6.why: 3...f6 does nothing for the c4 pawn, which falls to 4.Bxc4, and it weakens the diagonal toward your king that 8.Qh5+ exploits later in that line. 3...e5 attacks White's centre and opens the dark-squared bishop, and White can't grab the pawn back at once: 4.Bxc4 runs into 4...Qxd4, and 4.dxe5 into 4...Qxd1.
987839445230107|f7f6.principle: When White builds a big centre with two pawns, strike at it with a central pawn rather than making flank pawn moves.

991686180194659|e2e4.headline: Nc3 before e4, or the f6-knight just takes it
991686180194659|e2e4.why: 4.e4 drops a pawn: the f6-knight hits e4 and no knight on c3 defends it, so 4...Nxe4 just wins it. After 5.Bd3 Nf6 6.O-O Bg7 7.Re1 you have a little development, but Black is simply a pawn up. 4.Nc3 guards e4, so after 4...Bg7 5.e4 you have the big centre with nothing hanging. After 5...O-O 6.Be2 e5 7.O-O Nc6 8.d5 you reach a main-line King's Indian with extra space.
991686180194659|e2e4.principle: Before you put a pawn on a square, count who attacks and defends it: e4 needs the c3-knight first.
sources: A Crash Course In Understanding 1.d4 (GM Max Illingworth, chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/blog/Illingworth/a-crash-course-in-understanding-1-d4

ideas.title: Nc3 before e4
ideas.text: Black's f6-knight hits e4. 4.Nc3 guards the square first, so 5.e4 comes with nothing hanging.

ideas.title: The f6-knight eyes e4
ideas.text: Any pawn or piece on e4 without a defender drops to 4...Nxe4.

ideas.title: ...Ne4 hits a bishop on g5
ideas.text: A bishop on g5 can be hit by the knight jumping to e4, as after 4.Bg5 Ne4 5.Be3.

ideas.title: The fianchetto plan
ideas.text: 4.g3 is the Fianchetto Variation: you skip e4 and put your bishop on g2.

habit.why: 4.e4 drops a pawn: the f6-knight hits e4 and no knight on c3 defends it, so 4...Nxe4 just wins it. After 5.Bd3 Nf6 6.O-O Bg7 7.Re1 you have a little development, but Black is simply a pawn up.

strays.text: Without a knight on c3, the e4 pawn just hangs.

taught.why: 4.Nc3 guards e4, so after 4...Bg7 5.e4 you have the big centre with nothing hanging. After 5...O-O 6.Be2 e5 7.O-O Nc6 8.d5 you reach a main-line King's Indian with extra space.

enforces.text: The knight guards e4 first, so 5.e4 is safe.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.g3 is the sound Fianchetto Variation: you skip e4 and put the bishop on g2, as in 4...Bg7 5.Bg2 O-O 6.O-O. Masters play it 22% of the time; there is a more popular move.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 prepares e4 and a big centre, while 4.g3 is a quieter plan. Both are good; masters pick 4.Nc3 77% to 22%.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.e3 is safe but modest: you give up the e4 push for now, and Black develops freely with 4...Bg7 and ...Bf5.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 keeps e4 in reserve with the knight backing it, so you get the bigger centre.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Bg5 runs into 4...Ne4, hitting the bishop, and after 5.Be3 Bg7 your bishop has lost time while Black's knight is active.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 covers e4, so the knight has no jump there, and 5.e4 comes next.
